11526-summer-on-the-lakes-in-1843:
Sarah Margaret Fuller, signing as S. M. Fuller, wrote this travel book after a summer journey in 1843 around the Great Lakes, published in 1844. Verse at the front sets a plain, personal tone, and an engraving of the arched rock at Mackinaw marks the northern ground she covers.

Chapters follow the lakes, their towns, and the people met on the way, with long passages of thought on nature, work, and the limits of what a traveller can know. The book still reads as a first-hand record of the region before rail lines remade it.
11745-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for April 1843 is number 330, volume 53. It opens with the practice of agriculture, called applied science in every chapter of a work then before the reviewer. Poems and ballads of Schiller follow, in Charles Mackay's version.

Contents also list The Last of the Shepherds and Ammalat Bek. Ammalat Bek is a true tale of the Caucasus from Marlinsky. An occupation of Aden is praised for its harbour at the junction of Red Sea and Indian Ocean. Caleb Stukely, part thirteen, appears as well. An imaginary talk with Landor closes the number, a monthly miscellany of farming, verse, and foreign tales.
12263-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood Edinburgh Magazine for May 1843, volume fifty-three, number three hundred thirty-one, mixes travel, fiction, criticism, and politics in the Tory magazine manner. Contents list Dumas in Italy, a true tale of the Caucasus from the Russian of Marlinski, and Reynolds Discourses concluded.

Other items include Leap-Year, a tale, and a piece on the paving question called The Battle of the Blocks. Schiller poems and ballads, a natural history of salmon and sea trout, Caleb Stukely concluded, and commercial policy on Spain follow. A mid-book note records that yards in various parts of London use the Metropolitan Company pavement system. The number shows a Victorian review at full range, serious and miscellaneous at once.
12511-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine number 332, June 1843, volume fifty-three, mixes fiction, history and review. Contents list Marston, or Memoirs of a Statesman, a translation of the Vigil of Venus, and chapters of Turkish history on the Kiuprili family and the siege of Candia. A passage in the life of a maître-d'armes, and Ammalát Bek, a true tale of the Caucasus from Marlinski, follow.

The Vicar of Wakefield illustrated by Mulready, an attorney's clerk in a monk's hood, a tale of civil war, a Sicilian tour and commercial policy on Russia complete the number. Blackwood's, Tory and literary, offered readers a thick monthly miscellany. The issue shows its range, from statesmen's memoirs to Caucasus romance, in one binding.
12761-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
This March 1843 Blackwood's opens with Ammalát Bek, a true tale of the Caucasus translated from the Russian of Marlinski. Schiller ballads, a Landor imaginary conversation, and the serial Caleb Stukely follow, with tales of Spain, London life, and a lost lamb. The contents show Blackwood's wide, Tory-flavoured range.

A sermon scene mid-issue, with a small congregation leaving church moved and chastened, hints at the magazine's moral seriousness beside its fiction. Readers get foreign romance, poetry, and social sketches in one thick number. The issue is a good sample of a leading Victorian monthly at full stretch.
14413-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
This July 1843 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine mixes fiction, criticism, and travel in the Tory monthly's usual blend. A serial memoir of a statesman continues, beside essays on English music and early Greek romance.

Other items include a Louisiana swamp adventure, a satirical poem, a Derby betting tale, and a review of Carlyle's Past and Present. The magazine's confident, combative voice runs through the reviews. The issue gives a full flavor of early Victorian periodical reading, where politics, literature, and sport shared the same pages. Blackwood's remained a leading Tory monthly for decades.
20023-the-letters-of-queen-victoria-vol-:
Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837, and her letters from 1837 to 1843 fill the first volume of her published letters. The book pairs those letters with background on her family and the House of Brunswick. Her father came from that old German house, which also ruled Hanover.

Readers see a young queen in her first years of rule, writing in her own words. The opening pages trace her birth and family ties before the letters begin. For anyone who wants the start of the Victorian age from the queen herself, the volume gives a direct, personal record.
20920-morale-a-story-of-the-war-of-1941-:
An Area Officer loathes his quiet coast watch in Morale, Murray Leinster's tale of the war of 1941-43. He longs for the west, where strange fighting flares each day. Guarding calm shores for the sake of civilian morale galls his young, keen spirit.

Leinster, a master of pulp science fiction, wrote this as a future-war tale. Odd weapons and new tactics haunt its imagined conflict's edges. Morale itself, the faith of plain folk, stands as a weapon in play. The story shows how writers between the world wars dreamed the next war, half right and half wildly wrong.
25065-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The August 1843 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 54, number 334, closes Sir Edward Lytton Bulwer's series of Schiller translations with a final set of poems and ballads. Bulwer's closing essay praises Schiller's earnest mind and varied genius, judging the poems a better window on the poet than his dramas.

Elsewhere the issue reviews the art world, weighing painters such as Roberts and Danby and the state of current exhibitions. Together, translation and criticism show the magazine's double role in Victorian Britain: bringing continental literature to English readers while passing judgment on the arts at home.
9992-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volu:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for January 1843, number 327 of volume 53, opens with Great Britain at the commencement of the year 1843. Its contents show the magazine's Tory range: Lesurques, or The Victim of Judicial Error, and Caleb Stukely, part ten.

Further pieces include an imaginary conversation by Walter Savage Landor, Tasso and Cornelia, The World of London, The Dream of Lord Nithsdale, and notes on the east and south of Europe. The Curse of Glencoe and Taste and Music in England close the set. Readers get a thick slice of early Victorian periodical culture.
a-lover-s-complaint-pg1543:
William Shakespeare's poem, in this edition's modernized spelling, begins with a voice of grief carried from a neighboring valley. The speaker finds a young woman by a river, tearing letters and breaking rings, her face marked by early sorrow. She tells the story of the youth who seduced her.

She remembers his looks, his tears, and his gifts, including jewels and locks of hair given him by women he had ruined before her. She weighs his false words and finds them persuasive still. The poem's forty-seven stanzas close with her confession that, knowing all, she would fall again. Its authorship has been debated, but the anguish is vivid.
arxiv-2412-03243:
Samuel Giuliani and co-authors wrote this nuclear physics paper in 2024. The r-process is the chain of rapid neutron captures that builds heavy elements in events like neutron star mergers. Its yields hinge on the masses of rare, short-lived nuclei that labs cannot weigh. Models must guess those masses, and the authors ask which part of the guess matters most.

They split each guess into a smooth bulk part, set by broad traits, and a local shell part, set by jumps at key neutron counts. Swings in the bulk part barely moved the yields, even when large. The shell part, though small next to total mass, drove nearly all the change. The team urges mass work aimed at such local jumps, since that is where merger yields are truly set.
arxiv-2412-03643:
Asher Berlin and co-authors propose a new way to hunt a faint background of exotic particles in a 2024 paper. Millicharged particles carry a tiny fraction of an electron's charge and arise in many dark sector theories. If they are light, the early universe, stars, and dark matter decay could fill space with a fast background of them. Such a wind is nearly invisible to normal detectors.

Their scheme starts from light-shining-through-wall setups that use superconducting radio cavities. A driven cavity's oscillating field shakes the millicharged plasma, parting its charges into waves. Those waves can escape the wall and ring a second, shielded cavity. Listening for that ring is a direct deflection search. The authors estimate a future version of an existing experiment could probe far deeper than current limits.
arxiv-2412-04143: Ben Jarvis studies pin classes of permutations in two thousand twenty-four. Pin sequences play a key role in the structure of permutation classes. A pin class holds all finite patterns found inside one infinite pin sequence. Jarvis asks how fast the count of such patterns grows with size. He proves these classes have proper growth rates. He also sets out a procedure to compute those rates. The paper is the first in a series on pin classes. It is short and focused on the growth question alone.
arxiv-2412-04643:
Ohad Lib and six co-authors certify high dimensional entanglement with randomized measurements in two thousand twenty-four. High dimensional states carry more data and resist noise better. Their many modes and touchiness to rotation complicate lab checks. The team certifies three dimensional entanglement inside a five dimensional photon pair.

Hundreds of Haar random measurements drive the certification. A programmable light converter with many planes performs them. The method holds up under arbitrary phase scrambling of modes. No shared reference frame is needed between the parties. Long range links with random twists are the target use.
arxiv-2412-05443:
Hiroki Kaifu and Sandra Troian derive simple power laws for how heat slips across the border between a liquid and a solid. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. The newest computer chips run so hot that liquid cooling is now essential, and the border itself resists heat flow.

No formulas existed for ordinary liquid-solid borders, so researchers leaned on costly simulations. The authors studied one hundred eighty model systems. They tracked order and vibration in the first layers on each side of the border. Scaled the right way, the data collapse onto two power laws. One captures gains from neater in-plane order; the other, from matched vibration rates. Surface sound waves emerge as the key carriers to engineer.
arxiv-2412-05643:
Andreas Nold, Benjamin Goddard, David Sibley, and Serafim Kalliadasis model the moving edge where a liquid, a gas, and a solid meet, in a 2024 paper. That contact line is hard to study because tiny scale effects shape large scale motion. Their model blends a statistical view of fluid density with flow equations, to see structure near the wall.

Simulations show the fluid forms layered patterns near the solid surface. As temperature rises, two zones appear: a compressed zone on the vapor side and a high shear zone that acts like slip on the liquid side. Both zones can reduce friction at the contact line. The compression zone spreads along the surface as temperature climbs.
arxiv-2412-06243:
Sungpyo Kim, Jeonghyeok Do, Jaehyup Lee, and Munchurl Kim wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It sharpens satellite images by fusing a crisp black-and-white view with a soft color one, a task called PAN-sharpening, through a diffusion frame that knows its own doubt.

Past methods lose fine detail, and diffusion ones underuse their inputs. A large teacher model reads frequency detail through selective attention and wavelet cues. Its knowledge is then distilled into a light student, steered by an uncertainty map that points at the hard spots of each image. The student learns to spend its effort there. Tests on varied sets beat the newest rivals by a clear mark.
arxiv-2412-06443:
Olimov Umrbek describes the fixed points of a nonlinear operator in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-four. The operator is infinite-dimensional and comes from a hard core model with countably many spin values. Finding fixed points of such operators is generally thought impossible.

Umrbek reduces the operator to a two-dimensional one, which makes full analysis possible. The parameter set is split into subsets that record how many fixed points lie on the diagonal line and how many lie off it. In total, the operator can have up to seven fixed points. He gives the explicit form of each one. The result turns an intractable problem into a complete classification for this model.
arxiv-2412-06743:
Harish Thangaraj and three co-authors segment childhood brain tumors in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Pediatric gliomas are a major cause of cancer death in children. Their infiltrative growth makes treatment planning hard. Early, accurate outlining of the tumor in scans is crucial for diagnosis and intervention.

The team presents a 3D U-Net architecture with a spatial attention mechanism. It works on multiparametric MRI data from the BraTS pediatric glioma data set. Multi-scale features are captured while attention focuses on tumor-relevant regions. That focus reduces interference from surrounding tissue. Performance was scored with the Dice coefficient and a boundary distance measure. Results showed improved delineation of complex tumor shapes. Readers get an automated aid for a delicate clinical task.
arxiv-2412-07043:
John Harrison and Richard Anantua compute neutrino flavor transition odds at high energy in two thousand twenty-four. Neutrinos shift flavor as they travel from their source. The team works out those odds in closed form. Sources span the Sun, supernovae, and cosmic rays.

They also weigh a jump to a heavier state past the standard three. A rough cross section for high energy neutrinos grounds the math. Oscillation lengths are compared across the three source types. Charts of flavor shares at Earth close the study. Each source leaves a distinct mix for detectors to find.
arxiv-2412-08243:
Bohan Li and co-authors present Hi-SOP, a method for predicting 3D scene occupancy from camera images, in this 2024 paper. The task labels each small volume of space with what fills it. Features gathered across video frames can misalign, since the same spot may carry different meanings in different frames. That makes context fusion unreliable.

Hi-SOP splits context into geometric and temporal parts and aligns each on its own. Depth confidence guides the geometric match, and camera pose guides the temporal match. Aligned features are then combined in a local to global hierarchy. The result is a steadier learning process and more reliable occupancy maps. Such maps help self driving and robot systems reason about hidden and visible space alike.
arxiv-2412-08443:
Yuan Liu and colleagues at Tencent set out POINTS1.5, a vision-language model built for real-world use. Vision-language models have grown fast. They show strong scores on tasks from reading text in images to studying complex diagrams. POINTS1.5 improves an earlier model with three new steps.

First, it swaps a fixed-size vision encoder for a NaViT-style encoder. That encoder supports native dynamic high resolution, so images of any size are handled with no tiling. Second, it adds support for two languages, which boosts Chinese skill a lot. Open Chinese vision-language data are scarce. So the team gathered images online and labeled them by hand and by machine. Third, it uses a set of filtering methods, tested with care, to build its tuning data.
arxiv-2412-08543:
Abdullah Hyder, Will Fox, Kirill Lezhnin, and Samuel Totorica wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on how to add a laser to a plasma code. Such codes, called particle-in-cell codes, track swarms of sample bits on a grid to fake a full plasma. A laser that heats the plasma is hard to add well, since its force is lost bit by bit in the gas.

Their way traces rays and drops the beam's force by inverse Bremsstrahlung absorption, in which electrons gain force from the light as they hit ions. The way copes with beams that hit at a slant, and with the bounce at the deep face past which a beam can not pass. The force won is handed to electrons as random kicks. Tests set the way next to sums done by hand and to an old two-space ray code: it matched both.
arxiv-2412-08943: Jiaqi Liu and Changhua Yang compute the higher-order long-time asymptotics of the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. They use the nonlinear steepest descent method in its d-bar form, a modern refinement of the classical inverse scattering approach. The analysis assumes initial conditions in a weighted Sobolev space with finite regularity and decay. The twenty twenty-four paper extends the known asymptotic description of this fundamental wave equation to higher order, sharpening what analysts can say about how its solutions settle over long times.
arxiv-2412-10543:
Siddhant Ray and seven co-authors build METIS, a system that makes retrieval-backed chat faster without dulling its answers. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Such systems fetch outside text so language models answer with facts. Fetching more text lifts quality but slows each reply.

Past work sped up scheduling or tuned quality, but not both at once. METIS plans each query's path and tunes its key settings together. Those settings include how many text chunks to fetch and how to blend them into the answer. On four question-answering data sets, it cut waiting time by a wide factor. Answer quality held steady against the best tuned rivals. The work shows speed and quality need not trade off so harshly. It suits live assistants that must answer quickly and well.
arxiv-2412-11143:
Akshay Singh and seven co-authors analyze a millisecond pulsar in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The source, IGR J17591–2342, is an accretion-powered X-ray pulsar found during its twenty eighteen outburst. They use timing and spectral data from India's AstroSat mission. Such pulsars spin hundreds of times per second while feeding on a companion star.

The timing analysis updates the binary orbital parameters. The average spin frequency comes out near 527.4 hertz. Pulse profiles fit well with four harmonically related sinusoid components. The fundamental pulse carries about thirteen percent fractional amplitude, with weaker overtones. Across the studied energy band, those amplitudes stay roughly constant. Readers get sharpened parameters for a fast-spinning neutron star caught mid-outburst.
arxiv-2412-12143:
Abdou Mohamed Naira and co-authors work, in twenty twenty-four, on language tools for Comorian, a group of four tongues spoken in the Comoros. Many African languages lack the data to build strong language tech. Swahili, a related tongue in the Bantu family, has much more data. Their idea is transfer learning: train on the rich tongue, then adapt to the poor one. They picked Swahili data closest to Comorian by word distance, then mixed the two.

They tested the mix on speech recognition and machine translation. Translation scores were solid for a first effort. Speech recognition still made many word errors. The authors frame the work as a first step for Comorian language tech.
arxiv-2412-12343:
Carla Henriquez-Baez and co-authors construct an exact rotating charged black hole with a toroidal horizon in this 2024 paper. The setting merges Einstein gravity with a Skyrme matter model carrying internal symmetry. A known static toroidal black hole with Skyrme hair gains spin through a coordinate trick. Charge is added with a coupled electric field.

Thermal behavior is worked out in the grand canonical ensemble. The number of internal flavors changes the heat properties in explicit ways. Stability receives discussion as well. Torus shaped horizons break the usual ball only intuition from basic courses. Exact solutions anchor numerical work on exotic black holes. Skyrme hair shows matter can dress gravity in stable patterns.
arxiv-2412-13043:
Franz Sattler and Jan Pawlowski bring in DiFfRG, a C++ frame to solve flow rules for a group named in the work. Such flows are strong for field rules for quanta but hard to cut up in a true way in broad cut plans. DiFfRG uses finite part ways to deal with field links in a fast and true count way.

It also backs large peak growths that hinge in full on push strength, and time cuts fit for breaks in same form that start on their own. A Mathematica pack makes flow rule code on its own, with GPU aid and wide splits of work in pairs. The text holds full code cases. They are a finite heat O(N) view, a quark-meson model, SU(3) Yang-Mills view, and four-Fermi flows in the QCD phase chart. Guides for new users come with them.
arxiv-2412-13943:
Adhane, Dehshibi, Vetter, Masip, and Roig tackle in twenty twenty-four a puzzle in how small AI models learn from large ones. In this training trick, a small student model copies a large teacher model. It works well, but no one could clearly see what knowledge moves across or how to judge its quality.

They offer a visual tool that maps where the student looks in an image as it learns. With teacher guidance, the student focused on true object parts and ignored stray background detail. They call the useful focus distilled features and the ignored parts residual features. Two new scores measure how alike and how apt the learned features are. Tests on three image datasets back the approach.
arxiv-2412-14843:
Bernardelle, Fröhling, Civelli, Lunardi, Roitero, and Demartini map in twenty twenty-four how fake personas steer the politics of large language models. Bias studies usually treat a model as one fixed voice, yet users often prompt models to speak as someone else. Using a big library of synthetic persona sketches, the team ran models through a standard political compass test under many personas.

Persona-prompted answers clustered heavily in the left-libertarian corner of the compass. When then pushed with explicit ideology prompts, models swung strongly toward right-authoritarian answers. Swings toward left-libertarian answers were much smaller, an asymmetry the authors flag. They read the lopsided response as a hint of leanings baked into training.
arxiv-2412-15043:
Ion Grama and Michael Nussbaum build a functional Hungarian construction for sums of independent random variables. The variables do not share one distribution. Their 2024 paper extends a classic strong approximation device. The partial sum process is indexed by functions from a class. The supremum over that class is taken outside the probability. That setup is just what a Komlós-Major-Tusnády inequality in bounded-function space requires.

Their build keeps the classic rate over wide classes of functions. Hölder balls are included, where the standard result strains. Keeping the rate at this breadth is the technical prize. Such strong fits power proofs that statistical experiments match in the limit. The result is core support for limit theory.
arxiv-2412-15143:
Antonia Seifert, Zachary Lane, Marco Galoppo, Ryan Ridden-Harper, and David Wiltshire published this cosmology paper in 2024. It re-examines the Pantheon+ set of type Ia supernovae, exploding stars used as standard candles to measure cosmic expansion. The team ran a fresh analysis that does not assume a cosmic model in advance, using only the standard equation that corrects each supernova's brightness.

They compare two rival pictures of the universe. One is the standard model, where dark energy drives faster expansion. The other is timescape cosmology, which drops dark energy and instead credits the uneven lumpiness of matter. Across the full sample, the evidence strongly favored timescape, and the preference held for distant supernovae alone. The authors argue that the foundations of cosmology deserve a fresh look.
arxiv-2412-17443:
Hoshu Hiyane, Giedrius Žlabys, Thomas Busch, and Shohei Watabe study driven strongly interacting bosons in two thousand twenty-four. The gas is of Tonks-Girardeau type, where bosons act near like fermions. A strong periodic drive shakes the gas out of balance. They compute its exact spectral function in that state.

Floquet theory and the Bose-Fermi map do the heavy lifting. New Lieb modes appear when the mapped fermions form a Floquet-Fermi sea. At low frequency the boson modes turn linear in the Lieb way. The mapped fermions show a wide Dirac like spread instead. The split between the two views is a core result.
arxiv-2412-17843:
Rafaela Scaciota and co-authors present a method to predict blockages in millimetre-wave communication links, in work from 2024. These high-frequency links carry fast data but fail when objects block the path. Knowing where a blocker sits lets the system react before the link drops.

Their approach labels radio data automatically using object positions taken from laser scanning data. A deep learning model then learns to predict an object's location from radio signals alone. Because the model predicts location rather than blockage directly, it adapts when the transmitter or receiver moves, with no retraining. Tests in changing environments reached accuracy up to about three quarters for blockage location. The authors present the method as a step toward reliable high-frequency connectivity in dynamic settings.
arxiv-2412-17943:
Yuli Wang, Victoria Shi, Wen-Chi Hsu, Yuwei Dai, Sophie Yao, Zhusi Zhong, Zishu Zhang, Jing Wu, Aaron Maxwell, Scott Collins, Zhicheng Jiao, and Harrison Bai wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It tunes how prompts are fed to the Segment Anything Model for cutting lesions out of medical scans.

More prompt points lift the cut quality by a large step, and where the points sit counts too: surface and union prompts beat center ones. Each tumor kind and scan kind has its own best count and layout. A reinforcement learning agent learns to place the points on its own. It tops random and rival agents and cuts the work time near tenfold next to hand use.
arxiv-2501-00143:
Cheng-Hau Yang and three co-authors brought a shifted edge method to heat flows. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with joined flow and heat runs on meshes that do not fit the body's shape. Their build uses an octree mesh, part filled, with the shifted boundary method. A half implicit form of the thermal flow laws keeps runs fast yet true. The method can pin both field and slope terms on cut cells.

That gives true flux reads near hard shapes. Slope terms, the hard case, held exact on their meshes. Runs span flow regimes from slow to swift. Readers in flow sims get a way to keep edge truth with no body fit mesh grind.
arxiv-2501-00443:
Yu Tong and Yongtao Zhan wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about how fast a quantum system settles into its thermal state. Preparing Gibbs states, the thermal states of quantum matter, is a key task for quantum computers. A recently proposed process, called a Lindbladian, can drive a system toward such a state, but its speed needed proof.

The authors study weakly interacting fermion systems, the setting of models like the Fermi-Hubbard model of electrons in a lattice. They show that, at any temperature, the key spectral gap stays above a fixed constant when the interaction is weak enough. That constant does not shrink as the system grows. Mixing time thus grows at most in step with system size, so the states can be prepared efficiently.
arxiv-2501-00743:
Mengran Li and a team of co-authors repair incomplete graphs in twenty twenty-five. Many real graphs lack attributes for some nodes. Graph neural networks trained on such data produce biased results. Feature propagation is the standard repair, filling gaps from neighbors. It suffers a cold start problem, worst for low-degree nodes and reset attributes.

Their method, AttriReBoost, rethinks how propagation begins. New boundary conditions and added virtual edges improve node connectivity. Propagation then converges more stably and efficiently. The reconstruction needs no gradient computation, so overhead stays low. Readers working with messy real-world graphs get a way to restore missing features without training a heavy imputation model first.
arxiv-2501-01843:
Yirong Wang and co-authors describe a simpler optical lattice in a 2025 arXiv paper. Optical lattices trap atoms with interfering laser beams for quantum work. Keeping several beams phase-locked is hard, needing delicate optics and electronics.

Their scheme passes a single beam through a prism with symmetric facets and large apex angles. The lattice forms from parts of the same beam, so no moving parts or phase locks are needed. They built both a triangular lattice and a ten-fold quasi-crystal lattice. Stability tests showed the lattice constant changed by barely one percent. Position drift was likewise tiny.
arxiv-2501-02043:
Petr Kisselev and Padmanabhan Seshaiyer model epidemic spread across the United States with a hybrid of classic and neural methods in a 2025 study. A metapopulation design treats each region as its own susceptible-infected-recovered pool, with human mobility carrying infection between pools. Graph neural networks estimate the movement-linked parameters that older fitting handled poorly.

Earlier hybrid versions already beat standard methods on data gathered before the period studied here. The authors extend that comparison for COVID spread across connected regions. Mobility-aware forecasts help officials judge where interventions matter most, since a purely local model misses infections arriving from elsewhere.
arxiv-2501-02343:
Maitri Mandal and co-authors show that a sheared colloidal glass can remember its past, in the manner of the Kovacs effect. Their paper appeared in 2025. The classic effect, seen in glasses after temperature jumps, reveals hidden memory in disordered matter. Whether it survives under shear, which keeps volume fixed, was unknown. The team combined experiments, simulations, and response theory on a dense suspension of tiny spheres.

A two-step shear protocol produced the telltale memory hump. With stronger, nonlinear pushes, the response drifted from the simple theory. That drift tracked microscopic flows in which particles stray from the smooth shear pattern. The authors conclude the memory effect extends to volume-preserving pushes, and that local flow patterns govern how strong the memory is.
arxiv-2501-02443:
Mustafa and Guvendi study a quantum oscillator in a space with spiral flaws. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses the Klein-Gordon equation, the relativistic wave rule for spin-free fields. Two flaw types are in play. One twists a radial line, and the other twists a circle. The authors test each flaw with and without a magnetic field.

The first flaw shifts the energy levels of the oscillator in all cases. The second flaw leaves energies alone unless a magnetic field is on. Wave shapes pick up the flaw's mark in both cases. The team solves the equations exactly in most cases. Some cases need a weaker exact form tied to Heun functions. For the second flaw, the field strength alone sets how fast the oscillator swings.
arxiv-2501-02643:
Tamás Pető, Ferenc Iglói, and István Kovács study a disordered magnet chain buffeted by two kinds of random field at once. The Ising chain carries random bonds, a random transverse field, and a random longitudinal field. Experiments on a lithium holmium yttrium fluoride compound motivate the model. Strong disorder renormalization, which decimates the strongest couplings step by step, reveals its low-energy fate at zero temperature.

Each field alone leads somewhere known: transverse randomness gives ordered and disordered fixed points plus an infinite-disorder critical point; longitudinal randomness gives the classical random-field fixed point. Together, the flows are drawn to one of two disordered fixed points. At the infinite-disorder point, the one relevant direction runs along the separatrix between them. The correlation length diverges there with an exponent near one.
arxiv-2501-03043:
A. Müller and a large team measured hollow-atom resonances in boron ions in 2025, jointly in experiment and theory. Firing photons at helium-like boron ions, they hunted states where both inner-shell electrons are excited at once, leaving a double core hole that quickly decays. The ion beam mixed ground-state and long-lived excited ions, so two resonance series appeared, one from each starting state, across hundreds of electronvolts.

Spectrometers reached resolving power in the tens of thousands, pinning the strongest resonance energies to about a milli-electronvolt. Relativistic many-body calculations, including electron correlation and radiative effects, reproduced the pattern level by level. Such precision benchmarks atomic theory in a regime where several effects compete at once.
arxiv-2501-04043:
Bogdan Dimitrov extends a math route for timing a GPS signal when all six orbit traits can change, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Past work let only the angle along the orbit vary, with relativity effects counted. The full set maps into three space coordinates through a known change of variables.

The travel time is cast as a squared form in the small changes of the six traits. A varied-form method plus a Stokes step needs second derivatives to stay nonzero. In shape terms that need matches the presence of Morse functions. No such function exists for the omega angle, the author shows. Readers get both the wider frame and its hard limit.
arxiv-2501-05243:
Chandan Kumar Sheemar, Symeon Chatzinotas, and a team of co-authors argue for merging two satellite jobs into one. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers joint communications and sensing for sixth-generation networks. Satellites now carry split gear for talking and for watching Earth. Demand growth makes that split wasteful in cost and spectrum.

A shared payload can do both jobs with less hardware. It also opens services that split gear cannot offer. The authors walk through one test case to show the idea can work. They then list the hard spots: design, signals, and rules. The paper aims to spark work on shared space systems.
arxiv-2501-07943:
Eline Honig and Emiel Lorist bring, in a 2025 paper, the tools of optimization to a corner of harmonic analysis. Their objects are collections of sets with a boundedness property called the Carleson condition, and a related packing property called sparseness. Both matter in the study of wave-like functions and operators. Computing the exact Carleson constant of a collection was previously only approximated.

The authors give an algorithm that computes it exactly and runs in strongly polynomial time. The method rests on minimizing a submodular function. A second method shows any Carleson collection is sparse, with the best possible link between the constants. The key move recasts the duality between the two properties as the classic duality between maximum flow and minimum cut in a network. The paper grew out of the first author's bachelor's thesis.
arxiv-2501-10743:
Songita Das and Gourab Ghatak analyze the trade-off between fresh data and energy in wireless sensor networks where devices live off harvested power. The devices draw energy from transmitter signals, then spend it sending data packets. The authors split each time slot by a chosen factor: the first part harvests energy, the second sends data. They define a joint success measure: the chance that harvested energy and signal quality both clear their thresholds.

Exact values for that measure are hard, so the paper derives lower and upper bounds. From the same framework they compute the peak age of information, how stale the freshest data can get. Longer harvesting starves transmission time, while shorter harvesting starves energy. Both queuing styles studied share the same best split point. The authors recommend that split for different power levels and deployment sizes.
arxiv-2501-15343:
Nicholas LaHaye, Anistasija Easley, and colleagues teach a model to find smoke and fire in airborne measurements without hand labels in a 2025 study. A major field campaign flew through wildfire and farm fire smoke to study air quality and climate effects, gathering far more data than analysts can annotate. Self-supervised learning lets the model learn structure from the unlabeled flights themselves, then surface smoke plumes and active fire fronts.

Automated spotting turns an archive too big to read into evidence about how fires pollute regions and warm the planet. The same approach suits future campaigns as fire seasons lengthen.
arxiv-2501-15643:
Jordi Lopez-Abad and co-authors study special families of sets in advanced mathematics, in work from 2025. The families are called ideals, and the ones they study can be described by series in Banach spaces, which are complete spaces used in analysis. Recent work had sorted these ideals by how they can be so described.

The team gives clear descriptions of these ideals inside two classic spaces of continuous functions. A space called c0 plays a key role in their work. They also study colouring ideals, built from sets where a two-colouring stays uniform. Among their results, they show one random ideal of this kind is badly behaved, build well-behaved universal ones, and link the two topics. The paper answers a question posed by other researchers in the field.
arxiv-2501-16043:
Michele Della Morte, Benjamin Jager, Sofie Martins, and Tobias Tsang test a spread flow on force fields. The work came out in 2025. They check how the flow reads the field's twist charge on a grid. The stage is a force field whose stuff mimics a super form of Yang-Mills thought. In the end, they want to call out its full scale of bits.

Slope flow smooths the field as it runs. The smoothed field's twist charge should settle to firm marks. The team studies part charges across more than one grid gap. With a boosted force step in the spread core, the charge firms up at mild flow times. With the stock Wilson flow, it does not. The point is of use in real work. The pick of step in the flow rules if the twist charge is read with trust.
arxiv-2501-18743:
Seyed Mehrinezhad Chobari, Hossein Aghababa, and Mohammadreza Kolahdouz design quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Their circuits build a special shared state, called a W state, across three or four particles, with any chosen weights and phases. They then teleport such states, sending each particle separately through a shared four-particle channel.

Pre-processing by the sender cuts the resources needed for the sending. The receiver uses extra helper particles to rebuild the final states. Running the protocol both ways at once improves efficiency further, since unknown particles held by users can serve as helpers. Simulations with a public quantum toolkit confirmed the protocol works as designed.
arxiv-2502-00143:
Ambre Chabert wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on wave patterns on spinning shapes. The shapes are surfaces of revolution, like a vase profile spun around an axis, and the waves are near-modes called quasimodes.

Chabert studies a projector that picks out waves in a very narrow band of frequencies. She bounds how large those waves can grow, measured by a standard norm, for a wide class of such surfaces. The proof adapts a microlocal method built for wider bands and leans on the special integrable structure of these surfaces. That reduces the work to careful bounds on explicit wavy integrals, for which she builds new tools. Small disks around the poles are left out of the claim. The result is the first sharp bound of its kind for such narrow bands beyond the most symmetric shapes.
arxiv-2502-01243:
Chengfeng Zhou and co-authors build OphthBench, a 2025 benchmark for testing large language models on eye medicine as practiced in China. Models are being eyed for clinic use, but their real competence and limits in this specialty were unmeasured. The benchmark follows a typical eye clinic's flow and splits it into five scenes: education, triage, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.

Across those scenes sit nine tasks and five hundred ninety-one questions of varied type. The team then ran thirty-nine popular models through the full set and dissected the results. A clear gap showed between what the models can do and what clinical work demands. The authors publish the framework so developers can see exactly where models fail, in which scene and which task type. They frame the benchmark as a map for closing that gap before any ward deployment.
arxiv-2502-02143:
Ruxuan Zhang published this paper in 2025. It advances a conjecture about the hidden symmetries of hyper-Kähler varieties, a prized class of geometric spaces. These spaces generalize the famous K3 surface. Zhang proposes that a twisted version of their derived category, a bookkeeping system for sheaves on the space, is governed by an associated lattice. The lattice in question is the Markman-Mukai lattice, a grid of numbers attached to the variety.

He proves the claim under stated numerical conditions. The proof leans on a special bundle built by Markman and on a recently settled twisted equivalence result. One payoff: two well-behaved moduli spaces of sheaves on a K3 surface share the same derived category whenever their dimensions agree. The paper speaks to the deep dictionary between geometry and algebra.
arxiv-2502-03443:
Francisco Arco, Thomas Biekötter, Panagiotis Stylianou, and Georg Weiglein study top quark spin links in two thousand twenty-five. Their case is a heavy new spin zero particle that decays at the LHC. It can split into a Z boson and a lighter spin zero particle. The lighter one then splits into top quark pairs.

Two chains are possible, with odd or even parity roles swapped. Current searches cannot tell the two apart if their rates match. The team shows that spin links in the top quarks can split them. Angles from the leptons in top decay do the work. With high volume LHC data, the split should be clear.
arxiv-2502-04843:
Feifei Li, Qi Song, Chi Zhang, Hui Shuai, and Rui Huang introduced PoI in twenty twenty-five, a filter that makes synthetic views safe for training camera localization systems. Scene coordinate regression predicts a 3D point for every pixel, demanding exact supervision. Rendered views from neural synthesis can augment training, but they blur and distort where the original capture was thin.

Their pipeline renders novel views with 3D Gaussian splatting, then refines them with a one-step diffusion model that invents plausible detail. A progressive filter then keeps only pixels whose reprojection error is small, discarding untrustworthy ones during training. On the 7Scenes and Cambridge Landmarks benchmarks, the method steadily improved localization over strong baselines and reached top performance with competitive training cost.
arxiv-2502-07943:
George Fletcher, Olha Nahurna, Matvii Prytula, and Julia Stoyanovich argued in 2025 that data models deserve the same close reading that literary scholars give texts. Every database, statistical model, and machine learning system rests on an underlying data model, and that model quietly records the material, social, and political conditions that produced the system. Reading it closely can reconnect analysts with a system's origins, craft, and design choices.

Borrowing from literary criticism, where no single correct reading exists, the authors still insist that beginners need systematic guidance, since computing training often teaches students to set social and political questions aside. Their work sets out to fill the gap: a methodology for reading data models closely, aimed especially at readers trained in computing and data science.
arxiv-2502-09643:
Mathieu Helfter proves a result in the study of fractal size in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. Size for rough sets is often read by two scales, the Hausdorff scale and the packing scale. Each scale uses its own gauge function, a rule that says how size shrinks with width.

Helfter shows that, under mild rules on the gauges, one set can hit two preset scales at once. He builds a compact set in the Baire space whose two measures are both finite and positive, one for each gauge. He then plants that set inside any Banach space with endless dimensions. This gives a yes to a question posed by Fan about spaces with freely chosen scales.
arxiv-2502-09743:
Arne Rubehn and Johann-Mattis List improve how computers map the meaning of concepts across languages. A concept can be stored as a point in a space, so that near points have near meanings. Past maps were built from words that carry two meanings in many languages. Those maps miss cases where only part of a word carries the extra meaning.

The new method adds these partial cases to the network that feeds the map. The maps were tested on word likeness scores, records of meaning change, and word link data. In each test, the partial cases gave better maps of concepts. The authors show the maps can capture distinct kinds of links between meanings, which helps work with sparse data and rare tongues.
arxiv-2502-10843:
Peter Holderrieth, Michael Albergo, and Tommi Jaakkola wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five about drawing samples from sets of discrete choices. Many tasks need samples from a known but unscaled chance distribution. Their method, named LEAPS, learns the jump rates of a process that moves between choices over time.

The hard part is scoring how good each path is, since standard network designs make that score too costly to compute. The authors build a compact form for the jump rates using networks with a local symmetry property. That design lets them train the system at scale while keeping the scores steady and low in spread.
arxiv-2502-11443:
Jing Niu, Peng He, and Tong-Jie Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It pins the Hubble constant with a full covariance matrix built by a neural net, from cosmic clock data.

The cosmic chronometer method reads the universe's growth rate from old galaxies. Past work dropped the off-diagonal terms of the error matrix, or used a short one, which blurs the Hubble value. A net built to keep the matrix well formed grows a small known matrix into a full one. Set by a leave-one-out test, it beats a Gaussian process rival as a maker. With the full matrix in hand, two methods then bound the constant. The center barely moves, but the width of the bound shifts in clear ways.
arxiv-2502-11743:
Real training data is messy: human labelers often give the same example several different labels, only one of them right. Partial-label learning trains a classifier anyway, without hand-cleaning the data, by treating the candidate set as a hint. Tobias Fuchs and Florian Kalinke note that leading methods break easily under heavy label noise, strange examples, and crafted attacks. Their method rests on subjective logic, which keeps uncertainty explicit instead of hiding it in one score.

Their method reads the sizes of the network's class activation values, the internal signals behind each class, and turns them into stated uncertainty. A new rule then redistributes trust among the candidate labels, and the authors prove this rule is optimal. In experiments, the approach kept its accuracy better than rivals when label noise ran high. It also handled out-of-distribution examples better and resisted adversarial tweaks.
arxiv-2502-11943:
Zheng and a large team studied in twenty twenty-five a light-only way to sense weak fields with flaws in diamond. Those flaws glow in a way that shifts with field strength and line. The light way needs no micro-waves, so kits can be small and plain.

They read glow at low fields in stones rich in such flaws at room warmth. Glow marks matched near-tied states of the flaw's spin parts and their kin in the stone. False runs of the field acts matched the reads in a fair way. Top glow strength rests on flaw count and light strength, they find.
arxiv-2502-15643:
Luka Grbcic, Juliane Müller, and Wibe Albert de Jong propose a new design method in a 2025 paper. Inverse design means starting from a wanted result and working back to the settings that give it. Such searches can be slow when the design space is large. Their method pairs paired neural networks with active learning.

Active learning picks the most useful new examples to add, so fewer are needed. The team tested the idea on three tasks: wing shapes, light-handling surfaces, and a heat spread problem. In each case their method beat standard approaches, reaching better accuracy with fewer training samples. That saving matters when each test run costs much time or computing power.
arxiv-2502-15743:
Tillman shows a fresh sieve that yields primes and their part splits with no cuts. Most sieve ways lean on split steps to sift whole counts. His sieve builds both primes and full splits in one pass. The chains it makes are the p-adic worth counts of n. Each such chain proves to be a self-like chain in form. Self-like chains are those that hold their shape at all scales.

Those chains then make shape fractals, like the Levy Dragon form. A link twixt the odd part chain and one more form caps it. That form is the Heighway Dragon in the text of the work. Count math and plane shape meet in that close link. The sieve thus ties prime parts to bent plane art.
arxiv-2502-17843:
Istiaq Ahmed Fahad and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on spotting vehicles on hard roads with a transformer model. Light, road type, and vehicle mix all shift as a car drives. Older vision tools, which mix plain networks with set rules, can strain in such mix. The team is the first to try a detection transformer for this task.

Their training scheme, named Co-DETR, sharpens how the model learns traits and focus. Extra heads in training give more signal and lift the yield of good picks. Tests on a data set of tough road scenes pit their method against transformer and YOLO forms. Their method won on scores. The authors say it is fit for real use in self driving stacks.
arxiv-2502-18443:
Jake Poznanski and co-authors release an open toolkit that turns PDFs into clean training text with a fine tuned vision language model, in work from twenty twenty-five. PDFs hold trillions of quality words for training language models, but messy layouts defeat cheap extractors. Top commercial models cost too much per page or cannot take private files.

Their seven billion parameter model trained on over a quarter million diverse crawled pages. It reads pages into plain text in natural order, keeping tables, lists, and equations. A million pages cost about one hundred seventy-six dollars to convert. A new benchmark of fourteen hundred hard PDFs showed the toolkit beating even the best commercial rivals. All parts are public.
arxiv-2502-19743:
Chen and a large team report in twenty twenty-five telescope observations of sudden X-ray bursts from a neutron star system. These bursts come from nuclear burning on the star's surface. During bursts, the hot cloud around the star may cool, causing a dip in hard X-rays. That dip had been seen in nine sources, but never in this prolific burster, which cast doubt on the idea.

A Chinese X-ray telescope watched the system in its hard state and caught ten bursts. Two bursts showed a double peak in soft X-rays, hinting at a brief swelling of the star's surface layers. The hard X-ray dip did appear above a set energy, and its depth levelled off partway. The authors read this as proof that only the inner part of the cloud cools.
arxiv-2502-21143:
Hyungi Lee, Seungyoo Lee, and Juho Lee shrink the data needed to train uncertainty-aware networks, in a 2025 paper. Bayesian neural networks report not just a guess but how sure the guess is. That honesty costs heavy computing, since the networks carry whole ranges of possible settings.

A pseudo-coreset is a tiny, learned stand-in dataset that mimics the full data. Earlier versions for Bayesian networks ate memory during training and gave weaker results. The new method uses variational inference, a principled shortcut for hard probability math, to learn the stand-in set with less memory and cost. Benchmark tests show better accuracy than the earlier approach. The work makes uncertainty reporting more practical on large datasets.
arxiv-2503-00543:
Xiaoshan Huang and co-authors published this study in 2025. It asks whether merging black hole pairs could flash light that telescopes might catch. The pairs LIGO hears are born, in this picture, with a leftover gas disk around them. As gravity waves shrink the orbit, tides squeeze the disk. The squeeze raises a two-armed spiral wave that stands still in the pair's rotating frame.

Simulations show the spiral drives gas inward far faster than normal. Even a weakly ionized disk drains away long before the holes merge. With the gas gone, the merger happens in the dark. The authors say this dims hopes for a glowing partner to the gravity wave signal, at least for this kind of system. Disk draining, in short, beats the merger clock.
arxiv-2503-01343:
Hui Gao confirms a guess about which graphs push a new degree based index, the complementary second Zagreb index, to its max for a set size. Such indices boil a graph's shape down to one number used in chem-ical graph work. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The index came from a fresh geometric view of graph edges, set out by Furtula and Oz. In that same work, the authors guessed which graphs of a given order reach the top value. Gao proves the guess holds, which pins down the extremal graphs fully. The result closes an open point in the study of these new indices.
arxiv-2503-01743:
A large Microsoft team introduces compact language models in a 2025 technical report. The text model holds under four billion parameters yet beats similar-sized open models and matches models twice its size on math and coding tasks. The secret is a curated diet of high-quality web and synthetic data, heavy on math and code. A much larger vocabulary aids many languages, and a grouped attention scheme speeds long outputs.

Its sibling adds vision and speech to the same core. Small adapter modules with routers let the modes combine without interfering. The report details the recipes and benchmarks for both models.
arxiv-2503-02243: Naokant Deo and Sandeep Kumar build a new family of approximation operators in a 2025 paper. Their sequence ties the construction to a class of polynomials through their generating functions. They compute the operators' moments, including what the central moments settle to as the sequence advances. Then they bound how fast the operators converge, using a standard smoothness measure, and prove further results in a Lipschitz-type space.
arxiv-2503-02743:
Urvisha Shethia, Vedali Inamdar, and Viraj Kulkarni check Eloquent, a digital speech treatment app for stuttering, in a two thousand twenty-five pilot study. Stuttering disrupts speech fluency and brings psychological and social difficulties.

The the research team compared speech samples before and after treatment using the Stuttering Severity Index-4 and the S24 communication attitude scale. Overall severity scores fell by more than half, with gains in reading, speaking, duration, and physical concomitants. Over three quarters of people taking part got better by at least one severity group. Attitude scores also got better, hinting structured app-based treatment can build fluency and confidence.
arxiv-2503-03043:
Andy Dong, Wei-Ning Chen, and Ayfer Ozgur wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It shows how the random choices already built into model training can be used on purpose to strengthen privacy for the data behind the model.

In many setups, each data sample takes part in only some training rounds, or updates only part of the model. The authors prove that this partial involvement hides each sample's influence more than past analyses credited. They apply the idea to federated learning, where phones or hospitals train a shared model by each updating a random slice of it. That trick, used to save memory, turns out to buy real privacy. They also add a new sampling scheme that gives each sample a fixed number of turns, beating random sampling on privacy.
arxiv-2503-04843:
Alessandro Pasqui, Hervé Turlier, and a team of co-authors sharpen 3D microscope images along their weak axis. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents ZAugNet. Microscope stacks often have fine detail across a slice but coarse steps between slices. Light damage limits and sample traits cause that gap.

Their method fills in new slices between real ones in a learned, curved way. Each pass doubles the depth detail. A rival-maker network plus a teacher trick keeps it fast and sharp. Tests across imaging types beat rival methods on most scores. A plus version fills gaps at any spacing, which suits uneven real data sets.
arxiv-2503-05143:
Wenhao Wang and colleagues released the first benchmark for training phone agents on scattered user data in a 2025 paper. Mobile agents learn to operate apps for users, but central data collection is costly and hard to scale. Federated learning trains on data that stays on each phone, yet the field had no standard test bed, so results could not be compared fairly.

FedMABench bundles several datasets with many subsets, a range of federated algorithms and base models, and hundreds of apps in a few categories. Experiments found federated methods consistently beat training on one phone alone. Which apps a user has drove much of the difference between users, and even unrelated app categories showed linked patterns during training.
arxiv-2503-05243:
Gianluca Passarelli, Angelo Russomanno, and Procolo Lucignano examine a quantum complexity measure in a boundary time crystal in a 2025 physics study. Time crystals of this kind settle into steady states whose entanglement can change sharply under monitoring. Those transitions were known to depend on how the underlying open-system dynamics is unraveled into individual histories.

The authors instead track nonstabilizerness, sometimes called magic, which measures how far a state lies beyond easy classical simulation. Unlike entanglement, it stays the same across unraveling choices for large systems. Its steady value shows a cusp at the mean-field critical point rather than a full transition.
arxiv-2503-06843:
The T2K team, a large group of physicists, report in 2025 on a hard-to-spot reaction of neutrinos, the tiny particles that pass through matter with ease. They study cases where a neutrino hits a target and makes a single charged pion, without the neutrino itself changing form. The work uses the ND280 detector near the beam source.

The paper explains how the team picks out this faint signal from a sea of other events. It then shows how to work out the rate of the reaction in a way that does not lean on one set model of how neutrinos act. Such rates help test the rules that guide neutrino science. They also help future experiments read their own data with less bias.
arxiv-2503-08443:
Alexandru Aleman and Alex Bergman wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on invariant subspaces. An invariant subspace is a part of a space that an operator maps back into itself. The paper studies two linked operators, one that takes derivatives and one, the Volterra operator, that builds up integrals.

The authors use an abstract setup where the two operators undo each other. One is compact and fades to zero with repeats, while the other is unbounded but well behaved. Their results cover many cases, from Schrödinger operators to large classes of systems. A key tool is a model built from spaces of entire functions. The work widens what is known about these classic operators.
arxiv-2503-08843:
Rajitha de Silva and five co-authors improve feature matching for farm robots in two thousand twenty-five. Their test ground is vineyards, where rows of vines look much alike. Like looks make image points hard to tell apart. That hurts pose checks and place finding for the robot.

The team adds semantic facts to each key point in the image. Points in regions with meaning get richer codes. That makes twins in looks easier to split apart. Tests span two tasks, pose checks and place finding. Match accuracy rose across all point and code types tried. Gains held over months of hard field work.
arxiv-2503-09843:
Gheorghe Craciun, Abhishek Deshpande, and Jiaxin Jin compute a special parameter region for chemical reaction networks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Reaction models can swing wildly, with multiple steady states or chaos. A lucky few behave like a tame class of systems with very stable dynamics, even when they do not look the part.

Such impostors are called disguised toric systems, and the set of parameters making a network one is its disguised toric locus. Until now, measuring that set was awkward. The authors give a general, efficient method for its dimension. They demo the method on models of biological networks, including a classic oscillator, feedback gene circuits, and circadian clocks.
arxiv-2503-11543:
Wystan Benbow and colleagues present recent highlights from the VERITAS active galactic nucleus discovery program, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. VERITAS is among the world's most sensitive very-high-energy gamma-ray observatories. About half of its good-weather observing time has targeted active galactic nuclei. Many sessions belong to an ongoing program hunting new gamma-ray nuclei.

When a discovery is made, the collaboration pairs spectral and variability measurements with broadband observations. Together these probe the jet-powered processes inside the nucleus. Recent highlights include four very-high-energy discoveries. They are the objects B2 0912+29, 1ES 1028+511, 1ES 1118+424, and RBS 1366. The report shows how a long-running discovery program keeps expanding the catalog of extreme galactic nuclei.
arxiv-2503-12543:
Andrea Longhin re-analyzed Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons in twenty twenty-five, comparing each entry of the Sidereus Nuncius against a modern sky simulator. Earlier studies had sampled the record; this one checks every observation. It uses both Galileo's sketches and his written angular measurements. The aim is to grade a seventeenth-century telescope and dataset by modern ephemerides.

The analysis measures the telescope's power to separate close moons and its blindness near Jupiter's disk. Sine fits recover the moons' orbit sizes to a few percent and their periods to a fraction of a percent. That precision suffices to infer Kepler's third law convincingly. It also pins the famous one-two-four resonance of Io, Europa, and Ganymede. Checks extend to the Moon and star clusters.
arxiv-2503-12843:
Haozhe Si and five co-authors lay groundwork for a scalable base model for geospatial data with many modes and fine color bands. Satellite raster data hold rich place and time context across channels. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past self taught methods adapt poorly as channels and modes grow, which wastes computing. The new vision transformer splits its focus step into low rank space and spectra parts. A place and channel code layer keeps the physical sense of each patch. A mask limits focus to near patches, which uses local links. The team also builds a broad test bench to check these ideas.
arxiv-2503-13843:
Trisanth Srinivasan and Santosh Patapati build a voice-driven web agent in twenty twenty-five. Web interfaces serve users with limited mobility poorly. Screen readers and scripts lack the flexibility for dynamic pages and cannot grasp high-level goals. Their system, WebNav, aims to turn spoken commands into actions on a page.

WebNav uses two large language models in separate roles. One, the Controller, plans the next step toward the user's goal. The other, the Assistant, fills in the exact parameters to run that step. Vision from screenshots is combined with a browser extension that labels page elements. That pairing helps the agent find the right buttons and fields. Readers get a design for hands-free browsing driven by intent, not clicks.
arxiv-2503-14643:
Shaik and co-authors track how spinons, fractional magnetic ripples, get trapped as a lattice grows from a line to a sheet in two thousand twenty-five. Spinons are proven in spin chains, where they roam free. Whether they survive in two dimensions was disputed, though square-lattice experiments hinted at them at high energy.

The team studies a trial wave state on a rectangular grid of spin-half atoms, tuning the coupling ratio between the two directions. Spectra and spinon spacing were read as the ratio shifted. Over most of the momentum map the spinons grew more confined as the sheet formed. At select wave vectors they stayed free. The result maps where fractional ripples can live in flat magnets.
arxiv-2503-15043:
Roger Balsach leads a large team sharpening the predicted rate for making a Higgs boson with two top quarks. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. This ttH process is a key probe of the Higgs coupling to matter. Precision matters because deviations could hint at new physics. The work follows guidance from the LHC Higgs Working Group. It represents the best current standard model prediction.

Quantum chromodynamics corrections are pushed to next-to-next-to-leading order. Soft gluon effects are resummed to matching accuracy in two frameworks. Direct QCD and effective theory approaches are compared in detail. Electroweak corrections complete the package. The combined result is the most precise to date. Collider experiments gain a firmer yardstick.
arxiv-2503-15643:
Dzero and Kamenev wrote in twenty twenty-five about a collective vibration in superconductors called the Schmid-Higgs mode. Superconductors carry current without resistance below a critical temperature. Their collective modes gave the first real example of the Higgs mechanism. This longitudinal mode sits right at the energy edge where single excitations begin. When kicked suddenly, it rings with oscillations that fade slowly as a power law.

The pair ask what happens when pair-breaking effects enter the picture. Magnetic impurities or in-plane fields can lower the excitation threshold. Even then, the slow power-law ringing persists with a changed form. Only when the superconductor becomes fully gapless does the mode decay fast. The result clarifies how robust this mode is against disorder.
arxiv-2503-15843:
Tianyi Hao, Amanda Xu, and Swamit Tannu present an algorithm that cuts the cost of fault-tolerant quantum computing, in work from 2025. Error correction makes quantum machines reliable but adds huge overhead. The priciest operations are T gates, which need costly distilled states to run.

Many algorithms need rotations by arbitrary angles, which are usually split into long chains of T and simpler gates. Fusing two rotations into one general operation is possible, but older synthesis tools handled it indirectly and tripled the T count. The new algorithm synthesises the fused operation directly using tensor network search. Across 187 benchmark circuits, it cut T counts by up to three and a half times and simpler gates by seven times. Overall circuit error improved up to fourfold.
arxiv-2503-17143:
Koliogiannis, Yüksel, Ghosh, and Paar use a lab gauge of atomic nuclei to pin down neutron star traits. Their paper from twenty twenty-five centers on electric dipole polarizability, a measure of how a nucleus's protons shift under a field. It is gauged with high care in neutron-rich nuclei. That trait tracks the slope of the symmetry energy, a key knob in nuclear matter theory.

Relativistic energy functionals carry the chain in two steps. First the polarizability fixes the symmetry slope range. Then that range maps to tidal deformability and radii of neutron stars. The mapped bands tighten the mass-radius plane by a wide margin. They also sit well with pulsar and merger observations. The authors call polarizability a key bridge between tabletop nuclei and city-size stars.
arxiv-2503-17443:
Hossein Hosseinabadi and co-authors offer a simpler way to track open quantum spin systems over time, in work from 2025. Their method builds on the truncated Wigner approach, a tool that treats quantum spins in a near-classical way. They show the tool links closely to a classic noise-driven law for open systems.

The team tests the method on key models, from lasers to driven atom arrays and shared light emission. It runs from early to late times at low cost on plain home hardware. In some models it beats a rival expansion method, and in others it matches it. The authors urge its use as a fast first pass.
arxiv-2503-17743:
Faguo Zhou and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on fast neutron transport sums on graphics chips. The method of characteristics traces neutrons along lines in three dimensions. It is prized for truth and stability, but big cases run slow. Chip memory caps add a second snag.

The team moves line making and line sums onto the chips as the run proceeds. Two more tricks help: lines are preloaded, and work is shared in a balanced way across the chip. Truth of the results stays high. Speed leaps by hundreds of fold against the classic route. The work targets reactor and shield design, where such sums are core.
arxiv-2503-18143:
Yassine Tahraoui studies the small scale turbulence limit of a Fokker-Planck equation in two thousand twenty-five. The equation tracks polymer density in a turbulent flow. Here the fast small scale part of the flow is sent to zero time. Past work took the space scale to zero instead.

Stochastic models of turbulence drive the limit here. For set ranges of the model knobs, the limit density is a generalized Cauchy law. It governs the end to end vector of the polymer. Cases with no density limit are also treated. Weighted energy estimates carry the proof of convergence.
arxiv-2503-19943:
Sakshi Dhankhar, Stefan Wittek, Hamidreza Eivazi, and Andreas Rausch wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a flood forecast model for two German towns, Goslar and Göttingen, in the wake of a harsh flood there in two thousand seventeen.

That flood gave a warning of mere minutes and did wide harm. The model feeds radar rain maps, which show rain across space and time, into a deep net that reads both image and sequence traits. A residual trick handles the bent link between rain and river height. Of note, the model needs no upstream gauge data, so it can move to other towns on the same radar net. Tests show it catches peaks well.
arxiv-2503-22643:
Francesco Versaci and Giovanni Busonera hide network latency in image loading in two thousand twenty-five. GPUs now chew data far faster than networks can feed them. Slow storage stalls deep learning jobs in costly idle time. Local disks near the GPUs get overloaded as a result.

Their plan stores data and metadata in fast NoSQL databases. State of the art loaders plug straight into those stores. Out of order, incremental prefetch hides long network delays. Tests span local, medium, and intercontinental latency links. Throughput held up even across the longest hauls in their runs.
arxiv-2503-23843:
Alberto Vecchiato and five co-authors give a brief account of a core task in star mapping: rebuilding the whole sky of star places from a stream of scans. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A great space mission scans the sky in a set mode, and its data must be solved as one huge, sparse set of equations. The authors sketch the mission's design and the math that flows from its scan mode. They set out the two ways the mission's pipelines now solve the task. They then list known flaws, most of all in fine tuning and in links between unknowns. They close by showing how a path-based way could ease some of these flaws.
arxiv-2503-24343:
Chaussidon and a large team of DESI collaboration co-authors test early dark energy against new sky survey data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses the DESI second data release. Sound wave fossils in galaxy maps measure cosmic expansion. The standard model fits those measures well. Yet its settings clash slightly with microwave background values.

Late-time dark energy tweaks are the usual fix. This team tries an early dark energy ingredient instead. The early component eases the mismatch between the two datasets. It also shifts other cosmic parameters in testable ways. The work widens the menu of explanations for the tension.
arxiv-2504-01243:
Jaskaran Singh Walia, Shravan Venkatraman, and Pavithra LK present FUSION, a deep learning method that cleans up underwater photos. Water dims colors, cuts sight range, and blurs fine detail as light fades with depth. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past methods work mostly in the plain image space. FUSION also uses the wave rate space, which holds broad color spread and long range links. Each color channel is handled at many scales with focus tools in both spaces, then the streams are merged and colors rebalanced. Tests on three known photo sets gave top scores for rebuild truth, felt quality, and boost gauges, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-01943:
Wasi Uddin Ahmad and co-authors published this machine learning paper in 2025. Reasoning models have transformed competitive coding, and a popular recipe distills their skill into smaller student models. Much of that progress hides in private datasets. The team instead built a large, open supervised fine-tuning dataset for coding reasoning, and trained student models of several sizes on it alone.

Their distilled models scored 61.8 percent on LiveCodeBench and 24.6 percent on CodeContests, beating alternatives trained with reinforcement learning. The analysis held surprises. Filtering training data by running the code and keeping only correct solutions actually hurt accuracy. Diversity of instructions mattered more than verified correctness. The authors also studied how efficiently the students use tokens and what reasoning patterns they adopt. Datasets and models are being released openly.
arxiv-2504-02843:
Mario Lino, Tobias Pfaff, and Nils Thuerey sample whole spreads of fluid states with a graph diffusion model, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. One mean flow hides the spread that stats work needs. Their model draws states straight from the settled spread, given mesh and settings.

Graph parts handle wild shapes on loose meshes, where gradients run sharp. A hidden-space diffusion core keeps learning and drawing cheap. Short training runs still taught full spreads well. Wing pressure spreads in rough flow came out true and fast. Readers get flow stats without marathon sims.
arxiv-2504-03243:
Yohsuke Imagi, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on how a class of odd spaces can bend and shift in shape. The spaces are compact Calabi-Yau conifolds, with a set sheaf trait and lone, mild singular points. Past work by two named authors mapped blocks to such shifts in kin cases. Imagi asks where the blocks live for this class.

He proves that, under a shape based term, all blocks to shifts pile up at the singular points. The bulk of the space shifts with ease. Under a second term, shifts that keep the local form fixed meet no blocks at all. The results extend the old picture to this wider class of spaces.
arxiv-2504-03843:
Luis Martinez-Medina, Eloisa Poggio, and Elizabeth Moreno-Hilario wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five mapping the Milky Way's spiral arms in three dimensions through star chemistry. Metal-rich young stars trace where arms lie. The team used a sample of young giant stars from the Gaia mission to build a map of metal excess across the disc.

The map reveals the arms' heights above and below the disc plane, with clear unevenness between the two sides. The Perseus arm's tilt matches the known warp of the galaxy. Most striking is a long, wavy, metal-rich structure that rises and falls in step with a famous chain of star-forming regions called the Radcliffe Wave. The new structure is larger and forms the inner edge of the Local Arm for much of its length.
arxiv-2504-04743:
Lu, Chen, and Xiong built a tool in twenty twenty-five that makes art letter forms in many tongues with fine user control. It moves the style of a guide pic to a letter while it keeps the letter's sense. Past tools can blur fine parts or get strokes wrong.

Their tool fuses font traits into a code for fine shape, and blends text and pic codes for the whole form. A coarse loss term keeps the form true to its base. In tests it made crisp, rich art forms that beat top rivals. The team plans to share the code in the open.
arxiv-2504-06343:
Aakash Kumar, Arnab Rudra, Manav Shah, and Rahul Shaw write a formula for Compton scattering off heavy bosons of any spin. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Compton scattering is the bounce of light off a charged particle. For particles with spin, the maths grow harder as spin rises, and a clean form for all spins was missing.

They give a closed form for the tree-level process, for a fully symmetric, trace-free boson in any number of space ways. Their study rests on the three-point part, which is fixed by low-energy rules and drives soft photon facts. They also set out a gauge for the theory and show it stays sound only for two gauge picks.
arxiv-2504-06443:
Lizhi Xiang, Omid Asudeh, Gerald Sabin, Aravind Sukumaran-Rajam, and Sadayappan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, the last author named with an initial. It speeds up sparse-dense matrix multiplication on the tensor cores of modern GPUs.

Tensor cores chew small dense blocks at vast rates, but filling a sparse matrix with zeros to suit them has mostly lost to plain cores. The team's kernel, cuTeSpMM, answers yes for a broad span of real sparse matrices. A new gauge, TCU-Synergy, reads a matrix's nonzero shape to foretell the gain. For high-synergy matrices the kernel beats the best plain-core code; for low ones it stays close.
arxiv-2504-06843:
Angela Lopez-Cardona, Sebastian Idesis, and Ioannis Arapakis review work that feeds human cognitive signals into language models in a 2025 survey. Eye tracking and related measures record how people read, offering a trace of attention and processing effort. Adding such signals to model training promises help with scarce data and the heavy cost of training large models.

The review covers language models and multimodal systems, sorting advances and applications across the young field. Cognitive signals can guide models toward human-like reading patterns and flag hard passages. The authors close with open problems and directions, including richer signals and fairer evaluation of the claimed gains.
arxiv-2504-08543:
De Leon, Wang, Feng, and Lee use adapter tuning for multilingual emotion detection in a shared task, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Emotion detection is hard in low-resource languages with scarce labeled data. Adapters add few trainable weights while freezing the base multilingual model. The team compares task-only, language-ready, and family-based adapter strategies.

Language-ready task adapters perform best overall across tracks. Strong ranks appear for several African languages, including Tigrinya and Kinyarwanda.
