In one track, the system places third for Amharic and fourth for five other languages. It beats large language models in eleven languages despite far fewer parameters. Cross-lingual transfer survives while compute costs stay low.
arxiv-2504-11643:
Maria Oprea, Alex Townsend, and Yunan Yang wrote a math paper in two thousand twenty-five on random dynamical systems. They set out a new tool, the Distributional Koopman Operator, for work with group-level data only. In such work no one tracks the path of each part, yet staff can still track the group as a whole.

The tool acts on observables of probability distributions and, by way of the transfer operator, moves them forward in time. It extends the stochastic Koopman operator and keeps its linear form and semigroup traits. The authors show that dynamical mode decomposition can converge to the tool when data grow large. The tool thus fits cases where path data are gone but snapshots of the group still exist.
arxiv-2504-11943:
Florian Bridoux, Christophe Crespelle, Thi Ha Duong Phan, and Adrien Richard divide sums of cycles inside the semiring of functional digraphs. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats each functional digraph, one outgoing edge per vertex, as an isomorphism class of finite dynamical systems. Sums and products make these classes a semiring with mysterious arithmetic. Even deciding divisibility lacks a known polynomial algorithm.

When the target is a disjoint union of cycles, the limit behavior of the dynamics, a naive sub-exponential counter lists the quotient candidates. Their divide-and-conquer algorithm improves it to polynomial time whenever the divisor is fixed. The technique is offered as a stepping stone toward the general division problem.
arxiv-2504-14743:
Edelsbrunner, Stephenson, and Thoresen define a new axis for smooth surfaces in space, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The classic medial axis holds points with two closest points on the surface. Their new mid-sphere axis holds points where two saddle points trade partners. The pairing comes from a tool that tracks shape across scales.

The new axis gives a discrete way to find ridge-like lines on a surface. It blends algebra with geometry across many scales at once. As a first test, they give a method that builds a stair-case estimate of the axis. The estimate is rough but shows the idea can be computed. The work may help map thin structures in scans and models.
arxiv-2504-14943:
Dilda Berdikhan and a large team study cloud cloud collision and star formation in two thousand twenty-five. Their region holds molecular clouds that show signs of a crash. Radio telescopes in China caught lines from ammonia and carbon species. Archive data round out the view of the gas.

Signs of collision span matched shapes, U forms, bridges, and V shapes in velocity. Position velocity plots show two gas parts in contact. The crash age fits the ages of young stars in the zone. Filaments feed a dense hub in the squeezed gas. That setup favors the birth of massive stars.
arxiv-2504-16443:
Duy-Tho Le, Trung Pham, Jianfei Cai, and Hamid Rezatofighi introduced MGIoU in twenty twenty-five, a unifying loss for fitting parametric shapes in computer vision. Overlap, measured by intersection over union, is the canonical score, but optimizing it is messy: regression losses ignore it, direct versions are unstable or shape-limited, and each field handcrafts its own fix.

MGIoU projects convex shapes onto their surface normals and computes a one-dimensional normalized overlap there — simple, fast, and fully differentiable. A plus variant handles unstructured convex shapes, and a minus variant penalizes overlap for tasks like collision-free path prediction. On standard benchmarks the losses beat existing ones while computing ten to forty times faster, and they keep clean metric properties like scale invariance.
arxiv-2504-17143:
Bethany Foxon, Sindhu Jammi, and Thomas Fernholz engineer a cleaner microwave transition between trapped atomic states, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The atoms are rubidium eighty-seven dressed by radio-frequency fields, a common setup for cold atom experiments that rely on steady superpositions.

The dressed states shift with the surrounding static magnetic field, and that shift blurs the transition. A single off-resonant microwave field already cancels the part of the shift caused by the nuclear magnetic moment, at least to first order. Adding a second microwave frequency suppresses the field dependence further, as the team demonstrates in the lab. The resulting transition is narrow and far less touchy about field drift. Such a stable link between trappable states is useful across cold atom schemes. It gives experimenters a sharper tool for controlling atoms held in traps.
arxiv-2504-19043:
Connor Jerzak, Priyanshi Chandra, and Rishi Hazra learn clear voting plans from conjoint data, with honest doubt bounds. Their 2025 paper faults the standard scores, which average over rival traits and hide the clash when both sides pick at once. The team learns them offline from randomized preference data. Each plan is a product of chance picks, one per factor level.

The plans seek the best average case, then extend to a two-player minimax game of rival picks. A closed-form optimizer solves a tractable two-way case, and gradient steps cover richer ones. The Delta method carries the doubt to the plan and its value. Primaries and party divergence enter as measured amounts. On a presidential conjoint, these plans yield vote shares in past ranges. Plain averaging plans miss that range.
arxiv-2504-19443:
Yejin Jeong and Donghun Lee built an AI system that grades knee arthritis from X-rays more consistently than human readers often manage. Doctors grade the disease with the Kellgren and Lawrence scale, but grades vary between observers. Their system adapts CLIP, a model that links images with text, so it learns from both the X-ray and written descriptions at once.

Two added training rules push the model to agree with itself: one checks that a flipped copy of the same knee gets the same grade, and one enforces steady predictions. The system reached about 72 percent accuracy, the best reported for the task, beating plain CLIP by more than two points. The authors argue such consistency checks matter for fine-grained medical diagnosis.
arxiv-2504-19743: Jianjun Jin introduces a wider family of Hilbert matrix operators on weighted sequence spaces. His paper, from twenty twenty-five, builds each operator from a positive measure on the unit interval. He proves an exact test, both needed and enough, for when these operators stay bounded. The result extends a recent theorem in the same line, which Jin cites from a twenty twenty-three journal paper.
arxiv-2504-19943:
İsmail Burak Ateş, Şengül Kuru, and Javier Negro organized light-matter Hamiltonians into supersymmetric families in a 2025 paper. The Jaynes-Cummings model, an atom exchanging energy with a single light mode, is quantum optics' basic building block, and its detuning, the mismatch between atom and light frequencies, tunes its behavior. Supersymmetric quantum mechanics pairs Hamiltonians whose spectra nearly coincide, and the authors wield those transformations as bridges between different detunings.

Pairs of Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonians with different detunings turn out to be supersymmetric partners, and the bridges even reach the anti-Jaynes-Cummings variant with its counter-rotating coupling. Whole hierarchies of models follow, their symmetries exposed, including a shape-invariant chain of near-resonant systems. One solved model now unlocks its relatives.
arxiv-2504-20843:
Mishra and five co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a model of atomic nucleus mass rooted in chiral effective field theory, a step-by-step theory of the strong force. The theory gives a force law with eleven dials, called low-energy constants, to fit. Binding energies test such laws hard, since each nucleus binds its parts by a set total.

The team use a Hartree-Fock method to compute binding energies from the law. Fast emulator models let them tune the eleven constants to the energies of eighteen even-even nuclei. They then test the tuned model on 107 even-even nuclei with mass numbers from 16 to 56. The overall miss runs at 3.5 MeV per nucleus on the scale used. The authors offer the model as a base for mass predictions beyond the test set.
arxiv-2504-20943:
Rudnei Ramos and Gabriel Rodrigues re-examine a minimal model of warm inflation, in a two thousand twenty-five cosmology paper. Warm inflation keeps the early universe warm during its rapid expansion, unlike the standard cold picture. The model studied couples an axion-like inflaton to Standard Model gluons, adding no other new fields.

The original analysis used several approximations. Ramos and Rodrigues redo the calculations with WI2easy, a precision tool for warm inflation dynamics. They scan the full parameter range compatible with observations. The earlier conclusions mostly hold. One important change appears in the weak and strong dissipation regimes, where the precise treatment shifts the results significantly. The paper clarifies how much trust the minimal model deserves.
arxiv-2505-02043:
Xinzhu Ma and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on rebuilding CAD models from point clouds. A point cloud is a spray of dots that traces an object's surface. Turning that spray back into an editable design file is a core task in engineering.

Common methods hide the design inside a smooth field, which blurs sharp edges and makes edits hard. Their system, Point2Primitive, predicts the design's basic shapes directly. A transformer decoder treats the shape set as one prediction task. Each primitive stays exact and parametric, ready for a designer to tweak. Tests judge how close the rebuilt models come to the originals.
arxiv-2505-02543:
Dimitris Kallis, Moysis Symeonides, and Marios Dikaiakos benchmarked the energy appetite of an industrial internet-of-things system in a 2025 paper. Factories are filling with connected devices, robotic arms, conveyors, smart cameras, that automate making. Their energy bills are becoming a real operating cost that physics-based models predict poorly. The authors put forth a benchmarking methodology for measuring and analyzing device and application power demands. Then show it on a teaching-scale cyber-real system: a robotic arm, a conveyor belt, a smart camera, and a work out node.

Micro-benchmarks and an end-to-end application generate a rich data set of speed and power readings. Used to train machine learning models that predict energy use from application and system traits. Data-driven energy models, the authors argue, are the useful path to greener industrial automation.
arxiv-2505-05343:
Sooyoung Park, Arda Senocak, and Joon Son Chung teach a vision-language model to find where sounds come from, in a 2025 paper. Their base model, CLIP, was trained to match images with text. The team extends it to audio without giving it any text labels.

Sound clips are first turned into tokens the model's text side can accept, forming audio-based embeddings. These guide a mask that outlines the sounding object in the picture. Image features inside the mask are then pulled toward the audio embedding during training. A second variant learns from a larger model's scene descriptions. Across five tasks the method beat prior leaders and generalized well to new settings. It promises cheaper sound-aware video tools that need no hand labels.
arxiv-2505-05843:
Linda Scheu-Hachtel and Jasmin Zalonis strengthen, in a 2025 paper, a cryptographic tool for learning from private data. Functional encryption lets an analyst compute one approved function of encrypted data and nothing more. A noisy variant also scrambles the answer just enough to guarantee differential privacy. The authors extend the idea to many data holders whose number can change over time, with labels controlling who may run which analysis.

Their concrete scheme, DyNo, covers everything earlier noisy schemes could do. It runs leaner in space and time, and it holds up even when some clients are corrupted, a stronger promise than before. To show the point, they build a privacy-preserving logistic regression protocol on top of it. The paper targets settings like hospitals pooling data, where the math must protect patients while the analysis still gets done.
arxiv-2505-08843:
Marco Corrias and a team of co-authors present a way to clean up microscope images, in two thousand twenty-five. Images from microscopes carry noise and other unwanted signals. Those flaws can hide the fine features that scientists need to see.

The workflow rests on a method that splits an image into parts and removes the unwanted ones. The team tested three forms of the method on images from three kinds of microscope. One form proved the most flexible, while another was best for plain noise removal. Their code is shared as part of a public tool, for use during or after image capture.
arxiv-2505-08943:
Philip Ernst and Oleksii Mostovyi studied the value of partial information in pricing in two thousand twenty-five. They look at a pricing rule for income streams and claims, and ask how it changes when an investor gains insider-type knowledge. Their model allows the risky asset to jump suddenly.

They derive the state price density for three kinds of agents. One knows nothing about the jumps, one knows exactly when each jump will occur, and one has partial knowledge of jump sizes. For each, they characterize the pricing rule and give a formula for it. That lets them quantify how much partial information is worth, and how that worth differs across income streams and claims.
arxiv-2505-09543:
Ram and six colleagues run a learned energy model inside dynamical density theory with no retraining in twenty twenty-five. The theory tracks how particle crowds flow using a free energy rule. Exact rules are out of reach for most real systems. A neural rule learned from still bulk data by pair matching was on hand.

Moved into the moving version, it matched costly particle simulations well. Tests used a three dimensional fluid under tricky outer fields. A flow based extension handled a gas uptake setup drawn from real studies. The route promises cheap, true models of out of balance crowds.
arxiv-2505-10343:
Abril Sahade, Judith Karpen, and Spiro Antiochos report a new kind of solar eruption in twenty twenty-five. Coronal mass ejections and coronal jets are well-studied eruption forms with shared physics. Partial eruptions were known to produce jets. These three events did something different.

The eruptions segmented after they began, and went on to produce coronal mass ejections. Multiwavelength data from three solar observatories let the team rebuild the events in three dimensions. Magnetic field extrapolations showed the filaments lay under pseudostreamer structures. Splitting followed interaction between the filament's flux and external open field at null points. The breakout mechanism seemed to halt the system and split it. Readers meet a hybrid eruption that rewrites what partial eruptions can do.
arxiv-2505-10443:
Pedro Orvalho and Marta Kwiatkowska wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It asks if language models truly reason about code, or guess, by mutating programs in ways that keep their sense but change their dress.

Five such swaps are used: renaming, flipping comparisons, swapping branches, trading loop kinds, and unrolling loops. Nine models, open and closed, are graded on two benchmarks, with experts checking if right calls rest on sound thought. The top closed models lead, but the study finds right calls built on flawed thought in a wide share of cases. Calls flip often under the swaps, with drops that run deep.
arxiv-2505-11143:
William Denault introduces Nash, a regression method that learns how hard to shrink each predictor from side information about that predictor. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Sparse regression picks a few strong signals from many candidates. Flat penalties treat all candidates alike, which wastes structure like grouping or graph links.

Nash feeds each covariate's side information into a neural network that sets its personal penalty. No cross-validation is needed to tune the shrinkage. A split variational Bayes scheme separates prior learning from inference. That split cuts the heavy step to one batched pass, speeding things up hugely. Tests on real data beat existing methods on accuracy and flexibility. Biomedical data, with its many data types, are a natural home.
arxiv-2505-12143:
Arun Kumar and Paul Schrater ask where stable knowledge sits in a learning system. A model must hold some parts fixed as cases change. But it must not lose the facts that a task still needs. They argue that the fixed parts should be set at the level of relations. At that level, sense-making works through links between things.

The authors build groups by closing paths through an abstract space of relations. These groups form the core where knowledge is stored and where learning takes place. Links between groups then carry the shifts that a task calls for. To ground this view, they set out its math base. That base rests on a closed semiring, a structure from relational algebra.
arxiv-2505-15043:
Ze Wang and co-authors present a real-time planner for small flying vehicles in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The planner helps a human operator steer a micro air vehicle through cluttered spaces. It must avoid obstacles without building a full map of the surroundings, and with limited onboard computing.

The method builds a histogram of where obstacles lie around the vehicle and plans a path from that summary. A manager switches planning modes based on obstacle positions. The team validated the system in simulations and indoor flights for a teleoperation task. They also compared it against other planners on a purpose-built simulation platform.
arxiv-2505-15643:
Lan V Truong, writing alone, studies how to find the best option among many noisy choices when several options tie for best. The 2025 paper uses the bandit model, where each choice gives random rewards. The goal is to name a best choice with set confidence while using as few trials as possible.

Past work often assumed the number of best options was unknown. Truong takes the case where that number is known ahead of time. A new lower bound shows the least trials any method needs, and it is tighter than older bounds. A revised stopping rule for a known method meets that bound in the long run. The result is the first proof of that kind for this setting, with clear guidance for trial design.
arxiv-2505-16843:
Kalle Koskinen and Christof Külske study a classic model of magnetism under disorder in this two thousand twenty-five mathematical physics paper. They examine spherical ferromagnets in several dimensions when random magnetic fields act on the spins. Two versions are compared: one where the random fields grow with volume, and one where they do not. The analysis uses metastate frameworks developed by Aizenman and Wehr and by Newman and Stein.

The authors show that the metastates rest on a continuum of random product states, whose weights they describe. For the volume-scaled model, the overlap distribution shows spin-glass traits, including replica symmetry breaking and non-self-averaging behavior. Their proofs rest on concentration estimates, finite-volume Gibbs measure analysis, and the asymptotics of random walks and their spherical projections.
arxiv-2505-17643:
Ketabi and Ramachandram presented this paper in twenty twenty-five on joining two kinds of patient data. Hospitals store structured records, such as lab values and codes, plus free-text notes written at discharge. Models that use records alone can miss the context that notes carry. That gap hurts tasks like predicting whether a patient will return to hospital soon.

The authors train a model that pulls matched record-and-note pairs close together and pushes unmatched pairs apart. The record encoder, once trained this way, feeds standard prediction tasks. For predicting return visits within thirty days, it beat a strong standard model by a clear margin. The work shows that clinical notes can teach record-based tools useful context.
arxiv-2505-18343:
Yash Kumar Atri, Ahmed Alaa, and Tom Hartvigsen present a way to update language models without erasing old knowledge, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Models often hold stale or false facts, yet past edit methods overfit or cause forgetting. Their frame stores facts in a graph set in curved space.

Curved space keeps parent and child facts apart, so an edit to one does not spill onto the other. Updates move through the graph in a shape-safe way. Guards mask key settings and reset parts of the graph net on a cycle. Tests on three data sets showed steadier, more exact edits.
arxiv-2505-18643:
Steven Ndung'u and co-authors present a light-weight way to spot odd radio galaxies, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Radio surveys pour out vast data, and labeled odd cases are rare. Their method reads the shapes of radio sources with tunable filters that pick out set patterns.

An outlier tool then flags sources whose shapes stray from the normal run. No odd examples are needed during training, which solves a key snag. On a benchmark set the method scored above a heavy deep-learning system. The team sees promise for next-generation telescopes, where speed and open discovery matter most.
arxiv-2505-19443:
Ranjan Sapkota, Konstantinos Roumeliotis, and Manoj Karkee compare two styles of AI-assisted coding in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Both lean on large language models, but they split the work between human and machine very differently. Vibe coding keeps the human in a chatty loop; agentic coding hands whole goals to autonomous agents.

The review builds a taxonomy of design, feedback, safety, and debugging across the two styles. Twenty use cases show vibe tools shining in prototypes and teaching, while agents excel at enterprise automation and pipeline work. Hybrid designs that pair chat interfaces with agent back ends are rising. The authors predict success lies in blending both, inside a human-centered process, rather than picking a winner.
arxiv-2505-19943:
Huan Zhang and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on keeping pre-trained models limber as they learn task after task. Most routes freeze the base model and add small plug-ins like prompts. That spares old skill but caps how far the model can bend to new data. Full tuning bends well yet can wreck the base.

Their method, MIST, tunes a sparse slice of the base weights. Picks are guided by a mutual information aim, and random drops thin the flow more. Less than a twentieth of the weights move at all, and far less per step. Added ahead of freeze routes, it lifts scores across many continual tests.
arxiv-2505-22843:
Alexander Herzog, Aliai Eusebi, and Lorenzo Cavallaro argue that malware detectors must prove their confidence, not just their accuracy, in a 2025 paper. Modern tools adapt as malware drifts, and their headline scores look strong. But users act on a model's certainty: unsure cases get human review, while sure ones pass at once.

If certainty does not match real error, budgets burn on useless samples and risky files slip through with high confidence. The authors propose Aurora, a framework that audits a model's confidence for reliability and stability under distribution shift. Its metrics go beyond snapshots to how confidence behaves over time. A detector that cannot say when it is unsure is not trustworthy in use, whatever its score.
arxiv-2505-23243:
Pallis shows how tweaking the kinetic side of a Palatini gravity model rescues simple inflation theories from new data. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Recent measurements from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope tightened the allowed patterns for the early universe's burst of expansion.

Plain power-law inflation models clashed with those results under standard gravity. Adding a non-minimal link between the inflaton field and gravity, plus a matched kinetic mixing, restores the fit. The inflaton stays below the Planck scale, and energies stay within the theory's safe range. The model also embeds into supergravity with two chiral fields and a simple superpotential. A shaped potential term keeps the partner field stable during inflation.
arxiv-2505-23843:
Wenhan Dong and co-authors warn, in a 2025 paper, that current tests of lateral thinking in large language models can fool their own graders. Multi-round tasks with hidden facts are a key test of such thinking. Yet scores from automatic metrics may hide shortcut taking, rigid habits, and giving up too early.

Those hidden flaws make models look stronger than they are and weaken trust in the tests. The authors propose sharper standards for grading. They call for checks on the reasoning path itself, a wider set of scores, and direct comparison with human performance. Better grading, they argue, is needed before test scores can guide real claims about model thinking.
arxiv-2505-24243:
Joohwan Ko and Justin Domke present Model Informed Flows for Bayesian inference in this 2025 paper. Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution with a simpler family. Complex layered models create posteriors with awkward shapes that simple families fit poorly. Flow based families and a reparametrization trick each help in part.

The authors prove the two tricks together equal a certain autoregressive flow with an added shift. That insight guides a new architecture. It adds the shift mechanism, prior information, and the model layer order. Tests on layered and flat benchmark models gave tighter posterior fits. Performance matched or beat the best prior methods. The work turns a theoretical link into a practical inference tool.
arxiv-2505-24543:
Avila and four co-authors retested a basic law of the early universe in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The cosmic microwave background should cool exactly in step with cosmic expansion. The team rebuilt that temperature history from two data sets using Gaussian processes, a flexible statistical method. One set came from galaxy clusters bending the background light.

The reconstruction mostly matched the standard law. At low redshifts, though, hints of deviation reached about two standard deviations. The inferred present-day temperature also sat in mild tension with the precise satellite value. The authors float shifting fundamental constants as one possible cause. They treat the result as a prompt for sharper measurements, not a refutation.
arxiv-2506-00743:
Yeshwanth Venkatesha, Souvik Kundu, and Priyadarshini Panda speed up federated fine-tuning of language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains across many devices without gathering private data. Devices are weak and their data differ, which makes tuning large models costly.

Their method prunes attention heads inside each client model, guided by a confidence-based importance score. A weighted scheme then merges head updates, favoring crucial ones, and a strategy picks which clients join each round. Tests on four data sets reached ninety percent sparsity with under two percent accuracy loss. Communication needs fell and training operations dropped sharply.
arxiv-2506-01843:
Jonas Eidesen studies quantum error-correcting codes through a new mathematical lens, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Stabilizer codes and Clifford codes protect quantum information from noise. Their structure is usually described case by case.

Eidesen defines projective error models, which let representation theory organize both code families uniformly. He also introduces a third class, called weak stabilizer codes. Relationships among the three classes are worked out. The obstruction to a nontrivial stabilizer code turns out to be a class in group cohomology. Similar obstructions are found for weak stabilizer codes. For nice error bases, he characterizes exactly when a Clifford code is a weak stabilizer code. Two infinite families of non-stabilizer Clifford codes follow.
arxiv-2506-02743:
Thi Nhung Dao, Martin Gabelmann, and Margarete Mühlleitner compute corrections, in a 2025 preprint, to how the Higgs boson couples to itself in an extended model. The model is the next-to-minimal supersymmetric one, fitted with an inverse seesaw to give neutrinos their tiny masses. The Higgs self-coupling shapes the Higgs potential and future collider signals. The team adds one-loop corrections plus the biggest two-loop pieces. The treatment is applied to the Higgs mass, so the two stay consistent.

The new neutrino and sneutrino sectors leave marks. Effects reach about ten percent on the self-coupling of the standard-like Higgs. The Higgs mass shifts by up to four and a half percent. These numbers hold at points that pass all current data checks. The corrections also feed into decays of heavy Higgs states to lighter ones. Everything is coded into a public program.
arxiv-2506-02943:
Xu, Wang, Briand, and Liu built a tool in twenty twenty-five that writes code tests on its own with help from smart chat models. Hand-made tests for Java code take much time and care. Old auto tools check code acts but not what the code should do.

Their tool, CANDOR, splits the work among set chat agents that draft full tests as a team. A panel of such models talks through the right test answers to cut false claims. In trials it matched a top old tool on code reach and beat it on fault finds. It also beat a tuned rival on right test answers by a clear gap.
arxiv-2506-03143:
Qianhui Wu and co-authors presented GUI-Actor in 2025, a way for software agents to find the right spot on a screen. An agent that clicks and types must first ground a plan: pick the patch of screen where the act belongs. Most methods make the model spell out number pairs for the spot, a poor fit for coarse visual features and vague targets.

GUI-Actor skips the numbers. A small added head learns to match a special token against all patches of the screen at once, offering one or more candidate zones in a single pass. A checker then grades the candidates and picks the best. On screen tests, the method beat prior bests and held up on new screen sizes. A small model of theirs even topped a far larger rival, and training just the new head proved enough.
arxiv-2506-03443:
Ali Salloum and four co-authors study politics and polarization on the social platform Bluesky in a 2025 paper. Political talk now spreads across many fragmented platforms, each with its own users and algorithms. The team collected all platform activity from December 2024 to May 2025 and mapped political topics in English language posts.

About thirteen percent of posts touched politics, led by international conflicts, United States politics, and social technology debates. Structural polarization was high on several topics. Yet the most polarized topics were lopsided: the smaller side held only one to two percent of users. The authors find Bluesky users more politically uniform than on older platforms, even as familiar narratives repeat.
arxiv-2506-03643:
Lingjun Mao and four co-authors argue that images deserve labels in proportion to what they hold in a 2025 paper. Most vision encoders squeeze every image into the same fixed count of tokens, the chunks a model reads. A cluttered room and a blank wall get the same budget, which wastes effort on simple scenes and starves rich ones.

Their encoder, DOVE, gives each image a variable count of tokens sized to its content. It rebuilt images faithfully while using far fewer tokens on average, and its features beat rival tokenizers on probe tests and mixed media tasks. A second version takes a text query and spends its tokens on the parts the query asks about. Code and trained models are shared openly.
arxiv-2506-03843:
Fatemeh Taherasghari and Clifford Will work out how pairs of compact objects move in an altered theory of gravity, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The theory, Einstein-Aether gravity, adds a fixed time-like vector field to spacetime. The pairs in question are black holes or neutron stars in tight orbits. Such systems lose energy as gravitational waves, which slowly shrinks the orbit.

The authors derive the motion equations to high precision, reaching the order where radiation reaction shows up. They build on field solutions from a companion paper. The method tracks both gravity and the aether field near the pair. Their formulas match the order used for standard gravity tests. Waveform builders can use them to test whether real signals fit this rival theory.
arxiv-2506-05543:
Sethuraman and a team of colleagues introduced FRAME in twenty twenty-five, a video encoder trained to support dense prediction tasks such as tracking objects and labeling each pixel. Image encoders miss how scenes change over time. Existing video models, in turn, often trail image models on fine detail tasks.

FRAME learns by predicting present and future image features from past and present frames. The teacher features come from a strong image model, giving precise, stable targets. The encoder also aligns a summary token with a language-image model, enabling tasks such as video classification. Across six tasks and seven datasets, FRAME beat image encoders and prior video models. It stays compact, the authors note, suiting many downstream uses.
arxiv-2506-06243:
Benjamin Smith, Jianhui Gao, and Jessica Gronsbell build fairmetrics, a software pack for the R language that grades how fair a learning model is across groups. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A model can be right on the whole yet bent against a group set by race, sex, or age. Such bias can lock in the gaps of the world. The pack grades many group fairness marks at once. They span three views: that outcomes stand apart from the group, that errors match across groups, and that a score means the same in each group. It gives both point marks and ranges, through one plain call, on health data used as a case.
arxiv-2506-06643:
Moushumi Medhi and Rajiv Ranjan Sahay estimate scene depth from a single blurred photo. Their paper appeared in 2025. Judging depth from blur usually needs several shots taken with different focus settings. One shot leaves the task underdetermined, so few teams have tried it. The authors add a second clue: the dark channel, a measure of the darkest values in small patches of the image.

Blur softens contrast in a way that depends on distance, and the dark channel captures local contrast and structure. Joining the two cues lets their program infer depth from one image. The program is trained end to end with a rival-network setup. Tests on real photos showed the added cue gives meaningful depth maps. The method could help phones and small cameras that can take only one shot.
arxiv-2506-08043:
Ashkan Shahbazi and co-authors predict soft tissue bends in real time by wedding neural nets to a physics kernel, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Full physics solvers are too slow for live surgery tools. Pure data nets stray into shapes flesh cannot take.

Kelvinlet priors, drawn from classic force math, seed the nets with true bend shapes. Big solver datasets teach the rest, for one or many graspers. Across net builds, truth and bend shape both improved. Tests used standard keyhole grasp tools on hard tasks. Readers get a physics-aware tissue sim fast enough to steer by.
arxiv-2506-08243:
Zhenjiang Mao, Artem Bisliouk, Rohith Reddy Nama, and Ivan Ruchkin grade the confidence of reasoning models over time in a 2025 study. Language models answering math problems step by step often sound sure even when wrong. In classrooms that false confidence is risky, since learners may not spot the error.

Their framework treats confidence at each step as a signal unfolding in time. Rules written in a temporal logic language state what healthy confidence patterns look like. Robustness scores against those rules give structured, readable confidence estimates. Reshaping strategies then push model confidence toward the stated rules during evaluation.
arxiv-2506-09143:
M Siudek led a large team hunting black holes by full-spectrum fitting in a 2025 paper. Active galactic nuclei are usually found by X-rays, radio waves, infrared colors, or emission lines, and each route catches a different subset. Their study fit the whole light distribution of galaxies from a big survey and flagged likely hosts by the active fraction. The method recovered most line-selected and infrared-selected cases.

Adding clean infrared data cut contamination by star-forming galaxies sharply. Half the new candidates escaped all standard methods, yet extra checks classified most of them, often as faint or retired systems. The authors say fitting completes the census.
arxiv-2506-09743:
Nicolas Renaud presents software that lets neural networks help write molecular wavefunctions inside quantum Monte Carlo runs. The package is built on a mainstream deep learning library, so it is built for graphics hardware. Users can slot machine learning parts, such as neural backflow changes and flexible correlation factors, into the trial wavefunction. Links to two known quantum chemistry codes supply starting orbitals and exponents. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Renaud tunes wavefunctions for four small molecules, from hydrogen to carbon monoxide.

Breaking curves and the forces along them were worked out for each one. The results agree well with baselines and recover a large share of the correlation energy. The aim is rapid trials: new wavefunction ideas can be put together, tested, and checked quickly in one place.
arxiv-2506-10543:
Luiz Tizei and eight co-authors measure light absorption in nanowires of an unusual crystal form in a 2025 paper. Silicon and germanium usually crystallize in a cubic pattern, but a hexagonal diamond form could serve future lasers and quantum devices. Its light handling was unexplored, so the team combined electron microscopy, energy loss spectroscopy, and first principles simulation.

The wires, grown as branches inside the microscope, were nearly perfect single crystals, letting the team read their true optical response. Hexagonal silicon absorbed visible light more strongly than the cubic form, with a marked rise above a certain energy. Hexagonal germanium absorbed near one electron volt but showed no clear feature at its direct band edge, matching theory. The work links crystal structure to optical behavior.
arxiv-2506-10943:
Adam Zweiger and five co-authors let a language model rewrite itself in twenty twenty-five. Language models are powerful but static: their weights never change after training. New tasks and knowledge must be crammed into prompts. Their framework, SEAL, lets a model adapt its own weights instead.

Given a new input, the model generates a self-edit. An edit may restructure the information, set optimization hyperparameters, or call data augmentation tools. Supervised fine-tuning on those edits produces lasting weight updates. A reinforcement learning loop trains the model to make good edits. The reward is the updated model's downstream performance. No separate adaptation module is needed, since the model's own generation steers the change. Readers get a step toward models that learn continually from experience.
arxiv-2506-11243:
Santiago Góngora and a team of co-authors test how far small language models can go in grading tutor responses, in two thousand twenty-five. Their team joined a shared task on evaluating artificial intelligence tutors. They limited themselves to models under one billion parameters, to mirror labs in the Global South where computing power is costly.

Across five tracks, their models stayed within a modest gap of the winning teams. The smallest gap was about six points and the largest about thirteen, on the organizers' strict score. All their models can run on a cheap graphics card or even without one. The authors conclude that small models are competitive for tutor evaluation under tight budgets.
arxiv-2506-11943:
Amy Wayland, David Alonso, and Matteo Zennaro forecast how outside data can rescue cosmic shear measurements in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Weak lensing surveys map dark matter, but gas physics muddies the small-scale signal. Tracers of hot gas around clusters could calibrate that muddiness.

Using mock data for a future flagship survey, the authors ask how tightly the gas model must be pinned down. Key parameters need ten to twenty percent precision to keep lensing results intact. X-ray data from about five thousand clusters should reach that bar for hot gas content. The harder part, tracking ejected gas, needs sensitive microwave background data from a next-generation experiment. The forecast maps a route to self-calibrated lensing cosmology.
arxiv-2506-12243:
Lobo and co-authors ask whether a quantum clock can tell rival theories of gravity apart in two thousand twenty-five. Metric theories differ in set constants that tweak how mass bends space and time. A quantum clock that moves slowly through a weak field ends in a state shaped by those constants.

Quantum state tests can then sort the theories. The authors show that a single detection can rule out one named theory, and can split two theories with certainty. Success odds hinge on four factors: the gap in proper time between the two states, the clock's energy gap, path length, and speed. Long-lived nuclei such as thorium look best as clocks, and using many clocks at once lifts the odds further.
arxiv-2506-13543: Ofer Gabber and Shizhang Li proved a result in 2025 for families of varieties over a p-adic ring of integers. For a smooth proper family, they show the crystalline torsion in its cohomology can be controlled using its étale torsion. The control also draws on the cohomological degree and the ramification. The technical heart is a boundedness theorem for annihilator ideals of a certain torsion in Breuil-Kisin prismatic cohomology. The authors note that this result may be of independent interest.
arxiv-2506-13943:
Andy López-Oquendo, Joseph Hora, David Trilling, and Howard Smith commission an upgraded infrared camera on near-Earth asteroids in two thousand twenty-five. Heat glow reads an asteroid's size and reflectivity well, but ground infrared tools have thinned as upkeep grew hard. The MIRSI camera at the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility was rebuilt to help fill the gap.

First science runs reached out to twelve and a half microns. Forty-two looks at thirty-one near-Earth objects yielded sizes and albedos, with a paired optical camera fixing brightness at the same moment. The team also sized debris from the Didymos impact hours and days after the DART strike. A coming flyby target of Japan's Hayabusa2 mission got its measures too.
arxiv-2506-14043:
Nathaniel Hermann and Shane Hutson present analytic solutions for anomalous diffusion problems, in a two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Diffusion is the spread of mass from place to place. It shows up all through physics and engineering. In many real materials that spread is anomalous. It obeys fractional rules, not the plain rules of the old books.

Past work leaned on computer runs or on hard special functions. Hermann and Hutson give closed-form solutions for the time-fractional cases that come up most. Their answers use Mittag-Leffler and M-Wright functions. They also use generalized fractional error functions that they work out in the paper. They show this kind of spread can be seen as a two-parameter stretched-time process. A hands-on method then turns classic Fickian solutions into anomalous ones. The paper is the first in a planned series.
arxiv-2506-14543:
Bosco Garcia-Archilla, Alicia Garcia-Mascaraque, and Julia Novo wrote this numerical analysis paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on speeding up simulations of spread-and-react processes. Full simulations of such partial differential equations can be huge, so engineers compress them with reduced order models built from snapshots.

Most past error work assumed the simplest time stepping, implicit Euler. This paper studies backward differentiation formulas of orders one through five as the time engine for the reduced model. The authors prove the error shrinks at the matching optimal rate in time. Their snapshots come from finite element runs and are fed in as first-order difference quotients, a choice that is key to pointwise error bounds. The result widens the menu of proven time steppers for reduced models.
arxiv-2506-15543:
Hristo Papazov and Nicolas Flammarion wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It extends a classic theory of learning in the limit, asking what a learner can grasp when it can also watch how a program runs, not just what it prints.

Gold's framework asks which function classes a learner can pin down from endless examples. Plain input-output views cannot crack the class of all computable functions. The authors add time-bound views and views of an agent's action path. With cost caps, or rough time bounds, the wall falls. Learning from action paths turns out to match learning rational functions from inputs and outputs. A hard note closes the work: no neat test sets exist for fast functions, even with path views.
arxiv-2506-18943:
Andrew Kiruluta and Priscilla Burity rebuild vision-language models without two costly parts, in work from 2025. Most such models lean on convolutions to read images and on self-attention to fuse words and images, both heavy at scale. Their model swaps in a spectral dictionary mixer, which codes each patch or word bit as a sparse mix of wave atoms.

The billion-scale test model scored near top marks on image caption tests and fair marks on visual questions. It closed most of the gap to a strong rival while using far fewer weights, less memory, and faster runs. The shared wave code also makes word-image links clear to inspect.
arxiv-2506-19443:
Jian-Rong Li and Ayush Kumar Tewari connect two areas of algebra and geometry in this two thousand twenty-five paper. On one side stands the Grassmannian cluster algebra, with a prized basis called the dual canonical basis. Its elements match certain tables of numbers, called Young tableaux. On the other side stands a geometric shape, the hypersimplex, which can be cut into pieces in patterned ways. A map from earlier work links the two sides.

The authors show that each tableau induces one of these patterned cuts. For the smallest case, they prove the link is exact: certain prime tableaux match the coarsest cuts. Computer evidence extends the pattern to larger cases. They also guess a formula for counting the finest cuts. The paper deepens the tie between algebra and polyhedral geometry.
arxiv-2506-19743:
Shenbin Qian and co-authors shrink product search embeddings by nesting them, so stores can search huge catalogs faster. Their 2025 paper names the twin demands on shopping search: understand messy user queries and still answer in real time across millions of items. Large embeddings help accuracy but slow every lookup.

Their nested design lets one trained model serve at several embedding sizes, with the smallest running far more cheaply at query time. Training cost stays unchanged, and accuracy improved across several transformer encoders in their tests. The team checked the method under two training losses and on four test sets with hard cases like short, vague queries. Efficiency without an accuracy tax is rare in retrieval, and shops feel both sides daily.
arxiv-2506-20543:
Sanne van Kempen, Jaron Sanders, Fiona Sloothaak, and Maarten Wolf test a learning method for routing work in skill-based queues. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Such queues run call centers, data centers, and cloud services. Each job needs a server with the right skill. A recent reinforcement learning algorithm promised near-optimal routing, but only in theory so far.

The team runs the method on a real-world dataset as a case study. It learns fast and adapts when conditions change. It also beats fixed benchmark rules. A new heuristic rule added by the authors cuts delays further. The method can balance several goals at once, such as profit, fair server load, and shorter waits. The results suggest it could run live.
arxiv-2506-22943:
Siyun Liang and six co-authors raised the rate of a meaning-compressed transmission through a fluid antenna, in a paper published in 2025. Meaning-based sends ship the gist of data, not each bit, to save bandwidth. Their base station holds still antennas; the user holds one whose ports can switch on in a grid, near the base. Three dials must be tuned as one: the beam shape, the compression rate, and the port choices.

Their alternating method tunes each in turn. At each step the best compression rate falls out in closed form. Simulation runs support the gains of the method under a set power limit. The team presents fluid antennas as a gain for gist sends in tight near fields.
arxiv-2506-23543:
Hui Li and co-authors speed up image generation by changing how it is chopped into tokens as it is cleaned from noise. Diffusion transformers split the image into patches, and the patch size sets how many tokens the model must process. The design uses one patch size throughout. Their method, PPFlow, uses large patches early, when the image is noisy, and small patches late, when detail forms. A separate learned projection handles each patch size.

The approach works on the full image representation and needs no re-noising. Trained from scratch, it ran about one and a half to two times faster than a comparable model at similar image quality. Starting from a pre-trained model did even better with little extra training. The authors release code and a trained checkpoint. The savings matter because these models are slow and costly to run.
arxiv-2507-01443: Schmidt and Umeda check how grid Dirac math tools near their smooth kin in this twenty twenty-five paper. The grid tools live on cube nets in three-space, while the smooth kin rule free mote flow in the same frame. They prove the grid tools do draw close to the smooth ones in the strong sense, yet not in the stricter norm sense.
arxiv-2507-03643:
Jackson and five co-authors wrote this paper in twenty twenty-five on dust devils. These spinning dust columns occur on both Earth and Mars. A devil's width sets how much dust it lifts into the air. Yet what fixes a devil's width, and how widths are spread across a population, has stayed unclear.

The authors propose that widths follow a power law tied to a simple physical picture. Fits to several published Mars datasets support that form. They also model devils as heat engines. From that model, the number of devils per unit area scales with their efficiency and the heat flowing from the ground. The results help estimate how much dust devils add to the air of both planets.
arxiv-2507-04643:
Oleg Titov estimates the instantaneous Earth rotation velocity direct in two thousand twenty-five. Very long baseline interferometry tracks Earth with distant radio sources. Its standard reads are group delay and fringe frequency. Group delay serves most geodesy work, while fringe frequency sits ignored.

Titov shows fringe frequency can gauge spin speed on its own. Thirty years of routine data feed daily estimates from it. Two pole angles come out day by day with tiny formal error. Plain least squares does the analysis on the big network data. The series can track spin wobble beside classic length of day values.
arxiv-2507-04743:
Manuel de León and Rubén Izquierdo-López extend a classic tool of physics. Poisson brackets describe how quantities change in mechanics, and they sit at the heart of field theories as well. The authors build a theory of extensions for graded versions of these brackets, set inside graded Dirac manifolds, a layered geometric frame that mixes smooth structure with algebra.

They then show what the extension buys. The field equations of a chosen theory fall out of the bracket setup, and so does the time behavior of forms of any order built on the field. The result mirrors the role plain brackets play in mechanics, where one bracket generates the motion of the whole system. The paper is pure theory, aimed at giving field theory a cleaner geometric base.
arxiv-2507-05443:
Ashwin Rao, Sze Yuh Nina Wang, and Kristina Lerman study gender gaps in online talk about reproductive rights. Their 2025 paper draws on millions of posts on a major social platform after a landmark United States court ruling on abortion in 2022. The ideological split on abortion is well known, but how gender and place interact was less clear.

Using inferred traits of posters, they find gender shapes attitudes and emotional tone beyond ideology alone. The gap between men and women grew wider in conservative regions. A leaked draft of the ruling spurred a surge in posting, led by pro-abortion women in places where access was under threat. The study shows public talk in a crisis is structured by identity and place, not party lines alone.
arxiv-2507-06243:
Md Nahid Hasan, Md Monzur Murshed, Md Mahadi Hasan, and Faysal Ahmed Chowdhury build machine learning models that predict which breast cancer treatment a patient is likely to get. Choice of treatment is made hard by the varied nature of the disease. Choices rest on many factors tied to each patient. The study uses The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer clinical data set.

The models predict the chance of chemotherapy or hormonal therapy. They are trained with five-fold cross-validation. They are gauged on accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, sensitivity, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating curve. Bootstrap methods gauge model doubt, while SHAP values aid reading by naming key predictors. Among the models tested, gradient boosting hit the highest stable scores. It beat two other boosting methods.
arxiv-2507-06743: Dorin Popescu gives a short account of a special case of Zariski's uniformization theorem in prime characteristic, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The note is mainly an exposition. It treats extensions of valuation rings seen as a filtered union of smooth algebras. That view is the core of the uniformization claim in this setting.
arxiv-2507-06843:
Neeraj Kumar Tomar and co-authors add new separation axioms to topology. Topology studies spaces through their open sets, and separation axioms say how well points and sets can be told apart. The authors build two new families from special kinds of open sets. One family rests on sets they call SC-star open, and the other on H-star open sets.

The first family holds four kinds of spaces, in strong and weak forms. The second family holds three kinds, marked with subscripts from the classic scale. The authors prove basic traits of each new kind and show how they relate. Such sorting helps map the fine ladder of space types that pure math uses.
arxiv-2507-07243:
Kyle Celano leads a team of seven on this combinatorics paper from two thousand twenty-five. It counts parking functions where each car stops at most a fixed steps past its wished-for spot.

A parking function's displacement counts how far each car must drive on. The team sorts these ℓ-interval functions by inversion, displacement, and major index. For the tightest case they find a cyclic sieving effect at fixed displacement. Closed forms count that case by inversion count. They also show a classic map of Foata keeps the set intact just at the extremes of ℓ. There, inversion and major index turn out to be spread alike.
arxiv-2507-07543:
Chen Amiraz and four co-authors study why retrieval-augmented generation systems falter when a user's question and the document that answers it are written in different languages. Their paper came out in 2025. The test setting pairs Arabic and English, using real corporate documents rather than the open web.

Every combination of question language and document language was tried. Performance dropped substantially whenever the two languages differed. The failure sits in the retrieval step itself: the retriever ranks foreign-language documents badly, so the generator never sees the right page. Two simple fixes helped a lot: force equal retrieval from both languages, or translate the question first. The authors say cross-language retrieval deserves direct attention in practical systems.
arxiv-2507-08543:
Jianhao He and John Lui give quantum algorithms for sparse optimization in twenty twenty-five. The problem is projection-free convex optimization with sparsity constraints. It covers many tasks in machine learning and data science. The authors treat both vector and matrix domains.

For vectors, two quantum algorithms find near-optimal solutions with fewer queries than the best classical method. The savings reach a factor tied to the square root of the dimension, or even the full dimension. For matrices under nuclear norm constraints, two more algorithms speed up the update step. Their gains also scale with dimension. Sparsity here means most entries stay zero, which keeps solutions simple. Readers get quantum speedups for a workhorse optimization family.
arxiv-2507-08843:
Arpita Soni and co-authors propose a way to predict where a person will go next without taking their data off their device. Their 2025 paper joins federated learning, which trains models locally, with large language models. Location data is deeply personal, so central storage is a privacy risk.

Their system keeps user data on the device and uses a compact product trick to tap language model skill. It was tested on four public movement data sets drawn from location-sharing services. Scores led the field on each set, the authors report. The system also cut model size and memory use by large shares. The work speaks to app builders who want useful forecasts for maps and transport without pooling raw traces.
arxiv-2507-08943:
Pedro Lopes, Paola Accioly, Paulo Borba, and Vitor Menezes compare two ways teams use Git, the code tracking tool, to build software. One way keeps many side branches with set roles, while the other sends all changes to one shared branch. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Branch based flow, with GitFlow as the best known case, moves code from lone branches toward the main branch as it matures. Trunk based flow skips those steps. The authors gather proof on how developers in Brazil work with each flow and what helps or blocks each one. Their aim is to guide teams that must trade speed against code quality.
arxiv-2507-09743:
Riano Giribaldi and five co-authors ask how evenly the early Milky Way was enriched with new elements. Their twenty twenty-five paper looks at the oldest, most metal-poor stars in the galaxy's halo. Stars born then carry the chemical marks of the first rounds of star death.

Many past charts show wide scatter in the ratio of magnesium to iron for these stars. That scatter was read as proof that early enrichment was patchy. With sharper measures of the stars and modern 3D models, the team finds the spread is narrow in a key range. Their read: the early enrichment in magnesium was more uniform than thought.
arxiv-2507-11143:
Lam Pham and eight co-authors build a neural network that spots and outlines landslides in satellite imagery. Landslides are growing more frequent with extreme weather and land misuse, yet watching for them over huge, rugged areas is hard for people. An automatic system could scan remote sensing images as they arrive.

Their architecture, RMAU-NET, adds residual blocks and multi-head attention to a U-Net design. It handles both detection and pixel-level segmentation in one model. On three benchmark datasets the system posted strong F1 and overlap scores. The authors present it as an end-to-end tool for monitoring landslide events over large terrain.
arxiv-2507-11343:
Farhan Shah and a large team analyze light pollution across the northern Netherlands in this two thousand twenty-five report. They draw on a network of sky quality meters that track night sky brightness. Data span from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-three. The team joined the ground readings with satellite cloud data. Their region also covers part of the German Wadden Coast.

They ranked yearly brightness changes at twenty-seven sites. In the darkest areas, sky glow is growing by roughly three to seven percent per year. Clouds matter, since they bounce city light back down and brighten the sky. The report tracks this indirect form of light pollution in detail. Its findings can guide local policy to protect dark skies and the species that need them.
arxiv-2507-11543:
Iman Reihanian, Yunfei Hou, Yu Chen, and Yifei Zheng review how tools that make text and code are used in teaching computer science. Their review, from two thousand twenty-five, centers on truth, real work, and fair tests.

The tools speed work and aid fresh ideas by students. Yet they can state false things with ease, spread errors, hold bias, and blur the line between a student's work and the tool's. The authors stress that human eyes must stay in the loop. The works they read urge mixed tests that join tool and human marks, tools to spot bias, and skill in the use of such tools for both students and staff.
arxiv-2507-13343:
Yushu Wu and a team of co-authors make mobile video generation practical in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion transformers make strong videos, but they cost too much computing for a phone. On-device generation is even harder than running such models on big machines. The team offers a chain of optimizations to close that gap.

First, a highly compressed autoencoder shrinks the input data without hurting visual quality. Second, a pruning strategy guided by knowledge distillation cuts the model to mobile size. It is careful to spare the parts that matter most. Third, a step distillation method tailored to these transformers cuts the steps needed. Readers get a path to real-time video generation in seconds on a handset.
arxiv-2507-16343:
Pengfei Cai and co-authors build a sound detector that can find events named in words or shown by example clips, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most detectors know only a fixed list of sounds. Their model, DASM, treats detection as matching sound frames against query vectors from text or audio prompts.

One decoder branch decides which events are present, while a context branch pins down when each event runs. A masking trick at test time uses kinship between known and new classes to boost new-class skill. Scores beat language-based rivals on a strong public set and topped a trained baseline on a second set. Readers get open-list sound search that still times events well.
arxiv-2507-17643: Song, Xie, and Yang study maps of projective varieties and the orbits of points under them. They prove that the arithmetic degree of a point with a dense orbit must be a cohomological Lyapunov multiplier of the system. They then apply that result to draw a consequence for the dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture.
arxiv-2507-18643:
Syeda Tasnim Fabiha, Rubaiyat Jahan Mumu, Farzana Aktar, and Mainul Hossain model share prices on the Dhaka Stock Exchange, starting from what drives market liquidity. Investors favor liquid shares, and liquidity hangs on average share price. The authors ask which factors move that price, and how well simple models capture it.

A thorough linear regression analysis came first, with each factor's individual contribution to price variability identified and explained. A random forest model then outperformed the linear model on the comparison metrics they used. One negative finding stands out: the time series data alone could not support a predictive linear model. The paper separates explanation from forecasting in the Bangladeshi market.
arxiv-2507-21243:
Christopher Hill worked out quantum corrections to an other theory of the Higgs boson in 2025. In top quark condensation, the Higgs is not elementary but a bound state of top quarks and antiquarks, held by a new strong force carried by particles called colorons. A recent semiclassical treatment pictured the Higgs as an extended object with a mass scale of several trillion electron volts. Hill's paper asks whether that picture survives its own quantum loops.

Using source and Legendre transform methods and summing the leading fermion loops in a large-color-number limit through an auxiliary field. He derives the semiclassical theory as a working action from the underlying model. The theory stays natural, needing only a few percent of fine-tuning, and the loops substantially strengthen the working four-fermion coupling over the basic coloron coupling. A relatively weak underlying topcolor force, he concludes, can still bind the Higgs.
arxiv-2507-23243:
Sang-Eon Lee, Minkyu Park, and colleagues trace a change of regime in the Hall response of a magnetic layered crystal in a 2025 physics study. The anomalous Hall effect bends charge flow sideways in a magnet without any applied field, and its size can come from the electrons' geometric phase or from scattering off disorder. In clean crystals of this iron gallium telluride, the conductivity is large and steady.

Raising disorder drives a crossover between regimes, which the authors track experimentally. Knowing which mechanism rules at which cleanliness tells materials growers whether to purify or to roughen a sample for spintronic use.
arxiv-2508-00043:
Nhut Truong and Uri Hasson ask how a net forced to copy the brain's map changes what it learns. Such nets set units on a grid, like brain skin. Two loss rules vie here. Weight similarity fines grid mates whose in-weight lists diverge. Activation similarity fines mates whose reply shapes diverge. Both rules act on a grid layer just prior to the last one.

Weight similarity grew smooth maps with linked grid mates. Activation similarity made a two-hump link shape with no smooth map. Both nets stood up to weight nudges more well than plain nets. Each helped with one kind of image harm. Weight similarity also honed how keen each unit was and where skills sat, and expert units for set classes came out. The match shows a brain-like map is not one act but a range. The loss you pick rewrites the end state.
arxiv-2508-02343:
Wenyuan Liu and five co-authors squeeze large language models into mixed low-precision formats tuned for new Nvidia chips. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents MicroMix. Quantization swaps heavy matrices for light ones to speed inference. Stock kernels speak integer formats, while the Blackwell tensor cores favor floating microscaling forms. That mismatch wastes the new hardware's speed.

MicroMix pairs a quantization scheme with a custom matrix kernel. The kernel mixes several microscaling widths channel by channel. Thresholds flag values where low width would cost too much accuracy. Those channels get a higher width, the rest stay lean. On Llama and Qwen models, scores stay near full precision at a lean mean width. One large Qwen build lost no accuracy on its tests. Speed on laptop and desktop cards beat the vendor's stack.
arxiv-2508-02543:
Guillaume Quispe, Pierre Jouvelot, and Gérard Memmi design a signature scheme that lets group members sign anonymously yet transfer their signing identity safely, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Group signatures hide which member signed, except from a chosen auditor. A newer trick lets anyone mint fresh identities for a user, which only the recipient can trace.

Their scheme, nicknamed NGS, fuses the two so anonymous transfers stay auditable, curbing abuse. They spell out a security model and give a construction proven safe in a standard model of random oracles. As a proof of use, they built NickHat, a token-exchange prototype on the Ethereum blockchain.
arxiv-2508-03643:
Xiangyu Sun and ten co-authors rebuild three-dimensional scenes, meaning included, from a handful of photos with unknown camera positions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Older pipelines split shape rebuilding from meaning labeling, or tuned each scene at great cost, limiting their reach.

Their system, Uni3R, runs in one forward pass. A cross-view transformer fuses information across the images, then predicts a cloud of 3D Gaussian blobs carrying semantic features. The same representation renders fresh viewpoints, labels scene parts in open vocabulary, and estimates depth. It set new benchmark marks on standard indoor and street datasets. The authors present it as a step toward one general model for 3D understanding.
arxiv-2508-03843:
The-Anh Vu-Le and four co-authors audit a popular family of network clustering tools in a 2025 paper. Stochastic block models sort graph nodes into communities that should be both dense and well connected. Earlier checks found that leading tools can return communities that are internally split in two.

The team tests more software for the same flaw, including nested model variants, across real and synthetic networks. Every method produced some disconnected communities, though one leading package beat its rival. The study explains why the flaw arises and revisits a repair that trims weak bridges and re-sorts the pieces. Their message to network scientists is blunt: a community that falls apart when drawn is not a community, whatever the fit score says.
arxiv-2508-04643:
Dengke Qu, Quan Lin, Lei Xiao, Xiang Zhan, and Peng Xue certify indefinite causal order in an experiment reported in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum mechanics allows events to unfold in a blend of orders, not just one sequence. Past demos of this effect trusted the lab devices involved.

Their test uses entangled photons split across space, one acting as the control in a quantum switch. From measurement statistics alone, a causal inequality was broken by twenty-four standard deviations. No assumptions about the devices were needed, echoing how Bell tests certify nonlocality. The authors call it device-independent proof that causal order can be indefinite. The result opens a path to using such order as a certified quantum resource.
arxiv-2508-04843:
Shou proposes a unified flow matching method for forecasting long runs of timed events. Such sequences matter in health care, finance, and user behavior data. Standard neural models predict one event at a time, which is slow and lets errors pile up. The new method models gaps between events and event types jointly. It uses flows for both the continuous times and the discrete types. That joint design skips step-by-step decoding.

Generated event paths stay coherent over long horizons. Tests on six real-world benchmarks compared it with stepwise and diffusion rivals. The method improved both accuracy and generation speed. It offers a fresh base for long-range event forecasting.
arxiv-2508-06343:
Blažej and co-authors study fair division of indivisible goods in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. The goods sit on a graph, and each person's bundle must form a connected piece of it. Fairness is judged by the maximin share, the best a person can guarantee by splitting the goods themselves.

A perfectly fair split may not exist, so the team looks for near-fair ones that give each person a fixed fraction of that share. Such splits are known for some graph types but not for all graphs. The authors prove they exist for several more classes, including block graphs, cacti, complete multipartite graphs, and split graphs.
arxiv-2508-08843:
Bhat, Nayak, and Sahu estimate initial energy density in xenon collisions in twenty twenty-five. Nuclear collisions at high energy can create a hot, dense medium. The Bjorken formula estimates energy density from collision data. The team applies it to xenon xenon collisions recorded by the ALICE experiment.

They consider three cases that vary formation time and overlap area in unlike ways. Energy density patterns across centrality classes differ by case. Values above a threshold suggest a quark gluon plasma may form. Comparisons with lead lead collisions at lower energies are also made. Central xenon collisions give lower energy density than lead collisions at like settings. The authors judge the third case, varying both inputs, the most suitable.
arxiv-2508-09143:
Wagner da Rocha and co-authors build angle-based solvers for the distance geometry problem. The problem rebuilds a molecule's shape from a set of atom distances. NMR data gives those distances with slack, so each is an interval, not a point. Their two branch-and-prune methods turn interval distances into angle bounds on arcs.

One method cuts feasibility checks during the search with those bounds. The second adds torsion angle ranges that encode local twist and flatness. Test cases were built from real protein bank structures in a set way. Both angle methods solved more cases than the standard interval solver. The torsion form also gave the closest shapes on shared wins.
arxiv-2508-09743:
Yanick Tchenko and co-authors propose a 2025 way to make small neural networks stronger by letting them inherit knowledge from a big one. The usual trend grows models deeper and larger, which costs speed and ease of use. Their framework, called HKT, instead treats a large trained parent network as a source of traits that a smaller child model can take on in pieces.

The design borrows from biology, where traits pass from parent to offspring in modules. Network blocks act as the carriers of function. Transfer runs in stages and picks only the features the child's task needs, rather than forcing the child to copy all teacher outputs, as standard distillation does. The goal is a compact model that keeps much of the parent's skill and stays easy to deploy.
arxiv-2508-10243:
Taibiao Zhao and co-authors describe a hidden attack on transformer models in their 2025 paper. Transformers are the AI design behind most chat and image tools today. A backdoor attack makes a model act normally until a secret trigger appears, then it misbehaves.

Their method, called HPMI, needs no retraining of the model. It cuts out the least used head, a small part of the model, and swaps in a crafted bad one. Tests across data sets show the attack worked almost every time, while normal accuracy barely dropped. The attack also slipped past four known defenses. The authors warn that model owners should check parts they did not train themselves.
arxiv-2508-10643:
Helena Russello, Rik van der Tol, Eldert van Henten, and Gert Kootstra build a way to spot lameness in dairy cows from video, with no marks on the cow. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A pose tool tracks nine points on each walking cow: the hooves, head, and back. The paths of those points feed a network that reads time in both ways. It learns the marks of a lame gait on its own, with no hand-made traits. The best form named lame cows right in eighty-five of a hundred cases. That beat a known trait-based way, which scored eighty. The method also works with short clips and small training sets.
arxiv-2508-10743:
Ziwei Zou and colleagues present a training-free method for building a medical image atlas, an average anatomical reference that lets researchers compare scans across a population. Learning-based registration tools need large data sets and can fail on new kinds of images, while classical methods scale poorly to many three-dimensional scans. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team aligns a group of scans at once by updating one scan at a time in turn. A centering step keeps the atlas unbiased, and the warps stay smooth and reversible.

The atlas then does extra work. Labels drawn only on the atlas can be carried back to each person scan, and in tests that one-shot labeling beat leading few-example methods. New anatomical variants can be synthesized by warping the atlas mesh with invented deformations. The authors offer the framework as a flexible base for population anatomy studies.
arxiv-2508-10943:
Christian Düreth and co-authors build a pipeline for studying how woven fabric layers nest inside composite materials. Their 2025 paper concerns textile reinforcements pressed during manufacturing. How yarns of one layer sink into the next shapes stiffness, flow of resin, and damage tolerance, yet nesting is hard to measure in low-grade scans.

The team pressed dry fabrics inside a scanner and imaged them at modest resolution across several compaction levels. A tailored 3D network labeled the matrix and the two yarn directions in each scan, with strong overlap scores. A correlation method then extracted average layer thickness and nesting degree from the labeled volumes. Results matched microscope-based checks closely. The approach lets engineers quantify structure during pressing rather than after cutting samples apart.
arxiv-2508-11043:
Robert Dougherty-Bliss, Mits Kobayashi, Natalya Ter-Saakov, and Eugene Zima study a family of moduli built for fast computer arithmetic. Their 2025 paper works in residue number systems, which split big integer work across several moduli and recombine the results. The moduli they study have a three-term form with known bit-level advantages.

The task is to build large sets of such moduli, all of one bit length, that are pairwise coprime. They give a sufficient condition for coprimality based on polynomial resultants. That condition turns the search into a graph problem, where the largest valid sets are the largest cliques, found by known algorithms. Coloring arguments and cyclotomic polynomial facts then bound how large such sets can grow. Fast modular arithmetic underlies cryptography and signal processing hardware.
arxiv-2508-11643:
Tobias Kyrion derives recurrence rules for two classic number functions in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. The functions are the Dirichlet beta function and the Riemann zeta function, both central in number theory. His route runs through a family of integrals with hyperbolic functions.

He shows those integrals can be written as sums of Hurwitz zeta derivatives with polynomial weights. Setting a parameter to even integers then yields step-by-step rules for beta at even inputs and zeta at odd inputs. A related integral with the parameter's rate of change gets a simpler form, built only from digamma values with polynomial weights.
arxiv-2508-12143:
Hirons and five co-authors read in twenty twenty-five how free self-study tools moved grades in a first physics class on charge and magnets. The school built more than two hundred clips and a bank of past tests for all to use. Data spanned three fall terms, with class marks, a concept test, and student back-ground facts.

Past math prep was the best grade guide, with past physics next. Use of the old test bank was the second best guide of all. First-in-family students scored a bit low on their own. Those who used the old tests closed that gap in full, the models show.
arxiv-2508-12243:
Ponwitayarat and co-authors introduce SEA-BED, a benchmark that tests how well embedding models handle Southeast Asian languages. Text embeddings are often assumed to capture meaning the same way for everyone. Tests here show that assumption fails in practice. The benchmark spans 10 languages of the region and many task types. It checks performance by task, by language, and by their pairing.

No single model did well across all the region's languages. A task that was easy in one language could be hard in the next. Wins on one task rarely carried to others. The map of results is strikingly uneven. The authors urge region-specific testing before models are deployed.
arxiv-2508-13543:
