Samra Zafar, Shifa Yousaf, and Muhammad Shaheer Minhas present a study from twenty twenty-five on language model feedback on student writing. Most tools grade the final essay alone. The team asks if the writing process itself can ground the feedback more well. Key logs and time stamped drafts show how an essay grew, pause by pause and fix by fix.

They test fifty-two essays in two modes: final text alone, and final text plus process data. Rubric scores barely moved between modes. Feedback with process data judged the build of the essays more well, though. Its reasons leaned on how the text was made, not just its end state. The team backs process aware review tools.
arxiv-2508-14143:
Xin Li proposes a new model of computation in a 2025 study whose text presents the Urysohn Machine. The model targets classification, and it makes distance, boundary structure, and contraction part of the machine state itself. Its basic unit bundles a support region, a target split, and a separating classifier kept in a reusable library.

Li proves a realization result for finite settings, building separators from nested polyhedral regions arranged in steps. Boundaries between steps get their own calculus, and two width measures follow, one for a single classifier and one for a whole library. The proposal reframes computing in geometric terms.
arxiv-2508-14843:
Yijue Ding maps the energy landscapes that govern how diiodomethane breaks apart under light. The paper from twenty twenty-five builds potential energy surfaces for the ground state and the excited states reached by near-ultraviolet photons. Four dimensions are kept, enough to hold the key motions. Bond breaking and reshuffling among the methyl radical and two iodine atoms are the acts in view.

A spline interpolation scheme builds the surfaces with care and smooth slopes. Key resting points are located on the ground and three excited surfaces. Paths lead to a split into CH2I plus iodine by way of a CH2I-I isomer. The surfaces are packaged for dynamics runs. Photochemists gain a ready terrain for simulating this molecule's light-driven fate.
arxiv-2508-15243:
Yixin Gao and nine co-authors make image compression conversational in twenty twenty-five. Standard codecs offer few coding modes, chosen manually by engineers. That makes compression unfriendly for ordinary users with specific needs. Their system, Comp-X, is presented as the first interactive learned compression paradigm driven by a language model agent.

Three innovations define it. A multi-functional framework unifies coding modes for human viewing, machine perception, variable rates, and spatial bit allocation. An interactive agent learns from expert feedback, taught through augmented in-context learning. The agent interprets a user's request and selects settings accordingly. Readers in image coding get a glimpse of codecs operated by conversation, where expertise is supplied by the agent rather than demanded of the user.
arxiv-2508-15343:
Rishi Mishra and co-authors present a 2025 method for solving eigenvalue problems, the math tasks behind vibration and wave studies. Their tool, called Eig-PIELM, joins physics rules with a fast kind of learning machine. Old solvers need a mesh grid and long runs. Their method needs no mesh and solves in a single step.

The method turns the governing equations into one compact algebra system. Edge rules are built in exactly, with no penalty terms or slow training loops. One solve yields both the values and the shapes of the modes. Tests on set benchmark problems showed the results were sound and held up well. Fast, exact spectra help engineers who must scan many designs, as in machines, sound, and small devices.
arxiv-2508-16443:
Théo Lisart-Liebermann and Arcesio Castañeda Medina accelerate adaptive quantum optimization by seeding it with classically simulable Clifford circuits. Their paper from twenty twenty-five merges two known tricks. Clifford initialization pre-tunes parameters at points a classical machine can evaluate cheaply. ADAPT-QAOA, meanwhile, rebuilds the circuit's gate set while optimizing. Running Clifford approximations at several ADAPT levels compounds the gains.

Numerics show pre-optimization steering gate selection and sometimes easing convergence. Operator choice inside ADAPT can even go fully classical and parallel for MaxCut and the transverse-field Ising model. Approximating the costly T gates at ten to thirty percent error improves convergence quality, suggesting ansätze overuse them. Compilers may exploit that slack aggressively.
arxiv-2508-17343:
Abhik Roychoudhury surveys, in a 2025 preprint, how AI agents are reshaping software work, from the software engineering community's viewpoint. Public buzz centers on generating code from prompts. The author argues the real shift is broader. Agents now make small decisions across testing, repair, design, and requirements work, aided by program analysis tools. The vision is an AI teammate inside the development team. The hard core of the field, though, is reading developer intent. Agents that cannot infer what was meant will not be trusted, however fluent their code.

Roychoudhury predicts that future workflows will pair generation with AI-based checking of the generated code. Volume alone forces that pairing. Trust, he argues, will be earned task by task through verified output. The paper is a position piece: it maps where agentic tools help today and which research problems, above all intent inference, gate their wider use.
arxiv-2508-17643:
Krishna Vinod, Prithvi Jai Ramesh, Pavan Kumar B N, and Bharatesh Chakravarthi bring event cameras into a popular robot simulator in a 2025 study. Event cameras react in microseconds, handle harsh lighting, and use little power, suiting robots that move fast or face glare and shadow. Mainstream simulators, though, rarely model them, so event-based methods are hard to test safely.

Their open-source package links synthetic event vision with visual servoing inside the Gazebo simulator through standard robot middleware. Researchers can rehearse navigation and manipulation under motion blur, occlusion, and changing light before risking real hardware. The tool aims to be user friendly for robotics labs.
arxiv-2508-18143:
Yi Han proves the circular law for non-Hermitian random band matrices down to bandwidths well below full size, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In one regime, doubly stochastic variance profiles with symmetry or transitive invariance yield the circular law for Gaussian entries at explicit bandwidths, with no lower variance bound or mixing assumption. A comparison argument extends it to bounded-density entries, including nonperiodic graph supports and uneven weights.

In a second regime, periodic strips with a flat diagonal core get a least-singular-value estimate needing no density assumption. That yields the law for real sub-Gaussian entries, including coin-flip entries, at explicit sublinear bandwidths. Counting arguments with separator-tree elimination power that part. Coarse singular-value counting handles the logarithmic integrability throughout.
arxiv-2508-19943:
Nhat Nghiem brings quantum computing to a less-studied feature of data shape. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Topological data analysis reads the form of a dataset. Its best-known targets are Betti numbers, which count holes and links. Counting them is provably hard in general. Quantum speedups seem possible only in structured cases.

Nghiem turns to torsion, another part of homology. Torsion can reveal structure that hole counts miss. The paper gives a quantum algorithm that detects whether torsion is present. It builds on recent links between topology and quantum methods. The setting stays structured, in line with where speedups are plausible. The work widens the menu of shape questions quantum machines might answer. It also sets up later work on full torsion computation.
arxiv-2509-00043:
Md Faizul Bari, Yi Xie, Meghna Roy Choudhury, and Shreyas Sen show in 2025 that a repaired USB keyboard cable can leak keystrokes from afar. Devices shed faint radio signals as a side effect of their work, a leak called electromagnetic emanation. Such leaks were thought too weak to travel far or leave a room.

A standard cable repair forms a tiny rod antenna that throws the leak much farther. Tests with three cable types show signals can be caught past four meters and through a thick concrete wall. By logging seventy distinct keystrokes at varied distances in three settings, the team shows typed text can be pulled out. The find warns that cheap repairs can open a real spy path.
arxiv-2509-00143:
Andrew Robertson and Andrew Benson present a faster way to calibrate galaxy formation models in 2025, shown with the Galacticus code. Semi-analytic models grow galaxies inside dark matter halos by set rules. Fitting them to the stellar mass function, which counts galaxies by star mass, is slow, since each trial must evolve thousands of halos.

Their fast likelihood uses the stellar-to-halo mass relation, its mean and scatter, at a few target halo masses. Each trial then simulates only tens of galaxies. Sampling with a Markov chain method recovers the low-redshift mass function well. Extensions add higher-redshift and size data, and check survey traits such as emission line strength. Faster fits open larger model searches.
arxiv-2509-00243:
Pierre-Yves Goffin, Yves Dubief, and Vincent E. Terrapon follow the curvature of polymer stress in a steady arrowhead flow pattern in 2025. Dilute polymer solutions add elastic stress to a fluid, which can form organized sheets. The arrowhead is a steady coherent structure in a two-dimensional periodic channel flow.

In a frame moving with the arrowhead, streamlines double as pathlines and reveal two topological regions tied to two stagnation points. Stresslines, drawn parallel to the main directions of polymer stress, link the sheets' layout to polymer motion. A new form of the stress term ties local flow shape to how stressline curvature and stress variation interact. The view clarifies how polymers sustain the arrowhead pattern.
arxiv-2509-00543:
Jayakrishna Duggempudi leads five authors in total, with Lu Gao, Ahmed Senouci, Zhe Han, and Yunpeng Zhang, in drafting home floor plans from plain text. Their workflow uses large language models to turn a written request into a schematic layout with walls, doors, windows, and furniture.

Duggempudi and his co-authors combine prompt design, a refinement step for furniture placement, and Python scripting to make layouts that hold together in space. A case study on a mid-sized home shows functional output with little manual effort. The plans keep the parametric attributes, editable properties, needed for Autodesk Revit and building information modeling, and all key prompts are documented so others can copy the workflow.
arxiv-2509-01243:
Tennis players and fans often speak of momentum, a run of form that seems to carry a player forward, but proving it exists takes care. Chang Du, Caiya Zhang, and Likai Zhou propose a full framework for testing momentum in singles matches. A chi-squared test first checks whether point outcomes depart from independence.

Assuming momentum is present, the team builds a momentum score with an entropy weight method, then uses a control chart to spot change points in that series. A relative distance measure grades how strong each shift is. A neural network tuned by a swarm method predicts point outcomes, and feature importance is read with SHAP values. Applied to the 2023 Wimbledon men's singles, the tests backed momentum, and adding its features improved prediction.
arxiv-2509-01343:
Heavy and superheavy nuclei can decay by emitting an alpha particle, and the rate depends on the barrier the particle must tunnel through. S. Mohammadi, R. Gharaei, and S. A. Alavi study how the fuzziness of the nuclear surface, called diffuseness, changes that barrier. They examine three hundred parent nuclei, with atomic numbers from sixty-four to one hundred six.

Using two proximity potentials to model the nuclear force, the team traces how the interaction changes with distance, with and without surface effects. Diffuseness proved decisive near the touching point of the two nuclei, and its influence faded farther out. Including it lowered the chance of barrier penetration, and the computed half-lives matched measured data very well. The study sharpens predictions for the decay of the heaviest elements.
arxiv-2509-01543:
Conditional flow matching generates samples quickly and well, but many uses need those samples steered toward exact requirements. Konstantin Mark, Leonard Galustian, Maximilian P. -P. Kovar, and Esther Heid formulate that steering as tilting the output with an energy potential, favoring samples with desired traits. Steering tools existed for diffusion models, yet none had been extended to flow matching.

The team derives Feynman-Kac steering for flow matching for the first time, adapting a method from statistical physics. Tests include synthetic tasks and the hard case of tilted distributions in high-dimensional space. They then tackle an unsolved challenge: generating transition states of chemical reactions with the correct chirality, the handedness that decides which reaction paths are possible. The work opens guided generation in flow models to precise scientific demands.
arxiv-2509-01643:
Speculative design uses imagined artifacts to question the present. Minja Axelsson applies it to robots built by and for LGBTQ+ people. The format is an exploratory essay. It asks what aspirational queer robotics futures could look like, in art and in science. A brief review first gathers the state of queer robotics in fiction and research.

Three proposals follow. Robots could reflect and celebrate the identity of their queer users. Robots could perform a queer identity to engage outsiders, cutting bigotry through familiarity. A network of queer-owned robots could help a community reach each other and share resources. Axelsson then questions whether robots should be queered at all. The ethics of that step are weighed. Suggestions close the essay, offered to spark debate about equitable robotics.
arxiv-2509-02043:
Akihiro Higashitani, Masato Konoike, Norihiro Nakashima, and Satoshi Ono compute counting polynomials for deletions of Shi arrangements of types C and D. A hyperplane arrangement is a set of flat walls in space, and its complement holds the free regions. Characteristic quasi-polynomials count lattice points in that complement modulo growing integers. Deleting one wall from a Shi arrangement gives the cases at hand.

Type C follows by extending the team prior method for type B. Type D then reduces to type B through a direct link. As a corollary, they settle whether period collapse occurs for these deletions. Period collapse means the counting pattern repeats with a smaller period than expected. The results complete a family picture across the classical types.
arxiv-2509-02443:
A. S. Mikhaylov and V. S. Mikhaylov wrote a 2025 mathematics paper connecting the complex moment problem with an inverse problem for a discrete system. The moment problem asks how to rebuild a positive measure on the complex plane from a given list of its moments, which are averaged powers.

The discrete system in question is tied to a complex Jacobi matrix, a structured matrix with entries on three diagonals. The authors show that characterising the dynamic inverse data for that system yields sufficient conditions for solving the moment problem. In other words, knowing how the discrete system responds over time can certify that a matching measure exists. The link joins two classical areas of analysis.
arxiv-2509-02543:
Mert Can Cakmak and Nitin Agarwal present a 2025 computational social science paper on auditing bias in YouTube Shorts recommendations. Short video feeds shape what billions see, yet the ranking systems stay opaque, and small shifts can skew exposure on sensitive topics.

Instead of full videos or metadata, the authors extract perceptually salient keyframes, the still images that carry a clip's visual gist. Captions are generated for those frames, and both are embedded into one content space. Mapping recommendation chains then reveals drift and clustering patterns. Politically sensitive topics behaved differently from general categories, with consistent shifts suggesting filtering effects. The authors present keyframes as a cheap, readable lens for auditing short-form recommendation systems.
arxiv-2509-02643:
G. G. L. Nashed, Usman Zafar, and Kazuharu Bamba wrote a 2025 gravity paper constructing a black hole solution in a theory with higher-order curvature terms plus a scalar field. Modifying Einstein's gravity this way can soften the central singularity that general relativity predicts.

Their spherically symmetric solution is set by the gravitational mass. Curvature invariants, measures of how extreme the geometry gets, grow far more weakly near the centre than in standard theory. The authors then study heat and stability using Barrow entropy, a quantum-corrected entropy formula. Both quasi-local energy and Gibbs free energy come out positive, pointing to stability at the smooth horizon. A geodesic deviation analysis spells out the stability conditions explicitly.
arxiv-2509-02743:
Shuheng Liu and five co-authors wrote a 2025 quantum information paper on measuring how high-dimensional the entanglement in continuous-variable states really is. The Schmidt number counts that dimensionality and serves as a resource for quantum processing.

Most platforms with large Schmidt numbers are continuous by nature, yet they are usually chopped into finite pieces before measurement. The authors build witnesses directly from phase-space correlations and covariances, readable through characteristic or Wigner function measurements. The witnesses work for arbitrary mixed states, Gaussian or not, and need only a slice of phase space. Direct estimation proved more robust than discretising first. As a test, the method certifies arbitrarily large Schmidt numbers for a bound-entangled Gaussian state, a state whose entanglement cannot be distilled.
arxiv-2509-03043:
Sunho Kim, Chunhe Xiong, and Junde Wu proposed a 2025 purpose-oriented framework for judging quantum resources. Resource theories measure what makes a quantum state or process useful, such as entanglement. Their weak point is the free set, the class of things counted as costing nothing, which can be ambiguous.

The new approach measures deficiency instead: how far a state falls short of the most efficient option for a chosen task. That single measure can sort mixed states, estimate noise, and flag error-correction thresholds. The authors define a repair capacity that ties the measure to mission success even when the free set is fuzzy. Worked cases cover simple qubit systems and named test channels. Applications include repairing entanglement and switching on teleportation.
arxiv-2509-03143:
Kaidi Lõo and 3 co-authors ran a 2025 language experiment on how one Estonian speaker reads words aloud. Word naming, reading a printed word as fast as possible, reveals how the mind maps spelling to sound and meaning. The study followed a single person closely, combining naming with eye tracking.

Five measures were tracked, from where the eyes first landed to how long the spoken word lasted. Predictors came from a computational model of the mental lexicon that learns mappings between form and meaning. Those model measures predicted several outcomes strongly, and meaning clearly mattered in this task. Classic predictors like word frequency still fit slightly better overall. Deep and linear versions of the model performed much alike, and some eye measures resisted all predictors.
arxiv-2509-03643:
A 2025 research paper by Chao Pang and seven co-authors introduces CEHR-XGPT, a foundation model for electronic health records. Health records give a rich, time-ordered view of each patient's care. Most record-based artificial intelligence models are built for one narrow task, which limits their use in real clinical settings.

CEHR-XGPT unifies three abilities in one architecture: representing patient features, predicting outcomes with no task-specific examples, and generating synthetic record data. A time-token scheme encodes each patient's changing timeline directly into the model's structure, supporting reasoning over clinical sequences. Performance stays strong across all three tasks in their tests. The model also moves to outside datasets by expanding its vocabulary and fine-tuning. The authors argue such versatility speeds model development, cohort discovery, and outcome forecasting without retraining for every new task.
arxiv-2509-03743:
The statistics of dislocation links in a metal as it strain hardens is what Sh. Akhondzadeh and five co-authors examine in a 2025 research paper. Dislocations are line defects inside crystals, and deforming a metal multiplies them into a network. The segments between nodes, called links, track how that microstructure evolves under stress.

Data come from discrete dislocation dynamics simulations of copper. Link lengths are analysed for each slip system, the planes and directions along which dislocations glide. On active slip systems, lengths follow a double-exponential distribution with a long tail. On inactive systems, a single-exponential shape fits instead. The long tail is traced to long links bowing outward under stress, and vanishes when the load is removed. Both patterns follow from a one-dimensional Poisson process extended with different growth rules. When growth turns super-linear past a critical length, the double-exponential form emerges.
arxiv-2509-04143:
Cedric Perret and four co-authors separate trust from cooperation in a 2025 research paper on social dilemmas. Social dilemmas are games where helping the group can hurt the individual player. Many assume trust and cooperation rise together, yet models rarely measure trust on its own. The authors define trust plainly: a player who trusts stops watching a partner's every move once that partner has cooperated enough.

Simulated players using this shortcut evolved across the full range of two-player dilemma games. Where watching carried a cost, trust raised cooperation when temptation to cheat ran high. Where players sometimes acted by mistake, trust helped even in coordination games. Trust can now be measured as saved monitoring effort.
arxiv-2509-04243:
Wanfu Wang and four co-authors teach vision-language models to zoom in on the right part of a screen in a 2025 research paper. GUI grounding means finding the exact screen element a user's instruction refers to, such as a small button in a crowded window. High-resolution screens make that search hard. Their framework, LASER, trains models to look actively in steps, judging candidate regions by quality scores and overlap with targets, then building preference examples from the best searches.

Training rewards both accuracy and variety, and lets harder screens consume more reasoning steps. On two ScreenSpot benchmarks, scores rose steadily across versions. One tuned model set a new best result among its size class on the professional benchmark.
arxiv-2509-04543:
Eric Parsonage and two co-authors compress directed hypergraphs without losing their chain structure in a 2025 research paper. Hypergraphs link groups at once, modeling many-sided relationships in security work, but big ones resist being drawn. An older projection method can, oddly, add edges by flattening transitive chains. Their Transitivity Preserving Projection keeps only irreducible dominant metapaths, the routes that cannot be reduced, giving a minimal yet complete picture of ties inside a chosen subset.

An algorithm built on the set-trie data structure cuts the search from exponential to linear with polynomial filtering. Jobs finished in seconds where the older method failed within a full day. Network security and supply chain analysts gain readable maps of complex dependencies.
arxiv-2509-05143:
A network can fail by colour when a whole class of links shares one fault. József Pintér and one co-author study colourings that keep a graph connected after any single colour is removed in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Each colour represents edges or vertices that may fail together.

They characterise which graphs admit colour-avoiding connected colourings. For the basic connectivity case, the minimum number of colours and an optimal colouring can both be found in polynomial time. For stronger connectivity the problem becomes NP-hard. They also study orientations with the same robustness, plus vertex, multi-colour, and matroid generalisations.
arxiv-2509-05243:
When one star in a pair spills gas onto the other, the orbit itself changes, and A. Parkosidis and three co-authors model that process in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Mass transfer in round orbits is well studied, but many real pairs move on oval, eccentric paths where theory is thin.

Their framework gives orbit-averaged equations for both round and oval cases, treating stars as points or as bodies with size and spin. Checked against direct numerical runs, it predicts wider final orbits and more growth in ovalness than older models gave. The equations can plug into binary evolution codes used for studies ranging from ordinary stars to gravitational wave sources.
arxiv-2509-05343:
Attention modules, which let a network focus on the most telling image regions, are tested across five medical image networks by Zahid Ullah and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Ordinary convolutional networks can miss fine detail that matters for diagnosis.

Each base network gains either a squeeze-and-excitation block or a combined channel and spatial attention block, which reweight features by importance. The team evaluates them on brain tumour scans with several tumour types and on a tissue dataset with four categories. Attention versions beat the plain networks on all measures, with one efficient network plus hybrid attention scoring highest. Better feature localisation also helped the models generalise across different imaging types.
arxiv-2509-05443:
Psychological questionnaires usually measure several hidden traits at once, and R. Noah Padgett extends a flexible analysis method to that case in a solo 2025 statistics paper. Factor analysis links observed answers to latent traits, and moderation lets outside variables shift how the whole model behaves.

Earlier moderated models handled only one or two factors, while real measures often target three to five dimensions. Padgett's model lets moderation act on item intercepts, loadings, residual variances, and factor means, variances, and correlations across three or more factors. Estimation uses Bayesian computing in Stan and a penalised likelihood method, with exact analytic gradients replacing costly approximations. The penalties also help detect where measurement works differently across groups.
arxiv-2509-05543:
Splitting a video of human movement into its separate actions is improved by pre-training tricks from Haitao Tian and Pierre Payeur in a 2025 computer vision paper. Skeleton-based action segmentation works from joint positions over time, and labelled long videos are scarce.

Their DuoCLR framework pre-trains on short, single-action skeleton clips. A shuffle and warp augmentation creates varied multi-action orderings. Two surrogate tasks then teach the network: one matches the same action across different orderings, the other reasons about relative order between orderings. Pre-trained this way, the model beat leading alternatives on both multi-class and multi-label segmentation of untrimmed video. Ablation tests confirm each part helps.
arxiv-2509-05643:
Fuzz testing reaches closed factory firmware by running it inside an emulator, Carmine Cesarano and Roberto Natella show in a 2025 security paper. Guided fuzzing finds bugs by feeding varied inputs and watching which code runs. It usually needs source code to add probes, which closed toolchains deny.

Their system, FuzzBox, adds probes to code as it runs in the emulator, feeding inputs, catching failures, and tracking coverage without recompiling or real hardware. Tests target a closed hypervisor built to separate security levels in factory use. They also analyse fit across shop-bought device firmware. Being portable is the selling point: the same approach travels across products whose insides stay closed.
arxiv-2509-05743:
Integer-structured bases for the largest class of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras are built by Saeid Azam in a solo 2025 algebra paper. A Chevalley basis makes every structure constant an integer, which lets Lie groups be rebuilt over finite fields as Chevalley groups.

Such bases were known for finite-dimensional simple algebras and for affine algebras. Azam develops a uniform theory for extended affine Lie algebras of arbitrary type, consistent with both older cases. The theory explains how a Chevalley basis for a finite or affine algebra extends to one for the covering extended affine algebra. Uniformity matters: one construction now covers three levels of the Lie algebra family.
arxiv-2509-05843:
A new class of modules in abstract algebra is introduced in a 2025 paper by Mohammad Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh. Their notion, uniformly S-pseudo-injective modules, widens an earlier injectivity concept by allowing maps to be extended after multiplication by an element of a fixed set S. Injectivity questions ask when maps defined on a part can stretch to the whole.

The authors develop basic properties of the class and prove a clean test: a module is uniformly S-quasi-injective exactly when two copies of it joined together are pseudo-injective in their sense. They also introduce and characterize two families of rings connected with QI-rings, rings where quasi-injective modules behave in a special way. The results place the new notion inside the wider map of injectivity generalizations that ring theorists use.
arxiv-2509-06143:
Logic gates made of light, small enough for a chip, are demonstrated in a 2025 paper led by Adib Md. Tawsif with four co-authors. All-optical logic avoids slow electronic conversion, but plasmonic designs often suffer fabrication complexity and large footprints. The authors use magnetoelectric light funneling in grooved metasurfaces inside a metal-insulator-metal waveguide.

Their planar device, smaller than a micrometer across, implements NOT, AND, and OR gates with a high contrast ratio, all driven by one light source from one direction. It operates in the telecom band, around fourteen hundred nanometers. The single-source control and compact size ease integration into photonic circuits, and the authors present the design as a step toward scalable, high-speed optical computing.
arxiv-2509-06643:
Approximating integrals with very few sample points on a curve is studied by Cordian Riener and one co-author in a 2025 mathematics paper. A quadrature rule replaces an integral with a weighted sum at chosen nodes. When the underlying measure lives on an algebraic curve, the curve's shape should decide how few nodes suffice.

The authors take an optimization view, minimizing penalty functions over rules of a fixed strength so the best solutions use the fewest nodes. For plane curves they derive explicit bounds on node counts that depend on the curve's degree and its places at infinity, improving earlier results. For rational curves in any dimension, the parametrization's geometry sharpens the bounds further, and the classic Gaussian quadrature bound returns in the simplest case. Algebraic complexity and formula size are tied directly together.
arxiv-2509-06743:
Messages that must travel far across a graph are handled by wavelet networks in a 2025 machine learning paper by Filippo Guerranti and three co-authors. Graph wavelets borrow multi-resolution ideas from signal processing to capture both local clusters and global shape. Earlier wavelet networks approximated their filters with short polynomials, which kept their reach local.

The proposed long-range graph wavelet networks split each filter into two parts. Low-order polynomials handle nearby aggregation cheaply, while a flexible spectral component, defined in the frequency domain of the graph, carries long-range interactions. The hybrid keeps the wavelet framework principled while widening the receptive field. On long-range benchmarks the method set the best results among wavelet approaches, and it stayed competitive on short-range datasets, suggesting the split design loses little where long reach is unnecessary.
arxiv-2509-06843:
Pulling the three-dimensional structure of hadrons out of transverse-momentum data is made more systematic by Andrea Simonelli in a solo 2025 theory paper. The hard part is splitting effects that can be computed from truly non-perturbative ones, without bias from modeling choices. Standard work models the data in impact-parameter space and converts back, tangling the pieces.

Simonelli proposes doing the Fourier inversion by formula, summing transverse-momentum distributions and cross sections directly in momentum space, at next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. The method is checked against other prescriptions and tested on measured data. Two sources of non-perturbative effects are named: how the strong coupling acts at low energy, and how the parton distributions act there. The claim is a shift in practice, where hadron structure comes from QCD dynamics rather than flexible formulas fit by hand.
arxiv-2509-07243:
Li Li and 1 co-author survey recent work in 2025 on a class of solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations. These equations govern steady fluid flow. The solutions in focus are called minus-one homogeneous. They shrink in a set way when the space scale is stretched. Some of them have singular rays, lines where the solution breaks down.

The survey gathers what is known about such solutions for three-dimensional flow that cannot be compressed. One class gets close attention: flows with axial symmetry and no swirl. For these, the authors list the main types of singular behavior and show graphs of each type. As a survey, the value lies in one map of a scattered field. Readers can see which solution types exist, how they fail to be smooth, and where open questions remain.
arxiv-2509-07543:
Anna Van Elst and 2 co-authors develop gossip algorithms in 2025 for computing robust statistics across a decentralized network. Gossip algorithms spread information by repeated local exchanges between neighbors, with no central server. Decentralized AI and edge systems need them, but classic versions rely on means and sums that corrupted or adversarial data can easily poison.

The new algorithms compute a broad class of rank-based statistics, including L-statistics and rank statistics, which resist outliers because they depend on ordering rather than size. The team applies them to robust distributed two-sample testing and gives the first gossip algorithm for Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. They prove convergence guarantees, including the first rate bound for asynchronous gossip-based rank estimation. Experiments on diverse network topologies confirm the theory, supporting trustworthy statistics on edge networks.
arxiv-2509-07843:
Alexander Dorsey and 1 co-author present a missile guidance method designed to guarantee interception in a 2025 engineering paper. A pursuer chases a moving evader, each modelled as a simple point mass. Their law uses feedback linearization, a control technique that cancels nonlinear behaviour, driven by range and line-of-sight rate measurements.

One version of the law can hit a singularity, a point where the maths breaks down. A fuzzy logic system blends it smoothly with classical proportional guidance to avoid that failure. The line-of-sight version avoids singularities but can drift apart in some cases. Blending both ideas offers a practical route to guidance that stays stable while still promising a hit under the stated conditions.
arxiv-2509-07943:
Cleaning galaxy survey data so cosmic conclusions stay unbiased is the work of a 2025 Dark Energy Survey paper led by M. Rodríguez-Monroy and colleagues. As surveys reach extreme statistical precision, small observational flaws dominate the error budget. Varying sky conditions, such as seeing quality, change measured galaxy counts from place to place.

For the Year 6 MagLim++ lens sample, the team improves masking, the practice of cutting regions where conditions were poor or artefacts appear. Template maps of contaminants guide corrections, but extreme values can fall outside where corrections remain trustworthy. A carefully defined final footprint protects clustering measurements, which feed estimates of how the universe's large-scale structure grew under dark energy's influence.
arxiv-2509-08143:
Molten salts could store energy and process nuclear fuel, but predicting their behavior needs the electrons in the story. Harender S. Dhattarwal and Richard C. Remsing study molten silver iodide in a 2025 research paper. They compare three simulation approaches: quantum-level density functional theory, a universal machine learning model, and a classical pairwise force field.

Directional polarization fluctuations of the iodide ions turn out to boost silver ion diffusion. Silver motion ties tightly to the polarization of neighboring iodide. Iodide motion, by contrast, barely notices the electronic fluctuations. The machine learning model matched the quantum simulations on every quantity checked. The classical force field failed on cation behavior because it ignores those fluctuations. The findings link molten salt dynamics to the electronic paddle-wheel mechanism known in superionic solids.
arxiv-2509-08543:
Chérif Amrouche and 1 co-author revisit the Dirichlet problem for the Laplacian on rough domains in a 2025 paper. The domain is only Lipschitz, meaning its border can have corners but no wild cusps. Basic questions about traces and solution regularity are reopened.

A new function space gives a clean trace rule without relying on non-tangential limits. Using interpolation and known results, the authors claim strong regularity holds for a wide class of data. That claim conflicts with views held since the nineteen nineties. They also revisit existence in other spaces and a classic area integral estimate, which they argue cannot hold as stated.
arxiv-2509-08843:
Sidney Shapiro offers a comprehensive guide to pattern based file access with Python glob in a 2025 paper. Glob uses wildcard patterns to search, filter, and ingest files. The paper presents it as a basic but often under documented part of research computing.

Use cases include large scale data ingestion, organizational analysis, AI dataset building, and reproducible research. Examples use common libraries such as pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib. Glob is placed within wider data engineering and reproducibility practice. The author aims to give researchers a concise reference they can cite. The guide bridges basic concepts and applied workflows across fields.
arxiv-2509-08943:
Rahul Arvind and 4 co-authors study quantum error correction in adversarial regimes in a 2025 paper. Standard correction can fix only up to half a code's distance and must give one answer. An attacker who corrupts data on purpose pushes past those limits.

List decoding lets a decoder output a short list of possible errors, tolerating far more damage. Generalized Knill-Laflamme conditions tell which codes support list decoding. Using pseudorandom unitaries from quantum cryptography, the team builds a list decoding protocol secure against efficient quantum adversaries. Security holds across repeated attempts, unlike prior schemes. The work links coding theory with complexity based cryptography.
arxiv-2509-09043:
Ask a chatbot whether it would like to keep talking, and its answer turns out to carry a usable signal. Thomas Manuel Rost, Martina Figlia, and Bernd Wallraff define that signal, called SPICE, in a 2025 research paper. SPICE asks a model a yes-or-no question about re-engaging after it reads a short conversation transcript. The study crossed three user tones with ten interactions.

Four open-weight chat models were tested under four framings, giving hundreds of trials. Friendly conversations drew near-unanimous willingness to continue. Abusive ones drew strong refusal, and unclear ones fell between. The signal stayed decisive under careful statistics. Notably, when models failed to label abuse explicitly, they still usually declined to continue. SPICE thus offers auditors a cheap, reproducible probe of a model's relational state, distinct from its classification scores.
arxiv-2509-09243:
Giulio Peruginelli and 1 co-author classify Prüfer domains of integer valued polynomials on algebras in a 2025 paper. Integer valued polynomials map an algebra into itself while having coefficients in a larger field. When their ring is a Prüfer domain, a well behaved class of rings, is the question.

A complete classification is given for the base domain and algebra under stated finiteness conditions. In the semiprimitive case, the polynomial ring is Prüfer exactly when the algebra is commutative and a finite product of almost Dedekind domains. Those factors must also satisfy a double boundedness condition on ramification indices and residue field degrees. The work is pure commutative algebra.
arxiv-2509-09343:
Mohammed M. H. Qazzaz and 3 co-authors jointly optimize load balance and energy use in O-RAN in a 2025 paper. Open radio access networks can sleep radio units through controller apps to save power. Offloading users to free a unit, though, unbalances load across the net.

A classifier predicts unit setups and maps net state to three balance grades. Three threshold modes trade savings against service in line with operator aims. Tests use millions of real net measures from simulations. A random forest scores near top marks, a huge gain over standard baselines. Offloaded users keep their resource share by design of the framework.
arxiv-2509-09443:
Alexei Lebedev and 1 co-author argue in a 2025 mathematics paper that the Steenrod algebra cannot be realised as the enveloping algebra of any Lie superalgebra. Beyond that negative result, they list open problems pointing at the usual definition of an enveloping algebra itself. Some odd deformations in positive characteristic, they suggest, are artefacts of a definition that fits the setting badly.

P. Deligne added his own comments to the work, with hints and further problems for readers. Taken together, the piece serves both as a proof record and as an invitation. Algebraists interested in characteristic p structures get a clear statement of what fails, why the standard framing may mislead, and where revision might begin.
arxiv-2509-09643:
Yuhao Guo and 5 co-authors study clouds of ultralight bosons bound to pairs of compact objects in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Gravitational wave listening can reveal such surroundings, and boson clouds behave unlike star fields or ordinary particle dark matter. When two bodies of similar mass draw close enough, the bosons can settle into shared bound states much like a molecule, with an inner zone travelling alongside the pair.

Mixing simulations with a semi-analytic model, the team maps that shared zone and counts how orbital motion ionises it across different orbit shapes. The escaping bosons push back on the orbit, and one fresh effect stands out: lopsided orbits ionise the shared part efficiently, which quickly rounds the orbit out.
arxiv-2509-09943:
Zhu Chen and 3 co-authors track living cells through microscope movies without any hand-labelled training data in a 2025 biomedical imaging paper. Following cells and spotting divisions is essential work, yet footage fights back with low contrast, fuzzy borders, dense crowds, and cells that all look alike. Labelled training sets are expensive, and models raised on one laboratory's data often stumble on another's.

Their answer plugs Segment Anything 2, a general segmentation foundation model, straight into the tracking pipeline as a zero-shot tool. Nothing is fine-tuned, so no single data set's habits are inherited. Accuracy stayed competitive on both flat two-dimensional sequences and large three-dimensional time-lapse volumes, suggesting foundation models can carry specialised science further than expected.
arxiv-2509-10743:
Amit Kumar and Gojko Vujanovic wrote this 2025 nuclear physics paper on how a fast quark loses energy while crossing the hot, dense matter inside a nucleus. Such energy loss is a key signal in collisions that recreate conditions from the early universe.

Working in the higher-twist formalism at next-to-leading order, the authors compute every single-scattering emission kernel for a quark that interacts with medium particles called Glauber gluons and quarks. The calculation keeps the heavy-quark mass in both the incoming and outgoing states and includes coherence effects between scatterings. Four final states are covered, pairing the quark with gluons, antiquarks, or other quarks. The results feed into models of electron-nucleus collisions and the transport coefficients used to describe jets in nuclear matter.
arxiv-2509-10943:
Fernando Benito F. de la Cigoña and three co-authors ask a question in this 2025 paper. Which measures double as evenly as possible? A doubling measure assigns comparable mass to a ball and its double. Every such measure has a doubling constant. The authors study the minimizers. Those are measures whose constant is the least achievable on a given metric space.

Minimizers exist, they show. The setting is any complete metric space that supports at least one doubling measure. A bridge to superharmonic functions settles the Euclidean case. Lebesgue measure is the unique minimizer, up to scaling, in dimensions one and two only. In three dimensions and up, infinitely many independent minimizers appear. Similar uniqueness results hold for counting measure. The graphs there have a recurrent random walk. In every graph whose ball sizes depend only on radius, counting measure is also a minimizer.
arxiv-2509-11143:
P. Jishnu Sai, S. R. Haridev, and Rajeev Kumar Jain compute a subtle statistical signal from the early universe in this 2025 cosmology paper. During inflation, spectator gauge fields coupled to the inflaton can leave four-point correlations, a trispectrum, in the electric and magnetic fields they produce.

Using the in-in formalism and diagrammatic rules, the authors derive exact expressions for the full trispectrum built from scalar and tensor exchanges. For scalar exchange, the signal peaks in flattened arrangements of the four momenta, and its size ties neatly to a lower-order correlation. Tensor exchange adds a richer angular pattern that depends on how the momentum quadrilateral sits relative to the tensor polarization. Spotting such angular fingerprints in future observations would open a new window on interactions in the infant universe.
arxiv-2509-11543:
Zhengxi Lu and ten co-authors find a middle road for training interface-using agents. This 2025 artificial intelligence paper weighs two training styles. Live online learning is costly and its rewards are sparse. Offline training on recorded sessions is stable but blind to long tasks.

Their paradigm is semi-online reinforcement learning. It mimics online learning on offline records. A patch module repairs drift between model rollouts and expert records. Discounted future returns supply the long-term signal. A new metric tracks how well this predicts true online skill. Among models of its size, the approach set the best scores on four live test sets. Gains over its base model reached double digits on Android tasks.
arxiv-2509-11943:
In a 2025 paper, Antonin Sulc and Thorsten Hellert propose a multi-agent system for finding the root cause of a fault. Their design is neuro-symbolic, meaning it joins neural language models with formal logic. Each agent's beliefs are written as a Kripke model, a formal structure for reasoning about what is possible and what is necessary.

Domain knowledge that does not change is encoded as logical constraints, the rules a sound diagnosis must obey. The agents then reason within those rules to reach an explanation that can be checked step by step. The authors argue that improving the structure and consistency of agent reasoning matters as much as making models larger. Their target is diagnosis that is reliable and explainable, not just plausible.
arxiv-2509-12243:
Murray Cutforth and 4 co-authors tackle cheaper simulation for problems that can jump between distinct behaviors, in a 2025 paper. Multi-fidelity methods mix many cheap low-fidelity runs with a few costly high-fidelity ones. One such method, bi-fidelity interpolative decomposition, builds a reduced basis from the cheap data to approximate the expensive results.

The authors show that method can fail when responses are multimodal and which mode appears is random. They introduce an extension designed for that case. Their motivating example is a laser-ignited methane-oxygen rocket combustor studied over uncertain inputs, where behavior splits in a bifurcation-like way in parts of the parameter space. Handling that split correctly matters for uncertainty studies, design exploration, and optimization that rely on trustworthy approximations.
arxiv-2509-12543:
Harshit Rajgarhia and 4 co-authors join human checks with AI to speed up the review of ads made for new markets in a 2025 paper. An ad moved to a new language needs more than a word swap. Its look, layout, and style must stay intact, or the new ad seems broken.

Their system finds text in a scene, paints over the old text, translates it, and puts the new text back in place. People guide the machine steps and judge the end result. The authors say this is the first such joined system built just for ad work of this kind. Tests in six locales gave ads that kept the sense of the source and looked clean and whole.
arxiv-2509-12943:
Sayanho Biswas and 3 co-authors study doubling bifurcations of invariant closed curves in a 2025 mathematics paper. In dynamical systems, an invariant closed curve is a loop that a system retraces over time. Such curves can double in two reported ways: splitting into two disjoint curves that iterations alternate between, or becoming a single curve of double length.

Various methods have been proposed to analyze these bifurcations, which mark qualitative changes in a system's behavior. The authors show that existing methods are not always adequate for analyzing and predicting them. They propose a new method designed to overcome those difficulties. The work concerns three-dimensional maps, discrete systems whose state updates in steps, where predicting curve doubling matters for understanding long-term dynamics.
arxiv-2509-13043:
Antonio Vairo unifies quarkonia in 2025 via the Born and Oppenheimer effective theory. Quarkonia are bound states of heavy quarks. Types span plain pairs plus exotic four- and five-quark forms and hybrids. A single frame for all of them has long been sought.

The theory rests on slow-motion splits of the strong force. Lattice results supply key inputs. With one frame Vairo treats plain and exotic forms side by side. Threshold effects in the spectrum are weighed too. A shared tongue may sort which exotic peaks are true bound states. It may also guide where to hunt next and how to read new peaks.
arxiv-2509-13143:
Isabel Kain, Carlos Alvarez and 14 co-authors plan in 2025 to use twilight hours at Keck for the SCALES planet camera. Optical work stops at twilight, but infrared skies stay dark past sunrise. SCALES will image planets directly in mid-infrared light from 2026.

Current twilight use yields under twenty science hours per year. A staffed, ranked program could yield near ten times that. Two lead cases anchor the plan: watch of Solar System bodies, and a hunt for planets near bright close stars. Lessons from current twilight work shape scope. Tech and ops hurdles are listed for fix before launch.
arxiv-2509-13343:
Winston Chen and Yao-Guang Zheng build in 2025 a new Kerr-Sen solution class with rotational symmetry via Laurent expansions. The method starts from still Euclidean vacuum solutions. Variation and superposition tools generate stationary fields in one frame for study.

Fresh views on axial gravitational systems follow. The Kerr-NUT hierarchy extends under the frame. Dilaton and axion roles get detailed study, with numeric checks. A long history of axial exact solutions is surveyed. Theory and astrophysical stakes of Kerr-Sen metrics are weighed for current hunts, black hole tests, and exact solution catalogs.
arxiv-2509-13743:
Xiaoxiao Yang and five co-authors map routes into elastic turbulence in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Giant micelles, long wormlike chains formed by surfactant molecules, can flow in bands and then erupt into purely elastic instabilities and turbulence driven by hoop stresses rather than inertia. What controls that transition was known only qualitatively.

Using benchmark shear-banding micelle systems in Taylor-Couette flow, flow between rotating cylinders, the team quantified the effect of streamline curvature for the first time. Optical imaging and velocimetry revealed two distinct pathways into elastic turbulence, organized into a state diagram using curvature ratio and the Weissenberg number. Stress records suggest the transition changes character as curvature grows, and they derive a scaling law for its onset.
arxiv-2509-13843:
Paul Goulain and seven co-authors report light-matter experiments in a 2025 photonics paper. Inside non-dispersive mid-infrared cavities, intersubband polaritons can collide with optical phonons. Polaritons are hybrid particles of light and electron excitations in thin wells. Phonons are the crystal's own vibrations. The team look for light emitted when a polariton sheds exactly one phonon's worth of energy.

Under resonant optical pumping, they observe that faint scattering signal. It sits at the expected shifted frequency. Because the rate is extremely low, they built a custom quantum mechanical model. The model tests whether a pump-probe scheme could stimulate the process instead. The analysis identifies concrete lab conditions for optical gain. Under those conditions, polariton lasing in the mid-infrared might eventually be reached.
arxiv-2509-14043:
Marlon Bause and three co-authors listen for radio emission from quiet magnetars in a 2025 astronomy paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest known magnetic fields. They are leading suspects for producing fast radio bursts. Yet only six have ever been heard in radio. Most stay silent, and whether that silence is permanent was untested over long baselines.

The team observed thirteen radio-quiet magnetars regularly with the MeerKAT telescope. They searched as an interferometer making images. They also searched as a time-domain instrument, hunting single pulses and folded pulsations tied to X-ray timing. Nothing was detected. The value lies in the depth of the silence. They set strict upper limits on steady flux and single-pulse brightness. They argue for continued high-cadence monitoring regardless of X-ray brightness.
arxiv-2509-14143:
Zijian An and three co-authors build weight-aware grasping into a robot policy in a 2025 paper. Vision-language-action models follow instructions end to end. They are poor at stopping on a numeric condition, like lifting exactly a target weight. Nothing inside them explicitly watches the number. Tasks such as portioning ingredients hinge on exactly that kind of threshold.

Their framework, CLAW, splits the job. A fine-tuned CLIP model watches the digital readout of a scale. It issues discrete directives when weight thresholds are crossed. A flow-based policy turns those prompts plus multi-view camera images into continuous arm actions. Tested on single-object grasping and mixed-object tasks needing both arms, CLAW executed weight-aware behavior reliably. It beat both the raw and the fine-tuned base policy.
arxiv-2509-14443:
Kunal Marwaha and three co-authors study in 2025 how hard decoded quantum interferometry is to mimic. The method is a quantum algorithm for near best answers to hard choice tasks. Claims of quantum edge need care, since a method can beat some classic attacks yet stay low in the hardness ranks.

First, the method resists classic tricks that hunt for outputs with large chance. Next, the authors prove it can be mimicked at a low level of the polynomial ranks, which clouds standard supremacy claims. They also show it meets a coding bound tied to the MacWilliams identity in a direct way. Last, they read it as making low energy states of a quantum harmonic oscillator. That physics view may guide wider forms.
arxiv-2509-14543:
Zhengxiang Wang and four co-authors test in 2025 whether large language models can imitate the personal writing style of everyday authors from a few samples. Personal style is subtle and implicit, hard to state in a prompt. Writing assistants still promise to sound like the user.

Their evaluation uses several complementary metrics: authorship attribution, verification, style matching and AI detection. Tens of thousands of generations per model were scored across news, email, forums and other domains. Models captured surface traits better than deep habits, the results suggest. Faithful imitation of implicit style remains out of reach for the systems tested. Assistants that claim to write exactly like you are, for now, overselling what few shot prompting delivers.
arxiv-2509-14843:
Walter Briec gives an algebraic form for a limit kind of convexity in a solo 2025 math paper. B-convexity was first defined as a limit of standard convex sets, in the Painlevé-Kuratowski sense. That first form never spelled out the shapes that approach the limit, so no algebraic treatment over the full space was possible.

Briec builds on recent work to describe those limit shapes in algebraic terms. The result is a multi-point form of B-convexity ruled by a structure that is idempotent and non-associative. He also shows the limit shapes do not fit a symmetric convex structure proposed in past work. A broad separation result in Euclidean space comes from approaching convex sets by polytopes, and open points in the field are made clear.
arxiv-2509-14943:
Alessandra Stramiglio leads a team of six authors testing how well language models extract facts from biographies that state things indirectly, in a 2025 natural language processing paper. Information extraction systems traditionally rely on explicit statements. Human readers infer far more: a sentence about attending church every Sunday quietly signals a person's religion.

The team built two synthetic datasets of ten thousand texts each, one stating biographic facts explicitly and one implying them, all derived from Wikidata. They measured extraction performance for three pre-trained models and checked whether fine-tuning on implicit examples improves general reasoning about hints. The study probes the internal reasoning of the models, asking where indirect language breaks them. Findings matter for any system that mines real-world text, where facts are often implied rather than declared.
arxiv-2509-15243:
Muhammad Imran and Yugyung Lee make vision-language models show their work when they locate things in images, in a 2025 paper. Image tools are moving into safety-critical jobs. There, tangled links between objects and faint visual cues make clarity as key as hit rate. A model that points but cannot say why is hard to trust.

Their frame builds on gradient-based tools that explain Transformer models. A new module works at several scales at once. It weighs attention in a flexible way and lines up image and text cues. The design tracks links between image regions at more than one level of detail, from parts to whole objects. The goal is pointing that stays sharp while its reasons can be checked.
arxiv-2509-15543:
Xinwen Zhang leads a team that trains models across many machines under harsh noise. Their problem has two levels: an outer choice shapes an inner training task. Past methods assumed the inner task was nicely curved and the noise was tame. Real language data breaks both hopes, with wild, heavy tailed noise.

Their method is a two level descent that steadies its steps by scaling, with no clipping tricks. It cuts noise by mixing past steps across machines that hold split data. They prove it converges, with new bounds for the tangled step sequences. This is the first such method with firm proof under heavy tailed noise. Tests confirm it handles that noise well.
arxiv-2509-15843:
Alina Kostromina leads a team that releases a Python library for time series forecasting strategy. Most research chases new models, while the choice of how to train them gets little study. Their library, Tsururu, bridges research and industry use. It lets users mix global and multivariate training styles freely.

It also supports multi step ahead forecasting plans, where several future points are predicted in set ways. The library plugs into varied forecasting models without fuss. The code is public on GitHub. The paper is a short tool note, aimed at practitioners who must pick a training plan, not just a model.
arxiv-2509-16043:
Could the weak force hide a particle that no one has yet seen directly? Gia Dvali, Archil Kobakhidze, and Otari Sakhelashvili examine the case for such a particle, a pseudoscalar tied to the shape of the weak vacuum. Past work argued that removing a vacuum angle by a known symmetry calls for this particle to exist.

Here the authors test whether it could arise as a joint effect of instanton-driven terms in the vacuum. They argue a key term and its vacuum value match in a way that does not depend on cutoff choices. Puzzles about the particle's nature remain open, and they set out what to check next.
arxiv-2509-16343:
Satellite image questions in high-stakes work need more care than one quick pass by a vision model can give. Chung-En Johnny Yu, Brian Jalaian, and Nathaniel D. Bastian present a training-free agent frame that loops through think, critique, and act steps. Off-the-shelf vision-language models and a reasoning model check each other and refine answers step by step.

On a remote sensing question set, the frame beat single models by wide margins on hard question types. Joining three vision models through the frame lifted overall accuracy a lot, from near half to well over three quarters. More compute at answer time, not retraining, drove the gain.
arxiv-2509-16443:
Light-based chips promise fast, low-power math for language models, but someone must decide which parts of a model run on light and which on electronics. Ryan Tomich, Zhizhen Zhong, and Dirk Englund build LightCode, a compiler and simulator for such hybrid machines. Its stacked graph holds several hardware versions of each operation, and a solver picks the mix that best fits time or energy goals.

On two model workloads, photonic parts cut energy by up to half in simulation, and smart assignment cut delays by more than tenfold. Time-first and energy-first plans chose quite different mappings.
arxiv-2509-16543:
Yue Huang and a large team of co-authors aim to give language models real skill in chemistry in a 2025 paper. Good training data for chemistry is scarce. Made-up data often miss the strict rules and layered form of chemical facts. The team build a system that makes training pairs with those rules in mind.

Their system, called ChemOrch, first plans tasks under tight control. It then builds answers with the help of chemistry tools. Judges found the data varied and well matched to chemical rules. Tasks built this way exposed model flaws more clearly. Fine-tuning on the data raised model skill in chemistry by a clear margin.
arxiv-2509-16743:
Subhabrata Das, Bodruzzaman Khan, and Xiao-Yang Liu forecast power outages in a 2025 paper. Outages depend on weather, plants, animals, and swings in demand. Those inputs add noise that makes forecasts shaky. The team join several methods into one frame: a step that shrinks data, a rank step, and a sequence model tuned by a smart optimizer.

The sequence model reads long time patterns in outage records. Tests use real records from Michigan. Scores beat prior methods on accuracy and stability. Better outage forecasts could help grid crews stage repairs and warn customers sooner, before storms knock lines down.
arxiv-2509-17243:
Niclas Krupp, Moritz Huber, Cheng Luo, and Oriol Vendrell simulate molecules trapped in light cavities in a 2025 arXiv paper. Strong coupling between light and matter inside such cavities can shift how molecules react and how charge and energy move. Claims in the field clash, though, in part because studies pick distinct Hamiltonians and state forms.

The team runs numerically exact simulations from a first-principles light-matter Hamiltonian. Electrons, nuclei, and cavity photons are treated on the same footing. Their test system is a Shin-Metiu model with rotation, vibration, and electronic motion all live, handled by a tree tensor network method. A cavity does change single molecules a bit, mostly in rotation and nuclear motion. The change tracks the coupling per molecule, then fades as the group grows toward bulk size, which helps explain why lab claims are hard to reproduce.
arxiv-2509-17343:
Liyi Li and five co-authors introduce a programming language for quantum simulations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Simulations model quantum systems for work in physics, chemistry, and biology. Most compilers speak in Pauli strings or digital circuits, a low-level tongue that shuts out many of the scientists who need the simulations.

Their language, QBLUE, is presented as the first to describe quantum systems through second quantization Hamiltonians, the dialect those scientists already use. A new type system states clearly which states belong to which system, and it treats quantum computers as particle systems of set types. The typing stays compatible with compiling QBLUE programs for both digital and analog machines. The pitch is simple: let users name the system they want, and let the language map it onto hardware.
arxiv-2509-17643:
The IPPOG Collaboration presents its worldwide outreach network in a 2025 arXiv paper. IPPOG, the International Particle Physics Outreach Group, links students, teachers, and the public with particle physics. A gap yawns between the research community and everyone else, and the paper sets out how the network works to bridge it.

Three pillars carry the effort. International Masterclasses and the Global Cosmics hands-on network have together engaged hundreds of thousands of high school students in real data work. A curated resource database and web portal give teachers tested materials instead of raw papers. The paper describes the network's structure and reach across many countries. It argues that outreach at this scale needs shared infrastructure, not lone efforts by single labs, and it reports what that infrastructure has delivered so far.
arxiv-2509-17843:
Svitlana Ponomarova, Oleksandr Ponomarov, and Yurii Koval use machine learning to guess the Curie heat of metal mixes. That heat is the point where a magnet loses its pull. Their 2025 study covers iron with platinum, nickel, or palladium, and cobalt with platinum.

A voting group of models, each trained apart, gave the best guesses. Checks used the classic maths ways to work out the same heat. Mix ratio, atom order, and squeeze from outside each shifted the heat a lot. Those levers could help design mixes with a set heat in mind.
arxiv-2509-18143:
Mike Smart and 3 co-authors map trained net weights onto a low-energy analog chip neuron. Their 2025 paper deals with a dual-tree, single-clock capacitive neuron, built for frugal AI chips. Weights learned in software must turn into capacitor sizes on the chip, a step with hidden snags.

The team sets out those snags and what they mean for chip design and score. A best-practice map flow is proposed, aimed at smaller chips and higher score. Three trained nets were mapped with full match of function in their tests. Weight packing effects on chip space and choice quality are also probed.
arxiv-2509-18243:
Nicola Borghi and 3 co-authors study how missing galaxies in a catalogue weaken cosmic sums from wave events. Their 2025 paper deals with standard sirens, where a gravity wave plus its host galaxy pins the expansion rate. Real catalogues miss hosts, since faint galaxies escape our surveys.

Their open pipe, CHIMERA, keeps the host-weight logic firm as completeness varies. A hundred fake wave events in a next-run setup give tight rates when catalogues are full. As completeness drops, precision slides in an S-shaped way. Mass-based host weights sharpen both the best case and the slide. A fair rate stays in reach with part-full lists.
arxiv-2509-18343:
Quadratic Funding is a rule for splitting public money based on how many people back each project. Joel Miller, E. Glen Weyl, and Chris Kanich report how one crowdfunding platform moved past its flaws. Their 2025 paper argues the old rule treated people as lone and selfish actors. That view clashed with how the platform's community really gives.

The team built a new rule called Connection-Oriented Quadratic Funding. It rewards links between givers, based on a theory of plurality and pro-social motives. On the platform, the new rule won an 89 percent adoption rate and has handed out over four million dollars. In simulations it gave better total welfare than the old rule. The authors also argue the tool could serve public choices beyond this one site. Fair splits, they suggest, should count social ties.
arxiv-2509-18443:
The 5G core network is built from many software functions that must work as a chain. Ioannis Panitsas and four co-authors present 5GC-Bench, a tool for stress-testing those functions. Their 2025 paper notes that older tools test signaling or traffic alone. Many also use fake loads and cannot see fine resource use.

5GC-Bench drives signaling and service traffic together, under loads that mimic real use. It can profile single functions or the whole service chain end to end. By mapping bottlenecks and resource demands, it gives clear input for capacity planning. The team wired it into an open 5G core and ran it on a real testbed. The runs exposed resource limits and links between functions under load. All artifacts are released in public so others can repeat the tests.
arxiv-2509-18743:
LiDAR point clouds guide self-driving cars, but noise, blocked views, and attacks can corrupt them. Susmit Neogi presents TriFusion-AE, an autoencoder that cleans and rebuilds such clouds, in this 2025 paper. Autoencoders compress a cloud and rebuild it, dropping noise on the way. Under harsh real-world damage, standard versions degrade fast.

TriFusion-AE fuses three inputs: the LiDAR cloud, depth maps from camera views, and text cues. Cross-attention aligns the semantic, geometric, and spatial strands. Under mild damage the gains were small. Under strong attacks and heavy noise, the model held up while classic convolutional autoencoders collapsed. Tests used a small public driving data set to mimic low-data deployment. The design is model-agnostic and can wrap existing point cloud autoencoders. The author pitches fusion as the route to robust perception.
arxiv-2509-18843:
Hospitals want AI answers they can run in-house, without sending data to closed services. Damian Stachura, Joanna Konieczna, and Artur Nowak test whether small open-weight models can match big proprietary ones on biomedical questions. Their 2025 paper reports the team's entry to a BioASQ challenge phase. Several open models faced top closed systems.

The team boosted the open models with retrieved text snippets, in-context examples, and structured outputs. For exact-answer items, ensembles merged the strengths of several models. Results showed the open models were comparable to the closed ones overall. In some cases, above all with ensembles, the open models even won. All code is public. The authors argue that small open models are now a real option for biomedical question answering. Privacy-sensitive settings stand to gain most.
arxiv-2509-18943:
Hui-Qiang Liang and two co-authors report a new kind of localization in systems that do not conserve energy in the usual way. In known critical states, wave patterns keep their in-between character even as the system grows without limit. The states found here act critical only at finite sizes. As the system grows, they cross over into plain Anderson localization, where waves stay trapped in place.

The effect comes from a mix of weak localization and the skin effect, where waves pile up at an edge. The team shows the pattern in two simple models, one with a repeating mosaic pattern and one with one-way hopping. Tests with entanglement entropy, a measure of how linked two parts of a system are, confirm the size-dependent behavior.
arxiv-2509-19043:
Darko Mitrovic, writing alone, studies when a class of flow equations has solutions that behave well. The equations are scalar conservation laws, which track a quantity that is neither created nor destroyed as it moves. Their flux, the rule for how the quantity flows, can jump abruptly where the medium changes. Such jumps arise at interfaces in layered materials or changing road conditions.

Mitrovic allows the flux to be smooth on each side of a smooth interface, with the two sides tied to space and to the solution itself. The flux also vanishes at the edges of the range the solution may take. For this setting, and for a broader case where the flux varies with bounded variation in space, he builds a stable semigroup of solutions. That construction gives the problem a well-posed framework: solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on the data.
arxiv-2509-19143:
Alejandro Cuevas and four co-authors build a way to stress-test AI systems against disinformation in many languages at once. Safety probes, called red-teaming, are usually built around United States sources in English. Their method, named anecdoctoring, instead harvests real misinformation claims from fact-checking sites in English, Spanish, and Hindi, spanning the United States and India. Claims are clustered into broader story lines, and each cluster is mapped as a knowledge graph.

Those graphs then coach an attacker model to craft probing prompts rooted in real narratives. The method produced higher attack success rates than standard few-shot prompting. It also stays interpretable, since each attack traces back to a mapped real-world story. The authors argue that defenses against disinformation must scale across languages and cultures, grounded in how misuse actually happens rather than in invented examples.
arxiv-2509-19243:
Ahmed S. Alahmed and three co-authors schedule water and power together inside a desalination plant that also generates renewable electricity. The plant mixes thermal and membrane desalination, sells fresh water to a utility at a set price, and trades electricity with the grid in both directions. The question is how to run both technologies hour by hour to maximize profit as sunshine and prices vary.

The optimal policy, they show, has a simple threshold shape set by the plant's own renewable output. As renewable generation rises, thermal water output should shrink steadily while membrane output grows. The authors explain the intuition behind that split and examine special properties of the policy. Co-scheduling the two resources, rather than planning water and power apart, is the paper's central message for plant operators.
arxiv-2509-19443:
Modern sky surveys pour out spectra of stars faster than experts can analyze them, and J. E. Martínez Fernández and four co-authors speed up the most precise analysis method. Differential analysis compares a star with a near-twin to cancel errors, but it only works between stars with similar temperatures, gravities, and compositions. Finding those twins inside millions of spectra is the bottleneck. Their procedure projects spectra onto maps with the t-SNE algorithm, treating each pixel as a dimension, so look-alike stars cluster together.

They calibrated a similarity metric on thousands of high-resolution spectra from clusters, anchored to stars with trusted parameters. The metric finds matches within tight tolerances, with completeness up to ninety-eight percent in tests. The team also graded four published parameter catalogs, mapping where each needs improvement. The method promises to bring differential precision to survey-scale samples.
arxiv-2509-19543:
Some materials carry both magnetic order and electric response, and the two can talk to each other. Pavel A. Andreev studies spin waves in such a material whose ground state twists into a cycloid, a repeating spiral of spins. He works out the wave speeds with pen-and-paper math. The electric side enters through a link between spin patterns and electric dipoles.

The twist of the ground state weakens the grip of the material's preferred direction. Pushed far enough, that weakening can make the spiral unstable. Andreev also treats the straight-spin case to compare two forms of the electric link. He then computes how the material answers an applied electric and magnetic wave. Such results guide the search for materials where magnetism can be steered with voltage.
arxiv-2509-19643:
School rezoning plans draw thousands of public comments, and few residents ever feel heard. Cassandra Overney and eight co-authors built StoryBuilder, a human-AI pipeline that turns raw feedback into short first-person stories. The stories blend several real responses into one composite voice. The team drew on about twenty-five hundred responses from a live rezoning process and made over a hundred stories.

A phone-friendly reader, StorySharer, carried the stories to residents over a four-month field run. Studies with community members and a controlled experiment tested how story style shaped reactions. Stories grounded in lived experience helped readers relate across deep differences. The authors argue that narrative form can do what summary charts cannot: build shared understanding. The work targets civic choices where trust is as scarce as time.
arxiv-2509-19743:
Training sets can be distilled into tiny synthetic ones that teach models nearly as well. Xinhao Zhong and five co-authors clean up how the decoupled branch of that field is judged. Decoupled methods split teacher training from synthetic data creation, which scales better than older joint methods. But each team grades its results with a different protocol, so claims cannot be compared.

Their rectified method, paired with a systematic study of grading choices, exposes which tweaks truly help. Random augmentation and soft labels during grading turn out to matter greatly. Fair grading is unglamorous but decisive for a young field. Smaller synthetic sets cut storage and training costs across machine learning. The authors give the community a shared yardstick plus a stronger baseline.
arxiv-2509-19843:
A home robot that fetches your backpack, not just any backpack, must know who owns what. Filippo Ziliotto and five co-authors build PersONAL, a benchmark for personalized embodied agents. Episodes sit in over thirty photorealistic homes from the HM3D collection. Each scene description ties objects to named owners in plain language.
