They then ran over three thousand experiments themselves, crossing three datasets, four architectures, sixteen representative defenses, and five attacks, showing that a defense's measured strength swings a lot with the setup. Gaps they name include unreported overhead, untested behavior on benign inputs, and biased tuning choices. The paper closes with concrete recommendations to standardize testing. Its message to users is blunt: a defense is only as proven as the protocol that tested it.
arxiv-2511-13243:
Xiaoqi Han and 6 co-authors examine how editing multimodal models can quietly break their use of images. Editing aims to fix wrong facts, but older tests use random or weakly matched images and can overstate success. The authors build a fuller locality test with three image settings and seven data types.

Their dynamic test, De-VQA, reveals a flaw they call transient blindness, where an edited model leans on text and ignores the picture. Token checks show edits shift text tokens far more than image tokens. A new loss that guards locality cuts the flaw and improved locality by about seventeen percent on average over baselines.
arxiv-2511-13643:
Noah B. Frank, Joshua L. Pughe-Sanford, and Samuel J. Grauer ask how many measurements make a chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system observable for state reconstruction. When starting conditions are unknown, variational estimation rebuilds a path that fits both data and the governing equations. The open question is how sparse the data can be before reconstruction must fail.

Linking observability to embedding theory, they show a measurement count at the attractor's manifold dimension ensures local observability, and just over twice that ensures global observability for a gradient smoother. They also catalog optimizer pitfalls that persist past those thresholds and counter them with Newton updates plus a pseudo-projection step. Simulations confirm the practical limits.
arxiv-2511-13843:
Julian G. Soltes introduces QUASAR, a new evolutionary algorithm for hard optimization problems with many variables. Such problems resist standard methods because the search space grows so fast, an issue known as the curse of dimensionality. QUASAR builds on differential evolution and adds random mutation choices, rank-based crossover rates, and periodic restarts shaped by shrinking covariance.

On the CEC2017 test suite of 29 functions, QUASAR earned the best overall ranking against differential evolution and the L-SHADE method. Its final answers were on average several times better in quality, and it reached them faster as well. Soltes presents it as an effective and easy-to-use tool for complex high-dimensional tasks.
arxiv-2511-14043:
Chandrachur Bhattacharya and Sibendu Som describe AISAC, a multi-agent system built at Argonne National Laboratory to assist scientists with evidence-based reasoning. Rather than claiming autonomous discovery, AISAC supplies a governed runtime. Every agent has a declared role. Context and delegation are budgeted. Each step leaves a trace that can be replayed and audited.

The system enforces role semantics at runtime, gives agents tiered access to episodic, dialogue, and evidence memory, and validates tool calls against schemas. Retrieval is scoped per agent over hybrid storage with vector indices. Configuration files let new projects extend the platform without code changes, aiming at transparent, reproducible AI help for long research tasks.
arxiv-2511-14143:
An Yu, Weiheng Lu, Jian Li, and four co-authors present SMART, a system that finds the exact moment in a video matching a text query. Most retrieval methods read time coarsely and use vision alone, which fails on complex footage. SMART adds audio cues and respects the shot structure of the video, since shots are its natural temporal units.

A shot-aware compression step keeps only high-information tokens within each shot, cutting redundancy while preserving fine timing detail. Prompt design was also tuned to exploit the audio-visual signals. On the Charades-STA and QVHighlights benchmarks SMART improved over leading methods, including clear gains at both loose and strict overlap thresholds.
arxiv-2511-14243:
T. Liimets, D. P. K. Banerjee, M. Santander-García, and twelve co-authors catch a jet being born in the symbiotic binary R Aquarii. The system, a white dwarf orbiting a pulsating giant, passes closest approach only about every forty years, and this passage is the first watched with modern instruments. The team took hydrogen-alpha speckle images a month apart plus matching high-resolution spectra.

The images reveal a new two-sided jet pointing north-south. Its measured motion dates the launch to about January 2020, right at the passage's onset. A knot in the southern jet moves more slowly and was ejected slightly earlier. The authors also update the system's expansion-parallax distance to two hundred sixty parsecs.
arxiv-2511-14543:
Youran Zhou, Mohamed Reda Bouadjenek, and Sunil Aryal propose MissHDD for filling missing values in mixed type tables. Real tables mix numbers, categories, and discrete values in one data set. Most diffusion based imputers assume one uniform feature type. That leads to collapse for categories or unstable updates for numbers.

MissHDD splits features into two generative channels that work in parallel. A deterministic channel handles numeric values with stable denoising. A discrete latent path channel handles categories without leaving valid values. Together they preserve conditional structure across the whole row. The hybrid design aims for more reliable imputation on heterogeneous real world data.
arxiv-2511-14843:
Emmet Golden-Marx, Zheng Cai, and eight co-authors ask how living in a crowded young cluster changes the shapes of galaxies. In today's clusters, galaxies have mostly settled into smooth early forms, a pattern built as star formation shuts down over time. At the epoch studied here, about eleven billion years ago, that change was still under way.

Using sharp Hubble images of two protoclusters, the team measures the shape index of more than a hundred fifty galaxies picked out by their glowing hydrogen. Comparing these dense regions with emptier fields shows how far the shape change had come. Such snapshots pin down when environment began to sculpt galaxies into their modern forms.
arxiv-2511-15543:
Georgios Venianakis, Constantinos Theodoropoulos, and Michail Kavousanakis build a framework that decides where to place sensors and estimates unknown parameters at the same time. Measuring data can be costly, sparse, or noisy, so sensor placement matters most for systems that vary across space. Their tool is a physics-informed neural network, a network trained to respect the governing equations while fitting data.

Unknown parameters enter the network as extra inputs, so sensitivity of outputs to those parameters comes out through automatic differentiation. A classic D-optimality criterion then picks sensor spots that carry the most information. On two reaction and flow problems of rising complexity, the method estimated parameters more accurately than estimates from other placements.
arxiv-2511-15643:
Leonardo Ferreira, Haroon Mumtaz, and Gabor Pinter study United Kingdom business cycles over seven centuries with a time varying structural model. Data span from the thirteenth century to the present day. Shocks are identified as innovations that explain the largest share of future output variance. That long view reveals how cycle drivers changed with institutions and money.

Before the twentieth century, key shocks look supply driven and stagflationary. After that point they become demand driven, lifting output and inflation together. Output volatility peaks in the seventeenth century, then declines over time. Monetisation had large real effects early, turning more inflationary later. The results show business cycles are not timeless constants but products of their era.
arxiv-2511-15743:
Linnea Wolniewicz and ten co-authors release a machine learning ready data set that unifies ionospheric and heliospheric readings for forecasting. Working ionosphere outlooks suffer from sparse records and complex coupling between layers. Timely exactness supports guiding, radio links, aviation, and satellite operations. Their curated open data set integrates many sources into one coherent structure.

Inputs span solar imagery, irradiance indices, solar wind measures, and geomagnetic activity indices. Global ionospheric maps of total electron content provide the target variable. The workflow was built during a NASA heliophysics laboratory program. Gaps in current working approaches are addressed directly. A shared, ready to train resource should accelerate next creation space weather models across groups.
arxiv-2511-15943:
Zihan Li, Yiqing Wang, Sina Farsiu, and Paul Kinahan improve image-text pretraining for medical imaging with multi-granular language learning. Contrastive pretraining aligns pictures with text, but the standard approach links one label at one level of detail. Medical images instead carry many labels at once, from disease categories to diagnostic descriptions and clinical explanations at different granularities.

Their framework aligns vision and language across those labels and levels together. Structured multi-label supervision, text drawn from several granularities, and soft labels with point-wise constraints guide the alignment, while a smooth divergence measure keeps levels consistent. Built as a plug-in module, it was pretrained on large multi-granular data and beat leading methods on downstream tasks across data sets.
arxiv-2511-17043:
Rama Krishna Boya and seven co-authors test a medical image model on the job of sorting chest X-rays into normal and abnormal. Chest scans are among the most used tools for chest diagnosis, but rising scan counts strain the doctors who read them. The team uses MedImageInsight, a foundation model built for medical images, in two distinct ways.

In one route the model is fine-tuned to label scans directly, and in the other it supplies features that simpler classifiers then use. Tests mix a large public chest X-ray set with real scans from partner hospitals. The fine-tuned route scores best and stays better calibrated than the feature route, reaching a level the authors rate as close to strong established systems for this task.
arxiv-2511-17243:
Two classic matrix equations lie at the heart of control theory: the Lyapunov equation and the Riccati equation. Dongjun Wu and Yankai Lin read both through the lens of positive systems, systems whose variables stay nonnegative. Instead of attacking the equations head-on, they build positive systems whose long-run behavior encodes the answers. Claims about whether answers exist, and whether they are unique, then follow from positive systems theory.

For the Lyapunov case, under standard observability assumptions, the built system is strictly positive. It converges fast, in the Hilbert metric, to its Perron-Frobenius vector, which is tied to the solution. The Riccati case gives homogeneous positive systems with richer dynamics. Existence and uniqueness still follow there, but only slower, asymptotic convergence can be shown. The paper imports a fresh set of tools and intuitions into a well-trodden area.
arxiv-2511-17743:
Haytham Younus and four co-authors review efforts to modernize Failure Mode and Effects Analysis, a standard way engineers list how a system might fail and how bad each failure would be. Classic practice is manual and rests heavily on expert judgment.

Recent work adds machine learning, language tools, and ontologies, which are formal maps of system knowledge. Together they can automate failure forecasts, sort risks, and keep reasoning clear across teams. The review maps tools and case studies, notes problems with data and standards, and sketches a path toward smarter, model based safety work.
arxiv-2511-17943:
Zhiyu Xu, Weilong Yan, Yufei Shi, and five co-authors present SciEducator, a multi agent system for understanding and teaching from scientific videos. General video models struggle here because explanations need outside expert knowledge and careful step by step reasoning about experiments and phenomena.

Modeled on the Plan Do Study Act improvement cycle, the system reasons in loops and produces teaching material with text, visuals, narration, and references. The team also builds a benchmark of expert checked science questions across physical, chemical, and everyday topics. SciEducator beats leading closed models and video agents on that benchmark by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-18043: Kei Funano establishes two new universal inequalities for Neumann eigenvalues of the Laplacian on a planar convex domain. Eigenvalues in this setting are the natural vibration frequencies of a membrane with a free edge, and the Laplacian is the core operator behind them. Universal inequalities bound such values in ways that hold for every domain in the class, regardless of its exact shape. The note states the two results for flat, convex regions, adding to the family of shape-free bounds known for this problem.
arxiv-2511-18343:
Dongming Jin and eight co-authors help coders find ready made parts that fit a stated need. Reuse of open source parts saves work and tends to be more sound than fresh code. Yet a vast pool of parts makes the right one hard to spot, and search by keyword often misses the user's true aim.

The team build IntentRecBench, a test set for need driven part search across three large open source pools. On it they run five large language models and six older methods head to head. The study weighs how well each reads a stated need and ranks apt parts. Results guide when model based search earns its cost over older tools.
arxiv-2511-19243:
Dhruv Jain and six co-authors use gravitational-wave data to learn about luminous red novae, a class of stellar outbursts. These events are thought to mark the ejection of a shared envelope in a binary star system. That ejection tightens the orbit, sometimes leaving a compact pair that merges within the age of the universe and emits gravitational waves.

Rates of red novae from the Zwicky Transient Facility are compared with merger rates from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors, using delay time models for compact binaries. Only a tiny share, around a thousandth at the median, of red novae can end as the observed neutron star mergers. Most such outbursts must follow other paths.
arxiv-2511-19343:
Qihan Huang, Haofei Zhang, Rong Wei, Yi Wang, Rui Tang, Mingli Song, and Jie Song tackle weak training data in reinforcement learning for multimodal perception models. The popular GRPO method generalises well, but its samples often fail to draw diverse answers from the model, which narrows what the learner can explore. Entropy constraints treat the symptom, not the cause. Their system, Syn-GRPO, instead generates fresh training data during learning itself, evolving the data alongside the model.

A separate data server synthesises new samples from existing ones with an image generation model, working on a decoupled, asynchronous schedule so generation never stalls training. The workflow then trains on data chosen to provoke varied responses. The authors present the loop as a root fix for the exploration problem in perception reasoning.
arxiv-2511-19743:
Alexandru Hening and Siddharth Sabharwal study how populations spread across many habitat patches fare when both movement and environment are random. They prove when such populations persist and when they die out, even though dispersal rates themselves fluctuate. Beverton-Holt and Hassell growth rules serve as the test cases.

For slow and fast dispersal the authors find explicit formulas for the total population at stationarity. Random carrying capacity always hurts in the Beverton-Holt case but helps in the Hassell case. Fast dispersal can rescue populations from extinction. Switching environments, fast or slow, get their own approximations, with slow switching sometimes reversing the effect.
arxiv-2511-21143:
Taejun Kim and colleagues presented at UIST 2023 STAR, a text-entry method that lets augmented-reality users type on their own hands as if holding a phone. Bare-hand AR typing schemes usually demand new gestures and give no surface feedback. STAR instead borrows the two-thumb smartphone skill people already own. Hold the knuckle posture of gripping a phone, and a miniature QWERTY keyboard appears overlaid on the skin of the hands, tapped by the thumbs.

After 30 minutes of practice, study participants averaged 21.9 words per minute, which is 56 percent of their smartphone speed, with a mean error rate of 0.3 percent. An elicitation study with 29 participants had mapped the hand postures people choose for imaginary phone typing. For scale, smartphone typing averages 36.2 words per minute against 51.6 on desktop keyboards. The authors dissect the remaining performance gap, in tracking, feedback, and posture, and sketch how each factor could be narrowed.
arxiv-2511-21343:
Laura Boca de Giuli and five coauthors improve predictive control for systems that behave differently in different regimes, in 2025. Model predictive control steers a system by repeatedly forecasting its future, increasingly with neural network models learned from data. One network stretched across all operating conditions often predicts poorly in each. Engineers therefore train an ensemble of specialists instead. Then they face the question of how to blend the answers moment by moment.

Boca de Giuli and her coauthors propose blending weights based on the Mahalanobis distance, a statistical measure of how unusual the current inputs are for each specialist. The weights evolve across the prediction window using inputs alone, unlike schemes needing unavailable future states. They also build a moving horizon estimator, an observer that reconstructs the current state for the ensemble. Tests on a benchmark energy system running under multiple conditions validate the approach.
arxiv-2511-21443:
Sebastian Kilde-Westberg, Andreas Johansson, Anna Pearson, and Jonas Enger test a picture-based way to teach quantum teleportation in 2025. School quantum physics usually stops at century-old ideas, leaving students unready for modern quantum technology. The team taught teleportation with QPic, a simplified diagram language from the ZX-calculus, where quantum processes become wires and boxes that students can push around like a puzzle.

Working with 21 upper-secondary students and pre-service teachers, Kilde-Westberg and his coauthors analyzed recorded group work, written exercises, and an interview. They found four qualitatively different ways students experience teleportation, ordered as a ladder. Climbing it depends on grasping time's role in quantum processes, what entanglement contributes, that measurement actively changes the system, and how diagram moves map to mathematics. Diagrams gave an accessible entry point but did not by themselves dissolve the deep conceptual hurdles.
arxiv-2511-21643:
Gernot Akemann, Yan Fyodorov, and Dmitry Savin solve a random matrix ensemble that models open, lossy quantum systems, in 2025. Non-Hermitian random matrices describe dissipative quantum chaos and wave transport in complex media. The complex symmetric class, labeled AI-dagger, had resisted the exact analysis available for the classic Ginibre ensembles. Eigenvectors of such matrices are not orthogonal, and their overlaps control physical responses.

Using a framework recently proposed by Fyodorov, the team derives a closed-form joint distribution for a complex eigenvalue together with its right eigenvector. The result holds for any matrix size of two or more, across the whole complex plane. From it flow the overlap distribution and the mean eigenvalue density, at finite size and in the large-size limit. At the spectral edge, both quantities behave differently from the Ginibre universality class. Simulations with Bernoulli entries support the claim of universality.
arxiv-2511-21743:
Mukul Singh and three coauthors track how a language model's visible reasoning changes as fine-tuning turns it from novice to expert, in 2025. Reasoning tokens, the intermediate steps a model writes while solving, resemble human working memory. Cognitive science describes skill learning through four stages of competence, from failing blindly to performing without conscious steps.

The authors find models walk the same path. At first they answer wrongly with no reasoning. Then reasoning appears but answers still fail. Next, reasoning works, and its length peaks at this conscious-competence stage. Finally the model internalizes the task: reasoning shrinks away while accuracy holds. Even when reasoning is removed after training, performance persists, showing it scaffolded learning rather than propping it up. The practical payoff is diagnostic. Reasoning-length curves can signal which training stage a model sits in, flag convergence, and guide early stopping, turning model behavior into a training instrument.
arxiv-2511-21843:
Xi and colleagues build FLAWS, a benchmark testing whether AI language models can find serious errors in scientific papers. Human reviewers miss major mistakes, and output grows faster than the expert pool. The benchmark contains 713 paper-error pairs, made by using language models to insert errors that invalidate a paper's key claims into already peer-reviewed papers, inserted carefully, so spotting them takes real understanding.

An automated score checks whether a model identifies an error and locates it in the text. The team tested five frontier models, including GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and two others, on the benchmark set. GPT-5 did best, reaching 39.1 percent identification accuracy when allowed ten top-ranked candidate locations per paper in the evaluation setup. Even the strongest models thus miss most planted errors, so AI peer review has far to go.
arxiv-2511-22043:
Liu, Li, Xin, and colleagues present SwordRiding, a navigation framework that lets quadrotor drones fly through unknown, cluttered environments in real time. Most existing planners work open-loop: they compute a path, then follow it blindly. So wind gusts and surprises can push the drone off course. SwordRiding instead navigates in closed loop, continuously steering by a guiding vector field rebuilt online from what the drone's sensors currently see around it.

Onboard perception builds a signed distance map of obstacles, a global planner proposes collision-free waypoints. B-spline smoothing turns them into a feasible reference trajectory from which the adaptive vector field is synthesized, keeping compatibility with standard planning algorithms. In extensive simulations and real-world flights the system shows stronger robustness against external disturbances and better real-time performance than conventional approaches, including earlier guiding-vector-field methods tied to continuous paths.
arxiv-2511-22143:
An author team stacks fine-tuned convolutional networks into an ensemble that grades knee osteoarthritis severity from X-rays. A judgment clinicians make on the five-level Kellgren-Lawrence scale, from grade 0, no disease, to grade 4, severe. Manual grading is expert, slow, and subjective, yet early detection matters because treatments can only slow the disease. Three diverse pretrained networks, MobileNetV2, YOLOv8, and DenseNet201, serve as base learners, and a CatBoost model learns how to combine their verdicts.

Trained and tested on the Osteoarthritis Initiative dataset of 9,786 images spread unevenly across the five grades. The ensemble handles two tasks: binary detection of whether osteoarthritis is present, reaching 87.5 percent balanced test accuracy. Full five-grade classification, reaching 73 percent balanced accuracy, both above prior published results the authors compare against. Proposed extensions include bagging, feature-level meta-learning, and transformer-based backbones with more compute.
arxiv-2511-22343:
Dogoulis, Alizadeh, Kubler, and Cordy, power systems and machine learning researchers, fix neural power-flow surrogates at run time instead of trusting their raw output. Learned surrogates solve AC power flow far faster than numerical solvers. Their predictions often violate the physical equations and operating limits, which grid operators cannot accept. Their physics-informed test-time training takes a few gradient steps on each fresh prediction, refining it against the AC power flow equalities and operational constraints directly at inference, with no labeled data needed.

Across the IEEE 14-, 118-, and 300-bus systems and the PEGASE 1354-bus network, the refinement cuts residuals and constraint violations by one to two orders of magnitude versus purely learned models. It keeps the speed advantage over traditional solvers. Grid software gains predictions that are fast and physically reliable at once.
arxiv-2511-22643:
Wu builds a causal framework for settings where treatments spill over between peers. Standard analysis assumes one person's outcome depends only on their own treatment. That fails among friends, classmates, or competing firms, where peers' choices affect outcomes and decisions. Wu generalises the local average and marginal treatment effect frameworks to this world, defining controlled spillover and direct effects, in local average and marginal versions, for people whose behaviour responds to instruments.

Sufficient conditions are given for point identification of the local effects without restricting instrument support, clarifying why earlier binary-instrument studies needed extra restrictions. The marginal effects are nonparametrically point identified from continuous instrument variation, no functional form imposed on outcomes or unobserved trait distributions, and are building blocks for many policy-relevant effects. Estimators, semiparametric and parametric, are developed and applied to Add Health data, uncovering heterogeneity in education spillovers within best-friend networks.
arxiv-2511-22843:
Lee and colleagues expose a cheat in knowledge-based visual question answering benchmarks. In existing benchmarks, the query image almost always depicts the main subject of the answer's document, so models score well from visual matching alone. Real questions break that pattern: which beetle feeds on a pictured plant requires a document about the beetle, not the plant. The authors built RETINA to force the realistic setting.

RETINA, built automatically with a language-model pipeline, pairs queries about secondary, related entities with images of those entities: 120 thousand training examples and a 2 thousand human-curated test set. Existing models dropped significantly on it, confirming their reliance on the shortcut. They also propose MIMIR, a retriever enriching document embeddings with images of multiple related entities, handling RETINA effectively where prior retrievers fail. The pair resets expectations for what multimodal question answering systems actually know.
arxiv-2511-22943:
Xiao and colleagues teach AI systems to draw visual puns from idioms. The pictures show both the literal and the figurative meaning of a phrase at once, like butterflies for nervous butterflies in a stomach. No large public test set existed for measuring this skill, and one-shot image generators often miss the figurative side of an idiom entirely.

Their system loops three models together: a language model writes a detailed prompt, an image model draws it. And a multimodal model tries to guess the idiom from the picture, with the prompt revised until the guess succeeds. Using 1,000 idioms, they built a benchmark dataset and tested 10 language models and 10 multimodal models. They found that the multimodal choice mattered most, GPT scored highest, and Claude wrote the strongest prompts. Most improvement arrived within two or three refinement rounds in their experiments.
arxiv-2511-23043:
Nordhagen and colleagues present Bris, a data-driven weather model that produces probabilistic forecasts, an ensemble of many plausible futures rather than one best guess. Its stretched grid spends fine detail where it matters, resolving 2.5 kilometers over a region of interest while covering the rest of the globe at 31 kilometers. And it predicts 87 weather variables at any ensemble size.

The model is a stochastic encoder-decoder trained with a score called CRPS, applied both point by point and across spatial scales. And the across-scales part proved necessary to keep forecast fields spatially coherent instead of blotchy. Against the operational MEPS ensemble used in Scandinavia, Bris was competitive overall and scored up to 15 percent better on two-meter temperature at some lead times. And it has run operationally at MET Norway four times a day since October 2025.
arxiv-2511-23243:
Ethier builds a neural network that predicts not just how much a radio signal weakens along a link, but how uncertain that prediction is for this link. Path loss models, classical formulas and learned ones, assume the error spread is the same everywhere. Uncertainty depends on frequency, distance, and obstructions. The network is trained with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood to output a mean and a link-specific variance together.

Comparing shared, partially shared, and independent-parameter architectures on blind test sets from large public drive-test datasets, the shared design won on accuracy, calibration, and sharpness together. It reached a root-mean-square error of 7.4 dB with 95.1 percent coverage for its 95 percent prediction intervals and a mean interval width of 29.6 dB in the reported tests, close enough to honest to support per-link coverage margins and to flag where the model itself is weak.
arxiv-2511-23343:
Glücksam and Pardo-Simón construct entire functions whose dynamics contain a wandering domain of a shape and slowness prescribed in advance. Two controls that earlier constructions could not achieve together. A wandering domain is a region whose successive images under the function never return or overlap, a phenomenon rational maps cannot have. And the team shows any bounded simply connected domain with analytic boundary can serve as one.

For every prescribed order of growth strictly between zero and one, their construction realizes the chosen domain as a wandering domain of an entire function of exactly that order. With the iterates staying one-to-one on the domain throughout its wanderings. The results extend earlier work by Boc Thaler and give the first examples of bounded simply connected wandering domains for every order below one half. Pushing transcendental dynamics toward the slowest growth that still permits such behavior.
arxiv-2511-23443:
Huang and Li prove that sine activations are fundamentally better matched than ReLU to periodic tasks. Using modular addition, adding numbers modulo p, as the testbed for two-layer networks. They establish a sharp expressivity gap, since sine networks realize the task exactly with width just 2 for any fixed input length. And with bias terms the same width 2 works uniformly across all lengths simultaneously in theory.

ReLU networks, by contrast, need width growing linearly with the input length just to interpolate. And cannot fit two lengths whose residues differ at the same time, a hard structural failure. The authors add a Natarajan-dimension generalization bound giving nearly optimal sample complexity on the order of p for constant-width sine networks. Plus width-independent margin bounds, and experiments confirm sine networks generalize better and extrapolate strongly to longer inputs in practice.
arxiv-2512-00343:
Vision-language models such as CLIP are powerful, but they are also vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Zhongqi Wang and Jie Zhang study model-level backdoor detection for these pretrained models in 2025, under the banner that assimilation matters. A poisoned model behaves normally until a trigger appears.

Given a model fine-tuned by an untrusted third party, deciding whether a backdoor was injected is critical and challenging. Detection protects organizations that download models they did not train. The study speaks to a growing supply-chain problem in AI, where a single tampered model can compromise every application built on it. Backdoors are typically planted during fine-tuning, which is exactly the stage users outsource.
arxiv-2512-00643:
Milan Krömer and Stefan Müller wrote a 2025 paper on the math of elastic rods. Non-Euclidean elasticity studies bodies that have no stress-free shape they can fully relax into. The theory began with metal plasticity and dislocations, where inner strain is built in from the start.

Lately the same ideas have drawn interest in biomechanics, for living tissues that grow unevenly. Krömer and Müller focus on rods, the thin, one-dimensional case. They connect rod models to almost isometric embeddings of geodesic tubes, ways of placing curved tubes into space with little stretching. Their results help ground rod theories in careful math.
arxiv-2512-00943:
Jasveer Singh and Vardarajan Suneeta compute how nonlinear black hole vibrations can be in a 2025 paper. When a black hole is disturbed, it rings with characteristic tones called quasinormal modes. At second order, pairs of tones mix and produce quadratic modes, whose strength relative to the linear tones is the nonlinearity ratio.

Measuring that ratio tells physicists how far linear theory can be trusted for real signals. The authors revisit an analytic approximation scheme for computing these ratios. A reliable, fast scheme helps analysts interpret gravitational wave ringdowns without huge simulations, and tests where perturbation theory starts to break.
arxiv-2512-01043:
Thomas Bahder works through a classic problem in detail in a 2025 physics paper. The problem asks for the photon modes, the allowed patterns of light, inside a spherical cavity. It is iconic in electromagnetism, yet the literature reports conflicting answers for it.

Bahder starts from the Maxwell equations, the fundamental laws of electromagnetism. He applies the boundary conditions at the surface of the surrounding perfect conductor, where the field must behave in a specific way. By solving the problem carefully from scratch, the paper aims to settle which reported result is right. A clean reference solution helps students and researchers alike.
arxiv-2512-01343:
Shashank Landge and co-authors tackle the size of large language models. Big models are hard to run on cheap hardware. One fix shrinks each weight to fewer bits. If all weights shrink the same way, key weights get hurt and skill drops.

Their method keeps the most key weights at higher care. It uses a math split of each weight block to judge which parts matter most. Parts with strong inner form get more bits. The rest get fewer. This mixed plan aims to keep skill high while the model stays small enough for plain machines.
arxiv-2512-01443:
Xabier de Zuazo and co-authors decode brain waves for speech tasks. They used MEG, which tracks magnetic fields from the brain. Their entry targets a 2025 contest on the LibriBrain data set. Two tasks count: spotting speech and sorting speech sounds.

Their decoder is based on the Conformer model. It reads raw signals from hundreds of sensors at once. A light front layer shapes the input for each task. A form of data warping made for MEG was also tried. Strong decoders could one day aid speech aids for users who cannot speak.
arxiv-2512-01543:
Tomassini and co-authors study the binary star AFGL 4106 and its nebula with the SPHERE tool. The star is past its red supergiant phase. Its mass loss shaped a complex cloud around it. A companion star makes that loss harder to model.

SPHERE on the Very Large Telescope gives sharp views of the cloud. The team maps the cloud's form and the pair's traits. Those maps test how binary acts steer mass loss. They also show what yields the pair sends into space, which seed new stars and planets. Nebula maps also trace past outbursts, since each shell in the cloud marks an era when the star shed mass at a higher rate.
arxiv-2512-01843:
Zeqing Wang, Keze Wang, and Lei Zhang test whether text-to-video models obey physics. Video generators have grown in quality, length, and instruction following. Whether they grasp physics is open. Implausible motion can still look smooth at a glance.

Their PhyDetEx tool detects and explains physical plausibility in generated clips. It flags where motion breaks real laws. Explanations state what went wrong in plain terms. Physics-aware scores push generators toward clips that could train robots or teach science without false cues. Explanations name the broken law, like gravity or rigidity, which gives model builders a defect list they can train against next round.
arxiv-2512-02243:
Phishing pages steal credentials by impersonating trusted sites, and they increasingly hide behind obfuscated code and visual trickery. Md. Abdul Ahad Minhaz, Zannatul Zahan Meem, and Md. Shohrab Hossain present PhishSnap in 2025, an on-device detection system that judges a page by how it looks.

The system uses perceptual hashing, a fingerprint that captures a page's visual appearance and survives small changes. Because detection happens on the device, it preserves privacy instead of sending browsing data to a server. URL and HTML based detectors struggle against visual deception, so checking the picture itself attacks phishing where it actually deceives people.
arxiv-2512-02343:
A point that returns to itself after a fixed number of steps under a map is called periodic, and number fields measure the arithmetic cost of such points. Tien-Cuong Dinh and Jit Wu Yap prove in 2025 an exponential lower bound on that cost for polarized endomorphisms of smooth projective varieties.

The result extends earlier bounds to higher dimensions, covering maps of degree at least two on varieties over a number field. Galois orbits grow at least exponentially with the period, which limits how many low-cost periodic points a map can have. Such bounds feed the arithmetic dynamics program, which studies number theory through repeated maps the way dynamics studies motion.
arxiv-2512-03143:
Quasars from the dawn of time shine across the universe. M. Costa and co-authors study dust in the host galaxies of such quasars in this 2025 work. These bright objects help trace how giant black holes and their galaxies grew together early on.

The team uses infrared light from a quasar host at very high redshift. From that light they estimate the physical traits of its dust directly. Dust tells how fast stars form and how rich the gas is in heavy elements. Such clues help map galaxy growth in the first billion years. Dust measures also help date when heavy elements first spread through young galaxies.
arxiv-2512-03243:
Telling new behavior from normal behavior is a core task in data work. Ioannis Gasteratos and co-authors frame that task on path space in this 2025 work. Paths are sequences over time, like price curves or motion traces.

They treat novelty detection as a hypothesis test with signature-based statistics. Signatures summarize a path in a compact way. Using cost inequalities, they bound false positive rates beyond the Gaussian case. Reliable novelty flags help in finance, medicine, and engineering, where rare events can signal trouble. Tail bounds matter, since a novelty alarm that fires too often soon gets ignored.
arxiv-2512-03343:
Language models pick words one by one, which can blur ideas. Darshan Fofadiya proposes Idea-Gated Transformers in this 2025 work. He notes that people form abstract ideas first, then choose words to express them.

Standard models merge those two steps into next-token prediction. His design prunes the vocabulary in a differentiable way to enforce semantic coherence. Gating word choice by ideas could make text more consistent over long passages. The work explores a more human-like split in how models generate language. Vocabulary pruning is the gate, cutting words that do not fit the active idea.
arxiv-2512-03443:
Large magnetic fields shape how accretion disks evolve. Hongzhe Zhou, Yosuke Mizuno, and Zhenyu Zhu present a subgrid dynamo model in this 2025 work. Such fields drive turbulence, reconnection, and outflows from disks around black holes and young stars.

Simulations show the starting field strength and shape leave a direct imprint on outcomes. Resolving the dynamo that builds fields is too costly at full scale. Their model adds dynamical quenching inside general relativistic simulations. That lets big simulations include field growth more faithfully. Quenching stops runaway field growth, keeping simulated disks in a realistic balance.
arxiv-2512-03543:
Extreme events in many variables at once are hard to model. Pavel Krupskii and Boris Béranger present factor models for them in this 2025 work. Models must extrapolate beyond observed data, so their shape matters a lot.

Real extremes need flexibility, especially for asymmetric dependence between variables. They also need parsimony, few parameters, for clarity and for scaling to high dimensions. Factor models aim to give both. Better extreme models help in climate risk, finance, and insurance planning. Asymmetric dependence means crashes cluster while booms do not, a pattern factor models must capture to serve risk work well.
arxiv-2512-03743:
A robot hand that can rotate an object between its fingers needs the right shape as much as the right software. Kehlani Fay and colleagues present House of Dextra in a 2025 robotics preprint, a framework that designs the hand and its controller together. The field lacks agreement on which designs best support dexterous tasks, so the authors let the task decide.

Their search space covers joints, fingers, and palms, generating many candidate morphologies. A shared control approach, conditioned on each design, makes it feasible to evaluate that wide space at scale. Winning designs are built from accessible parts for real-world testing, including in-hand rotation trials in simulation and on hardware. The full pipeline, from design to deployed hand, runs in under a day. The framework and the hands it produced are released openly for other groups to reuse.
arxiv-2512-03843:
Geometric intersection graphs turn shapes into networks: each vertex is an object, and edges mark pairs that overlap. Malory Marin, Jean-Florent Raymond, and Rémi Watrigant design algorithms for path and cycle problems on such graphs in a 2025 preprint. Their setting uses similarly sized fat objects in multi-dimensional space, a class where exact solutions are usually far too slow.

The key invention is a lambda-linked partition, which splits vertices into groups whose members are highly connected to each other. It can be computed quickly and, remarkably, without ever seeing the geometric layout. With that tool the authors deliver the first robust, provably tight subexponential algorithms for Hamiltonian path and cycle. The result settles an open problem from 2018. They also build a randomised algorithm for long paths. A structural covering theorem for this graph family may serve other researchers.
arxiv-2512-04343:
Satyajit Movidi and Stephen Russell probe a trade-off they call the personalization paradox, using a student advising assistant named AIVisor. The assistant is an agentic system that fetches records and answers with a large language model. Making answers personal sounds like a pure win. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests whether that holds across many scoring dimensions at once.

The team posed a dozen real advising questions built to stress exact wording. They ran ten setups, with and without personalization, and scored word overlap, meaning match, and faithfulness to sources. Personal answers reasoned better and stayed closer to source facts. Yet they scored worse on meaning match with stock reference answers. The shortfall came from the metrics, which punish fair personal twists away from generic text. The finding warns that standard scoring is a poor judge of personal help.
arxiv-2512-04943:
Novanto Yudistira introduces an adaptive fusion method that teaches networks to recognize human actions by weighing several senses at once. Video alone can miss what sound or depth would reveal. His 2025 arXiv paper fuses four streams: ordinary color video, optical flow, audio, and depth. The hard part is balance, since the most useful stream changes from action to action and moment to moment.

Gating mechanisms act as learned mixers, turning each stream's share up or down as evidence warrants. Yudistira surveys many gated and weighted fusion designs to find the strongest recipe. The adaptive blend beat single-stream recognition in accuracy and held up better when one stream degraded. Such selective fusion suits surveillance, sports analysis, and home robots, where no single sense can be trusted alone.
arxiv-2512-05343:
Elisabetta Fedele and five co-authors introduce SpaceControl, a way to steer three-dimensional asset generation with geometry instead of words. Text prompts are vague and images are awkward to edit precisely, so generated objects often miss the intended shape. SpaceControl accepts explicit spatial input — anything from coarse primitive blocks to detailed meshes — and imposes it on modern generative models at test time, with no added training.

A single control knob lets the user trade fidelity of shape against realism. In measured evaluations and user studies, the method beats both training-based and optimization-based baselines on faithfulness to the requested geometry while keeping visual quality high. The authors also built an interactive interface for editing with deformable building blocks and generating assets in real time. The work points toward three-dimensional creation tools where designers sculpt the rough shape and let the model sweat the surface.
arxiv-2512-06043: Yongjie Pan, Baocheng Zhang, and Qingyu Cai ask whether a new effect can shield quantum entanglement from heat. Two detectors accelerated through a thermal field steadily lose their entanglement to the warmth, and no experiment can remove that background. Acceleration induced transparency, known to amplify a detector's response, is tested as a counterweight. The thermal field does erode the link, as expected. But the transparency effect protects it effectively. For Unruh hunters, that survival brings laboratory tests closer.
arxiv-2512-06143:
Marcus Noack and four co-authors refuse the usual bargain of large scale Gaussian processes: give up exactness, or give up scale. Exact training collapses under its own algebra long before a million points. Standard workarounds all approximate, and restrict kernel choice.

gp2Scale chooses kernels that are non-stationary and compactly supported. Sparse covariance carries exact computation past ten million points. It often beats the approximations outright. Any kernel, noise, and mean can be customized. Modelers can design the process the science wants. Speed, accuracy, and freedom are the three prizes.
arxiv-2512-06243:
Rohan Pandey and Eric Ye test whether shrinking a neural network for real world use can quietly break the guards that keep it safe. Many vision models are compressed by rounding their numbers to fewer bits, which saves memory and time. At the same time, hidden backdoor attacks can plant a secret trigger in a model, so it acts normal until it sees that trigger.

The team ran five known defenses against one standard backdoor attack, at three levels of compression, on two image data sets. At mid level compression, every defense stopped finding the attack, while the attack still worked almost every time. At the deepest compression, results split by data set, with one defense holding on one set and failing on the other. The study warns that safety checks done on full size models say little about the small models that actually ship.
arxiv-2512-06343:
Tong Xie and five co authors find a hidden skew in how reward models learn from human choices. Reward models score answers so that chatbots can be trained to please people. The standard training loss compares a chosen answer with a rejected one and nudges the model to rank the chosen one higher. That sounds clean, but the push each pair gives turns out to depend on more than whether the ranking was wrong.

Pairs whose inner wordings sit far apart get outsized pushes, while close pairs get weak ones even when they are ranked wrong. That is a problem, because close pairs are where fine taste lives. The team answers with NormBT, a fix that rescales each pair's update to even out the distance effect. Learning then heeds the ranking error itself, not the gap between the two answers' inner codes.
arxiv-2512-06443:
Xiangyu Li and five co authors speed up huge language models running on small devices, such as phones. To fit, the models are stored at very low bit counts, and a lookup table method lets a plain processor run them faster than a graphics chip. The snag appears when many tokens are handled at once, as in filling a prompt or scaling up test time trials. The old table method fetches memory in scattered scraps for each token, wasting bandwidth.

Their vector table method builds one shared table across the parallel tokens and does a single wide lookup per index. A new tensor layout built for that flow, plus cache aware streamed lookups, make it run well. Across five edge devices and three models, the method beat leading rivals by up to several fold. The code is folded into the llama.cpp project.
arxiv-2512-07243:
Anamika Singh and Abhay Kumar Singh extend a thrifty idea in error correction to the messiest kind of channel, one that inserts and deletes symbols. Classical codes protect a whole message; function-correcting codes protect only a chosen function of the message, spending far less redundancy when the rest does not matter. That economy suits DNA data storage and document exchange, where insertions and deletions are the natural errors.

The authors define function-correcting codes for insertion channels, deletion channels, and the combined insdel channel, then prove the three notions are actually equivalent. With distance matrices and irregular codes in hand, they bound the best redundancy such codes can achieve from both sides, including bounds in the style of two classic coding results. A simplified lower bound on optimal redundancy follows. Finally they price the redundancy for several concrete functions.
arxiv-2512-07643:
Ganesh Subramaniam, Avik De, and Jackson Levi Said wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on a modified theory of gravity. In non-metricity gravity, the way lengths change during transport drives the gravitational effect. Their version couples that quantity to a living scalar field.

Earlier work in this family mostly tracked smooth background expansion.  A full treatment of scalar wobbles in the coupled theory was missing. The authors derive the complete set of perturbed field equations. Under a quasi-static approximation, they extract the effective Poisson equation. A modified gravitational constant comes with that equation. Those pieces yield the density contrast equation. They then analyze how fast matter clumps and what growth index follows. Numerical checks show the theory tracks the standard cosmological model fairly closely. The work sets up tests against large-scale structure surveys.
arxiv-2512-07743:
Thomas DeGrand wrote this 2025 review chapter on lattice fermions in quantum chromodynamics. Simulating quarks on a space-time grid demands care with their spin and symmetry. Fermions obeying the Ginsparg-Wilson relation offer an elegant way through that thicket.

The chapter reviews the physics of those special lattice fermions. It explains how they connect to domain wall fermions, their close cousins. Domain wall designs add a fifth dimension to protect the same symmetry. The heart of the chapter is practical simulation methodology. Overlap fermions are the working realization of the Ginsparg-Wilson idea. DeGrand lays out how to run numerical simulations with them.  The chapter appears in an online book marking fifty years of lattice QCD. Its audience is researchers entering or using the overlap fermion craft. As a single-author review, it distills decades of method into one place.
arxiv-2512-07843:
Long Lian and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on making reasoning faster. Models think better when allowed more inference-time computation. Step-by-step decoding, though, is inherently slow, one token after another.

Earlier parallel schemes lost accuracy against their sequential cousins. They also demanded specialized inference engines to run at all. ThreadWeaver closes both gaps with three linked innovations. A two-stage generator produces high-quality parallel reasoning traces for fine-tuning. A trie-based rollout lets ordinary autoregressive engines run the parallel style. A reinforcement stage then teaches the balance between accuracy and parallel gain. The model learns when splitting thought helps and when it hurts. On six hard mathematics benchmarks, the tuned model matches top sequential rivals. Token latency drops by a wide margin at the same time.  Parallel thought need not mean sloppy thought.
arxiv-2512-07943:
Aris Tritsis wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper questioning a number astronomers rely on. The mass-to-flux ratio weighs gravity against magnetic support inside a molecular cloud. That balance decides whether the cloud collapses and where stars can form.

Tritsis asks how faithfully observers can recover the true ratio from outside. His laboratory is a simulated turbulent cloud, collapsing under its own weight. The simulation includes magnetic fields, chemistry, and motion in three dimensions. He views the fake cloud from many angles and at several life stages. The standard magnetic field versus column density relation supplies the mock measurement. Projection effects turn out to distort the answer severely. When the field lies mostly in the sky's plane, Zeeman readings overshoot hugely. They can pass the true ratio by more than tenfold in that geometry. Such measurements should be read as upper limits only, he warns.
arxiv-2512-08143:
Ali Lotfi Rezaabad, Bikram Khanal, Shashwat Chaurasia, and colleagues, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, PolyLingua, detects which language a short user request is written in. That first step matters for chatbots and voice assistants, and errors there cascade into later failures, as when a song title is in a different language than the request itself.

PolyLingua is a light transformer model trained with a two level contrastive method. One level separates single examples, while the other aligns whole language classes with adaptive margins, giving compact, well separated representations even for close languages. On a multilingual assistant dataset and a music request dataset with frequent code switching, it beat a large commercial language model. It did so with about ten times fewer parameters. That makes it a good fit for settings where speed and computing budget are tight.
arxiv-2512-08443:
Hithem Lamri and Michail Maniatakos, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about machine unlearning without any central server. Unlearning removes the influence of chosen data from a trained model, for privacy requests or to purge poisoned data. Certified versions carry privacy style guarantees, but only for central or server led setups, not for peers talking among themselves.

Their procedure, RR DU, runs as a random walk across the network. At the client asking to forget, it steps uphill on the forget set. Elsewhere it takes a random number of downhill steps on retained data, with noise added and the model kept inside a trust region. They prove convergence in the convex case and formal unlearning certificates for what each client sees. On image tests, it hit its privacy target with higher accuracy than decentralized private baselines, driving forgotten data accuracy down to random guessing.
arxiv-2512-08543:
Ivan Kostyuk, Stefano Carniani, Mahsa Kohandel, and Andrea Pallottini, astronomers, posted a simulation study on arXiv in December 2025. Webb telescope observations recently found warm ionized outflows in small galaxies of the early universe, but in fewer galaxies than simulations predict. The team asks whether the missing outflows are really missing, or just hard to see from certain angles.

They identify outflows in tens of thousands of simulated galaxies from the TNG50 and SERRA projects, using a mixture model over gas velocity, star formation, and position. Simulated outflow masses broadly matched the Webb survey values, though telescopes likely catch only part of the full wind. Simulated speeds, though, ran about ten times lower than observed, a real tension. Viewing angle mattered: face on galaxies showed detectable outflows more often than edge on ones, and the gap grew for massive disks. Part of the observation gap, they conclude, is geometry, not physics.
arxiv-2512-08743:
Shuyue Hu and coauthors argue that foundation models need native skill at working in multi agent settings, not just single agent tasks. Recent work has added single agent abilities such as interface use and tool use. The authors name four core abilities for multi agent work: understanding, planning, efficient communication, and adaptation to others.

Across many large language models and several hard benchmarks, they find that scaling single agent performance alone does not yield robust multi agent skill. That gap challenges a common assumption that such skill will emerge on its own. To close it, the authors outline research directions covering data construction, evaluation, training methods, and safety. Their message is that multi agent intelligence should be built and tested directly, rather than hoped for as a side effect of larger single agent models.
arxiv-2512-08943:
Singon Kim presents a method to make abstractive compression in retrieval augmented generation more robust to noisy retrieved texts. Compression with a smaller model condenses query relevant context and cuts compute cost. Retrieved texts often contain irrelevant or factually wrong passages, even when their relevance scores are high. Compressors can then drop facts that the correct answer needs.

The proposed method, ACoRN, sorts retrieved documents in a finer grained way and adds two training steps. Offline data augmentation teaches the compressor to handle two distinct types of retrieval noise. Fine tuning then centers summaries on key facts that support the correct answer, countering positional bias across texts. Tests show a large model trained this way improves exact match and F scores while preserving the answer string. Gains are strongest on data sets with many misleading texts.
arxiv-2512-09043:
Haoyang Gao and coauthors present a method to tune interactions directly in a strongly interacting ensemble of spins in diamond, for use in quantum sensing and many body physics. The spins are nitrogen vacancy centers, a leading solid state platform. Standard Floquet engineering can control dipolar interactions, but it usually weakens both the spin coupling and the coupling to the field being sensed, limiting sensitivity.

Their approach encodes qubits in dressed states under a magnetic field set perpendicular to the crystal axis. That encoding tunes the native interaction without the usual loss. The dimensionless coherence measure improves several fold over leading Floquet methods, and sensitivity in alternating field magnetometry improves by a similar factor. With the longer coherence, the team probes spin transport at intermediate to late times. The results give a powerful Hamiltonian engineering tool for nitrogen vacancy ensembles and for other interacting systems with higher spin.
arxiv-2512-09143:
Andrew Mummery and coauthors propose calorimetric tests of theories for the bright optical flares of tidal disruption events,. The population properties of those flares are now well mapped, and the origin of their X ray and long lived ultraviolet emission is fairly understood. The source of the early optical and ultraviolet light, by contrast, remains debated.

Each theory predicts how total radiated energy and peak brightness should scale with black hole mass. The authors contrast those predictions with the observed positive scaling in the data. No single theory describes observations across all black hole masses. Disk reprocessing and disk formation energy models perform best, but still need extension. Models that tie the flare directly to shocks between debris streams, or that scale light with the fallback rate, are ruled out at high significance. Calorimetry, proves a sharp discriminator.
arxiv-2512-09343:
Ashik E Rasul and seven co-authors describe the design and testing of a long-range QuadPlane that lands itself using vision. A QuadPlane mixes fixed-wing cruising with quadcopter-style lift, suiting it to long autonomous missions. Landing is the weak point: real sites are unstructured, GPS may be denied, and the aircraft must spot a safe spot on its own.

The team built a lightweight platform around those constraints. Neural networks learn landing-site features that generalize across varied visual conditions, while visual-inertial odometry estimates position during descent without GPS. Computing runs on a small edge device, so the whole perception and control stack had to be optimized for real-time use. Large QuadPlanes also respond slowly and carry heavy inertia, which complicates the final approach. The paper lays out the hardware, sensors, and embedded architecture as a foundation for autonomous landing in cluttered, GPS-denied places.
arxiv-2512-09443:
Chenyi Li and colleagues propose a workflow for doing mathematics with language models without giving up rigor. Language models can search for proofs and suggest theorems, but their output is not automatically trustworthy. The authors' answer is a human-in-the-loop process in which experts keep control of the problem's formulation and assumptions.

Within the workflow, the model hunts for proofs or contradictions, proposes candidate properties and theorems, and helps build structures meeting explicit constraints, backed by numerical experiments and checks. Experts treat that output as raw material, refining it into precise statements and rigorous proofs. The main case study connects manifold optimization with Grover's quantum search algorithm. It identifies invariant subspaces and search-compatible ways of moving on curved spaces, and uses a convergence analysis from companion work to show the refinement stage. The paper also documents failed and corrected routes, with an analysis of failure modes.
arxiv-2512-09643:
Sarah Thiele and colleagues introduce the CRASH Clock, a measure of how stressed Earth's orbit has become. The number of orbiting objects is climbing fast, driven by megaconstellations that launch and dispose of satellites rapidly, on top of satellite growth. Debris, collision risk, casualty risk, and pollution of the optical and radio spectrum all grow with it, and the authors wanted a timescale expressing the danger.

The CRASH Clock estimates how quickly a catastrophic collision could occur if satellites stopped maneuvering or situational awareness were lost, for instance during a solar storm. As of June 2025 they calculate it at about five and a half days, and falling. In 2018, before the megaconstellation era, it stood at one hundred sixty-four days. The contrast means a disruptive event now leaves far less time to recover control before collisions could cascade, which the authors present as an argument for better orbital management.
arxiv-2512-09743:
Luana N. Padilha and Rita C. Anjos model how massive star clusters contribute to the high-energy gamma rays observed across the Galaxy. Such clusters host many stellar winds and supernova remnants whose shock waves can accelerate protons to extreme energies. Those protons then produce gamma rays when they strike gas. The question is how much of the Galaxy's gamma-ray glow, up to the highest energies, clusters can explain.

They consider two populations: dispersed clusters and younger, compact massive clusters, both hosting supernova remnant shocks. Clusters within three kiloparsecs of the solar system are identified as the contributors. Using analytical methods, they calculate proton energy spectra and gamma-ray production rates for these populations. Their findings suggest young, compact clusters contribute emission from multi-tera-electronvolt up to peta-electronvolt energies, with the share coming from nearby populations, strengthening the case that star clusters are cosmic ray sources.
arxiv-2512-09943: Viktoriia Omelchenko calculates how fast charged particles scatter off a single wall carbon nanotube of zigzag type. The tube's atoms form a zigzag pattern around it. She obtains cross sections, which give the chance of scattering into each direction. The math covers tubes held at varied angles to the incoming beam. Two standard tools do the work: the eikonal approach from quantum electrodynamics, suited to fast particles, and the smooth potential approach, which treats the tube's atoms as a steady field.
arxiv-2512-10043:
João Lucas Luz Lima Sarcinelli and Diego Furtado Silva combine several language models to find named entities in Portuguese text. Named entity recognition, spotting people, places, and organizations, is a workhorse task. Language models are oddly weak at it, especially in lower resource languages like Portuguese. No single open model wins everywhere, which motivates an ensemble. Their pipeline runs three steps using similarly capable models deployed locally, with no task specific fine tuning and no labeled examples for the target task.

A heuristic picks good model combinations using minimal annotated data. On four of five Portuguese datasets, the ensemble beat every individual model. Ensembles tuned on one dataset also transferred: on new datasets they generally beat single models, suggesting labeled data for the new task may be unnecessary. The approach speaks to practical settings where data cannot leave the building and annotation budgets are tiny. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2512-10543:
O Benvenuto and co-authors review how stars evolve when they have a close companion. A single star can swell freely as its interior chemistry changes, but a star in a binary cannot grow past its Roche lobe. So the pair is forced to trade mass through the inner Lagrangian point. That one constraint rewrites both stars' lives.

The review walks through the standard picture for a normal donor with a compact companion. And shows where it fails, notably for binary pulsars, where it predicts long mass transfer that is not seen. Irradiation feedback and evaporation models are examined next. For black hole systems, the authors argue binary interaction cannot spin up a black hole born without rotation, so spin must be a birth property. They close with blue straggler stars in clusters and weigh mass transfer as their origin.
arxiv-2512-10643:
Tong Liu and co-authors speed up the classical simulation of bosonic Gaussian states, the states behind quantum optics and the famous Gaussian boson sampling experiments. Such states are easy to describe in the Gaussian formalism, but sampling from them requires amplitudes in the occupation basis. And that step runs into the hafnian, a famously expensive function to compute.

Their algorithm converts a pure bosonic Gaussian state into a matrix product state. It never computes a hafnian. It combines a Gaussian singular value decomposition with a projected creation-operator mapping. That mapping builds the local tensors directly. Benchmarked on the covariance matrices from the Jiuzhang 2.0 and 4.0 experiments, it beat earlier tensor-network methods clearly in the low-entanglement regime that lossy real devices live in. In that regime the needed bond dimension stays manageable, widening the reach of matrix product methods for bosonic systems.
arxiv-2512-10943:
Sharath Girish and co-authors give video makers a sense of timing. Subject-driven tools can place your chosen characters or objects into a synthesised video. But existing tools cannot say when each subject appears or vanishes, a control that storyboarding, synthesis, and animation all need. AlcheMinT adds explicit timestamps as a condition of generation.

A new positional encoding scheme encodes whole temporal intervals and ties each interval to a subject's identity, while slotting cleanly into the pretrained video model's own positional embeddings. Extra text tokens bind each visual identity to its caption, cutting mix-ups when several subjects share a scene. Joining token-wise keeps the design light, with no added cross-attention modules and tiny parameter overhead. On their new benchmark for keeping identity, fidelity, and timing, quality matched leading methods while precise multi-subject timing arrived for the first time.
arxiv-2512-11043:
Isabel Angelo, Erik Petigura, and Megan Bedell test whether data driven models of starlight can reveal hidden companion stars. Some stars that look single are actually close pairs whose light blends into one spectrum. Finding them needs models accurate enough to spot the faint second star's contribution.

The team trained a model called The Cannon on high resolution spectra from the Keck telescope, adding a wavelet processing step before training. The model predicted properties such as temperature, radius, and iron content as well as rival methods. Yet its ability to flag unresolved pairs stayed limited, because its per pixel flux predictions were only accurate to a few percent. The result maps a real limit for data driven binary hunting.
arxiv-2512-11443:
Yuan Li proves that error correcting codes can reach the theoretical limit of a noisy channel while being encoded by remarkably shallow circuits. Channel capacity is the fastest rate at which information can cross a noisy channel reliably, and codes achieving it usually demand heavy computation. Li's construction works for any additive noise channel over a finite field.

The encoder is an arithmetic circuit of linear size. Its depth grows like the inverse Ackermann function, a function so slow growing it stays at three or less for every useful input length. The construction layers a strong constant rate code, drawn from earlier work, with one extra layer built from a disperser graph. A probabilistic argument over that layer's weights shows a fixed encoder exists with vanishing error probability at any rate below capacity. The result ties information theory to circuit complexity in a striking way.
arxiv-2512-11643:
Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy presents Stateless Snowflake, a way to mint unique ID numbers across many computers with no central boss. Snowflake style IDs stay in time order and scale well, but each worker needs its own ID, often set by hand or by a registry service. That clashes with short lived cloud containers.

The new scheme reads a worker identity from its private network address, so no setup is needed. A reshaped bit layout, 1-41-16-6, makes room for that network clue while keeping IDs in order. Tests on AWS, GCP, and Azure hit about 31,000 IDs per second on a three node group. That matches classic systems, with far less setup work.
arxiv-2512-12043:
Yi Zhao, Chengyun Li, and Wanzhu Tu look for uneven mediation in a landmark blood pressure trial. SPRINT showed that aiming for 120 rather than 140 millimeters of mercury saves lives. One proposed pathway is early reduction of albumin in urine, a kidney stress marker. Standard mediation analysis gave mixed answers, perhaps because the pathway strength varies by patient.

The team builds a framework where mediation effects are functions of patient traits, with treatment interactions on both the mediator and outcome paths. A modified covariate trick plus a generalized lasso keeps the model lean. On SPRINT data the heterogeneity is real: a clear subgroup gains most from therapies that target albuminuria.
arxiv-2512-12343:
Sariah Al Saati, Karyn Le Hur, and Frederic Piechon build a local theory of orbital magnetization in a 2025 physics paper. Orbital magnetization comes from electrons circling within a material, and it can vary from place to place. Past theory mostly gave one global value for a whole crystal, hiding local patterns.

Their theory expands the local density of states in the magnetic field. It works for crystals, finite samples, and ribbons alike, and resolves magnetic textures at the sublattice scale. It also reveals a new local Berry curvature tied to how the field shifts electron weight in space. They identify ferro, antiferro, and ferrimagnetic orbital phases in insulators.
arxiv-2512-12443:
Akhmadillo Mamirov, Faiaz Azmain, and Hanyu Wang present an AI Transparency Atlas in a 2025 paper. Model documentation is scattered across platforms and varies in structure, blocking reliable checks of safety claims and data sources. They studied five frontier models, from Gemini 3 to Claude 4.5, plus 100 Hugging Face model cards, finding 947 unique section names.

Using the EU AI Act and the Stanford Transparency Index as baselines, they built a weighted framework of 8 sections and 23 subsections. An automated multi-agent pipeline scored 50 models for under 3 dollars total. Frontier labs reached about 80 percent compliance, while most providers fell below 60 percent. Safety categories like deception and child safety lost the most points.
arxiv-2512-12543:
Shaif Chowdhury, Soham Biren Katlariwala, and Devleena Kashyap prune neural networks by social network math before fine tuning in a 2025 paper. In social networks, a few key users sway whole communities, and small shifts in their behavior spread widely. The authors argue the same holds inside a neural network during fine tuning.

They build a graph where neurons are nodes and edges encode similarity, then score neurons by eigenvector centrality, a measure of influence through connections. Only the most central neurons are kept, and the smaller network is fine tuned. On VGGNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet, accuracy rose while complexity fell. On Oxford Flowers 102, accuracy hit 48 percent against a 30 percent baseline.
arxiv-2512-13043:
Tong Wei and co-authors present GTR-Turbo, a cheaper way to train vision-language agents over many turns. Such training suffers from sparse rewards and hard credit assignment. Recent methods ask a costly teacher model for step by step feedback, which limits who can repeat the work.

GTR-Turbo instead merges the weights of checkpoints saved during training itself. That merged model then serves as a free teacher for later rounds, through fine-tuning or soft distillation. The trick also eased the entropy collapse seen in earlier work. Across visual agent tasks, accuracy rose by 10 to 30 percent over the base model, while training time halved.
arxiv-2512-13443:
Davide Desio and Robert Seiringer present an abstract Dyson expansion for perturbations that are only form-bounded, a weak notion of smallness in quantum mechanics. Dyson expansions are series that express how a system deviates from a solvable reference. Extending them to such rough perturbations widens their reach considerably.

They apply the expansion to polaron problems, where an electron drags a lattice distortion with it, covering the Frohlich and Nelson models. For a large class of such models, the heat semigroup's vacuum expectation is a completely monotone function of the squared momentum. A direct corollary: the ground state energy is a concave function of the squared momentum.
arxiv-2512-13643:
Laura Kurek and co-authors run a field experiment on X with users who follow health misinformation accounts. They test whether ads can nudge those users to follow accurate health sources instead. The study covers 28,582 users who follow accounts that spread false health claims.

Four ad types varied by message style and by target: a health institution or a health influencer. A persuasive message urging users to follow a known health institution got far higher click rates than all other ads, with all p values below 0.001. Still, click rates were low overall and ad costs high. The authors conclude this ad format is not a cost-effective way to improve online information settings.
arxiv-2512-13743:
Oem Trivedi and Abraham Loeb extend the Loeb Scale, a scheme for classifying interstellar objects by how anomalous they look. The source framework was static, giving one score from the data at hand. Their version lets the score evolve as an object moves through the solar system.

Each anomaly metric becomes a function of distance from the Sun, and a relaxation equation governs the effective score over time. That adds memory, hysteresis, and predictive power to the rating. Early, stable forecasts of an object's final Loeb level become possible from sparse data taken far away. Such forecasts are most useful near Earth, when judging an object's true nature matters most. The paper is eight pages with no figures.
arxiv-2512-13943:
Anirban Roy and co-authors forecast how cross-correlating two kinds of intensity mapping can reveal the epoch of reionization. That epoch marks the universe's shift from neutral to ionized, driven by the first stars and galaxies. Line intensity mapping tracks atomic and molecular emission, while 21 cm mapping probes neutral hydrogen directly.

They study the cross-correlation of the 21 cm signal with multi-line mapping, using mock data for SKA-low and a FYST-like telescope. The carbon line and 21 cm cross-correlation can measure the ionization fraction across redshift bins at 9 to 40 sigma significance. Carbon monoxide lines give competitive constraints as well. The combined data also constrain metal enrichment and star formation links, raising the return of next-generation experiments.
arxiv-2512-14243:
Aaron Poole, Kostas Skenderis, and Marika Taylor give a full account of gravitational charges and radiation in a 2025 paper. They study four dimensional spacetimes that are locally like de Sitter space far away, with compact spatial sections and spacelike past and future infinities.

They show the variational problem is well posed once a conformal class is fixed at infinity and local terms, like holographic counterterms, are added. Radiation is possible only when that conformal class is nontrivial. Some symmetries give conserved charges, while general ones give flux balance laws instead. They derive results with Noether method and covariant phase space tools, then test them on exact solutions including a Robinson Trautman de Sitter class and a Bondi mass.
arxiv-2512-14543:
Changchun Feng, Laifa Tao, and Lin Chen use neural networks to reconstruct quantum states from measurements, a task called tomography. For several qubits the number of measurements explodes, and noise corrupts the answers. Their network is physics-informed: the rules of quantum mechanics are built into training through adjustable constraint weights, and a Cholesky-style output format guarantees every answer is a physically valid state.

On systems of two to five qubits it beat ordinary neural networks on fidelity, held up better under noise, and stayed steady as dimensions grew. Theory credits the constraints with shrinking the effective problem size. The authors report measurement needs dropping sharply, which would speed error correction and device calibration.
arxiv-2512-14943:
