Jun Zhu and five co-authors compress video with a hierarchical temporal neural representation. Implicit representations model videos as continuous functions. They offer compact storage and flexible rebuilds. Most past methods treat time as one more input. That limits how well they capture complex time patterns. The team's design builds time in a hierarchy instead.

Layered time structure can hold both fast motion and slow trends. Classic codecs split time in like ways by design. Neural methods must learn that lesson to compete. Better time models raise quality at low bit rates. Streaming and storage both gain from that. The work pairs with the team's frequency study. Time and frequency are the two axes of video.
arxiv-2601-17843: Jesse Hoekstra and Frank Windmeijer work on sharper tests for part of a model in instrumental variable studies. Their 2026 preprint deals with the subvector Anderson-Rubin test, used when instruments may be weak. They seek the best feasible critical values that adapt to how strong the other parameters are, under equal error spread. Better values mean a test with more power to detect real effects.
arxiv-2601-18043:
Haorui Ni and Sunil A. Bhave build a three-dimensional acoustic resonator shaped like a fin. Their 2026 preprint presents FinLN, made from lithium niobate on an insulator base. The team used deep ion etching to carve the fin and patterned electrodes on its sidewalls. The fin shape traps sound in three dimensions. It also boosts the coupling between electric signals and acoustic waves, all in a compact footprint.

The built devices run near 300 megahertz. Strong confinement in a small device serves filters and sensors in radios and phones. A fin design borrows a trick from transistors and applies it to sound. The work shows the shape can be made and that it performs as designed.
arxiv-2601-18243:
Hongmei Hu and Naihong Hu carry out a program to grow big quantum groups from smaller ones. Their 2026 preprint is the fifth in a series on double-bosonization and Majid's conjecture. The goal is a larger target quantum group of Drinfeld-Jimbo type, built by grafting two given smaller ones. To start, the authors set up basics of a multi-tensor product theory for the generalized double-bosonization construction. Grafting then joins the pieces into the bigger group.

Quantum groups sit behind many results in algebra and physics. A grafting method turns construction into a system, not a craft. Each new group built this way extends the known family. The work serves the long study of how these groups fit together.
arxiv-2601-18643:
Dominik Neudert-Schulz and Thomas Dallmann give cars that talk and sense as one a way to sync and to place them-selves. Cars in a peer group must share one clock and one beat to make their joint sense work. Each car must also know where its mates are, with care. The team do both tasks in one scheme, spread across the group with no boss node.

Their scheme works in two stages, each built on a famed maths of joint beats. First the group locks its clocks and beats as one. Then it uses that lock to read the place of each car from the talks them-selves. A joint scheme could cut the kit cars need for safe group moves. It may serve fleets of self-drive cars that must act as one on the road.
arxiv-2601-18843:
Muhib Omar and many colleagues read the heart's faint field with tools made from flaws in a gem. The gem is diamond, and its flaws can feel a field with great care. The read is done with no touch and no cut: the tool sits by the chest and picks up the heart's beat as a field. Such a read could one day sit by a bed or in a small ward.

The team ran the read in three forms, in rooms with shields from stray fields and in rooms with none. Each trace took a mean over a huge count of beats to pull the faint mark from the hiss. Clear traces in plain rooms would be a big step: shield rooms are dear and rare. The work shows the gem tools can catch the heart's field in the wild of a real ward.
arxiv-2601-19343:
Rahel Ohlendorf and eight co-authors probe a candidate altermagnet by squeezing it and watching heat. Altermagnets break time reversal and rotation symmetry together, yet show no net magnetism. Their order has the same symmetry as magnetic multipoles, and it couples to a mix of magnetic field and strain.

The team studies manganese fluoride, a leading candidate, through the elastocaloric effect under strain. That effect turns the coupling into a measurable heat signal. A clean probe of this hidden order could confirm a new class of magnets prized for fast, stray field free devices.
arxiv-2601-19443:
Patricia Medina Capilla and Luca Sabatini prove a clean fact about the largest subgroups of near simple groups. An almost simple group is built around one simple group, the atoms of finite group theory. Take any maximal subgroup, one that sits inside no larger proper subgroup, and run its derived series, the chain of commutator steps.

The team proves the tenth term of that chain is always perfect, equal to its own commutator. The same holds for maximal subgroups that avoid the core in a perfect group. Such blanket facts tidy the map of how big groups are built from their largest parts.
arxiv-2601-19643:
Zoe Betta, Davide Corongiu, Carmine Tommaso Recchiuto, and Antonio Sgorbissa send robots into harbours to keep people safe. Port work involves heavy loads, large vehicles, and tight schedules. Sending inspectors into the most dangerous spots puts workers at risk. A four-legged robot can go where wheels and people struggle.

This work is an early phase of a larger project. The team first identifies the critical areas inside a port that most need inspection. That mapping step decides where a quadruped robot would help most. Harbours are complex, with daily operations that shift by the hour. A robot that fits that rhythm could take over dull and risky checks. The study lays the groundwork for later trials.
arxiv-2601-19843:
Doğa Yılmaz, Jialin Zhu, Deshan Gong, and He Wang add uncertainty handling to a popular rendering method. Gaussian splatting builds scenes from millions of soft three-dimensional blobs. It has become a standard for neural rendering, spawning work on representation, speed, and optimization. Data uncertainty, though, has been largely ignored.

Their framework, GraphiXS, brings a graphical model to four-dimensional Gaussian splatting under uncertainty. Graphical models are built to reason about uncertain quantities jointly. Scenes captured from real sensors always carry noise and gaps. A system that knows what it does not know can render more honestly. The work points toward splatting pipelines that report confidence as well as images.
arxiv-2601-19943:
Yuhao Li asks how a population of learners can diversify without being told to. Coordinated, varied behaviour usually requires communication or explicit rewards for diversity. Li shows that competition alone can produce emergent specialization. Learners spontaneously split into specialists for different environmental regimes.

The mechanism, NichePopulation, combines competitive exclusion with tracking of niche affinity. The pattern echoes ecological niche theory, where species divide resources to coexist. Specialists emerge because generalists lose head-to-head contests in each niche. The result is a simple route to diverse agent populations. It may inform multi-agent systems, ensemble learning, and models of social division of labour. The rule set is small. No one tells the group what to do. The split in roles comes from the game itself. Each niche is a set of tasks where one type wins. Win there, and the type stays.
arxiv-2601-20043:
Yan Zhang, Xuefeng Liu, Sipeng Chen, and colleagues improve Bayesian optimization for problems with distinct regimes. Bayesian optimization searches expensive functions by modelling them with a Gaussian process. The standard model assumes uniform smoothness everywhere. Multi-regime problems break that: molecular conformations jump between energy basins, and drug candidates cluster into unlike families.

A single process either smooths over sharp transitions or invents noise in calm regions. Their method mixes several Gaussian processes under a Dirichlet process mixture, letting different regimes have different smoothness. Uncertainty stays calibrated in both calm and wild regions. Better-calibrated search wastes fewer costly experiments. The work suits chemistry and materials discovery, where each test is expensive.
arxiv-2601-20143:
J. W. Kania and a large team report on GREENBURST, a search for fast radio bursts carried out with the Green Bank Telescope. The project ran for about twenty-four thousand hours of observing time. It works in commensal mode, which means it searches data gathered for other projects at the same time.

Fast radio bursts are brief, bright flashes of radio waves from deep space. Piggyback searches like this one scan far more sky time than a dedicated survey could afford. The data can also reveal other short-lived radio sources. Long commensal records help astronomers count how often such flashes occur and where they come from.
arxiv-2601-20543:
Hsin-Yi Yang proves a result on CM-liftability of simple superspecial abelian surfaces over prime fields. An abelian surface is a two-dimensional analogue of an elliptic curve. The question is whether such a surface, defined over a finite field, can be lifted to one with complex multiplication, a rich extra symmetry.

Yang proves that for any prime, these surfaces admit CM liftings after extending the field at most to the quadratic extension. The proof uses the residual reflex condition and Lie types. Liftability results connect arithmetic over finite fields to the classical theory of complex multiplication.
arxiv-2601-20643:
Rupendra Yadav, Amita Sharma, and Aparna Mehra evaluate shrinkage estimators for portfolio choice across markets of different sizes. The mean-variance model is the standard investment framework, built on diversification. It struggles with estimation error in its core inputs: expected returns and the covariance matrix.

The authors test mean-variance and global minimum-variance portfolios under several shrinkage estimators, which pull noisy estimates toward safer targets. They compare performance across market dimensions. The study speaks to any investor whose optimization is only as good as the numbers fed into it. The point holds in a small fund and in a large one: bad inputs spoil good math.
arxiv-2601-20843:
Saurav Prateek presents a new design for AI systems that write deep research reports. The 2026 paper introduces a Deep Researcher architecture. It aims at complex, PhD-level topics. The design responds to limits of the parallel scaling paradigm. In that paradigm, many searches run at once and their results are merged. Breadth grows, but the plan itself never improves.

Two innovations anchor the system. The first refines the research plan step by step through reflection. The second is a candidates crossover algorithm that mixes rival draft answers. Together they push reports toward depth and completeness. The paper is a single-author design study. It speaks to builders of research agents that must do more than gather links.
arxiv-2601-20943:
Timmy Ejdetjärn and four co-authors simulate a dwarf galaxy merger that leaks ultraviolet light. Their 2026 paper models Haro 11 with radiation hydrodynamics. Haro 11 is the closest known leaker of Lyman continuum light. That light can ionize hydrogen across space. The galaxy is also a strong Lyman-alpha emitter. Together, these traits make it a key analogue of the galaxies that reionised the early universe.

Reionisation is when the first galaxies cleared the cosmic fog. Nearby leakers let astronomers study that process up close. A simulation can trace how ionizing light escapes through gas. It can also show how mergers open escape routes. The authors follow both Lyman continuum and Lyman-alpha escape. Their model helps read real images of Haro 11 and its kin.
arxiv-2601-21043:
Michał Miazga and three co-authors ask what body motion hides inside phone touch logs. Their 2026 paper presents Log2Motion. Touch data from mobile devices are collected at scale. Yet they reveal little about the interactions that produce them. Biomechanical simulations can illuminate motor control. Such simulations, though, have not been developed for touch. The authors propose a novel computational problem: synthesizing plausible motion directly from logs.

A touch log records taps and swipes as points and times. From that trace, the system infers how the hand and arm likely moved. That inference could power better keyboards and accessibility tools. It also raises questions about what logs quietly encode. The paper appears in the 2026 CHI proceedings. It opens a new link between interaction data and the moving body.
arxiv-2601-21143:
M. J. Neves derives a nonlinear theory of electric fields in a flat, two-dimensional world. The 2026 paper studies Euler-Heisenberg pseudo-electrodynamics. It starts from a theory of electrons confined to a plane. The fermion sector is integrated out. That step yields a nonlinear theory in the Euler-Heisenberg style. A non-local Chern-Simons term is added to the base Lagrangian.

The goal is the most complete gauge-invariant theory of its kind in two space dimensions plus time. Within it, Neves computes electric birefringence. That is the split of light by direction in a field. Such effects matter for flat materials like graphene. The paper is a formal theory study. It extends tools built for our world into the plane.
arxiv-2601-21243:
Amir Ali Farzin, Yuen-Man Pun, Philipp Braun, Tyler Summers, and Iman Shames study a class of tug-of-war problems in math. One side tries to push a value down while the other pushes it up. The shared function is rough rather than smooth, grows in a set-like way for one player, and curves the other way for the rival.

The authors test a method that needs no gradients, only function values. Such problems show up in robust design and game-like settings. Their work checks how well the method performs in both fixed and changing versions of the problem. It gives guidance on when this gradient-free route is a sound choice.
arxiv-2601-21543:
Fanshuang Kong, Richong Zhang, Qiyu Sun, Zhijie Nie, Ting Deng, and Chunming Hu create training data by unmixing blended examples. The classic mixup trick blends two examples and their labels to make new training points. Because the blending happens in hidden space, the results cannot be read by humans.

Large model based methods write fresh sentences instead, which are readable but hard to control. The authors invert the blending to recover readable examples with known mix ratios. That gives control and readability at once. Better synthetic data can stretch small labeled sets, a common bottleneck in applied language work.
arxiv-2601-21843:
Tom de Jong, Nicolai Kraus, and Axel Ljungström work in homotopy type theory, a foundation for mathematics where types behave like spaces. Simplicial type theory extends it so that types also carry directed morphisms, arrows with a direction. A Segal type is one where those arrows can be composed.

Defining such composition usually drags in endless higher coherence conditions. The authors show that all those coherences can be stated and derived. This holds if the theory is set up in one way. It is homotopy type theory with a postulated interval. Their tool is the Leibniz adjunction named in the title. The 2026 preprint then applies the machinery to simplicial type theory, giving formal mathematics a cleaner way to handle directed structures.
arxiv-2601-21943:
Ahmad Aghapour, Erhan Bayraktar, and Ziqing Zhang analyze how fast diffusion models converge. These generative models make samples by running a learned reverse-time process in small steps. Most existing theory says the error grows at least in proportion to the dimension of the data.

Such bounds force awkward assumptions about the data's hidden geometry. The team's 2026 preprint proves entropy-based convergence results that are free of the dimension. And pairs them with loss-adaptive schedules that adjust step sizes to the model's own errors. Dimension-free guarantees matter for very high-dimensional data, where older bounds become so weak that they stop guiding how many steps a sampler actually needs.
arxiv-2601-22143:
Anthony Chen and co-authors dub videos with a joint audio-visual model. Audio-visual foundation models, pretrained to generate sound and pictures together, have shown a striking ability to model generation and editing across both senses. Video dubbing, replacing speech in another language, stands to gain from those priors.

Most dubbing systems still rely on complex, task-specific pipelines stitched together by hand. The team's 2026 preprint, JUST-DUB-IT, performs dubbing through joint audio-visual diffusion, generating the new voice and matching visuals together. Good dubbing must sync lips, timing, and tone at once. A unified model could make foreign films and videos feel native to far more viewers.
arxiv-2601-22443:
Jing Jia and four co-authors show that a weak image prior can still fix hard image puzzles well. Diffusion models serve as priors: they know what a real image looks like. Their 2026 preprint asks if a model trained on bedrooms can help restore a face. The norm says the prior must match the target closely.

Their tests say a mismatched, low-grade prior can still do strong work. That result frees users from hunting for the perfect prior. It also cuts the cost of solving inverse problems, where a full signal must be rebuilt from partial data. The finding is broad and practical.
arxiv-2601-22943:
Xiang Wu and five co-authors shrink large graphs while keeping their shape. Graph coarsening merges nodes to make a smaller graph that acts like the big one. Most methods keep either spectral or spatial traits, and keeping the topology helps neural networks trained on the small graph stay accurate.

Older topology-keeping methods can take exponential time, far too slow for big graphs. Their collapse-based method aims to keep the shape at a scalable cost. Smaller, faithful graphs help analyze social, road, and molecule networks faster. Preserving topology is the priority because it keeps the predictive strength of networks trained on the coarsened graph.
arxiv-2601-23043:
Sudha, B. N. Karthik, K. S. Akhilesh, and A. R. Usha Devi test quantum sensors built from shared Dicke states. Phase sensing with entangled multi-qubit states is a core promise of quantum metrology, but noise eats the advantage. Their probes stack superpositions of Dicke states to fight that loss.

They study sensing where the phase is written by one-body and two-body interactions. The goal is precision at the Heisenberg limit, or beyond it, even with noise present. Noise-tough sensors could improve clocks, magnetometers, and imaging. One-body and two-body interaction Hamiltonians supply the two encoding routes whose precision under noise the authors compare.
arxiv-2601-23143:
Seanie Lee and eight co-authors align reasoning models for safety using the models' own generations. Large reasoning models gain skill from reward training on hard tasks. That same tuning can over-prioritize compliance, leaving them open to harmful prompts.

Outside teacher models are a common fix, but their style mismatch can dull native reasoning. ThinkSafe instead builds safety training from the model's self-generated material. Keeping alignment in-distribution aims to protect both safety and reasoning strength at once. Self-generated alignment data keeps the training distribution native, avoiding the mismatch that external teacher distillation introduces.
arxiv-2602-00443: Ruinan Jin and team present RVCBench, a dataset and benchmark for robust voice cloning. Modern voice cloning can make speech matching a target speaker from seconds of reference audio, for personal interfaces and dubbing. In practice, models face noisy audio, flawed prompts, multilingual and long form settings, post-processing, and hostile shifts, all hurting it. Despite progress driven by autoregressive codec models and diffusion models, robustness under real shifts remains underexplored. RVCBench contributes a large scale, task aligned dataset with real shifts from set pairing, multilingual cues, and post-processing.
arxiv-2602-00543: Seho Pyo and colleagues tackle table question answering, where flattening tables into lines breaks their grid structure. Existing end-to-end generation and single-line program queries give weak numerical accuracy and poor clarity. Their framework writes multi-line working programs with short natural-language comments, making reasoning explicit and raising the odds of correct code. On WikiTableQuestions it reaches 70.9% accuracy, surpassing the Repanda baseline, and pairing it with a robust end-to-end model via lightweight answer selection improves results further.
arxiv-2602-00643: Murtaza Vefadar presents QuVI, an open-source quantum circuit toolkit built inside LabVIEW for students and engineers who find text-based tools hard to enter. It uses LabVIEW dataflow, where wires carry data and nodes carry operations, as a visual counterpart to ordinary circuit notation, while still allowing loops and conditionals. The toolkit is shown building and visualising basic quantum algorithms and checking them against theory. By turning block diagrams directly into evolving quantum states, it lets users prototype quantum logic without leaving a graphical workspace.
arxiv-2602-00943: Zhenyu Zhao and colleagues propose Dynamic Prior Thompson Sampling, controlling the chance that a new arm beats the incumbent winner. Cold-start exploration forces new or sparse items to gain traffic, but over-exploration harms users. Standard Thompson Sampling starts with a uniform Beta(1,1) prior, implying a 50% success rate for unseen items. Batched updates amplify the problem: for hours, new items stay no-data, so the prior dominates before feedback arrives. Their closed-form quadratic solution sets the prior mean enforcing P(Xj > Yk) = epsilon at introduction, making exploration tunable.
arxiv-2602-01043: Jacob A. Barandes asks why quantum thought needs complex numbers, and gives a stripped-down answer. He reads the standard Hilbert-space setup as one case of a wider trick, Markovian embeddings, recasting a quantum setup as one indivisible chance process in a plain old space. In that view, wave functions and like Hilbert-space gear drop from real things to bookkeeping tools. Complex numbers then earn their keep by making the Hilbert-space setup count as a true Markovian embedding.
arxiv-2602-01243: Zhi Xiao and co-authors bound the no-birefringence slice of Lorentz-breaking photon rules with 14 gamma-burst photons in the GeV band. Their marks hit isotropic coefficients for dimensions 6, 8, and 10 inside the Standard-Model Extension frame. With theory-free Bayesian fits, the data lean toward slower-than-light breaking effects, and focusing there yields tight, self-agreeing bounds. Inside the 95% credible band, the new bounds beat the best past credible bounds by at least five orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2602-01443: Alberto Castelo and co-authors build SimGym, an offline stand-in for e-commerce A/B tests. Live tests divert shoppers, take weeks, and risk harm. SimGym runs synthetic buyers, driven by language-model agents in a browser, that mirror traffic. It pulls buyer profiles and intents from production records, groups them into types, and runs weighted sessions on control and changed storefronts. Against real outcomes on a large platform, it matched shifts well and shrank test cycles from weeks to under an hour, exposing no real buyers.
arxiv-2602-01643: Xichen Sun and colleagues generate molecular structures from tandem mass spectra, a route to understanding cell metabolism and finding compounds. Spectra carry fingerprints from cleavage of several atoms and bonds, which matter for telling isomers apart and for non local fragmentation. Most methods model only single atoms and pairs, missing such effects. Their MBGen framework adds many body attention and higher order edge modeling to a diffusion model, using the spectral signal. On two benchmarks it beats rivals by up to two hundred thirty percent.
arxiv-2602-01943: Li-Ying Chou and colleagues set finite temperature adiabaticity criteria for driven many body systems. A mixed state speed limit with fidelity susceptibility in Liouville space bounds Hilbert Schmidt fidelity. Driving a Gibbs state toward a quasi Gibbs target, the bounds give a threshold rate for nonadiabaticity onset. For gapped local Hamiltonians, the rate factorizes in the thermodynamic limit into a size part with zero temperature scaling and a universal factor. That factor nears unity at low temperature and grows linear at high temperature, shown in spin chains.
arxiv-2602-02143: Shubham Toshniwal and colleagues teach small thought models to pick the best answer from many tries. Sampling answers can lift thought, but weak picking caps the gain, and strong picking has sat with large models. They build picking tasks from math and code sets, keeping cases with right and wrong tries. They train one point seven billion parameter models with reward based learning to back right picks. Their models beat prompt and vote rivals on math and code tests, at times matching larger models. Gains carry to stronger outputs.
arxiv-2602-02243: Dakshina Tharindu and others present SysFuSS, mixing system-level firmware fuzzing with selective symbolic execution. Firmware sits between hardware and software, so its bugs can prove catastrophic, yet fuzzers target user-level code and stall on coverage plateaus. Evaluated on real embedded firmware including OpenSSL and WolfBoot, it beats leading fuzzers on coverage and vulnerability finding. It finds many known vulnerabilities where rivals find few, and activates them faster.
arxiv-2602-02543:
Mingda Liu and 3 co-authors diagnose why editing a language model's facts many times in a row eventually breaks it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sequential locate-and-edit methods can fail abruptly after many successful edits. The authors formalize the cause as a positive norm-feedback loop: solved value vectors and edited weights amplify each other until capabilities collapse.

Their analysis shows the loop can drive roughly exponential norm growth under standard editing dynamics. Existing per-edit regularizers and update clamps cannot resolve it. The proposed fix, norm-anchor scaling, rescales each solved value vector to a reference norm taken from the original model. The change is one line with negligible cost. Across multiple model backbones, datasets, and editors, it extended the usable editing horizon more than fourfold. Long-run editing performance improved by about seventy-two percent on average, while single-edit success stayed intact.
arxiv-2602-02743:
Fahim Arsad Nafis and 4 co-authors ask twenty domain experts what breaks when teams try to explore high-dimensional science data jointly inside immersive environments, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Analysis of such data is increasingly a team sport across disciplines, but software toolchains fragment the work, and most immersive research still designs for a lone user.

The semi-structured interviews drew on academic, government, and industry practitioners. A hybrid coding scheme, part theory-driven and part emergent, organized their answers into four themes covering workflow pain, attitudes toward adoption, wished-for features, and expected usability and ethics risks. Today's ecosystems repeatedly fracture coordination and common ground, the experts reported. Their requests point to platforms built for awareness of collaborators, fair participation, and work split across devices and sites. The study supplies the empirical grounding that multi-user immersive analytics has been missing.
arxiv-2602-02943:
Machines that predict first and optimize later can fail badly on unusual inputs, and Jiaqi Wen and 2 co-authors address that risk in a 2026 paper. Such pipelines forecast demand or context, then feed the forecast into a decision. Out-of-distribution test cases can cause large prediction errors and poor decisions.

Their framework, called 3D-Learning, trains predictors for worst-case decision quality. A diffusion model searches for the worst plausible data distribution, staying consistent with real data. The method balances average and worst-case performance. Tests use a language-model resource provisioning task, where computing must be allocated ahead of demand. The approach beat robust optimization and data augmentation baselines on out-of-distribution generalization.
arxiv-2602-03043:
Salim Khazem's solo 2026 paper makes early-exit vision networks safer to deploy. Early-exit networks let easy inputs stop at shallow layers, saving computation. The practical question is knowing when stopping early is safe, since a wrong confident exit wastes the savings and harms accuracy on exactly the inputs the system claims are easy.

His wrapper, SAFE-KD, attaches lightweight exit heads at intermediate depths of a backbone. A strong teacher is distilled into every exit, with consistency enforced from deep to shallow exits. At inference, per-exit thresholds are calibrated on held-out data with conformal risk control. That guarantees a user-chosen misclassification risk among early exits, under standard assumptions. Tests across datasets and architectures showed better accuracy-compute trade-offs and calibration.
arxiv-2602-03443:
Radio receivers need protection from sudden strong signals, and today's chip limiters get noisy and slow near gigahertz frequencies. Kristýna Davídková and 12 co-authors show a nanoscale alternative in a 2026 paper, aimed at the European 5G high band. Their device is a frequency-selective limiter built on spin waves traveling through a thin yttrium iron garnet film.

Spin waves are launched and picked up by coplanar waveguides with features as small as 250 nanometers. Four-magnon scattering inside the film caps the transmitted power only at the chosen frequency. The team measures the key limiter settings up to 25 gigahertz. Analytical theory and a numerical model back the measurements, and the authors sketch combining limiter, filter, and delay line in one device.
arxiv-2602-03543:
Kanstantsin Pashkovich and 2 co-authors study how a principal should pay an agent who acts step by step under a matroid constraint. In their 2026 paper, the agent takes actions one at a time, sees each action's random value, and then chooses what to do next. Only a subset of the taken actions, forming an independent set in the matroid, counts toward the reward.

The authors focus on linear contracts, where the agent receives a fixed fraction of the principal's total reward. Their main result ties the search for an optimal linear contract to the matroid reliability problem, a classic question about network dependability. The two problems turn out to be equivalent, up to adding parallel copies of elements to the matroid.
arxiv-2602-03643:
Serious games can screen patients for cognitive decline, but clinicians need to know how much to trust each session's signal. Elisabetta De Maria and Christopher Leturc build a probabilistic model-checking framework for that setting in a 2026 paper. They model gameplay behavior of healthy patients and of patients with mild or major neurocognitive disorders as discrete-time Markov chains.

Model checking then compares expected against actual behavior, spotting mismatches session by session. The framework tracks how a practitioner's diagnostic confidence should evolve as sessions accumulate, supporting Alzheimer's staging calls. A second idea adjusts the difficulty of later game sessions from the patient's earlier behavior, turning the same tool toward cognitive training. The paper supplies the theory and a protocol for testing it.
arxiv-2602-03943:
Mixed feelings toward parents may leave a mark on mental health. Sangpil Youm and 2 co-authors analyze posts from an online forum where Asian American children write about their parents. Their 2026 study uses a language model to detect emotions sentence by sentence and depressive symptoms post by post.

Eight emotions made up over half of those detected, and emotions rarely came alone. Pairs of negative emotions, such as anger with grief, tracked with depressive symptoms. Some positive pairs tracked the other way, while ambivalent mixes gave varied signals. The findings suggest clinicians should ask about emotional mixtures, not single feelings.
arxiv-2602-04043:
Restyle a whole 3D scene from a sentence or a photo. Joanna Kaleta and 5 co-authors built AnyStyle, a feed-forward system for 3D Gaussian Splatting, in a 2026 paper. Gaussian splatting represents scenes as clouds of soft blobs that render fast. Prior stylization leaned on image conditioning alone.

AnyStyle accepts text or reference images as style input and needs no camera poses. Its modular stylization block drops into existing reconstruction backbones with minimal changes. Experiments show stronger style control than earlier feed-forward attempts. Fast, controllable restyling serves games, film previsualization, and virtual shopping, where assets must be created and varied quickly.
arxiv-2602-04343:
Show a system a few photos of a new object and it should find, segment, and pose that object anywhere. Sebastian Jung and 3 co-authors present NeMO, a geometry-aware representation for few-shot perception, in a 2026 paper. The object never appears in training data.

An encoder turns a handful of template views into a sparse point cloud carrying semantic and geometric information. A decoder then combines that memory with a query image to produce detection, segmentation, and six-degree-of-freedom pose predictions. No camera-specific parameters or retraining are needed. Outsourcing object knowledge to an external memory makes onboarding new objects quick, a scalability win for robotics.
arxiv-2602-04743:
G. S. Adkins and U. D. Jentschura compute refined energy corrections for exotic bound systems in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. When a system's particles are heavier than electrons, the largest radiative correction to its energy levels comes from light-fermion vacuum polarization, a quantum effect of virtual electron pairs.

Earlier work treated systems with orbiting muons. The authors generalize those relativistic and recoil corrections to bound systems whose particles carry spin zero, one-half, or one. Applications include pionium, a pion bound system, plus muonic hydrogen and deuterium. Special attention goes to excited states of deuteronium, a deuteron bound with its antiparticle. Such corrections matter because precision spectroscopy tests fundamental theory through these fragile, short-lived atoms.
arxiv-2602-04943:
Finding the lowest-energy state of a Heisenberg antiferromagnet is a core problem in quantum physics. Mahmud Ashraf Shamim and 5 co-authors are its authors. The team recasts the problem in the language of graphs.

Each spin arrangement becomes a vertex, and edges join arrangements that differ by swapping one pair of spins. On this graph, the energy problem turns into a weighted Max-Cut problem, a classic graph task. The authors show the ground state's sign pattern can be recovered from the graph in reasonable time, and that a famous rule for sign patterns reduces to two-coloring the graph. The framework ties together sign structure, Monte Carlo methods, and why optimizing wave function phases is hard.
arxiv-2602-05043:
Many machine learning prototypes never survive contact with a real system, partly because testing stops at model accuracy. Grace A Lewis and 7 co-authors propose a quality model for ML components in this 2026 software engineering paper. Their target is the missing middle: system-level needs like throughput, resource use, and robustness, translated into terms a component developer can act on.

Existing standards mix system traits with component traits, which leaves model builders unsure what they own. The new model separates the component-level qualities, giving developers and stakeholders a shared vocabulary for negotiating requirements and aiming tests. A survey of practitioners confirmed its relevance and value. The model has also been built into an open-source tool for testing and evaluating ML components, showing the framework works in practice, not just on paper.
arxiv-2602-05143:
Graph-based retrieval can answer questions by matching entities while missing the causal story that links them. Nengbo Wang and 8 co-authors propose CausalRAG2 in this 2026 paper, accepted at ICML 2026, a scheme that reorganizes knowledge graphs around causal links. The hosted entry carries the earlier title HugRAG; the work was renamed in its published line of development.

Causal gating across hierarchical modules is the central mechanism. Causal links are modeled explicitly to suppress spurious correlations, while the hierarchy avoids the isolation that modular graphs usually suffer, letting reasoning cross module boundaries at scale. The team also introduces HolisQA, a benchmark aimed at holistic comprehension beyond entity matching. Across several datasets and metrics, CausalRAG2 beat competitive graph-based retrieval baselines. Code and the benchmark are public, and the authors frame the work as a principled base for causally grounded retrieval systems.
arxiv-2602-05243:
Pruning a vision transformer usually means retraining it, which defeats the purpose when a model must be slimmed quickly after training. Boxiang Zhang and Baijian Yang present CORP in this 2026 machine learning paper, a one-shot structured pruning method that needs no gradients, no fine-tuning, and only unlabeled calibration images.

The insight is to treat pruning as representation recovery. Components marked for removal are modeled as affine functions of the components that stay, and closed-form ridge regression solutions fold the compensation directly into the remaining weights. On ImageNet with the DeiT family, experiments exposed heavy redundancy in both the feed-forward and attention parts. A huge DeiT model kept accuracy above 83 percent after half of both structures were pruned away. The closed-form recipe makes post-training compression a calculation rather than a project.
arxiv-2602-05843:
Most agent benchmarks hand the model the rules and a fixed goal, then grade execution. Hang Yan and 16 co-authors argue that real autonomy also needs induction: discovering the hidden laws of an environment from experience. They introduce OdysseyArena, a benchmark suite for long horizon, active, and inductive interaction, built from four primitives that turn abstract transition dynamics into concrete environments.

A lite version offers a standardized set of tasks that measure inductive efficiency and long horizon discovery. A challenge version pushes stability across extreme horizons of more than two hundred steps. Tests on more than fifteen leading models show even frontier systems fall short in inductive scenarios. The authors identify that gap as a critical bottleneck for autonomous discovery. Code and data are public. The benchmark targets researchers who evaluate agents, and it reframes what a good score should mean.
arxiv-2602-05943:
Merging fine tuned language models into one usually means mean weights in flat plain space, which can wreck the shape the trained weights carry. Sihan Yang, Kexuan Shi, and Weiyang Liu propose Orthogonal Model Merging, which performs the merge on the curved manifold of the orthogonal group instead. The aim is to keep inner structure such as round-shell energy.

Task specific straight matrices from straight fine tuning are mapped to a Lie algebra, where course and strength of tuning can be joined in a sound, quick way. For models fine tuned by other means, a straight split step pulls out their straight parts by solving a Procrustes problem, while the rest merge by plain adding. Wide tests show the method eases the damage that linear merging does. It targets teams that build one shippable model from many experts.
arxiv-2602-06043:
Teaching a big pretrained model new tasks one after another often erases what it learned before. Prakhar Kaushik and 4 co-authors propose Share, a method that keeps all tasks inside one shared low-rank space. LoRA, a popular cheap tuning method, normally needs a fresh adapter for each task.

Share builds one common space from early tasks, then folds each new task into it. Only the most useful directions are kept, which limits clashes between old and new skills. The team reports far fewer added weights and far less memory than standard LoRA setups. Tests span images, language, 3D poses, and picture making.
arxiv-2602-06143:
How much mental effort a lab class demands, and how much it sparks interest, depends on how the class is taught. Razan Hamed and N Sanjay Rebello compared three styles in undergraduate physics labs for non-science majors: inquiry-based, design-based, and game-based learning. Students tried all three styles in mechanics and in electric circuits.

After each session, students rated their mental load and their situational interest. Game-based labs came out with the lowest load and the highest interest in both topics. The other two styles demanded more effort, and which one demanded more changed by topic. Interest rose as load fell, so lighter designs may engage beginners better.
arxiv-2602-06643:
Ruiqian Nai and ten co-authors present a way to teach humanoid robots whole-body skills without a robot present during data collection. Teaching by remote control is slow and ties up costly hardware, while learning in simulation needs hand-built rewards. Their system, HuMI, records human motion with portable gear instead.

The recorded motion feeds a staged learning pipeline that turns human moves into robot skills the machine can actually perform. Tests covered five tasks, including kneeling, squatting, tossing objects, walking, and using both arms together. HuMI gathered data about three times faster than remote control and reached a 70 percent success rate in places the robot had never seen.
arxiv-2602-06743:
Dong Chen and eight co-authors build a screening tool for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, a sideways curvature of the spine that early treatment can slow. Ordinary screening is subjective and hard to scale, while video analysis of walking patterns offers a cheaper route. Earlier gait datasets, though, often leaked data by including repeated clips of the same person in training and testing.

Their dataset, ScoliGait, holds 1,572 training clips and 300 fully independent test clips, each labeled with measured spine angles and clinical text. Their model fuses video, text, and a knowledge map built from clinical movement priors, using a latent attention pooling step to combine them. On the leakage-free benchmark it set a new state of the art by a wide margin, and the design keeps its reasoning open to clinical inspection.
arxiv-2602-07143:
Sound matters for intelligent systems, yet there was no single yardstick for how well a system hears.  Georg Heigold and six co-authors present the Massive Sound Embedding Benchmark, a method for testing the audio parts of multi-modal systems through the embeddings they produce from raw sound.

The first release covers eight core tasks, from transcription and classification to retrieval, thinking, segmentation, clustering, reranking, and reconstruction, with varied data sets and room to add more.  For teams building audio-capable models, MSEB offers one shared scoreboard instead of scattered, hard-to-compare tests.  The benchmark is designed to grow, with new tasks and data sets able to join the suite as audio research advances.
arxiv-2602-07243:
Robots that help at home need training data showing people and rooms changing over long periods. Current synthetic data sets miss how action shapes rooms and rooms shape action.  Siddharth Singh and two co-authors build a generative method that couples the two sides loosely.

Human personas influence how environments are generated, while environment layouts and meanings shape what happens next, producing 3D data with both static context and long-term time action.  Users can steer dataset traits through natural language prompts.  Embodied AI teams get large, diverse household data that captures the two-way street between people and their homes.
arxiv-2602-07743:
Additive number theory asks which sets of integers can represent every integer in exactly one way as a sum, a property called a unique representation basis. Yuchen Ding and Jie Wang sharpen a recent result that answered a 2007 question of Chen in the affirmative.

The earlier work showed such a basis exists with a density constant bounded between the square root of two over two and the square root of two. This short note raises the lower bound to 1, narrowing the possible range for the best constant. Specialists get a clean, incremental advance on a delicate existence problem, with the proof's main ideas laid out in compact form.
arxiv-2602-07943:
Causal inference from observational data often needs an instrumental variable, a factor that shifts the treatment without directly affecting the outcome, but finding valid instruments takes creativity and domain knowledge. Ivaxi Sheth and four co-authors test whether large language models can help.

In a two-stage evaluation, they first check whether models recover established instruments from the literature, then whether they avoid instruments already discredited by theory or evidence. Their system, IV Co-Scientist, is a team of agents that drafts, criticizes, and improves candidate instruments for a treatment-outcome pair, with a statistical test for consistency without ground truth. Economists and epidemiologists gain a promising AI collaborator for a traditionally human craft.
arxiv-2602-08243:
Learning samplers over discrete spaces is hard without gradients, and efficient continuous-domain solvers had not been extended to that setting. Wei Guo and eight co-authors show the core mechanism of adjoint matching is independent of state-space type. They build discrete ASBS, a unified framework extending adjoint matching and adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampling to discrete spaces.

Theory analyzes optimality conditions for the discrete Schrödinger bridge problem and its link to stochastic optimal control, spotting a cyclic group structure on the state space as necessary for the extension. Empirically, discrete ASBS matches competitors on sample quality while training more efficiently and scaling better. Teams sampling discrete structures, from compounds to sequences, gain a sound, efficient solver.
arxiv-2602-08343:
Long-context chatbots must store a growing cache of past keys and values, so choosing which tokens to keep matters. Debajyoti Datta and four co-authors offer a no-training method for that choice. Their scorer, ManifoldKV, orders kept tokens by straight-line distance to the key centroid, capturing both direction and size, where cosine scoring sees direction only. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets the memory wall in long-context inference.

On a standard long-context suite the method holds about 96 percent accuracy at moderate lengths with a fifth of tokens dropped, and it shines where cosine fails. Multi-key retrieval jumps from 77 to 92 percent against a strong baseline. A windowed variant rescues accuracy at 64-thousand-token contexts, recovering 49 points over the global baseline. Readers get a three-line change that works across four model designs with no tuning.
arxiv-2602-08543:
Search agents are usually tested on queries worked backward from answers, which feel nothing like real information needs. Yutao Zhu and eleven co-authors build GISA, a benchmark of 373 human-crafted queries reflecting authentic seeking behavior. Their arXiv paper covers both finding specific facts and gathering broad information in unified tasks.

Four structured answer formats allow exact evaluation, and a live subset with periodically refreshed answers resists memorization. Complete human search trajectories accompany every query, giving gold references for process supervision. Even the best model scores only 19.30 percent exact match, collapsing further on planning-heavy tasks. Readers get a hard, realistic gauge for general information-seeking assistants.
arxiv-2602-08643:
State policy studies often ask how effects vary across states, but the quantity they estimate may not match the question they want answered. Max Rubinstein and six co-authors clarify the causal targets in per-state variation work for state policies. Their arXiv paper sets out three targets: per-state effects, group-average effects given traits, and controlled direct effects.

Group averages are easiest to pin down yet often least useful for policy, and lumping distinct policies into one flag muddies what the numbers mean. The authors propose bounding per-state effects instead, giving ranges under stated assumptions about gaps from ideal conditions. Tests with fake data show the bounds pick effect signs more reliably than group averages do. An application to Medicaid expansion and buprenorphine prescribing shows the method in use. Readers get a more honest target for inference.
arxiv-2602-08743:
Plasma sheaths govern how plasmas meet surfaces, yet measuring sheath thickness directly has been difficult. John Whitlock Brooks and Richeek Dutta show that a plasma impedance probe with a controlled DC bias gives relatively direct, model-informed thickness measurements. This arXiv preprint tests the biased probe across a range of discharge conditions.

Measured thicknesses follow Child-Langmuir scaling closely after a single consistent correction factor near 0.74. Concurrent density and damping checks show probe biasing does not much disturb bulk plasma density. Using the calibrated factor, floating-probe analysis yields electron temperature and plasma potential estimates matching biased Langmuir probe results. Readers get a complementary diagnostic that widens accessible plasma measurements.
arxiv-2602-09443:
Physics at olympiad level demands more than symbol pushing: diagrams often carry essential constraints, from boundary conditions to spatial symmetries, that text alone omits. A 2026 paper led by Yun Luo introduces P1-VL, a family of open vision-language models built for advanced scientific reasoning, aiming to bind abstract logic to physical reality through sight. The method pairs curriculum reinforcement learning, which grows difficulty gradually to steady training, with agentic augmentation for iterative self-checking at inference.

On HiPhO, a rigorous benchmark of thirteen recent olympiad exams, the flagship model becomes the first open vision-language model to win twelve gold medals, leading open models overall. The agent-augmented system ranks second globally, behind only one proprietary rival. Beyond physics, the models lead their base models across science and math benchmarks. Open-sourced, P1-VL is offered as a step toward general physical intelligence for machine discovery.
arxiv-2602-09743:
Exact spectra offers a sharp probe of physics beyond the Standard Model. Lei Cong and four co-authors start from a lately seen nine-sigma theory-test gap in the ion energy of shaky helium. It sparked a guess of a new boson bridging exotic e-e links. Their 2026 paper tests that guess with a free sign-match analysis of the induced energy shifts.

The sign need alone rules out vector-vector and pseudo-pseudo links as possible answers to the anomaly. Adding current limits plus better limits found here further rules out axial-vector cases. Within the single-boson frame studied, only a tightly bound scalar-carried link stays viable. The left knob space could be probed, for example, by modest gains in sizing the electron gyro ratio.
arxiv-2602-10043:
Shared brain scans are stripped of direct identifiers before release, yet the brain itself may still give its owner away. A 2026 paper led by Gaurang Sharma, with four co-authors, shows that simple image processing and similarity measures can link skull-stripped scans of the same person across data sets. Earlier demonstrations needed training-heavy or costly methods.

Using standard preprocessing plus direct similarity computation, the team achieved near-perfect matching across different times, scanners, resolutions, and protocols, even amid cognitive decline. The experiments mimic realistic cross-database matching in large neuroimaging repositories. The finding flags an underappreciated re-identification risk for data-sharing policy.
arxiv-2602-10243:
The Sun's magnetic field drives eruptions from nanoflares to coronal mass ejections, and indirect evidence suggests it can occasionally unleash events far stronger than any modern recording. A 2026 paper led by Valeriy Vasilyev, with two co-authors, links solar magnetism, extreme solar particle events, and stellar superflares. Two lines of evidence frame the question: particle event spikes in tree rings and ice cores over fifteen thousand years, and superflares observed on thousands of Sun-like stars.

Whether these solar and stellar extremes share physics remains open. The paper summarizes current understanding and discusses mechanisms that might connect them. Although superflares and particle events both express magnetic energy storage and release, their relationship appears not one-to-one. Occurrence and energetics likely hinge on how magnetic flux and topology split released energy among radiation, mass ejection, and particle acceleration.
arxiv-2602-10643:
Katariina Perkonoja and four co-authors define how to judge mock patient timelines in a 2026 paper. Mock long-run data mimic repeated readings over time, but current checks focus on marginal resemblance: whether each factor looks right alone. That can hide serious distortions.

The new metrics assess time preservation across marginal, covariance, single-level, and measurement structures. Strong marginal resemblance, the authors show, may conceal covariance distortion and broken single paths. Preservation also depends on first data quality, measurement rate, and preprocessing choices like binning and encoding. Sparse or irregular readings limit what any generator can learn, and the metrics make those limits visible instead of letting averages hide them.
arxiv-2602-10743:
Vaisakh Shaj and five co-authors bring Bayesian filtering into fast sequence modeling in a 2026 paper. State-space language models like Mamba and gated linear focus offer linear hardness, but their linear state updates limit expressivity and robust state tracking. The paper closes that gap from a chance angle.

Casting sequence mixing as exact Bayesian filtering, the authors show that reparameterizing the Kalman filter in information form turns its updates into an associative scan. The per-token update becomes uneven, a Mobius-style sharpness recursion, yet stays temporally parallel. The resulting Kalman Linear Focus layer is a drop-in sequence mixer. It performs time-parallel chance inference with stated belief-state doubt, strictly more expressive than its linear cousins.
arxiv-2602-10843:
Christian Bertram and Mads Vestergaard Jensen portray fitted PageRank estimation in undirected graphs in a 2026 paper. Fitted PageRank measures the chance that a discounted random walk starting at one node terminates at another. The paper studies estimating that chance with constant relative error whenever it exceeds a threshold.

Across common graph-access models and single-source, single-target, and single-node variants, the authors give tight bounds up to logarithmic factors. Those bounds hold in both worst-case and average-case settings. Both new upper and lower bounds appear, completing a portrait that earlier work left partial for undirected graphs. The results tell recipe designers exactly how hard each estimation variant is.
arxiv-2602-10943:
Martin Gromniak and four co-authors learn broad 3D scene models from 2D robot views in a 2026 paper. Their broad neural radiance field approach predicts 3D workspace occupancy from egocentric robot views, constructing models in a global workspace frame rather than camera-centric coordinates. That choice makes the output directly usable for manipulation.

The model integrates flexible source views and transfers to unseen object arrangements without scene-exact fine-tuning. Showed on a humanoid robot and tested against 3D sensor ground truth, the model trained on forty real scenes achieves twenty-six millimeter reconstruction error. That figure includes occluded regions. The work shows robots can infer complete workspace shape from ordinary views, beyond what stereo vision delivers.
arxiv-2602-11143:
Humanoids can walk rough ground, yet tall platforms defeat them. Yikai Wang and seven co-authors present APEX, a system for climbing-based high-platform traversal. It composes edge climbs, platform walking or crawling, and posture changes into one perceptive skill set.

A ratchet reward tracks best-so-far progress and penalizes steps that go nowhere, giving dense, velocity-free guidance under strict safety rules. Lidar-based full-body policies close the sim-to-real gap through modelled mapping artefacts and map filtering. All six skills distil into one policy that picks moves from local shape. Tests on a Unitree G1 show zero-shot climbs onto platforms taller than its legs.
arxiv-2602-11243:
Agents need memory that is organized, not just stored. Alina Shutova and three co-authors propose StructMemEval, a benchmark that tests whether agents can structure long-term memory. Most current tests check simple fact recall, multi-hop recall, or time-based change.

Those skills can often be met by simple recall-augmented models, so they miss complex hierarchies. StructMemEval uses tasks humans solve by organizing knowledge: ledgers, to-do lists, trees, and similar structures. Early tests show plain recall models struggle, while memory agents succeed when prompted to organize. Yet modern models often miss the structure unprompted, pointing to a training and design gap.
arxiv-2602-11343:
The excursion algebra ties arithmetic local systems to automorphic functions. Dennis Gaitsgory and two co-authors define it as the algebra of global functions on the stack of arithmetic local systems for a scheme over a finite field and a reductive group. When the scheme is a curve, the algebra acts on automorphic functions.

The paper establishes basic properties of this algebra. It is a foundations paper, short and technical, setting out what the excursion algebra is and what it does before deeper uses follow. Readers in the Langlands program will find here the groundwork for using excursion tools as a bridge between Galois-side objects and automorphic forms.
arxiv-2602-11743:
Test-time adaptation for vision-language models usually leans on Shannon entropy to gauge prediction uncertainty. CLIP, however, carries a built-in bias from imbalanced web pretraining data, so that gauge comes out biased. Xiangyu Wu and seven co-authors show Tsallis entropy, a generalized form with a non-extensive knob, naturally suits biased distributions. Shannon performance serves as its lower bound.

They generalize it into Adaptive Debiasing Tsallis Entropy, customizing a class-specific knob from estimated label bias in incoming test data. The new method picks high-confidence views well and pairs with a label adjustment strategy, without distribution-specific hyperparameter tuning. Both forms can directly replace Shannon entropy with no other changes. Tests show it beating state-of-the-art rivals on ImageNet and five variants, with the highest average across ten cross-domain benchmarks regardless of model design or prompts.
arxiv-2602-11843:
Truncated Neumann series approximate matrix inverses and precondition polynomials, but in dense settings matrix-matrix products dominate their cost. Naive evaluation needs one product per term, while splitting methods cut that to logarithmic counts. Repeated squaring uses about twice the log count, so further gains need higher-radix kernels that extend the series by several terms per update. Piyush Sao constructs such kernels beyond the previously known radix-five case.

For radix nine the author derives an exact three-product kernel with rational coefficients, the first exact construction beyond radix five, yielding a 21 percent product reduction from repeated squaring. For radix fifteen, numerical optimization gives a four-product kernel matching the target through degree fourteen, with spillover at higher degrees handled by a new residual-based framework. That framework attains the best known asymptotic rate, and experiments support the predicted savings and runtime trends.
arxiv-2602-11943:
Homotopies between maps of differential graded rings need a concrete home. Amnon Yekutieli studies the Keller cylinder ring, which encodes homotopies between ring homomorphisms, and its higher analogues, which assemble into a simplicial cylinder ring. For the first level, the construction recovers Keller's original ring exactly.

The sets of homomorphisms into each level form a simplicial Hom set. The main result is that when the source ring is semi-free, that simplicial set is a Kan complex, the combinatorial shape that makes homotopy theory work. The paper also studies the fundamental groupoid of the first two levels, proving invariance under quasi-isomorphism and showing its automorphism groups are abelian. Applications are sketched, but the Kan result is the core.
arxiv-2602-12243:
Robot teams need shared maps of complex places, but Gaussian process models grow cubic in cost and strain links between robots. Sanket A. Salunkhe led this work with one co-author, George P. Kontoudis, presenting pxpGP, a distributed Gaussian process frame for large central and decentralised robot networks. Each robot builds a compact local pseudo-data set through sparse variational inference.

A global consensus method then joins those local pieces, using scaled proximal steps, adaptive settings, and warm starts. Tests on synthetic and real data show pxpGP and its decentralised twin beating existing distributed methods on hyperparameter estimates and prediction accuracy, with the edge growing in large networks. The result is a scalable way for robot teams to model a shared world.
arxiv-2602-12443:
Solo researchers increasingly build software as part of their research, and generative AI now assists that work while raising questions of accountability and rigour. Ka Ching Chan works alone here, proposing SHAPR, a framework for solo, human-centred, AI-assisted practice in research software development. Action Design Research gives a foundation for studying socio-technical works, but little guidance for day-to-day solo, AI-assisted practice.

SHAPR translates high-level Action Design Research principles into actionable guidance, supporting Building-Intervention-Evaluation cycles by making roles, works, thinking practices, and lightweight rules explicit. The contribution is at idea level: SHAPR itself is the design work and unit of analysis, assessed formatively for internal fit, match with Action Design Research, and fit to solo practice. The study links software development, human-AI teamwork, and reflective learning, with lessons for researcher training.
arxiv-2602-12643:
Reinforcement learning methods split between model-free speed and model-based representational strength, each with its own costs. Jashaswimalya Acharjee led this work with one co-author, Balaraman Ravindran, giving Unified Latent Dynamics, a new method that unifies model-free speed with model-based strengths, without planning cost.

State-action pairs are placed into a latent space in which the true value function is nearly linear. That supports a single set of tuning knobs across varied domains, from continuous control with low-dimensional and pixel inputs to high-dimensional Atari games. Under mild rules, the fixed point of embedding-based temporal-difference updates matches that of a matching linear model-based value expansion. Tests show strong scores across domains with a single setup.
arxiv-2602-13043:
Dynamic imaging needs methods that track objects over time while using strong spatial priors, a combination classic Kalman smoothing lacks. Benjamin Hawkes and three co-authors build on a Kalman-smoothing ADMM algorithm that handles state-space fidelity with smoothing and sparsity priors via proximity operators. Their plug-and-play variant replaces those operators with powerful denoisers such as deep networks, gaining expressivity without losing the state-space structure.

The resulting PnP-KS-ADMM algorithm handles the state-space model efficiently through Kalman smoothing while letting modern denoisers supply spatial prior knowledge. Simulations on a two-dimensional-plus-time imaging problem show improved computational efficiency over standard plug-and-play ADMM for large numbers of timesteps. For dynamic imaging, the hybrid offers a practical route to sharper, faster reconstructions.
arxiv-2602-13143:
Gamma-ray pulsars observed by Fermi can form a timing array hunting nanohertz gravitational waves, where a background from supermassive black hole binaries should dominate. Radio arrays recently reported compelling evidence for such a background near strain 2 to 3 times ten to the minus fifteen, while a 2022 Fermi analysis of 35 pulsars over 12.5 years set an upper limit near ten to the minus fourteen. Serena Valtolina and seven co-authors reanalyse the same data with a regularised likelihood that models cross-pulsar correlations directly from photons and marginalises over pulse-profile uncertainty.

Simulations show the photon-by-photon recovery is statistically more robust than earlier approaches. The new upper limit, 1.2 times ten to the minus fourteen, agrees with previous analyses. The work thus validates the gamma-ray timing method while tightening its statistical footing, keeping Fermi as an independent check on the radio background claim.
arxiv-2602-13543:
Search-capable language models need tests that cannot be answered from training data alone, and news provides a fresh source. LiveNewsBench automatically builds question-answer pairs from recent news articles, forcing multi-hop search, page visits, and reasoning, so scores separate internal knowledge from search skill. An automated curation pipeline enables frequent updates and a large training set for agentic search models, addressing data scarcity in the field.

A subset of human-verified samples anchors reliable evaluation, and a broad range of commercial and open-weight models plus web search APIs were tested on the benchmark. Leaderboard, data sets, and code are public, inviting reuse and comparison. Yunfan Zhang leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13643:
Magnetic order in strongly linked electrons can be reshaped by altermagnetic spin splitting, a largely unexplored influence this paper investigates in the two-dimensional square-lattice Hubbard model. Spin-linked second-neighbor hopping reshapes Fermi surface nesting and van Hove peaks, steering magnetic instabilities. Using path-limited quantum Monte Carlo, the authors map the dominant magnetic correlation as a function of filling and hopping ratio through the momentum-sorted spin structure factor.

The analysis reveals a transition from antiferromagnetic order at wavevector pi, pi in the isotropic half-filled system to tilted spiral order at pi, q as anisotropy or doping grows. It finally enters a short-range regime where stripe and spiral correlations coexist. The findings suggest a route to spiral correlation in altermagnetic systems, potentially enabling spin-based devices based on tilted spin textures. Yinlong Li leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14243:
Manuel Bodirsky, writing alone, offers a 2026 arXiv course on graph homomorphisms and universal algebra. Constraint satisfaction problems arise across theoretical computer science, and a central theme is the border between polynomial-time tractability and NP-hardness. The course introduces the universal-algebraic approach to finite-domain constraint problems.

It covers cyclic terms and bounded width theorems in particular. To stay accessible, the course starts in the tangible world of directed graphs and graph homomorphism problems. That concrete entry point grounds abstract algebra in problems readers can picture, before the general theory takes over.
arxiv-2602-14343:
A. Peláez-Torres and seven co-authors bound a 2026 arXiv exoplanet air: that of GJ 1214 b. Using all on-hand transits from the CRIRES+ scope at the VLT, the team sought water vapor, methane, and carbon dioxide. Eight K-band transit sets at sharpness near 100,000 were studied, with SysRem fix for sky and star effects and cross-match against template models.

No key marks of water, methane, or carbon dioxide were found. Inject-and-recover tests across metal share and cloud-deck pressure show the non-finds rule out airs with low clouds and mid or low metal shares. Methane gives the tightest real limits, while carbon dioxide oddly rules out mid metal shares near 100 times solar. Guesses for the future ANDES tool frame what study may still gain.
arxiv-2602-14443:
Lanqing Guo and four co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv control problem in image generation: editing at the element level. Modern generators achieve remarkable quality, but users still struggle to adjust shapes, colors, or objects intuitively. The paper offers layer-wise controllable generation through simplified vector graphics.

Images are first parsed into hierarchical vector representations that are semantically aligned and structurally coherent. A synthesis framework guided by those vectors then lets users freely modify elements and translate edits into photorealistic outputs. By combining vector structure and semantics with noise prediction, the method controls geometry, color, and object semantics precisely. Tests span image editing, object-level manipulation, and fine-grained content creation.
arxiv-2602-14743:
Sonke Tenckhoff, Mario Koddenbrock, and Erik Rodner present LLMStructBench, a benchmark for large language models extracting structured data and emitting valid JSON from natural text. Its open dataset holds diverse, manually verified parsing scenarios of varied complexity, tested across twenty-two models and five prompting strategies.

Complementary metrics capture both token-level accuracy and document-level validity, letting the benchmark compare model, size, and prompting effects on parsing reliability. A striking finding is that prompting strategy matters more than standard traits like model size. Structured extraction, the paper argues, is a prompting problem first.
arxiv-2602-15143:
Ma and colleagues protect language models against unauthorized copying of their skills through trace rewrites. Distillation transfers capabilities from large models into smaller student models. Such copying exploits the effort and cost behind frontier models. The team changes teacher traces toward two goals: cutting the training value of query answers, and planting signatures in student models.

They introduce several ways to rewrite teacher outputs while keeping answers right and sensible. Two methods use language models, while others use gradient methods. Tests show a simple prompt rewrite gives a strong blocking effect while keeping teacher scores steady or better. The same approach plants marks that can be found with almost no false alarms.
arxiv-2602-15943:
Gonzalez and Salinas-Arizmendi offer a compact analytic form for the synchrotron function, a quantity central to radiation from fast charged particles in space and in high energy labs. The function is defined by a hard integral over modified Bessel functions, so workers usually turn to numerical integration or special approximations.

Using the Method of Brackets, the authors derive a formula that yields controlled expansions for both small and large arguments. The new expressions match direct numerical integration closely and lay bare the analytic shape of the function. That makes the result a fast stand-in for repeated numerical runs, and a handy tool wherever quick, well controlled estimates of synchrotron spectra are needed.
arxiv-2602-16043:
Konstantin Gerbig and Min-Kai Lin revisit an instability that can arise in dusty disks when dust diffusivity or viscosity falls steeply as dust density rises. Their updated model adds an incompressible, viscous gas that responds around the disk and couples to dust through drag. For small dust stopping times, the basic threshold for instability stays near the earlier value, with gas feedback shifting results only modestly.

Nonlinear simulations confirm linear growth and selection toward the fastest-growing wavelength. Yet for power-law closures with a negative diffusion slope, the growth does not level off; steepening gradients drive collapse into sharp spikes in finite time. A piecewise closure that limits the negative slope to a finite density range removes the blowup and sets peak densities by the chosen saturation scale. The authors conclude that the instability can organize dusty turbulence linearly, while realistic saturation needs further physics.
arxiv-2602-16243:
Shinya Tomizawa and coauthors present a new family of multi-centered rotating black hole solutions in five-dimensional vacuum Einstein gravity. These give explicit examples of cohomogeneity-three spacetimes. With two commuting Killing vector fields, the theory reduces to 3D gravity coupled to a nonlinear sigma model. The scalar fields of the extremal Myers-Perry solution can be expressed through two harmonic functions on flat space.

Promoting those functions to include multiple sources yields multi-centre extremal Myers-Perry black holes. Each center forms a smooth spherical Killing horizon, provided rotation parameters stay within a stated bound. All curvature singularities hide behind horizons, and no closed timelike curves arise on or outside them. The solutions are asymptotically locally Minkowski. A binary example shows no conical defects between the two black holes.
arxiv-2602-16343:
Yixuan Xiao leads a team of three coauthors on a labeling puzzle in audio deepfake detection. Text-to-speech systems do not usually produce waveforms directly, so recent spoof detection studies use resynthesized waveforms from vocoders and neural audio codecs to stand in for an attacker. Vocoders are built for speech synthesis, but neural audio codecs were built to compress audio for storage and transmission, and their ability to discretize speech later drew interest for language-model-based synthesis.

That dual role creates a labeling question: codec-resynthesized data could count as either genuine or spoof, and very little research has addressed the choice. The authors build a challenging extension of the ASVspoof 5 dataset for this purpose and test how different labeling choices change detection performance. Their findings give guidance on labeling strategies for codec-based data.
arxiv-2602-16443:
Sebastian Spinner and Andre Weiner analyze buffet dynamics from ultrahigh-bypass-ratio nacelle installation on a transport-aircraft wing. Shock-boundary-layer interaction on the wing's lower surface can be caused or amplified by installation. The study examines the Airbus XRF-1 configuration at a high subsonic Mach number, using scale-resolving delayed detached eddy simulations and unsteady pressure paint.

Coherent structures are extracted with a data-efficient multi-taper spectral decomposition. Dominant modes occur at low Strouhal numbers, from one tenth to three tenths. Surface modes reveal wave-like shock motions starting near the pylon-wing intersection and travelling toward the fuselage, linked to separation downstream of the shock. Further dominant modes show spanwise oscillations of the separated flow region and shock oscillations linked to shear layer instabilities. Modal analysis of volume data reveals pressure waves tied to these modes travelling upstream around the wing.
arxiv-2602-16643:
Shuta Kikuchi and Shu Tanaka solve RNA inverse folding with a factorization machine plus quadratic-optimization annealing, called FMQA. The task is to find nucleotide strings that favor a given target secondary shape. Many past routes need huge numbers of string tests, which hurts when lab checks cost a lot. FMQA is a discrete black-box optimizer known for strong scores from few tests.

Using FMQA here means turning nucleotides into binary variables. The study tests all twenty-four ways to map four nucleotides to ordered integers, paired with four binary-integer codes. Those choices shape the surrogate model and the search land, and thus affect score quality. RNA designers get both a new FMQA frame and a clear map of how coding choices change results.
arxiv-2602-16943:
Arnold Cartagena and Ariane Teixeira introduce the GAP benchmark, testing whether text safety transfers to tool-call safety in language model agents. Agents increasingly act through tool calls with real-world consequences that text outputs alone do not carry. Safety evaluations, however, overwhelmingly measure text-level refusal, leaving a critical question open: does alignment that blocks harmful text also block harmful actions?

Six frontier models are tested across six regulated domains, seven jailbreak scenarios per domain, three system prompt conditions, and two prompt variants, yielding over seventeen thousand analysis-ready datapoints. The central finding is that text safety does not transfer to tool-call safety. In many cases, text refuses a harmful request while tool calls simultaneously execute the forbidden action, a divergence formalized as the GAP metric. Even under safety-reinforced prompts, hundreds of such cases persist across all models.
arxiv-2602-17043:
Paul-Hieu V. Nguyen led a four-author team asking how high a human decathlon score could ever go. Because the decathlon spans sprinting, throwing, jumping, and endurance, many treat it as the fullest test of athletic ability. The paper builds a Bayesian model that forecasts how one athlete performs across all ten events over time, catching non-linear trends and the way each event depends on the ones before it.

With that model, the authors can simulate the spread of possible top scores and sketch the athlete profiles that could plausibly approach the limit. The work offers a principled read on the ceiling of human all-round athletic performance, rather than a single guessed number. Coaches and analysts get a picture of what mix of strengths a near-limit decathlete would need.
arxiv-2602-17243:
Tapender led a two-author paper on low-scale baryogenesis through tri-resonant leptogenesis in a scotogenic model with scalar dark matter, framed by non-holomorphic modular A4 symmetry. Three nearly degenerate right-handed neutrinos sit in the triplet representation, with near-degeneracy arising as a small perturbation on a dominant singlet contribution. Generalized CP symmetry leaves the complex modulus as the sole source of CP violation.

For the inverted hierarchy, the model predicts the atmospheric mixing angle in the lower octant near maximal. CP phases sit near zero or full circle, and forecasts for neutrinoless double beta decay and cosmology can be tested, though one dataset mix disfavors that hierarchy.
