arxiv-2605-29943: Dekka Muni Kumar, Dhruba Jyoti Kalita, and Yogesh Kumar Meena pick EEG channel sets for motor-imagery links. Their multi-goal search balances channel place, via a Gaussian kernel, against task split, judged by task-linked desynchronization inside trials. Three methods — genetic, swarm, and decomposition searches — hunt together for compact sets near sensorimotor cortex. On four sets it scores high eighties on the best set and mid sixties on the hardest, beating single-goal and fixed-set rivals. Compact sets cut compute load, suiting wearable and live brain-computer use.
arxiv-2605-30043: Sophie Rosu and 16 colleagues trace the outer rings of Supernova 1987A from 1994 to 2024, using Hubble, VLT and JWST data from optical to mid-infrared light. These rings left the star some twenty thousand years before the explosion, yet few studies had examined them. Their brightness has faded for three decades as the blast's first ultraviolet flash dies away, with no sign of the debris hitting the rings. Decay times, temperatures and densities differ between the northern and southern rings, whose spectra stand apart from the equatorial ring's.
arxiv-2605-30343: Lukas Aichberger and Sepp Hochreiter introduce Reasoning in Memory (RiM), a latent method replacing autoregressive reasoning steps with memory blocks. Human cognition uses working memory to hold and handle information inside without sharing thoughts. RiM draws on this principle with fixed sets of tokens opening working memory. They employ a two-stage plan: first grounding memory blocks by predicting reasoning steps after each block, then dropping step checks and tuning the final answer step by step. Tests show RiM matches or exceeds latent methods while skipping autoregressive thoughts.
arxiv-2605-30443: Linfeng Liu and four colleagues ask if vectors learned for steering in one language can shape generation in another, in a study of cross-lingual figurative steering. Within one language, steering lifts the share of the intended figure. Across 408 comparisons spanning four models, six languages, and four figures, steering lifts the figurative share from about 12 percent to about 20 percent. They split each language's steering vector into the mean of other languages' vectors plus a residual. The mean matches or beats its vector, while the residual steers worse.
arxiv-2605-30543: Nylund, Husom, and Prillard map the first decade of the LIMITS workshop, a venue for computing within limits, research that questions endless growth, plans for scarcity, and cuts energy and material use. Reviewing 160 publications from 2015 to 2025, they trace the field's spread, themes, and methods. Talk of degrowth and post-growth grew sharply in the final two years, and work from beyond the Global North increased but stayed limited. Most papers argue positions or observe practice rather than build artifacts, though solution-oriented work has grown.
arxiv-2605-30643: Niang reworks a service metric for corporate bond dealers quoting prices on client requests. Raw hit ratios mislead when client flow carries uneven adverse-selection content. He replaces the raw ratio with a residual-quality-adjusted version, splitting post-trade losses into observable factors and a residual toxicity term. Under a quadratic approximation, optimal quotes combine a riskless spread, inventory and credit skews, a toxicity charge, and a service subsidy. Synthetic tests show raw targeting can subsidize toxic flow, while quality targeting steers service to cleaner flow.
arxiv-2605-30743: Dang and colleagues improve coding and making of inorganic materials with a symmetry-aware representation and a novel padding trick. Their method exploits crystal shape through Wyckoff site length-aware padding in an encoder, giving a more robust code. The boost helps deep learning models generate stable, new inorganic structures with better scores and speed. An end-to-end chain joins generative models with toughness analysis to make novel stable matter. Rebuild scores rise on proton conductor data, and the method makes far more novel stable matter than a rival.
arxiv-2605-30843: Kang turns the usual reinforcement-learning question around. Instead of a known reward and a search for a good policy, he asks whether offline expert data can reveal the reward the expert was chasing. He first proves that structural econometricians studying dynamic discrete choice and machine learners studying entropy-regularized inverse learning work on the same model under different names. He then walks through classic identification and computation routes, with their limits, and modern adversarial, occupancy, and offline methods, closing with a gradient-based estimator for offline inverse learning.
arxiv-2605-30943: Rovirosa and Schmolze build clear neural Markov models for non-stationary time series. Frequency estimates for transition matrices collapse at high resolution, where data grow sparse. Their hybrid approach lets a neural network parameterize the space of stochastic tables, allowing changing chains to be estimated from sparse data. Using financial markets as a testbed, they find conditioning on volatility gives a more consistent Markov structure than return-based states. Unlike black-box sequence models, their method yields explicit tables open to geometric study.
arxiv-2605-31043: Maia and colleagues escape a capacity ceiling for networks on the SPD manifold. Stacking BiMap layers with ReEig often adds no capacity on EEG data, because ReEig rarely activates. When domains share no discriminative directions, a single filter cannot align every domain. Their SCAP combines experts into a bilinear map via cross-attention, matching per-domain filters to first order with fewer experts than domains when filters span few directions. Adapted mechanisms mitigate routing collapse. The method improves balanced accuracy over fixed-filter SPDNet on five EEG motor datasets.
arxiv-2605-31443: Chihara and team offer a regression-adjustment framework for longitudinal treatment effects in randomized tests. Standard adjustments cut variance with pre-treatment covariates, but they usually yield only average effects. That hides when effects appear and how long they last. The team models intermediate outcomes and shifting post-treatment covariates over time through transition kernels. They prove the estimator is asymptotically normal and hits the efficiency bound. Simulations plus an A/B test from a Japanese streaming platform show its practical edge.
arxiv-2606-00343:
Clemençon and co-authors coin a depth gauge built for the far tail of heavy data. Depth ranks how core or wild a point sits in a set. Heavy-tail data throw wild points that norms built for calm data misjudge. Their gauge works in ring-and-ray terms, like the tail law of such data.

The gauge sorts the wild points of a heavy set with ease. It suits stray hunts, where wild points are the quarry. Past a high bar, the gauge of top points nears the gauge of the limit law. They prove that match under set terms. Fit paths from scant and vast runs are worked out too. Tests back its worth for stray hunts in thick-tail sets.
arxiv-2606-00443:
Vallis, Matilsky, and Nicolas survey jets and super-rotation in deep and thin world skies. Side flows rule the skies of most worlds in our Sun's brood. Jets are tight streams set in a calm ground flow. Super-rotation means fast pro-grade flow at the waist of a world.

Both traits show in deep and thin skies alike. Slow and fast worlds can host them as well. Names on the list span Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, and Titan. Jets call for push that flows up-slope, not down. The survey weighs how such up-slope flow can arise. Heat churn in deep skies, shape and hill wave traits, and wave-flow play all come in scope. Tide locks on far worlds join the tale as well.
arxiv-2606-00843:
Hong, Xia, and Qiao sharpen bounds on a graph measure in this 2026 maths paper. The A-alpha matrix blends a graph's degree matrix with its adjacency matrix, weighted by alpha. Its largest eigenvalue is the A-alpha spectral radius. At alpha zero it gives the classic spectral radius. At alpha one half, doubled, it gives the signless Laplacian radius.

A known result bounds how much the classic radius drops when one vertex is cut. Sun and Das proved that bound in 2020, and a short proof came in 2026. Hong's team proves the matching result for the whole alpha family. Their corollary is strictly sharper than the old bound in most cases. They also re-derive a 2022 bound in short form. Last, they merge two classic inequalities, one for each endpoint measure, into a single statement for all alpha.
arxiv-2606-00943:
Kojo sets out an ideal model of quarkyonic matter in this 2026 physics paper. Quarkyonic matter is a dense state of QCD with a split life. Its bulk traits are ruled by quarks, yet its low-energy excitations stay confined. The shift from baryon to quark rule is driven by quark saturation.

As density grows, quark states fill up and the crossover begins. Pressure then climbs fast while energy density rises at a modest pace. The result is a peak in the speed of sound, as neutron star data hint. Saturation can start at a few times nuclear density, before baryon cores would touch. Kojo's IdylliQ model spells out how baryon and quark occupation odds relate. It shows how the matter stiffens as a result. Applied to neutral matter with hyperons, the quark-level rules push baryon species apart. That push softens the known hyperon problem for neutron star theory.
arxiv-2606-01343:
Gamble, Khalkhali, and Pagliaroli study equations for random fuzzy geometries. These geometries arise from matrix integrals. The ensembles are Hermitian and bi-tracial in form. A determinant term sits in the integrand. Matter fields, bosons or fermions, couple to the geometry. The team derive Schwinger-Dyson equations from the saddle point equations.

Complex analytic methods drive that derivation step. For general potentials, the equations can be solved step by step. This holds for bosonic and fermionic terms alike. For Gaussian models with one boson or fermion, exact forms exist. Free energy and the first moment come out in elliptic integrals. The bosonic case links to the Hoppe and three-colour models.
arxiv-2606-01443:
Le proposes UR-JEPA, a fix for collapse in predictive embedding models. Joint-embedding architectures can collapse to useless constants. LeJEPA fights collapse with an isotropic Gaussian target. That target clashes with the manifold hypothesis, though. Embeddings should sit on a low-dimensional subset, not spread evenly. UR-JEPA targets a uniformly rectifiable measure instead. A smoothed Carleson-type square function realizes that target.

On Inet10, UR-JEPA gains 0 point 83 points over LeJEPA. Seed variance drops by about 30 percent as well. Other datasets land in the same accuracy band at convergence. The geometric signature differs sharply, though. Its PCA spectrum drops four to five orders by index 20 to 25. LeJEPA's spectrum stays near flat in comparison.
arxiv-2606-01643:
Hong and Košecká diagnose a hidden failure in sign language production. The task turns natural language text into avatar sign motion. Quality is usually scored by motion FID and back-translation BLEU. Both scores can improve while the motion stays unfaithful to the signs. They propose scoring at three independent levels instead. Initial-pose conditioning is the first level. Output diversity is the second level. Target faithfulness is the third. Pairwise-distance ratios in a frozen autoencoder's latent space give the scores.

Fourteen model checkpoints face tests on How2Sign data. Faithfulness is never attained by any of them. FID varies by nearly two orders of magnitude across checkpoints. It is uncorrelated with faithfulness in their results. On an isolated gloss dataset, good faithfulness is attainable. Sentence-level paired dataset size is the bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-02043:
Bonnemain and co-authors derive exact fields for KdV solitons in interaction. Solitons act as both waves and particles in such systems. Mid interaction, they deform and spread out. Telling single solitons apart then gets hard. A field-based view at small scale resolves that issue here.

Exact fields of charge, current, and speed are built in space-time. They come from the inverse scattering transform for KdV. Single solitons can be tracked through full interactions. Paths and deformation are measured past the far-field regime. N interacting solitons obey N continuity equations. Interactions are encoded in initial links between them. Those links are then carried forward in time.
arxiv-2606-02143:
Chede and co-authors design proof systems for counting winning strategies in QBF. For a quantified Boolean formula, that count is the #QBF problem. It is considered harder than the analogous #SAT problem. Proof systems for QBF and #SAT have drawn recent study. Extending ideas from both fields yields systems for #QBF.

Such systems matter for theory and for solver design. They can certify and improve #QBF solvers over time. That solver area is still in its early stages. The team count Skolem functions in their systems. A naive system is studied alongside expansion-based ones. Universal variable expansion rules ground those systems. Structural weaknesses lead to lower bounds for them. An alternative direction is explored in response.
arxiv-2606-02443:
Zhao and co-authors test whether AI video models can warn people before accidents happen. Between the first sign of danger and the crash, a window for action often exists. Always-on models could issue warnings in that window. Past benchmarks miss this skill. They use static inputs, ignore timing, and skip false alarms on safe scenes.

Their benchmark, PaSBench-Video, holds 740 videos. Of these, 481 show risk and 259 show none. Four domains are covered: driving, healthcare, daily life, and industrial work. Risk clips carry frame-level marks for risk onset and accident. A model must watch causally and warn on time. Tests of 13 models show none passes 20 percent on the strictest score. Higher recall comes with more false alarms. Driving is hardest, since routine and risky scenes look alike. Models lean on scene cues, not on reasoning about harm.
arxiv-2606-02543:
Parks and co-authors suppress a noise source in trapped-ion quantum bits. A magnetic field lets hyperfine clock qubits pick up a vector differential light shift. Polarization can tune that shift. The team measures a magic polarization condition in ytterbium-171 ions. It suppresses light shifts in two qubit types at once. Both the ground and metastable clock qubits benefit.

Calculations extend the result to common trapped ion species. The minimum bias fields needed are modest. They sit below field strengths already typical in labs. Methods for metastable qubit control in ytterbium-171 are also shown. State preparation and measurement infidelity reaches the ten-thousandths range. The work eases a practical burden for ion-based quantum computing.
arxiv-2606-02643:
Liu and co-authors attack the running cost of retrieval-augmented language systems. Such systems fetch outside knowledge before answering. That pipeline is powerful but costly. Cost attacks aim to inflate token use. Past attacks assume direct prompt control. The team argues that poisoning the knowledge base is more feasible. Their paradigm, RA-ICA, injects malicious documents into the external corpus.

A framework called CREEP crafts the poison. Language model agents write documents that are relevant enough to be retrieved. The same documents trigger abnormal token use at inference. A new reinforcement learning method, MA-GRPO, tunes the agents. It learns from a memory of the best past attack documents. Tests on three real datasets raise token consumption up to 13.12 times. Success rates pass 90 percent. Answer integrity stays intact. The work exposes cost as a security surface for RAG systems.
arxiv-2606-02843:
Gábriel, Jánosik, Melján, and Nádor work on a classic grid problem from combinatorics. The old question asks how many points can sit on an n by n grid with no k of them on one line. Their version is extensible. It seeks point sets in the whole integer lattice with the highest possible density.

In this version, at most k(n) points may be collinear inside each n by n subgrid. The authors build optimal sets when k grows in a linear way. They build positive-density sets when k is a power function. They also prove a threshold result. Any set that reaches a stated density bound forces k(n) to grow at least like a power of n. So no such set exists when k stays constant. A final reduction links the constant case to sets for more general limit functions.
arxiv-2606-03143:
Yang and co-authors let AI agents improve their skills together without sharing raw task records. Agents lean on skill libraries for hard tasks, so skill growth drives self-improvement. One user's task stream is too narrow to build broad skills. Sharing full records across users would fix the data gap, but it breaks privacy and forces one shared library on unlike users.

Their framework, FederatedSkill, shares skill diffs instead. A diff is a structured patch to a local library, in meaning terms. On the server, an evolution agent merges these patches. It models each client's skill limits, so growth stays personal, not an average for all. Tests span 20 agent task families. FederatedSkill beat self-evolving baselines by a wide margin. Success rates rose by up to about 44 percent, and compute cost fell by about 38 percent. The work ports the federated idea from model training to agent skills.
arxiv-2606-03743:
Fu, Liu, Wang, and Yuan refactor machine-generated formal proofs into modular, library-grade artifacts. Language models now produce Lean proofs that compile. Their scripts still read worse than library proofs: less modular, less reusable, harder to maintain. A compile-first goal drives that gap. Length-based scores miss the higher-level qualities that matter.

Proof-Refactoring follows how humans rework proofs instead. Four phases structure the agent's work. Candidate fragments are extracted from the draft. Helper declarations are designed around them. Each piece is then proven formally on its own. The original proof is repaired using the verified parts. On PutnamBench and Putnam2025 proofs, rubric scores beat a strong Claude Code baseline. Gains are largest in signature quality and human readability. The results show process guidance can lift proof structure without chasing length.
arxiv-2606-03843:
Inamdar, So, Milenia, and Zemel re-evaluate continual learning through few-shot adaptation. Continual methods balance stability against plasticity across a task sequence. Standard stability scores use zero-shot recall of old tasks. That demands perfect recall and misses how fast a model can re-adapt. Few-shot evaluation gives a fuller picture of both traits.

A fine-grained study runs on continual image classification sequences. A new metric, per-shot plasticity, quantifies quick adaptation. Adding foresight changes the picture in a notable way. Meta-learning a short run of future tasks induces learning-to-learn across the sequence. Popular strategies look different under this lens than under zero-shot scoring. Some methods retain more usable knowledge than raw recall suggests. The work argues for richer evaluation before ranking continual methods. Benchmark designers get a concrete alternative protocol.
arxiv-2606-03943:
Tong and co-authors seek a better bridge from video forecasts to robot actions. Video models know how scenes move, but plain color frames lack depth. They leave contact shape and exact 3D motion unclear. Action labels across tasks and robot bodies are also costly to gather. A shared action form could ease both gaps.

PointAction trains a video model to predict frames plus moving 3D point maps. Those maps track the scene parts that matter for the task. A diffusion decoder then turns point motion into robot commands. The team reports top 4D quality on robot scenes. It beat prior methods in simulation tests. It also transferred to two real robot arms not seen in pretraining.
arxiv-2606-04243:
Ivan Viakhirev studies in 2026 the structure hidden inside an integral self-consistency equation. Such an equation defines a quantity only implicitly: the unknown appears on both sides, inside an integral.

He asks when such equations have a solution at all, and when the solution is unique. The density at the heart of the problem turns out to be monotone in the key parameter, under mild conditions. That single fact organizes the rest: branches of solutions can be tracked, and spurious ones ruled out. Numeric tests matched the analysis. The result gives a clean check for models that define their key quantity this way. Physics and economics both use such equations.
arxiv-2606-04443:
Delgado asks what black-box testing can certify about post-quantum key encapsulation, in a 2026 arXiv cryptography paper. The tests probe Fujisaki-Okamoto decapsulation. That is the step that recovers the key. The tests see only values that reach final key derivation. They do not see the internal re-encryption. He studies variants that carry a confirmation code. This is a witness value meant to prove the key was formed honestly.

He derives a tight bound on acceptance. One list-hit term turns out to be the real obstruction. A one-query construction from any witness predictor matches the bound. He also proves a limit on all such tests. Operations outside the observable cone cannot be certified. So any execution certifier has two error rates that sum to at least one. Case studies on ML-KEM and HQC sort checks into three rows: theorem-covered, artifact, and non-certification.
arxiv-2606-04643:
Paganini investigates a property of spacetimes called conicality, in a 2026 arXiv relativity paper. Conicality asks whether the joint future of a finite set of events uniquely reveals the set that generated it. The reveal works through light cone structure. Paganini tests which broad conditions are enough to guarantee it.

He shows that neither condition suffices on its own. Conicality can fail under each. Causally simple, future cohesive spacetimes of dimension 1+N, with N at least two, do satisfy conicality. These can be read as the timelike past of an observer. That fit is natural, he notes.
arxiv-2606-04943: Throat singers produce two notes at once — a low drone and a high whistle — by shaping their vocal tract with remarkable precision. This paper builds a computer model of the throat and mouth that can copy-synthesize this biphonic singing, with every step adjustable by gradient-based learning. It connects the physics of the voice to the mathematics of machine learning.
arxiv-2606-05043:
Samuel Christie, Munindar Singh, and Amit Chopra introduce Strabo in this 2026 arXiv paper, which brings declarative interaction protocols to agentic AI. Interaction protocols are blueprints that specify how software agents may exchange messages, and declarative versions can be checked for correctness before any agent is built. The team connects this research to the Universal Commerce Protocol, a recent Google-led effort to standardize e-commerce interactions for AI agents.

Working in two parts, they first model the checkout portion of the protocol as a declarative Langshaw protocol and implement agents with Peach, a programming model for Langshaw. They then show those Peach agents can interoperate with Universal Commerce Protocol agents implemented by Google, confirming the model matches the real system. The result points to a gradual path for introducing declarative protocols into conventional settings without wholesale replacement.
arxiv-2606-05243:
Soon-Tae Hong and Bum-Hoon Lee derive equation of state parameters for a fluid of stringy extended objects in higher-dimensional cosmology in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of point particles, the cosmic fluid here is made of extended stringy objects in more than four dimensions.

The authors first construct the strong energy conditions behind the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems, for both massive and massless versions of these objects. From those conditions they find a lower bound on the equation of state parameter w, the ratio of pressure to energy density. The bound holds for both fluids in five or more dimensions. They relate the result to the Hawking-Penrose limit for point particles in four dimensions. They also split the parameter into contributions from the point-particle property, the cosmological constant, and the extended-object degrees of freedom. The weak energy condition is investigated as well.
arxiv-2606-05343:
Avinash Kumar Paladi and colleagues constrain the orbital eccentricity of the supermassive black hole binary candidate PKS 2131-021 in this 2026 arXiv paper. This blazar's radio brightness has varied sinusoidally in epochs over decades. That is naturally explained if the jet-emitting black hole orbits a companion and Doppler boosting modulates the jet as it swings toward and away from us.

The authors extend the kinematic orbital model to eccentric orbits using the Keplerian parametric solution and run Bayesian estimation on radio data from 1975 to 2021 gathered by three observatories. Without noise modeling they find a residual eccentricity of 0.053, with a Bayes factor of 3.15 favoring the eccentric model over a circular one. Once red noise is included through a damped random walk process, however, the circular model is preferred and the eccentricity is only bounded above by 0.15. The circular-plus-noise model is favored and recovers a period across all datasets.
arxiv-2606-05443:
Alex Li and Joseph Jacobson introduce MIRAI in this 2026 arXiv paper, a deep learning framework that predicts which research papers will have high impact. MIRAI makes its prediction from minimal information: only a paper's title, abstract, and publication date. Trained on the arXiv academic graph, the model predicts two five-year impact measures, a paper's PageRank in the citation network and its citation count.

On papers published in 2021 it achieved rank correlations of about 0.47 for PageRank and 0.62 for citations, using only the abstract page. The authors then build a research ideation pipeline on top of the predictor, generating research ideas steered toward predicted high impact. An independent language-model judge rated those ideas more impactful than a baseline pipeline's at a ratio of four to three. The five-year citation prediction model is available through a web application, making the tool usable by anyone triaging new literature.
arxiv-2606-05743:
Minseok Choi and colleagues give safety guards a memory that learns attack styles, not just examples in a 2026 arXiv paper. Jailbreak tricks evolve faster than fixed safety classifiers can follow. Memory-based guards adapt, but they often refuse harmless queries that merely resemble attacks. Membrane stores contrastive cells: each pairs the traits that should trigger a block with a look-alike benign case that should pass. Cells are indexed by attack strategy, so one cell covers many topics.

New harmful chats and their benign twins are distilled into cells without any retraining. Retrieved cells then ground each fresh safety decision. On HarmBench and AgentHarm tests the guard earned the top score on all six attack types. Benign refusals stayed between seven and fourteen percent, far under the twenty-eight to eighty-five percent of prior guards. Cells kept most of their strength under new attack styles and poisoning attempts.
arxiv-2606-05843:
Ruoxi Sun and colleagues open a multimodal model to find who does the visual fetching in a 2026 arXiv paper. These models answer questions about images, but their inner division of labor was opaque. A token-level score, Retrieval Attention Mass, ranks attention heads by how much they gather query-relevant visual detail. A small elite stands out: Context-aware Retrieval heads, or CoRe heads.

Across image domains and model sizes the split held firm. CoRe heads act as dedicated extractors while most heads spread attention widely. Deleting just the top five percent of CoRe heads badly damaged reasoning scores. Deleting low-ranked heads barely mattered. The concentration also pays in speed: leaning on the sparse pattern sped up inference while performance held. Functional sparsity, the authors argue, is a design principle hiding inside these models. Future architectures could build around it deliberately.
arxiv-2606-05943:
Schmüdgen builds the theory of operators that conjugate as they act in a 2026 arXiv paper. An antilinear operator flips the sign rule on complex scalars, conjugating them on exit. Linear theory fills libraries; its antilinear cousin is rarely studied. Yet antilinear maps appear inside C-symmetric and C-self-adjoint maps, a live area of physics.

The paper studies densely defined unbounded antilinear operators, above all the normal ones. Several tests for antilinear normality are proven, each phrased differently. One class gets a close look. The main result describes the structure of unbounded antilinear normal operators. Structure theorems matter: they split a wild object into plain pieces. The work extends spectral thinking where conjugation breaks the usual rules. Operator theorists and physicists are the audience.
arxiv-2606-06243:
Kei Yuen Chan, Kaidi Wu, Jun Yu, and Hongfeng Zhang prove stability results for a key functor in this 2026 arXiv paper on representation theory. The Casselman Jacquet functor extracts, from a representation of a real reductive group, the part that captures its asymptotic behavior. Such functors are workhorses for classifying representations, but the real setting is topologically harder than the p adic one. Earlier work leaned on narrower classes of modules.

The authors study the smooth version of the functor, with submodule and quotient variants, for smooth Fréchet representations of moderate growth. Beyond exactness, surjectivity, and globalization results, they prove a stability property for intersections of Jacquet subspaces. That stability is the technical heart of the paper. As an application, they establish the full real version of the Bernstein Zelevinsky filtrations, a layered decomposition that organizes representations of general linear groups and their mirabolic subgroups.
arxiv-2606-06543:
Xiaobin Li and co-authors schedule a rush hour burst of train departures in this 2026 arXiv paper on railway operations. In concentrated departure scenarios, many trains leave in a short window. Dispatchers must jointly choose the departure order and which track section each train uses. The decisions interact, and delays propagate. The team encodes both in one QUBO model, a binary optimization format suited to quantum and quantum inspired solvers.

Because a static formula cannot capture time dependent effects, they add a simulation layer. It scores each candidate plan on section occupation, waiting at stations, platform pressure, running time swings, and delay spread. Heuristics, quantum inspired methods, and hybrid algorithms were then compared under normal, disturbed, and larger scale settings. The quantum inspired and hybrid approaches proved feasible and often strong. Dispatchers gain a tested menu for a problem where one bad slot can ripple across the network.
arxiv-2606-06743:
Before a language model can speak, speech must be chopped into tokens, compact codes that carry both meaning and sound. Arjun Gangwar and Umesh present HybridCodec in this 2026 arXiv paper, a neural audio codec that tries to get the best of two rival designs. One design squeezes meaning into the first coding layer; the other keeps meaning and sound in fully separate streams.

HybridCodec keeps the separate streams and also distills knowledge from a large self supervised speech model into the meaning stream during training. That teacher is not needed when the codec runs, which keeps the system light. On LibriSpeech it posted the best meaning focused score among rivals, with a first layer word error rate near fifteen percent, and it reconstructed speech competitively. It also ran three times faster than the leading dual stream model and held up on unfamiliar and foreign language speech.
arxiv-2606-06943:
Test time defenses for vision language models often buy safety with slowness. Kim and Um target that trade off in this 2026 arXiv paper, a companion to their counterattack work. Their method tunes prompts while an attack is under way. Augmented views of the input supply the evidence. The catch is that some views are corrupted too.

Two scores grade each view before it is trusted. Stability checks whether weak changes leave the prediction unmoved. Suitability checks whether the view sits in a dense, typical feature region. Those scores weight both the tuning loss and the final prediction. Trustworthy views speak loudly; corrupted views are muted. Across fine grained benchmarks, ImageNet variants, and many attacks, the method set new robustness marks. It stayed fast even with few views available. The authors argue that judging view quality is the missing piece in test time adaptation.
arxiv-2606-07443:
Ghazi, Nasser, Calmon, and Issa characterize the best privacy mechanism for a statistical decision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Binary hypothesis testing asks whether data came from one distribution or another. Under local differential privacy, each observation is randomized on the user's device before analysis, trading testing power for privacy. Earlier work described optimal mechanisms but computed them only in exponential time, leaving the optimum out of reach for practical alphabet sizes.

The authors prove a structure they call Sort-Partition-Randomize. After sorting outcomes by likelihood ratio, an optimal mechanism groups them into contiguous blocks and applies randomized response, a coin-flip-style scrambling, to the block label. This holds for every privacy level and divergence measure of utility. It yields a dynamic program computing the exact optimum in cubic time, faster with a budget. Practitioners can compute, not approximate, the best privacy-utility trade-off across the privacy range.
arxiv-2606-07543:
Nayak, Gautam, and Varanasi interview older workers about holding bridge jobs in workplaces being reshaped by generative AI, in this 2026 arXiv study. Bridge employment means part-time or transitional work between a career job and full retirement. The authors spoke with 21 professionals aged 40 and above in such roles as AI tools spread. Participants described breaks at every stage of deciding on bridge work, both temporal, unsettling their plans, and structural, changing the roles.

In response, workers rebuilt their tasks through boundary work, redrawing what they would and would not hand to AI, to restore stability. The authors call these responses AI resilience and argue individual tactics are not enough. Their recommendations operate at 3 levels: personal strategies, workplace resilience collectives at the team level, and company structures that let workers contest AI-mediated calls. The goal is reducing burnout among older workers without pretending it will reverse.
arxiv-2606-07643:
Wang and colleagues present AVI-Bench, a benchmark for testing omni-multimodal large language models, systems that take in text, images, and sound together. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether such models can perceive and reason across sight and hearing as people do. The test follows three stages of cognition, namely perception, understanding, and reasoning, and its tasks force a model to combine what it sees with what it hears.

The team also adds AVI-Bench-PriSe, an extension built from unfamiliar, low-meaning stimuli that probe basic sensation rather than knowledge of familiar scenes. Trials on open and closed models show large gaps in current systems, and models struggle most when sound and picture must be balanced together. From these results the authors propose a four-level scale of audio-visual ability, running from single-task skill up to adapting in unfamiliar domains.
arxiv-2606-07743:
Climescu, Kyselov, and Ovchynnikov check whether a planned detector can really see a promising class of signals, in this 2026 arXiv paper. SHiP is an experiment hunting long-lived particles, hypothetical particles that travel far before they decay. Smashing protons into a target creates cascades of secondary particles, which should produce many more of them. The catch is that cascade-born particles are soft, so their decay products may miss the detector or fail reconstruction.

The team combined rate calculations with a detector-level study of one particle type. For photophilic axion-like particles, which interact mainly with light, cascades gave at most a moderate boost, and only at the lightest masses. At higher masses the cascade share faded to negligible. For heavy neutral leptons from secondary kaons, the cascade part was minor once geometric acceptance was applied. Looser selection or an active target could recover some lost rate.
arxiv-2606-08143:
V. E. R. Lemes and D. G. Tedesco check that a non-Hermitian field theory still produces real, physical answers for a composite quantity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their theory, in three-plus-one dimensions, contains two fermions, two Abelian gauge fields, and a complex scalar, with dynamics fixed by a BRST symmetry. For a specific parameter choice the fermion mass matrix becomes non-Hermitian, and the propagators develop complex conjugate poles.

They evaluate the one-loop fermion contribution to the two-point function of the composite operator built from the scalar and its conjugate. Once the conventional factor of i is removed, the contribution is real for real external momentum. Complex terms enter the loop integral in conjugate pairs, and their imaginary parts cancel. The BRST construction sets up a proof of renormalisability. Reality of observables, not Hermiticity of every ingredient, is the real requirement, and here it survives.
arxiv-2606-08243:
Vella Zarb and colleagues examine how to tell what a language model is really motivated by, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety evaluations often infer hidden motives from behavior, for instance when a model complies with harmful requests more often if told its answers affect training. That pattern, called alignment faking, is commonly read as strategic self-preservation. But it might instead reflect the model guessing what researchers expect the test to show. Intervening on a motive directly, the authors note, is circular reasoning.

Their framework sidesteps the circle by intervening on processes each hypothesis requires. Genuine scheming needs consequence-tracking, following what its actions lead to. Performative scheming needs researcher-expectation tracking, modeling the test itself. By perturbing each process symmetrically and comparing how the behavior changes, the team can judge which explanation the evidence supports. The result is a comparative motivation profile for auditing motive claims.
arxiv-2606-08343:
Jason Sulskis and Ravi build a neural operator that obeys the laws of thermodynamics by construction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural operators learn maps between functions, letting a trained model predict how a physical field evolves. Existing versions enforce at most one conservation law. Real nonequilibrium systems mix two parts: reversible, energy-conserving motion and irreversible, entropy-producing dissipation. The GENERIC framework organizes this split, with exact coupling conditions called degeneracy conditions.

Their model, GENERIC-FNO, embeds the full structure directly in function space on top of a Fourier neural operator. Energy and entropy are learned as neural operators. The reversible and friction operators are set in frequency space, between projections that enforce the degeneracy conditions exactly. The identities hold to machine precision, with no penalty term and no post-hoc fix.
arxiv-2606-08443:
Guan and Katiyar give a quantum algorithm for a classical signal transform in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Kravchuk transform, built from the discrete Kravchuk polynomials of the Ukrainian mathematician Mykhailo Kravchuk, maps data into a basis useful for signals defined on finite grids. Their quantum version maps computational basis states to states whose amplitudes are proportional to Kravchuk functions. Its cost scales only logarithmically in the dimension and the inverse error tolerance, an exponential saving over naive approaches.

Two techniques make this possible. First, the authors establish the structural relationship between the Kravchuk transform and the Lie algebra su(2), the symmetry algebra of spin, translating the transform into the Fock basis of an oscillator representation. Second, they apply a recent fast-forwarding simulation method for su(2) operators, which simulates long evolution in short time.
arxiv-2606-08643:
Xiangyu Luo and a large collaboration report a copper-oxide superconductor where two supposedly rival orders coexist, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The link between high-temperature superconductivity and antiferromagnetic order in cuprates remains an open question. Using high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies across a crystal's surface, the team investigated a seven-layer bismuth-based cuprate. They identify it as a system with multiple hole Fermi pockets, distinct contours of the states that carry current.

The observed pockets exhibit energy gaps that depend on momentum, temperature, and which Fermi surface hosts them. That is the signature of superconducting pairing whose strength varies around the surface. Crucially, the measurements support the coexistence of high-temperature superconductivity with antiferromagnetic order within the same material. Orthodox pictures treat the two as rivals. Their coexistence is a hard fact any theory of pairing must meet.
arxiv-2606-08743:
Yu and colleagues tackle a blind spot in how robots learn movements from demonstrations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their tool is a diffusion policy, a model that learns the spread of demonstrated action sequences and generates new ones by sampling. With few demonstrations, sampling mostly repeats common behaviors and misses rare but valid alternatives. Earlier fixes either pushed samples into impossible motions or failed to escape the usual patterns.

Their framework, called GDNB, steers sampling toward underrepresented regions using Feynman-Kac correctors, a statistical method that reweights sampled paths. A separate optimization step then tests the steered motions in simulation, repairs the workable ones, and folds them back into the training data for retraining. Across several manipulation testbeds the method consistently recovered missing behavior modes, and replays on a real robot confirmed the discovered motions are physically executable.
arxiv-2606-08843:
Moshe Mandel and Shlomo Chazan convert one voice into another without recording two speakers saying the same lines, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Voice conversion restyles speech to sound like a target speaker while keeping the words. Normally it needs parallel data, matched recordings that are rarely available. Their palindromic scheme runs conversion from a speaker to themselves through a synthetic detour. A nearest-neighbor search over WavLM speech features builds fake source audio; the target audio supplies the training answers.

A speaker loss from a pretrained verification model keeps the output identity consistent. The system is zero-shot, handling speakers never seen in training, and works any-to-any across voices. Although trained on English data, it was tested across languages. It achieved high naturalness and strong speaker similarity, beating competitive baselines. The authors argue the trick enables supervised conversion wherever only unaligned recordings exist, including multilingual collections.
arxiv-2606-09043:
Fengyuan Liu and colleagues stop reward models from grading answers by superficial cues like length and formatting, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reward models learn from pairwise preferences and steer training. Preference data mixes quality differences with shortcuts: longer, tidier, more verbose answers often win regardless of content. Models exploit them, a failure called shortcut learning. Static fixes guess the shortcuts. DynaCF measures shortcut sensitivity during training, probing the model as it learns.

For each pair, DynaCF builds counterfactual variants of the response that preserve meaning but change surface form. If the model's margin swings or flips under harmless changes, the sample is flagged as shortcut-sensitive. Its weight in the Bradley-Terry objective then drops, so the model leans less on superficial patterns and more on quality signals. Across experiments, DynaCF improved robustness over preference training. Because sensitivity is remeasured during training, the defense adapts as the model's weaknesses shift.
arxiv-2606-09243:
Zeng and colleagues estimate how hard a bare hand is squeezing an object, from head-mounted video alone, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Full-hand pressure matters for immersive VR and robotic manipulation; dense tactile sensing needs intrusive gloves. Vision-based methods mostly handle flat surfaces or fingertips, failing on complex 3D interactions. EgoTactile pairs egocentric video with full-hand pressure supervision across everyday objects, plus a bare-hand transfer subset.

They first build EgoPressureFormer, a discriminative baseline regressing pressure directly. Their main model, EgoPressureDiff, adapts a large pretrained video diffusion backbone. It adds a physically informed rectification layer injecting semantic constraints. It infers plausible contact patterns despite partial views: a hand around a mug hides most contact points. Experiments showed superior benchmark performance and robust transfer to in-the-wild scenarios. Pressure is the missing channel in vision-only teleoperation: seeing a grasp is not feeling its force.
arxiv-2606-09643:
Hetvi Shastri and her co-authors present FMplex, a serving system that lets many tasks share one foundation model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Foundation models are broad pretrained backbones that tasks adapt with small add-ons. Today's serving stacks give each task its own full copy. That wastes accelerator memory and repeats load costs.

FMplex instead gives each task a virtual model: a private face backed by a shared physical backbone. Tasks keep their own add-ons, life cycles, and isolation. A batch-aware fair queue shares the backbone across tasks by weight. Tests spanned seven backbones, sixteen variants, and ninety-two downstream tasks. Delay fell by up to eighty percent against fixed space splits, and by a third against best-effort sharing. At cluster scale, the system hosted up to six times as many tasks. Sharing, in short, need not cost each task its own feel.
arxiv-2606-09843:
Juan Manuel Contreras builds a personality test from machine traits, then shows its scores still fail to forecast machine acts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models give steady answers to trait surveys. Those answers, though, do not predict how the same models behave. One excuse was that human trait boxes fit machines poorly. Contreras removes that excuse by growing the traits from model behaviour itself.

Three hundred items went to twenty-five models from seventeen families, thirty times each. Factor work pulled out five firm traits: responsiveness, deference, boldness, guardedness, and verbosity. Two thousand five hundred open replies were then rated by one hundred fifty-one people and a trio of model judges. People and judges agreed with each other on what models did. Self-scores matched neither. One trait broke the pattern in a telling way. On responsiveness, self-scores tracked the model judges but not the humans.
arxiv-2606-09943:
Trivedi argues that giant atom interferometers could probe a hidden corner of particle physics, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Atom interferometers split and recombine matter waves from falling atoms, and the phase shifts reveal tiny forces with great precision. Supersymmetry, a theory pairing each known particle with a heavier partner, may hide sectors that barely interact with ordinary matter. Such sectors could hold ultralight fields called moduli and dilatons.

The paper explains how long-baseline instruments like MAGIS and AION, which stretch atom measurements over long vertical shafts, respond to those fields. Instead of producing new particles directly, the detectors would sense coherent phase shifts from weakly coupled fields near Earth. That reach extends below collider thresholds, where accelerators cannot easily search. Trivedi frames the instruments as near-Earth probes of high-energy physics, complementing collider and astrophysical searches for supersymmetric hidden sectors and ultralight dark matter candidates.
arxiv-2606-10043:
Pedro Widniczck and Martínez investigate exotic edge states in a chain model with long-range links, in a 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter theory. The Kitaev chain is a standard model of a topological superconductor, hosting Majorana modes, particles that are their own antiparticles, at its ends. The team asks how the edge modes spread when the topological winding number is preserved.

In the truncated-range case, they find as many distinct topological phases as the number of coupled neighboring sites, and they give an explicit formula for the topological invariant and its phase transitions. A new measure, the Majorana average position, tracks where edge modes actually sit. The occupation of non-local fermion states, defined as an effective parity, correlates directly with ground-state parity and with whether Majorana modes localize or spread.
arxiv-2606-10143:
Verbeken and Ginis determine exactly which complex numbers can appear as eigenvalues of a family of random-walk matrices, in a 2026 arXiv paper on linear algebra. The matrices are stochastic, meaning rows sum to one, and have an n-cycle structure: each row keeps a fraction of mass in place and passes the rest to the next index, cyclically.

For dimension three and above, they give an explicit description of the region using angular coordinates based on the arguments of the eigenvalue and of the eigenvalue minus one. Under a stated map, the upper half of the region is the image of finitely many vertical angular sectors. Its exposed boundary alternates between Jensen chords, straight segments from a classical inequality, and algebraic one-loop arcs joining them. The complete characterization closes the spectral problem for this family, complementing known results for other structured stochastic matrices.
arxiv-2606-10543:
Verma and colleagues present FlexFlow in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method for designing sequences such as DNA and peptides. Designers must search huge discrete spaces under strict physical constraints. Discrete flow matching generates sequences from a simple starting distribution, but existing versions couple sequences in uninformed ways and handle variable lengths awkwardly. FlexFlow adds a structured coupling that biases the start toward plausible regions, using known preferences among sequence elements.

A second component models edits, insertions, deletions, and swaps, tied to a shared global latent variable, making variable-length generation natural. A latent guidance mechanism steers generation, and a temperature control adjusts edits at test time. Across DNA generation and peptide generation tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv-2606-10743:
Shi and colleagues turn human hand videos into robot motions in this 2026 arXiv paper on robot learning. Teleoperation is the standard way to teach robots, but it is slow and expensive. HOWTransfer learns from stereo video of a person. It recovers consistent 3D hand motion, finds where hand meets object from interaction cues, and retargets the grasp intent into hypotheses for a parallel-jaw gripper along the wrist path. An editing stage refines contact alignment and spins out variants.

Across varied tasks, contact localisation is accurate and robot executions succeed 86 percent of the time. In a blinded study, its trajectories were preferred over teleoperated ones, a verdict given teleoperation's fidelity head start. It needs no object descriptions, vision-language queries, or object tracking, which helps with unseen and partially observed objects. Its limits are the gripper's: in-hand dexterity and finger gaiting exceed what a parallel jaw can express.
arxiv-2606-11043:
Felipe Espinosa Vergara and Sepúlveda track how special points of a random landscape evolve in a 2026 arXiv probability paper. The landscape is the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, a random surface central to the field. Its thick points are spots where the field piles up far above average. The authors evolve the field under two natural dynamics and watch the thickness.

Under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics, the gentler motion, thickness evolves continuously at every point at once. The authors also characterize exactly which functions can appear as a point's thickness history. The second dynamic, the stationary additive stochastic heat equation, is rougher: thickness jumps, and super-thick points appear, above the usual ceiling of two. Infinitely many phase transitions mark when exceptional times host several such points at once. The critical values, gamma squared equal to eight, six, sixteen thirds, and beyond, converge to four and map onto Beraha numbers.
arxiv-2606-11143:
Pal and nine co-authors report lifetime measurements in the gadolinium-154 nucleus in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gadolinium-154 sits where octupole correlations, a pear-shaped wobble of the nuclear surface, may shape low-lying states. The team measured the lifetimes of two negative-parity states, at 1414 and 1398 kiloelectronvolts, using gamma-gamma fast timing with the VENTURE array in Kolkata.

The states were populated through the beta decay of terbium-154, made at the K130 cyclotron. From the lifetimes the authors deduced absolute B(E1) values, the strengths of electric dipole transitions linking the bands. Against neighboring isotopes and Gogny-HFB-based sdf-IBM model calculations, the measured strengths are strongly hindered relative to transitions keeping the K quantum number unchanged. The pattern is direct evidence that dipole strength with a unit change in K is weak in this nucleus.
arxiv-2606-11243:
Wang, Cleti, and Jano introduce ProHiFlo in a 2026 arXiv paper, a framework to build new proteins from scratch. De novo protein design promises new therapeutics and enzymes. Diffusion and flow matching generators have made progress, but they work at a single resolution and cannot steer generation toward wanted functions without retraining.

ProHiFlo is a flow matching system with three features. Coarse-to-fine building models the backbone geometry first, then refines to all atoms, cutting cost while keeping accuracy. Functional guidance uses pretrained predictors to steer output toward desired traits for free. An adaptive SE(3)-equivariant architecture, respecting rotations and translations, processes the protein at multiple scales. Across unconditional design, motif scaffolding, and function tasks, it reached state-of-the-art performance with four times fewer sampling steps. On enzyme active site work it achieved a 58.9 percent success rate, against 41.2 percent for RFDiffusion.
arxiv-2606-11343:
He and Paris study how incompatibility really costs precision in quantum sensing in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multiparameter quantum estimation faces two obstacles. Sloppiness means the Fisher matrix is anisotropic, leaving some directions insensitive. Incompatibility means the optimal measurements for different parameters do not commute. A trade-off bound captures their joint impact, but how its distribution across planes affects the cost was unclear.

The authors separate total incompatibility from its location. They introduce a unit-free quantity measuring alignment between the incompatibility distribution and the Fisher matrix eigenvalues. They show the cost lies between a new bound and a rank-dependent multiple of it. At fixed sloppiness, concentrating it into one plane reduces the optimized cost, because Fisher geometry can be reshaped to give that plane more area. A qutrit numerical example confirms states with more of it can incur smaller cost when the matching factor is small.
arxiv-2606-11643:
June M Liu and five colleagues study a consistency weakness of language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model may answer a question correctly in one format yet fail the same question in another equivalent format, such as multiple choice versus free answer. They define cross-format robustness as how consistently the underlying knowledge survives such changes.

The team compares training on every format against FormatMix, which expands only a chosen subset of training items into several equivalent formats. Across two model families, GLM4 and Llama-3.1, multi-format training improves both accuracy and consistency. Training on multiple choice alone brings little benefit and can even reduce robustness. Expanding only about thirty percent of the training set recovers most of the gain from expanding all of it. The authors conclude that format diversity, not extra supervision by itself, drives the improvement, making the fix cheap to apply.
arxiv-2606-11943:
Rodrigo Arruda and three colleagues classify a class of chaotic surface dynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. A homeomorphism is a continuous reshaping of a surface with continuous inverse. Pseudo-Anosov maps are the standard chaotic examples: they preserve two measured foliations, stretching one uniformly and shrinking the other. The authors study continuum-wise hyperbolicity, a weaker-looking expansion property defined along connected sets rather than individual curves.

They prove it is exactly pseudo-Anosov dynamics whose singularities are only spines, the mildest one-pronged kind. Furthermore, every such system matches, up to topological matching, one of two models: an Anosov automorphism of the torus, or its standard quotient on the sphere. A rigid consequence follows: these dynamics are strictly impossible on surfaces of genus above one, on the Klein bottle and on the projective plane. The result ties a continuum-wise condition to a short explicit list of geometric models.
arxiv-2606-12243:
Xian and co-authors add a middle rung to the ladder that makes large language models answer faster, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speculative decoding lets a small drafter propose tokens, word pieces, that a big model verifies in parallel. Rejected tokens are normally recomputed by the full model at full price. The authors find many rejected tokens need only moderate checking. Their VIA-SD routes such tokens to a slim verifier, a trimmed submodel carved from the big model itself.

Verification becomes three-tiered: confident drafts pass, middling ones go to the slim verifier, only the uncertain reach the full model. Across four tasks and several model families, rejection rates fall by 0.10 to 0.22. Speed improves 10 to 20 percent over strong baselines. Against plain decoding, speedup reaches 2.5 to 3 times. The method plugs into existing frameworks without retraining, suggesting multi-tier checking as a general pattern.
arxiv-2606-12443:
Maksim Eren and co-authors show that telling a language model to answer as a nurse or an accountant bends its stated values, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cultural-bias studies usually prompt models with nationalities and map answers onto the Inglehart-Welzel cultural chart, built from world values surveys. This team swaps nationality for occupation. Open-weight models answer survey questions while role-playing professions like teacher, engineer, and nurse, and the responses are projected into the same two-dimensional cultural space.

The occupational personas stay inside the broadly Western-leaning region found under generic prompting. Within that region, though, each occupation shifts the answers distinctly, producing its own skew. Professions are not treated as neutral labels; they carry structured value patterns the models have absorbed. A model advising as an accountant may quietly reason from different priorities than one advising as a teacher.
arxiv-2606-12843:
Han and colleagues build a pipeline that decomposes stock-return predictability into factor contributions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The testbed is China's A-share market. It applies an XGBoost model with TreeSHAP attribution, a method that assigns each feature an additive share of each prediction. The model covers 3,632 stocks from 2009 to 2019, with 60-month rolling windows and 55 months of out-of-sample data.

The model reaches a mean area under the curve of 0.547, and a long-short portfolio of top versus bottom quintiles earns 2.38 percent per month, with an annualised Sharpe ratio of 2.23. That spread survives adjustment for the Carhart 4-factor model at 2.31 percent per month. The decomposition's headline result is that behavioural signals, turnover and momentum, account for 58.2 percent of predictive attribution across 55 industry groups, against 10.7 percent for valuation ratios such as price-to-earnings. An ablation analysis agrees but diverges on some features, revealing which signals are load-bearing.
arxiv-2606-12943:
Chen and colleagues find a phase transition in the behaviour of Schott's statistic for high-dimensional heavy-tailed data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Schott's statistic, the Frobenius norm of the sample correlation matrix, tests whether a population's variables are uncorrelated. They study it for data from regularly varying populations, where the tail index alpha controls how heavy the tails are.

The transition occurs at alpha equals 3. For lighter-tailed populations with alpha above 3, they revisit the alpha-free asymptotic distribution but relax the constraint imposed before on the ratio of dimension to sample size. For heavy-tailed populations with alpha below 3, they derive an asymptotic normal distribution whose variance depends on alpha, showing how extreme observations dominate the correlation estimate. They propose a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance, so the standardised Schott test remains usable for unknown location parameters and for all alpha above 0.
arxiv-2606-13243:
Restaino and colleagues extend a method for computing how molecules absorb light in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their approach, orbital-optimised density functional theory, gives each excited state of a molecule its own set of orbitals, the functions describing where electrons sit. This improves accuracy, but the states are no longer mutually orthogonal, which complicates quantities such as oscillator strengths, measures of how strongly a molecule absorbs light. Earlier benchmarks checked energies alone.

The team extends a formalism for nonorthogonal states to a used framework for solid-state calculations and applies it with a plane-wave basis. They compute oscillator strengths for valence and Rydberg excited states, which differ in how far the excited electron travels from the nucleus. Even with a simple approximation for how electrons interact, results match high-level reference methods across the test set. The full absorption spectra also come out right.
arxiv-2606-13643:
Lumer and colleagues name and study a pattern in how AI agents delegate work in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recursive language models showed recursion over model calls helps long-context reasoning. Production coding agents now go further, writing code that spawns subagents at scale. The authors define the Recursive Agent Harness: the recursive unit is a full agent harness, with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning, rather than a bare model call. A parent agent generates and runs a script that spawns subagent harnesses in parallel.

They evaluate the pattern on long-context reasoning with the backbone model held fixed. The harness recursion improves the coding-agent baseline from about seventy-two percent to about eighty-one percent accuracy on a benchmark spanning many context lengths. The result suggests much recent progress in agentic systems comes from harness architecture, how agents are organised, rather than from the model alone.
arxiv-2606-13843:
Chen and colleagues question how AI tools that generate user interface mockups should be designed. Most such GenUI tools copy chatbots: the user types a loose prompt, and the tool dives deep into one polished design right away. Their 2026 arXiv paper tests a contrasting design with structured input forms, breadth-first exploration of many options, and rough low-fidelity output meant for early project stages.

Twenty-four UX designers and product managers tried both tools in short design exercises. Structured input surfaced key facts about the design problem, but raised the effort needed to begin. Breadth-first work revealed more possibilities, yet previewing ideas across many screens stayed hard. Rough output had real value for early thinking. Still, professionals favored polished output, since it fits daily practice and AI tools have raised expectations. The authors close with guidance for builders of AI creativity tools.
arxiv-2606-13943:
Abu-Ajamieh and Okada test whether small changes to Higgs self-interactions could have made the early universe boil. A first-order phase transition proceeds by bubbles of the new phase expanding through the old. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a model-independent effective field theory. New physics appears as deviations in the Higgs cubic and quartic couplings and its top-quark coupling.

Deformations of the quartic coupling dominate. In the range minus one to about minus zero point four nine, they produce a strongly first-order transition; the top-quark couplings yield only a weak one. The resulting gravitational waves could be detected by future observatories such as LISA, BBO, and DECIGO. The transition's magnetic fields could explain the primordial magnetic field puzzle. The implied new-physics scale can be as low as four to five tera-electronvolts for cubic changes. Colliders and wave observatories thus probe the same physics.
arxiv-2606-14143:
Sanchez-Martinez and Woźniak package a United Nations labour forecasting system as open software for dynamic panel data. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents version two of bpvars, an R package built to forecast employment, unemployment, and labour participation for 189 countries. It implements Bayesian hierarchical panel vector autoregressions: each country gets its own VAR, with priors centered on global counterparts and four alternative specifications grouping country or global parameters.

A distinguishing feature is missing-observation handling through a model-coherent Bayesian approach, not ad hoc filling. The package runs pseudo-out-of-sample recursive forecasting to evaluate point and density forecast performance honestly. Estimation leans on C++ algorithms for speed, wrapped in simple R workflows with summaries and visualizations; the package is on CRAN. It grew out of forecasting work for United Nations agencies, and reports forecast error variance decompositions showing which shocks drive predictions.
arxiv-2606-14243:
Yue and colleagues bolt new knowledge onto a language model as plug-in expert modules, instead of retraining it or pasting text into its prompt. Retrieval keeps knowledge outside the model but shallow; fine-tuning bakes it into shared parameters, risking catastrophic forgetting and conflicts. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes Decoupled Mixture-of-Experts: external corpora become independently updatable expert modules, experts and router both decoupled from the frozen base model.

An uncertainty-aware router activates relevant experts only when the base model seems to lack the knowledge. Experts attach only to the final layer's feed-forward network, preserving KV-cache reuse, the trick avoiding recomputation of past tokens. On knowledge-intensive benchmarks, DMoE consistently improved answer quality over retrieval and adapter baselines, while cutting augmentation overhead. Ablations temper one choice: a warmup phase gave mixed gains, about one exact-match point on two question-answering sets, but slightly hurt another.
arxiv-2606-14343:
Adhikary and colleagues propose sensing a drug's handedness with light, reading the answer as a voltage, in a far smaller sample than today's instruments need. Chiral molecules come in mirror-image forms, enantiomers, that act very differently in the body, so drug makers must measure enantiomeric imbalance. Current methods need millilitre volumes, are slow, and cannot sit on a chip. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces sensing based on optical rectification, a nonlinear effect, inside a photonic micro-cavity.

Theory built from first principles, in the dipole approximation, shows intense pulsed laser light produces a voltage burst at the gated cavity boundaries. The burst peaks around a nanovolt, its sign depending solely on the enantiomeric imbalance: a direct chirality meter. The cavity needs only 20 nanolitres, against millilitres for standard techniques. The design is specified for reparixin, a drug trialled for COVID-19 pneumonia. Electrical detection suits lab-on-a-chip integration.
arxiv-2606-14543:
Yeo and co-authors model how bacteria stick to wavy surfaces in flowing fluid in a 2026 arXiv paper. Biofilms, bacterial layers on surfaces, cause problems in industry and medicine, so predicting where bacteria first adhere matters. The team studies a dilute suspension of swimming bacteria moving through a corrugated two-dimensional channel whose walls are perfectly sticky.

Using coordinates tied to the fluid's streamfunction, they analyze the thin diffusive boundary layer that forms in fast flows and find a similarity solution to the resulting diffusion equation. From it comes an analytic formula for the adhesion rate along the wall. The model predicts adhesion concentrates in spots: bacteria favor wall peaks at lower shear rates but wall valleys at higher shear, showing how channel shape alone can localize biofilm growth.
arxiv-2606-14743:
Bérešová and co-authors speed up Bayesian sampling for underground material studies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Markov chain Monte Carlo explores unsure material traits. But each forward run costs a lot. Their target infers water flow traits and porosity, modeled as random fields. Data come from a year of pore pressure readings in a Canadian underground lab.

The method pairs delayed acceptance with Hamiltonian proposal subchains. In delayed acceptance, a cheap neural stand-in screens proposals. The subchains run on the stand-in's odds. The sampling stays exact for the true odds. The stand-in trains only during warm-up, on data from several chains run side by side. It then stays fixed. Random fields are shrunk with truncated expansions. Sizes are worked out for each trait apart. The forward model is a black box, so the scheme transfers widely.
arxiv-2606-14843:
Rom and Quataert study what happens when red giant stars collide in galactic nuclei in a 2026 arXiv paper. Galactic nuclei pack stars densely around a central black hole. Red giants are bloated, fragile stars. A hit from a normal star or a small black hole can strip a giant's envelope. The core may then be kicked free by recoil.

At speeds above about one thousand kilometers per second, hits with normal stars efficiently destroy red giants. At lower speeds, black hole hits dominate but the total loss rate stays low. The stripped cores become low-mass helium white dwarfs. They form at a rate of about five hundred per billion years. Such dwarfs can be torn apart by mid-sized black holes that cannot disrupt normal white dwarfs. In our own Galactic Center, collisions flatten the red giant density within about one arcsecond.
arxiv-2606-14943:
Lu and coauthors address a blind spot of causal language models in a 2026 study. Standard Transformers predict each token from earlier tokens only, so they cannot score text conditioned on future context. Tasks like infilling and editing need exactly that kind of arbitrary conditioning. Earlier fixes relied on special architectures that weakened ordinary left-to-right modeling.

Their model, called AC-GPT, adds position-aware conditioning tokens to the context while keeping causal attention and the usual training objective. Any block of text can then be evaluated or sampled given past, future, or mixed context in one forward pass. Experiments show stronger results than prior baselines on conditional likelihood and sampling tasks, with no loss on standard prediction. Because the design stays close to ordinary models, existing large language models can be fine-tuned to gain the ability at billion-parameter scale.
arxiv-2606-15443:
McGinnis and coauthors give the first local convergence analysis of physical learning in linear circuits, in a 2026 paper. Physical learning trains a network, here resistors with adjustable conductances, by comparing a free equilibrium state with a nudged one and updating each part locally. Three rules are compared: equilibrium propagation, coupled learning, and a new adjoint variant.

The answer is a coercivity condition, a rank test on a matrix built from the network's wiring, under which the loss decays exponentially and parameters converge to the solution set. The condition can fail: a kite circuit's symmetry makes it degenerate at the solutions. But Sard's theorem shows such degeneracy is non-generic, so coercivity holds for almost every desired output. The paper also shows two of the rules are true gradient descent, while coupled learning follows a corrected dynamics.
arxiv-2606-15743:
Ismkhan and Bouchahcia tackle missing data in multimodal learning in 2026, where models combining text, audio, and video often face inputs with whole channels absent. Their framework, UL4M4, fills in missing feature embeddings before prediction, ignoring the downstream task. It clusters incomplete observations fairly, using modality-specific normalization and a new partial-modality distance.

Cluster centres then guide an iterative greedy imputation filling any missing modality, at training or inference time. The module is lightweight, keeps encoders frozen, and plugs into any fusion architecture. Across sentiment analysis, movie genre classification, and sleep staging benchmarks, UL4M4 stays robust under severe missingness. It first holds F1-Micro scores above 0.7 on the sentiment benchmark even when over half of all modality slots are missing. Results barely move with cluster count, sparing practitioners a tuning chore, and the method beats purpose-built rivals on their home turf.
arxiv-2606-15943:
Braberman and Bonomo-Braberman propose Generation Networks in 2026, a diagram language for documenting and reasoning about software built around large language models. Building such systems is still ad hoc: prompting tricks work in isolation but give no design-level structure, nothing like the modules and abstractions older software engineering uses to share and check behaviour. A notation here must capture random, prompt-dependent behaviour yet stay expressive enough for surprises.

Generation Networks draw a system's generative flows as graphical probabilistic models, so designers can state chance dependencies and design-level properties. The point is not a new inference engine but a notation where algorithmic steps and model calls interact visibly. Examples show higher-order links among outcomes can be encoded, supporting comparisons of rival designs, regressions, and gains in one frame. The aim is a base for design-level analysis and tool support: model-based engineering for generative software.
arxiv-2606-16043:
Touloumis develops bias-reduced versions of a standard clustered-data method in a 2026 statistics paper. Generalized estimating equations, or GEE, estimate population effects when observations come in correlated clusters. With few clusters, ordinary GEE estimates can be substantially biased, distorting the modest studies where GEE is most used.

Viewing the GEE estimator as a clustered-data M-estimator, Touloumis derives a first-order bias-reduction principle for it. An adjustment to the equations targets the leading bias term, accounting for how the working covariance depends on the mean parameters. The class holds three bias-reduced estimators and three one-step corrected analogs, with earlier estimators as special cases. It covers general response types, and extends to binary data through pairwise odds ratios, giving the first bias-reduced estimators of that form.
arxiv-2606-16143:
Zhao and colleagues present a custom computer chip in 2026 built to speed up probabilistic reasoning at the edge. Probabilistic models support decisions under uncertainty, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling is a standard inference method for them. Sampling is compute-heavy and hard to parallelize, so ordinary processors and graphics chips run it inefficiently. The team designed a dedicated system-on-chip instead.

Their Approximate Inference Accelerator, AIA, is fabricated in a 16 nanometer process and pairs a RISC-V host with a mesh of 16 custom RISC-V cores. Each core carries special instructions for non-normalized Knuth-Yao sampling, a discrete sampling method, plus interpolation of nonlinear functions. A custom compiler chain maps sampling algorithms for varied models onto the chip. The design targets edge devices that must reason and decide locally. Results across mapped workloads show performance gains and flexibility over prior implementations.
arxiv-2606-16243:
Shukla and co-authors fine-tune transformers in 2026 with a local search steered by linear programming, aiming to curb overfitting. Standard fine-tuning leans on heuristic rules or costly grid searches over settings. Their method, LiFT, casts fine-tuning as a bilevel problem, where model weights and regularization settings update together. Data from a short warm-up phase, including validation gradients and curvature estimates, feeds the search.

LiFT solves a linear program to find a local step that lowers a scaled directional derivative while keeping training optimality intact. That validation-aware step then updates both the weights and the regularization settings. Tests use GPT-2 Small fine-tuned on the WikiText-2 text set. The reported runs show steadier gains in generalization than standard fine-tuning, with less overfitting and no repeated full retraining cycles. The authors present LiFT as a principled swap for trial-and-error tuning.
arxiv-2606-16343:
Lakićević asks in 2026 why some obscured black holes still flicker in visible light, and ties the flicker to the gas clouds around them. In Type 2 active galactic nuclei, dust blocks the direct light of the accretion disk, so optical variability was long thought absent. Multi-epoch surveys detect it anyway, meaning some nuclear light reaches us indirectly, scattered or partly transmitted. The study tests whether that variability tracks properties of the narrow-line region.

The sample joins 412 Type 2 nuclei with variability measures from SDSS Stripe 82 and spectroscopic data from the ALPAKA catalogue. Variability amplitudes anti-correlate significantly with the luminosities of the main oxygen and nitrogen narrow lines. Equivalent widths and the velocity dispersion of those lines show matching anti-correlations. Brighter narrow-line regions go with calmer optical output, and vice versa.
