It stands in the original Spanish as a dated fragment of the brigade's paperwork, released through the CIA Reading Room for direct reading.
cia-0000135943: One CIA cable dated 1 January 1954 handles the identification of a contact, a name put to a face and reported by the Lincoln station. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136243: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 May 1954, long since declassified, on stated opposition to the bomb drop instructions, a pushback against the bombing plan. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136343: A message from the Guatemala station, relayed to CADICK in this 29 June 1954 cable, reports a junta figure seeking a cease-fire. He is sending a plane to Zacapa to enter negotiations directly with CALLIGERIS, and was warned it might be shot down unless it wagged its wings. The writer's impression is that the government is completely shaken and will make only a half-hearted attempt at conditions. Essence has many men ready, though without arms.
cia-0000136643: This Spanish-language item from the 2506 Brigade papers carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961, flagged in the catalog title. The brigade was then in winter training for the Bay of Pigs landing. The record states no subject for the document. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records that open the brigade's 1961 file.
cia-0000139043: Gerhart Eisler has found a job on Wochenpost, Reuters reported in July 1954 in a wire item preserved in this file. Since earlier prominence, he was reported to have lectured at internal party functions and some public lectures and contributed to newspapers and magazines as a freelance writer across the East German press. Wochenpost, the bureau said, is the first East German family weekly produced in Western style, launched the previous November. The item tracks the fallen propaganda chief's quieter afterlife.
cia-03163343:
China's communes open the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 8 July 1959. Peiping has retreated on a basic feature of the system. Peasants are no longer required to eat in communal mess halls. The brief calls this a significant admission of failure. Peasant compliance had never been won for that part of the programme.

Iraq follows, tensely. Communists reportedly plan a major Baghdad demonstration on the night of 9-10 July, near the revolution's anniversary. Qasim, answering a British arms offer, asks for fourteen Canberra jet bombers. Yemen's Crown Prince Badr leans ever harder on Egyptian help to keep his authority. The Imam may soon return from Italy. Bloc protests are expected as American personnel join French training of the Laotian army. Austria's Chancellor Raab decides to resign. A special committee's conclusions on Berlin close the issue.
cia-03189343:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 24 June 1960, marked Top Secret, leads with the Chinese address at the Rumanian party congress in Bucharest. The bulletin reports that the speech of 22 June was carefully worded, avoided sharp criticism of Soviet positions, and made no concessions to Khrushchev. Propaganda coming directly from Peiping, by contrast, stayed sharply critical of his foreign policies.

The Asia-Africa section reports that Prime Minister Kishi's coming resignation in Japan had calmed tension and shifted politics toward a contest inside the ruling party. It also notes a tour by top Indian officials along the Tibetan frontier. A Western item covers Jacques Soustelle launching a French Algeria group in France.
cia-03448343:
Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 22 July 1955 carries five items across four regions. The Far East lead sets out Tokyo's current China policy as stated by Japan. The bulletin reports that Japan was not weighing recognition of Communist China. It would keep friendly ties with Nationalist China. It would also observe Western trade controls. Many Japanese, though, believed dealing with Peiping was unavoidable in time.

Other Far East coverage reports South Korean instructions to break off talks. In Indonesia, the government could face an early vote of confidence, with the cabinet perhaps resigning rather than facing a vote it might lose. The bulletin also comments on Greece deciding to take the Cyprus issue back to the United Nations, and on the political situation in Argentina.
cia-06312743:
Sanitized email thread dated 15 March 2012 concerns a coming Ignatius column on documents from the UBL raid. Cynthia L. Rapp, writing as D/OPA, states she had not known of the release effort until a White House note arrived. She asks whether a set of the documents to be released could be obtained before press inquiries hit.

Replies in the thread, with most names redacted under (b)(3) and (b)(6), report that the list was in hand. Staff were looking for a copy of the set that had been declassified. A forwarded message from Tommy Vietor went to public affairs contacts at Defense and State. Another note in the thread asks whether the effort was known, and says the Counterterrorism Center probably needed to be informed.
cia-06554443:
Intelligence assessment dated November 1991, numbered SOV 91-10049 and marked Confidential, is titled Winners and Losers. Its subject is increasing social stratification in the former Soviet Union. The Directorate of Intelligence paper carries WNINTEL and NOFORN controls on its cover pages.

Inside, the assessment tracks how a widening gap between groups was reshaping daily life as the old system faded. One section covers children and the services once guaranteed to them, such as free health care, day care, and schooling. It reports that the base for those services was weak and falling fast. Day care sites were overcrowded, and one-fourth of schoolchildren studied on a second or third shift. Completions of new schools and hospitals had also fallen sharply in the prior two years.
cia-06626643:
Unclassified USINFO cable of September 1979 forwards a New York Times article for the embassy in Buenos Aires. The article, by Juan de Onis and dated September 23, is headlined in the cable as hopes rising in Argentina for Timerman's early release. It is marked for information only, with the article text following.

The article reports that Jacobo Timerman, described as Argentina's most prominent political prisoner, faced a second Jewish high holiday in detention with hopes of release soon to freedom abroad. It states the Supreme Court had told the military junta there was no legal basis for holding him. Timerman, former publisher of La Opinion, had been detained since April 1977. A military court had cleared him of ties to guerrilla funds, the article states, yet the junta held him and seized his newspaper.
copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543:
Nicolaus Copernicus published De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium in Nuremberg in 1543, the year of his death. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in its original Latin. The book placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the planetary system.

Copernicus set out a full mathematical astronomy on that single bold move, deriving the planets' order and periods from it. An unsigned preface, added by another hand, called the scheme a mere device for calculation. Readers such as Kepler and Galileo took it as truth instead. The book is widely read as the starting gun of the Scientific Revolution, and this is its full original form.
cours-de-philosophie-hermetique-ou-d-alc:
A French course in hermetic philosophy and alchemy by L.-P. François Cambriel fills this 1843 volume. The title promises the theory and practice of the science, plus steps said to be needed to find and make the philosophers' stone. Lacour and Maistrasse printed it at Paris.

Cambriel adds readings of parts of the first five chapters of Genesis, ascribed in his plan to Moses. Three additions argue for three lives in man, whom he calls a perfect animal. Salt, sulphur, and mercury are treated as three first principles that form one mercury. The book is a full, earnest guide for readers who want the old art set out as a system.
deleuze-practical-instruction-animal-mag:
J. P. F. Deleuze wrote the calmest guide to mesmerism of his age, and English readers got it in 1843 as Practical Instruction in Animal Magnetism. Deleuze, librarian at the Paris Museum of natural history, had watched magnetic practice for years. He set down a method meant to be safe and clear.

Step by step he covers the passes, the crises that may arise, and how to calm them. He also treats the ethics of the work, warning against showmanship and harm. At a time when animal magnetism drew both crowds and scorn, his manual gave sober readers a way to judge the claims for themselves.
dickens-christmas-carol-1843:
Charles Dickens published A Christmas Carol in 1843, in the first edition text used here. The ghost story of Scrooge's redemption became a Christmas fixture at once in England. Dickens wrote it fast, in debt, and it sold out by Christmas Eve that year.

Ebenezer Scrooge, a miser, scorns Christmas and all human warmth and cheer. Marley's ghost warns him, and three spirits show his past, present, and future. He sees Tiny Tim's plight and his own lone, unmourned grave in the churchyard. Scrooge wakes changed and keeps Christmas with a full and generous heart thereafter. Its plea for charity still lands each year in countless homes worldwide.
dumas-georges-1843:
Alexandre Dumas published Georges in 1843, just before his great serial triumphs of 1844 in Paris. The novel sends a mixed-race hero back to Mauritius to confront slavery and racism there. It is a pioneering abolitionist romance, and Dumas's most personal book on race and pride.

Georges Munier, schooled in Paris and rich, returns to Mauritius resolved to humble its planters. He woos Sara, a planter's niece, and challenges the island's color line at every ball. A slight at the races sparks a duel, a revolt of the enslaved, and a trial. Condemned to die, Georges is saved by his brother's ship in a last-hour rescue at sea. Dumas, himself of mixed descent, poured family pride and rage into its hero.
elliotson-surgical-operations-mesmeric-s:
John Elliotson put pain free surgery on record in his case book of 1843. Elliotson was a top healer in London who used the trance state in his wards. Arms and legs were cut with no cry from the sick, who slept in a deep trance wrought by passes of the hands and fixed gaze.

He prints case past case with names and dates. Peers mocked him and drove him from his post. Yet his tales helped pave the road to true sleep drugs in surgery. The book is a key step in that tale.
europmc-pmc10086443:
Zhao and colleagues review the central role of insulin resistance in metabolic disease in a 2023 paper. Insulin resistance means body cells respond poorly to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. The condition sits behind type 2 diabetes and is linked to high blood pressure, fatty liver, and some cancers.

The review explains how resistance develops at the cell level. It follows the damage as it spreads across organs and systems. It also covers drugs and lifestyle steps that restore insulin response. The paper frames resistance as a shared root worth treating early.
europmc-pmc10095343:
Twarowski and Herbet review inflammation in Alzheimer's disease in a 2023 paper, covering its mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia in older people and still has no cure. Inflammation in the brain is one of several forces thought to drive the disease.

The review explains how immune cells and their chemical signals act in the sick brain. It covers tests that can reveal this inflammation in living patients. It also surveys treatments aimed at calming it. The paper links lab science to the clinic in plain terms.
europmc-pmc10210743:
Wright, Fleming, and Colebrook studied whether the body's own fluids can clean a wound, in work from The Lancet of June 15, 1918. They grew wound microbes, among them streptococcus, staphylococcus, and B. welchii, in blood serum in fine capillary tubes. Normal serum and lymph, they found, form a poor food for most microbes found in foul wounds.

Stagnant discharge, digested by trypsin from broken white cells, feeds them all. Treatment follows from that split: clear away slough, flood the wound with wholesome lymph, and use a strong salt solution, which draws lymph and holds the second group in check. Necrotic tissue in gas gangrene still needs the knife. The result is an early plan for wound care built on the body's own defenses.
europmc-pmc10279643:
Zhang and a large team report iron-copper pair catalysts that turn nitrate into ammonia using electricity, in a 2023 study. Making ammonia the standard way takes high heat and pressure and heavy energy use. An electric route could cut nitrate pollution in water while making a valuable chemical under mild conditions, but rival reactions and weak nitrate capture have held it back.

The team's catalyst pairs single iron and copper atoms on a support. In their tests it converted nitrate to ammonia with high selectivity. The work points to cleaner fertilizer production.
europmc-pmc10436543:
Glaviano and a large team reviewed in 2023 a key growth signal chain in cancer and the drugs that block it. The chain, named PI3K/AKT/mTOR, tells cells to live, grow, and divide. It is the most often switched-on chain in human cancer. Faults in the chain also help tumours resist care.

Known faults include an overactive PI3K, loss of a brake called PTEN, and a stuck-on AKT. Glaviano sums up trial results for drugs that block each link in the chain. Some trials pair those drugs with other cancer drugs for a stronger effect. The review also covers how tumours learn to dodge the blocks. Immune effects of the chain get a look as well.
europmc-pmc10474743:
Liu and co-authors reviewed immune therapy for triple-negative breast cancer in 2023. This cancer form lacks the three marks that guide most breast cancer drugs. Immune therapy trains the body's own defences to kill tumour cells. It can boost a tumour's visibility to immune cells and lift signals that shield it.

Checkpoint drugs lead the field, Liu reports. They block brakes on immune cells, and gene tests now help match them to subtypes. Trials pair these drugs with chemo, radiation, and targeted drugs. Newer partners include nano carriers, RNA vaccines, and gene therapy. The review asks why some tumours resist immune attack. It maps paths to beat that resistance in future care.
europmc-pmc10514343:
Gao and co-authors reviewed microglia in 2023, the immune cells that guard the brain. In brain diseases, these cells switch on and change shape and acts. Fresh single-cell tools show that their states vary by place and time. Some states clear toxic protein clumps, a clear help to the brain.

Harm can follow when intake of clumps overwhelms the cells. Gao notes that strain can blunt their clearing skill and spark swelling. Immune cells from the blood can push them toward a harmful state. The cells can also spread clumps in tiny parcels they shed. The review weighs care ideas: boost clearing, calm swelling, and flip cells to a guard state.
europmc-pmc11075543:
Öztürk-Çolak and the FlyBase Consortium describe updates to the main fruit fly database in this 2024 paper. FlyBase holds genetic, genomic, and functional data on Drosophila melanogaster, the common fruit fly. Labs worldwide rely on it to plan and interpret fly research. Model organism databases must keep pace as data types multiply.

The update adds single-cell RNA sequencing data, which reads gene activity one cell at a time. Displays of functional information were improved, and the pipeline that matches genes across species was updated. New reports on chemicals and their effects on flies were added. Outreach resources for teachers and new users were enhanced. The authors present the changes as keeping the database current with fly science.
europmc-pmc1240543:
Fabricant and Farnsworth made the case for folk medicine plants in drug hunting in 2001. Traditional healers have used plants as medicine for centuries. That record may point chemists to useful new drugs. The authors compare ways to pick plants for study.

They counted 122 proven drug compounds drawn from just 94 plant species. For 80 percent, folk use matched or related to modern use. That match rate is far above random picking. Fabricant also weighs costs and limits of plant-based searches. Old remedies, they argue, remain a rich lead source. The review also lists the pros and cons of plant-based drug searches in full.
europmc-pmc1367843:
Main and co-authors measured phthalates in breast milk and infant hormones in 2006. Phthalates harm the male reproductive system in animals. The study asked whether milk contamination affects the newborn hormone surge. Samples came from a Danish-Finnish cohort on undescended testes from 1997 to 2001.

Milk from 130 mothers was collected one to three months after birth. Sixty-two boys had undescended testes and 68 were healthy. Six phthalate breakdown products were measured in each sample. All six appeared, with wide variation between mothers. Blood hormones were measured in three quarters of the boys.
europmc-pmc1810543:
Shea and colleagues developed AMSTAR in 2007, a tool for grading how well systematic reviews are done. A systematic review pools prior studies on a question, and weak methods can distort its verdict. Earlier grading tools existed, but none combined the best evidence and expert agreement.

The team merged two existing instruments and three extra items into a 37-item draft. They applied it to 99 paper-based and 52 electronic reviews, then used factor analysis to find the underlying components. That step yielded 11 components, and an expert group picked one item from each. The final AMSTAR tool has 11 items and was judged sound in face and content validity. The authors call for further studies of its reproducibility before strong advice on routine use.
europmc-pmc1821043:
Sommer, Salzberg, Pop and colleagues released Minimus in 2007, a small genome assembler for modest jobs. Genome assemblers piece sequenced DNA fragments back into whole sequences. Flagship tools had grown huge and hard to install, while many daily tasks, such as viral genomes or single genes, need far less.

Minimus was built to be fast, light on memory, and easy to run and embed in larger pipelines. Tests covered viral genomes, single genes, and BAC clones, which are large cloned DNA pieces. On bacterial genomes it made notably fewer assembly errors than tools then in use. The trade-off was a more fragmented result, with the genome left in more separate pieces. The authors released it as open source within the AMOS project.
europmc-pmc1828143:
Brickner and colleagues found in 2007 that yeast cells remember recently active genes by parking them at the edge of the nucleus. Many genes move to the nuclear periphery when switched on. The team asked what that move does, using two genes named INO1 and GAL1.

Both genes moved to the edge quickly, even without being transcribed, and they stayed there for generations after switch-off. A gene held at the edge restarted much faster than one long buried inside, even after six generations of repression. A variant protein called H2A.Z, built into the gene's packaging after repression, proved required for both the parking and the fast restart. Removing H2A.Z erased the memory. The authors call this an epigenetic memory of past activity.
europmc-pmc1885943:
Carrasco, DePinho and co-authors showed in 2007 that one stress factor can drive the blood cancer multiple myeloma. Myeloma grows out of a common, harmless precursor state called MGUS, found in up to ten percent of adults. What flips that state into cancer was unknown.

The factor is XBP-1s, a protein that manages the cell's response to unfolded proteins and guides plasma cell development. Mice engineered to overproduce it in antibody-line cells developed raised blood antibody levels and skin changes. With age they showed textbook myeloma signs: bone lesions where tumor eats through, and antibody deposits under vessel linings. Their cells also mis-set genes known to go wrong in human myeloma. Since human tumors often overproduce XBP-1s, the model implicates it in the disease.
europmc-pmc2124843:
J. The cause of acute lethal anaphylaxis in the intact animal, he argues, is failure of the heart. That failure sits in the heart itself, not in the central nervous system.

The changed heart is described by touch and eye. It loses translucency, changes consistency, and stops answering stimuli, a state Auer classes as probably a chemical rigor. The right ventricle shows it most: gray, stiff, very tough to a fingernail, and unresponsive. Digitalis-type stimulants seem to harm rather than help. Blood clotting is delayed, forming only a loose clot after half an hour to two hours. When death is delayed about an hour, even thigh and diaphragm muscles stiffen while the animal still lives. Readers get a precise account of allergic death as a heart event.
europmc-pmc2125043:
Albert A. Epstein published further studies on the chemistry of blood serum in 1913, sorting his cases by disease. Minor surgical cases, treated as normal, matched the standard values for serum proteins, and repeated samples from them did not vary. Their non-clotting nitrogen fraction, though, wandered widely from case to case.

Enlarged prostate cases, with or without chronic kidney inflammation, kept a normal protein pattern and normal ratios between fractions. Their non-protein nitrogen swung markedly, some swings tracking how badly the kidneys worked. Local infections of the kidney changed the serum two ways at once: globulins rose, as they do in infections elsewhere, and non-protein nitrogen rose with the amount of kidney destroyed. Disease of the kidney itself, his tables argue, does not alter the serum's proteins. Readers get blood chemistry used as a sorting tool, separating infection's mark from failing function.
europmc-pmc2125143:
Charles Krumwiede and Josephine S. Pratt of the New York Health Department's research laboratory watched bacteria grow on dye-laced media in 1914. Gentian violet and its fellow anilin dyes, they found, sort bacteria into two camps that generally match the Gram stain: the dye-tolerant and the dye-stopped. The reaction is a matter of dose, stronger in some species than others.

Exceptions sharpen the tool. Now and then a Gram-negative strain refuses violet agar entirely, setting it apart from its own species. The streptococcus and pneumococcus group stands out among Gram-positive germs by growing in dye amounts that stop the rest. The dysentery bacilli vary widely, and with fuchsin the variation nearly splits dysentery from paradysentery kinds. Bleaching the dyes with sodium sulphite robs them of some stopping power. Readers get dyes used as a cheap sorting sieve for bacteria, with its quirks honestly mapped.
europmc-pmc2125343:
Edward B. Krumbhaar, John H. Musser, and Max M. Peet ran the control study of their spleen series in 1916: instead of removing the spleen from dogs, they diverted its blood from the liver. The splenic vein was tied off, or transplanted into the inferior vena cava, or bypassed by an Eck fistula. The blood answered as if the spleen were gone.

Anemia followed, resembling the post-splenectomy kind in degree and duration. Red cells quickly grew more resistant to weak salt solutions, sometimes before the anemia appeared, and eased back as it cleared. White cells surged first in the polymorphonuclear forms, then shifted toward small lymphocytes and eosinophils, a pattern unlike ordinary post-surgical change. Tying the vein shrank the spleen considerably but caused no death of tissue or clotting. Readers get splenectomy's effects reproduced by plumbing alone.
europmc-pmc2128143:
Margaret Reed Lewis, of the Carnegie Institution's embryology department at Johns Hopkins, showed that tissue cultures need sugar to live. Her paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. Connective tissue cells grown with no dextrose in the medium formed odd vacuoles, clear bubbles inside the cells, and died. This happened even with plenty of protein at hand.

Small amounts of dextrose held the vacuoles off and kept the culture alive longer. Large amounts stopped the bubbles from forming at all, but they often soured the medium as the cells wore out, which brought its own harm. Lewis would not settle what the vacuoles are, lacking proof of their exact nature. Whatever they are, they are not normal cell parts, and their coming marks a medium missing something the cells need. Dextrose, in measured amount, belongs in the recipe.
europmc-pmc2130943:
David T. Smith and Leslie T. Webster traced a common middle ear infection of rabbits to the snuffles germ of the nose. Their paper is the sixth in an epidemiological series on rabbit respiratory infections, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. Autopsies at the Rockefeller Institute had repeatedly found pus in stock rabbits' middle ears.

In the great majority of cases the ear condition goes with snuffles, the upper respiratory inflammation, and with Bacterium lepisepticum in the passages. Put that germ into the nostrils of rabbits hitherto protected from it, and a pus-forming middle ear infection follows, indistinguishable from the natural one. The rabbit's anatomy makes the path easy. Nose and middle ear connect, so an agent planted in the nose can invade the whole group of cavities tied to the upper respiratory tract. Snuffles, the work shows, is not confined to the nose it names.
europmc-pmc2131343:
Harry Sobotka and Mae Friedlander opened a 1928 study of the precipitin reaction in antipneumococcus sera, in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. When such a serum meets the type-specific sugar from pneumococcus, a visible precipitate forms. Part one defines a number, the precipitin index, meant to measure the strength of that reaction in a clean, repeatable way.

The reaction's sensitivity stayed generally constant when expressed as the product of the two reacting strengths, and the index is built from that product. Uneven zones at high and low strengths can distort plain readings, and the index lets them be spotted and set aside. Adding normal serum or raising acidity shifts the zones in known directions, which the measure helps correct.
europmc-pmc2140843:
Southworth and Redfield, at Harvard Medical School, studied gas transport in turtle blood in a 1926 paper, using the turtle Pseudemys concinna. Blood must load oxygen in the lungs and carry carbon dioxide away. Turtle blood differs from mammal blood in makeup, and the pair set out its working traits as a transport system.

Its red cell content is low, a tenth to a fifth of the volume, and it holds much base bound as bicarbonate. Those two traits fully explain the shape of its carbon dioxide curve and how oxygen loading shifts its carbon dioxide power. Weight for weight, turtle corpuscles combine with as much oxygen as human red cells. The oxygen curve resembles the mammalian one and bends with carbon dioxide in the same way.
europmc-pmc2173943:
Kroth and a large team modelled carbohydrate metabolism in 2008 in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Diatoms are single-celled algae fixing about 20 percent of global carbon. Their cells arose by secondary endosymbiosis, one cell engulfing another alga, giving them complex structure. The team annotated sugar-pathway genes using the new genome plus expressed gene tags, and compared a second diatom, Thalassiosira pseudonana.

They predicted where each enzyme works, in plastids, mitochondria or cytosol, from targeting signals in its sequence. Genes pointed to a possible C4-like photosynthesis route, a carbon-concentrating trick. Calvin cycle enzymes appeared in up to five versions spread across cell compartments. One photorespiration enzyme, glycerate kinase, was missing in both diatoms. Diatoms store energy as lipids or as chrysolaminaran, a glucose polymer kept outside the plastids.
europmc-pmc2198943:
Rustad, Harrell, Liao and Sherman studied in 2008 how tuberculosis bacteria endure low oxygen. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can lie latent for decades, and oxygen-starved pockets in the host are suspected triggers. A regulator called DosR controls the first hypoxic response. Deleting dosR blocks that response fully. The team tested whether the mutant still survives oxygen starvation in culture and in mice.

The mutant entered bacteriostasis, a dormant non-growing state, with only mild loss of viability. In mouse infections it behaved like the normal strain. Gene activity studies showed the DosR response fades within 24 hours for nearly half its genes. A second, larger wave follows, called the Enduring Hypoxic Response. It covers 230 genes switched on at four and seven days, and it runs normally without DosR.
europmc-pmc2216043:
Huson and colleagues introduced Dendroscope in 2007, a program for viewing very large evolutionary trees. Phylogenetic trees show relationships between species, and modern data sets can hold hundreds of thousands of entries. Existing viewers often handled only small trees, lacked editing features, or were hard to install. The team aimed for an interactive tool that runs on all major operating systems.

Dendroscope provides all standard tree visualisations. It is optimised for trees with hundreds of thousands of taxa, the named groups in a tree. It stays responsive during interactive exploration of the data set on screen. It includes tree editing and graphics export. A magnification tool helps inspect dense regions closely. The software is written in Java, with installers for Linux, Unix, Mac OS X and Windows. The authors call it user-friendly for both small and large data sets.
europmc-pmc2556743:
Lopes and colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2007 on guiding fluid therapy during high-risk surgery by watching pulse pressure variation. Surgeons knew that loading patients with fluid until heart output plateaus can improve recovery, but judging that point is tricky. Pulse pressure swings with each ventilator breath, and the team tested whether keeping that swing at 10 percent or less would steer fluids well.

Thirty-three patients were randomised to guided care or usual care. The guided group received far more fluid, about 4,600 millilitres against 1,700, and their pulse pressure swing fell as intended. They left hospital after a median of 7 days against 17 for controls. They also suffered fewer complications per patient and spent fewer days on ventilators and in intensive care.
europmc-pmc2825543:
Fulda, Gorman, Hori, and Samali reviewed in 2010 how cells answer stress, choosing between survival programs and orderly self-destruction. A stressed cell may repair itself or die on purpose, and the choice depends on the kind and length of the stress and on the cell type at hand.

The review maps the main death routes, including apoptosis, the tidy self-dismantling most cells use, plus necrosis, pyroptosis, and death tied to self-eating. Survival and death programs talk to each other constantly, and that interplay settles the cell's fate. The authors then trace what these responses mean for major diseases, among them diabetes, Parkinson disease, heart attack damage, and cancer.
europmc-pmc2831043:
García-Campayo and colleagues adapted the GAD-7 anxiety screening scale into Spanish in 2010 and tested how well the version works. The GAD-7 is a seven-question self-rating for generalized anxiety disorder, a condition often missed in clinics. A careful panel process with paired forward and back translations aimed for equal meaning, not just equal words.

Two hundred twelve people, half of them patients with the disorder, filled in the scale in about two and a half minutes, leaving nothing blank. Scores formed a single dimension, and a cut-off of ten caught about eighty-seven percent of true cases while clearing about ninety-three percent of people without the disorder. Scores also matched closely with three established anxiety and disability scales.
europmc-pmc2860243:
Van den Berg and colleagues mapped in 2010 the full set of proteins that work alongside Oct4, a master switch that keeps embryo stem cells able to become any tissue. Oct4 is a transcription factor, a protein that turns genes on and off. The team fished Oct4 and then its partners out of mouse embryo stem cells and identified each catch.

Their network held one hundred sixty-six proteins, including many known self-renewal factors and many never linked to stem cells before. Some partners connect Oct4 to major growth signal pathways used across the body. Removing Oct4 quickly loosened its partners' grip on their target genes. The map shows that staying pluripotent, able to form any tissue, depends on a wide team rather than one switch.
europmc-pmc2873343:
Callaghan, Ford, and Schneider reviewed in 2010 whether shifting medical tasks to less specialized staff can widen HIV treatment across Africa. A shortage of doctors and nurses had slowed the rollout of antiretroviral therapy, the drug mix that keeps HIV in check. Task shifting hands jobs like starting and monitoring treatment to nurses, other non-doctor clinicians, and community caregivers.

Searching several databases, the team gathered eighty-four core studies, with outcome data from ten African countries. Shifting treatment tasks to nurses was the most studied model, and five studies showed it expanded the number of patients who could start therapy. Care quality in the reported programs held up well. The authors back the approach while calling for stronger training, supervision, and pay structures to sustain it.
europmc-pmc2944843:
Tilghman and co-authors tested how the stiffness of the surface beneath cancer cells shapes their growth, in a 2010 study using plates lined with gels spanning a wide stiffness range. Body tissues vary from soft to firm, and tumours feel that difference.

Cancer lines fell into two camps: some grew faster as gels stiffened, others grew alike on soft and stiff gels. Poor growth on soft gels came with less spreading and movement. Growth on soft gel also predicted growth after seeding into mouse lungs, a naturally soft tissue. One lung line even regained a mature surface marker on soft gels.
europmc-pmc3032643:
Walker and colleagues sequenced gut bacteria in depth in this 2011 study of inflammatory bowel disease, which covers Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. They took paired tissue samples from sore and healthy looking spots in patients, plus samples from people without the disease. More than ten thousand bacterial gene sequences were read from the tissue lining itself.

Diversity of microbes was lower in patients, most sharply in Crohn disease. One major bacterial group fell while others rose, and in Crohn disease a family linked to inflammation grew. Sore and calm spots in the same person did differ, but the pattern varied so much between people that no single microbe marked the sore spots. The authors suggest the imbalance may partly result from the disturbed gut, yet still help keep the disease going.
europmc-pmc3069743:
Evans summarized in 2011 how to run the data reduction step of X ray crystallography within the CCP4 suite. After a crystal is measured, its diffraction images must be converted into a clean, scaled list of spot intensities, and the crystal's symmetry group must be pinned down. Errors at this stage poison everything that follows, so the choices matter.

The guide explains what the reduction programs do with those choices. It explains how scaling merges repeated measurements into one consistent set, and how intensity statistics reveal problems such as twinning or wrong symmetry. It is written as a practical companion rather than a theory text. Beginners get a route through the standard programs, while experienced users get the reasoning behind the defaults. The piece belongs to a special issue documenting the whole suite.
europmc-pmc3081743:
Zrenner and a large German team reported in 2011 that an electronic chip placed under the retina let people blind from inherited retinal disease perceive shapes, letters, and even words. The chip holds fifteen hundred tiny light sensors, each with its own amplifier and stimulating contact, and sits where dead light sensing cells once worked. Scenes fall on it naturally through the eye's own lens.

Three volunteers received the implant near the central vision zone. All could point to bright objects on a dark table, and two could tell apart striped patterns. One patient named everyday objects, told fruits apart, read shades of grey at low contrast, and, after years of blindness, read large letters joined into words without prior training. The authors call it the first proof that a high count subretinal array can restore useful, detailed sight.
europmc-pmc3166743:
Eleni Andreou and colleagues validated a standard stress questionnaire for Greek adults in a 2011 paper in a public health journal. The scale asks how often life feels unpredictable and overloaded, and it comes in long, medium, and short versions. Nearly a thousand Greek adults completed it alongside a companion distress scale and a symptom list.

The two-part structure of the longer versions held up, and their scores were consistent and repeatable. The shortest version scored only marginally well. Stress scores tracked closely with depression, anxiety, and stress subscales, and rose with the number of physical symptoms people reported. Women scored higher than men on average. The authors approve the two longer Greek versions for research and care.
europmc-pmc3192843:
Yu Chen and colleagues solved the structure of a SARS virus enzyme pair that disguises viral RNA in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Human messages wear a chemical cap, and the virus copies that cap in two steps to hide from immunity and stay stable. The second step needs two viral proteins working together, one of them only as an activator, which is unusual.

Bench tests showed the enzyme pair accepts only correctly pre-capped RNA, unlike its partner enzyme that accepts any start. The activator proved necessary for gripping both the RNA and the chemical donor. The crystal structure shows the activator propping open the donor pocket and lengthening the RNA groove. The authors propose the protein interface, rather than the enzyme's active site, as the sharper target for anti-coronavirus drugs.
europmc-pmc3204243:
Megan Hardin and colleagues characterized patients who have both COPD and asthma in this 2011 study in Respiratory Research. The overlap of the two lung diseases is widely recognized but poorly described. Within a large study of smokers, the team compared those reporting a doctor's diagnosis of asthma alongside COPD against those with COPD alone.

About one in eight of the COPD subjects also had asthma. That group was younger and had smoked less over a lifetime, yet reported worse quality of life and suffered more frequent and severe flare-ups. Chest scans showed more trapped air in their lungs, while lung-function tests, emphysema, and airway wall thickness looked the same as in COPD alone. The authors argue this overlap group deserves recognition as a distinct clinical population.
europmc-pmc3267043:
Nikolaos Balaskas and colleagues worked out the gene regulatory logic that reads a developmental signal in the spinal cord, in this 2012 paper in Cell. A secreted protein called Sonic Hedgehog spreads from one side of the embryonic neural tube, and its fading gradient tells cells which neuron type to become. The team combined a live reporter of the signal in mice with genetics and mathematical modeling.

They show the gradient changes in both space and time, and that a network of three transcription factors interprets it. The network's wiring explains why different genes switch on in different places and at different times. It also buffers cells against wobbles in the signal and gives them hysteresis, a memory of past exposure. Morphogen reading, the authors conclude, is a property that emerges from the network's architecture, lending tissue patterning its reliability.
europmc-pmc3307043:
Rehm surveyed the health risks tied to drinking alcohol, in a review published in 2011. Alcohol is a direct cause of more than thirty conditions and adds to the risk of many more, making it a major driver of illness and early death worldwide. Heavy regular drinking accounts for most of that burden, though single heavy occasions also do real harm.

Disease areas covered range from infections, cancer, and diabetes to mental disorders, heart and blood vessel disease, and liver and pancreas damage. Injuries, both accidental and deliberate, add further losses. Drinking also harms people other than the drinker, through crashes, violence, and family strain. Rehm notes that knowing these risks shaped official low risk drinking guidelines, and argues for stronger prevention efforts.
europmc-pmc3349743:
Ottenhoff and Kaufmann reviewed the search for a better tuberculosis vaccine, in work published in 2012. The only vaccine in use, BCG, dates from the early twentieth century. It shields young children from the worst forms of the disease but works patchily against the adult lung form, which is the form that keeps the disease spreading.

The review surveys what might come next: booster shots built on viruses, reworked BCG strains, and subunit vaccines meant to top up or replace the first dose. The authors weigh the lack of clear immune markers for protection and the slow, hard task of proving that a new vaccine works in large trials.
europmc-pmc3380943:
Achtman and a study group argued in 2012 that Salmonella typing by gene sequences should replace the old serum-based system. Salmonella enterica has long been split into serovars by surface traits and feeding tests. The team typed thousands of isolates from hundreds of serovars using several housekeeping genes.

The isolates fell into just over a thousand sequence types, grouped into clusters that follow true family lines. Most serovars, by contrast, were scattered across unrelated clusters, and many clusters mixed several serovars. Problem cases such as Paratyphi B showed serotyping lumping strangers together and splitting kin apart. Because sequence typing tracks descent, the group recommends it as the new standard.
europmc-pmc3385443:
Thayer, Heindel, Bucher, and Gallo recapped a 2011 national workshop on whether chemicals in our surroundings feed the twin epidemics of diabetes and obesity. Experts reviewed human and animal evidence for arsenic, several pollutant families, nicotine, and everyday chemicals such as bisphenol A. Screening data helped flag cell pathways worth testing.

Several exposures were linked with type 2 diabetes in the literature reviewed. Evidence also backed the idea that early exposure can steer fat-cell growth and appetite circuits, raising weight risk, especially with a rich diet later. Research on type 1 diabetes was almost absent, a gap the group flagged as stark. The review sets a research agenda.
europmc-pmc3405143:
Reinius and colleagues warned in 2012 that DNA methylation measured from whole blood can mislead, because blood is a mixture of cell types. Each white cell lineage carries its own methylation pattern. If illness studies compare blood samples with different cell mixes, apparent disease signals may just be cell counts in disguise.

In healthy male donors, the team profiled whole blood, its two great cell families, and seven purified lineages. For most immune-related genes studied, at least one site differed sharply between the two families. Some control-region sites even flipped direction between cell types. Disease studies, they conclude, must account for cell mix before claiming a methylation link to illness.
europmc-pmc3407643:
Lai and colleagues profiled the protein cargo of tiny vesicles shed by mesenchymal stem cells in 2012, hunting the source of their healing effect. Such exosomes shrink heart damage in mice after a blocked artery reopens. The team suspected a select team of proteins inside does the work together.

Mass scanning found the complete 20S proteasome, the cell's protein-shredding machine, riding inside the vesicles, along with parts of its immune variant. The carried machine still worked, and its presence matched lower levels of clumped, damaged protein in injured mouse hearts. Human blood vesicles carried it too. A working shredder delivered by vesicle, they propose, helps clear wreckage after injury.
europmc-pmc3478843:
Rampersad reviewed the many uses of Alamar Blue, a dye that shows whether cells are alive and active, in Sensors in 2012. Living cells change the dye's chemistry, so its signal tracks cell health. Labs had used it for fifty years across bacteria, yeast, fungi, and animal cells, for tasks from drug screening to testing water safety.

The review weighs the dye's strengths against rival tests and flags the traps in its use. Results can shift with cell type, dose, and timing, so each new setup needs its own checks. Rampersad gives design advice and a checklist for judging whether the assay fits a planned study. Used with care, the dye offers a cheap, gentle way to follow cell health over time.
europmc-pmc3548743:
Quality-of-life research speaks in many competing frameworks, and Tamilyn Bakas leads a nine-author systematic review sorting them out in 2012. From 1,602 titles screened, 100 articles from 21 countries met the criteria, and the team identifies which health-related quality of life models researchers actually use, then critiques the leaders against published standards.

Three models dominate: Wilson and Cleary at 16 percent, the World Health Organization model at 5 percent, and Ferrans and colleagues at 4 percent. The Ferrans model, a revision of Wilson and Cleary, looks best placed to guide future work. The advice is blunt: use one of the three unless strong reasons demand a new model.
europmc-pmc3549243:
Shrinking one liver lobe can grow the other, and K. P. van Lienden and six colleagues systematically review portal vein embolization before liver resection in 2013. Blocking portal flow to the diseased side forces the future remnant to enlarge, making large resections safer. The search covers 1990 to 2011 across Medline, Cochrane, and Embase.

Forty-four articles report 1,791 patients. Technical success reaches 99.3 percent, and the remnant grows by about 38 percent on average. Surgery is abandoned in 3.9 percent, major complications touch 2.5 percent, and mortality is 0.1 percent. Cirrhosis blunts the growth response, while n-butyl cyanoacrylate glue seems to strengthen it.
europmc-pmc3579743:
Lambertus Klei and a large team of collaborators weighed the genetics of autism in Molecular Autism in 2012. Autism spectrum disorders begin early and affect social contact, communication, and behavior. Rare gene changes, especially new ones, were known to raise risk, but whether common gene variants matter much stayed open, and arguments over genes versus environment ran hot. The team used statistical genetics on families with one affected child and families with several.

Common variants spread across the genome added up to a major share of risk, they found. Their estimate put narrow-sense heritability above sixty percent for children from families with several affected members, with simplex and multiplex families showing different mixes of risk. Relatives' data fit the model of many small effects adding together. The result does not deny rare mutations or environment a role; it shows the everyday variation in everyone's genome carries much of the load.
europmc-pmc3579943:
Irena Pastar and colleagues studied mixed bacterial infections in wounds in PLoS ONE in 2013. Two germs often share chronic wounds: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, in its USA300 form the top cause of community skin infection in the United States, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Together they delay healing, yet how they affect each other inside a living wound was largely unknown. The team used a pig wound model, which heals much like human skin.

Mixed biofilms slowed the regrowing of skin over the wound, partly by suppressing a growth factor that skin cells need. In dishes, Pseudomonas held USA300 back, but in living wounds both species settled in side by side. The presence of Pseudomonas also switched on two USA300 toxin genes, raising its attack strength. Wound care, the authors argue, must reckon with germs acting as a team, not alone.
europmc-pmc3598943:
Andreas Kranis and a large team of collaborators built a high-density genotyping chip for chickens in BMC Genomics in 2013. Chips that read hundreds of thousands of DNA letters at once are standard tools in cattle and crop genetics. Chickens, among the world's most important farm animals, had no such high-resolution array. Building one meant first finding enough variable DNA letters spread across the whole chicken genome and across its many breeds.

The group re-sequenced 243 birds from twenty-four lines, commercial meat and egg stock plus experimental flocks, and found about 139 million candidate variants. Strict filters for quality and even spacing cut the list through validation trials on fresh samples, where about sixty-four percent proved reliably readable. The finished array carries 580,954 markers, including over twenty-one thousand inside protein-coding regions. Breeders and researchers gain fine-grained maps for traits from growth to disease resistance.
europmc-pmc3617543:
Sofia Santos Costa, Miguel Viveiros, Leonard Amaral, and Isabel Couto updated the science of bacterial drug pumps in The Open Microbiology Journal in 2013. Staphylococcus aureus, a germ behind everything from skin infections to deadly sepsis, increasingly resists whole shelves of antibiotics. One defense is the efflux pump: a protein that bails incoming drugs out of the cell before they can kill. Pumps handle many unrelated compounds at once, making them prime suspects in multidrug resistance.

The review gathers what is known about each pump in this species, whether carried on the chromosome or on mobile plasmids, and the tangled control circuits that switch them on. Pumps may serve as a first line, buying the cell time at low drug levels until a stronger resistance change appears. Open questions dominate the close, including how to measure each pump's true contribution.
europmc-pmc3709543:
Lin and colleagues compared the epidemiology of esophageal cancer in Japan and China, ahead of a joint study of the disease's causes. In both countries the squamous cell form dominates, while the adenocarcinoma common in the West stays extremely rare. Drinking alcohol and smoking raise risk in both populations.

The differences are just as striking. Rates of illness and death run higher in China, with far wider regional variation, though Chinese mortality fell faster between 1987 and 2000. Risk factor patterns vary between high- and low-incidence areas inside China but not Japan. Genome studies also diverge: several risk regions emerged in China, while Japanese risk centred on alcohol-processing genes.
europmc-pmc3733843:
Garance Di Pasquale and co-authors reported a bee study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on pollen nutrition and honey bee health. Bees depend on pollen for the nutrients a colony needs, but farm intensification has made pollen supply uneven. The team asked whether the quality of pollen, and the variety of pollen types, change bee health.

They fed young nurse bees single-flower pollens or a mixed blend, with and without a gut parasite called Nosema ceranae. Pollen quality changed the bees' body development and their tolerance of the parasite. Variety alone did not change healthy bees, but infected bees on the mixed diet lived longer than most single-pollen groups. Survival also tracked the activity of enzymes tied to defense and metabolism.
europmc-pmc3738443:
Devin Absher and co-authors reported a genome-wide study in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on DNA methylation in lupus. Lupus is an autoimmune disease shaped by genes, environment, and epigenetic marks such as methylation. The team took three immune cell types from 49 lupus patients and 58 controls and scanned their methylation with a large array.

T cells showed the most changes, with over a thousand sites strongly altered. Across all three cell types, genes tied to interferon signaling had lost methylation marks. The loss showed up in both active and quiet phases of the disease, and in several T-cell subtypes, which suggests the state is set early in cell development. T cells also showed a broad, smaller shift near genes for cell division, hinting at changed cell mix.
europmc-pmc3751743:
Andreas Schmitt and five co-authors described a new questionnaire in Health and Quality of Life Outcomes in 2013 for measuring diabetes self-care. Good questionnaires should track blood sugar control, but older tools often linked only weakly to HbA1c, the standard blood sugar marker. The team built the 16-item Diabetes Self-Management Questionnaire to do better.

The questionnaire has four subscales: glucose management, dietary control, physical activity, and health-care use, plus a total score. It was tested in 261 patients with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes. Internal consistency was good overall, and the four-part structure held up under statistical checks. All of its scales correlated with HbA1c more strongly than the matching older scale. The authors present it as a reliable, valid, and efficient tool.
europmc-pmc3760643:
Chris Gardiner, Yannick Ferreira, Rebecca Dragovic, Christopher Redman, and Ian Sargent wrote a methods paper in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2013 on nanoparticle tracking analysis. The technique shines a laser through a liquid sample and tracks the jiggle of single particles on camera to size and count extracellular vesicles quickly. As a new method, it had been criticized for poor standardization.

The authors propose silica microspheres as calibration standards for the measurements. They then set out a detailed protocol for preparing and measuring vesicle samples, designed to cut the variability and imprecision that had dogged the method. Reliable sizing and counting matter because vesicles are candidate markers for diagnosing and tracking disease, yet their small size and mixed sizes make them hard to measure.
europmc-pmc3788343:
Bryan Troxell and Hosni Hassan wrote a review in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2013 on Fur, the ferric uptake regulator in pathogenic bacteria. Iron is essential but hard to get: inside a host, iron is locked away from invaders on purpose. Bacteria answer by making siderophores, small molecules that grab ferric iron with extreme strength.

Fur uses ferrous iron as a co-signal to switch siderophore production off when iron suffices. It also controls, directly or indirectly, enzymes that defend against reactive oxygen species. Though long known as a repressor, Fur can also activate genes, through small RNAs, through direct binding that helps the transcription machinery, or by blocking other repressors. Related family members govern peroxide defense and the uptake of zinc and manganese. Mutants in these regulators are less virulent in many infection models.
europmc-pmc3861043:
Richard R. Stein leads a team of co-authors in a modeling study in PLoS Computational Biology in 2013. The gut hosts a dense microbial ecosystem that guards against gut infections. Antibiotics can shatter that guard, letting the germ Clostridium difficile take hold. The team build a way to read the ecosystem's rules from time-series data.

Their method extends a classic species interaction model to handle outside shocks such as drugs. Fit to data from a mouse infection study, it measures how gut groups help or hinder each other and the invader. The healthy mix proves stable on its own, yet a drug shock can flip it into a lasting bad state. A small group of bacteria looks key to holding the invader off.
europmc-pmc3891543:
Shashank Kumar and Abhay K. Pandey review flavonoids in The Scientific World Journal in 2013. Flavonoids are plant compounds found in fruit, vegetables, tea, and wine. Their health promise has drawn wide study, tied to the ring shapes and hydroxyl groups their molecules carry.

Small shape changes decide how well the body absorbs a flavonoid and what it does once inside. Reported gains include antioxidant action, heart protection, liver protection, calmer inflammation, and some anti-cancer and anti-virus effects. In plants the compounds fight oxidative stress and steer growth. Microbe-based production now makes bulk supply cheaper for drug use. The review links structure to function across this large family.
europmc-pmc3935943:
Alex Iranzo and colleagues follow 174 patients who act out their dreams in sleep. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The condition is called idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Patients were tracked at a sleep center in Barcelona. Records ran from 1991 to 2013. The team asked how many would later develop a brain disease. They also asked how long that took.

The risk was about one third at five years. It rose to about three quarters at ten years. At fourteen years it passed 90 percent. The middle time to conversion was seven and a half years. Dementia with Lewy bodies was the most common outcome. Parkinson's disease came next. A few patients developed multiple system atrophy. Others showed mild cognitive impairment. Brain checks after death confirmed Lewy-type disease.
europmc-pmc4015143:
Steve Horvath builds a clock that reads age from DNA tags, in Genome Biology in 2013. DNA methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, shifts with age at many sites. Whether those shifts could date most body tissues, and whether the date means anything for biology, was not known.

Horvath trained his predictor on eight thousand samples from eighty-two data sets, spanning fifty-one healthy tissues and cell types. The clock reads near zero for embryo and reprogrammed stem cells, and it tracks how many times cells have divided. Its speed-up over real age runs in families, so the trait is heritable. In six thousand cancer samples, all twenty cancer types showed age speed-up, on average by decades. Slow speed-up went with more mutations in one group, while certain hormone receptor faults sped breast cancer samples sharply. The clock rests on a few hundred tag sites.
europmc-pmc4051243:
Heather J. Lee, Timothy A. Hore, and Wolf Reik review how embryos erase and rebuild their DNA methylation patterns, in Cell Stem Cell in 2014. Methylation marks act as a molecular memory, locking in each cell's programme through division. A maintenance enzyme copies the pattern to new DNA strands as cells divide.

Yet twice in each generation the memory is wiped. Germ cells and the early embryo undergo genome-wide stripping of methylation. That blank slate underlies the naive state of stem cells, able to become any tissue. As cells leave that state, fresh marks are laid by de novo enzymes, and the spread of patterns helps sister cells break symmetry and choose fates. The review links the methylation machinery to the pluripotency network through shared partners.
europmc-pmc4054843:
Jacob M. Riveron and ten colleagues pin DDT resistance in a major malaria mosquito to a single letter change in one gene, in Genome Biology in 2014. Anopheles funestus spreads malaria across Africa. Its growing ability to detoxify insecticides is the largest threat to control programmes, yet no DNA marker for that metabolic resistance existed.

Gene activity scans of resistant mosquitoes from Benin put one detox gene, GSTe2, at the top. A single amino acid change in it tracked tightly with DDT survival across the continent. Fruit flies engineered to make the mosquito gene gained resistance to DDT and cross-resistance to pyrethroids. The purified changed enzyme broke down DDT faster, and its structure showed a widened pocket that admits more of the poison. The marker is under strong selection where spraying is heavy.
europmc-pmc4086143:
Douglas E. V. Pires, David B. Ascher, and Tom L. Blundell built DUET, a web server that predicts how a single-letter protein mutation changes protein stability. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Cancer genome projects were producing floods of such variants, and no single prediction method proved dependable in every setting.

DUET merges two complementary methods into one consensus answer. One method reads the local structural environment; the other derives energy rules from related protein families. A support vector machine, a type of learning algorithm, combines their outputs in an optimised way. The combined predictor beat each method alone and matched or beat similar tools. The server is free and aimed at experts and non-experts alike.
europmc-pmc4181643:
Doğa Gürsoy, Francesco De Carlo, Xianghui Xiao, and Chris Jacobsen described a software framework called TomoPy in the Journal of Synchrotron Radiation in 2014. Synchrotron facilities scan objects with intense X-ray beams and rebuild three-dimensional images from the slices, a method called tomography. Each facility had its own patchwork of analysis code, which wasted effort and made results hard to compare.

TomoPy gathers the needed steps, from cleaning raw data to rebuilding the image, in one open-source Python package. It runs on different systems, reads varied data formats, and can spread work across many processor cores at once. The authors built it as a shared project so beamlines at different centres can pool improvements instead of each solving the same problems alone.
europmc-pmc4300843:
Chirayu Pankaj Goswami and Harikrishna Nakshatri describe PROGgeneV2, an updated web database that links gene activity in tumors to patient survival. Their paper appeared in BMC Cancer in 2014. The first version let users ask whether a gene's expression level in a cancer tracked with better or worse outcomes, drawn from public studies.

The update nearly doubles the catalog of studies and widens what users can test. Survival can now be checked for single genes, multi gene signatures, and ratios between two genes, and models can adjust for patient factors such as age. Published gene signatures are included ready made. The tool serves cancer researchers who want a fast prognosis check before deeper work.
europmc-pmc4307243:
Raynoo Thanan and nine co-authors review oxidative stress in brain degeneration and cancer. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species damage lipids, proteins, and DNA, and the scars of that damage show up across inflamed tissue, failing brains, and tumors.

The authors draw on their own work on oxidized proteins, including heat shock proteins whose protective role fades once damaged. In brain diseases, DNA damage may kill cells or shorten chromosome ends and halt cell division. In inflammation linked cancers, the same damage helps start the disease. The review ties these threads into one account of how chemical stress ages tissue.
europmc-pmc4328143:
Verena Ruprecht and ten co-authors found a fast, balloon shaped style of cell crawling and the switch that turns it on. Their study appeared in Cell in 2015. Amoeboid migration, movement without firm anchors, drives embryo development and cancer spread, and the team found this stable bleb form in early zebrafish embryo cells.

The cells hold a polarized balloon shape and move with unusual speed and persistence. Raising the contractile protein myosin II, by chemistry or by squeezing, flipped ordinary progenitor cells into this mode. Random pulses in the cell's contractile cortex trip the switch, and a feedback loop between cortical flow and contractility keeps the cell polarized. Theory and experiment together explain the motion.
europmc-pmc4452143:
Ewelina Golebiewska and Alastair Poole reviewed platelet secretion in Blood Reviews in 2015. Platelets, the small blood cells that plug wounds, release hundreds of active substances from storage granules when they switch on. Some released chemicals, such as ADP and polyphosphates, drive clotting, and the same contents can also help cancer spread through the blood.

Another granule type holds growth factors, immune signals, and both pro- and anti-inflammatory molecules that shape the growing clot and many disease processes. How platelets choose what to release, and when, is still partly unknown. The review sums up granule formation and the release machinery. It covers the roles of secreted contents in clotting, wound healing, and disease. It also weighs ideas for how one cell type can serve so many settings with the same stored cargo.
europmc-pmc4489243:
Mark Davies and seven co-authors described the ChEMBL web services in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. ChEMBL is a large open database that curates molecules, their biological activity, their targets, and approved drugs, extracted by hand mainly from the medicinal chemistry literature. Drug discovery teams worldwide mine it, but many need to pull data into their own programs rather than browse pages.

The updated services expose far more of the database through a standard web interface, so software can query compounds, activities, targets, and drugs directly. A companion utility service offers common cheminformatics operations, such as structure conversions and similarity calculations, through the same style of access. The two services can be used together or separately to build applications and data pipelines for drug discovery and chemical biology. The article documents the endpoints and shows example workflows.
europmc-pmc4585843:
Ang Yuan leads an eleven-author team showing that macrophage flavor can speed or slow lung cancer, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Tumors are full of macrophages, which come in attacking M1 and healing M2 forms. Using the lung cancer cell line A549, the team tested what each form does to cancer behavior.

The M2 forms pushed A549 cells to invade and grew larger tumors in mice. M1 macrophages did the opposite: they cut vessel growth, made the cancer cells more sensitive to the drug cisplatin, and drove them into death or senescence. Each form rewired different gene programs in the cancer cells. The resulting M1 and M2 gene signatures tracked how long lung cancer patients survived, suggesting a prognostic test.
europmc-pmc4711343:
Kai Zhang presented Gctf, a program for measuring a key imaging distortion in cryo-electron microscopy, in the Journal of Structural Biology in 2016. Cryo-EM rebuilds molecular structures from thousands of fuzzy particle images. Each image passes through the microscope's contrast transfer function, which scrambles detail in a known way. Estimating that function exactly is essential for near-atomic results, and doing it live is better still.

Gctf runs on graphics processors and matches simulated functions against each micrograph's spectrum. A two-step search adds speed, on top of gains the paper puts at ten to fiftyfold. It then refines focus values for single particles and single movie frames. Built-in consistency checks flag bad estimates. Outputs drop neatly into the field's standard packages, making Gctf a practical front step for high-resolution work.
europmc-pmc4752443:
James B. Pease and four co-authors use whole gene readouts in a PLoS Biology study from 2016 to trace how wild tomatoes split into new species at speed. The group covers all 13 species of the wild tomato clade. Bursts of splitting like this one remain hard to explain with genes alone.

Their tree dates the spread to about two and a half million years ago. Three sources fed the change. Genes crossed between lineages, old and new. Fresh mutations arose in single lines, among them genes for red fruit. Old variants also sorted by habitat across species lines. Each source supplied a small but real share of the genome, so rapid splits drew on all three at once.
europmc-pmc479043:
Sara L. Sawyer, Michael Emerman, and Harmit S. Malik trace an arms race in primate DNA in PLoS Biology in 2004. The enzyme APOBEC3G edits viral DNA and can wreck HIV as it copies itself. HIV fights back with a protein, Vif, that marks the enzyme for destruction. Such paired attack and defense should leave a mark: fast change at the contact surface, as each side adapts.

Reading the gene across primates, the team found exactly that mark, strong and old. The pressure ran through much of primate history, far deeper than today's lentiviruses can explain, so older viral foes likely drove it. Five sister genes in humans show the same fast-change signal, among the strongest in the genome. DNA editing, the authors argue, is an ancient primate defense, not a new one.
europmc-pmc4819943:
Anu Kauppinen and four co-authors review inflammation in age-related macular degeneration in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2016. The disease is the leading cause of severe vision loss in older people in rich countries. It destroys the retinal pigment layer that nurses the light sensors, so central sight fades.

The pigment layer faces steady oxidative strain, and its recycling machinery weakens with age. Waste builds inside its cells and in deposits beneath them, and the immune alarm systems that sense damage stay switched on. Local and blood markers of inflammation run high in both the dry, wasting form and the wet form where new vessels invade. The review ties the disease's stages to that slow-burning inflammation and weighs where calming it might help.
europmc-pmc4820843:
Amit Grover leads a twelve-author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on how blood stem cells age. Old stem cells make more of the myeloid line, the infection-fighting white cells, and fewer of the lymphoid line that underpins adaptive immunity. Whether that shift comes from each cell changing or from the mix of stem cell types changing was unsettled.

Reading single stem cells and testing them one by one, the team found aging chiefly boosts platelet bias. Old stem cells are primed to make platelets, blood's clotting fragments, and a whole class that makes only platelets grows common. Cutting a switch that drives the platelet program restored lymphoid output. The platelet tilt, they argue, may be a main reason adaptive immunity fades with age.
europmc-pmc4893743:
Javier García-Nafría, James F. Watson, and Ingo H. Greger presented IVA cloning in 2016, a one-tube DNA building method that uses bacteria's own assembly skill. Standard cloning needs enzyme kits and many steps. Their system exploits a recombination path found in common lab E. coli strains, one that works without the classic RecA protein.

One PCR step, under two hours from setup to cell transfer, now covers insertions, deletions, point changes, and sub-cloning. Five changes at once, multi-piece builds, and whole libraries run in about half the usual time, still in one step. No special strains are needed. Labs gain speed and lower cost on the DNA builds that underpin most modern biology work.
europmc-pmc5009743:
John F. Atkins, Gary Loughran, Pramod R. Bhatt, Andrew E. Firth, and Pavel V. Baranov review ribosomal frameshifting in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. When a ribosome reads a gene, it can slip into a different reading frame, so the tail of the protein is built from a shifted code. Once seen as an error, this slip is now known to be used on purpose by many genes.

Viruses and moving DNA elements use frameshifting to make extra products from one gene. Stable genes in cells use it to control levels of polyamines, small molecules cells need in set amounts, from yeast to humans. Signals in the RNA itself, such as loops and knots, can raise the slip rate at set spots. A twin process in copying, called transcriptional slippage, does the same job. The review gathers these cases into one account of how cells stretch their genetic code.
europmc-pmc5023043:
Daniel Franke and Dmitri I. Svergun present a faster shape-finding program in the Journal of Applied Crystallography in 2009. Small-angle scattering bounces X-rays or neutrons off tiny particles in solution to reveal their rough three-dimensional shape, with no prior guess needed. Their earlier program, DAMMIN, rebuilt shapes from the scattering pattern but ran slowly. DAMMIF is its rebuilt successor.

The new program cuts average run time by a factor of 25 to 40, mainly through smarter step choices rather than parallel computing. A fixed search box gives way to a search space that grows and adapts as the shape emerges. Symmetry and stretched-shape constraints remain available, and results can be exported as chain-like files suited to the Protein Data Bank. The speed gain makes shape work that once took long sessions a routine step in scattering studies.
europmc-pmc5034643:
Mary Kay Kindhauser, Tomas Allen, Veronika Frank, Ravi Shankar Santhana, and Christopher Dye chart the spread of Zika virus in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2016. The team searched the medical literature and cross-checked official reports filed with WHO. Their coverage ran from the virus's discovery in 1947 to February 1, 2016, when the outbreak was declared a public health emergency of international concern.

By that date, 74 countries and territories had reported human infections. The timeline runs from isolation in Uganda and the first known human case in 1952, through a first big island outbreak in 2007, to the arrival in the Americas from 2015. Along the way, the illness changed character: a mild mosquito-borne fever became an outbreak disease linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome and to babies born with small heads. The authors expect travel and wide-ranging Aedes mosquitoes to carry it further.
europmc-pmc5034743:
A. P. Betran, M. R. Torloni, J. J. Zhang, and A. M. Gülmezoglu present a World Health Organization statement on caesarean section rates in BJOG in 2016, for the WHO Working Group on Caesarean Section. A 1985 WHO meeting had said no region needs a rate above ten to fifteen percent, and that range hardened into a supposed ideal, often misapplied to single hospitals. The statement revisits it after thirty years of rising rates.

When medically needed, a caesarean saves mothers and babies, but no evidence shows benefit when it is not needed, and surgery carries risks for present and future pregnancies. Rates keep climbing past medical logic in many places. The statement stresses that the right rate depends on the population served and a facility's case mix, not one worldwide number. Care should aim at giving the operation to every woman who needs it, rather than chasing a set percentage.
europmc-pmc5059543:
Pedro Romero-Aroca and five co-authors review diabetic macular edema in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2016. The condition swells the center of the retina and is the leading cause of blindness in diabetic patients. Two engines are blamed: leaking blood vessels, driven by the factor VEGF, and low-grade inflammation. Whether vessel growth causes the inflammation or follows it was unresolved.

Their reading of the evidence is that the two act together, each feeding the other as the disease develops. Sugar damage breaks the blood-retina barrier and starts leakage, while inflammation switches on alongside and makes the damage chronic. About thirty percent of cases resist treatment. Both anti-VEGF drugs and steroids work, but on different arms of the disease, so knowing which arm dominates in a given patient should guide the choice. Today's scans cannot tell the two apart, a gap the authors want closed.
europmc-pmc5125043:
Jonathan E. Millar, Jonathon P. Fanning, Charles I. McDonald, Daniel F. McAuley, and John F. Fraser reviewed inflammation during ECMO in Critical Care in 2016. ECMO machines take over heart or lung work for short spells, and their use has spread fast, yet patients still face high rates of harm and death.

One harm is the body's reaction to blood running over the machine's foreign surfaces. That contact wakes the innate immune system widely, in a response much like the body-wide inflammation seen after heart bypass surgery, and unchecked it can injure organs. The review traces how immune arms, blood vessel linings, and clotting interact in this response. Understanding the chain, the authors argue, should guide gentler circuits and better risk calls at the bedside.
europmc-pmc5192343:
Sha Li, Ming Hong, Hor-Yue Tan, Ning Wang, and Yibin Feng examine how oxidative stress and inflammation feed each other in liver disease. From early fat buildup through fibrosis and cirrhosis to liver cancer, both processes persist and reinforce one another. Together they form a vicious cycle that drives the disease forward. The review follows the classic mediators and signaling routes, then gives special attention to immune suppression as a possible bridge between the two.

Because the pair act together, treatments that target only one side often disappoint. The authors survey herbal medicines and their compounds that act on both fronts at once. They argue that understanding the interdependence, not just each process alone, is what will yield better targets. The review closes by pointing to combined antioxidant and anti-inflammatory strategies as the most plausible direction.
europmc-pmc5210543:
Gautier Koscielny and a large international team introduced Open Targets in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017, a free platform for picking and checking drug targets. Drug projects often fail late because the link between a target molecule and a disease was weak from the start. The platform gathers genome-wide evidence from many sources so teams can judge that link before spending heavily.

A user can start from a target and find diseases tied to it, or start from a disease and find candidate targets, and can switch between the two views freely. Evidence is scored and shown in visual form to support ranking and follow-up choices. The design work put end users at the center, and planned growth includes tissue-specific expression data, a richer disease vocabulary, and sharper scoring for likely new links.
europmc-pmc5279443:
James Sherren, assistant surgeon at the London Hospital, lectured on surgery of the peripheral nerves at the Medical Graduates' College in London, printed in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1906. Nerve injuries were growing rarer in civil life, yet nerve surgery was widening, with operations now used against paralysis and spasm as well as wounds. The hardest problem is a divided nerve whose ends cannot meet.

Sherren sorts the fixes into five groups: transplanting a nerve piece, flap operations, laying a path to guide regrowth, borrowing neighboring nerves, and shortening the limb by removing bone. He complains the naming is a muddle across languages, then turns to joining nerves for paralysis. For a dead facial nerve, joining it to the tongue's hypoglossal nerve, first done by Ballance, had become the operation of choice. Patients could recover even emotional smiling after five or six years.
europmc-pmc5285743:
