Arthur Robinson delivered the Sir John Struthers Lecture on prenatal death before the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh on December 17, 1920, printed in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1921. The lecture series, endowed by Struthers' will, covers anatomy or embryology and excludes pathology. Earlier lectures by Arthur Keith and by Symington dealt with life after birth; Robinson turns to the period before it.

By prenatal death he means the loss of mature eggs, or of the fertilized cells formed from them, at any point before the normal end of pregnancy. Such losses sometimes end in abortion. The topic matters beyond science, he argues: to animal breeders, to those worried by falling birth rates in several countries and keen to raise them, and to obstetricians advising patients. Popular discussion of the birth rate, he observes, often ignores how much conception is lost before birth even begins to be counted.
europmc-pmc5321743:
Hong Xu led a large team in testing a cancer drug in Nature Communications in 2017. The drug, CX-5461, locks onto odd DNA shapes called G-quadruplexes, where DNA folds into four-strand knots. The team asked if locking those knots could kill tumors that lack working BRCA repair genes. Such tumors already fail at a key DNA repair path.

In lab cells and in grafts grown from patient tumors, the drug hit BRCA-lacking tumors with sharp force. It blocked DNA copying forks and left gaps and breaks in the DNA. Healthy repair paths, BRCA-led repair and a backup joining path, were needed to fix that harm. Without them, the cells died. Even tumors that had shrugged off a standard drug class for BRCA tumors still fell. The drug had reached early trials in patients with BRCA-linked tumors.
europmc-pmc5413843:
Sjödahl and co-authors compare two ways to sort bladder cancer into subtypes. Their research article appeared in The Journal of Pathology. One method reads gene activity across the whole tumor. The other stains tumor cells for marker proteins. Whole-tumor reads can mislead. A tumor mixes cancer cells with normal tissue. That mix can blur the cancer's own traits. The team tested both methods on the same cases.

They studied 307 advanced bladder cancers removed by surgery. Each case got gene expression profiling. Each also got staining with antibodies for 28 proteins. From the protein data they define five tumor-cell types. The types are urothelial-like, genomically unstable, and basal/SCC-like. Mesenchymal-like and small-cell/neuroendocrine-like complete the set. The two methods often disagree on the same tumor. The authors argue that both views are needed for sound subtyping.
europmc-pmc5424143:
Morgens and co-authors turn a flaw of CRISPR screens into a measuring tool. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Cas9 cuts DNA at guide-matched sites. Cuts at wrong sites also occur. Each cut can harm the cell. That harm muddies large screens for gene function. Standard controls do not cut DNA at all. They thus miss the main source of harm.

The team built a library with ten guides per gene. It added thousands of safe-targeting guides. Those guides cut quiet, non-gene regions. They capture pure cutting harm with no gene effect. The library picked out growth and ricin-sensitivity genes cleanly. The authors then used harm itself as a signal. With tens of thousands of guides, they mapped how single mismatches cut off-target activity. Mismatch position mattered greatly. Shortened guides cut less off target. The design gives screens a simple specificity check.
europmc-pmc5429943:
Gilpin and Yang review how to strip cells from tissue while keeping its natural scaffold. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International. Organ donors fall far short of patient need. Over 100,000 people wait for organs in the United States alone. Decellularization offers another path. It washes cells and genetic material out of tissue. What remains is the extracellular matrix. That frame keeps the tissue's shape and chemical cues.

New cells can then be seeded onto the frame. The hope is a working tissue or organ. Methods fall into three groups. Chemical and enzyme treatments dissolve cell parts. Physical methods use force, cold, or pressure. Many protocols mix the two. Each route trades cell removal against matrix damage. The review compares those trade-offs by tissue type. It also shows uses for cell sheets, tissues, and whole organs. The field aims at transplants without donor shortage.
europmc-pmc5446243:
Hansen and co-authors watch CTCF and cohesin at work and find chromatin loops are restless structures. Their study appeared in eLife. Mammalian genomes fold into spatial domains. Loops shape which genes can be reached. The protein CTCF and the ring complex cohesin control those loops. They sit at the same sites and touch each other. Loops were widely assumed to be stable. Single-molecule imaging told another story.

The two partners move at very different speeds. CTCF stays bound for about one to two minutes. Cohesin stays for roughly 22 minutes. After release, CTCF rebinds within about a minute. Cohesin needs some 33 minutes to find a site. The pair thus forms a rapidly exchanging complex. Parts swap in and out constantly. Loops must therefore break and reform often. Domain structure is dynamic across the cell cycle. Gene control inherits that restless character.
europmc-pmc5458943:
Reidy and co-authors critically review how silver nanoparticles release, transform, and exert toxicity. Their review appeared in Materials. Nanosilver fills roughly 30 percent of registered nano products. Its tiny size speeds ion dissolution. Dissolved ions can concentrate inside cells. Particles also generate reactive oxygen species. They adsorb biomolecules and disturb proteins and DNA. Size, shape, and coating all steer these effects. Particles age and change during exposure.

That flux defeats easy comparison across studies. Characterization data are often missing or thin. Time-resolved records of dissolution are rare. The authors issue design guidelines for future work. Studies must describe synthesis, coating, and stabilization fully. Ageing under assay conditions needs tracking. Concerns about nanosilver overuse are growing. Bacteria may evolve resistance to it. The review calls for risk-benefit analysis per application. Uses without clear benefit may face restriction.
europmc-pmc5545843:
Bala and co-authors present clinical guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery. Their subject is acute mesenteric ischemia. In that condition, blood flow to part of the small intestine is cut off. Untreated, the bowel tissue dies and death is common.

The guidelines stress fast diagnosis with CT angiography. They cover ways to restore blood flow to starved bowel. They also cover removal of dead intestine and damage control surgery. Such steps let surgeons recheck bowel health before final repair. Though the condition is rare, death rates near 50 percent make speed vital. Readers get practical, graded advice for emergency teams.
europmc-pmc5556343:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Stem Cell Research & Therapy. Their subject is osteoarthritis, a joint disease that wears down cartilage. Stem cell treatment has shown promise, but the reason was unclear. The team tests whether tiny vesicles from the cells do the work.

The stem cells came from human embryonic stem cells. In mice with a knee injury model, injections of the cells eased cartilage damage. Lab tests then showed the effect came from their exosomes. Those vesicles raised collagen output and lowered a matrix-cutting enzyme in cartilage cells. Injections of exosomes alone also protected mouse cartilage. Readers see a possible cell-free path for joint treatment.
europmc-pmc5613143:
Ivanova and co-authors test an RNA reader protein in Molecular Cell. YTHDF2 binds mRNAs tagged with m6A marks. Binding marks those messages for breakdown. How much this path matters in living mammals was unknown.

Mice lacking YTHDF2 grew up mostly fine. Females, though, proved infertile. Targeted deletion pinned the fault to the germline itself. Their eggs could not mature into competent MII oocytes. Egg maturation normally clears a wave of maternal RNA. Without the reader, that cleanup failed for a whole gene set. The spared messages carried the reader's binding pattern and m6A marks. Embryos from such eggs could not sustain early development. Readers see timed RNA decay as a built-in quality test for eggs.
europmc-pmc5634543:
Pearce and co-authors report a prospective cohort study in PLoS ONE. The study tracked chemotherapy side effects in routine care. It took place across treatment centers in Australia. Patients had breast, lung, or colorectal cancer. Side effects came from patient self-reports, not clinician notes. Follow-up had a median length of 5.64 months.

Data covered 449 eligible patients. The authors report that 86 percent had at least one side effect. About 27 percent reported a grade IV side effect. Fatigue was most common, at 85 percent. Diarrhoea and constipation each reached 74 percent. Rates were much alike across cancers and side effects. Older patients reported side effects less often. The study gives Australian decision makers real-world rates.
europmc-pmc5660143:
Maass and co-authors present a resource study in Journal of Molecular Medicine. It maps circular RNAs across human tissues of clinical interest. Twenty tissue and cell types were profiled. Samples ranged from artery cells and heart atrium to brain cortex. Blood cells, placenta, and stem cell samples were included. Circular RNAs form by head-to-tail splicing and resist decay.

Expression proved highly specific to each tissue. Many circular RNAs outnumbered their linear host transcripts. The team validated 71 circular RNAs from the catalog. Some look like candidate biomarkers. Samples from two immune deficiency diseases showed altered expression. The affected genes fit the known disease mechanisms. The authors stress testing circular RNAs in disease research.
europmc-pmc5702643:
Thair and co-authors wrote a beginner's guide to transcranial direct current stimulation. The guide appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. The method passes weak current through the scalp. It can raise or lower cortical excitability. Results between studies often disagree. Polarity effects prove hard to reproduce.

The guide explains what the method is used for. It walks through how to run it safely. Design choices get practical coverage. Electrode placement and current settings matter. So do session length and control conditions. The authors survey varied approaches and outcomes. Their aim is to help new researchers plan sound studies. Better design may cut the confusion in results.
europmc-pmc5748643:
Nazzaro and co-authors review essential oils as agents against fungi. Plants make these oils to guard against attack in nature. Folk medicine and food science have used them for ages. The brief review centers on how the oils act on fungal cells.

The oils can block the talk between fungal cells that builds biofilms. They can also cut the making of fungal toxins. The authors describe the main modes of action of the oils and their parts. Rising resistance to synthetic drugs adds weight to the search, they note. Food keeping and human health uses are both covered.
europmc-pmc5769543:
Shan and co-authors build yearly carbon dioxide accounts for China from 1997 to 2015. China is the world's top energy user and emitter, yet it had no official yearly series. Published estimates differed by a gap as large as a major country's yearly output. A shared account was needed for policy.

The team follows the IPCC accounting method within China's borders. The accounts cover energy emissions from 17 fossil fuels across 47 sectors. They also cover process emissions from cement making. Inventories are given for the nation and for 30 provinces in one uniform format. The dataset will be updated each year.
europmc-pmc5780443:
Grundmann and co-authors test whether arrestins can signal without any working G proteins. A long held view says GPCR receptors can signal through beta-arrestin alone. The team built human cells stripped of whole G protein families by gene editing. Partner cells lacking both beta-arrestins served as the mirror test.

Across many receptors, arrestin still arrived and receptors still entered the cell at zero G. Yet ERK activation and whole cell responses failed completely, they report. The result reshapes how these receptors are thought to work. In particular, it reframes how they switch on ERK signaling.
europmc-pmc5820343:
Zimeo Morais and co-authors present fOLD, a toolbox for placing fNIRS sensors. fNIRS shines near-infrared light through the scalp to track brain work. It is portable, cheap, and tolerant of movement. Each study can place only a few light probes, though.

Probe spots must match the brain areas under study. Guessing that match is a common design headache. The toolbox runs photon travel simulations on two head atlases. It then picks the predefined spots with the best aim. The free tool borrows mapping advances from MRI research. Readers get a practical way to design sharper fNIRS experiments.
europmc-pmc5833343:
Denisenko, Budkevich, and Zhivotovsky review treatments that kill lung adenocarcinoma by forcing cell death. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. This cancer is the commonest form of lung cancer. It is often found late and resists standard chemo and radiation.

The authors map the driver mutations behind it, such as KRAS, EGFR, and ALK fusions. They then survey targeted drugs built on those faults. A full section weighs how each therapy triggers cell death. Resistance is the thread throughout. Combined attacks on several pathways, they argue, beat single-drug strikes.
europmc-pmc5841843:
Lawlor, Tilling, and Davey Smith set out triangulation, a way to firm up causal claims in epidemiology. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Epidemiology. Random trials often cannot test what habits or exposures do over decades. Single observational designs carry known blind spots.

Triangulation combines several approaches on one question. Each approach must fail in a different way. When their answers still agree, confidence grows. The authors ask researchers to state each bias direction up front. Three worked examples show the method in action. Mismatches, too, teach where new studies are needed.
europmc-pmc5887043:
Henriksen and co-authors survey fitness trackers and smartwatches for research use. Their article appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. New wrist devices reach the market every year. They differ in sensors, algorithms, and apps. The team searched six device databases for wrist wearables. They mapped 423 devices from 132 brands, from 2011 to 2017. Only devices with accelerometers were counted in the survey.

Nearly half of brands released a single device. Sensor support grew each year of the window. Heart rate sensors were the commonest extra feature. Fitbit, Garmin, Misfit, Apple, and Polar led research use. The team also checked developer access to health data. Fitbit appeared in twice as many validation studies as rivals.
europmc-pmc5895643:
Srivastava and co-authors review T cells in osteoporosis, a field they call immunoporosis. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Osteoporosis affects more than 200 million people worldwide. Immune cells are now known to shape bone health. Helper T cells rank among the major players. Activated T cells release cytokines that tune bone remodelling. The review sorts out each T cell subset in turn.

Subsets covered include Th1, Th2, Th9, and Th17 cells. Regulatory, follicular helper, and killer T cells also feature. Each subset's role in bone loss is weighed. Earlier reviews stressed inflammation in broad terms. This one pins down subset-by-subset effects. New prevention and treatment ideas follow from that map.
europmc-pmc5949843:
Lewis and co-authors argue that implementation science must move from classification to causal models. Their perspective piece appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. The field knows little about how implementation strategies work. Better outcomes need precise, testable theories of change. The authors set out a four-step approach. It builds causal pathway models for a given strategy.

First, the strategy must be specified by its core component. Next, links from strategy to mechanism must be drawn. Proximal and distal outcomes then need naming. Effect modifiers show where and when a strategy works. The piece also calls for stronger measures of mechanisms. Precise terms and better evidence curation close the agenda.
europmc-pmc5956843:
Bokulich and co-authors optimise taxonomic classification of marker-gene sequences with a QIIME 2 plugin. Their methods paper appeared in Microbiome. Naming microbes from short gene reads is a core step in microbiome work. The plugin, q2-feature-classifier, offers machine-learning and alignment-based tools. The team compared old QIIME 1 methods with new QIIME 2 ones. Targets were bacterial 16S rRNA and fungal ITS sequences.

The new naive Bayes, BLAST+, and VSEARCH classifiers matched or beat rivals, they report. Tests used 19 mock communities and error-free simulations. Simulated novel sequences were included too. Parameter tuning proved vital for good results. The authors give settings for a range of common conditions.
europmc-pmc5980143:
Li and co-authors overview antibacterial hydrogels, from structures to clinical prospects. Their review appeared in Advanced Science. Hydrogels are three-dimensional polymer networks that hold much water. Antibacterial versions are a main focus in biomaterials research. They offer high oxygen permeability and good biocompatibility. Drugs load into them and release with ease. Their structures can be varied in many ways.

The review covers how these gels are built and how they act. Loading and release behaviour gets close attention. Uses across biomedical research are surveyed in depth. The authors close with prospects for clinical use. Such gels may help where resistant bacteria defeat antibiotics.
europmc-pmc6028743:
Hanlon and co-authors measure frailty in middle-aged and older adults. Their study appeared in The Lancet Public Health. It drew on 493,737 UK Biobank participants aged 37 to 73. Frailty was scored from weight loss, exhaustion, grip strength, activity level, and walking pace.

About 3 percent of participants met the frailty mark. Another 38 percent counted as pre-frail. Frailty clustered with multiple long-term conditions and deprivation. Multiple sclerosis and chronic fatigue syndrome linked to it most strongly. Frail and pre-frail people died at higher rates in nearly every age group. That held after adjusting for condition counts and lifestyle. The authors urge care to target middle-aged patients with complex needs.
europmc-pmc6066743:
Dearden and co-authors review sex differences in how early life shapes metabolism. Their review appeared in Molecular Metabolism. Conditions in the womb and newborn period set later disease risk. Too little or too much nutrition both raise the odds. Obesity, diabetes, and heart disease follow from that programming.

The effects land differently on males and females. Females exposed to undernutrition gained more fat as adults. High sugar settings disturbed female glucose control most. The male placenta proved most open to damage. The review weighs candidate mechanisms for these gaps. It also covers intervention studies in animal models. Readers get a plea to study both sexes in early-life research.
europmc-pmc6111543:
Barratt and co-authors wrote an overview in Journal of Clinical Medicine on idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lung disease marked by steady scarring. The scarring pattern is called usual interstitial pneumonia. Damage to the lung's air sac cells is thought to start the process. Cases are rising worldwide.

The overview covers how the disease is diagnosed, which takes a team effort and ruling out other lung diseases. It also covers the burden the disease places on patients and health systems. Two antifibrotic drugs, pirfenidone and nintedanib, now give many patients a treatment option. More drugs are in early trials. The authors point to biomarkers that may one day guide care tailored to each patient.
europmc-pmc6162343:
Mendel and co-authors present a research article in Molecular Cell on METTL16, an enzyme that marks RNA. The mark, called m6A, controls how genes are expressed. A known enzyme pair adds it to loose RNA strands. What the second writer, METTL16, targets was unknown.

The team solved the human enzyme's crystal structure. A deep groove lets it grip folded RNA where the target base sits in a bulge. In mouse embryos, removing Mettl16 lowered levels of its target, the Mat2a message. Embryos lacking the gene could not develop normally. The study shows structured RNA marking is essential for early life.
europmc-pmc6163243:
Geerlings and co-authors wrote a review in Microorganisms on Akkermansia muciniphila, a gut bacterium that eats mucin. It lives in the mucus layer of the large intestine and helps keep the gut wall intact. Low levels of it track with several disease states. The title asks when, where, and how it colonizes us.

Using gene sequences and metagenomic data, the team tracked its presence across the body. Signs of it appear in the colon within weeks of birth and likely persist for life. Related sequences also turned up in human milk, the mouth, and other sites. The review assembles a colonization map for a microbe of growing medical interest.
europmc-pmc6202443:
The GBD 2016 Lower Respiratory Infections Collaborators measured lung infection deaths world-wide. The group covers pneumonia and bronchiolitis in 195 countries. Their study spans 1990 to 2016. It was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. It gives counts by age, sex, place, and cause.

The group used three model types for deaths and cases. They report about 2.38 million deaths from these infections in 2016. About 653,000 were in children under five. Streptococcus pneumoniae caused more deaths than all other causes combined. Child wasting was the top risk for young deaths. The authors say cleaner air and more antibiotics could cut the toll.
europmc-pmc6273543:
Du and Shim review a cell change that helps cancers resist drugs. Their review appeared in Molecules. The change is called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or EMT. Cells that switch gain traits like cancer stem cells. They pump drugs out faster and resist death signals. That shift has become a key cause of treatment failure.

Many signalling pathways feed the switch. The review maps how each pathway supports drug resistance. It also gathers new work on blocking the switch. Targeting EMT could restore drug sensitivity in resistant tumours. The authors note debate over EMT's role in spread itself. Its role in resistance is now much firmer. The review gives researchers a map of pathways to target. It also warns that blocking one path may not be enough.
europmc-pmc6329843:
Lee and co-authors pin a brain immune sensor to neuron loss in a Parkinson's model. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. Parkinson's disease kills dopamine neurons in a midbrain region. Brain inflammation likely helps drive that loss. The team used MPTP, a toxin that mimics the disease in mice. They focused on the NLRP3 inflammasome in microglia.

Mice lacking NLRP3 fared far better after the toxin. They kept more dopamine neurons and moved more normally. The toxin also failed to summon microglia without NLRP3. Key inflammatory signals, IL-1 beta and caspase-1, stayed off. In cell cultures, mitochondrial reactive oxygen drove the sensor. Blocking this pathway may slow Parkinson's damage, the authors suggest.
europmc-pmc6332843:
Jiang and co-authors review how tumors use the PD-1 pathway to escape immunity. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. PD-1 is a brake on T cells, the immune attackers. Its partner, PD-L1, sits on tumor and nearby cells. When they engage, T cell attack is blunted. Drugs blocking this pair have changed cancer care.

Yet many patients gain little from those drugs. The review explains why responses stay weak. It maps what drives PD-L1 levels in the tumor setting. Signals from immune cells, genes, and stress all play in. The surrounding tissue shapes the pathway at every step. Understanding that web may sharpen drug use. It may also suggest pairs of drugs that work better together.
europmc-pmc6347843:
Hussain and co-authors review cholesterol and sphingolipids in the brain. Their review appeared in Lipids in Health and Disease. The brain is rich in these two lipid classes. They form much of the myelin wrapping nerve fibers. They also sit in membrane rafts, signaling hubs on cells. There they help run cell communication.

Both lipids guide neuron growth and synapse building. Steady supply and active turnover keep nerves healthy. Faults in their handling feed neurological diseases. The review covers their roles in brain development. It also covers disease links across the lifespan. Membrane rafts get special attention as shared ground. The authors stress balance: too little or misplaced lipid harms signaling.
europmc-pmc6351943:
Barbieri and co-authors review biogenic amine production by lactic acid bacteria. Their review appeared in Foods. Lactic bacteria ferment many foods and drinks. Some strains turn amino acids into biogenic amines. Those compounds can sicken sensitive people. Headache, palpitations, vomiting, and diarrhea are known effects.

The review details which bacteria make these amines. It covers starter cultures added on purpose. It also covers wild strains from ripening and spontaneous ferments. Groups range from lactobacilli to enterococci and oenococci. The enzymes and genes behind production are explained. Conditions that raise or lower amine levels get attention. The authors aim to help makers keep foods tasty yet safe. Foreknowledge lets producers pick safer starter strains.
europmc-pmc6384243:
Lewis and co-authors report a cohort study in The Lancet Psychiatry on trauma in young people. They used a birth cohort of 2,232 children born in England and Wales in 1994-95. At age eighteen, each person was asked in detail about trauma and its effects.

The study measured how common trauma exposure and post-traumatic stress disorder were. It also mapped the signs of the disorder and the risks that raised its odds. Such base rates in youth have been poorly known, the authors note. Their results give services a firmer base for planning youth trauma care.
europmc-pmc6405943:
Dashti and co-authors report a genome-wide study in Nature Communications on sleep length. Why people habitually sleep long or short is poorly understood. The team searched DNA from 446,118 adults in UK Biobank for sites tied to self-reported sleep duration.

They found seventy-eight such loci, forty-three of them with very strong support. Results repeated in a second cohort for several loci. Watch-based measures in 85,499 people backed the self reports. The loci also linked to daytime rest and sleep quality. The authors offer the map as a start for finding the biology that sets sleep length.
europmc-pmc6417243:
Volarevic and co-authors review cisplatin kidney damage in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Cisplatin is among the most effective cancer drugs, but it harms the kidneys. The drug builds up in kidney tissue and changes form there.

Hydration, magnesium, and forced urine flow are the current guards against that harm. Each has limits, and mannitol can cause excess urine loss and dehydration. The review maps how cisplatin injures kidney cells step by step. It also weighs drugs that might protect kidneys without shielding the tumor. Balancing those two goals is the core problem.
europmc-pmc6472943:
Cassetta and co-authors map gene activity in the macrophages and blood monocytes of breast and endometrial cancer, showing that cancer retrains both, body-wide and on the spot. Profiles of the macrophages inside tumors differed from blood monocytes and from the resident cells of the matching healthy tissue.

A gene signature from breast tumor macrophages sat mostly in harsh subtypes and predicted shorter survival in public tumor data. The team also caught a self-feeding loop: tumor cells and macrophages trade TNF-α, CCL8, and CSF1 signals, raising SIGLEC1 and pulling in more monocytes. SIGLEC1 plus CCL8 together marked a poor outlook on their own, marking the loop as a target worth attacking.
europmc-pmc6479943:
Baglieri and co-authors review how liver fibrosis and the fibroblasts it breeds prepare the ground for hepatocellular carcinoma, among the most aggressive cancers, with five-year survival under 12 percent. Most cases grow out of chronic injury, from hepatitis viruses, alcohol, or fatty liver, and scarring is the common soil.

Hepatic stellate cells wake into matrix-producing myofibroblasts during fibrogenesis and likely give rise to cancer-associated fibroblasts inside tumors. Those fibroblasts stiffen the matrix, secrete growth and angiogenic factors, blind immune surveillance, and push cancer cells toward invasion. Mapping each contribution matters because the premalignant environment forms years before any tumor, a long window for interception.
europmc-pmc6570943:
Giaimo and co-authors review the histone variant H2A.Z and its grip on gene activity, writing in Epigenetics and Chromatin. DNA spools around histone proteins, and swapping the standard H2A for this variant changes how a stretch of genome behaves. H2A.Z turns up at promoters and enhancers across species, and mice cannot develop without it.

The puzzle the review works through is its double life: H2A.Z can help switch genes on or keep them off. The resolution lies in its chemical marks and partners — acetylation favors activation, ubiquitin tags favor repression — and in machinery that loads and evicts it on demand. The authors describe a buffering role, holding genes poised for rapid, measured response, and close with its misbehavior in cancer.
europmc-pmc6582343:
Meng, Li, Yang and Liu present MitoZ, a one-stop toolkit for animal mitochondrial genomes, writing in Nucleic Acids Research. Mitochondrial DNA anchors studies of evolution, ecology and species identification, but building a finished mitogenome from raw sequencing reads usually means chaining several separate programs, each with its own quirks.

MitoZ links the steps into independent modules: de novo assembly, a scaffold finder that fishes out mitochondrial pieces, annotation, and visualization. Feed it raw reads and it returns an assembled, annotated, drawn mitogenome. The authors benchmarked it on 50 samples whose mitogenomes were already public. MitoZ recovered more complete genomes, and with higher accuracy, than the available rival assemblers. The software is free and open source.
europmc-pmc6618043:
Gabelica and co-authors offer a guide to reporting ion mobility mass spectrometry. Their recommendations appear in Mass Spectrometry Reviews. The method drifts ions through gas under an electric field. It adds a separation step ahead of mass measurement. Instruments from rival makers work on different principles, which can confuse readers.

The guide explains what is measured and how results should be reported. Mobility values hinge on ion structure, gas, temperature, and field strength. Collision cross sections come from mobility through a physical model, not direct reading. Calibration-based methods can give method-dependent values. The authors stress reporting uncertainties for both quantities. They also urge the field to build primary standards and reference materials. Clear reports, they argue, let others reuse data with confidence.
europmc-pmc6618143:
Viola and co-authors review the metabolic wiring of macrophage responses. Their article appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Macrophages patrol tissues, eat debris, and steer immune reactions. They shift shape and duties with local signals. Two poles frame the range: inflammatory M1 and resolving M2.

Each pole runs on a distinct fuel plan. M1 cells lean on glycolysis, with two breaks in their TCA cycle. Those breaks pile up itaconate and succinate. Succinate steadies HIF1α, which keeps glycolytic genes switched on. M2 cells favor oxidative phosphorylation with an intact cycle. Lipid and amino acid routes also differ by pole. The authors argue that these fuel choices drive what macrophages do.
europmc-pmc6631643:
Yin and co-authors trace a message that helps pancreatic cancer spread. Their research article appears in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma kills most patients soon after diagnosis. Tumor-linked macrophages gather inside its tissue and track with metastasis. Their tiny exosomes can carry regulatory microRNAs to cancer cells.

The team found miR-501-3p raised in tumor tissue and macrophage exosomes. Exosomes from M2 macrophages sped cancer cell migration and invasion. They also boosted tumor growth and spread in nude mice. The microRNA targets TGFBR3, a tumor suppressor gene. Silencing it switched on TGF-β signaling. Blocking the exosomal microRNA slowed tumor formation and metastasis in mice. The authors propose the pathway as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6723943:
Hernández and co-authors review acetate, a short-chain fatty acid made by gut microbes. Gut microbes ferment fiber and release these fatty acids. Acetate is the most common one in the colon and the blood. It may help control body weight and blood sugar.

In animals and humans, acetate triggers gut hormones that curb appetite. It also lowers fat breakdown, calms inflammation, and raises energy use and fat burning. The review compares ways to raise acetate: vinegar, direct infusions, fermentable fiber, and probiotics. Human data remain scarce, the authors note. Still, these routes are being tested hard against obesity and its complications.
europmc-pmc6742443:
Kozik and co-authors challenge the standard picture of plant mitochondrial DNA. Textbooks draw these genomes as single rings. Yet plant researchers have long known the real molecules take many forms. Repeats in the DNA let it recombine into alternate arrangements, called isoforms. Older assembly methods missed most of that variety.

The team used long-read and short-read sequencing to assemble mitochondrial genomes of farmed and wild lettuce. Each species held a complex set of isoforms. Microscope images of the DNA showed linear, branched, and circular forms side by side. Comparing species showed how these structures evolve. One ring, the authors argue, does not rule them all.
europmc-pmc6779243:
Smith and co-authors tested whether gut microbiome diversity tracks with sleep in humans. Signals along the brain-gut axis can sway health, and sleep quality may be one target. Past sleep deprivation studies disagreed with each other. This team used wrist actigraphy to measure sleep objectively. They sampled gut microbes alongside immune markers and behavior tests.

Total microbiome diversity rose with sleep efficiency and total sleep time. It fell as wake time after sleep onset grew. Diversity also correlated with interleukin-6, an immune signal known to affect sleep. Specific bacterial groups added detail to the pattern. The work supports a real, if still murky, link between gut communities and how people sleep.
europmc-pmc6799843:
Wang and Xu review targeted treatment options for HER2-positive breast cancer. HER2 is a growth receptor overexpressed in 20 to 25% of breast cancers worldwide. Over two decades, anti-HER2 drugs transformed care for this subtype. Four agents anchor current practice: trastuzumab, pertuzumab, lapatinib, and the antibody-drug conjugate T-DM1. The review gathers the key trials behind them.

Studies before surgery, after surgery, and in metastatic disease are all covered. Promising strategies get critical attention rather than hype. Vaccine approaches aim to raise anti-HER2 immunity, and early trials showed strong T cell responses in immunized patients. Ongoing trials are listed for readers tracking what comes next. The authors frame the evidence for everyday clinical decisions.
europmc-pmc6872443:
Prior and co-authors review liver organoids in Gut. Organoids are miniature tissues grown in a dish from stem cells. Mouse models and flat cell lines have taught much about the liver, yet each misses parts of human liver function, above all its layered structure and chemistry. Organoids promise a closer copy.

They can now be grown from several starting materials, including adult liver tissue and reprogrammed stem cells, and in multiple species. The review traces what these cultures have revealed about liver development and disease. Tumour organoids keep a patient's drug responses, hinting at personalised testing. Limits remain in maturity and in missing cell types, which the authors set out plainly.
europmc-pmc7005843:
Garber and co-authors present FeGenie, a tool that finds iron genes in genome data. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Iron feeds nearly all life, serving as fuel, waste sink, and working part of core processes. Yet in oxygen-rich settings it rusts and drops out of reach, so microbes fight over it.

Sequencing now floods researchers with environmental genomes, but standard annotation misses iron genes, especially those for iron oxidation and reduction. FeGenie pairs a broad library of gene profiles with software that scans genome and metagenome assemblies and maps iron gene neighbourhoods. It was checked against 28 isolate genomes and applied to 27 metagenomes plus oral biofilm and candidate-phylum genomes. Results were accurate and showed how iron toolkits differ by environment. The aim is linking lab knowledge of model microbes to wild communities.
europmc-pmc7019743:
Głąbska and co-authors present a systematic review in the journal Nutrients. They ask whether eating more fruit and vegetables is linked to better mental health in adults. Most work in this area studies whole diets. Their review isolates these two food groups instead.

The team searched PubMed and Web of Science for observational studies published up to June 2019. After screening 5,911 records, they kept 61 studies. Most dealt with depression or depressive symptoms. Others covered mood, stress, anxiety, sleep, and life satisfaction. The authors report that higher intake was mostly linked to better outcomes. Berries, citrus fruit, and leafy greens stood out. They also warn that the studies used varied methods, which limits firm conclusions.
europmc-pmc7077443:
Hoang Thi and co-authors argue for alternatives to polyethylene glycol in the journal Polymers. PEG is the gold standard coating in drug delivery and bioconjugation. Attaching it to proteins, nucleic acids, and nanoparticles, a process called PEGylation, stretches the time a drug stays in blood and improves efficacy. Such products have served clinics for decades. A problem has surfaced: the immune system can learn to attack PEG itself.

Some patients form anti-PEG antibodies after treatment with PEGylated drugs. Others carry them from everyday products that contain PEG, without ever receiving such a drug. For those people, treatment can mean fast clearance of the drug, weak effect, hypersensitivity, and at times life-threatening reactions. The review collates recent literature to alert polymer chemists, then discusses several promising but imperfect replacement polymers. The authors call for joint work between chemists and biomedical scientists to build a satisfactory substitute.
europmc-pmc7090843:
Lai and co-authors surveyed mental health among Chinese health care workers treating COVID-19 patients, in JAMA Network Open. Their cross-sectional study covered 1,257 workers in 34 hospitals with fever clinics or COVID-19 wards. Standard questionnaires measured depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress.

A large share of workers reported symptoms on all four measures. Women and nurses were hit harder than other groups. Staff in Wuhan, the outbreak's centre, fared worse than those elsewhere in Hubei or outside it. Front-line workers who diagnosed, treated, or nursed infected patients carried the highest risk. The authors argue these groups need psychological support or intervention during such outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7094943:
Wu and co-authors report a new coronavirus found in a patient in Wuhan, China, in Nature. The patient was a 41-year-old market worker admitted to hospital in late December 2019. He had fever, cough, chest tightness, and weakness.

The team sequenced RNA from fluid washed from his lungs. They found a new virus, first named WH-Human 1 coronavirus. Its full genome ran to 29,903 nucleotides. The virus was closest to SARS-like coronaviruses found before in bats in China. The authors present the case as a warning that animal viruses can still spill over into people and cause severe lung disease.
europmc-pmc7105343:
Russell and co-authors systematically reviewed whether immune-suppressing and immune-stimulating drugs change COVID-19 risk or outcomes, in ecancermedicalscience. Cancer and transplant patients face hard choices, since their treatments alter immunity. The team searched the medical literature for evidence on drug classes from chemotherapy to cytokine blockers.

Eighty-nine studies were included. For most drug classes, the review found no conclusive evidence of help or harm in COVID-19. Low-dose prednisolone and tacrolimus might bring benefits, the authors suggest. Tumour necrosis factor blockade showed no sign of harm. The honest bottom line is how thin the early evidence was, a warning against stopping vital immune treatments out of fear alone.
europmc-pmc7137343:
Zheng and co-authors show that a circular RNA called circSEPT9 helps drive triple-negative breast cancer, in Molecular Cancer. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped molecules increasingly tied to cancer growth. The team compared tumor tissue with nearby normal tissue from four patients and screened for changed circular RNAs.

CircSEPT9 was raised in tumors, and higher levels tracked with later stage and worse survival in two patient groups. Lowering it in cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion while raising cell death, and shrank tumors in animals. Two factors, E2F1 and EIF4A3, control its production. It works partly by soaking up a small RNA, miR-637, freeing a leukemia-related gene. The authors flag it as a marker and target.
europmc-pmc7145543: Immune genes differ across peoples — AFND charts the variation. The Allele Frequency Net Database holds HLA and related gene frequencies worldwide. The 2020 update adds open data and better tools. Diversity, mapped for all to explore.
europmc-pmc7145643:
Malik-Sheriff and co-authors mark 15 years of BioModels, the repository for computational models in the life sciences, in Nucleic Acids Research. Founded in 2005, the archive lets researchers share mathematical models in formats such as SBML, CellML, MATLAB, and Python. Curators check each model reproduces its paper's results.

The collection now hosts about 2,000 models from the published literature, roughly 800 of them fully curated and annotated to community standards. The authors say it is the world's largest curated model repository. Large batches of automatically generated models are now accepted too. The paper argues that checked, standard-format models are what make published simulations reusable rather than decorative.
europmc-pmc7178943:
Shao and co-authors surveyed medical students in China about depression and anxiety. Their study appeared in BMC Psychology. The team questioned 2,057 students at a medical college in Chongqing. Students filled in scales for depression and anxiety. They also rated family function, social support, and coping style. The aim was to map how common these symptoms are. The team also tested which life factors track with them.

The authors report that 57.5 percent of students showed depression symptoms. About 30.8 percent showed anxiety symptoms. Older students reported worse scores than younger ones. Heavy money strain, study stress, and poor sleep also tracked with worse scores. Students living alone reported more symptoms as well. Both symptom types tied closely to family function and social support. Coping style mattered too. The authors urge colleges to offer counseling and support.
europmc-pmc7222643:
Wynants and co-authors review and grade the flood of prediction models built for COVID-19. Their article appeared in The BMJ. Models promised to diagnose infection, forecast patient outcomes, or flag high-risk people. The team ran a living systematic review of papers and preprints. Sources were searched up to April 7, 2020, and the review was designed to update as new models appeared.

Two reviewers independently extracted each model's details. The appraisal checked how models were built and validated. Outcome definitions varied widely between studies, complicating comparisons. A model tuned in one hospital may misfire in another with different case mixes. The authors warn against rushing unproven models into care. Their work became a reference point for judging pandemic prediction tools.
europmc-pmc7230343:
Galanakis examines food systems under the strain of the COVID-19 pandemic. The article appeared in Foods. One third of the world's population was under lockdown when it was written. The article first reviews food and herb ingredients that may support the immune system. It then asks whether the virus can travel through the food chain.

Markets selling live animals pose monitoring problems, the article notes. Bats form a vast reservoir of SARS-like viruses, a risk flagged years earlier. Lockdowns also threatened food security for millions of people. Supply chains built for efficiency proved fragile under stress. The author argues for more sustainable food systems. Stronger, cleaner chains could prevent or soften the next food and health crisis.
europmc-pmc7267243:
Koehler and co-authors warn that severe COVID-19 can be followed by a fungal lung infection called aspergillosis. Their chart review appeared in Mycoses. Patients with viral lung failure are known to risk this secondary infection, as seen with influenza. The team reviewed cases at the University Hospital of Cologne in Germany.

Among 19 consecutive critically ill patients with moderate to severe COVID-19 lung failure, five had invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. That is a high share for patients without classic immune suppression. The fungus Aspergillus can invade lung tissue already damaged by the virus. The authors urge doctors treating such patients to test respiratory samples thoroughly for fungal co-infection, so antifungal treatment is not delayed.
europmc-pmc7322843:
Xie and co-authors trace how a circular RNA shipped between cells drives gastric cancer progression. Their study appeared in Molecular Cancer. The molecule, circSHKBP1, was increased in tumor tissue and blood, and higher levels tracked with advanced stage and poor survival. Its level in blood exosomes fell significantly after the tumor was surgically removed.

Boosting the molecule made cancer cells grow, migrate, invade, and sprout blood vessels faster, in dishes and in mice; suppressing it did the opposite. It works two ways: soaking up a small RNA to raise a factor that stabilizes the VEGF growth message, and binding the chaperone HSP90 to shield it from destruction. Exosomes carrying it also push neighboring cells to grow, spreading the tumor's influence beyond its own cells.
europmc-pmc7369943:
Gualano and co-authors survey mental health in Italy during the national COVID-19 lockdown, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Italy was the first European country to lock down nationwide. The survey ran in the lockdown's last 14 days and drew 1,515 participants.

Symptoms of depression appeared in 24.7 percent of respondents and anxiety symptoms in 23.2 percent. Sleep disturbances affected 42.2 percent, and among them 17.4 percent had moderate to severe insomnia. Being female, spending more time online, and avoiding activities under peer pressure raised the odds of problems. Older age, marriage, and freedom from work troubles lowered them. Readers get a national snapshot of the psychological bill for a pioneering lockdown.
europmc-pmc7381543:
Liu and co-authors review memory T cells in Protein and Cell, with an eye on cancer immunotherapy. Memory cells are the long-lived T cells that remember past targets. Two kinds, stem cell memory and central memory, persist longer and fight tumors better than short-lived effector cells in several studies.

The ratio of central memory to effector cells may even predict responses in some tumors. The review explains where memory cells come from and how they form, including a role for gut microbes. It then gathers practical strategies for growing memory-rich cells outside the body for treatment. Readers get a guide to making cell therapies last, not just strike.
europmc-pmc7407943:
Yadati and co-authors review cathepsins in Cells, the most abundant enzymes of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. Inside that acidic space they digest proteins and support energy metabolism and immunity. The surprise of recent decades is that they also escape and stay active outside.

Outside the lysosome, in the cytosol and beyond the cell, cathepsins take on versatile new roles. In disease states they are strongly upregulated, with links to cancer and cardiovascular disease. That differential makes them candidates for diagnostic markers and drug targets, and selective inhibitors are emerging. New proteomic methods for finding their natural substrates promise to clarify how they act. Readers get the ins and outs promised in the title.
europmc-pmc7466243:
Jimenez-Lopez and co-authors review bioactive compounds and quality in extra virgin olive oil. This oil anchors the Mediterranean diet and many of its health gains. Strict rules earn it the extra virgin title.

The oil must come from mechanical pressing alone. Its free acidity cannot pass 0.8 percent of the oil weight under the rules for this grade of oil. It must show no sensory flaws and hold a fruity taste. Its chief compounds are unsaturated fatty acids, led by oleic acid. Minor parts, such as tocopherols and phenols, act as natural antioxidants. These give heart, anti-inflammatory, and gut benefits. Light, heat, oxygen, and pack choice can spoil quality in storage, so care extends shelf life.
europmc-pmc7501843:
Xia and co-authors map how SARS-CoV-2 evades type I interferon, the cell's early antiviral alarm. Viral growth and host response together shape COVID-19. Work on the virus's evasion tools was lacking.

An unbiased screen found three proteins that block interferon production, each by a distinct trick. Nsp6 binds the kinase TBK1 and mutes a key activation step. Nsp13 binds TBK1 and blocks its own activation mark. ORF6 binds an import protein and stops IRF3 from entering the nucleus. Two more protein sets block interferon signaling at STAT1 and STAT2. Nsp1 and nsp6 from this virus beat their SARS and MERS kin at suppression. Test replicons with those swaps grew better under interferon.
europmc-pmc7598943:
Liu and co-authors present CONSORT-AI, a reporting guideline for trials of AI health tools. The CONSORT statement sets minimum reporting rules for trials. AI interventions need added detail for fair judgment.

The extension was built through a staged consensus process. A Delphi survey drew 103 stakeholders from many fields. A consensus meeting had 31 stakeholders present. A checklist pilot involved 34 participants in refinement. The extension adds 14 new reporting items. Reports should describe the AI tool and its setting. Inputs, outputs and human interaction must be clear. Error cases need analysis in trial reports. The aim is fuller and clearer reporting for AI trials.
europmc-pmc7692443:
Stojanov and co-authors review how probiotics shift a key gut microbe ratio in two conditions. The ratio compares two large bacterial groups, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes. A high ratio tends to come with obesity. A low ratio tends to come with inflammatory bowel disease. Balance in this ratio supports gut health.

Probiotics are live microbes that can restore a skewed gut mix. Their effect on the ratio varies by strain, so the choice of species matters. Strains of Lactobacillus are the most tested for this aim. The review weighs which products led to weight loss or to calmer gut inflammation in past studies.
europmc-pmc7732843:
Dai and co-authors show how iron-driven cell death can help start pancreatic cancer. The death type is ferroptosis, which relies on iron and oxidative damage. The team fed mice high-iron diets or removed a guard enzyme, Gpx4, in the pancreas. Models included inflamed pancreas and a Kras-driven cancer model.

Both tricks raised release of a DNA damage mark, 8-OHG. That mark fired a DNA sensor path tied to the protein STING. Macrophages poured in and switched on, aiding tumor growth. Blocking ferroptosis, removing macrophages, or cutting the sensor path all curbed tumor forming. GPX4 levels also mark outlook in patients.
europmc-pmc7749743:
Zhang and co-authors review mutant p53, a warped form of a famous tumor guard. The p53 gene is mutated in more than 50% of human cancers. Most changes swap a single amino acid. The mutant protein loses its guard role and gains new, cancer-driving powers of its own.

Mutant p53 piles up to high levels in cancer cells, which its new powers need. The review sets out how this buildup is controlled. It then lists the gain-of-function tricks the mutant performs, from growth signals to spread. Last, it surveys drugs that aim to remove or refold the mutant. The authors see it as a prime target for tailored cancer care.
europmc-pmc7796143:
Meng and co-authors review the anti-inflammatory action of resveratrol. Resveratrol is a natural polyphenol found in plants. It shows antioxidant and anti-cancer effects in lab work. The body absorbs it well but breaks it down fast.

Inflammation is a normal defense response. Germs and tissue injury can both trigger it. Harm comes when it runs too long or too strong. The authors examine how resveratrol calms that response. They gather lab and animal studies on its control routes. Its immune-tuning effects are discussed in depth. The data set out both promise and limits for this compound.
europmc-pmc7815643:
Dumanović and co-authors give a concise overview of reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defenses in plants. Reactive species can harm plant cells. A layered defense network keeps them in check. The network holds the cell in balance.

Enzymes of the glutathione-ascorbate cycle lead the defense. Phenolic compounds and fat-soluble antioxidants back them up. Carotenoids and tocopherols are in that second group. Plant cells can survive hydrogen peroxide levels that would kill animal cells. Defense parts cooperate and recycle each other into active forms. The authors also note human uses of plant antioxidants. These span anti-aging products, food protection, and new drug ideas.
europmc-pmc7817643:
Alquezar and co-authors review how chemical edits reshape the tau protein in health and disease. Tau is best known for tangles in Alzheimer's disease. Edits added after the protein is built change its work. The long-standing view blames excess phosphorylation for tau pile-up.

The authors question that simple story. Phosphorylation may be part of tau's normal life and disposal. Many other edits occur too. These include acetylation, ubiquitination, and methylation. Sugar-based edits and oxidation also feature. Each edit can shift where tau sits and what it binds. Edits can also change how fast tau is cleared. The review argues that cells choose edit patterns on purpose.
europmc-pmc7853543:
Kugeler and co-authors estimate how often Lyme disease is diagnosed in the United States. Reported case counts miss many treated patients. The team turned to commercial insurance claims. The window covered 2010 to 2018.

Claims suggest Lyme disease was diagnosed and treated in about 476,000 patients a year. That figure far exceeds the reported case tally. The gap points to wide testing and treatment in practice. It also raises questions about test accuracy. The authors stress the need for sharper diagnosis. Better prevention of tick bites matters as well. Their count gives health agencies a fuller sense of the burden.
europmc-pmc7859843:
Tesoriero and co-authors compare COVID-19 outcomes for New Yorkers with and without HIV. State databases on HIV, COVID-19 tests, and hospital stays were linked. The question was whether HIV raised risk. Diagnosis, hospital care, and death in hospital were all tracked.

People with HIV were more likely to test positive. They were hospitalized more often once sick. In-hospital deaths also ran higher. After adjusting for age and other traits, the gap shrank. Hospitalization stayed clearly higher for the HIV group, though. Death risk stayed somewhat raised as well. The authors call for priority care and vaccine access for this group.
europmc-pmc7898243:
Henschel and co-authors present a deep learning pipeline for brain scan analysis called FastSurfer. Standard tools for structural MRI are accurate but slow. They rely on heavy optimisation steps that do not scale to studies of thousands of people. The team set out to match the leading tool, FreeSurfer, at far higher speed.

Their network segments a whole brain scan into 95 classes. It blends local and global information to handle both outer and deep structures well. A new surface method then rebuilds the cortex and measures its thickness. Volume analysis takes under 1 min per scan. Surface analysis takes around 1 h. Tests on unseen datasets showed high accuracy and strong repeat reliability. The pipeline also proved sensitive to group changes seen in dementia.
europmc-pmc7982343:
Wong and co-authors report a study pinning down the part of the SARS coronavirus spike that grips its receptor. The spike drives infection of cells that carry the receptor ACE2. It is also the main target of blocking antibodies. The team cut the spike into pieces and tested which piece binds ACE2 best. A clear winner emerged from the tests.

A fragment of 193 amino acids bound ACE2 more strongly than the whole outer domain. Smaller fragments failed to bind at all. One point change in the fragment killed the binding. The winning fragment also blocked infection at a far lower dose than the full domain. The results define a self-folding receptor-binding domain. That domain is the piece vaccine and drug work must target. The paper dates from the first SARS outbreak and still frames the field.
europmc-pmc7984443:
Ankley and co-authors present a review of the ecological risks of PFAS, a large family of man-made chemicals. A few members, such as PFOS and PFOA, are known to persist, build up in bodies, and poison wildlife. For most of the family, the data needed to judge risk are missing. A workshop in August 2019 took stock of the science. This review sums up its findings.

The authors walk through the steps of risk assessment: framing the problem, exposure, and harm. They draw on regulatory work from around the world. Gaps and doubts are named at each step. Fixes include wider monitoring of wild sites. Models that predict build-up in bodies need better support. Lab and computer tests that can screen many chemicals fast are a third need. The path forward they propose is cross-disciplinary by design.
europmc-pmc8031743:
Mahmud and co-authors track post-COVID-19 syndrome in patients at a tertiary hospital in Bangladesh. Their prospective cohort study ran at Dhaka Medical College Hospital in mid-2020. Patients were followed for a month after clinical recovery. The team looked for lingering or new symptoms after the virus cleared. They also hunted for risk factors behind the syndrome.

Of 400 recruited patients, 355 were analyzed. The authors report that 46% developed post-COVID symptoms. Post-viral fatigue was the most common, present in 70% of those cases. Female patients faced a relative risk of 1.2. Severe illness at arrival also raised the odds. Fever, cough, respiratory distress, and lethargy at presentation all pointed the same way. Slow recovery and late viral clearance added further risk.
europmc-pmc8050743:
Eberly and co-authors check who actually receives SGLT2 inhibitor drugs among U.S. patients with diabetes. These drugs protect the heart and kidneys beyond lowering blood sugar. Guidelines recommend them for patients at high risk. Yet new therapies often reach some groups faster than others. The cohort study covered 934,737 patients with type 2 diabetes.

In the full cohort, only 8.7% received an SGLT2 inhibitor during the study period. Use climbed from 3.8% in 2015 to 11.9% by the end of 2019. Even patients with heart failure, artery disease, or kidney disease lagged far behind. Adjusted analyses found Black patients less likely to receive the drugs, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.83 for Black patients. Asian patients also trailed, at 0.94 in the same adjusted models. The authors frame the gap as an equity problem.
europmc-pmc8114143:
Chou and co-authors pool two global consortia to count neurologic trouble in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. The combined cohort held 3,744 patients from centers worldwide. Neurologic manifestations appeared in about 80% of them. The commonest self-reported symptoms were headache, at 37% of patients. Loss of smell or taste followed at 26% of the group. Charted signs told a heavier story.

Acute encephalopathy led the sign list at 49% of patients counted. Coma appeared in 17% and stroke in 6% of the cohort. Any captured neurologic sign or syndrome raised the risk of dying in hospital. The consortia built shared definitions so sites could pool data fairly. Earlier reports from single centers could not do that. The authors press for routine neurologic checks in COVID wards. Brain involvement, they show, is the rule rather than the exception. It also marks the patients in most danger.
europmc-pmc8252743:
Melamed and co-authors give best practice advice on fetal growth restriction for FIGO. Growth restriction means a fetus fails to reach its growth potential. Placental dysfunction is the most common cause.

Worldwide, the condition is a leading cause of stillbirth and newborn death. The guidance covers screening, diagnosis, and management in one document. Sections treat risk factors, biochemical and ultrasound markers, and growth charts. Doppler studies and delivery timing get detailed advice. Postpartum review and counselling for future pregnancies close the guide. The aim is consistent care across very different health systems.
europmc-pmc8263343:
Passweg and co-authors report the EBMT survey of blood stem cell transplantation over 30 years. Activity keeps rising across Europe and partner countries. In 2019, centres reported 48,512 transplants in 43,581 patients.

Seven hundred centres in 51 countries sent data. Allogeneic grafts made up 41% and autologous grafts 59%. Lymphoid cancers formed the largest indication group. CAR-T cell therapy jumped from 151 patients in 2017 to 1,134 in 2019. The first survey, in 1990, counted 4,234 transplants. The long view shows a field transformed in scale and kind. Thirty years of surveys give the trend its depth. The long run of years lets the reader see slow shifts in care that one year on its own would hide.
europmc-pmc8314143:
Wong and co-authors chart global gastric cancer incidence and deaths from 1980 to 2018. Stomach cancer stays among the most common cancers. It causes more than 1 million new cases worldwide.

Their cohort study covered over a million cases in the data. Overall patterns split sharply by age. Incidence rose in people younger than 40 in many countries. Sweden, the United Kingdom, and Ecuador stood among them. Older groups showed different trends. The authors urge prevention to gain priority in guidelines. Younger populations need a place in that planning. Mortality trends are charted beside the incidence picture.
europmc-pmc8494643:
Peng and co-authors chart the shape diversity of single neurons in known cell types. A neuron's dendrites and axon show what it hears and tells. That makes shape a defining trait of neuron types. Yet brain-wide data on full neuron shapes stayed thin.

The team built a pipeline of sparse labeling, whole-brain imaging, and rebuilding. They fully rebuilt 1,741 neurons from cortex, claustrum, thalamus, striatum, and other regions in mice. Eleven major projection types stood out, each with its own shape and gene identity. Wide variety sat inside each type too. Shape matched gene type at the broad level, but fine shape often broke from gene clusters.
europmc-pmc8770643:
Danaher and co-authors introduce SpatialDecon, an algorithm that counts cell types in spatial gene expression data. Mapping cell types across tissue is a central goal of spatial biology. Raw spatial data do not give cell counts directly. Their tool uses profiles from single-cell studies to infer the mix in each region.

The method rests on log-normal regression and a model of background noise. It beat classic least-squares tools in tests. The team built profile sets for 75 tissue types. They also flagged genes that suit immune counts in tumors. A lung tumor dataset with protein markers served as a benchmark. The tool pairs cell counts with rich gene data.
europmc-pmc8822843:
Dang and co-authors test whether edaravone can ease depression-like behavior in mice. Edaravone is a free radical scavenger. It is known for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. The team used a chronic social defeat stress model of depression. They ran a battery of behavior tests on the treated mice. Brain tissue came from the hippocampus and the medial prefrontal cortex.

The authors report that edaravone eased depressive and anxiety-like behavior. It also cut neuron loss, calmed microglia, and lowered oxidative stress. A signaling chain stood out: Sirt1, Nrf2, HO-1, and Gpx4 all rose. Blocking Sirt1 or Nrf2 erased the benefit. The work points to one pathway behind the drug's effect. It suggests a fresh angle on treating depression.
europmc-pmc8931543:
Oliveri surveys copper ionophores as selective weapons against cancer cells. Standard cancer drugs hit all fast-growing cells. Off-target harm follows. Copper ionophores carry copper into cells. Some preferentially kill cancer cells over normal ones. The death they trigger is called cuproptosis. Cancers often hold more copper than healthy tissue. Their growth, vessel building, and spread lean on it. That dependence may be a weakness.

The overview explains how the ionophores work. It asks why cancer cells prove more sensitive. Selectivity mechanisms are weighed one by one. Strategies to sharpen targeting follow. Better carriers and tuned chemistry both appear. Resistance and cancer stem cells are named as goals. The author keeps the tone measured. Promise is real but early. The piece maps a niche field for drug designers.
europmc-pmc8955843:
Lombardo and Kiselev analyze how liposomes are made and which factors control the result. Liposomes are tiny spheres of fat membrane around a water core. They carry drugs for medicine and diagnosis. Their makeup is friendly to the body. Cargo loading and release can be tuned. Making them at industrial scale is the hard part. Batches can prove unstable or load poorly. This article dissects the formation process itself.

Structural features and control factors come first. Conventional preparation methods follow. Downsizing and post-formation steps get full sections. Newer technologies are reviewed in turn. Drug loading methods are treated separately. Characterization tools tell makers what they actually built. A final section covers technology transfer and regulation. The authors update readers on a mature but lively craft. Stable formulation is the goal throughout.
europmc-pmc9012043:
Zhou and co-authors present LinDA, a method for finding which microbes differ in abundance between sample groups. Microbiome counts are compositional, so standard tests produce too many false positives. LinDA fits plain linear models to transformed data and then corrects the bias that composition creates. The method keeps the false discovery rate under control and extends to mixed models for linked samples.

In tests on simulated and real data, LinDA stayed accurate where rival methods slipped. Because it rests on ordinary regression, it scales to large studies and is simple to run. The authors offer it as a flexible default for a core task in microbiome analysis.
europmc-pmc9050543:
Smajić and co-authors profiled single cells from the human midbrain to map how Parkinson's disease strikes each cell type. They sequenced more than 41,000 nuclei from six patients and five matched controls. One neuron cluster stood out, marked by high CADPS2 and low dopamine machinery, and it appeared only in patient brains. Checks on dissected neurons suggest these are failing dopamine neurons.

Glial cells also changed: microglia grew in number and looked activated, while oligodendrocytes thinned out under stress. Inherited risk for the disease mapped onto both neuron and glia patterns. The study spreads the blame beyond dopamine neurons alone.
europmc-pmc9077443:
Delany-Moretlwe and co-authors report a phase 3 trial of long-acting cabotegravir to prevent HIV-1 in women. Daily oral pills can be hard to take due to stigma and fear of violence. The trial, called HPTN 084, ran at 20 sites in seven countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Women aged 18 to 45 who were at risk of HIV took part.

The team enrolled 3,224 women and split them between injections and daily oral tenofovir with emtricitabine. Injections came every 8 weeks after a short oral lead-in. The authors report 40 new infections in all, with four in the injection group and 36 in the pill group. Side effects were much the same, apart from more sore injection sites. They conclude that cabotegravir worked better than daily pills for these women.
europmc-pmc9106343:
Gonzales and co-authors review how basic aging processes drive cognitive decline and dementia. Alzheimer's disease and related dementias are top causes of disability and death in later life. Age is the strongest risk factor for them. Even people who never develop dementia often lose some mental sharpness as they age.

The review first tracks changes in thinking, brain shape, and protein buildup across the human lifespan. It adds proof from animal studies on the mechanisms at work. The authors then focus on processes gone awry, like faulty autophagy, cell aging, and inflammation. They argue that drugs aimed at aging itself might slow both decline and dementia. Readers get a linked view of two fields that often work apart.
europmc-pmc9189143:
Fernández-Castañeda and co-authors show that even mild respiratory COVID can disturb neural cells and myelin. Many COVID survivors report lasting thinking problems much like chemo-related cognitive harm. That syndrome centers on reactive white matter microglia. The team asked whether lung-only infection could trigger the same brain pattern.

In mice, mild respiratory infection left white-matter microglia reactive for a long time. New neuron growth in the hippocampus fell, and myelin-forming cells were lost. A signal called CCL11 rose in spinal fluid and, given alone, reproduced the harm. Patients with lasting cognitive symptoms also had high CCL11. Flu caused a like pattern, though most of it faded. The findings may explain cognitive trouble after mild COVID.
europmc-pmc9266143:
Wendimu and Hooks review microglia phenotypes in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Microglia are the brain's first-line immune guardians and drivers of neuroinflammation. Inflammation marks many brain diseases and shapes their onset and course. Chronically activated microglia appear in patient tissue and imaging studies.

The review stresses that microglia can harm or protect, depending on context. Which phenotype dominates turns on the insult, its length, and the disease stage. Evidence comes from animal models and from human postmortem transcriptome studies. Key receptors and pathways that could serve as drug targets are covered. Age, sex, and species differences get brief attention. Readers get a balanced view of cells with a biphasic role.
europmc-pmc9370143:
Shahidi and Hossain summarize how lipids create food flavor, both welcome and spoiled. Fats break down during processing, cooking, and storage into volatile compounds. They also interact with products of the Maillard reaction and Strecker breakdown. Oxidation is the main road, by air, light, or enzymes.

Unsaturated fats first form hydroperoxides, then split into aldehydes, alcohols, and ketones with strong odors. Hexanal flags flavor loss in omega-6 rich meats; propanal does so in omega-3 rich fish oils. Cooking methods such as drying and fermentation shift the balance of notes. The review also covers heterocyclic compounds that add roasted character. The aim is control: keep the good flavors, block the bad ones.
europmc-pmc9630343:
Bilotta, Antignani, and Fitzgerald argue that managing the tumor microenvironment can lift the power of cancer therapy. The setting around a tumor shapes its growth and spread. It also shapes how well each treatment works. Suppression inside the setting often blocks a good response.

The review first lays out what the setting holds. It then turns to tumors with extreme versions of it. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma gets a close study. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and glioblastoma follow suit. Each standard therapy class is checked for its interplay with the setting. Chemo, radiation, targeted drugs, and antibodies all appear. So do immune based biologics that fight suppression itself. The authors close with five plans to reshape the setting. Each plan aims to turn a hostile setting into a treatment ally.
europmc-pmc9830443:
Lu and co-authors review cellular mitophagy, its mechanisms, disease roles, and drug control by small molecules. Mitophagy wraps and degrades damaged mitochondria on purpose. It keeps the cell's power plants and inner balance sound. Faulty cleanup is now tied to many clinical diseases.

The review splits the cleanup routes into two families. One path uses ubiquitin tags to mark worn mitochondria. The other path works without those tags at all. Disease chapters cover brain, heart, and metabolic ills. Cancer and innate immunity get their own sections. Small molecule modulators fill the second half of the tour. Some compounds switch mitophagy on through known targets. Others act as proton shuttles or mild mitochondria toxins. Metal complexes and natural products join the inducer list. Inhibitor compounds that brake the process are also covered. The authors stress the therapy promise of tuning cleanup.
europmc-pmc9842643:
Ascensao and co-authors report a research study of how fitness effects shift in a young bacterial community. Their work draws on the E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment. It focuses on two closely related ecotypes, called L and S, soon after they emerged. The team asks whether the adaptive landscape stays fixed as a community forms.

The authors built genome-wide barcoded transposon libraries for both ecotypes and their ancestor. They measured invasion fitness for gene knockouts across many growth conditions. Individual knockouts behaved in varied ways, yet broad statistical patterns held across backgrounds. Fitness effects also matched later evolutionary outcomes under several conditions. The results show how ecology and gene interactions jointly shape adaptation.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Pages withheld in full number 482 in release 43 of the Special Counsel Mueller investigation records, freed through the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Its deleted-page sheet gives two grounds for most pages. The first is the pair b6 and b7C, the privacy marks. The second adds b7A to that pair, the mark for pages tied to a live proceeding. A short block is marked for referral to another agency. No names, reports, or findings appear in the part. It stands as a count of its own gaps.
feuerbach-grundsaetze-1843:
Ludwig Feuerbach set out his program in Grundsaetze der Philosophie der Zukunft, German theses from 1843. The title promises the principles of the philosophy of the future. Feuerbach had already argued that talk of God mirrors human nature itself. These short theses press that line into a new starting point for thought.

He calls philosophy back from abstract spirit to real, sensing human beings. Thought, he insists, grows from flesh, need, and community with others. The young Karl Marx read the theses and turned from Hegel toward materialism under their pull. No public domain English translation exists. The German original carries the full charge.
fielding-jonathan-wild-1743:
Fielding published The History of the Life of the Late Mr Jonathan Wild the Great in 1743, inside his Miscellanies. Jonathan Wild was a real thief-taker, hanged in 1725, who ran London crime while posing as its hunter. Fielding turns his life into dark satire.

Every crime of Wild's is praised in the language of statesmanship, since Fielding's target is the 'great man' in politics too. Prime Minister Walpole's shadow falls across the rogue's career. The irony never relaxes, which makes the book Fielding's coldest and most biting work. It remains a classic study of power, cant, and the worship of greatness.
fielding-journey-next-world-1743:
A Journey from This World to the Next, printed in Fielding's Miscellanies of 1743, is his afterlife satire. The narrator dies, rides a coach of spirits to the world below, and reports what he finds. Lucian, the Greek satirist, is Fielding's model here.

In Elysium the dead are judged by Minos, and fame on earth counts for little. The spirit then passes through new lives, including that of Julian the Apostate, across a comic chain of births. Fielding mocks pride, cruelty, and empty ambition in every rank. The work shows his learning and his laughter working together, years before Tom Jones made him famous.
franck-la-kabbale-1843:
Adolphe Franck gave the lore of the Jews its first stern study in La Kabbale, his book of 1843. Franck was a sage of thought at a top school in Paris. He read the old texts in their own tongues. He asked when they were writ, by whom, and what they claim of God and man.

His calm sifts myth from fact with care. Great names of the occult, from Levi to Waite, cite his work as their base. The book, in French, marks the start of true study of this lore. Its worth still stands. Franck taught at the great school of France in Paris town. His rank gave his calm study a weight no mere fan could claim.
frus-1861-d143:
Writing on 17 August 1861, William H. Seward reset his orders to William Dayton for a long war. The letter is document 143 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's mid August letters have a plainer, graver tone than those of June. The short war was gone, and the orders fit the new facts. This note to Paris shows policy reset for endurance: fewer boasts, firmer law, longer watch. The reset he describes governed the Paris file through the rest of 1861. Endurance as policy asked envoys to be dull on cue, and Dayton obliged. Endurance, as policy, asked for dull strength.
frus-1861-d243:
