James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 8 July 1861. It stands as Document 243 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d43:
On 27 April 1861, William H. Seward sent orders to Charles Francis Adams, his new envoy to Britain. The letter is document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams was then crossing to take up the London post. Seward's April orders framed the line he should take with the British government. Britain had yet to state its stance on the war, and each word from Washington would shape Adams's first talks. Adams reached London in mid May and found a government still making up its mind. Mind and map were both still open when Adams stepped ashore in May.
frus-1862-d143:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 15 September 1862. It stands as Document 143 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d243:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 October 1862, and the letter closes the Stuart run as Document 243 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart had led the British legation through the summer and early fall.

By mid-October, the British cabinet was moving toward a decision against stepping into the war, though Stuart could not know its final shape. His letters across these months form a distinct chapter in the record: an understudy handling a great post in a crisis. This last letter ends that chapter on the eve of the decision. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d343:
The third Seward dispatch of 4 November 1862 stands as Document 343 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its mates, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Within days, the British cabinet voted down the truce proposal, and the fall crisis ended. These letters were already at sea, written for a danger that was passing. The overlap is a fine lesson in 1862 statecraft. Policy had to be framed to hold in several futures, because no one could know which future had begun. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d43:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 3 April 1862. It stands as Document 43 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d443:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Norman B. Judd, the American minister at Berlin. The instruction is Document 443 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By May 1862 Union victories in the West and the fall of New Orleans gave Seward good news to send his ministers. Judd's post in Berlin was a friendly place to send it. Prussia had no wish to aid the Confederacy, but its court still had to be courted and kept informed. Instructions of this sort also told ministers how to answer Confederate claims abroad. The dispatch shows Washington working a friendly capital with the same care it gave to doubtful ones.
frus-1862-d543:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 August 1862, the second day of the battle of Second Bull Run. His note is Document 543 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

That a Dutch minister transacted calm formal business in Washington while a battle raged thirty miles away is itself a fact about wartime capitals. Van Limburg's errand remained the protection of Dutch interests, which the war touched through trade and shipping rather than armies. His note belongs to the late-summer Dutch file, where the tone stayed correct even as the military news darkened. Seward's department answered such notes as they came, and the printed sequence preserves that discipline.
frus-1862-d643:
Townsend Harris sent this dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 November 1861. It is Document 643 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Harris wrote in late November, as the Trent affair was breaking in the Atlantic world he could not hear of for months. In Edo his business remained the treaty relationship and the condition of the mission he had founded. He was by then a sick man nearing the end of his service. His remaining letters have the quality of a founder setting his house in order. The dispatch is among the last of his printed reports in the volume, closing the first chapter of American diplomacy in Japan.
frus-1863p1-d143:
On 3 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 143 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

The middle sheet of Adams's sets often held the day's weight. In April 1863 the weight was ships: Southern raiders built in Britain, and the Union's drive to stop them. This letter holds its place in that fight's record. Read with its mates, it shows the legation working all its lines at once in the war's most fraught spring abroad.
frus-1863p1-d243:
Washington's orders to London on 23 July 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 243 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d343:
In Washington on 22 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 343 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d43:
Judah P. Benjamin sent this letter to John Slidell on 28 October 1862. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state; Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris. The letter is document 43 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By late October the South's drive for foreign backing was losing ground, after Antietam and the first word of the freedom edict. Benjamin's letters to Paris kept the push alive on paper. This one is a late-fall piece of that effort. Printed by the Union in its own volume, it shows the other side's hopes in its own hand, at the hour they began to fade.
frus-1863p1-d443:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 3 April 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d543:
The letter printed as document 543 was written on 30 May 1863 by F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d643:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 23 October 1863 and wrote to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1941-43:
This conference volume opens with Arcadia's crowded days. Pre-conference papers set the Washington agenda first. Roosevelt and Churchill meet on December 22, 1941. Their chiefs of staff sit the same evening. Christmas week fills with councils at all hours. Dinners double as strategy sessions in the record. Beaverbrook and Mackenzie King join the circle. The proceedings run day by day, hour by hour. Casablanca's turn comes in the volume's later half. The same machinery travels to Morocco in 1943.

A mid-volume memo settles who minds the store. McNarney takes one general's duties in Washington. Styer acts for another during the trip. All plans, it notes, hinge on the conference. The volume is alliance at the summit. Its minutes show war run by conversation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d143: Roosevelt answered Churchill on November 19, 1943, and the letter is Document 143 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Replies that week were written from ships, ports, and borrowed desks as the parties converged. The record names the parties and the date only. In the Foreign Relations series the letter stands just before the volume's conference chapters begin, where letters give way to minutes and agreed texts.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d243:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on 21 November 1943 about sparing Rome. His letter carries a draft message to the Pope, ready for Roosevelt's signature, on recognizing Rome as an open city.

Hull argues that, for reasons beyond the military ones, America should make a sincere effort to save Rome from the ruin of modern war. If no deal is reached, she should leave the blame for refusal with the Germans. The draft letter tells the Pope that Washington accepts the Italian government's August declaration and its conditions, if Germany grants the same status. One reservation is spelled out: Allied forces keep full transit rights through Rome by rail and road.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d343:
The final text of the Cairo communiqué, dated 26 November 1943, is the agreed statement of the first Cairo Conference. Harry Hopkins handed the text to Ambassador Kirk that afternoon, and the White House released it to the press on 1 December, after the Tehran meeting ended.

The statement says the military missions have agreed on future operations against Japan, and that the three allies will bring unrelenting pressure by sea, land, and air. The three powers covet no gain and no territory. Japan will be stripped of all Pacific islands seized since 1914. The territories stolen from China, including Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, will be restored. Japan will be expelled from every land taken by violence and greed. Korea, in due course, will become free and independent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d43: A second Roosevelt letter to Stalin bears the same date, October 14, 1943, and stands as Document 43 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters to Moscow in one day suggests business too mixed, or too urgent, for a single sheet. The record does not separate their topics, and neither should a summary. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the last days before the foreign ministers met.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d443:
By December 5, 1943, the Second Cairo Conference was in full swing, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff met again that day. Their minutes, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, come from the joint body that matched American and British plans into one war effort. Turkey's possible entry into the war hung over the whole conference.

The record follows the chiefs through the day's military business, with positions stated, differences worked through, and decisions noted for the two heads of government. Read beside the Tehran documents, it shows the alliance moving from promises to planning. Few sources show wartime teamwork at this level so plainly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d543:
President Roosevelt addressed this message on January 10, 1944 to Patrick J. Hurley, his personal representative, then temporarily in Iran. Hurley, a former secretary of war, roamed the Middle East on the President's personal business. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Personal representatives were Roosevelt's way of cutting through department lines: Hurley reported to the President alone and answered to no embassy. Iran, occupied and restless after hosting the Tehran Conference, held his attention that winter. For readers, the message shows Roosevelt managing a sensitive country through a trusted agent in the weeks after the summit left its capital.
frus-1944-quebec-d143:
Churchill reported to Roosevelt on the Italian offensive in telegram 772, sent August 29, 1944. Four German divisions had been pulled from Italy since the Riviera landings, yet General Alexander had concentrated his armies for a blow at the Gothic Line. Churchill had gone forward with the advance himself and described the modern battlefield at first hand.

The Eighth Army, ten divisions strong on the Adriatic flank, had attacked on August 26 and gained about nine miles. General Clark's eight divisions around Florence would strike once the enemy reacted, and both armies would converge on Bologna. Churchill also looked ahead: a powerful army in Trieste and Istria within weeks, he argued, would carry effects far beyond military value.
frus-1944-quebec-d243:
Churchill returned Roosevelt's memorandum on Italian colonies with a short note dated September 16, 1944. The paper was Hull's September 11 memorandum, with the department's study of British proposals for Italy's overseas territories. The Foreign Office, Churchill wrote, would like to treat it as an official communication, if the president would allow London to keep a copy.

The usual broad and substantial measure of agreement existed between the two governments, he said, but the British wished to look into the details more closely. A handwritten note by Dorothy Brady, attached in the Roosevelt Papers, records the outcome: the president agreed the British could keep copies, and he wanted an answer from them on it.
frus-1944-quebec-d43:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Mackenzie King of Canada on August 31, 1944. Canada would host the coming conference at Quebec City, and King was its host prime minister. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Canada's part in these conferences was easy to overlook and wrong to forget: Canadian soil, Canadian hospitality, and a Canadian government carrying a major war effort of its own. Hopkins's message to King handled the host's side of the arrangements. For readers, it gives due place to the third country in the room, whose capital province framed the meeting.
frus-1945-50-intel-d143:
A memorandum dated 14 February 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (McCormack). The State Department prints it as document 143 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d243:
A memorandum by the Army Member of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee (Pixtou) bears the date 15 October 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 243 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d343:
A memorandum dated 17 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 343 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d43:
Ladd, an assistant director of the FBI, wrote to Hoover on 5 November 1945. Ladd ran much of the bureau's intelligence and security work and stood high in Hoover's trust. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Assistant directors' memoranda gave Hoover the bureau's own picture of events, filtered by men who knew his mind. Ladd's paper belongs to the FBI's watch on the central intelligence question, which touched the bureau's foreign operations directly. Readers building the FBI thread should set Ladd beside Tamm: two senior aides serving one director. Their stream of paper kept the bureau's position sharp through the long contest of 1945 and 1946.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d143:
President Roosevelt answered Churchill's Moscow dispatches on 22 October 1944 with warm approval and one request. His short top secret telegram, number 632, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Six of Churchill's messages are acknowledged in its first line.

Roosevelt says he is delighted at the success in Moscow toward a compromise solution of the Polish problem. When and if a solution is reached, he asks to be consulted on one point of timing. That is whether publication should be delayed for about two weeks. “You will understand,” he adds, and closes by reporting that everything is going well at home. The note is a small window on how the Polish settlement touched American politics.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d243:
What happens in China if Russia enters the Far East war? A briefing book paper of 13 January 1945 works through the map. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume under a long title on the political and military situation in China.

The Communists hold large parts of North China, the paper says, with further pockets to the east and south. They claim 500,000 regular troops and two million militia: ill equipped, but well trained in guerrilla war and in good physical shape. Their underground strength in Manchuria counts as considerable. One Russian line of attack might run from Outer Mongolia through Inner Mongolia toward Shanhaikuan, the gateway to Manchuria. Communist armies would then stand on the Russians' right flank.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d343:
One sheet of paper or several? The United States Chiefs of Staff argued for one in this February 5, 1945 paper on the Bremen-Bremerhaven area. The port enclave was to sit inside the British zone but serve American supply lines. The chiefs backed a single clean agreement text over a draft tied to a general's letter.

On the side points raised in that letter, the chiefs took a practical line. Whatever the zone commanders on the ground could not settle between themselves should go up to the Combined Chiefs for a ruling. Clashes of authority, they granted, were sure to come. The paper shows alliance housekeeping at its driest and most needed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d43: On 6 January 1945 Churchill sent Roosevelt another message, one day after his previous letter. It stands as document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Frequent short messages were Churchill's habit before a conference, letting him raise points for the agenda while there was still time to settle them by cable.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d443:
Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss reported back to the foreign ministers on February 10, 1945. Their subcommittee had been instructed two days earlier on two subjects. The first was how to consult France and China on the conference's decisions about the world organization. The second was the text of the invitation to the United Nations conference.

On consultation, they held that the United States should speak for the three powers to both governments. On the invitation, they attached a draft for the ministers' approval. The report is brief. But it closed the last piece of machinery needed to summon the founding conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d143:
President Truman wrote to Stalin about the surrendered German ships on May 29, 1945. His personal and top secret message, number 275, is document 143 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had proposed a way of dividing the German fleet in a message of May 23.

Truman thanks Stalin for the suggestion, then puts the question off to the summit. The subject suits discussion by the three leaders at their coming meeting, he writes, where he is sure a solution fully acceptable to all can be reached. He adds a practical point: the records of the German naval surrender are being examined by the commanders in the areas concerned. Like Churchill, Truman kept the fleet for face-to-face bargaining rather than cable trading.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d243:
Ambassador Winant confirmed delivery of the Italy message in a one-line telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 243 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had told him the day before to inform the Foreign Office, urgently, of the planned American announcement backing Italy's admission to the world security organization.

Winant's whole report reads: Foreign Office given substance of the Department's telegram this morning. The delivery set off the trouble that followed within hours, when London officials protested that the announcement was sprung on them with the Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary already in Berlin. The tiny telegram is the quiet first half of a small allied quarrel; the second half sits in the next document.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d343:
Reeducation of Germany is the subject Archibald MacLeish laid before the Secretary of State on July 4, 1945. The War Department had asked again and again for a long-range policy directive to guide its men in Germany. MacLeish's covering note sends the paper the Secretary had requested that morning at the Staff Committee.

The enclosed paper admits the problem's great difficulty. To frame a policy, the Department had called in leading citizens with deep experience in education. President Edmund Day of Cornell chaired the advisory group, and President George Shuster of Hunter College sat among its members. Their charge was nothing less than reshaping German minds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d43:
Stalin wrote to Prime Minister Winston Churchill from Moscow on May 30, 1945, in a top secret personal message. It is document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The two leaders were settling when the Big Three would hold their next meeting, weeks after the German surrender ended the war in Europe.

Stalin explains a mix-up over the date. Truman's envoy Harry Hopkins had told him the President favored a meeting around mid-July, yet the message first read as June 15. Stalin says he has no objection if Churchill also agrees. An added note by Charles Bohlen records how the error was checked with Soviet officials and confirmed as July 15.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d443:
Elections in Greece are the subject of a briefing book paper that begins at Yalta. There the United States agreed to act with Russia and Britain in helping Europe's liberated nations solve their pressing political and economic problems by democratic means. In Greece, America had no military commitments and only a limited relief role.

The paper recalls the Varkiza Agreement of February 12, 1945, between EAM and the Greek government. Its ninth article promised allied supervision for a plebiscite within the year, and for elections after it. Washington made no public comment at the time, the paper notes, but stood ready to look favorably on a Greek request to help run those votes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d543:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent a top secret wire to the Secretary of State on July 11, 1945. He wrote from aboard the Army transport Brazil, on his way to the Potsdam Conference. The wire is document 543 in volume one of the Foreign Relations series on that meeting.

Stimson says he and John McCloy are troubled by the President's new lend-lease order. As the War Department reads it, the order bars food and fuel for the French army of occupation in Germany. It also bars upkeep for British and French occupation forces. Yet those forces free far more U.S. troops to shift to the war against Japan. Stimson asks if that strict reading is right.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d643:
From Beirut on July 9, 1945, Minister Wadsworth reported a talk with General Pilleau on the Levant transfer. His confidential wire is document 643 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Pilleau was the British officer dealing with the handover of the Troupes Speciales.

Pilleau urged prompt study of a Ninth Army memo on the practical side of the transfer. Absent higher political reasons, he saw a security gain in finishing the transfer before any troop withdrawal. French forces, he noted, could hardly be asked to leave except alongside the British. Wadsworth asks Washington for its views on who should propose a joint withdrawal. Without some move, he warns, Syria will press its demand again and the security picture will suffer.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1043:
Richard Bissell, a War Shipping Administration official at Potsdam, cabled his Washington office on July 22, 1945. British shipping chief Lord Leathers had stated Britain's coal limit in early talks. After August shipments, Britain can export no coal at all for September arrival. Two small exceptions stand: anthracite duffs for briquetting, and special grades needed in North Africa.

Leathers presses instead to draw at least 90,000 tons a month of American bunker coal. Britain has taken on fueling captured and released ships, near 70,000 tons a month. Bissell warns cash payment may be demanded. He asks Washington's view on American supply, and on whether the British refusal is fair.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1143:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to President Truman on 16 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam Conference opened. Stimson was the cabinet's senior figure on war matters. His word carried weight with the president on every question the army touched.

A message sent on the summit's eve framed the picture Truman carried into the talks. The War Department ran the forces that held Germany and still fought Japan. Its chief's counsel, put in writing, fixed the armed forces' stand before the bargaining began. This letter is that counsel. It shows the president's brief being built, one paper at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1243:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 22 July 1945. The Washington end of the circuit answered the summit end on a near daily rhythm. Grew's messages carried the home office's news and needs to Byrnes in Germany.

By the second week, the circuit was a settled habit. Files moved, questions rose, and answers came back within a day or two. This cable is one turn of that habit. Small in itself, it belongs to a rare system. That system let one department sit in two places at once, in the most crowded fortnight of its year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1343:
A text handed in by the Soviet delegation on 29 July 1945 forms document 1343 of the Potsdam volume. It came in the last days of the conference, when drafting of the final papers was at its most intense. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Late texts at a summit often carry the hardest bargaining, since each side knows the clock is running out. What a delegation chose to put in writing at that stage shows what it valued most. Set beside the closing protocol, this Soviet text helps readers judge the talks. It shows how much of the Soviet program survived, and how much was traded away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-143: This editorial note appears without a number after document 710 in the second volume of Potsdam papers. The Foreign Relations editors wrote such notes to lend readers a hand. They name sources, connect related texts, and mark thin spots in the file. Here the note steadies a reader inside a long stretch of conference records.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-43:
Thompson's minutes record the plenary session of July 20, 1945, at 4 p.m. at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Molotov opened the session by presenting his report as rapporteur of the morning's foreign ministers' meeting.

The report was largely a tale of unfinished work. The subcommittee on German economic policy had not yet reported, Molotov said. The committee on Poland had likewise not finished, and was told to complete its report by July 21. On the peace settlement, the drafting group had run out of time as well. The foreign ministers had therefore met just before the session and agreed a text themselves, whose revised paragraph 3 Molotov then read. He closed by presenting a Soviet draft on carrying out the Yalta declaration on liberated areas. That text opened debate on Rumania and Bulgaria, and on Greece.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d743:
Gerig reported once more to Alger Hiss on August 9, 1945, in document 743. The United Nations Preparatory Commission still filled his days in London. His letter extends the volume's record past the Potsdam close. It was printed among the final papers of the second Potsdam volume's United Nations thread.

Late letters in a series carry the state of play at a moment of change. The war in Asia was ending; the new body's first assembly drew near. Readers see a planner's desk at that hinge. The document shows how the Potsdam generation passed its work to the institutions it had built.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d843:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 27, 1945, as document 843. It dates from the final week, as Attlee returned to the table. Soviet texts in the endgame defended gains and pressed the last claims. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A late Soviet draft lets readers weigh Moscow's priorities under time pressure. What a side tables when days run short reveals what it values. The document can be read against the final protocol for the answer. It also shows the Soviet team's method to the end: written claims, firmly held, traded only at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d943: The Pauley group prepared this table of capital removals needed to cut German war potential, filed with the July 28, 1945 papers. Figures are in millions of prewar Reichsmarks. Factory removals, armaments included, total 3,500 across the Reich. Transport removals add 2,250, and power and gas add 900. The full total is 6,650 million. Of that, 2,925 million sits in the eastern zone including Berlin, and 3,725 million in the rest of Germany. Dollar conversions at two exchange rates split the value 44 percent east and 56 percent west.
gao-gaoreports-b-298143:
Lawrence Drake protested a Labor cost study call in GAO decision B-298143, dated April 7, 2006. He led the local union branch for agency staff. The study would weigh in-house work versus a deal for accounts work. The count was 150 posts. No call had yet been set. He sought to block the study path.

GAO dismissed the protest. A union lead is not a party with a stake to file a buy protest. That rank is held for firms that bid or could bid. Staff leads lack that rank here. The fight thus could not be heard. Stake to protest is a gate rule. It bars claims by those with no bid stake.
gao-gaoreports-b-298543:
STG, Inc. protested a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency award to Beta Analytics, Incorporated. The contract covered support services for a security and intelligence office. The work aids the agency's management operations staff. GAO decided B-298543 and B-298543.3 on October 30, 2006.

STG alleged a bait and switch on staffing. It noted that the awardee swapped nine staff after award. GAO found no proof the firm had meant to mislead the agency. A swap alone does not show a false promise at bid time. STG also attacked the scoring and the source selection. GAO found both sound on the record. It denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-311143:
Harris Enterprises, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-311143, dated March 27, 2008. The Social Security Administration sought storehouse help in Maryland. The call asked that the winner hold ISO-9001:2000 marks. Harris held the past deal for the work. It called the mark rule too tight for a fair race. The work deals with goods that hold private facts on folks.

GAO denied the protest. The agency tied the mark to a real need. Strict care marks guard goods of a touchy kind. A firm with such marks can best keep that trust. Terms that track a true need are not too tight in law.
gao-gaoreports-b-311343:
Singleton Enterprises-GMT Mechanical, A Joint Venture saw its protest thrown out (GAO decision B-311343, dated April 23, 2008). The Veterans Affairs office sought a garage fix at its Jackson, Mississippi site. The call was set aside for firms owned by hurt veterans. The joint bid was tossed as unfit for that class. A past call had drawn the same call on this firm.

GAO dismissed the protest. The Small Business Administration had ruled the firm out of the class. A top panel in that shop backed the rule on plea. The rule stood in force when the bid was tossed. A firm out of the class has no stake to fight the toss.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-243:
Defense Acquisitions, GAO-05-243 of March 31, 2005, gives the yearly grade for the missile shield build in 2004. Since 1985, the Pentagon has spent $85 billion on missile defense. It plans $66.5 billion more through 2011. The first shield, to guard the land from long-range missiles from Northeast Asia, stood near switch-on.

Congress told GAO to grade the Missile Defense Agency each year through 2006. GAO tests its cost, time, test, and skill aims for fiscal year 2004. It checks each part of the wide shield web, from ground rockets to sea and space gear. Gains and slips share the ledger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-343:
Head Start, GAO-05-343 of May 17, 2005, grades a new national test for the youngest pupils in federal care. In September 2003, the Head Start Bureau gave its first land-wide skills test to over 400,000 children ages 4 and 5. The test aims to show how well each grant site helps its charges grow. First-year rows with sites and pros dogged the launch.

GAO tells what facts the test is built to give. It tells how the bureau met the first-year fears. It tests if the facts the test yields are sound enough to steer picks. More build work could earn that trust, the title says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-543:
Coordination of border aircraft and boats across three agencies is reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-543, issued on August 12, 2005. The Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement guard 7,500 miles of land border. They watch more than 361 seaports and 95,000 miles of coastline. GAO asked what the department has done to join up the fleets and how local units work together.

Department councils hunt for savings across the fleets. One aviation plan sets shared tracking, training, and upkeep. A boats group helped one agency buy six boats on a sister agency's contract, saving about $300,000. A merger plan would fold one air and marine unit into Customs and Border Protection by September 30, 2005. At four sites GAO visited, local teamwork rested on commanders who chose to cooperate. In South Florida the three agencies build one weekly schedule for aircraft and boats. GAO said such ad hoc gains need firmer backing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-943:
Smart traffic systems and congestion are assessed in GAO-05-943, a report issued September 14, 2005. These systems use electronics and computers to squeeze more from existing roads. Congress set up a program for them in 1991. In 1996, the transport secretary set a goal: full smart systems in the 75 largest city areas by 2005. GAO described the federal role and graded the goal and its measures.

GAO found progress toward the goal, but the goal and measures fall short. They do not capture whether the gear is actually run well once installed. Chicago built 10 traffic centers to watch and respond to jams. Six lack full-time operators, which likely blunts their effect. Studies suggest the systems can ease congestion and aid safety. Barriers to wider, well-run use remain. The department could better aid their strategic use, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-143:
The first consumer-directed health plan for federal workers is studied in GAO-06-143, issued on November 21, 2005. Since 2003 the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program has offered such plans. Each pairs a high-deductible policy with a savings account for care costs. Unused balances roll over, which rewards careful spending. Critics fear these plans draw the young and healthy. That would leave older, sicker workers to raise costs in standard plans. GAO studied the plan run by the American Postal Workers Union.

GAO compared that plan's enrollment with other new plans and national preferred provider plans. It weighed who signed up, how satisfied they were, and what care they could reach. It also compared provider networks and price discounts across plans. The study tests early claims on both sides of the debate. Supporters see smart shopping for care. Skeptics see risk sorting that could weaken the shared pool.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-343:
The civil rights watchdog's own credibility is examined in GAO-06-343, a report dated May 1, 2006. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights dates to the Civil Rights Act of 1957. It is an independent, bipartisan fact-finder with no enforcement power. Its influence rests entirely on being trusted as impartial. State advisory committees serve as its eyes and ears in every state. Since 1980 they have produced 200 of the commission's 254 reports.

Quality safeguards need strengthening, GAO found. Policies do not require balanced views in reports and hearings. No rule governs the use of outside reviewers. Leaders have reshaped projects without all commissioners' consent. Most state committees cannot even act: 38 of 51 charters have lapsed. Funds and staff for the committees have shrunk. GAO urged fuller use of the committees and an outside check on the commission itself. A fact-finder's facts must first survive scrutiny at home.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-43:
Workers laid off because of trade often need help finding new jobs. GAO wrote GAO-06-43 on January 31, 2006, about Trade Adjustment Assistance. Little was known nationwide about how much such workers use federal reemployment services. GAO studied workers hit by five trade-related layoffs. It tracked the services they reached and the mix they got.

GAO also measured the job outcomes those workers achieved. It checked use of new health insurance and wage insurance benefits. It weighed factors that shaped take-up of those benefits. Most workers in the five layoffs got services, GAO found. Better outreach on new benefits was still needed. Readers see limits of a small-case study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-643:
The military role in the Hurricane Katrina response is studied in GAO report GAO-06-643, released on May 15, 2006. Katrina was one of the largest natural disasters in United States history. Despite a huge deployment at all levels of government, many judged the federal response to be inadequate. GAO reviewed how well the armed forces had planned and trained for a disaster of this scale.

GAO found that pre-Katrina planning did not fully address the military capabilities a catastrophic disaster would need. The military response was massive, yet it faced several serious challenges. Coordination and clear tasking were among the weak points. The Department of Defense had begun fixes, GAO said, but some problems were complex and long-standing. GAO called for better plans and exercises.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-943:
Surplus military gear, and the risk in how it is passed on, is investigated in GAO report GAO-06-943, dated July 25, 2006. Past GAO work found lost and stolen sensitive gear, some of it sold to the public. Waste dogged the reuse program as well.

GAO ran follow-up probes. It tested whether outsiders could get sensitive gear that must be destroyed when the military is done with it. It checked if new systems stop sales of fresh, unused gear that troops still need. Control failures, GAO found, pose a grave security risk. The report ties loose stores control to both safety and cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-143:
Army chemical units are the troops meant to respond after a chemical or biological attack. GAO rated their readiness in GAO-07-143, issued January 19, 2007. Defense leaders call such response a top national priority. The Homeland Security Council lists 15 planning scenarios for attacks. Twelve of them call for chemical and biological response. GAO analyzed readiness data for 78 Army chemical units.

GAO found that most of the units were not ready for their missions. They lacked staff, gear, and training, the review showed. Shortages hit hardest in the chemical operations specialty. Guard and Reserve units also lacked much of their decontamination equipment. Transfers to units deploying overseas had drained people and gear. Some units could not train for their wartime tasks at all. The Army had no specific plan to fix the shortfalls. GAO urged the Army to build one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-43:
Getting low-income workers to their jobs is the aim of the Job Access and Reverse Commute program, reviewed in GAO-07-43, published November 17, 2006. The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) runs the grants. A 2005 law, SAFETEA-LU, set $727 million for fiscal years 2005 through 2009. It changed how funds are awarded and told FTA to judge the program by August 2008.

GAO found that FTA had made real headway on the new rules. It had sought wide public input on its guidance. But checks on grant users were not set. FTA planned to borrow review tools from other programs, yet the fit was not final. Some users sat outside those tools with no clear review cycle. GAO urged firm oversight so the aid stays fair and on target.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-643:
Work carried over between budget years is misstated at a Navy center, and GAO-07-643, dated June 26, 2007, shows the flaw. Defense working capital funds will roll about $6 billion of funded work from fiscal year 2007 into fiscal year 2008. Some roll-over keeps work flowing. Too much can hide idle funds. The Naval Air Warfare Center reports its own carryover each year.

GAO tested the center's reported figures for fiscal years 2003 through 2006. They did not hold up. The center also skipped the required reviews, held three times a year, that clean the data. Dead obligations and stale charges sat in the books. A new Navy accounting system was due in October 2007, which raises the stakes: errors moved into a new system can take years to root out. GAO pressed managers to own the accuracy of their numbers and run the reviews as required.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-243:
Transit aid after disasters is charted in GAO report GAO-08-243 (February 15, 2008). Storms and attacks can wreck buses, trains, and the stations they serve. Riders then lose their path to relief, care, work, and home. Two agencies lead the federal reply. The emergency agency holds broad disaster powers, and the transit agency funds systems.

After the 2001 attacks, rebuilding transit at the World Trade Center took over $4 billion in federal aid. The 2005 Gulf storms broke less track but stranded whole populations. GAO traced aid since 1998 and what slowed it after those storms. It urged preset mission plans and clearer funding rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-343:
Protecting personally identifiable information held by federal agencies is the subject of GAO report GAO-08-343, dated January 25, 2008. Lost personal data can lead to identity theft and fraud. GAO mapped the laws and guidance that guard such data and surveyed 24 major agencies on their safeguards for data taken off site.

Two laws anchor the duties: the Privacy Act of 1974 and the E-Government Act of 2002, with the Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002 adding security program duties. After breach incidents, the Office of Management and Budget told agencies in 2006 and 2007 to encrypt data on mobile devices, among other steps. Uptake was uneven: 22 of 24 agencies required encryption on mobile computers, but only 15 had policies for session time-outs on remote access.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-43:
GAO covers the digital television transition in its report GAO-08-43, dated November 19, 2007. By law, full-power stations must stop analog broadcasts by February 17, 2009. Viewers with analog sets will need converter boxes, and a federal program subsidizes those boxes.

The Federal Communications Commission and the National Telecommunications and Information Administration have set deadlines, issued a subsidy contract, and begun outreach. A private coalition of over 160 groups is also spreading the word. But GAO found no full plan for the shift and no way to measure progress or manage risks. Consumer education was still mostly at the planning stage. GAO recommended a joint comprehensive plan. Neither agency said whether it agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-443:
U.S. trade preference programs are covered by GAO report GAO-08-443, released March 7, 2008. Four programs cut U.S. tariffs for goods from over 130 poorer countries to spur their growth. Three of the programs were set to expire in part or in full during 2008, as Congress weighed renewal.

The programs have a small effect on the U.S. economy, though some U.S. firms depend on them and others face the competing imports. Beneficiary exports to the United States have grown faster than overall imports, and the poorest countries are using the programs more. Gaps remain for farm goods and apparel. GAO found the programs have grown complex, with no joint review of whether they meet shared goals. It urged periodic joint reviews by the agencies involved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-643:
Small firms in poor areas can win federal work more easily under the HUBZone program. GAO-08-643, dated June 17, 2008, checks whether the Small Business Administration aims the help at the right places and firms, and whether it knows if the program works.

The map the agency posts to show eligible areas is wrong in both ways: it lists some areas that do not qualify and misses others that do. Rule changes have nearly doubled the areas, and some are no longer very poor. Checks on firms are weak, so some unfit firms got in. GAO urged tighter checks and a real look at results.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
In the second part of chapter six, John Lothrop Motley sends Sir John Norris to Holland in his History of the United Netherlands. Antwerp has fallen, and Elizabeth writes encouraging letters with her own hand. She implores the States not to falter now. She had long promised never to desert them, Motley notes.

Yet her parsimony starves the help she sends, and Norris must make energy do the work of money. The chapter contrasts the Queen's warm words with her cold treasury. Dutch envoys learn to price English friendship exactly. Motley's American eye sees the pattern of all the alliance chapters: a republic saved by an ally it cannot trust. Military narrative and diplomatic irony proceed together, as reinforcements land too few and too late to retake what Parma won.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
In the Fire of the Forge opens in Volume 1 of the Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers sets the scene in 1281, on the eve of St Medard's feast, with a bright moon over the imperial free city. Emperor Rudolph is lodged there, along with princes, counts, and knights, yet the street by the Ortlieb mansion stays still and dark under its linden tree.

Chapter I explains the quiet: an imperial order keeps soldiers indoors at night, the city gate shut long before, and honest burghers, meaning town citizens, keep early hours. One drunken master weaver staggers home seeing the moon doubled. Into this stillness Ebers places the wealthy Ortlieb household, whose two daughters, Els and Eva, will draw knights, slander, and danger toward the forge of the title.
international-weekly-miscellany-of-liter:
German criticism on English women novelists heads the International Weekly Miscellany for August 5, 1850. That was volume one, number six, at New York. A letter to the Cologne Gazette ranks Jewsbury, Bronte, and Gaskell in the first rank. Jewsbury's Zoe and Half Sisters are praised for thought and feeling.

Brown University's fund reaches one hundred and ten thousand dollars in a news note inside. That was within fifteen thousand of the sum proposed for Dr. Wayland's college reform. Tales, poems, and educational news fill the number. The weekly mixed European letters with American college affairs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abenheim-joseph:
Joseph Abenheim was a violinist and orchestra leader, born at Worms in 1804. He died at Stuttgart on January 18, 1891. His first music lessons came from Schlösser, and in his early youth he joined an orchestra at Mannheim. In 1825 he entered the royal orchestras at Stuttgart, playing at the palace and at the theater alike.

After study in Paris under Reicha, Abenheim came back to Stuttgart and often stood in for the chief leader, Lindpaintner. In 1854 he was placed at the head of the orchestra himself. He wrote many songs and pieces, among them two Nocturnes and a hymn, "Der Deutsche Rhein." He also wrote the music for a drama staged at Stuttgart in 1842. Very few of his works were ever printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abo-343:
Abo was the capital of the government of Abo-Björneborg in Finland, Russia. It stood near where the Auraioki river meets the Gulf of Bothnia. Swedish law from 1782 had barred Jews from all Finland.

A Russian ukase of March 29, 1858 let Jewish army veterans settle in the province. Widows and children shared the right. Local merchants pressed in 1883 to end Jewish settlement, and a mob entered the synagogue that June. Permits later had to be renewed each year. In 1898 the town held 34,339 people, of whom 220 were Jews. The rest were mostly Finns and Swedes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-nahmias: One line of fact is all this stub offers about Abraham Nahmias. He translated Thomas Aquinas' Commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics. Readers who want the fuller account are sent to the first entry under Nahmias, Abraham. No dates, home, or language of the version is stated here. His name survives in the record through that single piece of learned work on a Christian thinker's reading of Aristotle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-absolute-the-fr:
The Absolute is a term in thought for a being free from chance and outside control. Thinkers define it in many ways. Spinoza calls it the cause of itself. Kant calls it the thing in itself. Fichte calls it the wholly unbound. Schopenhauer calls it the unlinked. Spencer calls it the Unknowable. Its reverse is the relative, which rests on other things.

From Aristotle on, the entry says, thought has linked God and the Absolute. God is seen as the uncaused cause of all else. Arabic terms for that first cause passed into Hebrew thought terms as well. Maimonides and other Arabic-Jewish thinkers hold that this top point of thought is God. Schelling, a German thinker, comes close to that same view. In it, the mind that thinks and the thing thought of become one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acosta-luis-d-7: Luis d'Acosta was a Marano of Villa-Flor, Portugal. He was born in 1587. At the age of forty-five he was condemned to the galleys. The charge was that he had kept the law of Moses in secret. The hosted text gives only those facts. It names his town, his birth year, his age at the sentence, and the cause of it. It says nothing of his family, his work, or what became of him after the sentence was passed on him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adonai-melek-84: Built from three short texts, the chorus Adonai Melek rings through the days of penitence. Two psalms give a line that says the Lord reigns. A line in Exodus adds that he shall reign for ever. Sung phrase by phrase, the chorus caps poems in three-verse stanzas. Two tune lines stand side by side in the entry. Sephardic tunes favor flock song in plain beat, much like folk song. Ashkenazic tunes favor the cantor's free art, rich with turns and old modes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agricultural-co:
Agricultural colonies in the United States start, in the main, with the great Russian Jewish move of 1881-82. One first try came in 1837. Thirteen Jewish families left New York city for farms at Wawarsing. They called the place Sholom, or Peace. For five years they farmed and added trade and small making to their gains. By 1842 they had sold out and left.

The first colony of Russian Jews sat on Sicily Island in Louisiana. It held 35 families from Kiev and 25 from Elizabethgrad. They came in October, 1881. A tract of about 5,000 acres was bought at $8 an acre. The land had been a plantation before the Civil War. Houses, horses, tools, and stock were sent from New Orleans. The entry then walks the states one by one. It ends on south New Jersey, where farm work plus mill work kept the colonies alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-jacob-943:
Aha b. Jacob was a Babylonian amora and senior contemporary of Abaye and Raba, a disciple of Huna, head of the academy at Sura. His study was so intense that it damaged his health, yet he kept at it, repaying by night any part of the day taken by worldly business. After ordination he settled at Paphunia, where he became an authority on ritual matters and a noted haggadist.

He was also a skilled writer of Torah scrolls and is quoted widely in halakic discussion. Legend adds a stranger gift: lodged in Abaye's academy, he met a demon in the shape of a seven-headed hydra, and at each genuflection in prayer one head dropped off.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akkum-1043:
'Akkum is a Talmudic word for a heathen or idolater. It is an abbreviation, built from words meaning "worshiper of stars and constellations." It was first used of Chaldean star-worshipers. The word later drew the entry into a long dispute about slander against the Jews.

Critics claimed that harsh Talmud rules about the 'Akkum meant all non-Jews, Christians included. The entry calls that claim an error. Every Talmud edition, it notes, opens with a rabbis' declaration on the point. The word covers the idolatrous nations of old or of far lands, not believers in revelation. Censors also swapped the word in for plainer terms, which fed the confusion. One professor, Rohling of Prague, even read it falsely as "worshiper of Christ and Mary" in 1883.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-jagel:
Alexander Jagellon was grand duke of Lithuania and king of Poland. He was born in 1460 and died at Wilna in 1506. He was a son of King Casimir IV. He took the Lithuanian throne in 1492. He took the Polish one in 1501, on his brother John Albert's death. On December 1, 1492, he confirmed the Jews' old privileges and added new ones. He even repaid his father's large debts to them.

Then, in 1495, without warning, he ordered every Jew out of Lithuania. It was the first persecution of the Jews in that land. The banished came from Brest, Troki, Wilna, Lutzk, Vladimir, and Kiev. Poland took them in, and they stayed near Ratno. In 1503 Alexander himself ordered them back to Lithuania. The entry calls him weak in character and ruled by favorites. His wavering shows in this swing from favor to expulsion and back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkabizi-abraha: Abraham Alkabizi worked as an editor in Constantinople. He worked in the first quarter of the sixteenth century. In 1516 he helped print a known rabbinic work. That work was the Toledot Adam wa-Hawwah by Jeroham ben Meshullam. Two men shared the task with him. They were Judah Sason and Joseph Hamon. The entry gives no more of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alyashar-jacob-: Jacob Alyashar was a Talmudist born at Wilna about 1735. He died in Safed about 1785. In 1765 the group at Hebron sent him out. He went as their envoy to Persia. War broke out in 1775 while he lived at Bozrah. That city came under siege that year. He fled with his wife and new-born son. The three reached Safed in safety. He marked his escape in Hebrew verse. His grandson printed those verses in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amsterdam-n-y-1:
Amsterdam is a city in Montgomery County, New York. It stands on the Mohawk River. It lies 33 miles northwest of Albany. In 1900 the town held 20,929 souls. Its first Jewish settlers are named in order. Harris Davis came first, then Isaac Mark. Julius Wasserman came to the town in 1865.

In 1886 Wasserman was named postmaster of the town. He built a broom works that bears the town's name. By 1900 about 250 Jews lived in Amsterdam. Half of them went to the Reform temple. The Temple of Israel was formed in Jan. 1874. A new temple site was bought in 1900. Three clubs for aid and letters are named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anjou-1543:
Anjou is an old province of France, bordered by Poitou, Brittany, Maine, and Touraine. Jews seem to have settled there early, as in the lands around it. One of the first known rabbis, Joseph Tob-Elem, about 1050, bore the title of chief of the community of Limousin and of Anjou.

Provincial rabbis joined synods led by Rabbenu Tam before 1171, and Samuel of Anjou studied under the famed Tosafist Isaac of Dampierre. Yet the entry admits that almost nothing is known of Anjou's Jews until documents speak. They tell of massacres in 1236, by Crusaders, in which 3,000 Jews were killed and 500 baptized. A rabbi's elegy for the martyrs is also recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ardashar-1743: Ardashar is a village in the government of Erivan, in Russian Transcaucasia, about sixteen miles south-southeast of the city of Erivan. It stands on the site of Artaxata, the old Armenian capital. Artaxata, the entry says, was built for King Artaxias I, who reigned 189-159 B.C., by Hannibal, in 180 B.C. Nero's army destroyed it, and Artashes, who ruled in 85-127, restored it. He moved captive Jews from Palestine there. When the Persians wrecked the city in 370, they carried off 40,000 Armenian and 9,000 Jewish families as prisoners.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arvad-the-class:
Arvad, the classical Aradus, helped make Tyre great, as Ezekiel chapter 27 reports. Its men rowed Tyre's ships and manned Tyre's walls. Genesis chapter 10 lists Arvad among the offspring of Canaan, which gives the name Arvadite. The city, now Ruwad or Ruweida, stood on so small an island that its builders were forced to raise tall structures.

Trade made it strong early. It held out against Thothmes and against Assurbanipal, yet in time it sank to second place behind Tyre. Standing did not vanish, though. First Maccabees chapter 15 records a letter from the consul Lucius to Aradus, ordering it not to oppress the Jews. The entry keeps to these points: island site, sea trade, and slow eclipse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asheri-the-ashe: Asheri is the name by which Asher ben Jehiel is often cited in rabbinical writing, above all in discussions of law. Modern historians use a formed plural, Asherides, when they speak of his sons and descendants. The entry states that naming use, points the reader to the main entry on Asher ben Jehiel, and gives no life facts of its own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assize-of-jewry:
Assize of Jewry was a term used in thirteenth-century England. It named the laws and customs that governed dealings between Jews and Christians in that country. Those rules bound the work of the Exchequer of the Jews, a special court. Like most early English law, the assize was never put together in one official book. It grew from written and unwritten sources.

The written part rested on church rules and on charters, the agreements made between the king and the Jews. The entry points readers to an attempt to rebuild the twelfth-century assize in Jacobs, "Jews of Angevin England." It notes that the thirteenth-century assize had not yet been collected.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aurum-coronariu:
Aurum Coronarium was a tax paid to the Roman emperor by all the provinces. It began as a free gift toward a golden crown for a general granted a triumph. In time it hardened into a set tax. Emperors who kept it light, such as Augustus, Hadrian, and Antoninus Pius, won praise for their restraint.

Rome also used the name for the yearly tribute Jews paid to support the patriarchate. Emperors disliked the name, since it hinted that the patriarch held royal rights. They tried to stop the payment. Even Julian, friendly to the Jews in other ways, asked the patriarch Julus to free the Roman Jews from it. The tax bore hard on Palestine. The Talmud tells that in the days of the patriarch Judah I., all the people of Tiberias fled to escape paying it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bank-joshua-ben: Joshua ben Isaac Bank was a rabbi at Tulchin, Russia, born at Satanov in the first half of the nineteenth century. The entry lists three works by him. "Sippurim Nifla'im" (Wonderful Tales), printed at Odessa in 1870, turns tales from other tongues into Hebrew verse. "Rosh Millin," printed at Jitomir in 1872, is a short Hebrew and Judæo-German dictionary. "Tebusat Abshalom" (The Downfall of Absalom), printed at Odessa in 1868, is a tragedy in verse, with a supplement of tales, legends, and epigrams.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnacle-goose-:
Barnacle-goose treats the medieval notion that this bird was generated from the barnacle, a shell-fish growing on a flexible stem on loose timber and ships' bottoms. Shakespeare alludes to the metamorphosis, and serious writers of the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries repeat it. Gerald of Wales and Gervase of Tilbury, in 1211, place the birds on the Kentish shore. Gerald turns the myth against Jews, urging them to accept a birth without male or female.

Jewish writers also took the story up. Joseph Caro treats it in the Shulḥan 'Aruk, and Solomon Luria and Yair Ḥayyim Bacharach cite it from non-Jewish sources. Phineas Elijah of Wilna, about 1790, reports geese growing on trees by the water in Scotland and seems to have believed the fable. As late as 1863 the story was still credited in Russia. The entry closes by weighing a possible Oriental origin for the myth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnett-morris-:
Morris Barnett, dramatist and actor, was born in 1800 and died at Montreal on March 18, 1856. Trained for music, he chose the stage instead. After a provincial tour he appeared at Drury Lane in 1833 and scored a success in Jerrold's "The Schoolfellows." His own musical play "Monsieur Jacques" succeeded greatly at the St. James's Theater in 1837, with himself in the title-rôle. It won him vogue as a portrayer of French characters.

He later joined the "Morning Post" and the "Era," serving as the latter's music critic for about seven years. In September 1854 he sailed for America after farewell performances at the Adelphi. Illness spoiled the tour and ended in his death. His later plays were chiefly comedies, among them "The Serious Family" and "The Bold Dragoons."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassevi-hendel-:
Hendel Bassevi was the second wife of Jacob Bassevi of Prague and a daughter of Ebert Geronim. She died in the summer of 1628. Her tomb bears the family arms granted to her husband by Emperor Ferdinand in 1622, a blue lion with eight red stars.

Hendel was known for wide charity. She took in orphans, gave dowries to brides, and backed poor scholars. She paid for lights in synagogues and put books in schools. When Hebrew books were seized early in the Thirty Years' War, she helped supply synagogues and prayer-books across Austria and Moravia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-solomo:
Solomon Abendana Belmonte was a jurist born in Hamburg in 1843. He died there on March 19, 1888. Schooled in his home city, he studied law at Berlin, Heidelberg, and Göttingen. He then practiced as an advocate in Hamburg from 1864.

Belmonte won a name as a gifted speaker in court and a popular counselor. Voters sent him to the Hamburg assembly in 1887, where he sat until his death. He also served on the prison board and the medical college and worked for Jewish charities. For a short time he also held the office of assistant public prosecutor in his native city of Hamburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benham-arthur-2: Arthur Benham, a writer for the stage, was born in 1875 and died at Brighton, England, on Sept. 8, 1895. He showed real promise as a playwright while still very young. Two of his plays reached London stages, one at the Garrick and one at Terry's Theater. He was only twenty years old at the time of those runs. He died of consumption soon past that age. His sister, the actress Estelle Burney, had worked with him on the plays and nursed him through his long illness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bered-3043: Bered is a name the entry treats in two short senses. First, it was a son of Ephraim, named in First Chronicles. In the genealogy of Numbers his place is taken by Becher, and the two may be the same man. Second, Bered was a place named in the story of Hagar. Beer Laḥai Roi is placed between Kadesh and Bered in Genesis. The old renderings tie the name to Shur, but the entry states the site has not been identified.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-israe:
Israel Bernstein, a Russian Hebrew publicist, was born about the middle of the nineteenth century at Velizh. He studied pharmacy at Moscow and worked as a druggist near Bobruisk. His long pieces in a Hebrew journal struck hard at the faults of teachers, rabbis, and communal bosses in the small towns.

A third piece urged that rabbis and rich Jews stop using foul means to keep their sons from army service. After the persecutions of the early eighties, a letter of 1886 shows his hopes for fair treatment in ruins and his own views confessed as errors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezalel-b-moses:
Bezalel b. Moses ha-Kohen was a Talmudist of Wilna. He was born there on January 14, 1820. He died there on April 13, 1878. At eighteen he already ranked as a competent Talmudist. He even criticized a leading scholar by letter. In 1840 he became an ecclesiastical assistant at Wilna.

The entry says the humble title hid real power. From 1860 he truly led Wilna's large community. Questions reached him from far and near. His answers fill the responsa literature of the time. His own book, "Reshit Bikkurim," appeared in 1869. Unusually, he also valued secular sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brann-marcus-36:
Marcus Brann was a German historian born in Rawitsch on July 9, 1849. He was a son of Rabbi Solomon Brann. He studied at Breslau's university and rabbinical seminary, finishing in 1875.

Brann served as rabbi and teacher in several places till 1891. On Graetz's death he took the chair of history and Bible study at Breslau. His books include a text-book of Jewish history and a history of the Jews in Silesia. He edited a Jewish almanac from 1890. From 1892 he co-edited the Monatsschrift, and from 1899 he edited it alone. A memorial volume for David Kaufmann also came from his hand in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burial-society-:
Burial society names an organization that provides proper burial rites. The entry says hardly a Jewish congregation in the world lacks one. Its members attend the dying, watch over the corpse, wash and shroud it, and walk with it to burial. They do all this without charge. The Hebrew name means holy association or society of true kindness.

Talmud passages already mention such a body, with townsfolk freed from the duty to stop work when a society handled burials. The entry follows the institution across many lands and centuries. It ends in New York, where one society founded in 1889 had 2,200 members by 1901. That body had given 8,263 free burials by Jan. 1, 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calvert-thomas-: Thomas Calvert was an English Hebrew scholar born in 1606. He died at York in March 1679. The entry names one work of his. Printed at York in 1648, it recast a well known letter tied to Samuel of Morocco. That letter itself likely grew from a polemical treatise by Samuel Abu Nasr ibn Abbas. The notice is only a few lines and gives no facts about Calvert's posts or teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalan-gerson-:
Gerson b. Solomon Catalan, an author who lived at Arles in the middle of the thirteenth century, died, possibly, at Perpignan late in that century. Zacuto and others call him the father of Levi b. Gerson, known as Gersonides. About 1280 he compiled an encyclopedia titled Sha'ar ha-Shamayim, the Door of Heaven.

Following Ibn Palquera, Catalan split his work into three parts. The first treats physics, with a chapter on dreams. The second treats astronomy, drawn chiefly from Al-Fergani. The third treats theology, and Catalan states plainly that it holds nothing new. It copies Maimonides' Book of the Soul. Greek and Arabic authors quoted range from Aristotle and Plato to Averroes, Avicenna, and Al-Farabi. The work was printed at Venice in 1547 and at Rödelheim in 1801.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colchester-4543:
Colchester, the county town of Essex, England, first names Jews in its records in 1185. They likely shared in the massacre of 1190. The community carried weight: it ranked ninth in its payment toward the ransom of Richard I in 1194. By 1220 it had a special bailiff, one Benedict, probably to gather its taxes.

An agreement of 1258 maps the Jewry in Stockwell street. A stranger tale comes from 1267, when Jews and Christians together broke forest law by chasing a doe. The Jews were fined more heavily, and one man's portrait was drawn on the Forest Roll itself. At the expulsion of 1290, nine houses and a school passed to the king, hinting the town stood about seventh among England's Jewries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dacosta-isaac-f: Isaac-Francis Dacosta was a musician and composer, born at Bordeaux on Jan. 17, 1778. He died there on Nov. 29, 1864. He entered the Musical Conservatory as a pupil in 1798. Later, as first cornet at the Paris opera, he was vice-leader of the king's bodyguard band under Louis the Eighteenth. He wrote several romances and concertos. In 1836 Meyerbeer composed a clarinet solo for him. It stands in the fifth act of The Huguenots. He is believed to have been a son of the musician Samuel-Franco Dacosta.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-gerson-49: Gerson David was rabbi at Reshid, Egypt, in the middle of the seventeenth century. His responsa appear in the "Darke No'am" of his contemporary Mordecai ben Judah ha-Levi. Abraham ben Mordecai ha-Levi, who had been his pupil, praised him as a great rabbinical authority. One ruling of his is remembered in detail: he ended the practice of lighting a pipe from a tallow candle. He said a dream had shown him punished as if he had eaten fat, because he lit his pipe that way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dob-baer-b-loeb: Dob Baer b. Loeb was a Polish rabbi who died at Lemberg in 1779. He held the rabbinate at Koznitz in 1745 and at Kroshnik in 1754. That same period took him to Yaroslav, where rabbis met to defend Jonathan Eybeschütz against Jacob Emden. In 1758 he became rabbi of Reshaw. He ended as rabbi and head of the yeshibah at Lemberg, staying there until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dove-12143:
The dove is among the most familiar birds of Palestine in the entry's account. The Hebrew yonah covers the pigeon family, while tor names the turtle-dove alone. Noah sent a dove out from the Ark in the flood story. Doves and turtle-doves were the only birds allowed as sacrifices.

The Talmud names about ten kinds of doves, from dovecot birds to house-kept attic birds. Herodian doves were bred in towers by Herod's palace gardens. Betting on dove races was known, and its players ranked with gamblers as unfit witnesses. The Temple kept a special officer for sacrificial doves. Mustard, the entry notes, was thought their favored food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dublin-5343:
Dublin's Jewish community is among the oldest in Britain since the Resettlement. It was founded in the first half of the eighteenth century. In 1748 Michael Phillips gave ground at Drumcondra for a cemetery. London's Bevis Marks congregation paid to wall that ground.

By about 1791 the congregation worshiped in Marlborough street, by a glass-works yard. It then decayed, and its goods were seized for rent. Two scrolls of the Law were saved by the brothers Cohen. In 1822 the few families left reopened worship at Stafford street. They later bought a meeting-house at Mary's Abbey for £300.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-efes-afes-or-pa:
Efes, also Afes or Pas, was a scholar of the third century. He served as secretary to the patriarch Judah I. He ranks among the last of the tannaim. After Judah died, Efes ran a college in southern Judea. That post earned him the name Efes the Southerner.

Efes then became head of the academy at Sepphoris. Judah had named Hanina ben Hama for the post instead. Hanina refused to displace a man two and a half years his senior. Among Efes's pupils stood Hosha'yah Rabba. He carried several of his master's sayings to later readers. Efes died not long after Judah, and Hanina followed him at Sepphoris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-eliezer: Eleazar ha-Kappar was a tanna of the second century. He belonged to the fourth generation of the tannaim. The Mishnah quotes Eleazar in the Sayings of the Fathers. Envy, lust, and ambition shorten a man's life, he taught. A longer saying of his is also kept there. The born must die, the dead rise, and the living face judgment, it runs. All men must give account before the King of Kings. Great is peace, he said, for it is the end of all blessings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emrich-solomon-: Solomon Emrich was a judge of the Jewish court at Prague. He lived in the late eighteenth century. His one book holds six talks on points of ritual law. One of them argues a point with Ezekiel Landau. That point is the law of halizah, the shoe rite. The book came out at Prague in 1789. Its title hides a small word play, the entry notes. The first letters of the title spell the author's own name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-expectation-of-:
Expectation of life means the years a person may expect to live past a given age, read from death tables. The entry studies Jewish and Christian figures side by side. Its earliest source is De Neufville's 1855 work on Frankfort deaths in 1846-1848. That study counted 3,213 Christian deaths and 263 Jewish ones. A United States inquiry under Dr. John S. Billings covered about 10,000 Jewish families.

The entry faults both studies for hiding their methods, which weakens the tables. Still, its survival table is striking. Of 1,000 born, 867 Jews reached age ten against 736 Christians. At age fifty, 540 Jews survived against 351 Christians. At eighty, the counts are 69 and 37. A second table sets United States Jews beside non-Jews in Massachusetts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-family-and-fami:
Family, in this long entry, means both a line traced from one ancestor and a household under one head. Houses of David, Levi, and Israel show the wide sense. The narrow sense takes in parents, children, in-laws, and dependents. Kinship grounds the whole order, though outsiders could join the union by a legal fiction.

Much weight falls on purity of descent, the entry notes. Abraham sent his servant to his own kin for Isaac's wife. Samson's family balked at his foreign match, yet such marriages stayed common.
