Seegert and colleagues read the contrast as evidence that broader orders carry clearer information. The study speaks to how governments communicate risk, beyond masks alone, during fast-moving crises.
plos-pone-0339543:
Esraa A Salim led a team of seven authors hunting drug combinations against a rare breast cancer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Inflammatory breast cancer is uncommon and aggressive, and new treatment options are badly needed. The team began with computer predictions, then tested the best candidates in real cancer cells.

Salim's pipeline identified drugs and paired combinations that slow the growth of these cancer cells, with synergy between partners. Moving from in silico screening to lab validation in one study strengthens the claims. The candidates now merit further testing toward clinical use. For patients with few options, a disciplined route from computation to bench evidence is exactly how new therapies start.
plos-pone-0339943:
Wenhao Guo and co-workers study why women in China sign up for adventure sports trips such as skiing, surfing, and rock climbing. Such travel is growing, yet social expectations still hold some women back. Their 2026 paper surveys more than five hundred women at well-known activity sites and asks how drive, confidence, and sense of standing shape their plans.

Both inner enjoyment and outer rewards raised plans to take part, but through different routes. Inner drive worked mainly through personal confidence and a sense of public standing. That standing, understood as earning respect and a fair place, proved the strongest path of all. Feeling that a sport was risky weakened these links, so safer planning may help more women join in.
plos-pone-0340243:
Corentin Lucas and six co-authors try a deliberately simple idea for finding Crohn's disease lesions around the anus on MRI scans, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Such lesions usually sit on one side, so the team measured how lopsided each scan looked in shape and brightness. Their features were designed to work across different scan types, which often trip up automated tools.

On a small, clear-cut test set the method performed strongly, but accuracy fell on harder validation cases, especially lesions wrapped around both sides. The authors present the work as proof of concept: asymmetry is a real signal, yet not enough alone for a dependable clinical tool.
plos-pone-0342143:
Changrong Lu and co-authors argue that large digital platforms quietly discipline public emotion and behaviour. Their 2026 study links interface design, recommendation systems, and feedback loops to standardised behaviour and growing dependence on platform cues. They built a daily measure of emotional polarisation from news sentiment and compared it with the research output of big technology firms.

Treating 2020 as a turning point, the analysis traces how platform governance tracks sharper emotional splits between online groups. The authors are careful that their measure reflects the information environment, not individual minds. Lu and colleagues frame platform design as a form of soft power that shapes how publics feel and argue, with consequences for democratic debate.
plos-pone-0342443:
Guido Catalano and colleagues survey in 2026 how well children and teenagers with impaired vision manage daily life, feelings, and quality of life across five specialist centres. Caregivers for about ninety young people completed trusted questionnaires on independence, behaviour, and life quality, split into younger and older age bands. Vision shapes social life, school inclusion, and self reliance from early years.

Both age groups scored in a medium to high range for independence and showed sound emotional and life quality scores. Teenagers scored lower on independence than younger children overall. Greater independence tied strongly to better life quality and fewer behaviour problems, making it a key rehabilitation target.
plos-pone-0343143:
Federico Zilia and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on turning leek waste into a plant-boosting extract for greenhouse lettuce. The work pairs two tasks. First, the team measured the full footprint of making the extract. They also measured the footprint of growing lettuce with it. Second, they asked how a firm could actually sell such a product.

Lettuce grown with the extract scored better on most measures of harm. Gains included less acid rain impact and less water toxicity. Making the extract itself carried some costs in resource use. The authors then mapped each problem spot to the actor best placed to fix it. The actors ranged from processors to farmers. They also sketched ways to pay for checks and upgrades. The approach links hard data to business choices for residue-based farm goods.
plos-pone-0343243:
Melissa Allen and colleagues test how age affects the split-second act of reading gender from a face, in this 2026 PLOS ONE psychology study. Six hundred adults aged eighteen to sixty-nine saw faces paired with the pronouns he or she, sometimes matching the face's stereotype and sometimes not, while the team timed their answers.

Older participants answered more slowly overall and reported more negative, more conflicted feelings about pronoun use, though also fewer worries about it. Crucially, the slowdown when pronoun and face mismatched was no bigger in older adults than in younger ones. Automatic gender reading, it seems, stays stable across adulthood even as stated attitudes shift with generation.
plos-pone-0344143:
Negar Mottaghi-Dastjerdi and Mohammad Soltany-Rezaee-Rad analyzed gene activity in stomach cancer tissue to show how the cancer rewires the organ at a structural level. Stomach cancer is a major killer worldwide and is hard to catch early. Their network approach linked gene expression data with clinical details such as stage, spread to lymph nodes, and metastasis.

Across patient groups the same signature appeared: the cancer switched on developmental genes, most notably the HOX family that normally pattern the embryo, while losing the identity genes of healthy stomach lining. In effect, tumor tissue partly reverts to an early developmental program. Signatures like this help explain the disease's behavior and may point to stage-specific markers worth testing in the clinic.
plos-pone-0345043:
Cao and Zha, in a 2026 paper, tackle a hard choice in instant delivery: some orders cost more to serve than they are worth. When fleets are stretched, trying to serve everyone can raise costs and break time promises. Their model lets a platform drop a small share of costly customers on purpose.

The team built a routing plan that weighs vehicle costs, travel costs, and penalties for late arrival. They solved it with an improved genetic algorithm, a search method that breeds better routes over many rounds. In a case study, their solver beat a standard genetic method and a tabu search on speed, cost, and stability, with no missed time windows. Dropping a small share of hard orders cut total cost sharply, mostly by shrinking the fleet. Tests at larger scale showed the same pattern. The authors argue that planned, selective refusal can use scarce delivery resources better.
plos-pone-0345143:
Matthew Boot and co-authors studied how a parasitic guest ant keeps the peace inside its host's nest. The guest lives long-term inside a fungus-farming ant colony, taking resources while also defending the shared home. Their 2026 study staged encounters, measured venom doses, and quantified how the guest presents its sting chemistry.

Guest ants make conspicuous, costly displays of venom during meetings with hosts. Because the display is expensive to fake, the authors read it as an honest signal rather than a bluff. Signalling may calm conflict by advertising the guest's value as a defender. Boot and colleagues argue parasite signals deserve study as negotiated communication, not only as manipulation, when both sides gain from calm.
plos-pone-0345343:
Victoria Manasevich, Daria Kostanian, Anton Rogachev, and Olga Sysoeva wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review of the EEG signs that track how the brain handles the rise time of sounds. Rise time is how quickly a sound swells from silence, a cue the brain uses in hearing speech and music.

EEG records the brain's electrical activity, and correlates are the brain signals that track rise time changes. Gathering the scattered studies into one review shows what is firmly known and what is still guesswork. Hearing scientists and speech researchers, including those studying reading disorders tied to rhythm perception, are the audience.
plos-pone-0345843:
Celine Brooks led a team of eight authors on this 2026 mouse study of a protein-folding machine inside the eye's light-sensing rod cells. The machine, called TRiC, folds many proteins these cells depend on. Using mice engineered so the machine could be fished out of retina tissue, the team catalogued over two hundred partner proteins.

Blocking the machine cut levels of its known folding clients and disturbed energy metabolism proteins. Brooks links proper folding to the rod cell's power supply, and shows how overloading the machine can tip the eye toward degeneration.
plos-pone-0347343:
Xiaoyu Huang and co-workers build a phone-based system that watches transplanted tissue flaps after surgery and warns of trouble early. A flap fails most often when blood pools and cannot drain, and fast rescue saves it. Their 2026 study trains a deep learning model on photos from hundreds of patients and wraps it in a phone app for remote checks.

In testing at the home hospital and beyond, the model sorted healthy and troubled flaps with high accuracy. It caught nearly all cases of dangerous congestion while raising few false alarms. In live ward use it kept that record. Nurses could check flaps from afar and act sooner, which matters most where specialists are few.
plos-pone-0347443:
Jaeeun Yoo analyzed immune patterns in lupus across several cohorts, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Lupus patients have immune systems already on edge, and transfused donor blood can provoke reactions called alloimmunization. Yoo linked the strength of the type I interferon signature, a marker of immune activation, to gene programs tied to that risk.

The analysis suggests the signature may predict which patients will react badly to transfusions before blood is given. A warning like that lets doctors choose blood products more carefully or watch high-risk patients closely. Multi-cohort work strengthens the claim, since the pattern held across groups. Transfusion is common in lupus care, so a predictive marker has everyday value.
plos-pone-0347643:
Yan Yan, Mingxie Chen, Chuanyong Tang, and Sheng Wang mapped soil erosion across the world's karst regions, the limestone landscapes that cover about fifteen percent of Earth's land. Thin soils and underground drainage make these areas unusually fragile. Using a standard ecosystem model plus satellite-era data, the 2026 study tracked erosion from 2000 to 2020 and separated the roles of climate and human activity.

Erosion eased worldwide overall, though it stayed harsh across the south-west of Asia and the south of Europe. In North America the worst losses sat in the north-west, and that region's rate actually rose. Rainfall drove erosion most strongly, while scenario tests credited human activity with nearly half of the changes. Russia, China, and Europe led the reductions, the authors report.
plos-pone-0347943:
Robert W. Hurley, Daniel Guth, Elaine L. Hill, and Meredith C. B. Adams checked whether a diagnostic code on insurance claims actually identifies patients on long-term opioid therapy. Researchers and regulators often treat the code as equivalent to pharmacy records showing ninety days of prescriptions. Using complete Medicare and Medicaid claims from 2016 to 2022, covering well over a hundred million people, they tested the code against the prescription standard.

The code missed about two-thirds of true long-term users in both programs, though it rarely flagged the wrong people. Worse, patients found by code alone carried different risks, with more opioid use disorder diagnoses than those found by prescriptions. The authors warn that code-based surveillance badly distorts the picture.
plos-pone-0348143:
Fah Lertkulvanich and two co-workers read the full gene sets of four spiders that live in a plant trap. The plant is a pitcher plant in a Thai park. Its cups hold fluid that digests bugs. These spiders live in the cups, eat the trapped bugs, and are not digested. Three are crab spiders, and one is a huntsman.

Some genes for cell power had changed fast in these spiders, a mark of life in a strange home. The crab spiders also held rare shifts in gene order. One had a doubled control stretch. The work gives fresh facts for kin charts and for the study of life in odd homes.
plos-pone-0348443:
Mohammed Abdullah Hamad, Ahmed J. Alfahdawi, and Basim Mohamed Manswr characterize a fowl adenovirus strain taken from Iraqi chicken farms. The virus causes a liver disease that threatens broiler flocks, and this type has been reappearing in several regions. Their 2026 study infects young broiler chicks with the local isolate and examines organs and virus levels three weeks later.

Infected birds developed swollen, pale livers and enlarged dark spleens, with milder changes in kidneys and little in hearts. Virus copies ran highest in the liver, matching the damage pattern. No birds died, which points to a mild strain. Regional data like this helps farms watch for the right virus types and plan protection that fits local strains.
plos-pone-0348843:
Haiyan Zhang and colleagues designed TransitNet, a compact computer vision network that labels every part of a street scene, such as roads, cars, and sidewalks. Large labeling networks are too heavy for the small computers inside vehicles. TransitNet aims to stay accurate while using far fewer resources.

Built on an existing design, it adds modules that link distant parts of a scene and blend fine detail with broad context. A star-shaped backbone keeps the parameter count low. The network also adapts across different kinds of scenes, from traffic views to remote sensing images. Lightweight scene understanding like this is what driver-assistance systems and roadside cameras need to run in real time.
plos-pone-0348943:
Sofie Meijer and colleagues compared the gut microbes of Swedish women with the two forms of preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy blood-pressure disorder that arrives either early or late, against healthy pregnancies. Earlier studies lumped the forms together and used shallow sequencing. Thirty-seven women in late pregnancy gave samples read by deep shotgun sequencing, which names species and functions rather than broad groups.

Both preeclampsia groups' gut communities differed measurably from controls', surviving adjustment for age and body size, with the late-onset form showing the stronger shifts and lower diversity. A few named bacteria emerged as leads, though none survived the strictest statistical correction, and function-level differences washed out entirely. The careful, mostly negative detail matters: microbiome links to this disorder are real but subgroup-shaped, and small studies should stop promising simple signatures.
plos-pone-0349343:
Youming Huang and colleagues show that the plant hormone abscisic acid controls how rice flowers close, a detail that matters greatly in hybrid seed production. Rice spikelets open and close on a daily rhythm, and poor closure wastes pollen and cuts seed set. The team sprayed fertile and sterile rice lines with the hormone and with a blocker of its production, at several strengths.

The hormone sped closure, shortened the open window, and raised final closure rates, with a middle dose range working best; the blocker did the opposite. Gene sequencing of the tiny organs that push the flower open confirmed the hormone's pathway was active. In breeding fields, combining the hormone with a second treatment improved seed setting, a direct yield lever for hybrid rice.
plos-pone-0349643:
Marta Sfulcini, Erminio Trevisi, and co-authors studied how weaning hits dairy calves' immune systems, and why some calves grow poorly through the transition. Weaning stacks diet change, separation, and new surroundings into one stressful week. Their 2026 study split forty female Holstein calves into high and low growers over the ten days after weaning and compared blood chemistry and immune gene activity in white blood cells.

Weaning switched on innate immune pathways in all calves. Low growers, though, mounted a bigger immune response and showed blood signs of energy shortage, burning protein for fuel. High growers passed through with a quieter profile. The authors say the difference points to unequal resilience, and that spotting vulnerable calves early could let farmers support them through weaning.
plos-pone-0349943:
Crowded sea lanes raise the risk of ships colliding, and Minmin Zheng and co-authors combine two methods to plot safer courses. Their 2026 PLOS One paper pairs a rule-based reasoning system with a velocity obstacle method, a geometric way of finding paths that miss moving ships.

First, ships moving alike and sailing close are grouped, so the planner handles fewer targets. Safety zones around each ship or group scale with vessel length. The path method then draws avoidance routes toward the destination. Tests in two busy scenarios showed safer, smoother sailing. The authors offer the approach as a step toward smarter bridge decision support.
plos-pone-0350043:
Machines that caption sounds learn from human-written descriptions, and Laura Hekanaho and colleagues compared those descriptions in English and Finnish. Their 2026 PLOS One study is among the first to inspect this training data as language, including descriptions written by blind and sighted Finns.

The Finnish collections varied far more than the English one, which the authors trace partly to English writers working in a second language. A close reading of one hundred fifty descriptions showed what people choose to mention about a soundscape and what they leave out. The findings matter for accessibility tools, since captions trained on thin descriptions will describe the world thinly.
plos-pone-0350343:
Yoann Zafiriou and co-authors tested whether resilience protects anaesthesia staff during a simulated crisis in 2026. The specialty carries high burnout, and resilience is often promoted as a shield, but its link to the body's stress response was untested.

Thirty-four anaesthetists, trainees, and nurse anaesthetists completed a resilience scale, then faced a high fidelity child airway emergency simulation. Heart rhythm measures and self rated stress were tracked. Resilience scores sat in a mid range, yet neither body nor mind stress responses tied significantly to them. The result questions easy claims that resilient staff simply stay calm under fire.
plos-pone-0350643:
Jorge Maurino and co-authors studied procrastination among clinicians who manage spinal muscular atrophy in Spain in 2026. Delaying hard decisions is a known failure of self control, worsened by stressful clinical work, and the team linked it to burnout and regret.

Thirty-seven professionals from a national registry completed standard scales for delay, regret, attitudes to evidence, and burnout. About a third showed moderate to high procrastination. Modelling explored whether burnout feeds delay through regret over past choices. Even a small study matters here: if delay is common in rare disease care, systems, not just willpower, need redesign.
plos-pone-0350743:
Ivan Nirmalaraj, Nicholas Sookhan, and J. Scott MacIvor test a new way to measure how worn a bumble bee's wings are, in this 2026 study from a Toronto-area national park. Wings fray with flight, so wear hints at a bee's age and foraging effort, but existing scoring is coarse and subjective. The team photographed the forewings of more than two hundred sixty worker bees from three species and measured edge complexity using fractal geometry.

Fractal scores tracked human visual wear grades more closely than a simpler perimeter-to-area measure, and unlike that measure they were not distorted by body size. Undamaged wings also differed between species, giving each a baseline. The authors propose fractal dimension as a sensitive, objective tool for judging bee condition in field studies, useful for tracking colony stress and pollinator health.
plos-pone-0350943:
Maria Clara Ferreira, Frederico Kremer, and Vanessa Galli built a software tool that guesses which circular RNAs, a loop-shaped class of RNA, help plants weather cold and drought. Loops are hard to study one by one, so prediction narrows the field. Their tool reads the RNA's letter sequence, chops it into short fragments, and turns those fragments into numbers using a technique borrowed from language software, then classifies with a random forest.

Trained on rice and maize loop RNAs with known stress links, the tool sorted independent test sets well enough to serve as a screening instrument. Breeders hunting stress-resilient crops face thousands of candidate molecules; a ranked shortlist from sequence alone saves seasons of bench work. The authors offer the tool as an open starting point for a corner of plant biology that lacked one.
plos-pone-0351143:
Adults and children may not value the same rewards. Money means a lot to adults. Its pull on children is less clear. Sebastijan Veselic and colleagues compared fifty-one adults with thirty-nine children. The children were aged seven to twelve. Three tasks tested value, effort, and attention control. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Adults responded more strongly to money-like rewards. Children reacted about equally to both reward kinds. Food and treats counted as primary rewards here. Tokens and money counted as secondary rewards. The gap suggests learned rewards gain power with age. The authors add a caution. The two reward types were not perfectly matched. Age studies must weigh what a prize means to each group.
plos-pone-0351243:
Christoph Steup and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One genomic study of bowel cancer that has spread to the liver and been treated with antibody drugs targeting the EGFR pathway. Such treatment can shrink initially inoperable tumors enough for surgery, but resistant cell clones may grow meanwhile. The team sequenced tumor samples from thirty patients, taken before and after treatment, and compared them with public cancer genome datasets.

Samples taken after treatment carried resistance-linked mutations more often, spread thinly across many genes rather than concentrated in a few. Neither the total mutation count nor the well-known RAS status predicted whether tumors became operable. Reassuringly, even where resistance mutations appeared in subclones, they did not block successful removal of the liver tumors. The authors question how much routine profiling adds in this setting.
plos-pone-0351543:
Many insects stop eating as adults, living only to mate, and their guts fill with air instead of food. Hollister W Herhold and colleagues scanned such insects with micro CT imaging to measure that hidden air, in this 2026 PLOS One study spanning several insect orders.

The inflated gut was known from mayflies and one other group; scans now show it in stoneflies, webspinners, dobsonflies, moths, and true flies too. Species that had lost adult feeding carried strikingly more gut air, a link statistics confirmed strongly. Why the air helps is unsettled: buoyancy, display, or flight balance are candidates the authors weigh for future tests.
plos-pone-0351643:
Ju Zhao and colleagues sharpened satellite estimates of soil moisture over China's Wujiang River Basin, a rugged karst landscape where fields and rock fracture the ground. A NASA satellite reads moisture coarsely, and one model for all seasons fits none of them well there. The team trained separate seasonal models, mixing satellite drought indicators with terrain data, and compared five learning algorithms.

The seasonal CatBoost models beat single-model baselines, doing best in spring and autumn. Reading the model's reasoning showed its logic shifting with the year: winter estimates leaned on terrain, summer ones on heat and water signals. That rotation matches how moisture actually behaves in the basin. Better seasonal soil moisture maps feed drought warnings and water planning in mountain country where ground sensors are sparse.
plos-pone-0351943:
Edita Garskaite and seven colleagues turn eggshell waste into fire-resistant wood. Their 2026 study closes a loop: shells that bakeries discard become mineral protection for timber. First, water-insoluble proteins were extracted from shell membranes and fragments by boiling with denaturing agents. The mineral shell was converted into a calcium solution. Pine sapwood then soaked in two baths, phosphate first, calcium second. Inside the wood, the two met and grew a bone-like mineral, carbonated hydroxyapatite, in place.

Microscopy showed modest saturation: the wood's channels stayed mostly open. Element maps, though, showed calcium and phosphorus spread evenly throughout. Diffraction confirmed the mineral's identity and its carbonate substitution. Fire behaviour was measured with two calorimeter instruments. Timber construction is booming as a low-carbon choice, but wood burns. A waste-derived mineral grown inside the fibres, rather than coated on top, could protect buildings while giving eggshells a second industrial life.
plos-pone-0352143:
Zhiqiao Cheng, Ping Li, and Jingsheng Pan ground steel slag asphalt under accelerated wear to learn how its skid resistance ages, and how much slag a road crew should use. Steel slag, a steelmaking waste, grips tires well but roads must stay grippy for years at real temperatures. The lab program crossed three slag contents with three temperatures and measured two standard grip indicators as abrasion cycles piled up.

Both grip measures fell steadily as wear accumulated, and heat sped the decline sharply, a warning for hot-climate highways. The two indicators moved together closely, so either can track the other in monitoring. With wear curves in hand, engineers can set slag doses by climate zone instead of habit, and schedule resurfacing before a polished road turns treacherous in the rain.
plos-pone-0352243:
Xiaorong Bai and five colleagues run a brisk walking trial for overweight older women in China. Their 2026 study is a cluster-randomised trial with fifty-four women aged sixty to sixty-nine. Half walked briskly three times a week for twelve weeks. Sessions ran from thirty-five to sixty minutes. The other half kept their usual routines. Fitness, balance, and life satisfaction were measured at the start and the end.

Walking delivered broad gains. Heart and lung fitness, flexibility, strength, and endurance all improved significantly. Balance got better too, a serious benefit at this age. Life satisfaction rose with the physical gains. Body composition, though, did not shift in twelve weeks. Between-group differences reached significance clearly only on the chair stand test of endurance, while effect sizes grew across measures. The prescription is refreshingly plain: regular brisk walking, no equipment, measurably rebuilds fitness and mood in older women.
plos-pone-0352443:
Elizabeth A McHuron, a single author, published this 2026 study estimating how much energy nursing costs marine mammal mothers each day. Direct measurements are missing for most species, blocking models of how disturbance affects populations. McHuron gathered published milk intake rates and milk energy values from marine mammals and their land relatives, tracking how both change across the nursing period.

Milk intake per body weight fell over time in all groups, fastest in bears and kin, slowest in seals. Whales and dolphins drank heavily early, then dropped fast. The patterns give modelers grounded estimates for species never measured.
plos-pone-0352643:
Mary Bitta and seven colleagues report a large trial of bringing mental health care into ordinary clinics in rural Kilifi County, Kenya, published in 2026. Specialists are almost absent in such regions. The team therefore trained non-specialist primary care workers using the World Health Organization's intervention guide. They then rolled the program out across more than one hundred public facilities in a randomized stepped sequence, with refresher supervision each quarter.

Detection rose sharply once facilities crossed over. Monthly diagnosis rates for epilepsy roughly doubled, while depression, dementia, and substance misuse diagnoses climbed from near zero, all statistically robust after adjustment. Psychosis and suicidality showed raw gains that did not survive adjustment. Health worker stigma fell and patient outcomes improved. The authors call the scale-up feasible and effective, while asking for tests in other settings before general claims.
plos-pone-0353143:
Li and colleagues combined several data layers to find drivers of irregular heartbeat caused by a cancer drug in a 2026 study. The drug, widely used against cancer, can trigger atrial fibrillation, a serious rhythm problem. The team started with drug safety reports, then layered gene, protein network, and immune data.

Candidate targets emerged where drug targets, disease genes, and changed genes overlapped. Hub genes were checked in independent data sets, and docking tests probed direct binding. Naming the mediators could lead to heart-protecting companions for the cancer drug, so patients gain the cancer benefit with less rhythm risk.
plos-pone-0353343:
Altınalan and colleagues combined gene studies of a benign inner-ear tumor in a 2026 analysis. The tumor grows on balance and hearing nerves and often causes gradual hearing loss. Pooling four public data sets let the team find gene changes too faint in any single study.

Thousands of genes differed between tumor and normal tissue, even under strict cutoffs. Changed genes clustered around tissue scaffolding, hearing and nerve signaling, immune activity, and cell growth. Some changed genes already have known drugs that act on them. The map offers fresh leads for biomarkers and drug ideas for a tumor that today is handled mainly by watching or surgery.
plos-pone-0353743:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, profile the chemistry of backfat in Ningxiang pigs, a prized local breed in China, as the animals fatten. Backfat chemistry shapes pork quality, yet the fattening months, from about six months to a year old, were poorly charted. Samples at four ages were scanned for small molecules and matched against carcass traits.

More than one hundred fifty compounds shifted significantly with age, including fats tied to appetite control and fat burning. Plant-derived and vitamin-like compounds built up over time, which the authors read as the fat quietly recording diet and environment. Some man-made chemicals from feed or surroundings also accumulated, a possible flag for pork safety. One network of compounds tracked carcass traits strongly, with an obscure plant alkaloid at its center. The team offers these molecules as candidate markers for breeding and quality checks.
plos-pone-0353843:
Patryk Ziobro led a team of seven authors on this 2026 mouse study of exercise wheels and social behavior. Female mice raised with a running wheel in the home cage from weaning were tested as adults meeting unfamiliar females, and compared with mice given a simple paper hut.

Wheel-raised females spent less time investigating newcomers and called less during meetings, and two weeks without the wheel did not undo it. Surprisingly, even a locked, immobile wheel produced the same effect, so the object itself, not running, changed social motivation. Ziobro warns mouse study designs to account for cage furniture.
plos-pone-0353943:
Michael Bazaco and colleagues track in 2026 how foodborne outbreaks in the United States changed over two decades, sorted by food type and germ. Four priority germs and seventeen food groups were followed with a Bayesian trend model that handles rare events and hard attribution. Prevention teams need such trends to see which foods are emerging as risks.

Listeria outbreaks tied to dairy rose while those tied to meat and poultry fell. A gut germ's outbreaks tied to dairy and poultry also rose, while a toxin producing gut germ tied to meat fell. Salmonella outbreaks tied to eggs fell as well. The method itself is offered as a reusable trend tool.
plos-pone-0354143:
Kim and Kim, in a 2026 computer study, mine the genomes of African swine fever virus for pieces that could serve in vaccines. The virus kills pigs in huge numbers across Africa, Europe, and Asia, and its strains differ a lot by region, which frustrates one-size vaccine design. The team looked for protein fragments that are common within one country's strains.

Genomes were chopped into short overlapping pieces of four lengths, and pieces enriched in each country with enough genomes were kept. Italy yielded the most pieces, while Russia's pattern differed oddly. The kept pieces were screened as candidate targets for three arms of the immune system, and many were predicted to provoke a response. They came from shell proteins, copying machinery, and large gene families. The resulting library is meant to help design vaccines tuned to each region's virus, and tests of diagnostics as well.
plos-pone-0354243:
Moohebat and Khormaei, in a 2026 study, reframe insomnia as a problem of disconnection rather than loud symptoms. Poor sleep is usually explained by an over-aroused mind. These authors asked instead whether the web of a person's psychological traits hangs together less tightly when sleep is poor. They surveyed about four hundred Iranian university students, roughly split between good and poor sleepers.

Each student's answers on twenty-seven mental traits were turned into a network, with traits as nodes and links as their ties. Poor sleepers' networks were sparser, with more isolated traits and traits that were harder to predict from their neighbors. Overall network strength, however, did not differ. In good sleepers, thinking-related traits sat closer to the center of the web. The authors suggest insomnia may mark a mind whose parts talk to each other less, a shift in how care might be aimed.
plos-pone-0354343:
Yiwei Ge and Jingkun Bi used machine learning to find what predicts whether American teenagers meet muscle-strengthening guidelines. Strength exercise is a core part of youth health advice, yet its drivers are less mapped than aerobic activity's. Their 2026 study drew on a national youth risk survey of about twenty thousand high school students.

About three in five students met the guideline of strengthening on at least three days weekly. The model sorted students well. Overall physical activity level was the top predictor, followed by sex and fruit intake. Explanation plots showed how each factor bends the prediction. Ge and Bi say explainable models can help schools target the habits that travel with strength training.
plos-pone-0354743:
Guolong Zhang, Qian Dan, and Yutian Zhang published this 2026 communications paper on drones kept aloft by laser power. A laser-fed unmanned aircraft can serve ground users, but someone must decide its flight path, its transmission power, and which user it serves at each moment, fairly. Their goal was to lift the weakest user's data rate as high as possible.

The joint problem resists direct solution, so they split it into three smaller problems and solved them in turn with approximation methods. Simulations showed the algorithm settling quickly and steadily on its answer.
plos-pone-0355043:
Di Zhao and three colleagues compare the mitochondrial genomes of gliding and climbing squirrels to see whether their different ways of moving left marks on their DNA, in this 2026 study. The team newly sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of one rare flying squirrel species and lined it up against published genomes from both flying and tree squirrels. Basic organization, gene order, and composition proved highly conserved across the family.

Beneath that stability, four energy-related genes evolved faster in the flying squirrel lineage, and codon usage bias ran stronger there too. These are signs that natural selection pulled the two lineages differently, plausibly matching their energy demands. The reconstructed family tree settled into four subfamilies with strong support and placed flying and tree squirrels as sister groups. The authors offer the genome as a foundation for future work on squirrel evolution.
plos-pone-0355343:
Lixian Mou and fellow doctors test a new scan for finding thyroid cancer that has returned or spread after treatment. Doctors usually track a blood marker for this cancer, but that marker can mislead in both directions. Their scan uses a tracer that sticks to a protein common on cancer-supporting tissue, and they compared scan results against the blood marker in patients checked over about three years.

The scan judged cases more accurately than the blood marker in patients whose hormone levels were held low, and it was flawless in a smaller group tested under stimulation. It also found spread in several patients whose blood marker read negative, mostly in neck lymph nodes. Mou and colleagues say the scan can catch disease the standard marker misses.
plos-pone-0355543:
Nina Wanča, Jakub Jehlička, and Anna Hála studied a new children's exhibition that opened at the National Museum in Prague in 2023. The display was built for children aged five to ten and mixes hands-on stations with more traditional presentation. Rather than lecturing, it asks young visitors to explore and figure things out for themselves.

Over two and a half months the researchers watched hundreds of interactions involving more than two thousand visitors. Older children engaged more deeply, but they made up less than a quarter of the child visitors; most were younger than the intended audience. Many of those younger children seemed to struggle with the exhibition's open-ended design. The authors suggest ways to better match the content to the children who actually come.
plos-pone-0355743:
Bounmy Keohavong and co-authors feed in 2026 four alternative poultry ingredients to specially fed roosters to see how processing changes their value. The ingredients included distillery grains and meals from coconut, palm kernel, and jatropha. Birds received each feed as loose mash or as pellets, and in a second test mash received an enzyme that breaks down a tough plant fibre.

Pelleting raised how much dry matter and nitrogen birds kept and raised usable energy for all ingredients. Adding the enzyme also helped, most for the coconut and palm meals rich in that fibre. Both steps could let feed makers use fibrous byproducts more fully.
plos-pone-0355843:
Getahun Tamiru Yirsaw and co-authors reviewed outcomes for newborn babies treated for meningitis in public hospitals in Harar, Ethiopia. Newborn meningitis kills and disables many infants in low-income settings, yet local outcome data were scarce. Their 2026 study extracted records for about five hundred admitted newborns across four years.

One third of the babies had a poor treatment outcome. Risk climbed with assisted vaginal delivery and with laboratory-confirmed spinal fluid infection. Very high white cell counts in spinal fluid also tracked with poor outcomes. Yirsaw and colleagues argue earlier recognition and closer watch on these flagged babies could improve survival in similar hospitals.
plos-pone-0355943:
Ali Sait Özer and three co-authors address a power problem in wind energy systems in their 2026 engineering paper. Wind-driven generators that excite themselves can produce rough, uneven voltage, especially when the loads attached to them are unbalanced or draw current unevenly. A device called a DSTATCOM is meant to smooth that output, but it only works well when it can estimate the load current accurately.

The authors propose a new control method built around an improved phase-locked loop, a circuit that tracks the timing of the electrical signal. Their design filters messy load currents more cleanly, so the compensator can keep the source current balanced and smooth. Tests using real-time hardware simulation, including changing wind speeds and noisy measurements, showed the controller held up well.
plos-pone-0356143:
Fengliang Chen, writing alone, builds a trust-centered influence model in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on public health communication. Health messages spread through repeated peer and institutional contact, yet many computer diffusion models treat trust weakly. Privacy shocks can also abruptly reshape who seems credible.

The framework treats trust as a bounded, directed, and spreading state on a time-stamped network linking users, physicians, and shock events. A temporal graph model learns influence pathways, and an optimizer assigns interventions under a budget. In controlled simulations matched to the model's own assumptions, it beat comparison methods and lifted simulated intentions more than simple heuristics. Real-world testing, the author stresses, is still required.
plos-pone-0357043:
Shambal Kassahun Ferrede, Mulatu Werkina Eticha, and Habtamu Molla Ayele review births delivered with forceps or vacuum help at a university hospital in northwest Ethiopia, counting harm to newborns. Assisted vaginal delivery can save lives when done well, yet local evidence on baby outcomes was thin. Charts covered about three hundred such births across two years, and the team modeled which maternal and delivery traits tracked with adverse newborn results.

The results section tallies how common adverse outcomes were in this group and which factors stayed linked after adjustment, forming the study's core evidence. Ferrede and colleagues argue that knowing the local rate and its drivers helps the hospital train staff and choose instruments more safely, rather than importing assumptions from distant settings.
plos-pone-0357443:
Odey Bsharat and co-authors compare essential oils from a Mediterranean thyme relative gathered at two Palestinian sites, Hebron and Bethlehem. The herb is prized for oils rich in thymol and carvacrol, two compounds with germ-fighting reputations. Oils were drawn from fresh and dried leaves by steam, checked for makeup, and tested against oxidation, bacteria, and crop-damaging fungi.

Site changed the oil's character clearly: Hebron oil leaned rich in thymol, while Bethlehem oil leaned rich in carvacrol. All oils fought oxidation modestly and blocked bacteria across a useful range, with the strongest antifungal effects against the crop fungi tested. Bsharat and colleagues say origin and drying must be stated when such oils are sold or studied, since both shift performance.
plos-pone-0358043:
Yuye Wu and five colleagues search bladder cancer data for a tissue pattern that keeps immune cells out of tumors, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack, but only some patients benefit. Working across several public datasets, including spatial samples that preserve where cells sit, the team tracked a combined signature. It joins support cells, a growth signal called TGF-beta, and blood vessel lining. Those are three ingredients of a barrier around tumors.

The barrier direction reappeared in every section of an independent spatial cohort, a clean replication. Tumors scoring highest on it leaned toward not responding to a checkpoint drug, though after full adjustment the evidence stayed suggestive rather than conclusive. The authors are candid about the limits, including that some pattern assignments tracked sample sections. Their contribution is a testable barrier score and a map of which cohorts support it.
plos-pone-0358243:
Kerong Wang led a team of eight authors testing bedside ultrasound after cardiac arrest, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a stopped heart restarts, called ROSC, families face an agonizing question: will the person wake up? Early signs of brain outcome are hard to read, yet they shape care decisions within hours.

Wang's team tested whether a quick ultrasound at the bedside can help judge neurological outcome early. A fast, noninvasive check would be valuable in crowded emergency settings. Honest early information helps doctors plan intensive care and helps families prepare. The study does not promise certainty, but any reliable early signal in this setting carries real weight for everyone involved.
plos-pone-0358343: Johnson and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on one of the hardest talks in medicine: delivering bad news in an emergency room. As a scoping review, it maps what studies say about how that talk is delivered. Emergency rooms are loud, fast, and public, which makes a gentle talk harder. A clear map can point to training that helps staff and families.
plos-pone-0358543:
Tendai N R Gwanzura leads a team of seven tracking COVID-19 deaths among Floridians living with HIV across the vaccine divide, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The cohort is vast, over one hundred twenty-two thousand people, followed from March 2020 through 2021. The authors compared the period before vaccines became available with the months after, asking whether the survival gaps between racial, ethnic, and neighborhood groups narrowed once shots existed.

Overall mortality actually rose in the vaccine period, driven by the Delta surge. Beneath that average, the gaps moved differently. Black patients carried about double the mortality hazard of white patients before vaccines, and a still elevated gap after. Hispanic patients' excess hazard, equally stark before, essentially vanished in the vaccine period. Living in a highly vulnerable neighborhood raised risk specifically once vaccines existed. Availability alone, the authors conclude, did not deliver equity.
plos-pone-0358643:
Nusrat Jahan and three colleagues build a decision support system that explains its own predictions and suggests what to change, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Managers like the accuracy of deep learning but distrust answers they cannot inspect. The framework combines a predictor with feature attribution, which shows what drove each call, and counterfactual reasoning, which finds the smallest changes that would flip an outcome.

They tested it on employee attrition and customer churn data, separately and combined. Accuracy reached roughly ninety-one percent for attrition and eighty-seven percent for churn, with well calibrated confidence scores. The explanations scored high on fidelity checks, and the suggested actions cost less than those from comparison methods. For a manager, that means not just a warning that someone may leave, but a plausible, affordable lever to pull first.
plos-pone-0358943:
Rania F Zaarour and six colleagues report laboratory findings on waterpipe smoke and lung cells in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Hookah smoking is widespread worldwide, yet its effects on the airway lining are still being mapped. The team exposed healthy human bronchial cells, grown in the lab, to condensed waterpipe smoke and watched how the cells coped.

Stronger doses lowered cell survival, but a weak dose mainly triggered autophagy, the cell's internal recycling system, rather than killing the cells outright. Blocking that recycling pushed more cells into death, which suggests it acts as a defense under smoke stress. The exposed cells also showed damaged DNA and raised inflammatory signals. The findings add cellular detail to concerns about waterpipe smoke, while hinting that cell survival pathways shape the harm.
plos-pone-0359643:
Barry Chioza and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on brain research methods. It presents an optimised method for fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting, a technique that separates cell nuclei using glowing tags. The sorting prepares cortical cell types, the cells of the brain's outer layer, for epigenomic analysis.

Epigenomics studies chemical marks that control genes without changing DNA itself. Sorting clean nuclei by cell type first makes those marks readable cell group by cell group, instead of a blur of the whole cortex. Neuroscientists mapping how brain cells differ beneath identical DNA are the audience for a sharper sorting method.
pmc-10436543:
Glaviano, Foo, Lam, and co-authors review a key cell pathway known as PI3K, AKT, and mTOR, often shortened to PAM. Healthy cells use this chain of signals to stay alive, grow, and divide at the right times. Signals from growth factors feed into the chain under tight control.

When control breaks down, the same pathway can help cancers grow and spread. The review explains how the chain works step by step, then surveys drugs built to block parts of it. Readers gain a clear map of a major cancer target and of the promise and limits of drugs aimed at it.
pmc-10656343:
Hideyuki Hotta, Yuto Bekki, Laurent Gizon, Quentin Noraz, and Mark Rast review large-scale flows inside the Sun in two thousand twenty-three. The Sun's surface spins faster at the equator than at the poles, and a slow flow runs from equator to poles. Both flows are thought to be kept up by swirling hot gas under the pull of spin, and both help sustain the solar magnet field.

Sound-wave probing of the solar interior has mapped the flow shapes in detail. Growth in computing power now lets models grow such flows on their own in spinning shells of gas. The review sums up what is known, adds newly found slow wave modes, and lists open issues for future work.
pmc-10693143:
Idayu Badilla Idris and co-authors review what shapes women's say in their own health care choices, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Eight studies from developing countries passed the screen from work in three databases. Story-style pooling joined the findings.

Age, women's schooling and jobs, and partners' schooling and jobs all tied to choice power. Home place, household wealth, culture, and faith also weighed in. All kept studies were cross-sectional, which caps cause claims. The authors urge laws, fair services, plain information, and health teaching to lift women's say. Support for at-risk women is named as a policy must. Readers get a factor map for a core equity goal.
pmc-10693543:
Subin Lin and eight co-authors describe a data set of district-scale surface temperatures from two thousand twenty-three. The data come from infrared cameras on rooftops at the National University of Singapore. Infrared thermography measures heat without contact, and a fixed post can watch a whole district over time.

The observatory sat on two buildings and ran for ten months in a tropical setting. It gathered well over a million thermal images, at about ten-second intervals on average. Users can track temperature trends for single features, such as buildings, roads, and vegetation. The platform also carries other sensors for urban processes. The authors offer the set for studies of the built environment at a scale between single buildings and whole cities.
pmc-10696043:
Heba El-Sabban and Deyab report a new anti-rust coating pigment in a 2023 paper. They built a hybrid nano-pigment that mixes polypyrrole nanotubes, a carbon nitride sheet, and zinc oxide. The pigment is meant to guard carbon steel when mixed into epoxy paint.

The team made three pigments of rising complexity and checked their structure with standard tools. Electrical tests then measured how well coated steel resisted corrosion. Each added part improved the coating's resistance. The full three-part pigment performed best of the three. The authors present it as a highly efficient option for protecting steel.
pmc-10696243:
Aditya Fuad Robby Triangga and co-authors report joint-saving surgery for a young woman whose hip bone was dying. Dead bone in the femoral head, often a side effect of long steroid use, can collapse the hip and force a replacement, a poor bargain at age 21. Their patient had lupus, five years of steroid treatment, worsening hip pain, and a limp.

Scans showed a medium-sized dead zone in her left hip head. Instead of replacing the joint, the surgeons cut and rotated the femoral neck. That moved the dead area away from the load-bearing surface. They entered through a supercapsular route that keeps the head's blood supply and uses a short incision. Three months on, her pain had eased greatly and X-rays showed the cut bone healing well. The authors present the modified method as a promising option for young patients.
pmc-10696743:
Horváth, Mårdh, and Schwarz study good care paths for germ ills in hosts who shoot drugs. Such hosts in Europe face high risk of HIV and hep B and C. Lung ill, TB, joins that risk set for those hosts in the land. The aim was to add proof from good paths run in EU lands. A good path is a pack of acts with shown force in a place. That pack must be apt to copy and last in new lands.

Fifteen good paths form the proof pool in the work set. Two EU hubs, ECDC and EMCDDA, found them by a 2020 call. Lands span Belarus, Norway, and Portugal in that call set. The Moldova land joins the pool in the same call set. A word read of those paths weighs path traits in the pool. It also weighs what lets the paths run well in lands.
pmc-10705343:
Alison Manchester and co-authors tested how bile acids shape dog immune cells in twenty twenty-three. Bile acids form in the gut and are shaped by gut microbes and diet. In people and rodents they sway immune action. The primary and secondary kinds act in unlike ways. The team treated dog macrophages, a kind of immune cell, with one primary and one secondary bile acid.

Both acids curbed one swelling signal and raised a calming one when cells were stirred. Neither acid changed the level of a bile acid sensor. Gene reads showed the two acids switched on unlike sets of pathways. One set was tied to interferon signals and one to cell cycle control. The authors say both kinds act on dog immune cells, in shared and distinct ways.
pmc-10709443:
Ivert and six co-authors study risk factors for compensated maternal injury claims in Sweden, in a cohort study from twenty twenty-three. Claims proxy for suboptimal care during delivery. Nearly one point eight million births from two thousand to twenty sixteen are included. Over four thousand claims were filed, with about sixteen hundred compensated.

Filed claims doubled over the period while compensated rates barely rose. About thirty-six percent of filed claims were deemed avoidable injuries. Perineal injuries and diagnostic errors dominate compensated cases. Prior cesarean, post-term birth, disease, and multiple pregnancy raise claim risk. The findings guide maternity wards toward safer organization of care.
pmc-10711543:
Sandy Sousa Fonseca, Ana Leticia Zero Santos, Ciro Pedro Guidotti Pinto, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It tests whether a soybean protein that blocks digestive enzymes can break the resistance that fall armyworm caterpillars have evolved to insect-proof maize.

Farmers plant maize engineered to make bacterial toxins, but this pest has evolved resistance in the field. Gut enzymes in the caterpillar help process those toxins, so blocking the enzymes might restore the plant's bite. The team made the soybean inhibitor in bacteria and fed it to susceptible and resistant worm strains on plain and engineered maize leaves. On plain leaves, the inhibitor changed nothing. The study's setup and early results examine whether the story differs on toxin-bearing leaves. The work speaks to keeping engineered crops useful as pests adapt.
pmc-10711843:
Five heart doctors led by Catalin Pestrea tested a pacing method that taps the heart's own wiring, in seventy-five patients with severe heart block. They compared blocks high in the wiring path with blocks lower down. The wire was placed at the His bundle, a small hub that spreads the beat signal.

The method worked in most high blocks but in less than a third of low blocks. Once placed, settings stayed stable over close to two years of follow-up. A wide beat pattern and weak heart pumping raised the chance of failure. The authors judge the approach sound for high blocks and worth trying in some low ones.
pmc-10712243:
Kidist Tesfaye and Temesgen Tsega studied whether fixing children's heart defects helps malnourished children in Ethiopia catch up on growth. They reviewed 148 children, from two months to eighteen years old, who had corrective heart procedures and were followed for six months. Before surgery, over half were underweight, wasted, or stunted. Most had heart defects that do not cause blue coloring of the skin.

By three months after the intervention, all three malnutrition rates had fallen, and they fell further by six months. Growth scores improved clearly from baseline. Children with high pressure in the lung arteries and those corrected at older ages were more likely to stay underweight or wasted. The authors conclude that malnutrition is very common in these children, and that timely correction brings real, quick nutritional gains.
pmc-10715943:
Letizia Bertoldi and a team of co-authors review care for cardiogenic shock, a state where the heart fails to pump enough blood, in two thousand twenty-three. The condition carries a high risk of death. New temporary support devices that help the heart pump have changed treatment in recent years, alongside long-standing drug care.

The review sets out how to choose among drug-only care, one device, or several devices, by shock severity and cause. It describes the main device types and how each is used. It also covers best practice for putting devices in, since bleeding and access-site harm can erase their benefit. Careful technique is presented as part of the therapy itself.
pmc-10719243:
Ünal Üstündağ and four co-authors test a garden herb against metal poisoning in onion plants in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Manganese in excess damages cells and chromosomes. Lemon balm extract is rich in antioxidants, but its shield against metal stress was little tested. The team exposed onion roots to manganese chloride, with and without the extract. They tracked rooting, growth, and weight alongside cell division rates.

Manganese alone cut growth and raised chromosome damage and cell death signs. The extract eased many of these harms. Its own chemistry was profiled to name the likely protective compounds. Onion assays are a cheap early screen for plant protection ideas. The work serves plant toxicologists and natural product researchers.
pmc-10721343:
Elsiofy and four colleagues report a clinical trial from twenty twenty-three on a hip operation for teens. The work treats a slipped growth plate at the top of the thigh bone. The team tested a method that cuts and resets the bone after a safe hip dislocation.

The trial covered twenty-four hips, split evenly by sex, with a mean age near thirteen years. Most cases were classed as hard or very hard, and three quarters were stable. After about one year, scores for pain, movement, and leg length got much better. Bone death arose in four hips, and all four were unstable cases. The team still calls the method safe and useful for hard cases.
pmc-10725643:
Hao Chen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study of nanoparticles for gentler cancer heat therapy. Heating tumours with light can kill them, but excess heat harms healthy tissue. Heat also triggers protective proteins that blunt later treatment.

The particles pair a copper-doped core with a coating made from platelet membrane. The core converts a common body chemical into damaging radicals, lowering those protective proteins. Under low-power laser light it also warms the tumour mildly. Cell and animal tests cleared most tumour growth with good safety. The design combines chemical attack with low-temperature heating in one disguised package.
pmc-10730443:
Adriana Neag and Eric Becker review, in twenty twenty-three, aluminium alloys for thixoforging, a way to shape metal in a semi-solid state. The process has drawn interest for making parts with good properties. Choosing an alloy needs two things: the expected mechanical properties of the part, and the alloy's semi-solid temperature window. The review summarizes wrought and foundry aluminium alloys in depth. It describes methods to evaluate how sensitive each alloy is to heating temperature. For industrial use, the reheating strategy is crucial and should be analyzed systematically.

The reheated microstructure governs how the semi-solid metal flows and how the final part performs. The authors say a future process model should integrate microstructure conditioning during reheating. That would link feedstock preparation to final mechanical properties.
pmc-10735743:
Danielle McDuffie studies whether gratitude softens the harm of hard life events for grieving Black adults. Her paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. Black adults face loss more often than other groups, along with racial trauma and childhood hardship. Faith is a common source of strength, and gratitude shares much with that outlook. Yet gratitude had not been tested in this group.

McDuffie surveyed just over one hundred Black adults aged forty-five and up who had lost someone. Both racial trauma and childhood hardship linked to more depression. Gratitude changed that link, with depression differing across levels of hardship and thanks. She argues that care built on strengths and gratitude may help grieving Black adults. More work on trauma and policy could build on these results.
pmc-10735843:
Igor Akushevich, Arseniy Yashkin, Vinit Nalawade, and Julia Kravchenko examine dementia risk after cancer in this two thousand twenty-three study. They used SEER-Medicare data on Americans aged sixty-five and older. The cancer cohort covered more than two million people diagnosed with one of nine slow-progressing cancers, including breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers. A matched non-cancer comparison group of over one million people completed the design.

The team compared Alzheimer's disease and related dementia risk across many age-specific groups for each cancer type. Cancer patients diagnosed between sixty-five and seventy-five showed higher dementia risk than the comparison group. That pattern weakened with older age at diagnosis and eventually turned protective at advanced ages. The authors discuss treatment effects, genetics, and diagnostic practices as possible explanations.
pmc-10738743:
Fumihiko Yokota and colleagues interviewed older adults in Japan about social life after retirement during the COVID pandemic. Little was known about how retired Japanese elders kept contact in that period. Writing in twenty twenty-three, the team held face-to-face interviews in two prefectures in early twenty twenty-one with people over sixty-five who had retired around age sixty. Nearly all still worked part time. Transcripts were translated and coded for patterns in contact and in the forces shaping it.

Everyone said contact grew distant after retirement and was disrupted further by the pandemic. Even so, people stayed in touch online and in person with neighbors and volunteer groups, former coworkers, old school friends, children and grandchildren, and hobby friends. Health policy, pensions, income, and family living arrangements all shaped how much contact people kept.
pmc-10744343:
Bander Albogami tests quercetin and chitosan, alone and combined, against Giardia gut infection in a 2023 rat study. Standard drugs against parasites carry side effects and sometimes fail. Natural compounds might treat infection while sparing the liver and intestine.

Fifty male rats were split into control, infected, and three infected-plus-treatment groups. Quercetin is a plant flavonoid and chitosan a shell-derived fibre, both with antioxidant names. Results covered parasite clearance, liver protection, antioxidant markers, and intestinal muscle structure. The study tests whether the pairing beats either agent alone as a gentler giardiasis therapy.
pmc-10747743:
Yang Xu leads a team on sugar genes in the tomato plant. Their study from twenty twenty-three traces genes after genome tripling. Sugar is the main carbon form moved in higher plants.

Gene counts were tallied for grape and tomato in seven gene groups. Group sizes varied a lot from one group to the next. Duplication and loss took distinct paths in the tomato. Tandem copies drove growth of two of the gene groups. Most tomato genes lined up with grape kin genes. All groups were under a weeding form of selection.
pmc-10751343:
Xunbo Zheng and co-authors study a gene called TICRR in lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer. The gene helps start DNA copying in cells and has been linked to tumor growth. The team measured the gene in tumor and nearby normal tissue. They also mined large cancer data sets to link its levels to stage, survival, and cell traits.

The gene was far more active in tumors than in normal tissue, and high levels tracked with worse survival. Its levels rose with tumor stage and with heavy smoking and high counts of gene changes. Lab work that silenced the gene shifted cell growth and immune signals. A risk score built on the gene sorted patients well, so the authors propose it as a marker and drug target.
pmc-10771943:
Hyemin Jung and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three nationwide study of heart attacks in Koreans with HIV who take their treatment faithfully. Modern therapy suppresses the virus in most patients. Heart outcomes in this well-treated group were little studied.

Insurance claims identified thousands of people with strong treatment adherence over a decade. Heart events occurred more often than in the general population. Traditional risks like blood pressure and diabetes still drove many events. Deaths after heart events were counted separately for heart attack cases. The findings argue for heart prevention even when HIV is fully controlled.
pmc-10800443:
Motoko Watanabe and nine co-authors report a woman whose mouth pain came before a form of dementia. Their case report, from twenty twenty-four, begins with burning mouth syndrome. That is a lasting burn in the mouth with no visible cause. The patient, aged seventy-four, ate less as the pain grew.

Two drugs eased the burn and her eating came back. The pain flared again when her and her husband's health worsened. New drugs helped once more over time. Later she grew anxious and at times failed to know her husband. Tests then pointed to dementia with Lewy bodies. The case shows mouth pain care and brain care can cross.
pmc-10806143:
Sophie Irwin and co-authors test a live bacterial therapy, ADS024, against ulcerative colitis in work dated two thousand twenty-three. The gut lining in that disease loses cells and turns leaky. ADS024 is one strain of Bacillus velezensis, a microbe being readied as a drug.

A sterile brew of the strain's secretions shielded colon tissue from colitis patients and human gut cells in the lab. It cut cell death and swelling signals, and blunted death caused by patient serum particles. It also eased a plunge in barrier strength from two swelling chemicals and kept a key seal protein at normal levels. Fed to mice with colon injury, the live strain cut weight loss and tissue damage.
pmc-10847843:
Ameneh Jafari and five co-authors review the hunt for protein fingerprints that could catch cervical cancer earlier and less invasively. Screening has cut deaths, but compliance stays low and a blood-based test could reach women whom Pap programs miss. Proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, has begun naming candidate markers and drug targets.

The review also takes up cervical cancer stem cells, the stubborn subpopulation blamed for tumor growth and resistance to therapy. Targeting those cells may matter as much as finding the cancer early. The authors concede practical challenges remain before proteomic tests reach clinics. They argue the approach could still reshape how this cancer is detected and treated.
pmc-10876443:
You-Jung Choi, Won Young Wi, Geum Joon Cho, and Jin Oh Na link pre-pregnancy heart rhythm disorders to gestational diabetes in Korea, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Arrhythmias are more common in people with diabetes. Whether they also precede diabetes in pregnancy was unknown. The team used national health insurance records for over a million births.

After exclusions, about three hundred sixty-six thousand singleton pregnancies without prior diabetes were analyzed. Under one percent of the women had cardiac arrhythmias before pregnancy. Gestational diabetes occurred in about nine percent overall, but nearly fifteen percent among women with arrhythmia. Adjusted analysis kept the association significant, with odds roughly seventy-eight percent higher. The link held across age, body size, and blood pressure subgroups. The authors argue arrhythmia history flags pregnancies needing closer glucose watch.
pmc-11199443:
Lünnemann and three co-authors studied romantic relationships of youth exposed to family violence in twenty twenty-three. Growing up with violence at home can shape later relationships, but the authors wanted a fuller picture, including strengths. They interviewed eighteen young people aged sixteen to twenty who had been reported to child protection services.

The young people described struggles with support, connection, trust, setting boundaries, handling emotions, and resolving conflict. The authors link these patterns to learning by watching others and to attachment theory. Yet many also described good experiences and learning better ways from a partner. With the right social or professional support, the authors argue, these youth can overcome many of the challenges they face.
pmc-11536543:
Kyoungwon Jung and five colleagues compare, published in 2024, three ways of pushing the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori into its round resting form. The spiral bacterium rounds up under stress, keeping its virulence genes, so the round form still matters for disease. Labs need reliable ways to make it. The team used starvation, the antibiotic amoxicillin, and the liquid left over from growing a mouth bacterium. They checked shape, aliveness, and whether cells could still grow colonies, and read protein profiles of each round form.

Starved cells stopped forming colonies within a week yet stayed alive and round. Amoxicillin drove cells fastest into a living but non-growing state. The mouth bacterium's broth kept cells growing longest, hinting it holds something that preserves the spiral. Protein sets differed by method, with some shared changes across all. The authors say the making method must be reported, since it shapes the cells.
pmc-11538243:
Assi and four colleagues test a gel plus stem cell broth for arthritic jaw joints in rats in twenty twenty-four. The broth is the fluid stem cells grow in, rich in healing signals. Fifty female rats were split into five groups: healthy, arthritic, gel alone, broth alone, and both together. Arthritis was sparked by two shots of an irritant into the jaw joint.

After four weeks, joints that got both treatments looked best on every measure. The joint disc thinned toward normal and the cartilage layer widened. Collagen rose and a key inflammation switch fell. Each single treatment helped less than the pair. The team says the combo merits study as a joint repair route.
pmc-11546743:
Juhong Xie and seven colleagues dissect a devastating fish virus with omics in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Grass carp reovirus causes bleeding disease that heavily damages the grass carp farming industry. The team profiled five tissues, gill, liver, intestine, kidney, and muscle, before and after infection, finding over ten thousand proteins and four thousand metabolites. Analysis of the changes then mapped how the virus rewires each tissue.

Across tissues, the changed proteins and metabolites centered on carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, with fatty acids, glycerophospholipids, and steroids prominent among the metabolites. Joint pathway analysis flagged glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway as clearly enriched, and blocker tests showed both pathways matter for viral copying, making them candidate drug targets. The kidney suffered most; its butanoate metabolism changes were studied in depth. The study supplies a tissue-by-tissue molecular map for designing treatments against the virus.
pmc-11576743:
Shuaijie Zhang and co-authors report a model from two thousand twenty-four for early lung cancer screening in Chinese populations. Many health records have missing fields, which can break standard prediction tools. The team built a model that can still judge risk when data are incomplete, without using radiation-based scans.

The model, called BOUND, uses a Bayesian network and was trained on records from more than nine hundred thousand people. It kept strong accuracy in checks split by time and by place, and it held up when large shares of data were removed on purpose. A simple risk scorecard built from the model raised detection rates several-fold. The authors offer the tool free online for use in basic care settings.
pmc-11576843:
Leyi Loh and co-authors published a study in 2024 on single-photon sources in a sheet material. Crystals one atom thick can host lone defects that act as tiny quantum light sources. The team seeded a tungsten-sulfur sheet with niobium atoms spaced far apart.

At that spacing, each dopant could be studied on its own. The lone dopants gave narrow light lines, tight in space, with the stop-start pattern that proves single photons. The lines sat in a narrow color band across many samples, unlike the wide spread seen in kindred materials. Magnetic splits in the lines pointed to a bound complex of a dark particle pair and the charged dopant. The authors say such dopants are steady, uniform quantum emitters.
pmc-11585243:
Fangfang Zhou and colleagues build a nanoparticle that mops up the chemical shrapnel of a brain bleed and delivers a protective drug on cue, in this study from twenty twenty-four. After intracerebral hemorrhage, oxidative stress and inflammation drive the second wave of injury. Their particle is a porous silica sphere stitched with selenium bonds, loaded with an anti-inflammatory plant compound, and sealed with a polydopamine coat.

The design is reactive in both senses: the particle itself scavenges reactive oxygen species. Those same species break its selenium stitches, opening the pores to release the drug where damage is worst. In dishes and in mice, it calmed the brain's immune cells, shifting them from attack to repair mode. Injected into veins, it gathered at the bleed's rim and protected the brain, with good safety. The authors pitch it as a two-in-one platform for hemorrhage care.
pmc-11585543:
Zhenpeng Shen leads a team that creates glycoside diversity from glycals. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with sugar building blocks. Tweaking glycosides can change or boost drug traits.

Blocks with many changeable spots were hard to make. A nickel driven reaction adds carbon and boron at set spots. The boron group at one spot can be swapped later. That yields rare sugars with changes at that same spot. Many groups and complex drug shapes were tolerated. Analogs of natural products and drugs were made. The route speeds access to varied sugars.
pmc-11585943:
Lin-Lin Tao and co-authors published this fertility study in 2024. In IVF, clinics choosing an embryo for a day-four single transfer can look back at how many cells it had on day three. The team asked whether that cell count predicts pregnancy and newborn outcomes. They reviewed 431 fresh single transfers, sorting them into three groups by day-three cell number: seven to nine cells, ten to thirteen, and more than thirteen.

Embryos from the middle group did best. Their pregnancy and live birth rates beat the seven-to-nine group across age bands and in the standard IVF subgroup, and after statistical adjustment the gap held. The newborn outcomes, by contrast, did not differ between groups. The authors recommend preferring embryos that held ten to thirteen cells on day three when a day-four transfer is planned. They note the fastest group was small, with only 34 cycles.
pmc-11600743:
Gaohan Yin, Tianhang Zhou, and Qingmei Kong report a rare brain harm case. Their case from twenty twenty-four deals with a girl of thirteen in China. She had five months of anorexia, an eating disorder.

Scans showed the classic marks of central pontine myelinolysis. That harm strips the coat from nerves in the brain stem. It can come from fast fix of low blood salt. Her case had no grave salt shift in the tale. Yet her outlook for both ills proved quite good. Care teams should watch for it in refeeding.
pmc-11600843:
Jingyi Yang, Yating Li, Xiaoyan Li, and Nari Wulan weigh two fixes for broken wrists in older adults in two thousand twenty-four. A distal radius break can be held by a surgically set locking plate or by a cast after the bone is nudged back. Which fix serves patients best over years was unclear.

Four randomized trials with four hundred twenty-three patients aged sixty or more, each followed at least two years, were pooled. The plate group scored better on two wrist rating scales, one patient-rated and one on arm and hand limits. Grip strength also favored the plate. Quality-of-life scores and repeat surgery were also tracked. The authors read the edge as real but modest.
pmc-11603743:
Isobel Todd and four colleagues pool thirty-one studies on over ten million children to ask whether caesarean birth raises infection risk through childhood. The question matters because caesarean rates are high, and early microbial exposure differs sharply by birth mode.

Children born by caesarean, emergency or elective, went to hospital with infections at somewhat higher rates. That included upper respiratory infections, with hazard ratios around 1.10 to 1.12. Effects on infections outside hospital were judged by direction rather than pooled numbers. The evidence comes all from high-income-country cohorts. The authors weigh bias carefully; the raw increase is small but consistent across very large groups.
pmc-11603843:
Liu and seven colleagues review armored CAR cell therapies for solid tumors in twenty twenty-four. CAR-T therapy engineers T cells to hunt cancer by a surface receptor. It has transformed blood cancer care over the past decade. In solid tumors, poor trafficking and a suppressive environment limit its effect.

Two newer variants aim to fill those gaps. CAR natural killer cells need no tissue matching and show lower toxicity. CAR macrophages can eat tumor cells and present their antigens to other immune cells. The review compares features, advantages, and limits of all three cell types. It also suggests ways to boost their performance in solid tumors. The authors frame the variants as complementary, not rival, strategies.
pmc-11603943:
Li and co-authors report a case where nerve damage in the eye was the first sign of acute retinal necrosis. This fast, severe eye infection is caused here by varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox virus. Starting with optic neuropathy is a rare way for the disease to appear.
