A 57-year-old man first lost vision in his right eye, with signs of optic nerve damage. Twenty days later, vision in his left eye also fell. The report follows his treatment and follow-up in detail. It warns eye doctors that early nerve signs can precede the classic retinal picture.
pmc-11604943:
Minyoung Kevin Kim and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study designing broad phage and antibiotic cocktails for resistant infections. Virus-like phages kill bacteria, but each phage targets few strains. Personal therapy dominates because coverage is narrow.

The team grouped phages by which bacterial docking sites they use. Mixing groups with complementary targets blocked resistance from emerging. Certain antibiotic classes paired predictably with certain groups. Their three cocktails each covered nearly all tested Pseudomonas clinical strains, including biofilms. A wound infection animal model matched the lab success. Similar cocktails were built for Staphylococcus as well.
pmc-11605843:
Conflict between families and staff is common in children's healthcare, where emotions and expectations run high. Training can soften such conflicts, but judging whether training works lacks standard tools. Juliette Phillipson and co-authors ask the people who commission that training: thirteen healthcare decision-makers and stakeholders from hospitals and charities, interviewed about what an evaluation should measure.

Four themes emerged. Evaluations should capture how trainees experience the sessions, and whether staff gain and keep real skill and well-being. They should also capture how patients and families experience conflict afterward, and what conflict costs in staff time and clinical resources. The themes line up with the classic Kirkpatrick training framework while reaching beyond it. Interviewees wanted both numbers and stories, plus follow-up long after the course ends. The authors advise shaping each evaluation to its program rather than copying a generic template.
pmc-11612143:
Mohamed Atalla, Ali Shebl, Bojan Ðurin, Nikola Kranjčić, and Wael AlMetwaly map where Kuwait might find groundwater in this two thousand twenty-four study. In semi-arid countries, locating groundwater potential zones is critical water management. The team combined Google Earth Engine with analytic hierarchy process decision-making, joining thirteen criteria from geology, slope, and rainfall to vegetation and water indices, drainage, land cover, and the water table itself.

The resulting map favors Kuwait's north and east. High potential covers about twelve percent of the country and moderate about thirty-seven percent, while extremely high suitability is under one and a half percent. Nearly half the country, over seventy-five hundred square kilometers, rates low potential, with chances better in lower areas. The authors argue that combining many factors in the cloud-based workflow increases precision and stability, offering planners a reusable template for arid-region water exploration.
pmc-11612443:
Yuvraj Maphrio Mao and four co-authors boost a miniature microbial fuel cell's output more than sevenfold by dusting its anode with graphene quantum dots. These tiny fuel cells, which harvest electricity from wastewater microbes, could power sensors and implants but remain too weak. The bottleneck is electron transfer at the electrode.

Electrodes were screen-printed on glass, a durable and fouling-resistant format, then the anode was drop-coated with quantum dots to enlarge its active surface. Fed reverse-osmosis wastewater, the modified cell produced about three hundred thirty-two nanowatts per square centimeter against forty-five for the bare electrode. Output held up over long operation. The authors present glass screen printing plus quantum dots as a practical manufacturing route.
pmc-11612843:
Miguel de Felipe and co-authors show, in a 2024 study, that the fate of one Spanish marsh echoes across an entire migratory flyway. The Guadalquivir marshes host wintering waterfowl from across the East Atlantic Flyway, and the team joined thirty-eight years of local and international counts with data from over four hundred protected wetlands. They asked whether local conditions track the fortunes of whole populations.

Local conditions do track them. The wintering community has shifted over forty years, from herbivores and one set of dabbling ducks toward another group crossing the Sahara. Nine of fifteen species declined in step with the decay of the natural marshes inside Doñana National Park. The other six answered mainly to global forces such as warmer winters elsewhere. The authors draw a double lesson: read local trends with flyway data in hand, and know that one wetland's care registers at continental scale.
pmc-11613543:
Carlos Gómez-Restrepo and eight co-authors test music workshops for teens with depression and anxiety in Bogotá, in this twenty twenty-four study. Teen mental distress is common, yet few community activities have been studied as routes to recovery. Music groups are cheap and social, which makes them worth a look.

Thirty-four teens aged fifteen and sixteen, drawn from a larger teen cohort, joined five weekly sessions of music learning and practice. They rated their anxiety and depression before and after, and shared their experiences in writing. Attendance and feedback were tracked as well. This early trial, run without a control group, maps promise and problems for a fuller test.
pmc-11615043:
Xingjian Zhang, Zhaokai Pan, and Guoding Liu prove a quantum magic edge. Their work from twenty twenty-four deals with shallow quantum circuits. Magic states are the key source of quantum power, theory says.

Yet if magic truly gives an edge was still in doubt. Their proof needs no unproven claims or black box tricks. They link shallow circuits to the strongest form of nonlocal play. In that game, magic is a must for matched scores. They then turn that play into computing tasks. Shallow circuits need magic to meet those targets.
pmc-11616143: Navarro-Aceves and five co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-four on retrieving a broken surgical tool tip from a spine disc. During disc surgery for a man's leg pain, the tip of a grasping tool snapped off inside the disc space. The team widened the entry path. It used hooks, forceps, and a magnetic probe to free the tip safely. The authors urge teams to weigh magnetic retrieval when instruments break mid-surgery.
pmc-11618343:
Paula Sosa-Guillén and four co-authors publish a fine-grained climate dataset for the Canary Islands, in a 2024 paper. The archipelago packs mountains, coasts, and many endemic species into small areas, so climate change will bite unevenly. Coarse global models smooth away exactly the local detail conservation needs.

The team ran a regional weather model at three-kilometer resolution, steered by three global models. Three time windows, past, mid-century, and late century, were run under two emission paths. From temperature, rain, sun, humidity, and wind they derived fifty-three bioclimatic indicators, the measures species actually respond to. The open dataset gives island planners and ecologists a shared, detailed picture of the climates their species will face.
pmc-11619143:
Margaux Lorillon and seven co-authors published a fertility study in twenty twenty-four comparing two hormone supports for women receiving donated eggs. After embryo transfer, progesterone support comes either as an oral drug or as vaginal capsules, alongside weekly injections. Patients prefer swallowing a pill, but proof of equal results was needed.

The Lille hospital team reviewed three hundred seventy-two donation cycles from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. Clinical pregnancy rates were thirty-six point seven percent with vaginal support and thirty point three percent with oral, a difference that vanished after adjustment. Ongoing pregnancy, miscarriage, and live birth rates also matched. The oral route appears a fair substitute in this setting.
pmc-11621443:
Marzieh Rashidipour and eight co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-four on tannic acid packed in chitosan nanoparticles. Tannic acid can fight tumors, but the body takes it up poorly. The team put it in tiny chitosan carriers to help it kill germs and cancer cells.

They made the particles by ionic gelation. They checked them with electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and size and charge tests. The particles killed several strains of bacteria and the fungus Candida albicans in dilution tests. They also harmed HepG2 liver cancer cells. They changed how genes that control DNA methylation act. That points to an epigenetic effect that needs more study.
pmc-11621643:
Seungjin Son and eight co-authors describe patchy hair loss that followed COVID-19 infection or vaccination. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The condition, alopecia areata, is an immune attack on hair follicles, and infections and vaccines are known triggers for such attacks.

The team reviewed patients whose hair loss began or worsened within three months of infection or a vaccine dose, from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-two. Fifty patients qualified: eighteen after infection and thirty-two after vaccination. Hair loss started on average about five weeks after infection and four after vaccination. Fever was the most common sickness sign before the loss. Treatment response was also charted. The study adds clinical shape to scattered case reports.
pmc-11621843:
Ai-Zhi Lin, Xian Fu, Qing Jiang, and a large team trace sugar damage to the gut in this two thousand twenty-four paper. High-sucrose diets injure multiple organs, but mechanisms and treatments were uncharted. Feeding mice a high-sucrose diet for sixteen weeks produced gut barrier dysfunction: colon inflammation and impaired tight junctions between intestinal cells. Metabolomics of colon tissue pointed at one enzyme, soluble epoxide hydrolase, which rose while its protective product, an epoxyeicosatrienoic acid, fell.

Blocking that enzyme chemically, or deleting its gene only in the intestine, significantly reduced the diet's intestinal injuries, easing inflammation and restoring tight junctions. In cell studies, the protective fatty acid itself prevented sucrose-induced inflammation and junction damage, while its breakdown product could not. The authors present the enzyme as both mechanism and therapeutic target: inhibiting it preserves the gut barrier against dietary sugar.
pmc-11635443:
Sun, Tang, Li, Wang, Yang, and Shen build in twenty twenty-four a rapid test kit for Epstein-Barr virus, a widespread virus that can quietly contaminate lab cell lines. One infected line can spoil others in the same lab, and standard checks are slow or costly. The team built three systems of rising convenience: a classic DNA test, a fast enzyme-copy method, and that method married to a paper strip readout.

The two fast systems spotted tenfold fewer virus copies than the classic one. On nearly two hundred cell lines, results matched industry-standard assays, turning up ten positive lines. The strip version shows results by eye in about fifteen minutes. The authors pitch daily strip checks for labs and cell banks.
pmc-11636443:
Kevin Matlock and five co-authors study stress, mood, and diabetes in Latinx adults in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Latinx people in the United States face higher risk of type 2 diabetes and depression. The team asked whether the strains of city life change how depression links to insulin resistance. They recruited one hundred twenty-one adults with type 2 diabetes in Hartford, Connecticut. Each person reported depressive symptoms and daily urban hassles.

Fasting blood tests gave insulin and glucose levels, from which the team computed insulin resistance. They then tested whether exposure to urban threat strengthened or weakened the mood link. Their framing treats unsafe or wearing city conditions as toxic stress. The results speak to community health work. Tackling neighborhood stress may be part of treating diabetes in this population.
pmc-11638243:
Marwa Abd El-Hamid and co-authors present a 2024 study of a smart gel for skin wounds infected with the yeast Candida albicans. Open wounds invite the yeast, which stalls healing and breeds complications. The team built a hydrogel loaded with silver nanoparticles, pomegranate peel extract, and hyaluronic acid. Silver fights germs, the peel brings plant actives, and the acid keeps the wound moist and skin-friendly.

One hundred rats with infected wounds were split into five groups, among them an untreated set and a shop cream set. Healing was tracked against the treated groups. A carrier that fights the yeast while it feeds repair answers two needs in one dressing. Plant-plus-metal gels could serve clinics where drug proofing grows.
pmc-11641043:
Tingting Liu and co-authors review the two-way links between bone and brain in Parkinson disease, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The disease wears down movement control, causing tremor, stiffness, and balance trouble. A bone-brain axis, where skeleton and brain signal each other, has become a hot research theme.

The review covers bone metabolism ties to the disease, plus messenger and hormone roles on the axis. Swelling, immunity, and tiny RNA regulators get their own sections. Treatment ideas that use the axis close the survey. The authors aim to ground fresh care paths in this cross-talk.
pmc-11641743:
Seyed Hesamoddin Bidooki and co-authors test a plant oil compound, packed in nanoparticles, against colon cancer cells. Their 2024 paper studies squalene, found in olive oil, which has shown promise against diseases tied to oxidative stress. On its own it mixes poorly with water and breaks down, which limits its use.

Packed in biodegradable particles, the compound left mature gut cells alone but slowed the growth of immature cancer cells. It pushed those cells into programmed death and halted their cycle early. The effect ran through a rise in reactive oxygen and the release of a key cell protein. Gene tests fit that picture. The work supports particle delivery as a way to give a food compound drug-like reach.
pmc-11642143:
Abdulkadir Kamal and co-authors measure how steady a pupil timing mark is in healthy adults, in work from 2024. Handheld pupil meters time each phase of the pupil's light reflex. One phase runs from light onset to peak squeeze. That phase shifts in brain injury, but its normal range was not known.

Fifty healthy adults gave paired readings in both eyes across four rounds over two days. Mean time to peak squeeze sat near one second in each eye. Spread within a person ran high, and match scores across rounds were low. The authors say the mark varies a lot even in health, which shapes its use in care.
pmc-11642843:
Silvia Cimino and colleagues followed fathers of toddlers in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Father involvement in feeding and care supports early learning and feelings, yet fathers with mental health symptoms may struggle, and programs for fathers are rare. Their program used online video feedback sessions held twice a week.

Fathers and children were checked twice, four weeks apart, for symptoms and behavior. The sessions aimed to improve feeding interactions and lower distress in both fathers and young children. Families and therapists gain early evidence that remote, father-focused help is workable during the toddler years, when habits form fast.
pmc-11643443:
Shing-Hwa Liu and three co-authors swap fiber and fat kinds in a fat-rich rat diet to ease fat burn harm. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Thirty-five young male rats sat in five packs for fifteen weeks: plain, fat-rich, fat-rich low-carb, the same with shell fiber, and the same with shell fiber plus fish oil.

The plain fat pack bore the most liver weight; the low-carb pack the most fat cloth. The shell-plus-oil pack cut body, liver, and fat weights, blood harm marks, and fat size, and set fat build and burn in line. The team back the swap.
pmc-11643643: Boris Mahltig and Andrea Ehrmann introduce the topic of nanomaterials in textiles, a field where the words nano and nanomaterials have become buzzwords for decades of rapid research and development advances. Both authors work in textile and materials research, and the piece frames the meeting point of nanotechnology and fabric science. The surviving text is brief, offering the framing rather than detailed findings.
pmc-11644243:
Chiara Botta, Corinna Grottola, Davide Amato, and Maria Acocella wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on how to keep used plastic strong. The plastic is polylactic acid, or PLA. It is made from plants, not oil, so it is sold as a green choice. Yet it breaks down slowly in the open air.

Used PLA can be remade, but the new goods are most often weaker. The team shows, for the first time, that a fill of biochar can fix that flaw. Biochar is a char made by heat from plant waste with no air. At fills of 1, 2.5, and 5 per cent by weight, the mix stayed easy to shape. Its stiffness rose by up to 20 per cent, and it held up far better under UV light. The char seeds crystals too: a near glass-like PLA grew to 30 per cent crystal.
pmc-11647343:
Rou Yu and Xuemei Lin published the protocol for a trial seeking the best epidural morphine dose after cesarean delivery. Spinal morphine is the gold standard for post-cesarean pain, but newer multimodal strategies, mixing regional blocks and patient-controlled analgesia, aim to cut opioid side effects and monitoring burdens. The single-center, double-blind randomized trial plans to enroll 310 healthy women scheduled for cesarean under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia. Different morphine doses will be layered onto multimodal regimens.

Recruitment was planned at a Sichuan university hospital across twenty twenty-four. Publishing the protocol in advance locks the design, outcomes, and analysis plan against later drift. Pain after cesarean competes with a newborn's needs: mothers must move, feed, and bond. Finding the lowest morphine dose that still controls moderate-to-severe pain would ease both recovery and the respiratory monitoring such doses demand.
pmc-11651443:
Zhao-Jun Zou and co-authors test a wearable nerve stimulator meant to keep leg blood moving, in a 2024 study. Stagnant deep veins invite clots, and squeezing devices help but are bulky. Their small stimulator zaps the common peroneal nerve to flex the calf. Thirty healthy volunteers tried both the stimulator and a standard compression device in random order, with ultrasound measuring vein and artery flow.

Both tools raised vein peak speed and average flow over rest, by similar amounts. Neither changed artery flow. Results matched across the two order groups. No safety problems appeared. The authors conclude the pocket stimulator rivals the bulky standard for boosting deep vein flow, at least in healthy legs.
pmc-11653143:
Ya-Wen Zhang and co-authors introduce, in a 2024 genetics paper, a software tool that finds genes whose effects change with the environment. Such gene-by-environment links matter for traits like flowering time, but past tools were not both flexible and accurate. The new tool builds on a mixed-model method for genome-wide association studies.

Simulations showed the new fixed-effect form had more power than two older methods. In a fresh look at flowering time in a small model plant across three heat levels, the tool found more known links than older methods. All of its top finds were backed by checks on gene variants and by past work linking them to heat.
pmc-11653943:
Sarah Waliany and six colleagues measured how patients with a rare HER2-mutant lung cancer were treated before any targeted drug existed for them. The retrospective study used a nationwide American clinico-genomic database. Among 9,206 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, 164 carried HER2 mutations without accompanying EGFR mutations. Their average age was sixty-seven, and most were women; about half had smoked.

Treatment patterns and survival were reconstructed from records spanning twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-one. Chemotherapy-era outcomes in this subgroup become the benchmark every new targeted therapy must beat. Eighty percent of eligible patients received first-line systemic treatment, detailed in the analysis. Rare-mutation cancers are invisible in aggregate trial data. Real-world cohorts like this twenty twenty-four one give drug developers and regulators the historical control arm they otherwise lack.
pmc-11654143:
Meysam Fallahnezhad, Mostafa Langarizadeh, and Afshin Vahabzadeh put out a full review in 2024 on tracking hospital supply chain results. Hospitals need indicators to track how supplies move and serve care. Choosing the right measures is hard without a ready evidence base. Supply chains had got less focus than care readings.

The team searched seven research data banks for matching studies. Thousands of papers were screened down step by step. A few dozen studies made it through the full screening. Back lists of those studies were checked as well. The team pulled and sorted the measures those papers used. The result is a map hospitals can use when building their own score cards.
pmc-11655143:
Yanjun Wang, Pengli Luo, and Tana Wuren review mesenchymal stem cell therapy for kidney disease in two thousand twenty-four. Acute kidney injury kills a large share of patients worldwide, and chronic kidney disease is set to grow into a top global burden. Dialysis and transplant, the current mainstays, have limited reach and real drawbacks.

Stem cells from connective tissue can calm immune reactions and support tissue repair, which suits damaged kidneys. The review gathers lab findings and clinical trial results on how the cells work and where they help. It weighs safety data and the hurdles still blocking routine use. New tools such as single-cell sequencing and gene editing may enable combined and personalized treatments with fewer side effects.
pmc-11656943:
İdil Alpat Yavaş and four co-authors study food knowledge among office workers in Türkiye in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Nutrition literacy means knowing enough about food to eat well. The team asked whether that knowledge tracks with diet quality and quality of life. They surveyed more than three thousand white-collar workers aged eighteen to sixty-five. Standard scales measured their nutrition literacy and their match to the Mediterranean diet.

The survey also captured body measures, eating habits, and activity levels. Workers with stronger food knowledge tended to eat closer to the Mediterranean pattern. Links with body measures and life quality were also tested. Employers run wellness programs for such staff, and this study shows where knowledge gaps sit. Dietitians and workplace health planners are the readers.
pmc-11660043:
Stefano Menasce and co-authors print silicone parts that are both strong and reprocessable in a 2024 study. Silicones serve everywhere from sealants to implants, but molding limits their shapes and cured silicone cannot be reshaped. A class of materials called vitrimers can flow under stress while keeping their network whole, which opens the door to recycling.

The team writes the silicone vitrimer directly with a printer, laying down ink in complex shapes. Tests of flow and strength show the inks can be tuned so parts resist creep yet can still be reprocessed at room temperature. Those two traits usually fight each other. Printed parts kept high strength after shaping. The work points to silicone goods that can be printed to order and later reworked instead of thrown away.
pmc-11663643:
Mohamed El Ouardi and colleagues analysed wormwood essential oils from Morocco in 2024. Morocco hosts rich Artemisia plant diversity. Two species supplied the oils here. Chemical makeup was profiled in full. Germ killing and antioxidant power were tested. Computer docking added a third angle.

Key compounds bound target proteins strongly. One compound, davanone, stood out especially. Simulated complexes stayed stable over time. Target enzymes included defence-related proteins. Oils showed clear biological potential overall. Traditional plant uses gain scientific support. Further product testing is still needed. Natural antimicrobials remain in demand.
pmc-11663743:
Hao Yuan and nine colleagues published a 2024 study of tinnitus patients treated with transient compound sound therapy. Tinnitus is the perception of ringing or noise without an external source. Sound therapy, which plays tailored sounds to the patient, helps some sufferers but not others, and doctors cannot easily predict who will benefit.

The team reviewed 991 patients with subjective tinnitus treated at their hospital's ear department between November 2019 and January 2022. Patients who responded to therapy differed significantly from those who did not on several clinical characteristics. From these differences the authors built a predictive model. Such a model could spare unlikely responders a long course of therapy and direct them to other options sooner.
pmc-11664043:
Shuying Xu and five colleagues study a blood ratio as a risk sign for stroke, using a large United States survey, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The ratio joins the share of neutrophils, a white cell type, with albumin, a blood protein. The team drew on survey data from 1999 to twenty twenty covering more than fifty-six thousand people. They modeled stroke odds across ratio levels and hunted for bend points.

Higher ratios linked to higher stroke risk, even after other factors were counted. The tie was not a straight line: past a bend point, the rise in risk slowed. The pattern held as curves in men but ran straight in women. The authors offer the cheap ratio as a prevention aid.
pmc-11670743:
Shuai Zhang, Chengyue Li, Almujiang-Yimitri Tarken, and Weiming Li tracked motor fitness in Xinjiang youth from nineteen eighty-five to two thousand nineteen. Data came from national student fitness surveys run in eight years across that span. The group covered ages seven to eighteen.

Tests covered speed, heart-lung fitness, strength, power, and flexibility. Overall fitness fell over the whole period. Speed, power, and heart-lung fitness improved in the first decade, then worsened sharply in the next. Decline slowed after two thousand five, and some parts improved, but most kept falling in the last years. The authors say trends differ by sex and age, which policy should reflect.
pmc-11671243:
Brooks Hibner and colleagues measured exercise responses in multiple sclerosis in two thousand twenty-four. Aerobic capacity drops in this chronic nerve disease. Blood flow responses at peak effort were unknown. Fitness itself might explain any differences found. Patients and controls had similar peak oxygen uptake. All pedaled through a maximal cycling test.

Heart and blood measures rose similarly in both groups. Heart rate patterns differed before age adjustment, though. That difference vanished once age was considered. Stroke volume, output, and pressure showed no group gaps. Fitness, not disease, seems to drive responses here. Keeping fit may normalize exercise circulation in MS. Training programs gain a reassuring evidence base.
pmc-11672343:
Mak and co-authors test group therapy for stressed parents during the COVID-19 years. The therapy, called ACT, teaches parents to accept hard thoughts and act on their values. The study ran at a Hong Kong family service center. Parents joined five weekly group sessions. Sessions ran in person or online based on rules and choice.

The study enrolled 250 parents of school-age children. Most were mothers, with a mean age near 41. Stress scores fell after the program, with a small to mid gain. Gains showed in parent stress and general stress alike. The flexible mix of online and in-person groups still worked in real-world use.
pmc-11672943:
Wanyu Tang and co-authors present a 2024 system that reads the actions of children with ADHD from video. The children take a standard attention test while a camera watches. Sudden, uneven moves are a hallmark of the condition, and set video tools often miss them. The team's system tracks body and face points instead of raw pixels, which cuts background noise.

One branch reads body points with a graph network tuned for jerky motion. A second branch turns face points into images and reads head and face moves with a phone-grade vision model. A fusion step joins both branches for the final call on each act. The calls map to the symptom traits in the standard diagnostic guide. Such tools could make attention tests more fair and less reliant on a watcher's eye.
pmc-11673043:
Ianis Boboc and colleagues test a diabetes drug in a mouse model of Alzheimer disease. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses semaglutide over four weeks. Alzheimer disease brings memory loss and anxious behaviour. The drug mimics a gut hormone that also acts in the brain.

Twenty mice split into healthy and disease groups, treated or not. Blood sugar and weight were tracked through the treatment. Behaviour tests measured exploration, recognition, social response, and anxiety. Semaglutide brought disease-group blood sugar down to healthy levels. Memory test results improved after treatment in the disease mice. Anxiety-related behaviour was also part of the outcome set. Early animal results justify deeper study, not clinical claims.
pmc-11673243:
Yiying Wang, Abhirup Banerjee, and Vicente Grau rebuild coronary artery trees in 3D from just two flat X-ray views. Heart doctors read vessel shape from angiograms during live procedures. Radiation limits scans to about two angles, so depth must be inferred. Their NeCA method learns a neural field of the vessel tree without any 3D training truth.

A hash-based encoder and a cone-beam projector make the learning self-taught. Test trees came from CT scans of two major heart arteries. Six scores judged shape and branch linking against known truth. NeCA matched a supervised rival on tree shape and branch joins. The result hints at safer, fuller guidance during heart procedures.
pmc-11675743:
Nazira Bekenova and six co-workers looked at heart rate change as a sign of nerve harm to the heart in Kazakhstan. This nerve harm, often tied to diabetes, is not often checked with heart rate tests in day to day care. Their 2024 study took in 5,707 adults from a city clinic group in the capital. Checks mixed forms that patients filled in, health records, and heart traces kept for a full day.

Nerve harm showed up in near 17 percent of those checked. Diabetes was found in near 31 percent of those cases. Rates rose with age. They tracked the same shape as diabetes rates by sex and by age. Two heart rate scores from the day long traces are put forth as handy signs. The team says such tests could flag this harm at an early stage in plain clinic care.
pmc-11676943:
Ángel Sanz-Felipe and Juan Vallés map the design and run settings that let an active waveguide Bragg grating lase. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The structure pairs the sharp bounce of a Bragg grating with the gain of rare earths, a mix that could yield a one-piece laser. Its response swings hard with design, so a model is a must first.

They trace light power through a grating doped with erbium and ytterbium by a numerical method. A full data base of responses is built across the key settings. From it, the critical value of each design and run trait for laser action is pinned down. The map guides later builds and tuning of such photonic parts.
pmc-11677943:
Xinyue Ren and five colleagues published a cell study in two thousand twenty-four on making the brain's insulation cells. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibres in myelin, and their parent cells often stall before maturing. Vitamin C and a signalling drug were each known to push maturation; together they work even better.

The team traced the effect to DNA demethylation, the removal of chemical tags that silence genes. The pair raised levels of an intermediate tag that marks active tag removal. Blocking that intermediate almost fully stopped maturation. One expected enzyme family member, TET1, proved uninvolved. The authors propose the combination as a future therapy lead for diseases where myelin is lost.
pmc-11678243:
Mateusz Urbaniak and co-authors test a bacterial pigment, pyomelanin, as a spur for bone growth. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The pigment comes from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and mimics deposits seen in a rare genetic disease where cartilage turns to bone. That likeness hints it could wake bone cells on purpose.

Two forms, one that melts in water and one that does not, both lift bone marks in human bone cell cultures. The team sees a path to new bone repair mixes built with the pigment.

pmc-11726543:

Their mice were bred to release the human form of the protein into the blood from vessel walls when switched on. At rest the mice seemed well, but a chemical in their drinking water brought on gut inflammation that closely matched ulcerative colitis. The colon lining broke down while the upper gut stayed near normal. The protein thus worsens inflammation once it starts, without starting it alone.
pmc-12734343:
Martino, Szmulewicz, and Birmaher ask in twenty twenty-five whether today's concept of bipolar disorder rests on valid ground. They reviewed a century of texts and studies on the criteria for manic and depressive episodes, judging both whether the illness is a real entity and whether the rules describe it well.

Mania holds up as a genuine construct, though its diagnostic rules need more testing. Evidence for splitting milder hypomania from mania as separate episodes is thin and contested. The modern idea of bipolar depression lumps together unlike episode types, with weak proof all belong to the one illness. The authors call the current definition's validity limited. Sharper definitions, they argue, would speed biology research and tailored treatment.
pmc-12734743:
Hyun Soo Kim and co-authors put a full-size aluminum electric vehicle battery case through punishing tests, in the lab and in simulation. Their study appeared in 2025. The case must survive bottom impacts, crushing, and constant vibration without endangering passengers. The team ran a bottom impact test, a 200 kilonewton compression test, and a random vibration test, then mirrored each in a finite element model with the same supports and loads.

Predicted stresses and bending matched the real measurements closely. Hot spots sat at corners and frame joints, and peak compression bent the case by less than a millimeter. Vibration shook hardest vertically but loosened no bolts and broke nothing. The authors say the design is verified, and the matched model can drive lighter future cases.
pmc-12735143:
Yizhou Hu, Leheng Zhang, Sirui Gong, and Zhenlong Wang polish titanium composite surfaces with an electrochemical finish after spark machining, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The mesh-structured composite suits aerospace work but its uneven makeup makes smooth micro-surfaces hard. Spark machining leaves pits ringed by raised rims.

Standalone electrochemical machining failed first: the fiber reinforcement and the metal base dissolved at wildly differing rates, chewing the surface unevenly. Applied after spark machining instead, the method under tuned settings (salt solution, modest voltage, fast pulses) erased the pit rims. Surface roughness halved, and the finish grew even. The authors present the two-step route as a practical way to machine this tough material cleanly.
pmc-12735243:
Yaoyao Liu leads a team that coats sea sensors with a hard film. Their work from twenty twenty-five uses a film of alumina laid by a strong sputter tool. Sea water wears and rusts sensors, which cuts their life.

Film tests in a sea like setting showed strong wear proof. Surface scans traced how the film changed with rubbing. With the film, a pressure sensor caught tiny forces under water. Mounted on a robot gripper, it sensed fine moves of held things. The coat could extend sea sensor life and skill both.
pmc-12736743:
Trey Coughlin, Koki Weng, Maria Laura Salum, Pablo Froimowicz, Chris Scott, and Hatsuo Ishida make heat-stable, flame-resistant resins from a plant compound in two thousand twenty-five. The starting compound, umbelliferone, comes from natural sources and carries a phenol group. Four resin building blocks were made from it, two of them new.

The new blocks use distinct amine partners, which lets the team test how the amine's ring and chain length shape the final plastic. Heat tests showed high char left after burning, a sign of strong heat stability. None of the four plastics could be ignited in flame tests, and their heat release rates were low. The results guide design of safer resins for hot settings.
pmc-12736943:
Magdalena Gaca and Magdalena Lipińska study rubber composites. In these mixes, an ionic liquid is used to improve the bond between polymer and carbon filler. Their base is a styrene-butadiene rubber, a type in wide use in rubber processing. It is cured with a standard sulfur system. Two fillers were tested, furnace carbon black and graphene nanoplatelets. Each filler was changed during mixing with a pyridinium-based ionic liquid. That liquid can stack onto the filler surfaces.

The study measures curing behavior, crosslink density, and mechanical properties. It then looks at rheology and damping at service temperatures, across a range of deformations. Fillers of distinct shapes and sizes interacted with the polymer in distinct ways. The ionic liquid also shaped contacts between filler particles. The authors map how a small additive reshapes viscoelastic performance in filled rubber.
pmc-12739843:
Ida Elisabeth Bang and co-authors hunt risk factors for tearing during birth in Norway, in work from 2025. Such tears hit the anal sphincter and can cause lasting harm. The team used a regional birth registry with over twenty-six thousand single births from 2012 to 2022. They tested known risk traits plus a new suspect: breaking the water sac by hand.

The hand-breaking step showed no added risk in this fresh group. Tool-aided birth stood out as the top fixable risk, with vacuum and forceps both raising odds a lot. A cut to ease birth and pain relief through the back each cut risk for first-time mothers. Tear rates held near two percent.
pmc-12739943:
Fangshuo Cheng, Jinghua Wang, and Fen Sun review tiny drug carriers cloaked in real cell membranes for treating ischemic stroke. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five. Stroke drugs struggle to cross the blood-brain barrier, and the treatment window is short.

The carriers pair a synthetic core with a natural membrane coat, gaining targeting and the ability to slip past immune patrols. The review weighs benefit against safety, a balance past work had left incomplete. Size and surface features steer where the particles end up and how long they circulate. Membrane proteins, natural or engineered, add homing power. The authors map which designs look safest inside the stroke-damaged brain.
pmc-12745443:
Youjin Kong and co-authors test a traditional granule against atrial fibrillation in a 2025 paper. Early clinical work hints that Shenlian Fumai Granule cuts rhythm problems after ablation and eases symptoms. The team probed how it may prevent the condition.

They combined network analysis, chemical profiling, and docking studies to find targets. In rats, fibrillation was induced with two drugs over five weeks. The granule was given daily at two doses, with a standard drug as a comparator. Heart tracings, ultrasound, and tissue checks tracked the effects. The work links the granule to changes in the atrium's electrical and structural remodeling.
pmc-12746843:
Atopic dermatitis, the itchy skin disease also called eczema, is driven by a tangled loop between nerves and the immune system. Zhongsong Zhang led a team reviewing how that loop works and how new treatments aim at it. Signals such as IL-31 and IL-4 talk both ways between skin, nerves, and brain, feeding the itch-scratch cycle that keeps the disease alive.

Fresh tools, from single-cell mapping to brain imaging and gut microbe profiling, are redrawing the map of these nerve-immune neighborhoods. The review gathers markers that could sort patients and track treatment, then surveys drugs old and new, from pathway blockers to microbe-based care. The authors argue that aiming at the nerve-immune axis could bring steadier, better-matched therapy.
pmc-12748443:
Rhian Graham and five co-authors published a 2025 interview study with neurodivergent women who also carry a personality disorder diagnosis. Autism and ADHD are common in this group, yet mental health services rarely offer a clear care path for them. The team asked ten women about their experiences of those services.

Five themes emerged, covering staff skills and attitudes, access barriers, feeling involved, the support offered, and the impact of diagnosis. Women described misdiagnosis and services that did not adapt to their needs. The study sketches a better pathway: person-centred assessment, peer-led support, adapted talking therapies, and patients helping to design services. It also sets priorities for clinical practice and future research.
pmc-12748543:
Rajan Kumar and co-authors chart cerebral palsy in children in eastern India in a 2025 paper. Cerebral palsy is a leading cause of childhood disability, with varied forms and added conditions. The team studied children aged four to fourteen at a tertiary center over one year.

Among 127 children, the spastic form dominated at about three quarters of cases. Severe motor limits were present in nearly two thirds. Hand ability worsened in step with motor severity. Factors tied to severe cases included no cry at birth, newborn seizures, and jaundice. Added conditions were common, marking where early help is most needed.
pmc-12748843:
Meng, Hu, and Li build a system that writes Yongju opera text in its own style. Yongju is a regional opera form from Ningbo. The team first built a data set of 100 old scripts and 50 new scripts. They added 500 lyric audio clips from local sources. Two models then split the work of writing and styling.

One model drafts text that fits Yongju grammar from modern Chinese input. A second model adds dialect words and rhythm through style controls. Drafting took 33.32 minutes, about 57 percent faster than a standard baseline. Human raters gave high marks for dialect truth and art quality. Style transfer hit 97 percent accuracy in their tests.
pmc-12750843:
Gong and co-authors show a Schwann cell gene loss that sparks face pain in mice. Face pain hits 10 to 15 percent of grown hosts in life. It stays a hard ward case with dim root paths. Schwann cells wrap nerves, yet their role here was blurred. The gene in view, Lrp1, sits in those wrap cells. Mice with that gene cut from wrap cells grew sharp pain sense. Both push and heat tests showed the spike in their faces.

Gene reads from nerve hubs showed wide shifts in those mice. Paths for cell power, rust signs, and lime hold all shifted. Flux tests and chem checks backed the power shift in the hubs. Two pain gates, TRPV1 and TRPA1, ran high in the hubs. Those gates were primed past stock in the gene-cut mice.
pmc-12752243:
Julia Koerber and co-authors map cannabis use among primary care patients with depression and anxiety in a 2025 Los Angeles study. The three conditions tangle together, yet few health systems ask about cannabis in a systematic way, so the links stay murky. This system screens routinely with a validated survey built into the medical record.

The team analyzed more than one hundred seventy thousand adult patients. They compared recent use, reasons for use, and risk of cannabis use disorder across patients with and without depression or anxiety diagnoses and related prescriptions. Systematic screening turns a hidden habit into chart data. The results can help primary care doctors counsel patients whose mental health and cannabis use may feed each other.
pmc-12752843:
Mahmud Mohammed, Tulio Fernandez-Medina, Manjunath Rajashekhar, Stephanie Baker, and Ernest Jennings review how well computers can outline jawbone in dental scans, in a 2025 paper. Dentists rebuilding lost gum bone need exact maps of the bone from cone-beam CT scans, and drawing those maps by hand is slow. The review gathered studies from the last five years that use machine learning for this outlining task, called segmentation.

From 834 papers found, 23 met the bar for inclusion. Deep learning methods, above all a design called U-Net, were the most common, and their accuracy scores ranged widely, from 76 to 98 percent overlap with hand-drawn maps. Only four studies used semi-automated methods. Bone with defects proved harder to outline than healthy bone. The authors call for better deep learning tools tuned to damaged bone, since exact maps guide regenerative treatment.
pmc-12753643:
Jae Hyung Woo and five co-authors probe how the brain picks between ways of learning in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Rewards can be learned by linking them to sights or to actions. Under uncertainty, the brain seems to run both systems at once. Some referee must weight them moment by moment. The team had monkeys play tasks with shifting uncertainty while models tracked their choices.

Monkeys with amygdala damage were compared with intact ones and with damage to a reward hub nearby. The amygdala set the starting balance between the two systems. It also proved key to adjusting that balance on the fly. The findings give the amygdala a managerial role in learning. Neuroscientists of decision making are the audience.
pmc-12757943:
Akihiro Nishi and Jon Stone write in twenty twenty-five about functional neurological disorder, known as FND. People with FND may have seizures, weakness, tremor, or loss of sight. It is one of the most common conditions seen in nerve clinics. For a long time it was called hysteria and was often dismissed or shamed.

The authors take a view based on evolution. They note that brain scans for structure are most often normal in FND. Studies of brain function, though, point to changes in brain networks. There is now broad agreement that FND has clear signs that let doctors rule it in. Readers get a fresh frame for a condition that sits between nerve care and mental health care.
pmc-12767443:
Meiying Zhu and a team of co-authors traced how a long noncoding RNA feeds a bile duct cancer's sugar burn and immune hide. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a fierce cancer with a poor outlook. The RNA, NKILA, was read in tumor samples by data scans. Its ties to two mito genes were set out. Cell lines and a mouse tumor graft then test its role in the flesh.

NKILA lifts the Warburg effect, the tumor's fast sugar burn, through that gene axis. It helps the tumor slip immune watch at the same time. Readers in liver cancer get a two front mark that could be hit by one drug aim.
pmc-12770543:
Seven authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on screening for thinking problems through speech. Fast, accurate checks for cognitive impairment are a major unmet need. Speech offers a cheap, non-invasive signal that software could screen at scale, but models must be explainable and must work on real-world recordings.

The team trained a random forest on features of speech from a standard benchmark set of two hundred ninety-one people. It caught about sixty-nine percent of cases while clearing about eighty-three percent of healthy speakers. They then checked the model on speech recorded in people's homes. Risk levels were split into bands to guide next steps.
pmc-12771843:
Maryam Koopaie, Mahnaz Fatahzadeh, and Sajad Kolahdooz combined studies on using saliva chemicals to diagnose pancreatic cancer. The cancer is usually found late and current tests can be invasive or inaccurate early on. Saliva is easy to collect and carries many small molecules that might betray disease. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team searched many databases without language limits and kept the few diagnostic studies that met their rules. Quality was rated with a standard tool, and results were pooled across thousands of patients and controls.

Pooled accuracy was moderate to good, with sensitivity and specificity each near four fifths and an overall ranking score in a useful range. Panels that combined several saliva chemicals beat single markers by a clear margin. The authors present saliva testing as a promising, painless aid, while the small number of studies argues for larger confirmatory work.
pmc-12774343:
Paul Alumbugu Tsaku and a large team of co-authors published this clinical trial in 2025. It tested raw honey dressings against standard saline dressings for the chronic foot ulcers that leprosy leaves behind. Honey helps other stubborn wounds, but it had never been rigorously tried on leprosy ulcers. The trial ran at two centers in Nigeria with 130 patients whose ulcers had lasted at least six weeks, assigned evenly to the two dressings.

Complete healing by 84 days occurred in 29.2 percent of honey-treated ulcers and 24.6 percent of saline-treated ones, a gap too small to rule out chance. Healing speed leaned toward honey without reaching significance, and recurrence at six months was similar. No treatment-related harms appeared. The authors conclude that honey is a safe, culturally acceptable option where resources are thin. They offer the trial as solid data for future evidence reviews.
pmc-12775843:
Palak Gupta and co-authors reported a surgical study in 2025 from a large hospital in western India. Their subject is holes or gaps in the skull base, the bony floor under the brain. Such gaps can arise by accident or be made on purpose while removing a tumor. A poor repair can let fluid leak from around the brain or let infection in.

The team reviewed 26 patients treated between 2018 and 2024. Fourteen had gaps at the front of the skull base and twelve at the side. All repairs used several layers, mixing the patient's own tissue, graft material, and flaps of living tissue. Every repair held, with no repeat failures. Two serious problems did occur: one case of air trapped inside the skull and one case of vision loss. No patient got meningitis or a new leak after surgery.
pmc-12780243:
Zhang and coauthors test melatonin as an aid to grow nerve cells for Parkinson care. Stem cell care is a rising hope for that brain illness. Melatonin guards nerve cells and tunes how mitochondria fuse and split. How it steers stem cells to dopamine cells was unclear.

The team honed a lab method to grow those brain cells from stem cells. Melatonin boosted that growth through a key gene path. Mitochondria fusion shifts sat in the middle of the effect. A toxin mouse model of Parkinson gave in vivo tests. Treated mice showed nerve repair gains in the brain. The work may lift cell therapy for Parkinson.
pmc-12780443:
Fatima Wilder, Miles McAllister, and six peers use maps to find the state zones where lung lump checks would do the most good. The work came out in 2025. The state is Massachusetts, in the far north-east of the land. Lung lump ends split hard by stock and by funds. To catch lumps young, when cuts and aimed drugs work, is the best lever. But take-up of checks is not the same in all zones.

The team pulled each lung lump case in the state list from 2004 to 2020. That is more than 72,000 sick folks. They tied cases to zip-code facts on stock mix and house funds. Their aims were firm. Test if zip code calls the stage at first find. Test if zip code calls the age at first find. Zones where folks show up late and young are the born marks for out-reach work.
pmc-12785843:
Ashokkumar Thirunavukkarasu and Ebtehal Mobarak Zawawi published a health study in 2025 on families caring for people with schizophrenia. The study ran in Jeddah, in western Saudi Arabia. Most earlier work on caregiver burden comes from Western countries. The authors wanted local evidence to guide policy.

They surveyed three hundred thirty caregivers with a validated Arabic tool. The tool measured five areas of burden. Only a small share reported no burden at all. Emotional strain scored highest among the five areas. Adult children caring for parents carried heavier burdens. Government workers reported lower burdens than others. The authors recommend workplace flexibility and financial help for caregivers.
pmc-12786943:
Irina Zvereva and colleagues studied iron-loaded zeolite crystals in 2025. Zeolites have tiny ordered pores inside. Alkali etching can add larger pores too. Extra pores may help iron enter channels. Optical and surface changes were then measured.

Etched samples took up more iron. Iron spread differently inside porous samples. Light absorption shifted toward visible range. The energy gap of the material shrank. Such changes suit light-driven catalysis. Pre-etching created a useful hierarchy of pores. The authors propose photocatalyst uses next. Cleaner chemical production could benefit. Iron placement inside pores was the core question.
pmc-12787943:
Alexander Gnutikov and co-authors unpick the parentage of a man-made wheat relative bred for hardiness. Their study appeared in 2025. The hybrid, Trititrigia cziczinii, came from crossing bread wheat with a wild wheatgrass, then crossing back to wheat. Using several DNA markers from nucleus and chloroplast, plus deep sequencing of one ribosomal region, the team asked which parent's genome dominates. The main nuclear ribosomal DNA and the chloroplast both came from bread wheat, marking wheat as the mother line.

One outer marker region, though, leaned toward the wheatgrass parent, hinting at reshuffling or mixed sequences in the hybrid. Deep sequencing confirmed wheat-type copies dominate, with a small wheatgrass-like minority. The authors say knowing the true genomic mix guides using this hybrid in breeding.
pmc-12800143:
Weihong Wu and colleagues report a 2025 study of roadbed filler made from coal gangue, a waste rock from mining. Roads need fill that survives endless wheel loads without sinking or cracking. The team improved the coarse material by mixing in fly ash, lime, and soil, then searched for the best recipe.

Tests found the densest mix at three percent fly ash, nine percent lime, twelve percent water, and five percent soil. Under repeated loading, samples soaked up energy in loops whose size grew as strain rose. Higher surrounding pressure shrank those loops and let the material bear more stress before failing. Lasting deformation also grew with stronger stress swings. The team fit the results to an improved stress-strain model. Their work supports turning mine waste into road foundations that hold up under traffic.
pmc-12811243:
Mayo and coauthors ask if brain sync with others softens trauma effects. Trauma harms mental health for years after the event. Social ties are known to buffer that harm. Brain sync during social contact may be the link.

Ninety-eight adults had brain sync read years before a terror attack. That read came from a joint task with a stranger. After the attack in Israel, each adult rated trauma exposure. Forms also gauged trauma signs after the event. Adults with high prior sync showed fewer signs at like exposure. The work hints sync marks social strength that guards health.
pmc-12811643:
Enayat Almasri and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, how inflammatory bowel disease may raise the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. The disease pair, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, inflame the bowel but act on the whole body. Past studies link them to rhythm faults such as atrial fibrillation and blocks in the heart's conduction system, independent of the usual cardiovascular risk factors.

The review weighs the mechanisms that may join gut to heart: systemic inflammatory signals, autonomic dysfunction, and structural remodeling of the heart muscle. Treatment effects split by drug kind. One gut drug class can at times inflame the heart, but the harm can reverse. Steroids act by dose and duration. Newer biologic drugs look safe for the heart in most data. The authors urge joint gut and heart care and long-term study.
pmc-12812243:
Kypraiou and co-authors turn a nose score form to Greek and test its worth. The form, SCHNOS, grades both look and work ends post nose jobs. It sees wide use round the world in that care field. No Greek form with proof of worth had stood till now. Turns ran front and back, with pro looks and pilot tests. In sum, 49 hosts sat in the set for the grade work.

Set hosts split as 24 nose-job hosts and 25 check hosts. Self-same marks came from a Cronbach count per sub-form. Repeat marks came from a class count on retest scores. The block sub-form scored 0.90, and the look form 0.98. Repeat marks ran 0.990 and 0.995 for the two forms. Nose hosts scored high past check hosts by firm counts.
pmc-12812443:
Gloria Venturini and eight co-authors compare two ways to pull tiny vesicles from mouse blood. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. These sacs, shed by most cells, hold proteins that may serve as disease flags. Mouse blood is a key source for such hunts, but the amount per draw is small, so the pull method matters.

One route sieves the blood through size columns. The other spins it fast through a density layer. The sieve route gives more sacs and more of their mark proteins, with fewer stray blood proteins mixed in. Plasma beats serum as the cleaner start. The work guides flag hunts in mouse models.
pmc-12812943:
Perennial ryegrass meets four kinds of salt in this study from twenty twenty-five by Gözde Hafize Yıldırım and colleagues, who ask how the forage grass copes at the gene level. Salt stress chokes growth through oxidative damage and water loss. The team dosed plants with calcium chloride, magnesium chloride, magnesium sulfate, and sodium sulfate, then read both stress-gene activity and seedling growth.

Higher salt turned up the plant's defense genes more strongly, including its antioxidant and metal-handling machinery. Yet the louder alarm did not save the plants: growth and water retention fell anyway. Mild to moderate salt told a better story, with balanced gene responses, less damage, and stronger development. The pattern suggests ryegrass can manage modest salinity with a measured response, but past a threshold, even full genetic mobilization cannot hold the line. Breeders now know roughly where that threshold behavior begins.
pmc-12813943:
Victoria Martinez and four co-authors report a case of seizures that were not epilepsy, in work from twenty twenty-five. The condition is functional neurological disorder, where brain network faults cause real symptoms without structural harm. It is common yet often missed and stigmatized.

Their patient was a woman aged nineteen with a seven year history of presumed epilepsy. She took many seizure drugs, yet brain scans and brain wave tests stayed unclear. Her history held trauma stress and family epilepsy, which clouded the picture. The authors stress early, correct diagnosis. A right label can stop years of needless drugs and point care toward what helps.
pmc-12819743:
Jia Zhou and colleagues published a 2026 study of a secreted protein driving liver cancer. Liver cancer mechanisms remain incompletely defined. The protein was newly linked to tumor signaling. Its levels were measured in tumors and healthy tissue. Cell and mouse experiments tested its effects.

Tumor tissue showed markedly higher levels. Raising the protein sped cancer growth. Silencing it slowed growth in models. The protein controlled the cell's recycling system. A well-known growth pathway carried its signal. Single-cell data mapped where it acts. Blocking this protein could become a treatment strategy. More work must confirm safety and reach.
pmc-12821543:
Aronis and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on shoulder strength in standing men. Overhead reaching strength matters for work design, rehab, and wearable support gear. Fourteen healthy men pushed with greatest effort at eight arm angles. A force sensor read shoulder torque at each angle. Wires on the skin tracked four shoulder and arm muscles. Torque fell steadily as the arm rose higher. One side shoulder muscle fired harder at higher angles.

A chest muscle's activity fell sharply as the arm rose. Two other muscles held high, steady activity across angles. The data set gives reference values for healthy male shoulders. The authors say the values can guide ergonomic checks and support gear design. They caution the sample is small and male only.
pmc-12821843:
Darci Phillips and co-authors explore, in twenty twenty-five, how parents view cardiovascular health for their families. Parents' views shape children's lifelong heart health, yet they are rarely studied. The team ran semi-structured interviews with twenty-one parents of children under eighteen, plus four children. Answers were coded thematically with a constant comparison method until no new themes appeared. Child interviews were analyzed separately, for context on how youth see heart health and how families talk about it.

Eight themes emerged, covering definitions of heart health, information sources, family and community roles, experiences, resources, and emotional links. Parents named real barriers, including limited access to fitness options, the head text notes. The findings aim to guide intergenerational heart health programs.
pmc-12821943:
Aishwarya Guha and co-authors show, in a 2025 study, how platelets educated by a breast tumor can feed the tumor's stem cells. Platelets are blood components that seal wounds. Tumors educate them, and educated platelets help cancers spread. Their grip on breast cancer stem cells, the seed cells that regrow tumors, was not mapped.

The team drew platelets and tumor cells from patients with two breast cancer types, plus mouse models and cell lines. Educated platelets bore more of an adhesion protein, P-selectin, and clung to the stem cells through its partner PSGL1. Under their influence, stem cells grew more aggressive: they seeded tumors, resisted drugs, and invaded. Aspirin calmed the platelets and cut that influence. The adhesion fires a signaling chain involving WNT and beta-catenin that steadies stemness. Blocking parts of the chain by gene silencing confirmed its role.
pmc-12822043:
Nine authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five that shortens a quality-of-life questionnaire. The full measure has sixty-nine items and covers well-being across four elements and eighteen domains. A shorter form would be quicker for patients and clinics to use, if it stayed just as sound.

The new form, called SigQOLM-36, keeps thirty-six items and the same structure as the original. The authors report that its scores hang together very well overall and acceptably in every domain. Checks on how the items group and how the model fits also came out strong. They conclude the short form can stand in for the long one.
pmc-12824143:
Fentaye Kassawmar and three co-authors surveyed the use of medicinal plants in Meketewa District, in northwestern Ethiopia, in a 2025 ethnobotanical study. Traditional medicinal plants remain an important source of health care for rural communities there, where access to modern medical services is limited. The team collected information from 360 informants across five kebeles, or sub-districts, in different agroecological zones.

The study documented 76 medicinal plant species in 46 families. Fabaceae was the largest family, and herbs were the most common growth form. Most species were used to treat human ailments, while others treated livestock or both. Most plants came from natural forests. Crushing was the most common preparation method, and oral administration was the most common route. The authors call for conservation of these plants and for further laboratory testing of their effects.
pmc-12824243:
Taya Lee and five colleagues published a device study in two thousand twenty-five on treating neck-of-womb cell changes by injection. The therapy injects an alcohol-based gel into the cervix to kill abnormal cells. It is aimed at poorer countries where surgery is scarce.

First the team checked that pig cervix tissue behaves like human tissue; stiffness tests matched. Then they compared two injectors that work with a standard examination tool. Shots placed at least ten millimetres deep, with under two millilitres of gel, leaked less and cracked the tissue less. An extender injector caused fewer cracks than a plain needle one. The findings set practical rules for future clinical use.
pmc-12830743:
Artem Oganov and Maksim Kostenko present a simple chemistry model in 2025 for predicting which pairs of elements form stable compounds. Since the time of Linus Pauling, scientists have used a trait called electronegativity to guess such behavior. Prior models worked only for narrow classes of compounds or grew complex when stretched further.

Their model gives each element just two numbers, one for electronegativity and one for chemical mismatch. Values fitted from many computed formation energies follow clear patterns across the periodic table. The model explains several odd cases, such as why reactive alkali metals form few compounds with most elements. Noble metals, by contrast, form stable compounds with most elements in this picture.
pmc-12830943:
Junhao Han and a large team show how one central light source can feed fast data links at the edge of a network. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Small sites such as edge computing rooms need high capacity but have little space, and adding more light channels runs into noise and weak signal quality.

The team used a tiny chip device that makes a comb of laser lines from one source. With it they sent data at very high rates on a single line and core. A wider setup with sixteen comb lines pushed the total far higher. Adding shaping chips and amplifiers shrank the whole system to about a hundredth of its size while still delivering strong rates. The work points to compact light gear for modular data centers.
pmc-12837043:
Wan and co-authors test whether poor sleep carries the effect of childhood trauma into depression in teens with bipolar disorder. Trauma in childhood worsens bipolar disorder in adolescence, above all by deepening depressive symptoms. The steps between early trauma and later depression, though, were still unclear to clinicians.

Sleep disturbance is a strong candidate for the middle step. The study enrolled 426 adolescents with bipolar disorder and measured trauma history, sleep quality, and depression severity. Statistical mediation tests checked if sleep problems explained the trauma link. A confirmed path would make sleep care a clear target for these teens.
pmc-12849143:
Zunqi Hu and co-authors explain in 2025 one way stomach cancer learns to resist the drug cisplatin. Immune cells called M2 macrophages sit near tumors and shed tiny parcels. Those parcels carry a small RNA, miR-668-3p, which the team found raised in drug-resistant tumor tissue.

Cancer cells take in the parcels and the RNA with them. The RNA silences a gene called ETS1, which lowers a growth receptor, EGFR. That drop switches on autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup, which helps the cells survive the drug. The chain held in cell tests and in mouse tumors. Blocking the small RNA is the authors' proposed route to restore drug sensitivity.
pmc-12849443:
Mohammad Aadil and colleagues report a malignant neck artery-body tumour in a young woman, with a literature review. Their 2025 case report covers a rare growth that is usually benign and slow-growing.

An eighteen-year-old from a non-mountainous region presented with a painless neck swelling growing gradually for two and a half years. The firm, pulsing lump sat in the front triangle of her neck with a palpable vibration. Imaging established the diagnosis, and complete surgical removal followed. Tissue examination confirmed the tumour type with spread to nearby lymph nodes, which established malignancy. The authors note the rarity of malignant change and its occurrence in so young a patient.
pmc-12853843:
Ipek Bulut and co-authors find a lever against drug-proof prostate cancer in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Once the cancer stops answering hormone therapy, taxane drugs are a mainstay, but resistance grows. The team built resistant cell models and screened epigenetic drugs.

Blockers of the Menin protein restored taxane power, halting cells at a division checkpoint and triggering death. Removing Menin hurt only resistant cells and stopped resistance from forming in fresh ones. Gene and binding studies tied Menin to the mTOR growth pathway. Pairing an mTOR blocker with the taxane worked even better together. Animal tests backed the idea. The authors propose the combo for refractory cases.
pmc-12859143:
Xu Han and a large team use inverse design to pack light circuits far more densely on lithium niobate chips. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The base film is prized for light work but hard to shrink to silicon-like density. The team used math search to shape tiny parts that split, cross, and bend light in many modes at once.

Built parts took just a small chip area yet held more than ten light path parts. A test chip sent data in many modes and, with built-in speed shifters, hit fast rates per lane. The team claims a ten-fold jump in part density for this film. Wide use in data links is the aim.
pmc-12859943:
Yanan Niu and ten co-authors study the genes behind flag leaf thickness in wheat and how that trait links to yield. Leaf size traits get much past study, but leaf thickness has had far less. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team measured thickness directly in a large set of wheat lines bred from two parents. Leaf traits rose along with spike length, grain count per spike, and grain weight and size. The authors map gene spots tied to thickness and to yield parts, with one main spot for thickness found near spots for other traits. The results can guide breeding for higher yield.
pmc-12866343:
Huiwen Xie and three colleagues ask whether a previous keyhole hernia repair blocks doing the same operation on the other side later, in a cohort study published in two thousand twenty-five. Totally extraperitoneal repair works behind the abdominal wall. Scarring from the first operation might obstruct a second.

Thirty-eight patients who developed a hernia on the opposite side after a first repair were reviewed. The average gap between operations was about four years. The second repair succeeded in thirty-seven cases. Surgeons found that identifying key vessels and dissecting the lateral space first made the reoperative field manageable. Recurrence and complication outcomes were tracked. Patients can be reassured that choosing this repair once does not burn the bridge for the other groin.
pmc-12907043:
Jiyeon Han reviews how metal ions work inside proteins and small protein-like chains in living systems. Metals are often framed as poisons, Han notes. Yet cells depend on tiny, tightly held amounts of iron, copper, and zinc. These ions sit in buffered pools, passed hand to hand rather than floating free.

Trouble starts when metals land in the wrong place. Loose iron and copper can spark reactions that damage proteins, fats, and DNA. Such damage is tied to nerve cell death, degenerative disease, and cancer. Foreign heavy metals like lead and cadmium can also push native metals out of their slots. Lead, for one, can take zinc's place in an enzyme and shut it down. The review traces how shape and grip decide whether a metal helps or harms.
pmc-12924443:
Annerstedt and seven co-authors compare two support bundles to help schools run a healthy habits program faithfully, in a trial report from twenty twenty-five. Childhood overweight has risen sharply in Sweden over recent decades. The program joins school lessons with family talks and checks. The trial tests whether extra support beats basic support.

Forty-five schools in Stockholm took part over two school years. Close to a thousand parents and over six hundred children joined. Schools followed the program at about three-quarter fidelity overall. Extra support did not beat basic support on fidelity scores. Two extra strategies never really happened for lack of time and interest. Fidelity improved over time, so early support matters most.
pmc-13087443:
Aroni and five co-authors report a gum surgery case with long follow up, in work from twenty twenty-six. The patient was a healthy man aged thirty-seven with many gum recessions on both sides of the upper jaw. Recession exposes tooth roots and can cause sensitivity.

Surgeons used a flap method with two pig collagen matrices as graft substitutes. One product went on the right side and the other on the left. Full root cover was seen in almost all sites within two months. One side gained more thick tissue. Four year follow up lets readers judge whether the gains lasted, which short reports cannot show.
pmc-13133243:
Miguel Marquez and colleagues build a microscope that films bubbles dancing at a million cycles a second, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Microbubbles driven by ultrasound are used in therapy, but their frantic motion is hard to catch: cameras must trade speed against sharpness and cost. Their instrument squeezes a whole high-speed movie into a single snapshot.

The method streaks the scene, darkens the background, and lets a neural network rebuild the film from the compressed trace. With it they recorded steady bubbling, wild oscillations, free ringing after the sound stopped, and violent collapse, in bubbles a few micrometers wide. In whole blood they watched, for the first time, vibrating bubbles shoving platelets around and squeezing out of shape against a red blood cell. The authors offer the compact rig for labs studying bubble-based therapies.
pmc-13146443:
Oshi Swarup and seven colleagues tested whether an enzyme used for mucus can boost a clot-busting drug. The enzyme, dornase alfa, chews up DNA webs that white cells cast into stroke clots. Those webs stiffen clots against breakdown. Earlier work paired the enzyme with an older drug. This study pairs it with tenecteplase, the newer standard.

The team worked on forty-two clots pulled from stroke patients during procedures. Clots soaked in buffer with the drug alone shrank to about forty percent of their weight in two hours. Adding a high dose of the enzyme cut them much further. In plasma, the boost faded and lost statistical strength. The results suggest the pairing can work, but blood proteins blunt it. The authors call for care in moving the idea toward patients.
pmc-13146543:
Emily E Farah and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six Australian cohort study of daily functioning in school children with spinal muscular atrophy. New treatments have transformed this once-deadly muscle disease. How independent treated children are in everyday life was unexplored.

Children aged four to twelve were found through newborn screening or later clinical referral. A standard disability inventory measured social, responsibility, daily activity, and mobility skills. Most children scored as expected for their age in social and responsibility areas. Mobility lagged, with fewer than half at expected levels. Screening-found children did better across all areas.
pmc-13147343:
Kadison Michel and co-workers report a rare case of a bad blood infection from a dog scratch. A 52-year-old woman who had been well got sepsis from Capnocytophaga canimorsus after a small scrape on her brow. The 2026 case report tells of a muddled mind, loose stools, and a sick feeling that got worse fast. She went into shock and her kidneys failed, though she had just had a drug from her own doctor to fight germs.

Blood tests then found the germ, and care was changed to match. She needed a breathing tube and a machine to clean her blood day and night. Scans showed dead tissue in both kidneys. That left her tied to dialysis for life. The team notes this is one of very few such kidney cases on record. It is the sole known case where the patient lived.
pmc-13150343: Sho Okamura and co-authors published a short technique note in 2026 on heart pacing tests. Some hearts have two backward paths for electric signals near the central node, a fast one and a slow one. Standard pacing can miss the slow path because the fast path masks it. The note shows that adding extra timed pulses to the pacing, while varying which tissue is captured, can reveal the hidden slow path. The trick gives doctors a clearer read on the wiring in such cases.
pmc-13157743:
Shukar and a large team study access to anticancer medicines in South Asia in twenty twenty-six. The region carries a high cancer burden with low health coverage. Patients often pay large sums out of pocket for drugs. The team examined essential medicines lists, registration, and local production in eight countries.

They compared sixty-seven medicines from the World Health Organization list with national lists. Median national lists held only about twenty-four of those medicines. Registration was broader, with a median of forty-five medicines. Local production stayed very limited, with a median of six point five medicines. Interviews with thirty supply chain stakeholders named key barriers. Financial limits, weak regulation, and poor strategic planning stood out. The authors urge better coordination and regional production.
pmc-13172843:
Thakshila Dasanayake and Nikki L. Hill lay out a planned study of education and Alzheimer's disease using the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center dataset. Clinical diagnosis and brain pathology at death do not always agree. The authors ask whether schooling helps explain the mismatch.

Participants will be sorted into four groups, from true Alzheimer's to people with pathology but no symptoms. Regression analysis will test how education relates to each group. The authors expect highly educated people to appear more often among those who stayed sharp despite pathology. Such a result would support the idea of cognitive reserve. It would also argue for including reserve factors in diagnosis and research.
pmc-13173643:
Hallward-Driemeier and coauthors track methane gas that leaks from a landfill in New Jersey. Landfills give off a large share of methane in the United States. Methane warms the air far more than most gases. Reports may miss much of what landfills truly emit.

The team read air from one tall tower near the site for two and a half years. That long run caught shifts that short plane or car checks miss. Their counts matched plane and ground checks done at the same times. Heat and air pressure drove much of the month-to-month shift. The work gives a new way to check landfill claims.
pmc-13176143:
Saeed, Siepker, Jang, Shahdadian, and Liu measure coupling between brain blood flow and fluid movement in twenty twenty-six. Alzheimer's disease involves vessel damage and poor waste clearance from the brain. Spinal fluid helps wash out toxins, but measuring it is invasive. The team used broadband near infrared light through the forehead instead.

Three groups took part: young adults, healthy older adults, and early Alzheimer's patients. Coupling between blood volume and free water signals was computed across rhythm bands. Coupling was weakest in the young and strongest in Alzheimer's patients. Older healthy adults fell in between.
