The authors suggest stiffening vessels and compensation for poor clearance explain the pattern. The cheap, non invasive method may mark early disease.
pmc-13178243:
Jinglu Wang and five co-authors build two zinc-based lattice materials that glow, for use in cell imaging and cancer care. Such lattices can be tuned by design, and their glow lets doctors track them. By varying the mix and fill of the reaction vessel, the team grew two forms from the same parts. One stacks in layers; the other weaves through itself in three dimensions.

Both glowed green in pure water, but the woven form glowed more than twice as strongly and held its glow amid the ions found in the body. The layered form killed cervical cancer cells in dishes through several death paths at once. The paper shows how small build choices tune one material family for seeing or for treating.
pmc-13179043:
Aharon Steffè and co-authors build tunable nanoparticles in a 2026 paper. Smart design of nanomaterials needs exact control of structure and of how surfaces react. The team made block copolymer nanoparticles in water that carry amine groups on their surface.

The amines could be counted and then linked to other molecules with high yield. One link added a dye; another added a heat-responsive polymer that switches at 41 degrees. The particles could also be assembled into hollow crosslinked shells called colloidosomes. The authors present the platform as a modular base for drug delivery, diagnostics, and tiny reactors.
pmc-13180543:
Chao Li and six co-authors link broken sleep, swelling, and a sharper sense of pain through one brain zone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Broken sleep is known to raise swelling signals and lower the point at which pain is felt. How the brain sits in that chain was not clear.

In a lab test, forced waking cuts deep sleep, raises a key swelling signal, and lowers pain thresholds. Brain scans show one zone, the precuneus, fires more when pain is felt after broken sleep. That zone's heat carries the link from the swelling signal to pain sense. In chronic pain patients, the same zone settles as pain and sleep improve.
pmc-13181243:
Wenxi Yu and four co-authors published a lung cancer study in twenty twenty-six on a circular RNA in tumor cells. Circ-FSCN1 helps the cells grow and dodge a fiery form of cell death. It was found at high levels in non-small cell lung cancer tissues and cell lines, and the team mapped its chain of action.

Silencing the circle slowed cell growth and migration and let reactive oxygen pile up, pushing ferroptosis. The circle normally sponges up a small RNA, miR-506-3p, which otherwise restrains a cystine transporter, SLC7A1. Restoring either downstream partner cancelled the silencing effects in two cell lines. Animal assays extended the story. The axis gives drug hunters three connected targets in one pathway.
pmc-13181343:
Min Cao and Glenn Masson review structural insights into the activity and inhibition of HRI kinase, a stress-sensing enzyme. Their 2026 review examines a protein emerging as a drug target in cancers and neurodegenerative disease.

HRI is one of four related kinases that switch off protein production by modifying a translation factor. It senses several proteotoxic stresses and prevents further rounds of protein synthesis. The review covers recent structural and molecular work on how the kinase activates and how inhibitors act. Regulatory interactions with other proteins and cofactors are also examined. Despite identification decades ago, the authors note surprisingly little is known about its regulation.
pmc-13184043:
Joyeeta Bhattacharya and nine co-authors reviewed plant chemicals packed in nano carriers as a breast cancer treatment path, in a paper published in 2026. The cancer is a top killer of women, and standard treatments cut hard at the whole body. Plant compounds are kind to healthy tissue but weak in reach: they dissolve poorly, fade fast, and land widely. Nano packs fix each flaw.

Fat bubbles, plastic beads, metal particles, and carbon dots all serve as packs in the studies. Packs keep the compounds stable, raise their uptake, and steer them to the tumor. Harm to healthy cells falls as tumor kill rises. The team sorts gains by pack kind and compound kind. They call for trials to carry the green path into clinics.
pmc-13194743:
Feng Zhu leads a 2026 engineering paper on making tiny hemispherical resonator gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation for precision navigation. Their quality factor, a measure of how cleanly the shell vibrates, and its frequency splitting decide performance. Standard coating lays a continuous metal film on the shell, which adds damping and drags quality down.

The team used patterned coating instead, depositing titanium and platinum films only in designed patches on the curved shell through three-dimensional masks. Coated devices lost little quality, reaching a quality factor above eight million, with even performance around the shell and tiny frequency splitting. Cutting film coverage reduces friction damping, the authors show, and a model links pattern to uniformity.
pmc-13196343:
Fangru Li, Xiaolei Liu, Weiguo Hou, and seven colleagues read archaeal communities as vent detectors in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Deep-sea hydrothermal sediments host archaea driving major chemical cycles, but how their communities differ along heat gradients from vents was unclear. The team sequenced archaeal genes in sediment cores from two different sites in the Tianxiu vent field, Northwest Indian Ocean. One site sat near a vent, the other far from it, with metagenomics added at the near-vent site.

The near-vent sediments were enriched in Hydrothermarchaeia, Nanoarchaeia, and Thermoplasmata, and formed a more complex, highly connected community network. Hydrothermarchaeia abundance tracked heat and chemical gradients closely, and its genomes carried the Wood-Ljungdahl carbon fixation pathway, with potential for methane production and hydrogen oxidation. The far site was led by Nitrososphaeria with simpler structure. The authors propose Hydrothermarchaeia as a marker lineage of hydrothermal influence.
pmc-13197443:
Ceren Demir and colleagues ran a 2026 trial of home posture exercise for fibromyalgia, a long-term pain condition. Guidelines pair the drug duloxetine with exercise for this condition. The team tested whether a home posture program adds benefit beyond the drug alone.

Fifty-one patients split into an exercise group and a control group, both on the drug. The exercise group trained at home three times a week for four weeks. Both groups improved in pain, mood, sleep, and quality of life. The exercise group gained more in sleep quality, physical quality of life, and trunk bending range. Pain and mood gains did not differ. The trial was short, with no later follow-up.
pmc-13200443:
Azza M El-Derby and colleagues review cancer-killing viruses for liver cancer in a 2026 article. Oncolytic viruses infect and burst cancer cells while sparing normal ones. Results in solid tumors still lag hopes, and liver cancer's dense, immune-suppressed setting is among the toughest.

The review covers natural and engineered viruses in lab and clinical work on liver tumors. Barriers include thick scar-like tissue, fast liver immune clearance, and uneven tumor traits. Fixes under study include stroma-targeting designs, viruses tuned to low-oxygen zones, and lab-grown tumor models to test delivery. Engineering now arms viruses to wake anti-tumor immunity. The authors map how these strands could yield stronger next-generation viruses.
pmc-13202443:
Stronger, water-resistant paper made from farm and mining waste is the aim of a 2026 study led by Oumaima Bendalahcen. The research article treats date palm fibers to enrich their cellulose, reinforces the sheets with phosphate waste rock, and coats them with a bio-based terpene phenolic resin.

The mineral additive, rich in calcium and magnesium oxides, bonded with fiber sugars to strengthen cohesion inside the sheet. After resin coating and heat pressing, the paper shed water far better and showed large gains in stiffness and tensile strength over the untreated material. Ductility also improved, and the authors present the recipe as a route to high-performance paper that valorizes two waste streams.
pmc-13203043:
Prescribing guidelines aim to trim opioid use, and a 2026 systematic review by Jihoon Lim measures whether they actually do. The review and meta-analysis gathers studies of opioid prescribing guidelines for adults, focusing on chronic noncancer pain, and pools their effects on use prevalence, dosage, and treatment duration.

From 190 records found in four databases, seventy-one studies entered the meta-analysis. After guidelines took effect, opioid dose per person and prescription duration fell year by year among chronic pain patients in the pooled estimates. Declines also appeared in the general population and in cancer and acute pain groups, showing effects spilling beyond the intended audience.
pmc-13204243:
Dana-Emanuela Pitic and ten co-authors compare two turmeric extracts with an eye to mouth care in a 2026 study. Turmeric's active compounds fight germs and help wounds close, which suits dental uses. The team made one extract with water and one with strong alcohol, then compared their make-up and their action on mouth bacteria and skin cells.

The alcohol extract yielded more material, held more plant compounds, and fought the two tooth-decay bacteria better. The water extract was gentler on yeast and kinder to skin cells, though the alcohol one closed a scratch wound faster at a low dose. The authors say the solvent choice lets makers trade germ power against tissue kindness in future products.
pmc-13205943:
Panagiota Peleka, Petros Galanis, and five co-authors review what shapes life quality after a heart event. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers acute coronary syndromes. Modern care saves far more lives than before. Many survivors, though, live with lasting limits on daily life.

From more than twelve thousand papers, fifty-five passed the bar. Most were group-follow studies from Europe and the Americas. Better starting life quality predicts a better later course. Past exercise habits, a sense of coherence, and coping style help too. Mood, social support, and heart limits weigh in as well. The map can guide rehab that targets what matters most.
pmc-13207843:
Ioana Roxana Codru and four colleagues published a study in two thousand twenty-six on a blood ratio that might flag ventilator pneumonia early. Lung infection on a breathing machine is common and deadly in intensive care, and early diagnosis is hard. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio comes free from routine blood counts.

Three hundred twelve ventilated patients were analysed, split between scheduled tube replacement and standard care. Pneumonia struck far less often in the replacement group. Within that group, patients heading for pneumonia showed higher ratios before diagnosis, with a cutoff near eight point three. In standard care the ratio predicted nothing. The authors call its value limited and context-dependent.
pmc-13209143:
A thyroid failure so severe it squeezed the heart is reported in a 2026 case authored by James Nelson Okema from northern Uganda. The article presents a 65-year-old woman with five months of worsening breathlessness, swelling, and slow pulse, arriving with chest pain and signs of cardiac tamponade from fluid around the heart.

Ultrasound confirmed a large effusion collapsing the right ventricle, and urgent drainage removed over half a liter of straw-colored fluid. Fluid tests argued against tuberculosis, the usual suspect in that region, while blood tests revealed severe autoimmune hypothyroidism driving the picture. Gentle thyroid hormone replacement followed drainage, her circulation recovered at once, and later scans showed the fluid gone.
pmc-13210143:
A two-faced enzyme in a tropical parasite appears impossible to delete, and a 2026 study headed by Juliana Martins Ribeiro works around that barrier in Leishmania infantum. Using CRISPR editing, the team tried to knock out an atypical phosphatase-kinase that tunes stress signaling, then studied parasites with lowered or raised expression instead.

Full deletion failed repeatedly, even with a spare copy supplied first, suggesting the gene is essential for the parasite's free-living stage. Halving expression stretched the parasites' shape, disturbed their cell cycle, and made them far more sensitive to oxidative attack inside host cells. Overexpression instead hardened them against antimony drugs, linking the enzyme to treatment resistance.
pmc-13210243:
Island mothers' DNA carries the timetable of early human settlement, and a 2026 genetics study by Anjana Welikala sequences it at full resolution in Sri Lanka. The research article analyzes 139 complete mitochondrial genomes from Sinhalese, Sri Lankan Tamil, and Vedda people, merged with 247 published genomes worldwide.

Four settlement phases emerged from the family trees reconstructed in the analysis. The earliest phase aligns with the first entry of modern humans into South Asia, backing the southern coastal dispersal route out of Africa for the region. West Eurasian lineages arrived later by way of India, and every studied population shows a marked shrinkage in effective size across its history.
pmc-13210743:
Sheng Yao leads a team that maps the NAC gene family in Masson pine. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with wood formation genes. The pine is a key timber tree in South China.

NAC factors form a large plant gene control family. Near a hundred members were mined from the genome. One member stood out as a core wood regulator. Tests placed its protein inside the cell nucleus. In poplar, it raised lignin and cellulose build up. Binding tests tied it to wall related genes. Pulp and paper value frames the tree's worth.
pmc-13211243:
Liu and co-authors present an adaptive algorithm for hybrid beamforming in joint communication and sensing systems. Massive MIMO arrays both send data and sense the surroundings in these JCAS networks. Hybrid beamforming splits the work between analog and digital parts, trading some gain for far lower hardware cost.

Design is hard because analog and digital precoders couple tightly, and huge arrays widen the search space. Their state-driven method unfolds a projected gradient algorithm into a deep network that adapts as conditions change. The approach seeks sharp beams for both tasks without the heavy cost of full digital arrays.
pmc-13211943:
Chatbot safety filters work unevenly across languages, and a 2026 vulnerability analysis led by Saubhagya Joshi measures the gap with disguised harmful prompts. The study attacks a health-oriented language model in English, Spanish, and transliterated Hindi, using emoji and letter-permutation ciphers across self-harm, violence, and drug abuse categories.

One thousand prompts per language became six thousand model interactions for human coders to judge. Hindi prompts broke through most often under both disguise styles, with Spanish and English resisting better in the comparisons. Violence-related prompts succeeded more than the other harm types overall, and the authors urge stronger multilingual moderation before such tools guide health decisions.
pmc-13212943:
Luyao Qu leads a team comparing in 2026 how accurately two clear aligner brands move teeth when a first premolar has been removed to make space. The brands use different plastics, which may grip crowns and roots with different fidelity.

Records for 29 patients combined cone-beam scans with mouth scans taken before and after treatment, aligned on stable palate ridges. Neither system differed clearly on pulling back the upper front tooth crown. One brand placed roots of two back teeth closer to plan, while the other controlled premolar tilt and torque better. Both showed the same unwanted tipping pattern. Material choice, the authors conclude, trades off by tooth and direction.
pmc-13213243:
Najeeb Ullah, Selom Doamekpor, and Liang Tong report a structure study from two thousand twenty-six on an enzyme called DXO. In cells, some RNA molecules wear unusual caps made from other cell compounds. The enzyme removes these caps, and how it grips each kind of cap was not fully known.

The team solved the crystal structure of mouse DXO holding one such cap, built from a sugar-linked compound. The shape explains why the enzyme removes the whole cap at once. Structures with short RNA pieces helped them model the enzyme at work. The model shows that a water unit held by a metal ion makes the first cut in the cap.
pmc-13214243:
Sadeed Hossain, Ahsan Ahmed, and Mohammad Sorowar Hossain sound an alarm in 2026 over measles sweeping back through Bangladesh, writing to the editor as an urgent call for an emergency response. The country had neared elimination before coverage slipped.

By spring 2026 the virus had reached nearly all districts, with tens of thousands of suspected cases and hundreds of suspected deaths reported nationally. Many sick children were too young for vaccination or had missed doses. The writers blame pandemic disruption, health system strain, and delayed policy action for weakened community protection. They demand stronger routine vaccination, catch-up campaigns for missed children, and tighter surveillance to regain control.
pmc-13214343:
Eördögh and co-authors validate a one-nostril surgical route to the central skull base in this 2026 anatomy study. Standard scope surgery through the nose often uses both nostrils and cuts more nasal tissue. Their transethmoid-paraseptal approach aims to preserve nasal function while keeping exposure.

The team performed the approach on 19 cadaver specimens and built a step-by-step checklist from the dissections. They also analyzed CT scans covering 104 sides from patients and further specimens. The corridor was established in every cadaver case, and key landmarks were found in all but one specimen. Variants like septal deviation in 36.6 percent of sides could affect the route. The study gives surgeons a tested map for the approach.
pmc-13215543:
Ruxandra Malina Petrescu-Mag and co-authors report a 2026 survey study of a little-noticed reaction to climate change: boredom with the topic. The authors ask what produces this boredom and whether it weakens people's intention to act.

Using a representative Romanian sample and structural equation modelling, the team traced boredom to beliefs about climate change, commitment to climate goals, and confidence in cooperation. Perceived health effects, living environment, and age also played a part, and together the six explained about two-thirds of the variation in boredom. The feeling itself cut the intention to act. The authors suggest that campaigns should fight disengagement, not only fear or doubt, if public motivation is to last.
pmc-13216443:
Celeste Boesjes and co-authors present a 2026 real-world study of baricitinib, an oral drug for moderate-to-severe eczema, pooling three national treatment registries from the Netherlands, Denmark, and Germany. Trial results do not always survive contact with ordinary practice, so registry evidence matters.

Across 264 patients followed for sixteen weeks, severity scores improved in all three countries, and about 62 percent of the pooled cohort reached mild disease or better. Benefit appeared in patients both new to biologic drugs and those who had used them before. Itch relief varied much more between countries than doctor-measured severity did. The authors call the drug effective in practice while urging longer follow-up and better targeting of who benefits most.
pmc-13216543:
Sherif A. Gabr and co-authors present a 2026 animal reproduction study on protecting frozen ram semen with a green tea extract packaged in chitosan nanoparticles. Freezing and thawing batter sperm through oxidative stress, and antioxidant additives are a standard line of defence.

Semen from five Ossimi rams was frozen in extender dosed with 0 to 200 micrograms per millilitre of the nano extract. The middle dose, 100 micrograms, came out best on nearly every measure: post-thaw movement, viability, and membrane integrity all rose significantly over control. DNA damage fell to about 5 percent, and pregnancy rates after insemination improved at 100 and 150 micrograms. The highest dose backfired on some measures, which the authors read as a dosing ceiling.
pmc-13216643:
J. Dominic and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their article on gadolinium-doped polyaniline and carbon nanotube composites for supercapacitors, fixing several unit and naming errors in the published record.

In the microscopy discussion, energy peak values for carbon, nitrogen, chlorine, and gadolinium were printed in electron volts and are corrected to kiloelectron volts. A table heading for entropy is corrected from kilojoules to joules per mole per kelvin. One methods sentence wrongly listed erbium among the elements mapped; the element was gadolinium. The notice supplies the corrected sentences and confirms the article has been updated.
pmc-13217243:
Deborah A. Osafehinti and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a rare hormonal complication of Ewing sarcoma: a tumour driving the adrenal glands into cortisol overproduction. Ectopic ACTH syndrome usually comes from neuroendocrine tumours; in Ewing sarcoma only a handful of adult cases exist.

Their patient, a 40-year-old woman with relapsed metastatic disease, developed swelling, low potassium, profound muscle weakness, and confusion over two months. Examination showed classic Cushing features, and scans revealed rapidly enlarged adrenals. The steroid synthesis blocker metyrapone improved her chemistry quickly enough to stop insulin and potassium replacement. With the cancer refractory, she moved to palliative care at home on metyrapone and died four months later. The authors urge prompt recognition of the syndrome.
pmc-13217443:
Jing Li and co-authors present a 2026 study of diabetic retinopathy that fingers the retina's Müller cells as drivers of a fiery form of cell death called PANoptosis. The team combined single-cell data from rats with bulk gene data from human tissue to find the responsible cell type.

Müller cells in diseased retina showed the highest PANoptosis activity scores, and one subpopulation stood out. The cells appear to send death signals through a ligand-receptor pair, PSAP and GPR37. Twenty-seven death-related genes differed in disease, and a network analysis produced ten hub genes and candidate drug targets. In rat and cell models, high glucose raised death markers as predicted, and silencing PSAP blunted that rise. The authors propose cell-specific intervention aimed at this axis.
pmc-13218143:
Zia Mehmood and colleagues test whether an angiography grade can predict living heart muscle in patients with a blocked coronary artery, in a 2026 study. When an artery closes entirely, the heart often grows collateral vessels detouring the blockage. Whether collateral strength, graded by the Rentrop scale during angiography, matches tissue viability was unclear.

The study enrolled 56 patients with chronic total occlusion who underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Viability meant scar tissue occupying no more than half the wall thickness in the blocked artery's territory. Higher Rentrop grades went with more viable muscle, rising from about 44 percent viability at grade zero to about 89 percent at grade two. Blood flow under stress also differed across grades. In adjusted analysis the Rentrop grade was the only independent predictor of viability, and a grade above one was the best cut-off. Collateral grading, the authors suggest, can inform decisions about reopening blocked arteries.
pmc-13219343:
Wang and colleagues compare in twenty twenty-six two heart-support drugs for a severe type of heart attack that also harms the right side of the heart. This attack pattern often leads to shock, where the heart cannot pump enough blood. Doctors lacked clear evidence on which of the two drugs serves these patients better.

The team reviewed records for over two hundred patients at one centre over many years. Death rates at thirty days were close in the two groups, with no clear gap after careful matching. Among survivors, patients on one drug needed support for fewer days, even though that group started out less stable. The authors advise choosing by each patient's state, not by a fixed rule.
pmc-13221143:
Megane D. Malieuze Nanfah and co-authors review infections that blood transfusion can pass on in Cameroon yet screening rules overlook, in a 2026 review. National guidelines cover four classic germs, while endemic germs such as malaria parasites go untested in blood banks. The team pooled rates and medical impact data for these neglected agents.

Eighteen studies covering about 12,500 donations met their criteria, mostly from three regions. Malaria parasites dominated the literature, found in roughly one in six donors in pooled estimates. Dengue virus, toxoplasma, and a filarial worm also appeared. Few studies measured harm to recipients, so the authors press for awareness, better diagnostics, and updated safety rules.
pmc-13221343:
Essi Hantikainen and colleagues link eating patterns to heart, kidney, and metabolic risk markers in a 2026 South Tyrol population study. Data came from 8,066 adults in the CHRIS study, who reported their diets on a detailed food questionnaire. Six established diet scores plus locally derived patterns were compared against blood pressure, blood fats, blood sugar, and kidney measures.

Diets rich in fruit, vegetables, and whole grains, and low in saturated fat, tracked with healthier marker levels. The healthy plant-based score tied to lower cholesterol and blood pressure and better kidney filtration. Western-style and unhealthy plant patterns pointed the opposite way. Some links ran stronger in men, smokers, and less active participants.
pmc-13222343:
Isabell Lang and co-authors present a nanobody recipe for building strong activators of tumor necrosis factor receptors, in a 2026 methods study. These receptors matter across immunity and cell death research, yet making activators for each one has required bespoke work. Antibodies often need extra binding partners to fire the receptors, which muddies experiments.

The team fused chains of three receptor-specific nanobodies onto scaffolding proteins, creating molecules with six, nine, or twelve binding arms. Designs covered nine different receptors and triggered signaling at sub-nanomolar doses. The formats also behaved well in production terms. A single recipe that works from nearly any nanobody could speed both research tools and drug candidates.
pmc-13223143:
Ian McMillan and co-authors track a bacterial disease in Sri Lanka across nearly two decades in a 2026 study. Leptospirosis spreads from animal urine into water and soil, and it enters people through the mouth, eyes, or broken skin. It can stay mild or turn severe and strike many organs. Sri Lanka saw a sharp spike of cases in 2008.

The team analyzed reported human cases from 2007 to 2024. Cases rose over the whole span, and they followed a yearly season. Heavier rain seemed to drive the seasonal spikes, which fits a germ that spreads through wet ground and floodwater. The study maps where and when cases cluster. Health teams can use that map to time warnings and stock care before the wet months hit.
pmc-13223943:
Mariana Carreira and co-authors identify the homing signal that guides engineered Delta One T cells into colorectal tumors, in a 2026 study. These donor gamma-delta T cells kill colorectal cancer in models, yet getting enough of them into solid tumors limits therapy. During manufacturing, the cells prominently gain the chemokine receptor CXCR3.

Colorectal tumors and cell lines produce that receptor's partner signals, and signal levels matched both natural and therapeutic cell infiltration. Blocking the receptor cut tumor homing in living models, while boosting signal production in tumors increased infiltration and improved tumor control. CXCR3 stands out as a dial developers can turn to strengthen cell therapy delivery against this cancer.
pmc-13224043:
Sarah Batson, Bethany Shinkins, and colleagues set out a 2026 position statement from the UK National Screening Committee on multicancer detection tests. Such tests promise to spot several cancers from one blood, urine, stool, or imaging sample. Several products are in development, and a large English trial is already testing one blood-based version in screening.

Because screening programmes are hard to reverse once launched, the committee lists the proof any test must supply before adoption. Considerations span disease burden, test accuracy, benefits and harms, cost effectiveness, and whether the health system can deliver the programme fairly. The statement gives policy makers a shared yardstick for judging claims made by test developers.
pmc-13225443:
Plant chemicals have been medicine for centuries. Mohammad Amin Rajizadeh, Siyavash Joukar, Farzaneh Rostamzadeh, and Maryam Doustaki Zaboli review what they do to ion channels, the gates that let charged atoms cross cell walls. Those gates drive the heartbeat, nerve signals, and gut motion, so plant effects on them matter for heart rhythm troubles, epilepsy, anxiety, pain, and gut cramps. The team searched the literature through twenty twenty-four.

Near fifty medicinal plants and their compounds shifted the flow through calcium, potassium, sodium, or chloride channels. That changed the electrical behavior of excitable cells and the working of whole organs. The review maps this scattered evidence into one frame for researchers, clinicians, and drug makers.
pmc-13226243:
Mengyuan Wang and five co-authors report enzyme engineering work in 2026 aimed at making a gas used widely in industry. The enzyme they study can turn a common cell chemical into ethylene gas, with help from the amino acid arginine. Prior attempts to boost its activity, at the active site or on its surface, had not gained much.

Guided by the enzyme structure and new clues about where arginine binds on the surface, the team changed one surface site. The new variant worked about one and a half times faster overall. Computer simulations showed the change loosened arginine grip at the surface and eased access to the active center. The study points to distant surface sites as useful targets.
pmc-13226843:
Paing Oo Htut and Naw ZuZae Nar Blue report a 2026 war-surgery case. A 23-year-old man arrived at a field hospital in shock with a shrapnel wound to the neck. He was bleeding heavily from the carotid artery and had stopped breathing. Carotid injuries kill quickly, and this hospital had no anaesthesiology support, advanced imaging, or intensive care unit to lean on.

Surgeons opened the neck and repaired the artery directly with sutures, relying on fundamental technique rather than equipment. The patient survived with no neurological deficit and went home on the fourteenth day after surgery. The authors present the outcome as proof that life-saving vascular repair stays feasible in austere conflict settings when basic surgical principles are applied decisively.
pmc-13227543:
Luisa Bertin and a large team review a 2026 map of the immune system inside eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic allergy-driven disease that stiffens and narrows the food pipe. Prevalence in Western countries now passes one in a thousand people. The review stresses that the disease runs far beyond the white cells that name it, involving alarm signals from the lining, multiple immune cell types, and scarring fibroblasts.

One newly described circuit, running from innate immune cells through a growth signal to its receptor, drives structural remodelling without needing eosinophils at all. That helps explain why some drugs clear tissue counts yet symptoms persist. Standard first-line options achieve tissue remission in a wide range of patients, and the first approved biologic roughly doubled placebo remission. The authors foresee treatment chosen by molecular subtype.
pmc-13230343:
Emilie W Kjeldsen and colleagues track in 2026 how often a common skin cancer returns after scraping treatment in Denmark. Registry data covered more than forty-seven thousand basal cell tumors treated in dermatology offices between 2013 and 2022. Some tumors also received a heat step after scraping, and follow-up ran up to eight years.

About one in ten tumors had returned by five years, rising further by eight years. Tumors on the head and neck returned most often, reaching about one in four by eight years. Larger tumors also fared worse, while the flat superficial type returned least often. Scraping stays a practical low-cost choice for well picked tumors, yet cutting out head and neck lesions may serve patients better.
pmc-13231943:
Nicolas Niessen and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry finding about boron compounds called NHC-boranes, where NHC is a ring-shaped carbon molecule that steadies the boron centre. They were heating a charged boron compound while trying to build a stronger acid catalyst.

Instead of the planned product, the heated compound pulled a fluorine-rich group off its own counter-ion, forming new chiral boranes, meaning versions that are mirror images of each other. The products showed an unusual cis and trans arrangement around a newly formed plane. The authors note the charged form is a very strong Lewis acid, a kind of electron-pair acceptor, and may prove useful as a catalyst.
pmc-13232843:
Tie Xu and colleagues design in 2026 a cooperative collision-avoidance system for several ships sharing busy water. Human rules for avoiding crashes at sea assign duties by situation, but crowded encounters strain simple planners. Their method first predicts nearby ships short-term motion and guesses how risk-tolerant each one is, using past tracking data.

A game layer then treats the give-way ship as leader and the stand-on ship as follower, choosing moves together. The sea rules are built into the allowed action set as hard limits rather than soft advice. Tests on real tracking records and simulated meetings showed advantages in crash rate, rule compliance, smooth paths, and average risk. Predictable, rule-following automation is the safety case being built.
pmc-13233143:
Pallavi Surana and colleagues published a 2026 computational study introducing TSProm, a deep learning system that reads the DNA switches controlling tissue-specific genes. They act differently in brain, liver, or testis partly because of promoter sequences near their start. The team adapted a DNA foundation model to separate general promoter rules from the signals that mark one tissue.

Two specialized models were trained, one for promoter biology overall and one for tissue-specific control, then interpretation tools highlighted the sequence motifs each model used. Applied to human brain, liver, and testis promoters, the system flagged transcription factors such as SP1, MYC, and HES6 in brain tissue, factors also tied to brain tumors. A family of zinc finger proteins stood out across tissues.
pmc-13233843:
Jun Gao and nine co-authors show a liver switch, ERR alpha, ties sugar make to gene tags gainst fat liver ill. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Lactic waste is both a fuel and a tag donor in liver cells, yet its link to fat liver was not clear. The switch ran low in sick livers as waste and its tag form rose.

In mice, drill raised the switch and its mate, which steered waste to sugar make in place of tags. Loss of the switch made the ill worse; its boost in liver cells set tag piles right and curbed the ill. Age and laze are named as tune knobs.
pmc-13234843:
Rohinee D. Hoval and a large team reviewed in 2026 titanium dioxide as a catalyst for cleaner chemical making. Titanium dioxide is a stable, low-harm semiconductor whose traits can be tuned by size and structure. Its large surface area and strong oxidizing power let it drive many reactions using light or mild conditions. The review covers oxidation, reduction, and coupling reactions that build useful organic molecules.

Reported systems often give high change while the catalyst can be recovered and reused many times. Tuning the band gap and charge separation in the material improves selectivity for desired products. Standard synthesis often depends on risky reagents and harsh conditions, which these catalysts may help replace. The authors position titanium dioxide systems as useful tools for moving industry toward looping, lower-waste output.
pmc-13235443:
Supranee Buranapraditkun and co-authors detailed in 2026 a gentle method for freeing single cells from human cheek tissue samples. The inner cheek contains skin-like cells, support cells, and resident immune cells that reflect local mucosal immunity. Small punch biopsies were digested with enzymes under controlled speed, temperature, and timing. The aim was a living, mixed single-cell suspension with minimal damage.

Typical preparations kept at least eighty percent of cells alive in the reported workflow. Resulting suspensions suit flow cytometry, which counts cell types by markers, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which reads gene activity per cell. Cheek cells offer a window on local immunity that blood cells cannot provide. Transport on ice within thirty minutes and work inside a safety cabinet protect viability and sterility. The protocol standardizes a technically tricky preparation for other laboratories.
pmc-13236543:
Meiling Zou and Shang Ju built in 2026 a machine learning tool to predict major amputation risk for hospital patients with diabetic foot ulcers. Models were developed on admissions from 2019 to 2020 and checked on a separate 2024 group at the same centre. Only information available within the first day of admission entered the models. Four model types competed, and an explanation method showed which factors drove each prediction.

A random forest model separated future amputation cases most accurately in both time periods tested. Blood flow grade in the limb and a simple circulation index ranked among the strongest predictors. Dialysis dependence, infection markers in blood tests, and prior minor amputation also carried heavy weight. Calibration of predicted risks stayed acceptable in the later validation group. The authors propose the tool for sorting patients toward timely team-based limb care.
pmc-13237443:
Kensaku Kashima and colleagues reviewed 95 adults who received donor stem cell transplants between 2017 and 2024, asking whether muscle weakness plus comorbidity predicts death from causes other than relapse. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength, was measured by grip, walking speed, and muscle index before transplant. The standard comorbidity score was combined with it into a single risk split.

Patients with both sarcopenia and a high comorbidity score faced about 42 percent non-relapse mortality at two years, against about 16 percent for everyone else, and their overall survival was far worse. Neither measure alone predicted the outcome in adjusted models, but the combination did. The authors suggest the pairing can guide conditioning choices and pre-transplant exercise programs.
pmc-13239043:
Keying Ding and team sorted 312 ICU patients with sepsis in 2026 by the shape of their body temperature over the first forty-eight hours. Path modeling found four patterns: hypothermia, fever with a rapid drop, temperature staying high, and normal temperature. The same exercise was repeated in the large American MIMIC-IV database as a check.

The hypothermia group suffered the highest death rate and the most hospital-acquired bloodstream infections. Staying-high temperature also carried raised odds of dying in hospital compared with the normal group. Similar pattern families appeared in the check data. The authors suggest that watching temperature's path, not just its height, could flag fading patients earlier. Sepsis, they note, hides several subphenotypes under one label.
pmc-13239343:
Zetao Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study of glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour whose rich blood supply helps it resist treatment. The group searched large datasets for transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on, linked to the tumour's blood vessel growth.

Their experiments point to a factor called SRF joining a partner protein, P54nrb, through phase separation, a process where proteins gather into droplets. Together they raise levels of OLFML3, a protein that remodels tissue around vessels and encourages new vessel growth. Those vessels then draw in immune cells that suppress attack on the tumour. Blocking this chain could offer a fresh angle for anti-vessel therapy.
pmc-13239443:
Stephanie Ströbele and colleagues ran a 2026 crossover trial on breathing support for extremely premature babies. Such infants often pause breathing during nasal pressure therapy, so backup breaths kick in, and the question was how those backup breaths should wind down once the baby breathes again.

Twenty-four infants in a level three intensive care unit tried both strategies in random order. One stopped backup breaths at once, while the other reduced them step by step. Time spent inside the target oxygen range was similar under both approaches. The gradual method raised average airway pressure and slowed breathing rate slightly, yet offered no clear overall advantage.
pmc-13239643:
Troy Francis and co-authors set out a 2026 scoping review protocol on judging stem cell technologies while they are still young. Early health technology assessment weighs clinical, economic, and social value during development, guiding whether a product deserves investment and how it might reach patients.

The review will search medical, economics, and policy databases plus grey literature, with no language limits, for work published up to April 2026. Reviewers will extract data independently on a standard form and combine findings in counts and narrative. Results will circulate through stem cell networks and assessment conferences. No ethics approval is needed since no new personal data are collected.
pmc-13240343:
Soma Elefánti and team test a catchy idea about crab larvae riding sea snakes in a 2026 study. A 2012 report found crowds of young crabs, their kind unknown, rafting on pelagic sea snakes off Costa Rica. The prime suspect was a crab species famed for rafting on turtles and driftwood as an adult.

Gene barcoding of 106 larvae told a new tale. It named three shoreline grapsid crabs and none of the suspected rafter. Rafting, it seems, suits the shore-dwelling grapsid family as a route to new homes. The authors suggest that larval rafting in this family may have paved the way for one fully raft-bound species to evolve.
pmc-13240943:
Tianfei Yu and co-authors publish a 2026 methodological critique of a Canadian study on COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among university students. The original survey framed hesitancy as part of a syndemic, where social and biological problems reinforce each other. Yu and colleagues accept the value of that framing while urging caution.

Their concerns include memory bias in how earlier hesitancy was recalled, and a one-time design that cannot show change over time. A low response rate raises selection worries. Splitting key measures into two groups and assuming straight-line change also draw criticism. The authors still back trust-building and misinformation work. They call for long-term studies that measure hesitancy as it happens.
pmc-13241643:
Abdullah Langgeng and co-authors publish a 2026 study of worm infections in Javan slow lorises under rehabilitation. These critically endangered primates suffer heavily from the illegal wildlife trade. Parasite patterns during captive care are rarely documented, yet they may affect release decisions.

Repeated droppings samples from nineteen adults were checked for worm eggs. Four worm groups were identified by egg shape. Overall parasite variety did not track with release readiness, sex, or housing. Instead, the chance of infection rose as time passed since deworming treatment, and egg output for one group followed the same pattern. The authors recommend ongoing parasite monitoring rather than one-off checks before release.
pmc-13242143:
Okubo's team at Kanagawa Cancer Center warn thyroid pathologists against overreading a negative gene panel. Hotspot assays catch common mutations but can miss RET and NTRK fusions entirely. Morphology or clinical course may still scream fusion-driven cancer. Their correspondence sets out a panel-negative framework for exactly that gap.

Reports should state the assay's scope and any residual suspicion explicitly. Pan-TRK staining may triage cases but never rules fusions out. When suspicion persists and management hinges on it, RNA fusion testing should follow. The aim is killing false reassurance, not mandating more tests.
pmc-13242843:
Godwin Nimusiima and a large team publish a 2026 cross-sectional study of harmful effects among self-medicating cancer patients in southwestern Uganda. Patients often add their own drugs or herbs to prescribed cancer treatment while seeking relief. Data from this setting were limited, so the team interviewed patients at a regional cancer unit.

About four in five participants had experienced an adverse event, mostly mild or moderate. Events linked more strongly to certain chemotherapy drugs, to self-medicating with acid-relief drugs, and to herbal product use. Medication histories were reconciled against records to catch unreported items. The authors urge routine full medication review at the unit, with closer monitoring for patients on the flagged drug classes or using herbs.
pmc-13243043:
Erkan Acar, Zeynep Özdemir, and Pinar Yalinay Dikmen publish a 2026 study asking whether being a night owl raises migraine disability. Body clock preferences interact with sleep and pain pathways, making the question plausible. Two hundred migraine patients and a smaller healthy control group completed sleep and chronotype questionnaires.

Migraine patients slept worse than controls, and chronic migraine patients carried by far the highest disability scores. Chronotype distribution, however, did not differ between patients and controls. Morning types showed somewhat lower disability than intermediate and evening types, but the gap was not statistically significant. The authors conclude that clock preference itself does not track with disability. They instead urge sleep-focused care, especially for chronic migraine.
pmc-13244243:
Charlotte Heurlin and co-authors report what young adults want from long-term rehabilitation after brain injury in 2026. Their service takes patients aged 18 to 25 after standard medical rehabilitation ends. The team asked which daily life problems matter most to these young patients.

Forty-six patients named 122 problems they rated as important at entry. Social life, community activity, and finding work topped the list. By discharge, patients rated their own performance and satisfaction much higher. A broad disability scale also showed wider outcomes at discharge than at entry. The results argue for patient-led goals as young adults rebuild adult lives.
pmc-13246043:
Chan and co-authors describe a puzzling physical sign in this 2026 ACG Case Reports Journal article. Jaundice, the yellowing caused by excess bilirubin in the blood, normally colors the whole body evenly. Their patient, a young man, turned yellow unevenly: days after fluid was drained from the right side of his abdomen, the yellowing and swelling both favored his left side.

Earlier reports blamed a channel between the abdomen and the skin left by the drainage procedure, but the authors argue that cannot be the whole story here. They present the case as an extremely rare, poorly documented phenomenon whose cause is likely several factors combined, and offer the details to help others recognize it.
pmc-13247843:
Wu and a large international team compare clinical diagnoses with brain pathology and genetics across parkinsonian disorders. Their 2026 cross-sectional study draws on 3,353 brain donors who had movement-disorder diagnoses or were healthy controls. Conditions covered include Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, and corticobasal syndrome.

Autopsy often told a different story from the clinic. Among people diagnosed with Parkinson disease, 3.1 percent actually had supranuclear palsy pathology, while 7.1 percent of clinical supranuclear palsy cases showed Lewy body disease instead. Nearly 17 percent of clinical multiple system atrophy cases had Lewy body pathology, and corticobasal syndrome most often reflected supranuclear palsy or Alzheimer pathology. The authors also examined how variants in genes such as GBA1 and LRRK2 tracked with these pathological patterns.
pmc-13248743:
Shah and colleagues describe a rare surgical emergency in this 2026 Cureus case report. A sixty-one-year-old woman arrived after a fall with low blood pressure, confusion, and a hugely swollen abdomen. Scans showed a massive cystic pelvic tumor pressing on a major vein and pushing her bowel aside, with signs of spread elsewhere.

Surgeons drained about six liters of fluid and removed her uterus and ovaries to relieve the pressure. Her recovery was stormy, with kidney injury, clots in both legs, and a bowel infection. Biopsy later confirmed a high-grade ovarian-type cancer. Too frail for drug treatment, she moved to comfort care and later died.
pmc-13248943:
Sun and co-authors report a dangerous bile tract infection in a 2026 surgical case. Their patient, a seventy-year-old man with diabetes and weak kidneys, arrived with abdominal pain. Scans found gallstones blocking his bile duct, an inflamed gallbladder, and a large abscess inside the abdomen, all driven by a highly virulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strain.

Doctors first drained the duct and removed the stones through an endoscope, then took out the gallbladder and drained the abscess. Cultures confirmed the aggressive bacterium. Bleeding from a stress ulcer and clotting problems followed, but the man recovered well. The authors stress early imaging, fast source control, and team care in such high-risk infections.
pmc-13249643:
Abel Ruiz-Giralt and colleagues propose an updated method for archaeology in this 2026 paper. Their toolkit, called Anthropic Activity Markers, reads chemical and biological traces left in old soil layers to work out what people once did at a site.

The update argues that soil chemistry values should be treated as parts of a whole, not as stand-alone numbers, since raw values can create false patterns. Using an older study of herding communities as a test case, the authors show the new maths gives firmer results. They say markers should be read as ratios mapped across space, giving a stronger base for claims about past behaviour.
pmc-13251143:
A large team of co-authors reports a study dated two thousand twenty-six on two brain diseases that share a common genetic cause. The diseases are frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The cause is a repeated stretch of DNA in a gene called C9orf72, which leads cells to make toxic short proteins.

Those proteins disturb the cell's stress response and the granules it forms under stress. Using fruit fly models that carry realistic repeat lengths, the team found one toxic protein switches the stress response on early and keeps it on. Blocking that response, or lowering a linked protein called Ataxin-2, eased the nerve damage in the models.
pmc-13252843:
Sebastian Klavinskis-Whiting and colleagues present a 2026 model of the brain's dorsal visual pathway built on temporal prediction. The guiding principle is that sensory areas represent whatever best predicts the input arriving a moment later. Earlier prediction models lacked the feedback connections that real visual areas send to one another.

The team's model stacks prediction units in a hierarchy and adds both local recurrence and feedback between areas. It reproduced hallmark tuning properties of dorsal pathway neurons, including sensitivity to pattern motion and the suppression of responses by surrounding stimuli. Head-to-head comparisons found this model fit neuronal tuning better than several alternative accounts of visual processing. It also explained responses to natural scenes most successfully. The authors argue that prediction, wired with feedback, is a strong candidate principle for how the visual brain is organized.
pmc-13253843:
Annalena Ulsperger and colleagues test what makes science writing seem credible in a 2026 study. Readers often judge a text by its author rather than its facts. Across three experiments, with about 200 people in each, the team varied the author's stated gender and kind of expertise.

In the first test, texts said to be by high-expertise authors were rated more credible, with no gender effect. A second test found no effects at all. In the third, academic expertise raised credibility while personal expertise, meaning lived experience, did not. The authors urge care in how expertise is presented to readers.
pmc-13255043:
Anna C. Prins and colleagues present a 2026 treatment-planning study for vulvar cancer, comparing proton therapy against a standard photon technique. Patients receiving photon radiation for this cancer often suffer severe skin, urinary, bowel, and blood side effects. Protons can stop inside the body, which in theory spares healthy tissue beyond the tumor.

The cohort covered 30 patients treated at Erasmus Medical Center in Rotterdam with advanced or recurrent disease. For each patient, the team built both proton and photon plans and compared doses to organs at risk, along with estimated complication chances. No earlier planning studies had tested protons for this cancer. The authors aim to show whether the expected sparing is real enough to guide bringing proton treatment into the clinic.
pmc-13255743:
David Wilson and colleagues argue about emergency medicine training length in a 2026 letter to the editor. The letter responds to a study of board exam pass rates for the American qualifying exam in emergency medicine. Debate in the field centers on whether all residencies should move from three years to four.

The authors say pass rates differ little between three- and four-year programs. What seems to matter more is program age and maturity: seasoned faculty, refined curricula, and stable support. They warn that forcing longer training targets the wrong problem, and urge stronger standards and help for newer programs instead.
pmc-13256143:
Un Ju Jung and Sang Ryong Kim review brown seaweeds as a source of diabetes-fighting compounds in a 2026 paper. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and failing insulin-producing cells, and it damages many organs over time. Brown seaweeds carry unusual compounds, including fucoidan, alginate, phlorotannins, and fucoxanthin, that are drawing research interest.

Evidence gathered in the review shows these compounds act on several fronts at once. They support pancreatic cell function, adjust gut-driven metabolic signals, and tune glucose handling in liver, fat, and muscle. They also calm chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, and improve the abnormal blood fats that accompany diabetes. The authors frame seaweed compounds as functional-food candidates that complement, rather than replace, standard diabetes care and deserve fuller clinical testing.
pmc-13256843:
Mengmeng Wang and co-authors show in a 2026 study that mild heat stress makes methamphetamine far more damaging to heart muscle cells. Their setup models the crowded, hot settings where the drug is often used. Methamphetamine heart injury is a leading cause of death among users beyond overdose, yet environmental factors in that injury are rarely studied.

Mice exposed to methamphetamine at 28 °C fared worse than those at 22 °C, with stronger heart dysfunction and mitochondrial damage. The chain ran from excess mitochondrial reactive oxygen through the protein BAX to leaked mitochondrial DNA that triggered inflammasome-driven cell death. A mitochondria-targeted antioxidant blocked the aggravation, pointing to mitochondrial redox control as a treatment angle.
pmc-13257343:
Sara Ussia and a large team review plant compounds and fat-based signals in weak heart muscle disease in 2026. The signals, called eicosanoids, steer swelling, calcium balance, and heart cell survival. Their dock points on cells can pull the heart toward harm or toward safety.

Two dock points link mostly to weak squeeze and more cell death. A third, called EP4, guards the heart, aiding calcium use and cell power plants. Plant polyphenols, flavonoids, and carotenoids act through anti-swelling and anti-rust routes that cross the same paths. Heart doctors and plant-product researchers share the audience. The authors see a bright pairing of sharp dock drugs with food compounds. Firm patient trials are the missing proof for both halves.
pmc-13257643:
Rui Gao and colleagues build hollow carbon spheres that strip toxic chromium from acidic wastewater in a 2026 study. The resin-derived spheres were templated and alkali-activated to open vast internal surface, measured above two thousand square meters per gram. Tests ran in acidic solutions matching industrial effluent from plating and chemical plants.

Removal of hexavalent chromium passed ninety-nine percent in a fifty parts-per-million solution and stayed strong across the acid range tested. Surface oxygen groups grabbed metal ions through bonding and reduction reactions, joining physical trapping in pores. Spectroscopy and microscopy confirmed the porous build and the chemistry behind uptake. Water treatment engineers gain a high-capacity adsorbent tuned for the hardest, most acidic streams. Regeneration and real effluent trials remain the practical next hurdles.
pmc-13257743:
Katarzyna Dominiak and co-authors build vein-ready fat drops that carry magnolia compounds in a 2026 study. The two compounds, honokiol and magnolol, may guard the liver, yet they dissolve poorly in water. Clinic fat feeds rich in omega-3 oils served as the base for single and paired loads.

Two-step mixing gave drops that met drug-book rules, with tight size spread and strong surface charge for shelf life. The drops did not break red blood cells and mixed safely with feed bags for a day. Liver cells bore them well, and harm ran lower than with clinic feeds in dishes. Folk fed by vein for months often face liver harm, so a guard add-on counts. Tests in live animals must come next.
pmc-13258143:
Jiye Kwon and co-authors test whether virus genome watching can forecast COVID vaccine protection in a 2026 study. More than ten thousand viral genomes from Connecticut cases between 2021 and 2024 were compared with each vaccine formula's spike sequence. A Bayesian weekly model joined those distances with over a million test results.

Greater amino acid distance in the spike gene tracked lower vaccine effectiveness over time. Sharp drops matched new variant arrivals, while slow drift within variants eroded protection gradually. Each block of added spike changes corresponded to a measurable protection loss in the fitted model. Public health teams gain a forecasting frame: sequence surveillance could warn of waning protection before outcome studies catch up. Updating vaccine formulas might then start earlier, guided by genomes already being collected for other reasons.
pmc-13258643:
Dong Yu and colleagues teach computers to rewrite enzyme genes so bacteria produce more usable protein. When foreign proteins are made in Escherichia coli, they often clump instead of dissolving. Simply picking the most common codons, the usual fix, ignores how codons sit together. Their 2026 framework learns better patterns.

One model learned codon habits from the bacterium's own genome, while a partner model ranked rewrites by predicted soluble output. Two industrial enzymes were rebuilt and tested, one starch-processing and one starch-cutting. Soluble yields jumped several-fold, and in the best case more than tenfold. The winning strategy avoids certain codon choices rather than chasing favorites.
pmc-13258743:
Yüksel Furkan Yildirim and Mehmet Emiroğlu test lightweight cement mixes with volcanic pumice or expanded perlite in a 2026 study. Lightweight grains replaced normal aggregate at four levels up to full replacement. Strength, stiffness, density, and sound insulation were measured for each mix.

More lightweight material lowered strength while improving sound performance. Gains were clearest in middle and high sound frequencies. Full perlite replacement gave the best overall acoustic result in their tests. Pumice mixes followed the same general trade off pattern. Builders seeking quieter rooms can weigh the strength cost against the acoustic benefit with direct numbers.
pmc-13258943:
Tianran Hao, Xiao Zhang, and Bing Zhou build a drone image detector tuned for tiny objects in a 2026 computing paper. Small targets in aerial photos carry few pixels and drown in background clutter. Their transformer design processes features progressively across several enhancement stages.

One module merges spatial and frequency details to sharpen small targets. Cross layer gathering counters detail loss from image shrinking steps. A gated sequence model weighs local detail against broad scene context. Final stages rebuild fine features that earlier steps weakened. Scores on two aerial benchmarks support the design choices for crowded small object scenes.

Ilias Miltiadis leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of spleen anatomy, combining data from 64 studies. The spleen is a blood-rich immune organ that surgeons find hard to stitch and easy to damage. Knowing its normal size ranges and vessel patterns helps plan operations and preserve the organ after injury.

Pooled averages put spleen length at roughly ten and a half centimeters, with width near seven and volume near two hundred nineteen cubic centimeters. In most people the spleen's artery branches off the celiac trunk and runs above the pancreas before splitting into two or more branches. Variation is wide, so the authors stress careful imaging and planning for each patient.
pmc-13278243:
Sofija Pejkova leads a 2026 study of a nerve-release operation for diabetic foot ulcers. Ten patients with diabetes and chronic foot ulcers, lasting about seventeen months on average, had Dellon decompression, surgery that frees a pinched nerve tunnel at the ankle. The team checked feeling, artery flow, and foot blood supply with a tracer scan before and twelve months after surgery.

Feeling improved clearly, judged by how close together two touch points could be told apart. Flow in the main ankle artery nearly doubled on ultrasound. Tracer scans showed higher uptake in the operated foot at rest and under stress, by roughly a third. All foot ulcers had healed by the twelve-month follow-up.
pmc-13278443:
Andrea Nucita leads a 2026 study of whether AI tools can reliably classify social media posts for sociological research. Human coding is slow, and categories can be ambiguous. The case study covers Facebook posts by two Italian universities from March 2020 to March 2023, sorted into eight types of public communication. Three researchers coded the posts independently as a benchmark.

Human coders themselves disagreed on several categories, showing real interpretive ambiguity. Automated models matched human classifications about as well as humans matched each other. The findings support using AI as an extra coder inside hybrid workflows, the authors say. That pairing could make large-scale, transparent analysis of complex social media data practical for sociology.
pmc-13278943:
Zhi Wen and colleagues review how ageing immune cells drive chronic bone disease in a 2026 article. Senescent immune cells multiply less, clear debris poorly, and release a changed mix of signals. That slow-burning inflammation tilts the bone environment toward loss.

The review organises evidence across osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes-related bone disease. The link looks most direct in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis, and more of an amplifier in the other two. Candidate treatments include rebalancing macrophages, clearing senescent cells, and stem-cell-based repair of the local environment. Most remain preclinical or early in translation. The authors call for single-cell mapping to build biomarkers for precision care.
pmc-13279943: Remi Sieskind and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their 2025 Scientific Reports study. That study used a phage virus own DNA polymerase, its DNA copying enzyme, to sequence its hypermodified genome, meaning DNA with heavily altered bases. The error sat in Figure 5B, where the formula in the glycosidic bond, the link that joins a DNA base to its sugar, was drawn wrong. The notice reprints the figure and caption on related phages and their DNA changes. The sequence work and its claims stand.
pmc-13280343:
Katharina Helena Morawitz and colleagues report a 2026 study of biological age after bariatric surgery. Bariatric surgery, weight loss surgery, cuts body weight a lot, yet health gain in the first two years was less studied. The team modelled mortality associated biological age from standard blood markers. Age acceleration is the gap between biological and calendar age. A prospective cohort of five hundred five surgery patients was tracked to two years.

At baseline, age acceleration rose with smoking load and with body mass, most in males. Twelve months after surgery, patients scored on average about five and a half years younger in biological age. The gain held stable to twenty four months. After adjustment for body mass change, the gain shrank to about three and a third years at twelve months. Part of the rejuvenation thus runs apart from weight loss itself, a gain the authors call independent in the title.
pmc-13280543:
James Kaufman-Cook and team give a 2026 review of stem cells in pituitary tumour formation. Pituitary tumours are brain area growths that pose challenges from recurrence, drug resistance and hormone dysfunction. In the normal front pituitary, resident stem cells aid tissue homeostasis and cell turnover. How much they add to tumour growth is not known. A growing set of studies aims to answer that.

The review sums evidence that links pituitary stem cells and tumour stem like cells to tumour start, upkeep and growth. It sets practical criteria for defining tumour stem cells. It weighs work from human tumour function studies, new single cell and spatial gene data sets and mouse lineage tracing models. A curated list of single cell RNA studies flags stem groups across tumour subtypes. Targeting stem like cells is the care hope at the close.
pmc-13280643:
Constance Delaugerre and colleagues reported in 2026 on a French program for people whose HIV no longer responds to most drugs. Forty-two adults got lenacapavir, a drug that blocks the shell of the virus, plus other drugs picked for them. Care ran from 2021 to 2023 under a program for hard cases. Thirty-three patients had HIV type one and nine had type two.

By week twenty-six, about two in three patients with type one had the virus under full control. Results for type two were much weaker, at about one in five. A few patients developed drug resistance, and about a third had sore spots where the shot went in. No severe harm was tied to the drug.
pmc-13282043:
Michele Tizzani and Yelena Mejova present a 2026 study of how viewers engage with vaccine videos on YouTube. Over six months they tracked more than seven thousand vaccine-related videos, posted from November 2024 to May 2025. They classified each video and its comments as for or against vaccination, checking machine labels by hand. They also noted who posted the video and what moderation the platform applied.

Vaccine-hesitant videos drew far more likes and comments than strongly pro-vaccine videos. They also gathered most of their views faster, reaching ninety percent of views in about eighteen days against about thirty-two. Comment threads under hesitant videos tended to agree with the video, forming echo chambers. Pro-vaccine threads drew more open argument. Pro-vaccine content came mostly from news and health bodies, while hesitant content came more often from lone creators. The findings matter for how health groups plan online outreach.
pmc-13282443:

Tumors often silence NLRC5 to lower their MHC-I display that lets killer T cells recognize them. Engineered tumors were controlled in both host types, proving host antigen-presenting cells do not need NLRC5. The tumors filled with CD8 and CD4 T cells, natural killer cells, grew vessels, and switched on chemokine genes. Depleting T cells or NK-lineage cells weakened control. Protein profiling showed reshuffled antigen-processing machinery and quieter autophagy. In human data, NLRC5 tracked with NK cell markers. The authors argue tumor-intrinsic NLRC5 opens doors for immune attack.
pmc-13283043:
Jorge A Valdivieso and Rebecca K Hicks reported in 2026 a rare skin cancer case in a 44-year-old man. He had a growing lump on his scalp that came back after an earlier removal, when it was read as a different, benign growth. Wide removal followed, and lab study showed a low-grade trichoblastic carcinoma, a cancer arising from hair follicle germ cells.

The cancer sat close to the cut edge, so he received focused radiation after surgery, given in twenty sessions. This cancer closely mimics the far more common basal cell carcinoma under the microscope, which makes exact lab reading vital. The authors say wide removal is the main treatment, with radiation worth weighing when margins are narrow.
pmc-13283843:
Avaniyapuram Kannan Murugan, Hindi Al-Hindi, and Ali S Alzahrani studied a long non-coding RNA in 2026 in differentiated thyroid cancer. These RNA strands do not build proteins but tune gene activity. The strand GAS8-AS1 had an unclear role in this cancer, so the team measured it in tumour and normal tissue and ran cell experiments that lowered or raised its levels.

The authors read GAS8-AS1 as a brake on this cancer.
pmc-13283943:
Gonzalo Roig-Ferreruela and co-authors set out a case of punctate inner choroidopathy in a woman who carries the gene form for RP2-associated retinopathy. Their 2026 case report uses retinal imaging in more than one form, electrophysiology, and genetic testing.

Tests showed she held the same pathogenic RP2 variant as her brother. Imaging showed chorioretinal atrophy and lesions that looked punched out. Those signs hinted at choroidopathy that was not active. Tests of the eye's response to light showed that rods and cones did not work as they should, in both eyes. The case picks out what imaging adds to diagnosis, and the course that care took.
pmc-13284043:
Li Shao and co-authors characterised in 2026 a protein from a salt-loving bacterium that boosts salt and alkali tolerance in other bacteria. The protein, HadS, comes from Halobacillus andaensis, a moderate halophile, meaning it thrives in salty settings. It belongs to a broad enzyme family, and few members had been tied to salt tolerance before. The team found it by screening a gene library in a salt-sensitive E. coli strain.

HadS has 220 building blocks and no membrane-crossing segment, and tests showed no typical salt-pumping activity. Still, it turned up in membrane-rich cell fractions, and early tests hinted at dehalogenase activity, meaning it may strip halogen atoms from acids. When produced in the sensitive strain, it cut sodium build-up inside cells and clearly improved growth under salt-alkali stress.
pmc-13285543:
Marat Fudim and colleagues offer a practical guide, published in 2026, for giving intravenous iron to heart failure patients who lack iron. Guidelines from major cardiology groups recommend the treatment because it eases symptoms and cuts hospital stays. Views from a cardiologist, a nurse, an advanced practice provider, and a pharmacist show how each role keeps treatment moving. Ferric carboxymaltose can deliver a large dose in one rapid visit. Teamwork, the authors argue, closes the gaps between settings.
pmc-13285743:
Zhaochen Zhang and co-authors review artificial intelligence for osteoporosis care in a 2026 overview of the field. Weak bones are often found late, since standard scans are scarce and reading them takes expert time. Smart software promises faster screening, sharper risk forecasts, and help in finding new drugs.

Programs now read plain X-rays, CT, MRI, and ultrasound images to flag thin bone and grade fracture risk. Other tools sort risk factors, hunt for gene targets, and predict how patients will fare on treatment. Gains in speed can be large, with some measures done in a fraction of the usual time. Yet studies vary widely in patients, methods, and scoring, and outside checks are often thin, so the authors urge shared standards before wide clinical use.
pmc-13286043:
Elodie E Baumgartner and co-authors report a 73-year-old woman whose aorta became infected with salmonella around a stent graft placed earlier to repair the vessel. The 2026 case report shows why such infections hide: symptoms are vague, and standard blood cultures often miss the germ. The woman had a weakened immune system and worsening abdominal pain.

Her likely exposure was daily unpasteurized eggs from backyard chickens. Surgery was judged too risky, so she received a month of intravenous antibiotics followed by long oral suppression. Scans three months later showed clear improvement.
pmc-13286143:
Tzu-Fei Wang and a large team of colleagues study language and end-of-life care in Ontario in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Most dying cancer patients in the province receive home care, yet care in a language the patient does not share can warp hard choices near death. Records sorted patients by their preferred tongue: English, French, or another language entirely.

They also faced more emergency visits, more admissions, and more aggressive steps in their final thirty days. pmc-13286843:
Xiaoyi Chen, Xuchen Luo, and Jiehua Deng review how digital tools can strengthen referral and follow-up for children's surgery in low-resource settings. Their 2026 mini review covers teleconsultation, mobile messaging, image sharing, and remote check-ins after operations. Evidence remains thin, dominated by pilots and small observational reports, and follow-up has drawn more study than referral. The authors stress equity, privacy, workflow fit, and durability as conditions for real impact.
pmc-13286943:
Talisa F. Their 2026 narrative review surveys policies, guidelines, and frameworks. Exclusion punishments have faded, yet suspension gaps by race and disability persist, and childhood trauma keeps rising.

Guidance that does merge the lenses rarely treats all three together. The authors propose an integrated framework that weaves trauma principles and equity checks through every tier of support and every discipline decision, with concrete recommendations and research directions.
pmc-13287143:
Natalia Muklewicz and colleagues present a 2026 case-based review of granulomatosis with polyangiitis when the illness first affects the bladder, cervix, or urethra rather than airways or kidneys. Their own patient, a woman aged 58, had bladder surgery before the immune cause was recognised.

For nearly half, genital or urinary signs came first and often looked like cancer, and many underwent operations that later proved avoidable. Steroids and cyclophosphamide were common treatments. Rituximab controlled disease that kept returning, and the authors urge early rheumatology input.
pmc-13287243:
Xu Bai wrote a letter in 2026 about a study by Utami and others. The study described a life-skills teaching module meant to keep Indonesian teenagers away from drug misuse. Activities are not mapped tightly onto theory ideas such as confidence to refuse. Expert approval scoring, reported as 82%, needs plainer handling of disagreement and of weak readability scores for young readers.
pmc-13287543:
Changik Lee, Young-Jin Kim, and Jin-Sung Kim report in 2026 two hard cases of keyhole spine surgery through two small ports, where scar tissue stuck fast to the nerve covering. Working one-handed is a known limit of the method, since the other hand holds the camera.

In one case scarring followed earlier surgery; in the other, a joint cyst caused long-term inflammation. A scope retractor either held sticky tissue steady or served as a dissecting tool, giving an effect much like a second hand. Both cases ended with full freeing of tissue and good nerve relief. The authors recommend the tool for severe sticking in port-based spine work.
pmc-13287843:
Kyungseok Park and co-authors analysed emergency visits in 2026 by 1,445 people aged 24 or younger. All came to a Seoul psychiatric emergency centre after self-harm or a suicide attempt. Most visitors were female, at 75.4%, and most acts were impulsive. Severe medical outcomes hit 8.7% of visits, tied to planned attempts and to high-harm methods. Returns within sixty days hit 7.1%. pmc-13288043:
Sanjida Haque, Rosanna Cavalletto, and Mohammed Ali Alomshani surveyed green dental practice in Saudi Arabia in 2026. They mixed a questionnaire for 200 dentists and clinic directors in Riyadh with six in-depth interviews across the country. Dentistry uses much energy, water, and single-use gear, so the team mapped what clinics already do.

Lack of training was the top barrier, followed by weak motivation and cost worries. The authors call for training, money incentives, and firm clinic policy to close the gap.
pmc-13288143:
Hongyang Zhang and co-authors coated copper oxide films in 2026 with a thin platinum skin to stop sunlight from eating the material away during water-splitting tests aimed at making hydrogen fuel. The porous films were cast from a gel mix, with a mild acid used as a helper for the first time.

pmc-13288543:
Farahwahida Mohd Kasim and co-authors study drug prices in Malaysia in 2026. The work deals with public buying of drugs. Records came from 19 ministry sites. Years ran from 2017 to 2021. Eight costly drug groups were covered.

The data held 97 drugs in all. It held 4,702 purchase records and 28 suppliers. East Malaysia had the widest price spread. Small buys spread more and cost more per unit. Imported generics spread most in price. Yet they cost less than brand or local drugs. More rival drugs steadied paid prices. Bid spreads grew at the same time. Rivalry works past headline price, they say.
pmc-13288943:

About 35 minutes in, panic struck hard. She felt chest tightness and doom. Her heart raced and her blood pressure spiked. Staff thought of stopping the surgery. The lead doctor used calm talk and breath work. Grounding and guided images helped too. Her symptoms cleared in eight minutes. Surgery then finished with no more trouble.
pmc-13289143:

Low sense of control played a part too. Low income and weak support also counted. The authors urge joined-up help after birth. Such help may break a long chain of hardship.
pmc-13289343:
