pmc-13377643:
Brendon Larson, Jesse Peterson, and René van der Wal published a 2026 essay on what natural history becomes in the Anthropocene, the age of dominant human influence on Earth. Many ecologists have praised field-based natural history for keeping first-hand knowledge of nature alive. The authors argue these accounts assume a stable Holocene world that no longer exists.

The Anthropocene unsettles assumptions about who naturalists are, where they work, and what they offer society. The authors synthesize earlier arguments and propose six ways for naturalists to adapt: widening what counts as nature, questioning data collection habits, engaging emotions consciously, ensuring justice and diversity, and more. The essay is a call to rebuild a beloved practice for a changed planet.
pmc-13378343:
José Araque-Gallardo and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of computer methods for grading diabetic eye disease from retinal photos. The disease, called diabetic retinopathy, is a leading cause of preventable blindness, above all in poorer countries. Experts can grade the photos reliably, but reading them by hand takes a long time.

The review covers 146 studies from the years 2019 to 2025, all of them peer-reviewed. It compares methods that grade the whole image at once with methods that first find and measure damaged spots. The authors also map where the research was published and which countries produced it. Their aim is to help researchers choose sound approaches for building screening tools.
pmc-13382443:
Semyon Kurkin and Alexander Hramov wrote a 2026 letter challenging a study that claimed very high accuracy in diagnosing autism from brain scans. The original study used deep learning on a shared scan data set and reported accuracy above ninety-eight percent. The letter writers checked the authors' publicly shared code and found a critical flaw.

Feature selection, which narrows thousands of scan measures to a smaller set, was run on the whole data set before the data were split for validation. That leaks information from the test cases into training and inflates the reported scores. The letter sets out the code evidence line by line and argues the published performance figures cannot be trusted.
pmc-13383543:
Moon-Jong Kim and Hong-Seop Kho test a soft mouth appliance for burning mouth syndrome in this 2026 paper. The syndrome causes chronic mouth pain with no visible cause. Drugs are the main treatment, but some patients keep hurting despite them. A soft guard worn in the mouth might help as an added therapy.

Charts covered nine women with stubborn symptoms despite drug treatment. Five chose to wear the appliance, and four stayed on drugs alone. Pain was rated on a ten centimeter scale over about four months. Most appliance users felt early discomfort that faded as they adapted. The case series weighs early response in both groups. As a small exploratory study, it points to a low risk option worth a larger trial.
pmc-13384743:
Sai Harshini Rathod and co-authors describe a stomach tumor that masqueraded as advanced liver disease in a 2026 case report. A 63-year-old woman had six months of growing belly swelling, and fluid tests first suggested decompensated liver disease. Scope exams instead found a polyp-like stomach growth plus enlarged esophageal veins.

Detailed scans showed several stomach lesions, spread to liver and spleen, and clotting in the portal vein system. A biopsy confirmed a neuroendocrine tumor arising from hormone-related stomach cells. With surgery deferred for health reasons, her team chose fluid drainage, portal pressure care, nutrition support, and watchful scope follow-up.
pmc-13385443:
Songqin Yang and co-authors show that the enzyme KDM8 strongly boosts cell reprogramming in 2026 work. Turning adult cells back into stem-like cells with the classic Yamanaka factors works, but slowly and rarely. KDM8, a histone-editing enzyme, had no known role in that process before this study.

Added KDM8 raised reprogramming yields sharply, and paired with OCT4 alone it sufficed to reprogram adult cells. Part of the effect came from its cutting activity lowering epigenetic barriers. A larger share came from partnering with the factor SOX2, strengthening its grip on DNA and its activation of stemness genes.
pmc-13385543:
Yoshihara and colleagues test how accurately cone-beam CT measures the gap between implant and nerve canal, in 2026 dental imaging research. Surgeons keep implants clear of the mandibular canal to avoid nerve injury, and software reports distances to a tenth of a millimeter. The team built a phantom allowing distances from zero to one millimeter in steps of a tenth of a millimeter. They scanned it at varied positions and had dentists measure gaps on two monitor types to find where imaging stops being trustworthy.

The scans could not reliably distinguish distances of 0.4 millimeters or less. Instability peaked at 0.3 millimeters, where readings scattered, with an interquartile range of 0.121 millimeters. A trend held across that range, but the sub-half-millimeter zone is where safety margins live. Yoshihara cautions that readouts imply precision the scanner cannot deliver, so clinicians should keep a bigger safety margin than the screen suggests.
pmc-13386843:
Chunqing Cao's team offers CWAGS, a neural network for multi-trait genomic selection in crops, in a 2026 paper. Genomic selection speeds crop improvement, but catching complex links among genetic variants remains hard. CWAGS uses channel-weighted focus to reveal trait-specific genetic patterns, depthwise split filters for speed, and DropPath with skip links to aid transfer across diverse genetic backgrounds.

Channel attention weights showed distinct genetic patterns for different traits, backing the model's genetic insight. Across four test sets, CWAGS beat the best rival models by about 1 to 5 percent in average scores. By weighing scores with insight, CWAGS offers a model toolkit for exact genomic selection and faster crop breeding.
pmc-13386943:
Yafei Xu and colleagues find a host protein that marks a pig diarrhea virus protein for destruction in 2026 work. Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus kills newborn piglets, and its ORF3 protein helps drive disease by stressing the cell's folding compartment. A screening method fished out HERPUD1 as an ORF3 binding partner.

HERPUD1 recruits a tagging enzyme that marks ORF3 for disposal, easing cell stress and curbing virus growth. A single site change on ORF3 escaped that disposal, raising viral output by about half a log in their measure. The mutant virus also suppressed interferon more strongly, which confirms the pathway's defensive value.
pmc-13389243:
Sarah B. Carey's team assembled phased sex-chromosome genomes for cannabis and hop, crops whose visibly different sex chromosomes were spotted a century ago but whose sex-control genes stayed obscure. The XY chromosomes share an origin predating the two genera's split about thirty-six million years ago.

The Y's male-only region proved heavily degenerated with major gene loss, and no clear sex-determining gene sat on the Y. Instead, an X-linked copy of an ethylene-pathway enzyme gene, an ACS homolog, decides female flower fate. The sex chromosomes also shaped ecological and physiological differences between sexes and played a part in domestication and breeding.
pmc-13390143:
Pengfei Liu and Liang Xiao built a goal-aimed multi-agent chat system to support patient-centred medical choices, an area where most chat tools serve doctors instead. Poor patient grasp can erode sticking to treatment and spark conflict, while existing systems lack clarity or scale rigidly.

Their system splits work among agents for goal grasp, argument reasoning, and interaction. Grounded in a medical knowledge map and recent literature, it was tested on a Graves' eye disease platform. Goal spotting scored an average F1 of eighty-five percent with over ninety-five percent reply hit rate by doctor judgement, matching doctor-led online systems and beating usual medical Q&A tools.
pmc-13390943:
Shuangshuang Yang and colleagues test, in 2026, whether two simple body and blood indices can predict cognitive decline and dementia. The triglyceride-glucose index reflects insulin resistance, while a body shape index captures abdominal shape beyond weight alone, and their combined form has rarely been used for brain outcomes.

Using UK Biobank data from more than three hundred seventy thousand participants, the team related the indices to scoring in the lowest quarter on cognitive tests. They also related them to later dementia diagnoses, including subtypes. Preventive medicine readers gain large-scale evidence on whether two cheap, routine measures can flag dementia risk early enough to act.
pmc-13391443:
L Campiglia's team tracked brain oxygen levels during robotic prostate surgery in steep head-down tilt, a pose plus belly gas pressure that may raise in-skull pressure. Forty adults having robotic-aided keyhole prostate removal at thirty degrees tilt were tracked with near-red scans and optic nerve cover sound scans.

Brain oxygen levels, blood-pigment signals, and cover diameter were tracked at start. Further checks came at forty-five and one hundred twenty minutes into tilt, during the join, and before tube removal. Phase-dependent changes and their links clarify how the brain bears long steep Trendelenburg, informing sleep-drug watch during long robotic cases.
pmc-13392043:
Jianxing Zhou's team presents ice-phase light-heat tweezers, a deep-cold platform that moves micro- and nano shapes at the ice-water edge. Brownian motion, surface sticking, and stuff constraints had blocked exact rebuilding of mixed shapes.

A laser-induced mobile melting zone in ice moved nano bits, proteins, DNA, and even micro bubbles at ten to one hundred microns per second with nano-scale detail. The team built multi-stuff mixed builds with tailored uneven and twisted optical responses, enabling twisted light tech and angle-controlled nano light under deep-cold conditions. The tweezers moved particles at ten to one hundred microns per second.
pmc-13392643:
Sefi Lestyo Harini and a large team tested a pairing of green tea and turmeric alcohol extracts against the giant liver fluke Fasciola gigantica in laboratory dishes. The fluke sickens cattle and can infect people, and heavy use of synthetic dewormers has bred resistant worms. Adult flukes and eggs came from naturally infected cattle, and six groups compared extract blends against salt water and a standard drug.

Damage rose with dose and time: the strongest blend produced the most egg breakdown, with cracked shells and failed development, and adult deaths climbed the longer worms soaked. Microscope work showed torn outer skin and internal tissue injury in treated worms. The authors see the plant pairing as a promising natural candidate, while noting that dish results must still be proven in living animals.
pmc-13392943:
Firas A Jamil and Saif S Abdulrazzaq reviewed studies of tooth socket preservation, the grafting done after extraction to hold jaw shape, tracking two molecular signals that steer bone rebuilding. One signal, RANKL, promotes bone-eating cells, while its decoy partner OPG blocks it, so their ratio hints at whether bone is being lost or gained. Twelve studies survived screening from an initial pool of just over three hundred.

Grafted sockets generally pushed the signals in the bone-friendly direction compared with ungrafted healing, and combined grafts did best. The lowest, most favourable ratio came from a biologically boosted graft of the patient's own bone, while a purely synthetic graft posted the highest ratio. The authors see promise in grafts pairing active agents with scaffolds, while warning that the ratio's value as a prediction tool remains unproven.
pmc-13393243:
Wen-Yu Jao and colleagues link bone drugs after shoulder replacement to fewer implant problems. Their cohort study from twenty twenty-six uses a large American health network. Osteoporosis weakens the bone holding shoulder implants. Fractures, loosening, and repeat surgery follow more often.

Patients starting bone drugs within a month after surgery were compared. Matching balanced age and other conditions between groups. Total and reverse shoulder replacements both entered the study. Revision surgery was a key complication tracked. Earlier work mostly studied drug use before surgery instead. Starting treatment right after may protect the new implant. Orthopaedic and bone teams should coordinate that timing.
pmc-13393743:
Carmen Cumpăt and six colleagues surveyed managers of Romanian public hospitals to test how leadership style and hospital traits shape accreditation scores, the formal quality grades hospitals must earn. Their analysis layered several stats methods over the survey, from cross-tables and rank correlations to ordinal regression and clustering. Items ranged from hospital size and manager education to staff consultation, team motivation, and information access.

Administration type, the manager's field of study, and team motivation each predicted success, while larger hospitals scored lower, suggesting scale makes standards harder to meet. Oddly, consulting staff and sharing information openly showed no real link to scores. The authors recommend spending on leadership training and team-based quality work, urging policymakers to treat manager growth as a direct lever on hospital quality.
pmc-13394143:
Shim and co-authors re-examine, in 2026, the mechanism of the urea oxidation reaction on nickel catalysts, a partner reaction that makes hydrogen with less energy. Textbooks long assumed the reaction converts urea fully into nitrogen and carbon dioxide through a six-electron pathway, but that story lacked proof. Pairing lab tests on a beta-NiOOH catalyst with density functional theory calculations, the team traced what the reaction makes.

The catalyst delivered current densities of 500 milliamps per square centimeter at 1.53 volts, while the competing oxygen evolution reaction needed 1.79 volts for the same output. The math showed oxygen vacancies, missing oxygen atoms in the surface, are favored sites where urea binds, with an energy barrier of 1.49 electron volts against 3.25 for oxygen evolution. Chemical analysis confirmed the main products are cyanate and nitrite, not nitrogen gas. The findings give designers a corrected target: engineer vacancy-rich nickel surfaces.
pmc-13394543:
T. Bertolin and co-authors test, in 2026, salty liquids that could carry protons in fuel cells run near boiling point. Hotter cells ease water and heat control, but the liquids must work with no water present. The team made six liquids from phosphonium cations paired with two anions. They measured how much oxygen each liquid holds and how fast it moves.

The new liquids held more oxygen than a close nitrogen-based cousin. Some let oxygen move more slowly, while others matched the cousin. Top samples passed higher peak currents for turning oxygen into water. One anion family proved stable enough for the heat. The authors back these liquids for the next fuel cell designs.
pmc-13394643:
Ding Li and Song Ye challenge the conclusions of a trial comparing two pain relief methods in endometriosis surgery in a 2026 letter. The original randomized, double-blinded trial found no opioid-sparing benefit for laparoscopically guided nerve block over local wound infiltration, with equivalent analgesia, recovery, and safety.

The letter writers argue the trial was fatally underpowered: its sample size assumed a 50 percent opioid reduction based on a historical control of 15.4 milligrams, yet the actual wound infiltration group used 27.5 milligrams with wide variability. With only 46 patients, genuine differences could not be detected. Readers gain a caution against accepting negative trial results without checking the power calculation.
pmc-13394743:
Ondřej Strýček and co-authors report, in 2026, real-world results for cenobamate in hard-to-treat epilepsy. Five hundred adults at three Czech centres took the drug after many others had failed. Most had ultra-resistant disease with heavy seizure loads. The team tracked seizure cuts, full freedom, side effects, and how long patients stayed on the drug.

After a year, about three in five patients had at least half as many seizures. About one in six were fully free of seizures. Gains shrank as past drug counts climbed, yet held up even in the toughest group. Most patients stayed on the drug at one year. The authors back its use in routine care.
pmc-13395843:
Carli Peterson and co-authors model, in 2026, the seasons of Oropouche virus in Amazonas, Brazil. The virus, carried by biting midges, has infected more than half a million people across the Americas. Their maths model links climate, midge behaviour, and spread between wild hosts and people. It was fitted to weekly case counts from the 2023 to 2024 outbreak.

Many season shapes were tried, from rain-driven curves to plain pulses. A fading pulse on midge recruitment fit the case curve best, with error near twelve percent. Noise in case counts could shuffle the ranking of rival shapes, tests showed. The authors say season timing must sit inside outbreak plans. Midge surges may be brief but sharp.
pmc-13396043:
Yili Wang and co-authors asked how well a single baseline test day predicts concussion over the next school year for cadets and midshipmen at United States service academies. Their 2026 study uses data from the CARE Consortium, a joint project of the NCAA and the Department of Defense.

Machine learning, using a method called extreme gradient boosting, turned baseline scores into risk estimates. The authors checked how accuracy fades as months pass after testing, and whether prediction works equally for varsity and club athletes versus intramural players. They also compared blows from sport with those from military training, giving academy medical staff a clearer sense of when a baseline result still counts.
pmc-13396343:
Xiang and team trace, in 2026, how broken calcium control inside cells drives aging, and show an old antidepressant can push back. When calcium homeostasis fails, the calcium-binding protein S100A6 accumulates in the cytoplasm, recruits a partner called CacyBP, and triggers destruction of the DNA repair protein PARP1. The damage then switches on inflammatory pathways and the release of senescence signals. The chain operates in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, the premature aging disease, and in natural aging alike.

The antidepressant mianserin, in use for over 50 years, blocks serotonin receptors HTR2B and HTR2C and lowers cellular calcium in their experiments. It reduced senescence in cells from progeria patients and naturally aged humans. In both progeroid mice and normally aging mice, mianserin improved multiple aging phenotypes and significantly extended lifespan. Progeria patients age five to ten times faster than normal and die at 14.5 years on average, underscoring the stakes.
pmc-13397743:
Zhuo-dong Tang and others map where postoperative deep vein thrombosis strikes and what raises its risk after tibial plateau fracture in a 2026 retrospective study. This clot snag is common after fracture surgery, yet its usual sites and predictors needed clarifying.

Among 890 patients treated from 2023 to 2025, 207 picked up postoperative thrombosis, including 186 distal, 4 proximal, and 17 mixed cases, all without symptoms. Age, injury factors, fracture type, waiting time, operation time, and incision length differed strongly in single-trait reads, with multivariable models naming lone predictors. Surgeons gain a site and risk map for targeted clot prevention.
pmc-13398143:
Suvodeep Sen and co-authors review how catalyst design steers carbon dioxide reduction toward the products industry wants. Their 2026 survey covers electrochemical routes that turn CO2 into hydrocarbons and oxygenates, the dense, valuable feedstocks chemical plants prize. Progress is real, but steering selectivity, keeping catalysts alive and scaling up remain the hard trio.

Copper and non-copper catalysts, down to single-atom and molecular designs, are compared along with how each breaks down. Shaping the local reaction setting (the mix of water, ions and fields at the surface) emerges as a lever as strong as the catalyst itself. The review closes with what must hold steady before such reactors leave the lab bench.
pmc-13398643:
D C Deeming measures bird breastbones to test whether keel and rear sternum trade off against each other. His 2026 study photographs the pectoral girdle and sternum of 62 species across ten orders. The sternum is the bird body's largest bone, anchoring the flight muscles, yet its shape varies in ways body size alone explains poorly.

Keel area was expressed as a share of total sternum area, and bony coverage of the rear section against its maximum possible spread. Family-tree-aware models then tested body size and flight style effects. The guiding idea is thrift: a lighter skeleton may deepen the keel for muscle while hollowing the rear plate, matching each species' way of flying.
pmc-13398943:
Shubin Li and co-authors build three editing platforms that make cyanobacteria keep engineered changes instead of shaking them loose. Their 2026 study uses the fast-growing Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 2973, a promising carbon-fixing workhorse. Single crossover swaps, the standard editing route in such microbes, often reverse themselves and destabilise engineered strains.

The three marker-free systems (T4CROSS, TRIPLEARM and CRISPRARM) stack crossover rounds or pair CRISPR cutting with recombination to lock changes in. As proof, the CRISPR route ran a three-step build of the sucrose-making pathway inside the cells. Stable, repeatable editing turns this photosynthetic microbe into a platform for making sugar straight from carbon dioxide.
pmc-13399343:
Dayvion R. Adams and colleagues built a community science program to track tick encounters across North Carolina, reporting in 2026. Working with 22 county public health agencies, the team handed out submission kits so residents could mail in ticks they found on themselves. Submitted ticks were tested for bacteria including the Lyme disease agent and Ehrlichia species.

Over two years the program received 444 ticks in 319 submissions. Species patterns mostly matched earlier records for the state, with one exception. The lone star tick, Amblyomma americanum, turned up in the mountainous west for the first time in print, hinting at a range expansion into cooler, higher country. Risk modeling tied recreational activities most consistently to higher submission likelihood. They present the framework as a workable template for community-based tick surveillance.
pmc-13399943:
Abdullah A AlShammari surveyed the leaders and staff of transfusion services in Riyadh hospitals about why blood components run short, in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Saudi Arabia. A structured questionnaire covered the problem and its fixes. Ninety-four responses came in, and the 64 from staff directly involved in shortage management formed the main analysis.

Shortage registered as a recurring operational burden, with average scores of 3.68 out of 5 for how it is perceived and 3.69 for the barriers around it. Confidence in countermeasures ran higher, practices scoring 4.03 and improvement strategies 4.44 in the survey results. The top barriers were scarce donors, heavy workload, thin staffing, high demand, and limited authority to act. The strongest support went to public donation awareness, patient blood management programs, and a national blood service. The authors read the findings as a system problem, not simply a donor problem.
pmc-13400143:
Chengming Qu and team engineered light-activated vesicles to break through the dense scar-like barrier around pancreatic tumors. Their 2026 work targets pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, whose cancer-associated fibroblasts build a stiff stroma that blocks drugs and immune cells. Overcoming that barrier could unlock chemo and immune therapy for a notoriously resistant cancer.

The team built extracellular vesicles carrying a light-sensitive drug, chlorin e6, and aimed them at midkine, a protein overexpressed in tumors. Light triggered immunogenic tumor cell death, activated an innate immune pathway in macrophages, reprogrammed fibroblasts, and eased low oxygen and poor blood flow. Joined with checkpoint blockade, T cell therapy, or chemo, the platform prolonged life in several preclinical tumor models. Human translation still requires safety and manufacturing work.
pmc-13400443:
Shao-Yu Peng and colleagues explore, in 2026, tiny parcels released by pig womb cells that may help embryos grow in the laboratory. The parcels, called extracellular vesicles, carry small RNA molecules that can change how cells behave. Lab-grown pig eggs mature and develop less well than those in the body, a problem for breeding and research.

Fluid from the womb cells improved egg maturation. One carried RNA, miR-21-5p, raised the rate at which artificially activated eggs reached the blastocyst stage, acting by lowering a brake gene and raising a key embryo gene. Another RNA lifted early cell division rates. The work points to natural signals that could make lab embryo production more efficient.
pmc-13400543:
Yuqing Tang and colleagues compare, in 2026, four pre-cooling methods for beef shipped in insulated foam boxes for online orders. Steaks were chilled in a fridge, supercooled just below freezing, sub-frozen, or deep-frozen, then spent 48 hours in passive distribution at room temperature before cold storage. Quality changes were tracked in detail.

Deep freezing protected color at first, but ice damage later sped up moisture loss, pigment oxidation and texture decline once temperatures rose. The frozen groups deteriorated fastest overall. Supercooling just below freezing performed best, holding redness, texture and taste acceptance longest while delaying protein damage at the molecular level. The authors back gentle supercooling over hard freezing for this delivery style.
pmc-13400743:
Shriya Singh and co-authors review, in 2026, the tug of war between mycobacteria and the internal compartments of the cells they infect. These bacteria, including the tuberculosis agent, survive inside host cells by exploiting organelles, the cells own miniature organs. Host cells, in turn, use the same structures to fight back.

The Golgi apparatus, the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria all influence who wins, beyond their textbook jobs in energy, calcium balance and protein shipping. They also steer immune signaling, metabolism and inflammation. The review sorts organelle roles into host defense mechanisms and pathogen hijacking strategies, and points to drug targets that might tip the balance toward clearing infection.
pmc-13400943:
Silas Forrer and colleagues chart, in 2026, how brain network growth diverges in young people with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, a genetic condition carrying high psychosis risk. Brain wiring matures abnormally in those who develop symptoms, but the timing pattern was unclear. The team used repeated brain scans and a fingerprint method. It gauges how distinctive each persons wiring pattern is.

Sixty-two affected participants and sixty-three controls, aged eight to thirty, were scanned multiple times. Controls showed a clear teen dip in fingerprint stability, then recovery. That arc reflects coordinated maturation. Those without psychotic symptoms partly followed it. Those with symptoms showed disorganized paths and decline on one growth axis. The contrast suggests lost coordination as networks mature.
pmc-13401143:
King and colleagues publish the plan for a project that will co-design a communication aid for aged care. The project will study the co-design as carefully as the product. Communication failures between residents, families, and staff are a complaint. Involving users in the fix is recommended, yet evidence on how taking part creates impact is thin. Their 2026 protocol describes a study inside a cluster randomized trial of an experience based co-design program.

The study will compare what residents, families, care workers, and managers experience during workshops, using surveys, interviews, focus groups, field notes, and observation. Findings will be checked against a model of how co-design should change services. The program's reach and upkeep will be tracked through the RE-AIM framework. A group of care recipients and family shaped the protocol. The aim is an account of which parts of co-design earn their cost.
pmc-13401543:
M van den Berg wrote a 2026 mathematics paper on the gradient of the torsion function for long cylinders with an elliptical cross-section. The torsion function solves a classic partial differential equation tied to heat flow, and the question is where its slope, the gradient, reaches its largest values.

Working with a cylinder of length L built on an open ellipsoid base, van den Berg uses heat equation tools to prove two contrasting results for sufficiently long cylinders. When the base ellipsoid has small eccentricity, meaning it is nearly round, the gradient maxima sit at the centres of the two end faces. When eccentricity is large, meaning the base is strongly stretched, the maxima move to the lateral side of the cylinder. Keywords list convexity alongside the torsion function, placing the work in geometric analysis.
pmc-13401643:
Martin Krsak and colleagues wrote a 2026 narrative review of the conceptual problems in designing clinical trials for psychedelic therapies. These treatments bundle a drug with preparatory and follow-up psychotherapy plus support during dosing, and every part of that package can move the outcome.

The therapeutic relationship itself is often stronger and more influential than in ordinary drug trials, a further complication. The deepest problem is blinding: patients almost always know whether they received the psychedelic, so functional unblinding is complete or near-complete in placebo-controlled studies. That makes it hard to separate the drug's true effect from positive expectancy in the treated group, compounded by negative expectancy in those who realise they got placebo. The review works through approaches that have been tried to reason about mechanisms despite these obstacles.
pmc-13402043:
John Sprockel Díaz, Sharon Sotomonte, and Alberto Buitrago built a custom GPT tool that reads antibiograms, the lab patterns showing which drugs stop a bacterium, for Gram-negative germs. They tested it in a retrospective accuracy study on 210 antibiograms balanced across control patterns and five resistance mechanisms, from simple penicillinases to carbapenem resistance. A Gemini-based rival, expert reading, and standard accuracy measures set the bar.

The custom GPT reached 95.7 percent accuracy with a kappa of 0.948, ahead of the rival at 91.9 percent and 0.902 on the same material. Its mistakes also did less clinical harm, nine against seventeen for the rival tool. The authors call the work proof of concept only, since checks at other hospitals and on wider germ types must come before ward use.
pmc-13402243:
Sara G. Creemers and colleagues report the first use of a lumboperitoneal shunt to sustain leukemia therapy complicated by raised brain pressure. Their 2026 case concerns a 19-year-old woman with high-risk acute promyelocytic leukemia who developed recurrent pseudotumor cerebri syndrome during treatment with all-trans retinoic acid, a life-saving drug that can raise intracranial pressure.

Acetazolamide and lower drug doses failed, and repeated lumbar punctures were ruled out by severe procedural anxiety and distress. A shunt draining spinal fluid to the abdomen kept brain pressure stable, allowing uninterrupted retinoic acid therapy and successful completion of consolidation. The case offers a cerebrospinal fluid diversion option for refractory cases, while a single patient cannot establish safety for broader use.
pmc-13402343:
Xu and co-authors make, in 2026, a nanoporous zirconia composite membrane for alkaline water electrolysis, the workhorse route to green hydrogen. Zirconia membranes trade ion flow against gas tightness. Their one-pot sol-gel method disperses yttria-stabilized zirconia nanoparticles evenly through a polybenzimidazole matrix, with phosphoric acid bridging the phases. The result is a sponge-like membrane of about 85 percent porosity that still resists gas crossover.

Despite the openness, bubble-point pressure stayed above 25 bar, and the interconnected pathways let hydroxide ions migrate without pause. In electrolysis tests the membrane delivered a current density of 13.1 amperes per square centimeter at 2.0 volts, performance at the top of the field, and worked across a range of alkali concentrations. Reinforced with a polyphenylene sulfide mesh, it operated for 7,000 hours and scaled to a large-area single-cell stack. The authors present the route as scalable manufacturing for hydrogen production at scale.
pmc-13402743:
Haoyang Shi and colleagues demonstrate a sliding metasurface, a flat engineered sheet that steers radio beams across a wide angle while also filtering frequencies sharply, all without electronics. Crowded airwaves demand better use of both spectrum and space. Instead of retuning each tiny element, their design slides two complementary patterned layers against each other, shifting the whole response in one motion.

The stack reuses its layers as a quasi Fabry-Perot cavity inside each unit cell, giving phase control and frequency selectivity at once. Bench tests confirmed sharp spectral cutoffs, strong suppression outside the band, and steady steering over a scan range of plus or minus 57 degrees in the reported runs. Because the trick is geometric, the authors argue it can scale to other frequency regimes, offering compact wave control for next-generation wireless and radar systems.
pmc-13402843:
Syamantak Ghosh, Kamalika Mukherjee, and Suvendra N Bhattacharyya lay out a step-by-step protocol for measuring how microRNAs cross the endosomal membrane inside cells. MicroRNAs are tiny gene-tuning molecules, and their movement between endosomes, multivesicular bodies, and export routes shapes how much silencing they can do. A shared, quantified method has been missing for comparing that traffic across labs.

The protocol follows the standard format for reproducible methods papers. It lists reagents, cell culture in Dulbecco modified Eagle medium, and the protein players of the endosomal sorting world, from early endosome markers to vesicle machinery. Atomic force microscopy and gene editing tools appear among its listed methods. Readers get a bench-ready recipe for turning miRNA movement across one membrane into numbers that other groups can repeat and contest.
pmc-13402943:
Matthew A Reyna leads a large team releasing the ECG-Image-Database, a library pairing pictures of electrocardiograms with their true digital signals, built to teach computers to read paper heart tracings. Archives hold mountains of ECG printouts, but scanning them back into data is foiled by wrinkles, stains, and bad photos. The team generated printouts from records held at Emory Healthcare, the PTB-XL collection, and Akershus University Hospital in Norway.

A toolkit rendered 1977 records into realistic printouts, then physically abused them with soaking, staining, and mold before rescanning under varied light; hospital thermal printouts from 266 patients added natural wear. The release totals 37,191 images from 2243 records across three countries, each tied to its signal. Parts already powered the PhysioNet Challenge 2024 and a Kaggle follow-up, and the design allows steady growth.
pmc-13403343:
Pavel Brož and co-authors rebuild the phase diagram of the niobium-antimony system. They pair fresh experiments with CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling and quantum calculations. Knowing exactly which compounds form, and at what temperatures they melt or transform, underpins any alloy or electronic use of the pair. Their reinvestigation confirmed three intermetallic compounds. It also mapped the niobium-rich phase Nb3Sb across a narrow band near 74 to 75 atomic percent niobium at 950 degrees.

Thermal analysis, fighting antimony evaporation above about 1300 degrees, fixed the breakup of Nb3Sb at 1840 degrees, give or take 25. It also showed Nb5Sb4 forming at 1550 degrees where older literature said otherwise. A low eutectic at 624 degrees was confirmed in sealed ampoules. The computed diagram matched the measured one well, and the thermodynamic database ships with the work for engineers to reuse.
pmc-13403543:
Anton Kubala and co-authors asked in 2026 whether dried morel mushrooms bought in shops still hold living spores. Morels are prized for food yet hard to farm, and fresh stock can be hard to source. The team soaked and blended four retail packets from separate sellers.

Spores from every packet sprouted on growth plates, at rates from about 2 percent up to near 20 percent. DNA checks named two morel species among the grown samples. Some labels did not match the species found, which hints at origin mix-ups. Still, cheap dried packets offer labs an easy source of living morel material.
pmc-13403743:
Luigi Camerano and a 20-author team studied in 2026 what happens when iron atoms slip between the layers of a magnetic crystal. Layered materials can be tuned this way, yet how added atoms change the flow of electrons was unclear. They used iron placed inside tantalum sulfide as their test case.

X-ray and light tools, backed by calculations, showed a new shared electron band linking guest and host. That band runs across layers and crosses the key energy level for conduction. It gives magnetism a moving channel between layers. The result breaks the simple lone-atom picture and offers a design rule for layered magnets.
pmc-13404243:
Saachi Bhattessa and colleagues reported in 2026 an adult whose deep brain cleft was found by chance during care for a mental illness. The birth defect leaves a fluid-filled split running through one side of the brain. Such clefts usually surface in childhood through seizures, weakness, or slow development.

This patient's scans showed the open kind of cleft, plus hints of other midline faults. He also carried a schizoaffective disorder, a mix of mood and psychosis signs. Links between the cleft and mental illness are reported, yet cause is unproven. Care stays aimed at symptoms, with surgery kept for pressure problems. Sorting which signs come from which condition is the hard part.
pmc-13405343:
Kosuke Arita and co-authors study steroid-related bone death at many body sites at once, in a 2026 Japanese report. Bone death in three or more places is uncommon but severe, and its background may differ from single-site disease. Whole-body MRI hunting found the extra lesions.

Among 107 patients operated on for hip bone death between 2019 and 2024, thirty-one, or 29 percent, had multifocal disease. Those patients were younger and had taken higher steroid doses, averaging 59.5 milligrams against 48.5 in the reported comparison. Blood diseases carried a sharply raised odds in the regression model. Serum protein profiling adds an exploratory molecular layer to the clinical contrast.
pmc-13406343:
Ching-Yu Wang and co-authors describe weight patterns in young gay and bisexual men in a 2026 United States cohort study. These men face two pressures at once: social conditions that raise obesity risk and appearance cultures demanding thinness. Data cover 2,704 participants aged 17 to 29 in a digital cohort.

Self-reported height and weight were compared across five racial and ethnic groups. Average body mass differed significantly between groups in the reported tests. White non-Hispanic and Asian non-Hispanic men showed lower average values and different weight category mixes. The authors read the spread through both structural inequality and body image pressure, arguing neither lens alone explains it.
pmc-13406543:
Francesco Vari and co-authors review lactate as a hormone-like signal from exercise, in a 2026 article. Long dismissed as a waste product of hard work, lactate now looks like a fuel and messenger in its own right. In the heart it feeds energy production directly.

Beyond fuel, lactate adjusts vessel tone, lining function, new vessel growth, inflammation and heart remodelling. Routes include the HCAR1 receptor, shifts in cell chemistry and a tagging process called lactylation on proteins. The review gathers evidence across heart physiology and disease. Clinical implications are weighed for exercise prescription and for drugs that might copy lactate's helpful signals.
pmc-13407743:

Their 2026 split-mouth work looks at children aged 6 to 9, weighing a decayed lower baby molar with pathological root loss against the healthy opposite side with normal root loss. Pulp infection can eat away baby roots, but effects on successor teeth were unclear.

Root loss was greater on distal roots of first molars and mesial roots of second molars. The authors conclude that pathological root loss speeds successor root growth and eruption, a finding that helps dentists time extractions and space care. The split-mouth design strengthens the comparison.
pmc-13407943:
Yulong Chen and co-authors compare, in 2026, two robotic approaches to removing part of a lung in 418 patients. Total-port surgery works entirely through small ports, while the utility-incision approach adds a working cut. Which is better was unsettled. No objective check of anatomical thoroughness existed either, so the team also validated a 3D-CT airway reconstruction score reviewed blindly by radiologists.

The total-port group, despite tackling more complex segments, achieved verified completeness in 95.8 percent against 80.0 percent after statistical weighting, lost less blood, and suffered fewer early complications, 3.6 against 10.3 percent. Radiologists agreed substantially on the score. The authors offer both a preferred technique for complex cases and a reproducible audit tool for thoracic surgical quality.
pmc-13408143:
Dhruba J. Deka and co-authors pinpoint, in 2026, why too much ammonia chokes the catalysts that scrub diesel exhaust. Copper-loaded chabazite catalysts convert nitrogen oxides using ammonia, but excess ammonia suppresses the reaction at low temperatures. Kinetic tests plus live magnetic-resonance spectroscopy and computation located the blockage. It sat in one half of the chemical cycle.

The reduction half-cycle proceeds nearly unaffected. Inhibition strength shifted with temperature and copper loading, as the mechanism predicts. Smarter catalyst design and operating windows that respect copper mobility are the practical upshot for emission control.
pmc-13408443:
Yun Lin, Weiming Chen, Zhihong Wang, and Pengwei Cai published a study in 2017 on emodin, a plant compound. They claimed it halts the growth of human lymphoma Raji cells through a chain of gene-control proteins. In 2026 the journal Molecular Medicine Reports retracted the article. A reader had flagged problems in its western blot figures. Several bands in different figures looked strikingly alike, where they should have shown separate tests.

An outside check by the journal judged the reader's concerns well founded. The editor then withdrew the article, citing lost trust in the data shown. The authors were asked to explain the likenesses and did not reply. The notice closes with the editor's apology to readers for any trouble caused. The record now stands as a retraction, kept in place so the scholarly trail stays visible.
pmc-13409043:
Zhi-Yong Yang and colleagues feed juvenile minnows in 2026 to find how much fish meal their diet can lose to soybean meal inside a biofloc system. In such a system, microbial flocs recycle waste in the water. Five diets replaced from none to over two thirds of the fish meal protein over an eight-week trial, with glucose feeding the flocs. Growth, digestion, antioxidant defences, and gut barrier health were all tracked.

The heaviest replacement clearly stunted growth and thinned muscle protein. At about half replacement, digestive enzyme activity and antioxidant protection in the gut already sagged while a damage marker climbed. Blood chemistry at the top level signalled liver strain and weakened immunity. The authors therefore cap the recommendation at about a third replacement, the highest level that kept growth and intestinal defences intact in their system.
pmc-13410743:
B. Y. Roukema and colleagues record in 2026 expert agreement on sinus problems in scuba divers, reached through a structured Delphi process in Malta. Sinus trouble is a frequent diving complaint, yet no dedicated guidance existed for diagnosis, treatment, or judging fitness to dive. Fourteen Dutch ear, nose, and throat specialists took part.

Agreement passed the set threshold across four areas. Diagnosis should rest on full ear, nose, and throat examination with a nasal scope, plus low-dose scanning when problems persist. First-line care follows standard sinus guidelines, with surgery kept for cases that resist medicine. After surgery, divers should wait at least eight weeks, prove healing by scope check, and pass a controlled test dive before returning.
pmc-13412143:
Rochelle Veldhuizen and Maria Belen Rabaglino survey in 2026 how omics tools can reveal better fertility traits in cattle. Classic measures such as conception rate and calving interval describe outcomes after the fact instead of predicting which animals will breed well. Genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics each read a different layer of biology, from DNA variants to the small molecules active in tissue.

Gene studies have tied DNA markers to sperm production, womb readiness, and embryo signalling. Protein and metabolite profiles track egg quality, fertilization capacity, and energy balance more closely in time. The authors argue these measures could become quick farm-side tests, guiding breeding choices within assisted reproduction programs.
pmc-13412343:
Simon-Pierre Corcostegui and colleagues described medical support inside France's elite GIGN police unit across 242 operations from 2018 to 2022. Since 1984 a military doctor and nurse team has traveled with tactical units, yet how often casualties occur and how fast help arrives had not been tallied in this physician-led system.

At least one casualty arose in 21 percent of missions, totaling 90 people cared for, with law-enforcement missions riskier than judicial ones and explosives linked to the highest risk. Median access ran 15 minutes to a doctor-staffed unit and 40 minutes to a hospital, giving planners hard numbers for staffing high-risk operations.
pmc-13412543:
Neele Kufeld and co-authors measure in 2026 how often patients with chronic non-cancer pain develop a substance use disorder tied to gabapentinoid medicines. These drugs are prescribed more widely each year, often off-label, and their misuse risk in ordinary pain patients was poorly quantified. An anonymous questionnaire went to patients treated with gabapentinoids at eleven general practices in two German regions, with 93 responses analysed.

About 27 percent met criteria for at least a mild disorder, and 5.4 percent scored in the severe range on the diagnostic items used. Male sex stood out as the clear predictor in their regression model, roughly quadrupling the odds. The authors advise care when prescribing these drugs for chronic pain and flag the sex difference for study.
pmc-13412643:
Alexandra Carloni and colleagues describe in 2026 a workflow that pulls school testing records into the medical charts of children with spina bifida. Learning difficulties are common in this condition, yet most centres never collect psychoeducational data in a systematic way. Their centre in central New York asked schools directly for records, then filed IQ scores both in the electronic record and in the national spina bifida registry.

Records arrived for 29 of 57 school-aged patients, and 62 percent of those files contained IQ scores. The share of registry entries holding an IQ score climbed from 5.4 percent to 29.7 percent under the new routine. Clerical staff ran most steps at about fifteen minutes per patient, and most schools replied within a week.
pmc-13415343:
Sara Vitale and colleagues review what handwritten signatures reveal about brain and mental disorders, in a 2026 systematic review. Signing is a deeply practiced act that often survives when other writing fails. The team searched three databases through December 2025 and kept sixteen papers on signature traits in patient groups.

Signatures seemed largely spared by general cognitive decline yet changed in specific conditions. Parkinson's disease shrank writing size, small vessel disease made strokes more winding, and shifts appeared in mania, delirium, and obsessive compulsive disorder. Movement and space traits changed most often. No sign pattern proved unique to one ill, so court use stays a guess.
pmc-13415543:
Liang Qu and colleagues ranked power options in 2026 for self-driving ocean platforms that watch marine pollution for months without servicing. Hybrid systems, wave converters, solar panels, fuel cells, and small wind turbines were scored on technical merit, cost, and environmental impact, with weights set by data spread rather than opinion.

Two ranking methods agreed, placing hybrid systems first and wave energy second, with solar and fuel cells in the middle and small wind last. The order held when weights shifted by up to 30 percent. Designers gain a defensible, numbers-first basis for powering remote sea sentinels.
pmc-13416543:
Ma Xiaoxiao and Jiang Erlie wrote a review dated two thousand twenty-six, in Chinese, on a gene change that worsens outlook in a childhood leukemia. The cancer is B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Faults in the gene IKZF1 are common in it and track with higher relapse risk and poor prognosis.

The review explains what the gene does and what its many change types mean in the clinic. It then builds a decision framework that runs from diagnosis through transplant planning and beyond. Immune therapy serves as a bridge to transplant, and the choice of transplant type is guided by how fast measurable disease clears. Follow-up care keys on the same measure.
pmc-13416743:
Tramontana and colleagues report a 2026 case study of drug levels in spinal fluid during treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis meningitis, an infection of the membranes around the brain. A drug mix called BPaL has transformed care for resistant lung tuberculosis, but proof for the brain form is thin. One patient was cured on a ten-month course of BPaL plus two added drugs.

The team measured the three BPaL drugs in blood and spinal fluid across a full day. Pretomanid entered freely, matched its free blood level, and stayed above the bacteria-killing level most of the day. Linezolid also entered well, close to its free blood level. These readings give rare hard numbers for dosing, where too little drug can mean death or lasting harm. One case cannot set doses for all, but it supports formal trials.
pmc-13417643:
Samuel Ford and co-authors lay out a trial protocol comparing glucose only treatment with standard insulin plus glucose for high blood potassium, published in 2026. High potassium can be life threatening, yet insulin treatment often drops blood sugar too low, especially in people without diabetes. The trial runs in one Australian emergency department with blinded treatment.

Ninety five adults without diabetes will receive either strong glucose alone or insulin with glucose, followed by infusions. Main checks are low blood sugar within six hours and potassium change at two hours. If glucose alone proves no worse at lowering potassium, it may offer a safer option.
pmc-13417843:
Majid Naderi and colleagues count clotting events in a large Iranian cohort with rare bleeding disorders, in a 2026 study. Bleeding dominates these illnesses, yet clots have been reported. Records for 1,251 patients at one centre during 2025 covered factor deficiencies, von Willebrand disease, and platelet disorders, with imaging proof required for each clot.

Twelve patients, about one percent, had at least one confirmed clot, all in veins. Leg veins and brain veins were commonest sites. Most events arose in risky settings such as pregnancy, surgery, infection, or clotting factor concentrates. Treatment balanced blood thinners with minimal factor replacement to avoid renewed bleeding.
pmc-13418143:
Tang and colleagues report a 2026 study of forsythoside A, a natural compound from the plant Forsythia suspensa, tested in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The mouse model shares many features of that nerve-insulation disease. Mice got the compound from day seven, and the team tracked symptoms, tissue damage, immune cells, and spinal cord gene activity.

At the higher dose, mice had milder symptoms, less nerve inflammation, and less insulation loss; the lower dose helped only slightly. Treated mice also carried fewer Th1 immune cells, which drive this disease. A plant compound with a named target gives drug developers a concrete lead against nerve inflammation.
pmc-13418543:
Jan L Klee and co-authors image striatum neurons in mice pressing a lever either spontaneously or after a cue, in a 2026 study. Parkinson disease impairs self started movement more than cued movement, raising the question of separate circuits. Calcium imaging tracked the same neurons across both modes in the dorsolateral striatum, a movement hub.

The same neurons encoded the press in both contexts, so the code is shared. Population patterns diverged before movement began, though, showing context specific preparation. Both major neuron classes joined in, with one class responding more at cue time. Flexible dynamics inside shared circuits may support both drive types.
pmc-13418743:
Ping Xu and colleagues identify a protein that helps colorectal cancer resist a standard chemotherapy drug. Oxaliplatin-based treatment remains the first choice for most patients, since immune therapy helps only a small share. The same effect held in mouse tumor models and in organoids grown from patient tissue. Tex10 normally holds a non-standard form of the BAF complex together, and blocking that link broke the shield around the cancer cells. The findings mark Tex10 as a possible drug target for patients whose tumors no longer answer to standard care.
pmc-13420343:
Russo and colleagues report a 2026 case, written as a letter, in which a rare blood variant made the standard diabetes test useless. The variant, hemoglobin Lepore-Boston-Washington, forms when parts of two globin genes fuse into one. She carried two copies of the fused gene, so her blood held none of the normal adult hemoglobin the HbA1c test measures.

Fetal hemoglobin made up about three quarters of her hemoglobin, softening what would otherwise be severe anemia. With HbA1c impossible, the team used fructosamine, a marker of sugar control over the past few weeks that does not depend on hemoglobin type. Its high level showed poor control and guided treatment choices. Gene tests confirmed the exact defect. An unreadable HbA1c can thus signal a hidden hemoglobin disorder, not a broken test.
pmc-13420643:
Katherine Makaroff and co-workers report a 2026 case where a rare heart tumor hid behind repeat pericarditis and killed a 47-year-old patient. Months of short breath, chest pain, fatigue, and high swelling markers followed an initial pericarditis episode, while serial heart scans missed the tumor.

Six months on, tamponade and hemorrhagic shock led to death from right atrial rupture, and pathology showed primary cardiac angiosarcoma. The case urges advanced imaging when pericardial fluid keeps returning with systemic symptoms, since scan alone can miss a lethal tumor before a returning effusion turns fatal.
pmc-13421243:
Maciej Kolodziej and colleagues followed tandem radioligand therapy safety in 2026 for neuroendocrine tumors over up to 20 years in Poland. Among 89 patients treated from 2002 to 2016, severe kidney toxicity hit 3.4 percent, kidney disease incidence reached 51 percent by ten years without any end-stage failure, and severe low platelets hit 5.6 percent. The paper supports tandem therapy as tolerable long term, with kidney function deserving lifelong watchfulness after treatment ends for all patients.
pmc-13422643:

Data came from 8,314 American adults followed for a median of about twelve and a half years, during which 1,606 died. pmc-13422743:

Where the valid share was 12 percent, best-of-128 selection cut violations from 88.2 percent of samples to zero in the cardiovascular tests, matching theory exactly, while a generator with zero valid support stayed hopeless. Their favored pairing hit zero violations on all three datasets with strong fidelity to the real data.
pmc-13423143:
Cherian and colleagues present a 2026 viewpoint arguing that child health services should keep refugee-background teenagers for longer before handing them to adult care. Adult services rarely match that joined-up, trauma-aware style. Extending the paediatric age limit, the authors argue, protects care at the very stage where these young people are most likely to fall between systems.
pmc-13424243:

At 30 degrees with nutrients, the yeast Kluyveromyces marxianus Y-6860 produced ethanol faster than the industrial standby Saccharomyces cerevisiae PE-2, reaching a productivity of 3.25 grams per litre per hour. pmc-13425543:

pmc-13426243:

Faulty citations, muddled content, and a compromised review process also appear. Such signs, the publisher said, break trust in the article as a whole. The findings should no longer be cited as sound evidence by readers.
pmc-13426943:

Subgroup checks by sex, age, and diabetes status rounded out the analysis.
pmc-13427543:

pmc-13427643:

pmc-13428043:

pmc-13428443:

Results on real dosage forms matched published reference methods in both precision and accuracy. Scores favored the new approach, backing its claim as a cleaner routine test for drug quality labs.
pmc-13429543:

pmc-13430743:

Starting ages averaged 51 years, ranging from 27 to 82, and starting motor and breathing function varied widely. Motor and breathing measures tracked change over time, giving adult clinics a realistic picture beyond trial volunteers.
pmc-13433843:
Aung Zaw Moe and co-authors checked stool germs in 2026 from sound alpacas and llamas on German farms. They hunted for drug proofing and harm traits. Pet trade lifts human touch with these herds. Proof rates ran low across more than seven hundred picks: the top rate hit a drug at under one in twenty. Rare picks shrugged off three or more drug classes. Sieve hunts caught proof genes for two watch drugs, all colistin-proof picks from one farm, and none for the last-line drug class. The authors call the herd risk low yet worth a watch.
pmc-13433943:

By weaving project stages with six IDEO design steps, they built the DTH-AI model and its use pathway. Heritage teams get a stakeholder-first route for AI rebuilding that aims to last, not just to dazzle.
pmc-13434443:
Baniowdeh and colleagues, writing as a letter in 2026, pool the head to head evidence comparing metabolic bariatric surgery with incretin based drugs for weight loss in type 2 diabetes. Only four studies qualified, and just two, covering twelve to twenty four months, could be pooled. The pooled result favored surgery by a wide margin in percent of body weight lost. But the confidence range stretched from slightly favoring drugs to hugely favoring surgery. The studies also disagreed strongly with each other. pmc-13434543:

Confidence in one's own ability, called self-efficacy, stood out as by far the strongest driver of precaution use. Knowledge of the precautions, older age, and past contact with hospital infections also mattered, in smaller measure. Together the factors explained about 65 percent of the differences between students, so Son backs training that builds confidence.
pmc-13434643:

The team capped the work with a full build of a plant lignan. Bench and computer studies agree that the cobalt coat sets the fork in the road. Predictable choice replaces trial and error.
pmc-13436143:
Julia Ienes-Lima and coauthors survey a needle like weapon across 399 genomes of gut escaping E coli in 2026. These strains cause urine, blood, and newborn brain infections in people and birds. The weapon, a type six secretion system, stabs rival cells and host cells alike.

Strains with the weapon tend to carry less drug resistance, which hints at a fitness trade off. Evolution pressures differ by infection niche, the pattern suggests. Lab work must now test when the weapon fires.
pmc-13436243:
Lamichhane R and coauthors map a booster switch on MAIT cells, a large unconventional T cell group, in 2026. These cells sense a vitamin byproduct that microbes make, shown on a display protein. The switch 4-1BB appears on their surface soon after sensing.

Switch levels peak early, within six hours, and mark the strongest responding cells. Blocking the switch dims cell activation and cytokine output, while extra switch ligand boosts both. Two gene switches tied to killer function also rise with 4-1BB signals. Vaccine designers may use this booster to tune MAIT cell help. The data fill a gap in co stimulation research.
pmc-13436443:
Wataru Yamori's team tested in 2026 whether extra Rubisco activase helps rice cope with flickering light under future high carbon dioxide. Rubisco activase restores the key carbon-fixing enzyme after inhibitors block it, and light that shifts quickly can leave photosynthesis lagging. Transgenic rice lines making different amounts of the activase were compared with normal plants under low and high carbon dioxide.

Extra activase sped enzyme reactivation and photosynthetic ramp-up, lifted water use efficiency under long flickering light, and improved growth under high carbon dioxide with flicker, while growth under steady light stayed similar. Crop scientists get a targeted trait for a warmer, higher-carbon world where clouds and canopy shade make light jumpy.
pmc-13436643:
Shivam Shah and coauthors describe an emergency led chat care platform at Mount Sinai from late 2023 to late 2024 in 2026. The platform handles six low risk needs, from urinary infections to contraception. Nearby emergency visits for like complaints totaled 19,204 in the window.

The platform took 343 visits from 277 patients, a small first slice. Urinary complaints led at 45.8 percent, with yeast infections and eye complaints next. Median age was 32.6 years, and ninety three percent of patients were female. About five percent of visits were bumped up to in person care. Seven day return visits form the safety gauge.
pmc-13437343:
El-Sayed El-Shafaey and colleagues describe a fungal-like infection of the genitals in Saudi Arabian horses. Pythiosis, caused by the water mold Pythium insidiosum, forms stubborn ulcerated growths on skin, yet genital cases are rarely detailed. Their 2026 study reviewed 123 horses brought to one hospital with ulcerated skin growths between late 2022 and late 2025. Seventeen male horses had confirmed disease of the penis or its sheath.

Growths sat most often on the sheath, then at the urinary opening and the tip of the penis. Tissue study, antibody staining, and culture all confirmed the culprit, and microscope images showed its reproductive forms. About eighty-two percent of horses recovered fully, while about eighteen percent saw the disease return, mostly with larger or multiple sheath growths. The authors urge fast, exact diagnosis and complete removal, presenting their series as one of the closest looks yet at this uncommon site.
pmc-13437443:
Gloria Straub, Wolfgang Prinz, and Brigitte Lueger-Schuster reviewed what helps soldiers stay resilient when trauma exposure cannot be avoided. Research on military resilience has leaned on the lone soldier, yet strength may also live in units and the whole organization. Their 2026 systematic review sorted findings into three levels: personal, team and leadership, and structural. Only nine studies qualified, two of them based on interviews.

Most sat at the personal level, such as flexible coping and individual traits. Far fewer studies touched leadership behavior or structural conditions, and none modeled the levels together as nested data. The authors argue this imbalance quietly shifts the burden onto soldiers themselves. They urge military organizations to fix structures and culture first, secure support access, build belonging, and cut stigma around help-seeking. Resilience, in their reading, is something an institution builds around its people, not a trait it demands from them.
pmc-13437543:
Lei Deng and colleagues asked how much of a brain bleed surgeons should clear during keyhole surgery for the best thirty-day outcome. Bleeding inside the brain is among the deadliest stroke types, and gentle suction can remove the clot through a small track. Their 2026 study reviewed 148 adults treated at one center between 2020 and 2024. Half ended the month with a fair outcome and half with a poor one.

Clearance mattered steadily: each added percent of clot removed lowered the odds of a poor outcome, even after other factors were weighed. It sorted patients well, with a rough threshold near sixty percent clearance. A rival rule based on leftover clot volume proved more specific when it fired. The authors propose clearance near sixty percent as a yardstick, paired with the volume rule rather than replacing it. Planned studies must test it before it becomes a set target.
pmc-13438143:
Gillian P Boyce's team demonstrated film transfer in 2026 using sacrificial polyvinyl alcohol substrates for atomic layer deposited oxides. Thin dielectric films are hard to move intact to new surfaces, limiting device designs. Alumina films were grown directly on PVA, then peeled and transferred to silicon oxide or gold, yielding continuous 32-nanometer films over millimeter areas with angstrom-scale roughness that survived repeated peeling.

Thermal study found a clear PVA melting point, no glass transition, and a suggested ceiling near 226 degrees, while expansion mismatch and processing heat were weighed for film quality. Residual PVA-derived carbon at the interface, even after oxygen plasma, likely degraded dielectric performance. Device engineers get a workable transfer route plus a named contaminant problem to solve next.
pmc-13438443:
Aryan Wadhwa and co-authors examined the ethics of trials that proved clot removal for stroke. Pulling a clot from a blocked brain artery, called thrombectomy, helps many patients, yet testing it meant randomizing people who often could not consent, with minutes deciding outcomes. Their 2026 analysis read the practice-changing trials and ethics literature from 2003 to 2024 across three pressure points.

After 2015 the proof piled up so fast that honest doubt collapsed, and several trials stopped early to spare the control group, at some cost to the precision of their estimates. Standard consent, signed by patient or family, also skewed who entered: the most severe cases, often voiceless, were shut out. The authors back deferred or presumed consent for such emergencies, arguing that rigid respect for autonomy can breach fairness by excluding the most vulnerable from research on their own rescue.
pmc-13439243:
Rachel Frost and colleagues map how symptoms link in people who live with both psychosis and trauma stress, in a 2026 network study. Trauma after-effects are thought to feed delusions and voices, yet which symptoms pull hardest was unclear. The team used baseline data from a therapy trial with 305 adults who had schizophrenia-spectrum illness, distressing delusions or voices, and post-traumatic stress. A Bayesian network model charted links among trauma symptoms, complex trauma symptoms, beliefs, and psychotic symptoms.

Early guesses missed the mark: no symptom clearly outranked others in predictability, and voices showed no direct tie to trauma memories or trauma beliefs. Self-blame did track with delusions, while poor control of feelings pointed toward voices. The authors argue that mixed symptom patterns across people may hide clearer links, and that sorting patients into subgroups could sharpen care.
pmc-13439343:
Seyed Alireza Mostafavi's team studied scale buildup in 2026 in produced water from two oil fields, asking how reaction time changes what precipitates before reinjection. Produced water is voluminous and toxic, reinjection is the favored disposal route, yet mixing incompatible waters drops mineral scale that clogs systems. Samples were mixed and filtered after one day versus fourteen days under field conditions, with scale chemistry checked by electron microscopy.

One-day scales exceeded five hundred milligrams per liter, while fourteen-day scales fell below one hundred fifty, meaning over three hundred fifty milligrams redissolved, though some scale types grew instead. Oilfield engineers get a kinetics lesson: holding time reshapes scale, so retention design can cut or worsen clogging. Pre-treatment plans should account for time, not just water chemistry.
pmc-13439443:
Yunwei Lu and co-authors test a Chinese herbal formula in worms that model Alzheimer's-linked harm. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six, with a title in Chinese in the pack. The formula, Bushen Yijing, is a blend used in Chinese medicine. The team asks if it can cut the build-up of amyloid beta, a protein that clumps in the disease, and guard cells from stress.

In worm strains, some bred to make the protein, the formula lengthens life and delays paralysis. It cuts protein deposits in the throat zone. Stress defence levels rise, while harm marks fall. Two defence switches move into the cell core, as the model would want. Computer docking ties two of its parts to key targets.
pmc-13439843:
Yang Chen's team mapped research in 2026 on Epstein-Barr virus DNA as a biomarker for nasopharyngeal cancer immunotherapy. Response to immunotherapy varies widely, and viral DNA in blood tracks tumor biology, yet no full map of the field's growth and themes existed. One hundred sixty-four articles were analyzed for trends, countries, keywords, collaborations, and citations using bibliometric software.

Work surged after 2017, led by China and the United States, with hotspots around PD-1 drugs, tumor activity, and mechanisms, shifting from tumor burden and prognosis toward dynamic monitoring and trials. The paper frames viral DNA as a living biomarker joining virus, tumor load, and response. Oncologists get a field atlas for choosing monitoring strategies.
pmc-13441743:
Shoichi Shiota, Takahiro Ohitokata, and Hiroshi Harada follow children's self-esteem and gratitude through a school morning yoga program in Kitakyushu, Japan, reporting in 2026. Four hundred one elementary children took part across seven public schools, as part of the regular curriculum. Sessions ran fifteen minutes once a week from September 2025 to February 2026, mixing postures, breathing practice, attention meditation, and loving-kindness meditation. Standard child scales measured self-esteem and interpersonal gratitude before and after.

Both scores rose significantly across the program window. The authors read the pairing as consistent with yoga acting as an embodied regulation practice, settling body and attention together. Because no comparison group was tracked, they caution against causal claims: growing up, school events, or expectation could share credit. The pilot is offered as groundwork for controlled school-based trials of brief morning yoga.
pmc-13441843:
Yaacov Biton and colleagues simulate waves crossing tissue where cells randomly flicker off and on, hunting for the tipping point where orderly waves break, in a 2026 modelling study. Flickering excitability is increasingly blamed for unstable conduction in heart-like tissue. Their two-dimensional FitzHugh-Nagumo model, a standard stand-in for excitable media, subjected one region to random switching between keen and weak excitability. Density of flickering cells inside that zone was the dial under test.

Three regimes appeared in clean sequence. Sparse flicker, under four percent, merely dented passing waves, which healed afterward. Middle densities, roughly four to eighteen percent, snapped waves into breaks that seeded lasting spiral activity. Beyond eighteen percent, conduction shattered into fragments and failed outright. The authors argue that purely functional, time-varying patchiness can by itself manufacture the re-entrant dynamics behind rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation.
pmc-13442443:
Wanbing Zhao and colleagues track whether one gene variant shapes the course of Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. The gene, TMEM106B, makes a membrane protein and is known to shift risk in a related brain illness. The team followed 241 patients over time and typed each person at a spot called rs3173615, which sorts people into GG, GC, or CC groups.

At the first visit, the CC group felt more daytime sleepiness than the other two groups. Most other traits showed no clear link to gene type at that point. Across later visits, the GC group slid faster on mood, space sense, and life quality scores than the CC group. The GG group leaned the same way, though less firmly. The authors read gene type as one quiet force that may steer how the illness unfolds.
pmc-13442543:
Lema Delara and colleagues build the first survey that asks children about hiding autistic traits in a 2026 paper. No tool had measured how children mask or play down such traits to fit in. The team built the Children's Masking Questionnaire with families, young people, and experts through shared design work.

Two pilot studies asked users whether the survey felt useful and fit for use. Users backed the tool and gave pointed tips that shaped the final form. That form holds two parts, one for adults to answer and one for the child, plus a good practice guide, all free for research and care use. The authors call for tests in larger groups and across other mind-health states. Their hope is a shared yardstick for a habit that can tax a child's well-being.
pmc-13442643:
Ling Qin and colleagues survey infection experts in China on shared choices for fever of unknown origin in a 2026 study. Such fevers hide their cause for weeks, so care choices carry real doubt. An online survey in July 2025 drew 429 replies, and 386 of them passed the checks for this work.

Just 27.7 percent of the experts knew the shared-choice method by name beforehand, and only 8.5 percent had formal training in it. Views on the method scored high at 4.46 points out of 6 on the attitude scale. Scores for felt gains also ran high, while block scores sat mid-range. The authors say most experts back joint talks with patients yet lack training and time. They urge skill courses and clearer steps so shared choice can enter fever workups for real.
pmc-13443543:
Younghun Kim and colleagues find gas that freezes into lattice order inside porous crystals in a 2026 paper. Gases in metal-organic frameworks were long read as loose crowds, yet tight pores can pin them into crystal-like ranks. Their pipeline screens hosts with a lattice-aware score, using xenon as the test guest.

One host, Co-CAU-36, held a pore-wide xenon lattice in the screens. Uptake curves split the build into shell growth, pore fill, and joint lattice lock steps. In xenon-krypton mixes the host split the pair into core and shell zones at pore scale. Math runs found a low-wall path for krypton through the core. The authors cast gas lattices as a true phase that design can aim at for sharp separations.
pmc-13443643:
Ekkaphot Khongkla and coauthors report the first 2026 isolation and testing of nanovesicles from Bacopa monnieri, a healing plant prized for its chemistry but never before mined for these tiny carriers. The team mapped the vesicles' cargo by mass spectrometry and protein analysis, then tested them against neuroblastoma cells in the lab.

The vesicles ran about 112 nanometers across, carried mainly triterpenoids and triterpene saponins plus the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase, and were taken up by tumor cells, clustering near the nucleus. They suppressed neuroblastoma growth and altered cell shape. The work opens a plant-based route to cancer nanotherapy, though animal and safety studies must follow.
pmc-13443843:
K Nithya and C R Dhivyaa present a 2026 federated system for detecting fake news without pooling raw articles from rival outlets. Their COASBC model blends character-level embeddings with convolutional and attention-based recurrent layers under cost-sensitive learning, then trains across news sources while keeping each source's data local.

Character-level vectors handle rare and odd words better than word-only embeddings, and the federated design cuts central compute cost while improving security and scale. Tests on LIAR, FakeNewsNet, WELFake, and other sets, plus a 2023 tweet collection, showed the model beating leading rivals on accuracy, precision, and reliability. Newsrooms gain a privacy-aware filter, though adversarial headlines remain a moving target.
pmc-13444143:
Yunhan Lin and colleagues read depression in the voice with a self-taught speech model in a 2026 study. Major depression lacks firm lab marks, so clinics lean on talks and scales. Their cohort held 1,816 people, split 910 patients and 906 healthy peers, with 23,608 standard speech clips in all.

A deep frame learned from raw speech through self-supervised steps, set against named voice models and classic feature kits. Inside checks gave an AUC mark of 0.932 for the new frame, well past classic routes. Outside checks at fresh sites held an AUC mark of 0.879 in the report. Voice traits numbered 6,373 in the classic kit, yet learned marks won. The authors pitch voice as a fast, cheap aid for depression screens.
pmc-13444243:
Zehao Yao and colleagues build a space-tied gene atlas of the growing human heart in a 2026 study. Heart form needs gene programs that differ by zone, yet how zones sync their growth stayed vague. Their atlas profiles 30 slices from hearts at 8 to 15 weeks after conception.

Each spot acts as a small multicell unit, and zones fall out in clean anatomic ranks. Rare crews surfaced, from papillary muscle cells to plane cells at the valve ring. In the ventricle, a smooth gene slope runs from inner lining to outer wall, with factor and signal shifts in step. Shared ripening marks rose across zones: more contractile and fuel programs, fewer growth programs. The authors share the map as a base for heart birth and disease work.
pmc-13444443:
Yunrui Li and colleagues set a fair test frame for antibody-antigen binding forecasts in a 2026 paper. Binding calls guide drug hunts, yet past tools fade on new targets and on sets that lack true non-binders. Their frame grades sequence and structure tools by pair accuracy and retrieval marks across varied antigens.

Their own tool, MochiBind, reads sequence alone and calls pairs head to head. It matched or beat structure tools such as Boltz-2, GeoDock, and Graphinity on the shared tests. That tie matters, since sequence tools scale far past structure rigs. The authors offer the frame as a shared yardstick for the field. Fresh antibody design may lean on sequence-first screens if the tie holds in wider tests.
pmc-13444743:
