Nearly everyone received the test before listing.

Of those tested, 96 percent completed screening, and 22 people, about 4 percent, tested positive for the infection. Positive results clustered among people with diabetes, people born abroad, and people who used alcohol. Seventeen patients started preventive treatment, with few side effects and no liver damage reported. No one developed active tuberculosis after transplant. Helbo supports keeping universal screening even in a low-incidence country like Denmark.
pmc-13483243:
Gina Chaput and co-authors describe a 2026 lab system for watching microbes settle on eelgrass seedlings. Seagrass meadows shelter coasts and young sea life, yet seedling microbes stay poorly known while restoration leans on seeds. The team grew Zostera marina in fabricated ecosystem chambers that hold the water and germ setting under tight control.

Seed washing with bleach and alcohol stripped surface microbes while sparing those living inside the seed. Even so, washed and unwashed plants still diverged by the sixth growth stage across many microbe types, which shows seed coat riders steer the whole assembly path. Twenty-six microbe markers flagged set life stages. Growers gain both a standard rig for plant-microbe trials and first targets for seeding helpful microbes in restoration.
pmc-13483443:
Punduk Yilmaz and colleagues surveyed working mothers in Turkey about anxiety in the year after childbirth and how maternity leave felt to them. Their 2026 study gathered 287 employed mothers, who completed a 47-question scale built specifically for postpartum worries. The team compared anxiety levels with how long leave lasted and whether mothers judged that leave long enough for recovery.

The average anxiety score sat in the moderate band, and about 81 percent of mothers landed in the moderate or high anxiety groups. Three quarters of the mothers rated the statutory 16-week leave as insufficient for their needs. Mothers who wanted to extend their leave showed the clearest link to higher anxiety categories. Punduk Yilmaz argues that felt adequacy of leave matters alongside its length when employers and lawmakers shape postpartum support.
pmc-13483543:
Moazama Shakeel Ahmed presents a single-patient account from 2026 of neurosarcoidosis that shut down pituitary hormone production. The patient was a 42-year-old man who had lived with sarcoidosis for 12 years. He arrived with belly pain, low blood pressure, low body temperature, high blood sodium, and heavy urination with strong thirst. Skin plaques, joint pain, and earlier drug-resistant seizures formed part of his history.

Blood tests showed broad hormone shortages matching failure of both the front and rear pituitary, and scans found lesions above the sella and in the brainstem. Replacement treatment with thyroid hormone and desmopressin brought clear improvement. The account reminds clinicians to consider brain involvement when people with sarcoidosis develop hormone or nerve symptoms, since prompt treatment can prevent lasting harm.
pmc-13483743:
Sarah Hug and co-workers describe a joint design push to lift referrals to lung rehab for people with COPD, a long-term lung disease. This 2026 study spans three large hospitals and three time spans. The spans cover a base phase, a design phase, and a phase after changes went live. Four patients and six care staff built the new steps side by side.

The new steps include promo goods for the rehab programs, plus more steps set out in the full text. Referral rates before and after are compared with a method that strips out drift over time. A cost model asks how many hospital stays must be saved each year for the push to pay for itself. Class turnout and health gains sit outside this study's scope.
pmc-13483843:
Nabisere and team translated a grief questionnaire into Kiswahili and Luganda so health workers in Kenya and Uganda can measure how intensely mothers grieve after losing a baby. Bereavement support after stillbirth or newborn death is scarce in the region, and imported English tools may miss local expression. Their 2026 study adapted the Perinatal Grief Intensity Scale with community groups, then tested it through think-aloud interviews and repeat questionnaires.

Final testing covered 160 bereaved women across the two countries, including a smaller group who answered twice to check consistency. Scores proved stable between repeats and consistent within the scale, which the authors rate as good reliability. Translations were agreed through stakeholder review rather than literal word swaps. Nabisere says the versions are ready for screening use, though cutoff scores and deeper validity checks still need work.
pmc-13485643:
Miguel de Oliveira reports use of a platelet-boosting drug to prep patients with rare low platelet counts for planned surgery. Low counts raise bleed risk, and donor platelet bags carry risks of their own. This 2026 series covers nine patients with four gene-based platelet diseases across fifteen operations. The drug eltrombopag was given at 50 milligrams a day from about three weeks pre-surgery.

Counts rose well in fourteen of fifteen cases, and ten met the strict top mark. Median counts climbed 143 percent from a low base to a sound peak. No bleeds and no donor bags were needed in the whole series. One patient with one gene type failed to respond and needed extra help. The series also gives the first report for one rare gene type.
pmc-13486043:
Ilaria Milani and co-authors study a blood protein across metabolic diseases in a 2026 paper. Fetuin-A may link obesity, both types of diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The team measured it in patients and checked livers with ultrasound-based scans.

The study covered 105 patients plus 13 controls. Fetuin-A ran higher in every patient group than in controls, highest in obesity without diabetes. It tracked with body size, waist measures, and blood fats. It also rose with liver fat scores but not with scarring. The authors propose it as a marker of fatty liver with fair accuracy.
pmc-13486443:
Weijie Chen reviews the two-way conversation between lymphatic vessel lining cells and immune cells in health and disease. Published in 2026, the synthesis covers the lymphatic system's twin jobs of draining tissue fluid and ferrying immune traffic. Lining cells set chemical gradients, tune local metabolism, and display docking molecules that steer immune behavior.

In calm conditions the lining partners with dendritic cells to start immunity, guides T cell fates and homing, supports antibody responses, and keeps tissue peace with macrophages. During infection and autoimmunity the same cells recruit fighters yet may also break tolerance by presenting the wrong antigens. Cancer twists the dialogue both ways, building suppressive networks that aid spread or, in other contexts, helping anti-tumor immunity take hold.
pmc-13486743:
Mary Amir Bishara and Giordano de Guglielmo argue in a 2026 commentary that lab-made cooling agents in nicotine goods merit the same hard look as menthol. That compound has long held a special place in tobacco rules. Its cool feel makes smoke and vapor go down with ease. Strong proof links it to heavier use and to more failed quit tries.

As bans spread, makers turned to lab-made coolants such as WS-3 and WS-23. These hit the same cold nerve switch as menthol but leave no mint taste. They now fill goods sold as non-menthol or ice, at times past menthol strength. Yet no rules guard their use in lungs. Brain work shows menthol boosts nicotine reward in three ways at once. If lab coolants share those brain acts stays an open, pressing point.
pmc-13487243:
MohammadNezhad-Aghdam and co-authors ran twenty-seven laboratory tests on inclined drop structures, the sloped chutes that carry water down in channels, to learn what controls the scour hole dug below them. Scour undermines the structure itself, so its depth and length drive design. Their 2026 experiments varied slope angle across three settings, tailwater depth across three levels, and flow rate, filming how each hole grew over time.

Steeper slopes concentrated the jet and deepened maximum scour by up to about 32 percent versus gentler slopes in the test series. Shallower slopes instead stretched the hole longer, by more than 36 percent in the comparisons reported. Deeper tailwater cushioned the jet and cut both depth and length, by up to about 17 and 14 percent respectively. Over eighty percent of final depth dug during the early phase. Regression models predicted outcomes within about ten percent.
pmc-13487343:
Yubin Xue uses gene clues to test if body weight itself makes hearing worse. Plain watch-and-see studies can't split cause from shared traits like wealth or noise at work. This 2026 study sets five gene-based metabolic traits against self-reported hearing strain in a large genome data set. A second hearing data set checks the result.

Gene-based higher body mass raised the odds of hearing strain by a small but firm step. The check data set pointed the same way for weight. The other traits span swelling marks, blood pressure, bad blood fat, and diabetes risk. Their results sit in the full text with checks that weigh the traits side by side. Weight care is urged for heart health in any case. A true push toward hearing harm adds one more ground to act.
pmc-13487943:
Lisanne Hut-Mossel and colleagues study how clinical audits shape trainee doctors in a 2026 case study from a Dutch university medical center. Residents in two departments carried out audits, which are structured reviews of care against set standards. Interviews followed with residents, supervisors, program directors, and a quality officer within two years of the audits.

Residents grew in awareness and skill mainly by presenting findings and urging colleagues to change practice. Progress toward full improvement cycles, where changes are put in place and checked again, stayed limited. Department leadership, role modeling, and shared ownership decided how far teams went. The authors argue that audits teach best inside a learning culture that treats improvement as daily work.
pmc-13488243:
Nazife Nur Ozer Sensoy and Yavuz Ayar report severe adenovirus pneumonia with kidney failure in a healthy young adult in a 2026 case report. Adenovirus usually causes mild illness in people with normal immunity, so severe lung and kidney involvement is unusual. An 18-year-old woman arrived with severe pneumonia, strong inflammation markers, and kidney function already badly reduced before antibiotics began, while cultures stayed negative and a throat test found adenovirus.

A kidney biopsy showed preserved filtering structures, no antibody deposits, and mild tube damage, which fits injury from infection and body-wide inflammation rather than immune attack on the kidney itself. Steroid pulses and broad antibiotics were given, and kidney function recovered fully during the hospital stay.
pmc-13489943: The MULTI Consortium and colleagues published an author correction in 2026 to their Nature article presenting a sleep chart of biological ageing clocks for middle and late life. The notice adds two relevant prior studies that were missing from the original reference list: a 2022 study and a 2025 study, both by Li and coauthors. The authors state their regret for the omission. Nothing else in the article changes: no data, analyses, figures, or conclusions are altered, and the correction concerns citation completeness only.
pmc-13490243:
Zongkuo Li and Jianting Cai show that zinc calms gut inflammation by pushing harmful T cells toward a rust-like death in a 2026 mouse and cell study. Inflammatory bowel disease is driven by overactive helper T cell subsets, and zinc deficiency tracks with worse disease in patients. The team fed zinc to mice with colitis and grew human helper T cells in dishes, then sequenced gene activity to find the mechanism at work.

Zinc sharply reduced gut damage and stopped pathogenic T cells infiltrating the bowel lining in the reported experiments. Rather than merely blocking their development, zinc stripped their defenses against ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, by lowering two protective proteins and raising a driver gene. The mucosal niche cleared as a result.
pmc-13490343:
Xiaowei Hu leads a large team uncovering a three-part growth circuit in bladder cancer in a 2026 study blending tumor databases, patient tissue, cell sorting, and mouse models. Two cell-division proteins, NEK2 and ZWINT, rose together in high-grade tumors and marked a stable, aggressive cell subgroup enriched in invasive lesions. The team then traced how they cooperate with a third protein, NDC80, that helps chromosomes separate during division.

Silencing both lead proteins together crippled growth, spread, and tumor formation, while silencing either one alone helped only partly in the reported experiments. Removing NDC80 also slowed tumors and restored sensitivity to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine. Tissue from drug-resistant cancers carried more NDC80. The authors propose the circuit as a drug target.
pmc-13491443:
Susan Musau leads an author group reporting a 2026 study of drug-resistant tuberculosis bacteria from western Kenya. Routine testing in the region relies on narrow gene probes and culture methods that can miss resistance. The authors set those results against whole-genome sequencing of stored samples drawn from twelve counties.

Among 1,053 samples, about one in eight stood up to at least one drug. The largest group no longer answered to isoniazid, though rifampicin still worked on it. Sequencing of 290 good-quality genomes tied rifampicin failure mainly to the rpoB change S450L and isoniazid failure to katG and inhA promoter changes. Resistant samples grouped in four counties and in lineages 4 and 3. Routine tests and sequencing differed often enough that the authors urge using both methods.
pmc-13492343:
Que Kong revisits a 1998 Plant Physiology paper that reported wrinkled-seed mutants of Arabidopsis with drastically reduced seed oil, and traces how it reshaped plant oil research. Plant seeds store oil as triacylglycerol to fuel germination, and vegetable oils matter for nutrition and industry. Their 2026 retrospective follows the science that grew from that single mutant phenotype.

Cloning the responsible gene in 2004 identified WRI1, a transcription factor that switches on late sugar-breakdown and fatty-acid-building genes, showing seed oil depends on developmental control of carbon flow. Later work mapped the DNA element it binds, its upstream regulators in seed maturation, its partner proteins, and the modifications governing its stability, plus the structure of its DNA recognition. Recent studies extend WRI1 into non-seed tissues, hormone and nutrient processes, and crop engineering. Kong presents WRI1 as a central node linking seed development, carbon metabolism, and oil accumulation.
pmc-13492843:
Durman and colleagues surveyed in 2026 sports science students in Indonesia on self-efficacy and study burnout. These students face dual study and athletic demands, and confidence in one's ability may buffer stress. The cross-sectional study enrolled 233 junior-year students at the State University of Makassar in 2025. Burnout and self-efficacy were scored with validated Indonesian forms.

Most students reported moderate confidence, at about seventy percent, and about half showed moderate burnout, with no severe cases. Higher confidence was tied to lower burnout, though the link was modest. Each step up in self-efficacy cut the odds of burnout by about half in the full model. The authors conclude that building student confidence is a plausible lever against burnout in dual-demand courses. They suggest schools screen for low confidence early.
pmc-13494543:
Wanyi Wang and others tune DNA copy enzyme theta to improve exact genome editing by tiny-match repair. In 2026, the study builds editors from the copy enzyme part and the unwinder-like part of the enzyme, aiming for thousand-base-scale aimed inserts that match-guided repair handles poorly in non-splitting cells. Short tiny-match strings guide donor entry.

The copy-enzyme-part editor tripled knock-in rates over standard Cas9 editing, while both part editors cut on-target insert-loss rates by about thirty percent and raised precise inserts by up to eighty percent. The copy enzyme part beat other setups and boosting factors. The work moves forward healing gene inserts with fewer stray edits.
pmc-13495143:
Kang An, Marc Gillinov, Lars G Svensson, and Miralem Pasic present a 2026 case report of valve infection after a catheter-based aortic valve replacement, known as TAVR. An 82-year-old woman arrived with fever and weariness, and scans found a large, loose growth of infected tissue swinging on her implanted valve. Such growths often break off and block arteries, with the brain a feared target.

Scans showed clots had struck her spleen, kidneys, and gut arteries, yet the brain stayed clear. At surgery the growth was gone from the valve, proof it had broken away, and the team removed the valve, cleaned the area fully, and sewed in a tissue valve. She recovered well. The authors muse that her arch shape and the growth's central seat may have steered debris away from the brain. They warn that no one should count on such luck, and early surgery stays the rule.
pmc-13495543:
Poorva Kulkarni and colleagues compare, in a 2026 survey, what dental and medical postgraduate students in Maharashtra, India know about gum disease's links to gut disorders and pancreatic cancer. Gum disease is a chronic inflammation, and proof keeps tying it to illness far beyond the mouth. The team sent an eighteen-question survey to 202 postgraduates, 108 dental and 94 medical.

Medical students scored clearly higher on overall awareness of these body-wide links. Knowledge scores, though, sat close between the groups, both middling. Awareness of the tie between gum disease and gut cancers was thin in both camps, and answers about liver disease and pancreatic cancer swung unevenly from question to question. The authors read the pattern as a training gap on both sides and argue for teaching the mouth-body connection across both curricula.
pmc-13495843:
Geonhui Lee, Bingjie Sun, Nicholas Fang, and Chunguang Xia present a bioengineering study, published in 2026. They built a tumour-on-a-chip. It keeps breast cancer tissue alive. Densities match real tumours. The chip is printed in fine detail. It has vessel-like channels and tiny pores. Nutrients flow through cancer tissue packed very densely. Up to four hundred million cells per millilitre are supported.

The crowded tissues reprogrammed key cancer genes. The patterns matched high-grade patient tumours. Ordinary cultures fail to do this. Resistance to the drug elacestrant also matched patient levels. Clinical drug concentrations were used. The authors say the chip is a better test bed for aggressive cancer treatments.
pmc-13498743:
Harkoo and co-authors describe a single puzzling case from a phase 1 trial of anti-HIV monoclonal antibodies, lab-made immune proteins tested for prevention and treatment. A woman volunteer developed a sharp but temporary rise in liver enzymes, the blood signal of liver cell injury, after receiving the antibodies. Her team stopped her other medications and ran an extensive workup covering infections, autoimmune markers, pregnancy, and ultrasound imaging, all of which came back unremarkable.

Enzymes began falling within three days, then rose again about three weeks later. Around then she reported drinking household white vinegar for heavy menstrual bleeding, a folk remedy the authors flag as a confounder. Everything eventually settled and her symptoms cleared. The case, reported in 2026, is offered as a lesson in how many rival explanations must be excluded before blaming a new antibody for liver injury.
pmc-13499043:
Omar Saleh and colleagues review in 2026 the revived role of balloon widening of a narrowed aortic valve as a short-term bridge for very unstable patients. Severe narrowing can tip suddenly into heart failure, shock, or cardiac arrest, a state the authors call acute valve syndrome. Valve replacement is the only lasting fix, yet the sickest patients may be too unstable for the usual planning steps that replacement requires.

Registry data show lower death rates with emergency replacement than with balloon treatment, though sicker patients and differing severity cloud that comparison. Smaller studies with detailed heart measures suggest patients who stabilise after balloon widening and then proceed to replacement can fare about as well as those treated directly. The review maps where evidence is thin and urges heart teams to weigh real-time stability when choosing the path.
pmc-13499943:
Kshitij Bang and co-authors present in 2026 a jaw case treated with a vibration-based surgical tool in a young child whose jaw joint had fused to the skull. Temporomandibular joint ankylosis locks the mouth shut, and in children early surgery prevents distorted facial growth. Their patient was a six-year-old girl with one-sided advanced bony fusion. Treatment used gap arthroplasty, which removes a block of fused bone to free movement, with a pad of cheek fat placed in the gap.

Cutting used a piezoelectric device, which slices bone with ultrasonic vibration while sparing soft tissue, giving finer control than rotary drills near vital structures. The same-side jaw projection was also removed to improve motion, and physiotherapy began early to hold the gain. At follow-up her mouth opened beyond twenty millimetres in the reported measurement, with good function, supporting the tool as a safer cutting option.
pmc-13500143:
Nawanon Chantaprasarn, Wiriya Loongyai, Sornthep Tumwasorn and Phongthorn Kongmun published this 2026 feeding trial on cassava factory leftovers as cattle feed. They tested ensiled total mixed fiber, a silage blend, made with cassava pulp or cassava bioethanol waste. The blends fully replaced guinea grass, the usual roughage, in diets for dairy cows that had recently calved and were giving milk.

Eighteen Holstein Friesian crossbred cows were split into three groups and fed for 90 days. Cows on the bioethanol-waste blend ate the most, reaching a dry matter intake of 15.6 kilograms a day, with higher energy intake than the grass group. Digestibility of the feed did not differ between groups. Milk makeup stayed the same across diets, while the cassava pulp blend showed a trend toward more milk, at 15.5 kilograms a day on average. The authors conclude the blends can replace grass without harming milk output.
pmc-13500443:
Xinzhao Zhao and co-authors map, in twenty twenty-six, the gene networks through which benzo[a]pyrene, a carcinogen in tobacco smoke and exhaust, may drive bladder cancer. They mined public gene expression data sets for genes changed by the compound. Network toxicology, machine learning, docking, dynamics simulations, and single-cell data were combined. Nineteen significant genes emerged, and seven were prioritized as key players. An explanation method ranked two genes, GSK3B and SKP2, as top contributors to the predictive model.

Single-cell data showed where those genes act in the tumor microenvironment. Simulations detailed how the compound binds its target proteins. The study names candidate mechanisms and therapeutic targets for this exposure-driven cancer.
pmc-13500643:
Zongyun Yang and co-authors propose in 2026 a hybrid forecasting network for the steep karst terrain of Guizhou in southwestern China, where mountains cover most of the province and wreck weather models. Local terrain effects and broad atmospheric dynamics must be captured together. Their design fuses a convolutional recurrent network, good at nearby patterns, with a transformer, good at long-range links, joined by a cross-attention module bridging space and time. A preprocessing pipeline splits jagged weather signals into steadier trend and seasonal parts.

Validated at 33 stations over a 51-year record, the model beat a standard recurrent baseline clearly in the reported tests. It cut temperature forecast error by roughly a fifth and precipitation error by more than a quarter, with a large gain on a precipitation skill score. Robust behaviour across half a century of data supports operational use in topographically complex regions facing flood and farming decisions.
pmc-13500843:
Anay Sinhal, Amit Sinhal, and Arpana Sinhal present a 2026 method for training chest X-ray classifiers across hospitals without moving patient images. Two problems meet here: privacy law blocks pooling raw scans, and models updated on new tasks tend to forget older findings. Their system, DP-FedEPC, combines federated averaging with elastic weight consolidation, which penalizes changes to weights that mattered for earlier tasks, and a small bank of class prototypes rather than stored images. Each hospital trains under differentially private stochastic gradient descent, which adds noise to protect individuals.

Training used CheXpert data, with outside checks on MIMIC-CXR. Beyond macro-AUROC accuracy, the authors report per-finding scores, forgetting scores, prototype geometry, failure cases, and a cost comparison with baselines. The design targets hospital settings where neither public substitute data nor image replay is acceptable.
pmc-13502743:
Chen and colleagues reported a woman in her late fifties whose stomach lymphoma cleared after bacteria-eradication drugs. Tests had shown no trace of the culprit bacterium. Their 2026 report concerns gastric MALT lymphoma, a slow lymph-system cancer normally driven by Helicobacter pylori. Guidelines differ on whether patients without the bacterium should try eradication first.

Biopsies confirmed lymphoma confined to the stomach lining, while breath and tissue tests for Helicobacter were negative, though one value sat near the cutoff. After discussion she received a fourteen-day, four-drug eradication regimen including an acid blocker and two antibiotics. Two months later she was symptom-free, scans were clean, and biopsies showed remission, maintained at six months. The authors suggest other helicobacter species, drug effects on tumor cells, or immune changes may explain the response. They argue a negative test alone should not rule out a trial.
pmc-13503143:
Meng-Chieh Lin leads a nine-author team with a 2026 Alzheimer's mechanism in which a kinase's phosphate tag turns a chaperone into an accomplice. The co-chaperone DNAJB6b partners with Hsp70 to keep the tau protein from clumping. Brain tissue from Alzheimer's patients showed more phosphate tags on DNAJB6b at tyrosine 53, inside its J-domain. The team traced the tag to YES, a Src kinase, and measured what the tag does to the chaperone's partnerships.

The tag strengthened DNAJB6b's binding to Hsp70. Oddly, the tighter partnership tracks with more tau aggregation, suggesting the complex mishandles tau disassembly, holding clients instead of clearing them. The finding reframes a piece of Alzheimer's failure to manage proteins: not a broken chaperone but a re-regulated one, activity dialled by kinase signalling. The authors propose the YES-DNAJB6b axis as a contributor to risk and point of attack.
pmc-13503743:
Asmita Singh leads a team studying how two cell-cleaning proteins shape the release of tiny parcels from cells, in a 2026 paper. The proteins, ATG9A and ATG2, supply fat-like parts for the sacs that clear waste inside cells. Those sacs can merge with other cell parts that shed parcels to the outside.

When the team deleted either protein, cells shed far more small parcels, and the parcels were smaller than usual. The flood depended on a known export protein. Under stress, normal cells loaded parcels with waste tags, while altered cells could not. Fat profiles inside the cells shifted a great deal, with more waxy fats stored. A drug that blocks one fat path brought parcel output back to normal.
pmc-13503943:
Ying Lu and three colleagues present a neural network that forecasts crypto token prices, in a 2026 paper. Token prices swing wildly and jump between calm and stormy phases, which breaks plain forecast tools. Data also comes from many streams that interact in tangled ways.

Their network joins 47 inputs, from chain activity and mood scores to broad economic gauges and chart patterns. An attention part reweighs inputs as market mood shifts, and a dropout trick gives uncertainty ranges with each forecast. Tests on six big coins from 2022 to 2025 gave mean errors under two percent for Bitcoin. The ranges covered the true price about 94 percent of the time. Mood and chain data ruled in stormy phases.
pmc-13504043:
Yongzhong Li leads a team reviewing the shifting roles of a long non-coding RNA called JPX across human cancers, in a 2026 paper. JPX helps switch on XIST, the RNA that shuts down one X chromosome in female cells. Reports on JPX in cancer have pointed in opposite directions.

Scanning studies to late 2025, the team found JPX mostly cast as a cancer promoter in ten tumor types, often by soaking up small RNAs that would otherwise brake growth genes. In liver, breast, and eye tumors, the record instead fits a growth-restraining role tied to XIST. Much of the proof rests on single studies with thin checks. The authors urge caution: JPX looks like a context-bound marker, not a proven drug target.
pmc-13504143:
Shawn S Goodman leads a team modeling how the inner ear's echo grows with sound level, in a 2026 paper. The echo, a faint tone the ear itself makes, reveals how healthy the cochlea is. Its growth curve shape shifts with the test setup, which clouds what the curve says about hearing.

Their method fits the curves with a hidden growth model borrowed from structural equation work. A smooth S-shaped curve stands in for the ear's hidden nonlinearity, while a linked fit handles noisy readings. Data from twelve young adult ears, plus simulated tests, showed the fit stayed sound when signals were weak. It also recovered standard curve traits like slope and threshold. The team aims the tool at future hearing diagnosis work.
pmc-13505043:
Hongyi Shen and Bo Zhang link early-onset diabetes to early high blood pressure and early death in U.S. adults, in a 2026 study. Both conditions are rising in younger people and shorten lives. Whether diabetes that starts young drives the other two was the question.

The team used a national health survey spanning six cycles, with more than twenty-two thousand people in the blood pressure analysis. Early diabetes went with more than four times the odds of early high blood pressure. In the death analysis, early diabetes tripled the hazard of dying before old age. Poverty level changed the strength of both links, and drinking habits changed the blood pressure link. The authors urge early, broad intervention for young diabetic patients.
pmc-13505143:
Dilek Hacıvelioğlu and colleagues surveyed 724 midwifery students across Turkey about empathy and attitudes toward migrants. Students answered an empathy tendency scale and a xenophobia scale in an online survey, along with questions about their background and training. The team looked for background factors tied to each attitude and for any link between the two.

Empathy scores varied with the university attended, citizenship, income, cross-cultural friendships, and experience caring for a foreign patient during training. Xenophobia scores varied with university, income, the kind of place students grew up in, family type, and whether they had taken a course on care across cultures. Surprisingly, empathy and xenophobia showed no clear association with each other. The findings give midwifery programmes concrete factors to work with when shaping training for work with migrant patients.
pmc-13506543:
Blair profiles rovadicitinib, sold as Anxu, in a 2026 first-approval review marking the drug's debut in China. Developed by Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group, the small molecule blocks two signalling enzymes at once, JAK and ROCK. That dual action is aimed at myelofibrosis, the marrow-scarring blood cancer that enlarges the spleen and drains patients with fatigue and weight loss. On 25 February 2026 it won approval as first-line treatment for adults with intermediate-2 or higher-risk disease, including cases arising after other blood disorders.

The review walks through the development milestones behind the decision, from the biology of the overactive JAK-STAT pathway that drives the disease to the clinical programme supporting registration. The same drug is being developed for graft-versus-host disease, the transplant complication where donor cells attack the recipient, and for a rare hyperinflammatory syndrome.
pmc-13507143:
Hanif Ullah leads a 2026 team that reports a bacterial enzyme able to turn non-edible plant oils into biodiesel under mild conditions. The bacterium came from waste-oil sites and was named Stenotrophomonas maltophilia strain HO5 by gene reading. Its fat-cutting enzyme, a lipase, was purified and tested on wild olive and taramira oils, which do not compete with food crops.

The enzyme kept full activity in methanol, a key reaction partner that often harms enzymes, yet a metal-binding blocker shut it down strongly. Product checks confirmed true biodiesel, with wild olive fuel led by methyl oleate at near half the mix. The natural methanol tolerance, without genetic tweaks, suits green fuel making.
pmc-13507943:
Tommaso Volpi leads an eleven-author team using brain scans to measure a key chemical receptor in people with schizophrenia, in work published in 2026. The receptor, called M1, sits in brain circuits tied to thinking and memory. Tissue studies after death had hinted at M1 shortages, and a newly approved drug pair acts partly through this receptor. The team used a new tracer with PET scanning to count M1 in living brains. Sixteen patients were matched with sixteen healthy volunteers by age and sex.

Patients showed clearly lower M1 levels across many brain regions, including the front and side cortex and deep structures. Drops ranged from about one eighth to nearly one fifth, depending on the region. A subgroup of patients showed much deeper losses across the whole brain. The findings back M1 as a drug target and a possible marker for sorting patients.
pmc-13508243:
Yavuz Selim Kahraman and three co-authors test whether simple blood inflammation scores can predict how hard a gallbladder operation will be, in 2026 work. Surgeons grade difficulty during keyhole gallbladder removal on the Parkland scale, from easy to severe. The team reviewed 1,054 patients who had planned surgery for gallstones between 2018 and 2025. Blood tests taken before surgery were turned into several inflammation ratios. Those scores were then matched against the grades given in the operating room.

Higher grades came with longer operations and more switches to open surgery. Three blood scores stood out as independent predictors of a high grade, along with type 2 diabetes. One score, the inflammatory burden index, sorted patients best, with the other two close behind. The authors suggest that cheap pre-surgery blood scores could warn teams to expect a hard case and plan staffing, time, and consent talks with patients accordingly.
pmc-13508343:
D Scognamiglio and four co-authors present MuSA, a software pipeline that labels genetic variants and ranks them for clinical meaning, in 2026 work. Reading a patient's variants means merging forecasts, population rates, and past case evidence from many sources. Older tool chains demand fiddly setup, spew hard-to-review output, and lean on one-off scripts. MuSA automates the whole path in a standard workflow system, with a light mode for routine diagnosis and a deep mode for full workups. It blends annotation tools, over twenty add-on predictors, and automated rule-based classification.

Output lands in tables with up to 920 data columns per variant, plus web reports matched to a patient's traits. On a test set of more than twenty-two thousand variants, deep annotation finished in about twenty minutes on a large server. The authors pitch MuSA as a way to make variant reading faster and reproducible.
pmc-13508443:
Paula Domínguez-del Olmo leads a thirteen-author protocol for testing whether machine learning tools that predict early preeclampsia dangers hold up in new hospitals, in 2026 work. This pregnancy disorder, arising before 34 weeks, can turn severe fast and drives early delivery and maternal deaths. The group's three earlier models predict mother complications, delivery within a week of diagnosis, and a dangerous syndrome pairing or placental separation. None had faced a true outside test. The new study runs across centers from 2024 to 2027 and enrolls diagnosed women who consent.

The first hundred cases will check the models head-on, with clinicians also rating case risk by eye. Those cases then retrain the models, and the updated tools are applied live to the next hundred women. Predictions are made through a secure web app and revealed only after delivery. The design treats validation as a loop, not a one-off stamp.
pmc-13508543:
Guang Xu, David Strom, and Sumathilatha Sakthi-Velavan test whether scores on in-class interactive quizzes predict final exam results in a first-year medical course, in 2026 work. The course covered heart, lung, and kidney systems and ran across two years with 156 and 160 students. Sessions opened and closed with low-stakes quizzes worth a small slice of the grade. The team related average quiz scores to final exam performance, then surveyed students split by final grade band about the experience.

Quiz scores tracked exam results with moderate to strong consistency in both years. The link was already visible by the sixth session, early enough to flag strugglers. Survey replies, though only a quarter of students answered, were broadly positive. Lower performers felt the quizzes helped their learning most. The authors suggest teachers can use early quiz patterns as an early-warning gauge, while easing the pressure middle students feel.
pmc-13508643:
Azahaf and colleagues report a 2026 study of breast implant illness, a set of body-wide symptoms some women link to silicone implants. One theory blames mast cell activation, an immune overreaction. The team measured two blood markers tied to mast cells and allergy, tryptase and total IgE, in 71 women before and about eight months after implant removal.

In the full group, neither marker changed significantly after removal. Subgroup checks by allergy history and by high starting IgE were also run to look for hidden patterns. The null result matters: if mast cells were driving symptoms through these pathways, removal should move the markers. It does not clear implants of blame, since symptoms were not the measure here, but it narrows the search for a mechanism and warns against selling marker-based tests to these patients.
pmc-13509943:
Liu and colleagues review in 2026 how lipid nanoparticles, tiny fat-based carriers, can deliver nucleic acid medicines through the moist linings of the lungs and gut. Such medicines, including mRNA and gene editing tools, face enzymes that chew them up, poor entry into cells, and fast clearance from the body.

The review explains design rules that help carriers slip through mucus, the sticky layer guarding these surfaces. Particles smaller than the local mucus mesh, near-neutral surface charge, and a soft coating that sheds at the right moment crossed mucus several times better than older charged designs. Remaining hurdles include tailoring carriers to diseased tissue. The authors propose AI-guided, personalized carriers that adapt to each site as a future direction.
pmc-13510143:
Pasvanis and colleagues charted in 2026 how a growth signal switches eye fibroblasts into scar-forming cells. The culprit is the myofibroblast, a contractile scar cell arising from Tenon's fibroblasts under the signal TGFβ. The team treated human Tenon's fibroblasts from three surgical patients with TGFβ1 for five days and profiled all gene activity.

They found 3,362 genes changed activity, with more switched down than up. Pathways involved covered scar-cell formation, TGFβ signalling, collagen and matrix organisation, cell identity change, and cell cycle control. Named genes rising included LDLRAD4, CDKN2B, FZD8, and MYOZ1, while SOD3 and LTBP4 fell, among others. The map gives drug hunters specific targets for anti-scarring therapy after glaucoma surgery. The authors present the dataset as a detailed characterisation of the transition.
pmc-13511443:
João N. A. Dias, Daniel A. Marinho, Luís B. Faíl, Konstantinos Papadimitriou, and Henrique P. Neiva compare three warm-up styles in elite water polo players, in 2026 work. Ten international-level athletes each completed a dryland warm-up, an in-water warm-up, and a combined version, in a shuffled order across sessions. After each warm-up they swam an intermittent shuttle test built for the sport, while distance, speed, lactate, heart rate, ear temperature, and felt effort were recorded.

Players covered far more distance after in-water and combined warm-ups than after dryland work. The two water options showed no clear gap. Body responses after the test mostly matched across conditions, though lactate ran higher later after the dryland warm-up. Heart rate, temperature, and felt effort showed no gaps. The authors say warm-ups should include pool time to prime repeated sprint swimming.
pmc-13511643:
Pengji Zhou and six co-authors use a plasma-based mutation method to breed a bacterium that breaks down an algal toxin faster, in 2026 work. The toxin, microcystin-LR, pollutes rich, bloom-prone lakes, and oxygen-free bacteria that degrade it often work slowly. Starting from a Citrobacter strain taken from Lake Taihu sediment, the team ran three rounds of mutation and screening.

The winning mutant cleared the toxin fourteen percent faster than its parent under oxygen-free conditions, and the gain held steady across repeated transfers. Genome re-reading found ten changed sites in genes tied to cell wall building, movement sensing, and other jobs. Activity checks showed genes for sulfur handling, wall synthesis, and adaptation switched higher. The authors say the method shows multi-gene tuning can lift toxin cleanup for lake repair.
pmc-13512343:
Chia-Yen Hsu and four colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare cause of pain near the sitting bone. Pain in that area is most often blamed on hamstring injury or an inflamed bursa. A tear in part of the adductor magnus muscle, deep in the thigh, is easy to miss.

Their patient was a 63-year-old woman whose back thigh pain began after sprinting and grew worse when she sat. High-detail ultrasound scans showed a partial tear where the muscle meets the bone, plus swelling and fluid nearby. Step-by-step scan views found the tear, and care without surgery was planned. The case shows ultrasound can catch this uncommon injury.
pmc-13512443:
Nahyun Kim, Jooyeon Park, In Deok Kong, Tonda L. Hughes, and Dae-Kwang Kim compare mitochondrial DNA patterns and white cell telomere length in teenage boys with and without internet gaming addiction, in 2026 work. Questionnaires sorted 206 male adolescents into addiction and comparison groups. Blood tests measured repeat patterns in two control regions of the mitochondrial genome, mitochondrial copy number, and telomere length, the cap that shortens as cells age.

One repeat pattern at the first region was rarer in the addiction group and at first looked protective in adjusted models, yet the link faded after strict correction for many tests. Mitochondrial copy number did not differ between groups. Telomeres ran clearly shorter in the addiction group, above all in boys carrying either of two repeat patterns, and addiction stayed tied to shorter telomeres after adjustment. The authors call the gene link preliminary and the telomere link the firmer signal.
pmc-13512543:
Mingxuan Yao, Yuhao Chu, and Xiaokang Dai survey a whole family of potassium transporters across eight oilseed rape varieties, in 2026 work. These HAK/KUP/KT proteins pull potassium into cells and help plants handle salt and other stress. Earlier catalogs leaned on single genomes, missing variety-level differences. The team found 269 family members in total and sorted them by how widely each branch is shared across the eight genomes.

Family trees split the proteins into four large clades shared with model plants. Most branches evolved under purifying selection, which trims harmful change, while variety-specific branches varied more freely. Gene shapes, shared motifs, and promoter switches were mapped, and expression data showed tissue, hormone, and stress responses. Blending those clues with salt-tolerance data flagged one locus near salt-linked variation as the top candidate for breeding work.
pmc-13516243:
Mihal and colleagues test isorhamnetin, a plant flavonoid (a natural compound found in foods such as sea buckthorn and onions), on human ovarian cells in a 2026 laboratory study of female reproduction. Earlier work credits the compound with antioxidant and anticancer effects, but its influence on the ovary was poorly known. The team treated three cell lines: normal granulosa cells, which support egg development, a granulosa tumor line, and an ovarian cancer line.

Cells received isorhamnetin doses from 5 to 80 micrograms per milliliter for 24 hours before the team measured survival, hormone output, and signaling proteins. Viability fell steadily as the dose rose, and the two cancer lines proved more sensitive than the normal granulosa cells. The researchers also tracked progesterone and estradiol secretion, plus growth factors linked to cell survival and programmed cell death. Their results map where the compound helps or harms ovarian tissue.
pmc-13518843:
Jae Ryong Song leads a very large team reporting the AURA Korea study in 2026 on SB15, a biosimilar copy of the eye drug aflibercept sold as Afilivu. Injections that block blood vessel growth treat several retinal diseases, and cheaper biosimilars could widen access. Real-world proof across diseases was still thin.

Records covered 1,083 eyes from 984 patients at three South Korean centers, most switching from the original drug. Retinal thickness fell by an average of 47.5 micrometers while vision held stable over about five months. Treatment-naive eyes improved more than switchers. Fluid cleared significantly in macular degeneration, vein occlusion, and diabetic swelling groups, with only one serious event noted.
pmc-13518943:
Ziyang Ren and colleagues tracked frailty, low mood, and thinking decline in older adults to see how they foreshadow Parkinson disease. Published in 2026, the study followed 49,039 people aged fifty and over in a large European ageing survey, finding 624 new Parkinson cases over up to nine years. A second English ageing survey supplied a check on patterns before diagnosis.

Physical frailty more than doubled the risk of later Parkinson disease, while severe low mood and severe thinking problems each raised risk by roughly two thirds to nearly double. Risk climbed highest when all three problems struck together or when a person worsened across all three domains, while recovery toward better health lowered risk. People heading toward diagnosis also slipped faster beforehand, with a sharp worsening near diagnosis itself. The work backs repeated checks across body, mood, and mind to sharpen early risk grading.
pmc-13519443:
Hemadri S and colleagues tested how far a curing light can sit from a braces bracket before the bond weakens. Published in 2026, the lab study bonded brackets to two hundred premolar teeth, varying both bracket type and light-tip distance from zero to fifteen millimeters. Bracket types covered stainless steel, polycarbonate, and two ceramic forms, and bond strength was measured with a universal testing machine.

Bonds were strongest with the light tip touching the bracket and fell steadily as distance grew. Steel and ceramic brackets kept clinically adequate strength across the range, while polycarbonate brackets faded at greater distances. Both material and distance mattered, so the authors urge clinicians to keep the light tip as close as possible. Readers get a simple chairside rule with numbers behind it.
pmc-13519543:
Alymkulova and co-authors investigated a 2026 signalling molecule, CXCL14, in muscle regeneration, where stem cells must fuse into new fibres. Fusion repairs damaged muscle throughout life and is steered by growth factors and cytokines, small immune messenger proteins. The team worked with mouse muscle stem cells and the C2C12 myoblast cell line.

CXCL14 significantly enhanced myocyte fusion in their cell experiments, a key step in building mature muscle fibres. Tracing the mechanism, Alymkulova showed the molecule switches on a pathway running through focal adhesion kinase to the enzyme ERK5. Neighbouring support cells called fibro-adipogenic progenitors proved to be the main source of CXCL14 in muscle tissue. The findings cast this support to stem cell signalling as a positive regulator worth exploiting in regeneration research.
pmc-13520143:
Ming Jin, Yongping Lu, Jing Yang, and Zhiqiang Wang profile Traditional Chinese Medicine nursing skills in 2026 among clinical nurses at a Chinese tertiary hospital. Demand for joined-up long-term care is rising, and ward leads need to know where TCM nursing competence sits. Valid questionnaires from 457 nurses fed a latent profile analysis.

Overall self-rated skill was moderate, stronger on TCM techniques and weaker on advanced clinical practice. Three profiles emerged: low at 12.3 percent, moderate at 64.3 percent, and high at 23.4 percent of nurses. Schooling level, willingness to train, and felt importance of training steadily predicted a place in higher profiles. Jin's team urges tiered training aimed at real ward use, while noting self-reports measure perception, not proven skill.
pmc-13521143:
Dongming Qi and colleagues catalogue in 2026 drug resistance genes inside gut microbes of free-range chickens across four Chinese provinces. Outdoor birds meet people and soil microbes closely, so their gut may shuttle resistance widely.

Faecal sampling covered 120 birds, yielding more than two thousand reconstructed microbe genomes across 660 species. Detected resistance copies numbered in the hundreds of thousands, spanning 159 genes and 35 drug classes. Regional patterns varied sharply with environment and farming habits. Mobile DNA pieces averaged about 34 per genome and tracked with resistance load. Certain E. coli and Klebsiella genomes carried hundreds of resistance and virulence genes.
pmc-13521943:
Chin-Yun Lee and colleagues grow in 2026 feather-light gels made from gas alone. Solid mixes are turned to vapour first. The vapour then forms a gel coat on surfaces. Such gels may serve in insulation and health care. Older liquid routes limit shapes and added extras.

The gas route coats complex shapes in an even layer. It takes in varied added extras in one step. Trial gels held living cells, stored gases, or mixed parts. Cell gels kept stem cells alive and able to grow into spheres. Gas gels tuned uptake and release. Final gels were very light, mostly air, with huge surface area.
pmc-13522343:
Abdoljalil Kalantar-Hormozi and colleagues survey in 2026 diet and food access among mothers in Iran whose infants have facial clefts. Mothers joined at a Tehran referral hospital in 2019 and 2020. Diet in pregnancy may shape cleft risk, so intake and home food access both matter.

Poor intake was widespread in the group. Iron fell short in about nine of ten mothers. Vitamins D and A, folate and calcium also fell short often. B12 shortfall split by cleft type, with palate cases hit harder. Hunger peaked near 43 percent in the joint lip and palate group. Cleft severity rose step by step with food stress in all models.
pmc-13522443:
Zhen Cui and co-authors work on automatic pain assessment for intensive care patients in a 2026 study built around facial movements. Video was recorded from sixty-one patients at rest, during daily care, and during procedures known to cause pain. A detection system measured facial action units, meaning small, defined movements of facial muscles linked to expressions.

Six action units selected by the team outperformed the units used in a widely used facial pain scale on accuracy and related measures. Models that learned patterns over time further supported the chosen combination. The authors argue that pairing these facial signals with temporal deep learning could make pain monitoring in intensive care more reliable, especially for patients unable to report pain themselves.
pmc-13523243:
Chilochibi Chiziba and co-authors propose a new way to group areas for malaria control in Zambia in a 2026 study. Malaria is unevenly spread across small health facility catchment areas, and current targeting uses incidence alone. Data from 2017 to 2024, drawn from the national health system and public sources, covered environment, access, disease patterns, and social conditions at catchment level.

A statistical model picked out significant drivers, including walking time to a facility, shares of cases in pregnant women and young children, bednet coverage and use, elevation, vegetation, rainfall, and housing quality. Clustering produced four area archetypes that stayed more stable over time than incidence-only grouping. The authors recommend embedding these archetypes into stratification so that interventions can be tailored to each area's defining features.
pmc-13523343:
Celal Sayilir and Emre Ilker evaluate Anatolian safflower germplasm under Mediterranean winter growing conditions in a 2026 field study. Sixteen local genotypes and five registered cultivars were grown over two seasons and scored for agronomic traits, oil content, and fatty acid composition. Safflower is valued as a resilient oilseed for dry regions, yet local material was poorly characterized.

Genotypes varied significantly on most traits. One accession led on seed and oil yield, another held the highest oil content, and a third stood out for linoleic acid, while two cultivars led on oleic acid. Statistical analysis showed the balance between those two fatty acids, together with yield traits, drove most variation, cleanly separating high-oleic from high-linoleic material. The authors offer the collection as breeding stock for Mediterranean oil quality and productivity.
pmc-13523443:
Babatunde Ishola Gabriel Adejumo leads a large author group in a 2026 systematic review on whether islet autoantibodies can predict who will develop type 1 diabetes, with special attention to Africa. These antibodies signal immune attack on insulin-producing beta cells. Early identification of high-risk people is a public health priority, yet evidence from African populations has rarely been gathered together.

Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, the team searched four major databases for studies from 2000 to 2026 and included 47 studies in qualitative synthesis. Eight addressed African populations or African diabetes patterns, and a smaller comparable subset entered quantitative pooling. Across studies, higher antibody levels and positivity for several antibodies at once were consistently linked with later disease. The review discusses what screening would require in African health systems.
pmc-13523543:
Glaser and co-authors mapped breast cancer rates in 2026 across Ohio counties sitting above the Great Miami Buried Valley Aquifer, a large underground water source. They asked whether communities drawing water from this aquifer show higher cancer incidence than state and national averages. The study is ecological, meaning it compares whole county rates rather than measuring what any individual woman was exposed to.

Montgomery County stood out with an incidence of 141.4 cases per hundred thousand people, above the Ohio rate of 132.3 and the national rate of 130.8 per hundred thousand, roughly eight percent higher than the country overall. Other counties over the aquifer showed smaller elevations. Because the analysis uses county-level proxies rather than personal exposure data, the authors cannot prove the aquifer caused the pattern. They frame the results as a reason for closer environmental and health monitoring in the region.
pmc-13523843:
Yuan Tao and others benchmark, in a 2026 review, how regression modeling choices affect how plant medicine extraction is tuned. Teams often pick models by goodness of fit alone, which can mislead choices about how to run the process. The team built its datasets from systematic screening of past papers.

The benchmark used 1,148 extraction datasets and tested seven models, from full quadratic regression and leaner subset models to ridge, support vector, partial least squares, and Gaussian process methods. Checks covered fitting, leave-one-out testing, behavior, and stability of predicted best conditions. Leaner parsimonious regression models gave the most balanced profile. Some machine learning models cut training error without better checked prediction or stability. The authors argue model choice itself adds doubt and should be judged as a choice in its own right.
pmc-13525643:
Hamidreza Badeli, Mahsa Motiei, Azita Tangestani Nejad, and Afagh Hassanzadeh-Rad pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, how common chronic kidney disease is after heart surgery in childhood. Survival after pediatric cardiac surgery has improved, shifting attention to long-term kidney harm. Scattered studies left the true burden unclear.

Searches of three databases through March 2025 found five prospective studies with 1,002 patients, published between 2016 and 2022 in France, Canada, Belgium, and the United States. Pooled prevalence of chronic kidney disease was 16 percent, with moderate variation between studies, and sensitivity checks left the estimate stable. The authors call for long-term kidney monitoring in this group, plus better studies using standardized definitions and longer follow-up before the figure can be refined.
pmc-13526643:
Rachel Morgan and a team of co-authors study early lead exposure and the brain in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Lead exposure in early life is a suspected contributor to dementia, which involves amyloid beta plaques and disturbed metabolism. The team tested that link in mice.

Female mice got lead in drinking water during pregnancy and nursing, and offspring were checked at three weeks and eighteen months. Exposed mice had more diffuse amyloid beta and more positive cells in the cortex at old age. Chemical profiles in blood and brain shifted toward markers of oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipid changes. The authors say developmental lead may raise dementia risk through these routes.
pmc-13527043:
Imara and nine co-authors study an immune switch on tumor-linked white cells in brain tumors in this twenty twenty-six paper. The tumors are a fast, harsh type with bleak odds and wide gaps in how long patients live. The switch sits in the body guard system and shapes how immune cells act near a tumor.

Inside, the team checked tumor samples from one hundred fourteen patients for levels of the switch. Tumors with high levels held a mixed set of white cell types, not one plain type. Patients with high levels lived longer on the whole, even after age and care traits were weighed. The authors say the link is a clue, not proof, and needs fresh tests.
pmc-13527143:
Olivia Surgent leads a large team in a 2026 longitudinal study of what predicts spoken vocabulary growth in autistic children. Many autistic children speak late, affecting communication during key developmental windows. Brain and behavior predictors had usually been studied separately, so the team measured both together in 122 children first seen between ages two and four.

Children were grouped by starting vocabulary size, and nearly half fell in the smaller group spanning emergent and non-speaking children. Within that group, faster vocabulary growth over about two years tracked with stronger early fine motor skills, better joint attention, and lower white-matter coherence in three specific tracts. Models combining brain and behavior predicted growth best, explaining roughly half the variation. The authors argue early brain scanning adds predictive value beyond behavior alone.
pmc-13527343:
Martje Van Neste and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on iodine levels in human milk after a mother took high doses of potassium iodide. Iodine is a normal and needed part of milk. The mother took the drug to prepare for thyroid surgery while breastfeeding, and infant exposure in such cases was poorly studied.

Milk samples were gathered during treatment and for months after it stopped, then measured with a precise mass method. Iodine levels in milk were very high during dosing but fell fast once dosing ended, returning to the normal range within about a week. Feeding was paused during treatment and partly resumed after. The study gives rare direct data to guide care for nursing mothers who need this drug.
pmc-13527943:
Zichen Wu and five colleagues report a 2026 animal study testing whether a gut bacterium, Parabacteroides distasonis, can protect weaned piglets against diarrhea caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli, a major killer of young pigs. The bacterium was isolated from Ningxiang piglets, a Chinese breed known for low diarrhea rates, and given to piglets challenged with the pathogen.

Treated piglets lost less weight and had fewer bouts of diarrhea, with fewer pathogen cells colonizing the gut lining. Inflammatory signals in the small intestine fell, protective antibody levels rose, and the proteins sealing the gut wall were strengthened. The bacterium also shifted gut microbe communities toward helpful species and raised short-chain fatty acid levels, supporting its use as a feed-based defense.
pmc-13528043:
Alexandra Brentani and eleven colleagues test a support package for Brazil's national home visiting program in a 2026 feasibility trial. The program, Criança Feliz, visits families to boost early child development. Past reviews found no fixed curriculum, thin training, and weak supervision. The trial ran in eight varied municipalities.

The package added forty hours of hands-on training for visitors. Supervisors got eight hours of their own training. Standard visit guides and an activity book came with it. Home visit quality scores rose by about fifteen points after the package. Families and staff rated the changes highly acceptable and workable. Suggested tweaks included matching activities to each child's level and shortening training. The authors draw lessons for home visiting programs elsewhere.
pmc-13529643:
Pankaj Deka and thirteen colleagues detect parrot bornavirus in captive parrots across India in a 2026 study. The virus causes a wasting disease that swells the stomach organ. Eighty-three birds from thirteen species were tested. Groups covered sick birds, healthy cage mates, and dead birds with past suspicion of the disease. Swabs and tissues went through gene testing.

Forty-four birds, about fifty-three percent, carried the virus. Dead birds tested positive most often, at about eighty-eight percent. Sick live birds hit about fifty-five percent. Healthy mates still reached about nineteen percent. Gene reading named the strain as PaBV-4. The authors call this the first report of its spread in Indian captive parrots. Endangered species bred in captivity face real risk, they warn. Screening should enter breeding programs.
pmc-13530843:
Bram and the PLUTO Study Group present in 2026, as conference poster 18, a multicenter check on knee ligament reconstruction in pre-pubertal children. It asks whether the surgery bends the growing leg out of alignment. The two operations studied both deliberately avoid the growth plates.

The prospective cohort compared 77 children who had the modified MacIntosh reconstruction, which uses the iliotibial band, with 35 who had an all-epiphyseal reconstruction. Alignment films were taken about a year after surgery. No alignment measure differed between the techniques, and the between-leg changes were generally tiny. Yet about a third of children in each group shifted at least one alignment zone, and up to a fifth shifted a key angle by five degrees or more. Three children developed growth disturbances needing monitoring or corrective surgery, all after the MacIntosh operation.
pmc-13531743:
Faris A Alshahrani and colleagues test in 2026 how cleaning methods affect the bending strength of 3D-printed denture plastic. Two printed resins formed 200 bar samples split among water storage, cleanser tablets, microwave, ultraviolet light, and ultrasonic cleaning. Strength was measured after 90 and 180 days of each routine.

Cleanser tablets weakened both resins at both time points. Microwave and ultrasonic cleaning also cut strength by the later check in most cases. Ultraviolet light preserved strength best, holding steady across the full period for one resin. The authors favor light-based cleaning for printed dentures.
pmc-13532243:
Faridath Massou and nine colleagues published this 2026 study testing whether tuberculosis gene variants of uncertain meaning actually confer drug resistance. Genome sequencing flags many mutations in genes tied to four TB drugs, but the World Health Organization catalogue calls most uncertain or harmless. The team took isolates from the DIAMA cohort in sub-Saharan Africa, from patients never treated with these drugs, and measured drug response in the lab.

Of 1,475 sequenced isolates, 89 carrying variants were tested by broth microdilution. For bedaquiline and clofazimine, only variants in the mmpR5 gene pushed response past the resistance threshold; variants in three other genes did not. For delamanid and pretomanid, variants rarely produced resistance-level results, though they often appeared in mixed bacterial samples. Protein stability modelling showed no clear link to the lab results. The authors conclude most uncertain variants showed no resistance under their test conditions.
pmc-13533843:
Xiaochen Dai and colleagues re-examined alcohol's health effects with a conservative, cross-outcome method. Published in 2026, the Burden of Proof study ran sixteen systematic reviews across four databases, re-analyzing 843 cohort and case-control studies for twenty health outcomes. Drinking guidelines differ widely, leaving drinkers unsure what intake, if any, counts as safe.

Current drinking tracked higher risks for ten cancers plus pancreatitis, cirrhosis and other liver disease, lung infections, tuberculosis, and atrial fibrillation. For type 2 diabetes, dementia, and several heart and stroke outcomes, risks dipped at low-to-moderate intake before rising, forming J- or U-shaped curves. High intake raised risk across every outcome. The authors offer a single comparable evidence base for guidelines, with observational limits acknowledged.
pmc-13534143:
Hua and co-authors fabricated a 2026 granular hydrogel dressing for infected wounds, where bacteria stall healing and lock tissue in inflammation. Their green method mixes a synthetic prepolymer with tannic acid, a natural plant polyphenol, which triggers self assembly into grains without extra crosslinkers. Agarose was added in steps to probe how the structure forms.

More agarose gradually flattened the grains into a sheet network, so the lowest agarose mix keeping the granular form was selected. That version, A/MP@TA3, killed bacteria strongly, quenched oxidative stress, and sped skin cell migration in Hua's laboratory tests. In infected animal wounds it accelerated closure while boosting collagen deposition and new blood vessel growth. Released tannic acid reprogrammed immune cells toward a healing type by activating a protective pathway and suppressing an inflammatory one.
pmc-13534643:
Carmen Pisano and colleagues simulate in 2026 at atomic scale how a magnetic field changes the A2A adenosine receptor, a cell sensor tied to inflammation. Pulsed field therapy raises receptor numbers on cell surfaces, yet the physical reason was unclear. Computer models used a steady field as a stand-in for the slow part of therapy pulses.

The field mainly reshaped the outer region of the receptor, opening the entry path for binding partners. The entrance widened and took in more water, and three key residues swung their electric orientation. Readers gain a physical account that fits lab findings on field effects.
pmc-13536243:
Kentie and colleagues untangle why lesser black-backed gulls shun an offshore wind farm. Do the turbines repel them? Or does restricted fishing inside the farm simply remove the discarded fish they love to scavenge? Their 2026 study GPS-tracked 58 breeding gulls and compared where they flew against both turbine locations and fishing vessel activity. It exploited the fact that fishing runs heavily on weekdays and rests at weekends.

At population level the gulls avoided the wind farm through most of the season while actively selecting areas with fishing. The avoidance did not melt away at weekends, when the fishing explanation would predict re-entry. The authors read that as genuine turbine avoidance. Individuals varied a lot, though: several males were actually attracted to the farm during and after breeding.
pmc-13540443:
Ran You and colleagues trace a kidney injury pathway in a 2026 study. A protein called WWP2 harms the filtering cells of the kidney. The setting is lupus nephritis, the kidney complication of lupus. Lupus itself is an autoimmune disease. Damage to these podocyte cells lets protein leak into urine.

WWP2 levels rose in the kidney filters of patients. The rise matched how much protein each patient lost. Lowering WWP2 in lupus-prone mice eased the leakage. Raising it did the reverse. The protein tags a histone, H2A, at one specific site. That tagging disturbs the cell's inner actin skeleton. A new WWP2 blocker cut protein in the urine of nephritic mice.
pmc-13542143:
Begizew Golla and colleagues run a field trial in 2026. The crop is maize in western Ethiopia. Nine improved varieties faced acidic soil. Acidity quietly caps yields there and threatens food security. Breeding has usually tested varieties on good soil only. This trial asked which varieties tolerate acid.

Plots at Bako grew each variety at two acidity levels. Blocks were replicated for fairness. Acid soil hurt every variety in the trial. Losses still differed widely between varieties. Three varieties lost the least yield. They were BH5211, BH661, and BH547. Their yields also stayed stable across both soils. BHQPY545 lost the most under acid stress.
pmc-13542243:
Danial Fotros and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study linking how strongly a person's diet and lifestyle raise insulin levels to their odds of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. All participants had type 2 diabetes, a group where this liver condition is especially common. Diet and habits were captured with validated questionnaires and converted into four scores covering eating patterns and wider lifestyle, each scored for both insulin release and insulin resistance.

People in the highest quarter for the insulin-resistance diet score had notably higher odds of the liver condition, with an odds ratio near 7.8 in the fully adjusted analysis. The lifestyle score for high insulin release gave a similar figure near 8, while one diet score showed no clear link. The authors argue that eating patterns chosen to calm insulin demand may help prevent liver complications in diabetes care.
pmc-13542443:
E Sarmikasoglou and colleagues published a 2026 feeding trial on corn silage made from a short-stature corn hybrid carrying the brachytic2 mutation, which makes plants shorter and sturdier than tall conventional corn. Lactating Holstein cows received silage from either the short hybrid or a tall one, at high or low dietary fibre levels. The team tracked feed intake, milk output, how completely nutrients were digested, and greenhouse gas emissions.

Cows on the short-hybrid silage ate more and produced more energy-corrected milk than cows on tall-hybrid silage, with the advantage largest in the high-fibre diet. Low-fibre diets raised intake and milk yield but lowered feed efficiency, and they cut methane output per cow and per unit of feed. Methane did not differ between corn hybrids. The short hybrid therefore improved cow performance without a methane penalty in this trial.
pmc-13542943:
Xi Lin and colleagues published a 2026 animal study testing nanovesicles from honeysuckle, Lonicera japonica, as a treatment for acute lung injury. These tiny plant-derived sacs were isolated and given to mice whose lungs had been injured with a bacterial toxin. Much of the damage in this condition comes from neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA that white blood cells throw out and that can harm lung tissue when produced excessively.

The vesicles gathered in lung neutrophils, and treated mice kept their weight and activity better while lung injury eased. Inflammatory signals fell, fewer neutrophils crowded the lungs, and fewer traps formed. Markers suggested the vesicles calmed a self-digestion process in cells that feeds trap formation. When a drug that forces trap release was added, the benefit vanished, supporting the proposed mechanism. Plant nanovesicles aimed at the lung could become a new treatment direction, though human testing lies ahead.
pmc-13543543:
Tao Luo's team published a 2026 study combining an approved iron medicine, ferumoxytol, with a gene-silencing therapy to kill acute myeloid leukaemia cells by ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. The gene target, GBA, maintains the chemistry of lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments; blocking it leaks iron that fuels the death process. Their plasmid was designed to switch on mainly where NF-kappaB, a signalling protein overactive in this leukaemia, is already active, sparing normal cells.

In laboratory tests the iron particles amplified the silencing effect greatly, and markers plus microscopy confirmed ferroptosis as the killing route. Mice carrying the leukaemia lived significantly longer on the combination, with no obvious harm to organs, blood counts, or liver and kidney tests. Turning a tumour's own signalling addiction into the trigger for its destruction is the elegant core of the approach.
pmc-13545043:
Sanjana Parikh and colleagues published a 2026 modelling study of vedolizumab, a gut-selective antibody drug for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, asking how inflammation severity changes the drug's path through the body. Exposure varies with disease activity because the drug is consumed by binding its target. Their physiologically based model, built in a standard simulation platform, included that target-mediated disposal and was first checked against healthy-volunteer data.

The model reproduced observed blood levels closely across a wide dose range in healthy adults, with predicted-to-observed ratios mostly between eight- and eleven-tenths. For patients, the team let the amount of target rise with inflammation, as the biology dictates, and predictions for mild-to-moderate colitis again landed near the observed values. A verified model of this kind can forecast dosing in sicker patients before trials enrol them, the authors argue.
pmc-13545143:
Patricia Grant led a 2026 evaluation of a self-guided eye movement training program for adults who have lost central vision. Thirty-three people with retinal disease and a documented blind spot in central vision enrolled, training two hours a week for eight weeks. Twenty-five trained in a clinic, while eight used the same platform at home.

Reading speed, measured with standard low vision charts, rose by about 23 words per minute on average, a gain near 55 percent. Home users improved about as much as clinic users, which suggests the program can reach people who cannot travel for rehabilitation. Vision, mood, and self-reported function were also tracked before and after training.
pmc-13546543:
Qin Deng and colleagues reported in 2026 on adding the targeted drug apatinib to standard chemotherapy after surgery for stage III stomach cancer. The study covered 112 patients whose tumors showed high levels of VEGFR-2, the molecule apatinib blocks, treated at one Chinese hospital between 2015 and 2021. Fifty-seven received apatinib plus the two-drug SOX regimen, while 55 received SOX alone.

Patients on the combined treatment stayed free of disease far longer, with five-year disease-free survival near 63 percent against 32 percent for chemotherapy alone, and overall survival showed a similar gap. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate in both groups. Because treatment was not assigned randomly, the authors call for a large randomized trial to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13547343:
Shion Masuda and colleagues tested in 2026 whether simply limiting how far the shinbone slides forward after a torn knee ligament can protect the joint's sense of position. The torn ligament normally carries tiny sensors that report joint movement, and surgery restores stability better than it restores that sensing. Rats were split into sham surgery, ligament cut, and ligament cut plus an internal suture brace that controlled the sliding.

Braced rats kept better balance beam performance and healthier-looking sensors at the ligament's attachment points, while unbraced injured rats lost coordination and grew more abnormal sensors. Sensor counts tracked behavior closely, supporting their role in recovery. The authors suggest bracing-style control as a foundation for treatments focused on function, not structure alone.
pmc-13548143:
Nawal Tahir and a large team compare two sedative drugs for older patients who need a gut scope test. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Sedation keeps the patient calm and helps the test go well. Propofol is long in use, while remimazolam is newer and may be safer for the old.

They pool trials that set the two drugs head to head in older adults. Low blood pressure, the main harm checked, came far less often with the new drug. Slow heart rate, low breathing, and pain at the shot site were also less common. Wake-up time and sickness rates were much the same. More strong trials are still called for.
pmc-13548543:
Natasha Beer and colleagues review how injury from transvaginal mesh affects women's sexual lives and relationships, in a 2026 systematic review. Mesh once commonly treated pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence, yet it left many women with chronic pain and lasting harm. The authors searched five databases plus grey literature and combined findings thematically from nine reports covering roughly fifteen hundred women.

Seven themes emerged, covering pain-driven changes in sexual function, shifts in sexuality and self-image, strained relationship satisfaction, and altered roles between partners. A central theme tied these together as a disrupted sense of the sexual and relational self. Most reports rated high in quality. The authors note that psychological flexibility may soften relationship distress, and they call for research that can shape proper support and therapy for injured women.
pmc-13548643:
Yanting Chen and colleagues hunt for what predicts lingering neck pain after front-of-neck spine fusion surgery, in a 2026 risk factor study.
