Axial pain is a recognized nuisance after this operation, though it is more often blamed on back-of-neck surgery. The team reviewed patients operated between 2020 and 2023, comparing imaging measurements of neck curve, disc height, and joint spacing between those who developed the pain and those who did not.

About one in six single-level patients and one in five multi-level patients reported the pain. For single-level surgery, how much the facet joint gap changed after surgery predicted trouble, with a clear cutoff value. For multi-level surgery, the size of the change in neck curve was the culprit. The authors advise surgeons to disturb joint spacing less in short fusions and to avoid over-correcting the curve in longer ones.
pmc-13549343:
Nanrui Yang and colleagues propose flipping the polarization of synchrotron light thousands of times per second, in a 2026 accelerator physics paper. Their trick is to wiggle a magnetic field. The work targets the planned Hefei Advanced Light Facility. Experiments that probe magnetism in materials need rapid alternation between polarization states, yet mechanically shifting magnet arrays is slow, and workarounds with twin devices are bulky and costly.

The proposal adds electromagnetic coils to the undulator, the magnet array that makes the beam. Wiggling its field directly switches polarization at kilohertz rates. The paper lays out the design against the landscape of existing strategies, from hybrid magnet devices at other facilities to beamline switching schemes that pick between two beams. The authors argue source-level switching promises cleaner, faster results for magnetic spectroscopy at the new site.
pmc-13549443:
Tomoki Tanabe and co-authors name in 2026 a new species of gut bacterium found in human feces. The genus Anaerostipes is known for making butyrate, a food for the gut lining. The strain came from a healthy adult during a broad effort to culture gut microbes.

Gene comparisons placed the strain inside the genus but well apart from every known species. Its body chemistry, enzyme set, and narrow range of usable sugars also set it apart. The authors name it Anaerostipes stercorihominis and deposit the type strain in two collections. Along the way they found two named species that look identical by gene measures, and propose merging them.
pmc-13550443:
Mohammed Jamal Mohammed, Javad Rahmani-Fard, and Ali Mohammed Ridha design a silent, sensor-free controller for a hybrid electric motor used in vehicles and industry, in a 2026 engineering paper. The machine needs rotor position to run well, but physical sensors add cost and fragility, while the usual signal-injection trick whines and wastes energy. Their scheme estimates position from the motor's own electrical ripple at low speed, using an adaptive flux observer. At higher speed it hands over to an improved model-based estimator through a smooth weighting curve.

On a six hundred watt prototype, low-speed position error stayed under two and a half degrees with no injection noise. The handover bump shrank, torque ripple fell by more than half across the speed range, and speed sag under sudden loads dropped by over sixty percent compared with the conventional hybrid. Stability proofs accompany the experiments.
pmc-13550543:
Victoria Paredes-Orejudo and colleagues read the sugar decorations on antibodies to tell apart critical illnesses and guess their course, in a 2026 biomarker study. Sepsis and severe COVID-19 both fill intensive care units, and who will crash is hard to foresee. The sugars attached to immunoglobulin G steer immune behavior, so the team profiled them in healthy volunteers, sepsis patients, and COVID-19 patients, splitting the last group by whether they survived.

Chromatography and mass spectrometry revealed distinct sugar patterns linked to which disease a patient had. Within the COVID-19 group, particular structures also tracked survival outcome. pmc-13555943:

pmc-13558343:

pmc-13558643:

pmc-13559643:

pmc-13568043:

pmc-13570443:

pmc-13572443:

pmc-13572543:

pmc-13573343:

pmc-13574143:

pmc-13613443:
Nisha Makani and colleagues built a supercapacitor electrode composite in 2026. Supercapacitors store charge very quickly. Two-dimensional MXene sheets offer large surfaces. A conducting polymer adds further capacitance. The MXene here holds two transition metals.

The base sheet came from a MAX phase. Polymer was integrated in tuned amounts. A full device was then assembled. It used the composite as positive electrode. Capacitance and energy density were high. Power density was also strong. Results point to efficient storage uses. Flexible electrodes are a further promise. Charge storage gains were the headline result.
pmc-13616743:
Lukas Thiele and colleagues watch a chemical messenger called cGMP at work inside tiny blood vessels of living mice, using a glowing indicator protein that shifts its light when the messenger rises. cGMP relaxes arteriole walls and is made when nitric oxide from the vessel lining switches on an enzyme, while other enzymes, called phosphodiesterases, destroy it. The team imaged vessels in the thin muscle of anaesthetised mice and bathed them in nitric oxide donors and acetylcholine, with and without blockers of the destroying enzymes.

Two nitric oxide donors raised the glow quickly and in step with dose, by 4.0 percent at a mid dose, and the signal faded slowly after washing. Blocking the maker enzyme confirmed the glow meant cGMP. Mice lacking that enzyme showed how vessel widening depends on it. Live readings like these separate the roles of making and breaking the messenger in real time.
pmc-13617543:
Md Asik Uzzaman Asa and seven colleagues turn groundnut shell waste into a treated biochar that pulls methyl violet dye out of wastewater. The shells, already extracted once with methanol, were functionalized with tartaric acid to load their surfaces with oxygen-rich groups that attract dye molecules. Microscopy, spectroscopy, and charge measurements confirmed a porous, favorably charged material.

Batch tests mapped how acidity, dose, time, and concentration shaped removal, and the biochar's maximum capacity came to nearly eighty-nine milligrams of dye per gram. Two kinetic models both fit the data, suggesting several cooperating pathways rather than one mechanism, and the process proved spontaneous and heat-absorbing. Statistical optimization showed the operating factors interact strongly, so settings must be tuned together. The authors present the sorbent as a cheap, eco-friendly option that also advances a zero-waste use of farm residue.
pmc-13618343:
Antti Marttinen and Manu Lahtinen design two nickel-based metal-organic frameworks, crystalline sponge-like materials, as photocatalysts that use sunlight to split water toward hydrogen fuel. The two frameworks share nearly identical building units and absorb visible light alike, yet their layouts differ: one is flexible and the other rigid. Single-crystal X-ray analysis mapped both in detail.

Both survived boiling water, showing strong chemical and thermal stability. The flexible framework also did an unusual reversible trick, collapsing to an amorphous state in solvent and recrystallizing afterward. Under simulated standard sunlight, both made hydrogen without any helper catalyst. Their durability split sharply, though: the flexible framework partly degraded over repeated cycles, while the rigid one stayed fully stable with no real activity loss. The authors judge the rigid framework the better candidate for solar hydrogen production.
pmc-13619043:
Kexin Zhu and seven colleagues review the 2026 state of a quiet regulatory practice: the surveys drug makers run among healthcare professionals to check whether safety measures worked. Guidelines say companies should predefine the success threshold before surveying. Searching the European post-authorization study catalogue, the reviewers found seventeen industry studies from 2022 to 2024 evaluating the measures through knowledge surveys.

Nearly all, sixteen of seventeen, did predefine thresholds, most often eighty percent correct, a marked improvement over an earlier era when half did. Yet only three in ten studies ran within the recommended twelve-to-twenty-four-month window after the measures launched, and fewer than half explained why their threshold was chosen. Six cited comparable studies or regulatory guidance; two rested on subjective judgment. The authors warn that an unjustified threshold makes a pass or fail verdict hard to interpret, undercutting the exercise of proving that risk communication changed clinician knowledge.
pmc-13619343:
Julia Azanza-Ricardo and nine colleagues report triplet embryos found in a wild green turtle nest on Cuba's Guanahacabibes Peninsula. Three embryos shared one continuous yolk mass inside a single egg, each with its own yolk blood vessels. The authors read that pattern as evidence the triplets came from one fertilized egg, a process called polyembryony.

The nest as a whole hatched very successfully, and most hatchlings performed normally. Among the unhatched eggs, three held embryos with birth defects, including this triplet set. One triplet showed strong uneven development and face malformations, which the authors link to limited shared food and uneven competition between siblings. Tissue checks found ovary-type organs in all three. They present the case as the first such record from natural incubation in a sea turtle nest.
pmc-13619843:
Ethan Napier and co-authors test in monkeys if a disturbed lung microbiome or TNF-blocking drugs make nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease worse. These germs live in soil and water and cause lung infections, worst in older people. Cases have also risen in patients on immune-damping biologics. The team's past work found that aging lungs lose a key friendly germ, and that loss tracked with worse disease.

Young rhesus macaques were split three ways. Some breathed in antibiotics to upset the lung microbiome. Some got a TNF blocker to mute a core immune signal. Some got no pretreatment. All were then given Mycobacterium avium in one lung. Germ load, scans, immune responses, and microbiome makeup were tracked over time. The setup pulls apart two suspects, a thinned microbial community and a blocked cytokine, in a primate model close to the human disease.
pmc-13619943:
Ming-Shih Tu and co-authors report a mouse study, published in two thousand twenty-six, on broken sleep during gut inflammation. Mice were given a drug that causes colitis, a swelling of the colon. Some mice also had their sleep broken often, and some had it broken less often.

Stress hormone levels rose in both sleep groups, while one immune marker was higher with less frequent breaks. A type of helper T cell was more common when breaks came more often. Clear signs of worse disease did not appear. The authors conclude that how often sleep breaks may shape which body systems react, rather than simply making colitis worse.
pmc-13620443:
Savaş Karataş, Jana Vietze, Chiara Ceccon, and Ughetta Moscardino followed ethnic minority teenagers in Italy to see how peer discrimination and identity feed into each other over time. The group held 280 adolescents, averaging about fourteen years old, most of them born in Italy to immigrant parents. The researchers tracked three things: perceived ethnic discrimination from peers, negative feelings about one's own ethnic group, and overall identity coherence, a settled sense of self.

Discrimination and negative ethnic feelings pushed each other upward in both directions. Negative feelings and weak coherence also dragged each other down over time. Discrimination lowered coherence in one direction only, without the return push. The picture the authors draw is a loop worth breaking early. Being treated badly can sour a teenager's view of their own group, and that sour view then leaves them more exposed to the next slight.
pmc-13623443:
Stephanie Gallard and colleagues present a perspective article, published in 2026. It identifies obstacles to good care in the United Kingdom. Two conditions are covered. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune hair loss condition. Atopic dermatitis is a chronic eczema. Both carry heavy physical and psychological burdens. The authors drew on a landscape review. Interviews with patients and clinicians were included. An expert survey and an advisory board also fed in.

They found system-wide gaps across primary and specialist care. Service availability was uneven. Psychological support was limited. This matches national findings on dermatology access. The article sets out practical steps for both care levels. Earlier recognition and clearer referral routes would close much of the gap. Attention to mental health would help too.
pmc-13623843:
Dechuang Jiao and thirteen co-authors published a phase two trial in twenty twenty-six on a targeted drug given before surgery for a common breast cancer type. SHR-A1811 is an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at HER2, tested here in hormone-sensitive tumors with low HER2 levels. Sixty-six women with untreated, sizable tumors enrolled.

Patients received eight cycles of the drug every three weeks before surgery. The response rate reached about eighty-two percent, comfortably above the trial's preset bar. Pathological complete response and survival endpoints were also tracked. Safety data accompanied the efficacy analysis. The single-arm design lacks a comparison group, but the shrinkage numbers support moving this pre-surgery strategy into larger randomized trials.
pmc-13623943:
Nathan A Chin and colleagues published a 2026 soil study showing that the border between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor soil is a hotspot for rotting plant litter. Litter breakdown controls how much carbon soil stores, and textbooks credit oxygen-loving enzymes as the main drivers. The team suspected a reactive form of manganese, a common soil metal, does heavy work where the two zones meet.

In controlled soil reactors, the researchers pushed microbes to make reactive manganese right at that border. Gene activity for litter-chewing enzymes rose many-fold at the same spot. Litter broke down about twenty-nine percent faster where metal and enzymes worked together than elsewhere, and the boost was predicted better by the interface activity than by conditions in either pure zone. The authors say decomposition models that ignore these borders will miss a major control on soil carbon as climates shift soil wetness.
pmc-13624043:
Ludovico Miccoli and six colleagues ask whether the dyes used in brain scans for Alzheimer's disease stick to the wrong targets inside cells. These PET tracers are meant to light up amyloid clumps. But lab work had shown one tracer also binds a family of enzymes called sulfotransferases.

Gene and protein maps showed three of these enzymes are common in the human brain, even in the region used as the scan's clean reference zone. Computer models showed all three tracers fit snugly into the enzymes' pockets, with mixed stability. The authors say this off-target binding could add noise to scans and help explain why readings vary between people.
pmc-13624843:
Muhammad Adnan Ayub and co-authors tune a steam method for pulling essential oil from mastic resin, the gum of Pistacia lentiscus, a Mediterranean shrub. They used superheated steam and a statistical tuning method to vary heat, grain size, and run time in search of the strongest antioxidant power. Oils from the new method were then compared with oils from two older water and steam methods by chemical profiling.

The best run used moderate heat for two hours on fine grains, and its oil beat the older methods on three separate antioxidant tests. Pinene and a handful of related scent compounds dominated the oil's makeup. Because makeup and strength hinged on the extraction route, the authors present superheated steam as the better choice for food and health uses.
pmc-13625443:
Nasriah Zakaria and eight colleagues, publishing in 2026, test a reusable digital lesson on mental health literacy for young people in two countries. Literacy here means spotting disorders, knowing where to seek help, and understanding treatments, and it runs low among youth in both Saudi Arabia and Malaysia. Teenagers and young adults aged sixteen to twenty-four in Riyadh and Kuala Lumpur either worked through the interactive object or simply answered the survey twice.

Scores rose clearly in both countries after the lesson, with Saudi participants shedding mistaken beliefs about mental illness as one gain. Malaysian participants improved the most on several measures in the cross-country comparison. A single well-built digital lesson, the study suggests, can travel across cultures, though local tuning may decide how far it lands.
pmc-13626943:
Ziyu Zhai and co-authors test an off-label migraine drug against vertigo and ear symptoms in everyday practice, in a 2026 study. Rimegepant blocks a peptide signal tied to migraine. Fifty-four adults with vertigo took it daily or every other day for eight weeks. Charts were reviewed for vertigo days, headache days, ringing, hearing measures, and mood scores.

By week eight, 94 percent had at least halved their monthly vertigo days, and relief typically began within six days. Ringing eased, hearing averages improved, and mood scores fell. Daily dosing beat alternate-day dosing on vertigo days. The authors call the results preliminary and uncontrolled, urging a proper trial of the drug class for balance and ear disorders.
pmc-13627743:
Ivan Lin and colleagues ask what helps or hinders a culturally grounded way of talking with Aboriginal patients in Western Australia. Clinical Yarning mixes story, relationship, and biomedical exchange, and the Midwest region, a vast rural area, has been rolling the training out. The team interviewed fifty-three health workers across four centers, about one in six of them Aboriginal, and sorted their answers through a behavior framework into barriers and enablers.

Views clustered in three bands: what staff know and believe about yarning, how training is delivered, and the surrounding conditions, from cultural safety to executive backing. Goodwill toward the approach ran strong, while rosters, turnover, and thin local expert availability bit hard. The authors turn each finding into an implementation move, a playbook other services can borrow.
pmc-13628143:
Lilith Abrahamyan Empson and nine colleagues lay out the design of an urban Living Lab in Lausanne, Switzerland, built to support recovery from psychosis. Patients, psychiatrists, geographers, community actors, and public authorities are designing the project together, on the idea that city surroundings themselves can help or hinder recovery.

The pilot follows fifty-five patients from two psychosis cohorts as they use small, co-created city interventions in daily life. Researchers collect field notes, recorded walks, workshops, and focus groups, alongside questionnaires and clinical rating scales taken before and after. The team aims to learn which interventions suit which patients, to inform city mental health planning and to size a future controlled trial.
pmc-13628443:
Kassoum Dianou and seven colleagues compared ways of counting deaths of young children in Burkina Faso. Armed conflict there blocks standard home surveys from large areas. For their 2026 study they ran a phone survey from September 2021 to October 2022. They spoke with over eleven thousand women. They then set the results beside the 2021 national survey.

In calm regions the phone figures tracked the national survey closely. In conflict regions the phone data told a grimmer story. Child deaths had climbed steeply from the late 2010s into the early 2020s. The national survey missed that rise. Its teams could not enter the most unsafe areas. The authors say phone surveys can stand in, or add support, when unrest shuts out face-to-face counting.
pmc-13629343:
Allen and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-six comparing lab platforms for blood markers of brain injury. After cardiac arrest, such markers help forecast recovery. Thirty-two critically ill patients supply blood samples. Four markers are measured on two main platforms and one bedside device. The two main platforms agree tightly on all four markers. The bedside device agrees poorly to moderately with the reference platform. Cross-checks between the other pairings fall in between.

Cutoff values cannot travel between devices safely, they conclude. Each platform needs its own thresholds for prognosis. The study is a secondary analysis of a care-withdrawal cohort. Platform choice becomes a clinical decision, not a detail.
pmc-13629543:
Nabil Abdul Majeed and eleven colleagues describe how know-how was built while scaling a peer-led lifestyle programme. The programme targets high blood pressure and diabetes across Kerala, India. The project gave structured lifestyle support through state primary care centres. The paper records the learning process, not health outcomes.

The authors drew on stakeholder talks, documents, and field watching. They show know-how being made jointly. Researchers, health workers, officials, and local people reshaped formal proof with lived experience. Local context steered repeated rounds of change. So did social learning and power dynamics. The account names practical aids and barriers to using know-how in routine practice. It offers guidance for similar chronic disease programmes in like health systems.
pmc-13629643:
Bison Lim and four colleagues report the crystal structure of a bacterial enzyme's catalytic domain, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The enzyme sits at the core of a multi-enzyme complex breaking down a metabolic intermediate. Its catalytic units assemble into trimers that expand into a twenty-four-part assembly. The crystals grew in a highly symmetric space group.

Near one lysine residue, the electron density fit a sulfate-like ion. That spot lies at the threefold junction between subunits of the trimer. Comparison with earlier structures marks it as an oxyanion-sensitive hotspot. A nearby helix reaches toward the active site pocket. It sits shifted relative to other crystal forms of the same domain. The authors link the ion density, the junction, and helix positioning within the assembly. The structure frames how local chemistry may tune this enzyme core.
pmc-13630243:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues publish the plan for a worldwide review of telemedicine teaching. The teaching targets medical students and residents. Virtual care is now core practice, sped up by the pandemic. Yet training for it stays patchy and uneven across schools and specialties.

The review follows set scoping methods. Two reviewers will screen six databases plus reference lists, each working alone. They will extract data on course content and teaching methods. Assessment plans count too. So do the barriers and aids programmes report. Results will be charted by learner group, specialty, and region. Tables and narrative will summarise them. The authors aim to give course designers, researchers, and policymakers a first full map. The literature on this teaching is fragmented today.
pmc-13630843:
Ahmed Wael Moftah leads a nine-author team pooling trials of dye-guided thyroid surgery, in a systematic review from two thousand twenty-six. Thyroid removal puts the neighboring parathyroid glands at risk. Temporary parathyroid failure strikes up to half of patients. Permanent failure is rarer, but it means lifelong treatment for those it hits.

Five databases were searched for studies in the field. They had to compare fluorescence guidance against conventional surgery. The technique joins the glands' natural autofluorescence with injected indocyanine green dye. With both, the team can judge the glands' blood supply live. Randomized and observational studies were pooled into one whole. The quality of the evidence was graded in a formal way. The question is a hands-on one. Does the glowing view preserve hormone function more well than a trained eye on its own? Meta-analysis is how scattered surgical trials can answer as one.
pmc-13631243:
Longjiang Qiao and thirteen colleagues built and stress-tested a machine learning pipeline for drug hunting. It targets one specific enzyme, AKR1C3. The enzyme helps cancers grow and resist chemotherapy. Their framework, called TAME-VS, expands sparse activity data using related enzymes. It then trains its classifiers. The study appeared in 2026.

The honest tests came in two waves. Looking back, the model faced inhibitor families it had never seen. It still prioritised well beyond simple similarity searching. Looking forward, its picks beat designer intuition under a tight synthesis budget. Two flagged compounds proved potent and selective. They restored sensitivity to a standard chemotherapy drug in resistant breast cancer cells. A public web server now runs the workflow.
pmc-13632343:
Whether longer exercise habits improve student sleep over time is examined by Zhang and three colleagues. College students often report poor sleep, late bedtimes, and daytime drowsiness, and short studies cannot show how those problems shift as exercise accumulates. The team followed 687 students at the start of an exercise programme and again at four and eight weeks, tracking sleep quality, bedtime delay, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness.

As total exercise time grew, sleep quality scores fell steadily, meaning sleep improved, while bedtime procrastination, daytime sleepiness, and insomnia severity also declined. Students who began with worse sleep or stronger bedtime delay showed distinct later trajectories, which suggests one-size exercise advice may fall short. Zhang and colleagues recommend pairing regular exercise with behavioural support, tailored for students with the most severe sleep problems.
pmc-13632743:
Leandro Soria and a large team of researchers uncover a new control on sugar storage in the liver in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Glycogen, the storage form of sugar, also builds up inside cell nuclei. Its role there stayed murky for nearly a century. The team found such stores in the livers of mice and people with a metabolic disorder called argininosuccinic aciduria. Breaking down this nuclear glycogen, they show, supports chemical marks on histones and keeps the liver healthy.

The breakdown is governed by a small chemical change to the enzyme that frees sugar. Nitric oxide drives that change, which sets how much enzyme reaches the nucleus. In metabolic liver disease, this control is impaired. The finding links a gas signal, sugar stores, and gene regulation in the liver.
pmc-13636143:
Murat Kaan Erdal led a 2026 engineering study of a self-adjusting drug dosing system that learns each subject's drug handling in real time, rather than relying on population averages. New sensors can report drug levels in tissue every few seconds. That opens the door to closed-loop dosing. Controllers built on average pharmacokinetics must be set cautiously and can still overshoot when a subject differs. The team built an adaptive controller that estimates an individual's kinetics early in infusion and keeps updating that model.

Tested on the anesthetic procaine in the brain ventricles of live rats, the system faced a hard target because drug transport into the brain lags. It reached target levels in twenty to thirty minutes. It held them within roughly five to twelve percent deviation, including sensor noise.
pmc-13636643:
Jakob Heyer-Müller and four colleagues published this 2026 methods study on tracking protein clumping during purification. Clumped protein is a critical flaw in biologic medicines; makers want to spot it mid-process. A light-based probe can watch protein structure during column purification, yet shifting salt levels bend the signal and confuse standard software. The team built a physics-based model of the signal, with a built-in account of the salt-driven background drift.

Applied to nearly three hundred in-line spectra across varied column conditions, the model rebuilt the data faithfully while keeping each component's identity stable. One derived feature, the center of the main structural band, proved a sturdy clumping marker even while concentrations swung hard. The features predicted the share of single proteins well and lumped forms acceptably. The authors offer the approach as an interpretable alternative for real-time quality watching.
pmc-13638043:
Oliver Umney and eleven colleagues map three proteins inside the Z-disc, the narrow boundary structure that links muscle fibers' contractile units. The team tagged three residents with fluorescent binders in pig heart fibers: an actin crosslinker, a segment of the protein titin, and a width-regulating protein. A super-resolution microscopy method then located each tag within ten nanometers.

Pattern analysis separated the trio. The crosslinker and the width regulator shared a similar repeating arrangement. The titin segment followed a different but equally regular pattern through the disc. Knowing which proteins march together and which keep their own rhythm constrains models of how the disc bears force and signals. The authors also release their analysis approach for groups imaging crowded protein assemblies.
pmc-13639643:
Hidetaka Wakabayashi and four colleagues present a 2026 paper from the Japanese group for rehab nutrition, setting out version 3.0 of their field. Rehab nutrition pairs exercise care with food care. It aims to help people with illness, frailty, or disability live and move better.

Early versions stressed body function, first as an idea and then as a set care routine. The new version adds mind, social life, and spirit to the frame. It also welcomes digital health tools and smart software. The group calls the update full, personal care for patients and the staff who serve them.
pmc-13643143:
Sami S Zoghbi and Robert B Innis wrote a letter questioning how a recent brain inflammation imaging study should be read. Kalita and colleagues had presented a PET tracer aimed at GPR84, a marker on immune cells, using systemic bacterial toxin injection to provoke inflammation.

The letter warns that toxin in the bloodstream also inflames vessel walls, trapping white blood cells inside brain capillaries where the tracer can bind them. That vascular signal could be mistaken for activation of resident microglia. Blood-brain barrier leakage adds further doubt. The authors ask for checks such as direct brain injection models or correcting the vessel contribution.
pmc-13644543:
Reo Ikumi and five colleagues present a 2026 laboratory comparison of four ways to take digital impressions for a full arch of dental implants. Complete-arch scanning is error-prone, and a two-part scan joined at a palate marker might do better.

On an upper jaw model holding six implants, each workflow was repeated ten times and matched against a laboratory reference scan. The segmented scan with the palate marker agreed best, the conventional tray impression worst. A marker alone without segmentation added nothing, and far-back molar sites suffered most in one-piece scans. The authors present segmentation as an accessible accuracy boost.
pmc-13645743:
Hospitals can jointly study survival without pooling patient records, Veeraragavan and two colleagues show. Survival analysis across hospitals usually stalls because privacy rules forbid pooling sensitive health data. Simpler sharing methods can leak single counts by subtraction. The team built a federated Kaplan-Meier framework using threshold homomorphic encryption. This method lets a coordinator add coded tallies from many sites. Only the combined result is decoded, using shares from a group.

In tests with synthetic breast-cancer data spread across five hundred sites, the coded curves matched the pooled gold standard closely. Message sizes grew in a steady way with site and time-point counts. The authors also prove correctness, stability, and efficient packing of the encrypted vectors. Veeraragavan and colleagues present the design as a way to run high-quality multi-institution survival studies with far less privacy risk than plaintext collaboration.
pmc-13647243:
Rhyan Ouaddane Alami and six colleagues present a step-by-step dissection guide to the carotid region of the neck, the corridor carrying the brain's main arteries and several key nerves. Safe surgery here demands a true three-dimensional grasp of vessels, nerves, and tissue layers. The team dissected one side of a preserved adult cadaver from surface to deep structures in six stages. Landmarks anchor each stage, from skin marks through muscle release to the artery fork.

The sequence exposes the jugular vein and a named anatomical triangle, manages small vein branches, opens the carotid sheath. It finishes by mapping the hypoglossal and vagus nerves and the small carotid body. Clinical notes tie each landmark to what a surgeon meets in vascular, head and neck, and spine operations. The authors offer the protocol as a teaching scaffold for trainees who must learn this crowded anatomy before operating on it.
pmc-13647643:
Ji Liu and seven colleagues compare two ways of giving a last-resort antibiotic to patients with pneumonia caused by carbapenem-resistant germs, in a 2026 study. The drug, colistimethate sodium, reaches the lungs poorly when injected because of its chemistry, while breathing it in as a mist delivers it straight to the air spaces. Records from several centers covered 209 patients treated between 2021 and 2023, split between injection alone and injection plus inhalation. Response, cure, stay length, death, and harms were compared.

The combined route produced a clearly higher clinical response rate. Cure rates, hospital stay, and twenty-eight-day deaths did not differ significantly between the groups. Side effects, including kidney and nerve toxicity, skin darkening, and airway spasm, appeared at similar rates. The authors conclude that adding the inhaled route improves response without adding measurable harm. The result supports a practical tweak for infections where few drug options remain.
pmc-13649443:
Yangyang Qian and five colleagues report two women whose breast cancer had spread to the lungs, with drug picks guided by a test on tumour cells caught from blood. Spread tumours can drift from the first tumour, and tissue is not always in reach. Both women had the HER2-positive form of the disease.

The test grew the caught cells and tried drugs on them in the lab. Its calls matched the tissue reads and each woman's past drug proof well. Care then bent to those calls. The authors claim the first such report in far-spread breast cancer. They pitch blood cell tests as a way to pick drugs when tissue is out of reach, with more proof still owed.
pmc-13649743:
Jeevan Yoganand and three colleagues upgrade a zero-trust login frame for vehicles that talk to roadside fog computers. Car networks shift fast, so trust checks and handovers between zones must keep up without slowing traffic data. Their upgrade adds three parts to the base frame.

First, fog nodes now train a shared trust model in a split way that keeps raw data local. Second, a cipher design built to resist future quantum attacks guards trust messages in transit. Third, a token lets a car reuse past proof when it crosses into a new zone, which cut login delay by nearly half in tests. Trial runs also showed steadier trust scores and better catches of behaviour-based attacks.
pmc-13650143:
Radka Roubalová and thirteen colleagues, publishing in 2026, test whether gut microbes help drive anorexia nervosa, a severe eating disorder with low recovery rates. They used a mouse model in which animals with access to running wheels and limited food lose dangerous amounts of weight, echoing features of the human illness.

Germ-free mice received stool transplants from healthy donors, from patients with acute anorexia, or from patients with a severe long-lasting form. Mice given acute-phase microbes showed weaker hunger signals in the brain and ate less. Mice given microbes from the long-lasting form ate normally yet ran much more than the other groups. Neither transplant changed whether the full anorexia-like state developed. The authors read this as evidence that the microbiome shapes parts of the illness course, and that restoring a healthy gut community may be needed for complete recovery.
pmc-13650743:
Zhihao Wu and one colleague review ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, as a thread running through osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease of aging and hormone loss. In ferroptosis, iron fuels the peroxidation of membrane fats while the cell's defenses against that damage fail, and the review asks how this process plays out in each bone cell type.

Bone-forming cells and their stem cell parents suffer: their growth, matrix production, and mineralization falter when ferroptosis strikes. Bone-embedded sensor cells may pass distorted remodeling signals. Bone-eating cells, by contrast, might be usefully killed by ferroptosis when resorption runs too high. Triggers span estrogen loss, sugar and fat toxicity, steroid drugs, aging, and iron overload. Candidate treatments range from iron chelators to targeted delivery of protective vesicles. The authors insist the goal is selective control by cell type, not blanket switching of the pathway.
pmc-13672943:
Hayley Alderson and co-authors report on a police program for first-time domestic abuse suspects. The program, called CARA, settles lower-risk cases out of court with workshops on relationship abuse. It now runs across police forces in England and Wales. The team held interviews and group talks with thirty-one staff, from police to workshop leaders.

Staff across areas backed the program with strong, shared support. They also urged changes to sharpen how it runs. Risk checks should split cases with more care, they said. Training and rollout steps need tweaks to fit local needs. Views from voluntary groups that aid victims should be heard more fully. The authors frame the study as a guide for the next stage of delivery.
pmc-13677743:
Pin Lyu and colleagues published a 2026 structural biology study of a protein pump that moves zinc across cell membranes. Zinc is essential in small amounts but poisonous in excess, so cells control it tightly. Using advanced imaging, the team captured the pump's shape at fine detail while it faced inward, ready to collect zinc.

Experiments and computer simulations showed that the pump's tail acts as both a brake and a sensor: it holds the pump still until zinc levels rise, then releases it. A rich supply segment appears to hand zinc ions to the pump's core binding site. The findings revise older models of how cells import zinc.
pmc-13678843:
Zhang and co-authors review the m6A mark and how crops cope with stress. The m6A mark is the most common inner edit on plant RNA. Three protein groups write, erase, and read the mark. Those acts tune RNA life span, splicing, and protein output. New sequencing tools now map the mark across whole crops.

Studies show shared rules plus species-level twists in the network. Proof of function still rests on a few model plants. Field tests in real farm crops lag behind lab work. The review weighs breeding plans that use the mark. It also lists blocks that slow use in stress-proof crop design.
pmc-13680843:
Kathrine Sullivan and a large team described in two thousand twenty-six how they reshaped a trauma-focused parenting program for military-connected mothers of young children. These mothers, including service members, veterans, and partners, face more trauma than civilian mothers. The original program, Parenting-STAIR, targets trauma, emotion control, and parenting skills.

Interviews with clinic staff, clinicians, and mothers pointed to four needs: shorter treatment, more flexibility, less stigma, and respect for military culture. The team cut the program to a shorter modular form with plainer language and wrote a companion guide for clinicians. Health workers gain a version families are more likely to start and finish.
pmc-13694143:
